THE GOOD-
Possibly my favorite 2d action game on PC. Terraria provides an enormous array of weapons, items, enemies and bosses that will see you through easily 100+ hours of play for the complete experience.
I did have some issues early on with multiplayer, but found out later it was due to a NAT setting on my router. Once I resolved that, the gameplay couldn't be smoother (with some lag due to whatever the ping was).
Although I'm not much of a sandbox gamer, I found myself dabble in some extravagant designs from time to time, and can conclude that the assortment of placeables is mind blowing. If you want a 2d sandbox game, this can certainly fit the bill. If you don't mind the occasional zombie, or eater of souls popping by for a visit, that is.
Surprisingly, the game's soundtrack doesn't grind on you, even in the long hours of mining. It's a masterful blend of interesting and subtle, that feeds extended play in an amazingly natural way.
THE BAD-
If there is anything bad to say about the gameplay, it's that the combat can become somewhat repetitive. If you get lost underground, you're likely to run into hidden caches and chest, but if you don't, it can become a monotonous search for a way back to the surface as you battle many of the same types of enemies. I didn't find this particularly irksome, but I didn't get lost often (marking with torches and all).
THE VERDICT-
The game isn't for everyone, but if you're after an exploration focused, 2d action platformer, I can't recommend it more. Especially if you love the idea of many hours digging through the rock, beating back baddies alone, or with buddies!

I have tried to get into this game, multiple times on multiple platforms. The issue is not the plot or the characters, persay, as I have played far more immature and hilarious games. The issue is that this is a first person shooter desperately trying to be an rpg. Resource management is practically non-existant, and the weapons system is based on a number of slots that can be upgraded over time. This system requires minimal effort, and though it appears to be a central point of the game, it just seems to be a clunky, poorly-built weapons wheel. The plot takes forever to move forward, and the side missions consist purely of kill and/or collect. Pardon me, but I'll stick with my bethesda rpgs.
Still, not to grossly underrate the game, it is still a fairly fun shooter, with a few elements of an rpg that are well done, for example the skill trees and character creation systems are well made, and offer a variety of specializations and appearances. Still, I would not recommend this game, at least not to someone with similar tastes to myself.

It has very good art and sound design with pretty good animations, but it is a sadly very boring and forgettable experience. Enemies are generally very simplistic with low variety and lack challenge. The first thirty minutes of the game are extremely boring, backtracking for collectables feels pointless and unnecessary because the only thing you get is more HP and some gold that you can farm from killing enemies and breaking barrels. Early on the core game mechanic of swapping soldiers is even temporarily removed to force you to get them back, for no real good reason. Level designs aren't interesting, platforming challenges aren't challenging, bosses (at least up until 50% of the game is completed) are easy and tedious bullet sponges that require little to no thought. At least two of them look like direct rips from the movesets of Mega Man X bosses.
I still intend to finish the game and I'm not mad, per-se, about my purchase. For five dollars on sale I think it was okay enough, but for the game's full asking price I would never recommend this game to anyone who likes old platformers. And that's a specific point I'd like to make more clear. People will buy this game because they played and liked Super Nintendo/Genesis era platforming shooters and Metroidvania games, and those people will probably not be satisfied with how easy and slow this game is.
Despite a few problems here and there, Omega strike is overall a good metroidvania.

A cozy semi retro game. Good art and animations, decent fitting music, a comfortably stereotypical plot, gameplay is simple but enjoyable. For a linear game the price is decent although it could be more humble.
The main problems the game has are the multiple playable characters and the bosses.
Like in almost every single situation, the multiple characters only make the gameplay more tedious. Even more so in this situation because the multiple characters essentially translate to having multiple different loadouts. So your default is the rapid fire gun, with a dodge roll. Press the button and you get slow bouncy ball launcher with the ability to move heavy objects. Press the button you get shotgun with double jump, press it again the cycle repeats.
This exclusively serves to break up the players abilities and only functions as an inconvinience. Want to be able to dodge roll, have to play as the rapid fire gun guy. Want to double jump, have to play as shotgun guy. Not only does it limit the player, but it is also tedious since players have to swap characters just to pass certain obstacles. And even more problematic is that you can only use certain abilities with certain characters, so you have to adjust to the abrasive fact that you can't do certain things while doing other things. So if you need to use a character for their specific ability or weapons, you have to lose access to other abilities or weapons. It also means if you upgrade a specific character, but need to use another for a specific situation, you are forced to be weaker then you could be otherwise.
Having to switch between characters multiple times in a short period of time just to traverse obstacles that require different characters to pass each individual piece of it; is also very tedious and disruptive.
The developer could have easily just allowed players to buy and swap between guns and unlock progression abilities instead of forcing players to swap between three different loadouts which force specific guns and specific abilities in specific situations. Having multiple characters players need to all use, especially like this, only makes the game more tedious.
The other significant problem is the boss battles. They are completely barren of any developer empathy for the fact that the player does not have the attack pattern and all the mechanics of the boss memorized from the beginning. Each boss has around three attacks, and fighting the boss comes down to following an extremely strict pattern of response to its attacks because of how tight, unforgiving and overbearing the attacks are. The bosses often require extreme jumping or movement precision and require players to be able to react instantly to attacks which have almost no telegraph. They are very unfun and arbitrary, basically being trial and error gates to progression. It seems like the developer wanted the bosses to be challenging so they designed a boss pattern that was challenging to them as the developer, without taking into account that players have to fight these things without all that knowledge the developer has from the start.
There is also the minor flaw that the game gives players the ability to return to previous areas or sections of a map to take new paths you can only unlock using abilities slash characters you unlock after progressing past that point. But honestly the game does not feel gripping enough nor are the rewards meaningful enough to justify backtracking for those things, so it is really dead content.
Game is still enjoyable though despite the issues it has, worth playing especially for the comfortable retro feel it has.

A joke of a game, when all is said and done about the game.
The game offers a lot that many other games do not, meaning it's near endless levels of customization from your character, to your vehicles and your weapon (albeit pre-made skins upon your weapon.)
The gun game, whilst often subject to horrid servers is satisfying, regardless of it's Call of Duty-like TTK (Time To Kill) meaning that most fire-fights will be over very swiftly.
The game suffers from a plethora of issues however, and many of them are game-breaking.
There is a heavy influence of cheaters in the game, and they are not removed appropriately quickly due to the anti-cheat measures put into the game prioritizing microtransactions from the cheaters instead of increasing the quality of the game by banning them as quickly as possible - which is a very shady practice seeing how it's a lose-lose situation.
The community is probably the most toxic and vile you can find. I have never seen such a hateful community anywhere else which directly affects gameplay as you will find many people griefing your mission and other missions just for the fun of it for them. This is also why it is almost impossible to stream this game and have a remote amount of viewers, as many will target you for griefing.
The development behind the game is barely there, and they also do very shady practices. They falsely ban players with zero evidence of them cheating or the like, or simply ban them because they receive too many reports about the players without checking into their playstyle and seeing if they are good, or cheaters.
GMs are non-existant, they are very few and very rarely around - even when they display themselves, they hardly do anything against blatant cheaters.
The development team has zero clue about the metagame, what should be fixed and what should not be fixed, along with pretending some things are not an issue - server issues being a particular subject they prefer to avoid.
If you have a severe case of masochism, it is worth trying out. I have played it for many hours, and I have an entire channel dedicated to the game on YouTube. If you want a game that is as new player hostile as Dwarf Fortress without one ounce of it's depth, this is it. This game breaks friendships faster than Mario Party 2.
If you want to play a third person shooter that's free to play and something to just calm down to, I would probably keep looking elsewhere.

I've been a fan of the franchise for a long time. The concept was always good but the execution was often frustrating and made certain parts of some titles nearly unplayable -- and often unenjoyable. This new release is by far the best edition in the franchise yet. They've really balanced the gameplay to remove the most frustrating, capricious aspects of the game. Playing the new edition, the logic of the game's world -- which guards are paranoid, when an action has made a guard suspicious, etc. -- make this new title much less frustrating while preserving all of the sneaky, covert aspects that the franchise is known for. The levels are bigger and more detailed than ever, the graphical detail is spectacular, and the new and more detailed achievements for each level had me replaying levels over and over. ★★★★★

Fantastic game.
That's the short version. A longer version is that this game has brought me some really good times. It's a very pleasant and satisfying sim with many great features that create huge depth for this minimalistically stylized game.
Just when you think that you have the perfect, most stable running prison in the world, the inmates take advantage of your arrogance and point out the flaws in your system and kill the mole that was supplying you with information about gangs and escape attempts. This hurts your prison's value, you walk on the razor's edge of being halled off to jail yourself for criminal negligence. For being a sim game it actually brings a huge element of a power struggle between you and the inmates. No other game has played on my ego as much as Prison Architect.
The devs have put in a lot of time and hard work in this game and it doesn't seem like they are about to stop. Even after the 1.0 release they keep updating with new features and balances that make the game more enjoyable, more intricate, and pushes the "end-game" portion slowly out of the equation.
Each build of this game makes your prison more and more into a living, breathing world. You easily forget about the minimalistic (but beautifully designed) sprites and look at your population and staff as real people.
The AI's actions feel planned out and specifically designed for the prison that you built yourself. Back to the drawing board.
A must-have for any fan of management games.

Having been playing this game since Alpha (early 20s) I've put in more than a couple hundreds hours of gameplay, and I still find myself immersed in the game. I'm all about rehabilitating my prisoners, so I find a real enjoyment catering to their needs, and seeing them off as succesfull citizens. However, having taken a hiatus due to the fact that large projects and prisons aren't possible to due to the largely reported performance issues everyone is facing, but hopefully in time that issue will be addressed, and solved. The game is still very much playable for new players, and offers many many hours of fun, strategic gameplay.
With a large modding community, nearly every aspect of the game can be altered to your own liking. Though it really doesn't need to be, because the developers have done a spot on job communicating with their audience, and responding appropriately to improve the game.

Sister Location is way different from the other FNAF games, it's different in a good way. As usual this game isn't too long it's FNAF game length. I was shocked when i found out that the game pretty much guides you through everything. I had thought that the system where you shock the animatronics would be a regular mechanic, but I was wrong. I thought we would at one point even if it was on the final night, Have to do what nights 1 and 2 taught us to do. Hiding under the desk, shocking animatronics that aren't on their stage, ect. But no, Baby and the robot voice guide you through everything. But when you do get to do your own thing, it is terrifying. Like when you are trying to get past Ballora. Okay so Sister Location Review.
Scott clearly felt that the original formula had been done to death so it's easy to see why he changed things up for this game. Truth be told if it ended up being the same game play style then it probably wouldn't of been a game I'd of enjoyed as much, but the fact Scott pretty much reinvented the series for this game not only worked in his favour, but in my opinion is the scariest game in the series so far. The scenarios you're put into are nightmarish (often being only inches away from an animatronic while you have to do something else) and I genuinely felt tense throughout each night and was dreading what the next night had to bring. The addition of vocice acting added a new layer of depth and discomfort to playing, navigating hallways and rooms while hearing animatronics tease and taunt you as they grow ever closer brings more terror to an already uncomfortable scenario.
The secret night however was the games one weak point for me ( mainly because it took me this long to beat it ) but naturally it had to be there due to the previous games and I don't have a problem with that, it was still a tense experience and the feeling of beating it is so joyful.
Overall I just wanna say that whatever Scott's planning (and we all know he is) for the next game, if it's anything like this game I'm extremely excited.

When I got Ori and the Blind Forest last year about a week after it came out, I fell in love immediately. I loved the characters, I loved the stories, I loved pretty much everything about it. I've been thinking of doing a review for a while but now that I've played through the original game countless times and the Definitive edition a couple times, I think it is about time that I do a review. AHEM!
Ori and the Blind Forest makes you feel like you're playing through a fairy tale. The visuals, the music, and pretty much everything in it is absolutely stunning and it is simply a work of art. The story is told through facial expressions, gestures, and music, not something you see in every game and it does it without fail. The story is also pretty simple and vague, but not the bad kind of vague. It leaves so much up to player interpretation but is also detailed enough that you can connect the dots and never be lost in what is going on. Because of this, the Ori community has so many headanons and original characters. The tale of Ori and the Blind Forest will make you feel emotions you completely forgot you had and will leave you wanting more.
The soundtrack... oh god the soundtrack! Composer Gareth Coker has really outdone himself with this work of art. Each track has so much soul and love put into it and not one track feels out of place in the game. I listen to the OST every now and then and I never get tired of it. Each track perfectly fits the mood of each area in the big world of Nibel and doesn't ruin any immersion you have, which you will have. The game is very immersive and lovely.
The gameplay and animations are smooth and flawless and very, very responsive. They are so responsive, it is never the game's fault you died. Oh speaking of things being the game's fault, the game is pretty much bug-free. I haven't encountered game breaking bugs at all.
The Definitive Edition of the game takes everything that was good about Ori and the Blind Forest and makes it BETTER. Every single thing in it is an improvement on the old. The Definitive Edition adds in stuff the community has asked for and more. It adds in difficulty modes, behind the scenes, fast travel, new levels, a backstory for Naru, an adorable idle animation, and the ability to re-enter dungeons after completing them. Let's have a look at the difficulties and what they do:
Easy: Ori doesn't take as much damage from the environment and there are checkpoints in the escape sequences, making things a lot easier. This is basically for people who don't really want a challenge and just want to play for the story and stuff. Newbie difficulty.
Normal: Normal Mode is basically the original game's difficulty. If you've played the first game, Normal mode is that difficulty. It is for returning players who like the story and want a mild challenge.
Hard: Hard Mode is for experienced players who want a good challenge. Ori is a glass cannon in this mode. If you don't know what a glass cannon is, it is basically you are a ♥♥♥♥ing piece of glass with power. You die easily. Don't do this mode if you can't handle constant death.
One Life: One-Life uses the Normal difficulty except as the name implies, you have one life and one life only. If you die, you have to start back to the beginning of the game(don't worry. You don't have to replay the prologue). Despite it using the Normal difficulty, it is harder in that you have to be really, really cautious and make sure not to take too much damage.
The Definitive Edition adds on a good amount of extras in the main menu. It gives you a look behind the scenes at early concepts from the game such as cutscenes, ability, and enemy concepts as well as concept art(the spirit tree had a face and his roots were like hands. It was WEIRD).
There are a lot of more things I could cover, but I want you to find out for yourself what Naru's backstory is and what the abilities are as well as the changes. Let's go over the pros and cons.
Pros:
-No piece of extra content feels unnecessary or out of place. Everything fits together perfectly.
-The soundtrack is beautiful and you could just sit in one place forever.
-The save system is handy and great.
-Gameplay is smooth and responsive.
Cons:
-They had a chance to allow for button layout changing, but they failed to deliver with that. Not much of a big deal since the controller's buttons are very well placed and perfect. The keyboard on the other hand.... not exactly the best. That is where button mapping would be very useful.
9.25/10 get this game. It is absolutely perfect and you WILL love it to death.

I am an Army infantry combat veteran. I don't say that to brag, only so that you'll know when I critique the realism of this game, I know a little of what I'm talking about.
I love shooter games but I have never had the emotional connection to any game before this one. Normally it doesn't take much thinking to blow away animated bad guys. But in Spec Ops you quickly get drawn in to what you are doing. I read a couple articles about this game before playing it. Most talked about how the creators of the game wanted to create a game where players thought about what they were doing when they killed in the game. In that, they succeeded. I have never played a game that sucked you into the battle the way this one did. Normally in a game I would clear an area and then poke around for ammo and secrets. The first few times I played this game I got so caught up in the rush of the game that I routinely charged forward without stopping to pick up ammo and often found myself with little ammo left which would be more similar to real life than most games. With that said, here is my review of the game. Do not read further if you want to avoid spoilers....
GAMEPLAY:
I'm normally not a fan of 3rd person shooters, but this game worked pretty well. The controls take some getting used to, specifically in the moving to and from cover aspects and cycling through weapons. But I thought overall the game really sucked you in to the emotion and the adrenaline. This is actually a very short game, though I was glad it was after my first time through as I felt I had literally been through a war zone playing it. It took me a while before I could play it again. Ironically I've actually come to enjoy replaying this game which is probably not what the creators intended. I'm fairly good at separating games from reality and this is actually a pretty good shooter in my opinion.
WEAPONS:
One of the things this game gets right in my opinion overall is the weapons. For the most part you can pick any weapon and get through the game with it. M4's are accurate but don't have the stopping power of AK-47's. M2 .50 cals kill anything but overheat quickly. For the most part it's pretty realistic.
GRAPHICS:
The graphics are pretty good, even for a game that is not very new. Once you've played through it and can stop long enough to take in the scenery it's actually pretty cool and very well done.
THE NITTY GRITTY:
Overall I really liked this game but the grunt in me couldn't let everything pass without complaint....
STORY:
If you can suspend disbelief the story is actually pretty compelling. But if you stop to analyze it falls apart pretty quickly... The premise is interesting and serves the purpose of creating the scene needed for the game to work. But...a more or less never ending sandstorm??? Your character is sent to see if there are any survivors in Dubai but at several points in the game you can see clear skies above you. Why couldn't recon satelites be used to see what was going on??? You can also see the ocean nearby at some points. What would stop a submarine from getting in close to land a recon team or a rescue force and maintain communications?
CHARACTERS:
Everybody has to be a Delta operator or a SEAL these days, but a captain, a lieutenant, and a sergeant as the team? Come on guys. I can buy the early fights against the "insurgents" but once the team meets and kills Lt. McPherson of the 33rd, how does the rest of the 33rd know the "Delta" guys are bad guys? Why can't the Delta guys talk to the 33rd soldiers they run into???
CHOICES:
One of the main themes of the game is that you shouldn't just mindlessly charge forward killing everything in sight as most shooter games want you to do. The game tries to imply that you have a choice, specifically to stop playing, killng, etc. Unfortunately the game doesn't give you a choice most of the time. There are one or two occasions where the "choice" you make can lead to slightly different outcomes, but overall you don't have a choice unless you stop playing the game altogether.
The mortar/white phosphorous scene is the prime example of this and the pivotal scene of the game. I admit, the first time I played through that scene it got to me more than any other game scene has. The problem is, in real life you would have a choice. In the game you can either use the mortar to masacre the 33rd troops or you can try to shoot it out with them with small arms, in which case you are guaranteed to die eventually. Why can't you go around them? Or sneak by them? I can think of several other options other than the ones you are permitted to choose.
Again this is a powerful scene but as a mortar man myself, it strays pretty far from reality. Your using a 60mm mortar... regardless of the round it's not going to do much to a Striker. The game makes a big deal of white phosphorous/willy pete rounds. Sure, against unprotected infantry WP rounds can be pretty deadly but its primary function is to be used after high explosive (HE) or delayed impact rounds have been fired and have opened up fuel lines and other combustible material. Then the WP is shot in to light the combustible stuff on fire. I understand what the creators were trying to do here but the scene stretches reality quite a bit.
As a military man I have to complain about the game not being EXACTLY correct but as I said in the beginning I really recommend this game to anyone that wants to really feel a game pull you in. You will hate yourself for liking this game but in the end it's worth at least one play through.

This game is the definition of casual. What drew me in initially was the visual style. Every level has an uncanny level of detail, making the experience very pleasing to the eye. Gameplay involves travelling from room to room, solving simple puzzles and searching for puzzle pieces along the way to complete a virtual puzzle that advances you to the next world. It's a simple formula, and probably would start to get boring if the game were any longer, but it works and is engaging while it lasts.
There were definitely a couple of downfalls. There were a couple puzzle pieces in levels that were simply impossible for me to find. After long periods of searching every inch of the level, there were instances where I was forced to look up tutorials on YouTube, which really took me out of the experience. Most likely you will experience this once or twice, and maybe you will be more perceverent than I was and succeed, but it will still be frustrating nonetheless. Also, there is no reason to play this game a second time, for you will know the location of the puzzle pieces. There are a couple of minigames that become available upon completion of the main story, but those are only a minor distration.
If you're looking for a super casual game that's accessible and pretty to look at, this is definitely your cup of tea.

This game is probably one of the dankest memes of my childhood. Unfortunately, I was not one of the lucky people who didn't have the game spoiled before they bought it, but everything that I heard or saw about it just pulled me in. I had to finally play it for myself. When I did, I was pleasantly surprised by a vibrant cast of characters with a simple yet unique art style and a stellar compostion of music. The references to modern internet culture are plentiful and nicely incorporated into the underground and its characters, just like the tropes of many teens and young adults they portray with cheesy yet also inviting personality. Underneath the inviting exterior, Undertale has considerable depth and those who inhabit the world have relatable struggles. For a game that appears so kid-friendly on the outside, there are a lot of mature themes if you pay close attention.
Compounded with the fact that this game was almost entirely made by one individual--Toby Fox--Undertale is a fine work of art with notable time and effort put into its making. For how short the game is, it has a great amount of plot development and is lush with lore for those who love to analyze. Rather than being its downfall, its short length is a great benefit. Undertale's cliffhanging endings, in combination with its lore, leave lots to interpret and speculate for the future of each and every playthrough, and has led to some compelling theories by its fanbase.
Even when I think my love for this game has faded, I always come back to it. For as cancerous as the fanbase is, this game is not one to (always) be taken lightly.

This game is a standalone game in the Mad Max universe.  It shares the names, characters, style and locations but is not linked to any of the films.
The game is presented fantastically the graphics are gorgeous and the audio while sparse is very good.
Taking down your first few convoys is great fun, especially with the slow down game feature that shows the action.  When you realise you have to do this umpteen more times then it's not so fun.  When you get to the next big base and see you have to do all the upgrades AGAIN.  Nope, not so fun.
The entire game gets boring and repetitive very quickly.  You can break up the car sections with bouts of exploring on foot and melee action.  Here again the game fails.  The control system is too consoli-fied  After unlocking a plethora of skills and moves it just comes down to mashing a few buttons with very little skill involved, invariably not pulling off the impressive block, parry or finishing move you wanted to.
A few odd design decisions.
The crowbar for example.  It's a required piece of kit from the start of the game but isn't in your starting inventory.  Also, If i have a crow bar on my person i'm going to hit people with it.
Balloons.  Again.  Why?  Drive out of my way for a vantage point to see interesting things.  I understand this.  But why a tedious slow mini game every time of working out how to release and fuel the balloon and then slowly wait to ascend and descend.  Then that feeling of utter boredom when you get to the balloon, get told it's out of fuel and have to re navigate all again with a canister from your car.
Scrap.  Go out of my way for 2 pieces of scrap when most initial upgrades cost 100s and end game 1000s.
Bosses.  They are all the same.  A guy in a gimp mask with a different colour texture.
Optional stuff that's not actually optional because you need to grind 1000s of scrap to upgrade the car.
For me the game screams rushed to deliver / ran out of budget / ideas.  It was polished up and shipped out.
Rating 6/10 - A wasteland of opportunities.

This is one of those games with some really nice art and music but is utterly boilerplate. One of those games you would see on the list of obscure old games and say "why haven't I heard of this before." then play it and go "ah, that's why."
There's something that just feels off about the way it controls, it's level design, and gimmicks. It becomes a real slog of slowly going through rooms fairly early on. It's a metroidvania, but it doesn't really advantage of large interconnected world. The levels feel more like something from a platformer like Mega Man. Backtracking to old areas when not required to progress offers small rewards like some money or the game's version of heart pieces. It would have probably been better off as a level based game. Going through each room feels slow.
The gimmick of having three character you switch between isn't really utilized well. I tended to just play as the guy who can double jump because the added mobility was way better than any thing else. It's too easy to forget which character has what ability in the heat of the moment. "I'll just double jump up there. Ah, dang it, that's not this character." Switching between them is done with one button (the shoulder buttons are not used at all,) and that makes switching characters more of a chore.
It's feels like the game thinks it's faster paced than it actually is.
It has some good ideas, but it doesn't quite know how to implement them.

Lastly, I got lost about 2/3 the way through the game and had to go map-by-map to find out where I was supposed to go next. I'm not sure I see myself replaying this game any time soon.

I played this almost nonstop for the past 2 days. It's really fun! Nice metroidvania with good shooting mechanics. The most distinguished mechanic of the game is the ability to swap between 3 characters on the fly (literally, you can change characters mid air) and each has their own weapon. At first I thought it was just a cute way of doing weapon selection but each character can do different things, like one pushes blocks, the other double jumps etc. So it's nice, feels like juggling, it keeps me on the edge of my seat the whole time and create some pretty fun action. When you get used to it you'll be swapping characters 10 times in seconds, to shoot an enemy on the floor, double jump to the platform above and switching to the long range guy to shoot someone else. Later you'll also find upgrades for each character that allows you to explore different areas, like any metroidvania.
I found that some abilities were very little explored on the game. I hope it's not considered spoiler to mention you'll unlock a dash ability, because which metroidvania doesn't have a dash ability to unlock, right? Anyway, you dash on these narrow corridors with lasers. These corridors are the "door" opened by the dash. And aside from a couple of other places that requires dashing it really felt less like a new ability and more like a key. And the same can be said about other upgrades. There's one where you explode the ground by laying bombs. I think I can count on my fingers how many times I used that upgrade. My point is replacing keys with abilities is the art of metroidvanias, and one really expects the ability to be more than a key. This is a light criticism though, as it doesn't take value from the game. Also, I did find myself using almost all abilities on boss fights at least.
It's worth  mentioning the game is easy. I played on normal though, so I don't know about the hard setting. Allow me to illustrate that by sharing a moment I had around halfway through the game. So I was noticing the game was getting harder, as I died for the first time even. Then I discovered that those 25 cubes in my inventory that I have been hoarding since the beginning of the game were actually the means to get health upgrades. I didn't know because apparently I didn't talk to a specific NPC that does the thing. So the game was 'starting to get a little hard' because I was still playing with only 8 hit points instead of 28 I could have! as soon as fixed that I sailed through the rest of the game without breaking a sweat. Not to mention I was filthy rich and had a huge stock of health packs in my inventory.
If you want a hardcore challenge or even a soft core challenge this isn't it. But I like easy games, as long as they're not boring easy, and I think Omega Strike stays right on the limit. I just finished Cuphead before this and I'll be totally honest, I take a fun easy game over a frustratingly hard any day! I had a much better time with this game.

Omega Strike is a metroidvania that features a good deal of exploration and colorful characters. However, you'll need to be patient to see the game be what it should be. Early in the game, like in many games of the genre, powers are taken from you and must be reclaimed. In this case, two characters of your squad are kidnapped and need to be rescued. These multiple characters create the crux of the gameplay. You can freely switch between three squadmates to utilize their unique weapon and abilities. With all characters and their abilities unlocked, the game shows it's potential. The player can rapidly swap characters to defeat enemies and overcome light platforming and puzzles to find and defeat the boss characters. However, there are no other weapons, powerups, or combat upgrades availible beyond simply damage, range, and hp (at least not for the time I played). This makes the initial hour or two where the player can only control one of the characters excruciatingly anemic.
The bosses are colorful and unique, and remind me greatly of classic Mega Man bosses. The enemies also display a great deal of variation, both mechanically and visually. The player characters don't quite keep up, and look and feel awfully generic. Exploration is critical, and is assisted by a good, but simple, map. A great deal of backtracking is required, as you'd expect of a metroidvania. Presentation wise, the music does a great job matching the environments, and the visuals are competent; at worst it looks like a bland SNES title.
Omega Strike, while lacking in innovation, is a fine metroidvania for fans of the genre that can provide several hours of play, as long as you have the patience to pull yourself through it's initial dullness.

Borderlands was a game from 2010 about a prolonged second-hand gun bring-and-buy sale which some people liked and I didn't very much. There's a longer version of this story obviously, but basically while shooting Jason Vorhees in a scrapyard might sound like a stimulating escape from the workaday world, it loses something when it's all you're supposed to do for about twelve hours. Borderlands? More like Bored...rlands!
*pause*
But now it's time for the sequel and just to remind you of my personal formula for sequels, a good sequel leaps off from the original spreading silvery wings to explore uncharted skies while a bad sequel spends most of its runtime motorboating the original's ♥♥♥♥♥♥s and rubbing its head in the gravel. So in what category sits Borderlands 2? Well, from the comfortable territory of shooting Jason Vorhees in a scrapyard, Borderlands 2 has shyly thrown aside its dressing gown and taken its first nervous tentative step into the unexplored realms of shooting Jason Vorhees in a scrapyard and also it's been snowing a bit. Borderlands? More like Snore-derlands... 2!
*pause*
Anyway, we return to the planet Pandora (or to give it its full name, the planet Pandora-No-Not that one) with four Vault hunters of varying skill sets, different superficially from the four Vault hunters from the previous game but not in any practical sense, and after the Vault that drove the first game's plot was revealed to be short on treasure and long on tentacles, it turns out there's actually more than one treasure Vault on Pandora-No-Not that one, some of which actually do have treasure in. So that means that everyone in the game gets to keep calling you Vault hunter. Phew, thought we'd have to change our stationery!
But now your quest is to end the tyrannical regime of one Handsome Jack who lures you out to Pandora-No-Not that one and then try to kill you because he hates Vault hunters! Oh no, wait, actually he wants to manipulate Vault hunters, but then why would he try to kill you? Oh stop thinking about it and kill some more Jasons, Mr. Picky-Pants! After Rage demonstrated that you can't ask someone to hate a villain who spends most of the game quietly minding their own business behind a big wall, Handsome Jack's job is to call you up every five minutes and be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at you, although come to think about it, that might describe the behaviour of every character in the game.
The hilarious thing about Borderlands 2 is that its main strategy for ramping up the stakes is to tell you the stakes are ramped up and that's about it. The player characters from the last game show up as NPCs just to confuse matters, let's call them Team Widdlebiscuit, and when a big robot boss shows up some way into Borderlands 2, they make a point of going, "Oh no, not that guy! He defeated all of Team Widdlebiscuit off-screen, no really!" And then I took him down inside five minutes! Now bearing in mind Team Widdlebiscuit basically defeated Shub Niggurath last time around, either we take from this that the new characters are all super-powered in the least apparent way possible or maybe Team Widdlebiscuit have spent the last two years sitting around drinking pints of cream with ring doughnuts hooked over the rims.
Or alternatively, Gearbox is trying to dress up the sequel as bigger and better despite it being neither of those things and not having significantly evolved in the slightest degree, and if that's the case, then the really insulting part is the halfheartedness in the disguise. It's like a small boy sitting half-in and half-out of a bear's mouth and trying to get into a nightclub by claiming to be Robin Williams.
So like its predecessor, Borderlands 2 is a game that's all wallpaper and keeps introducing new quirky characters with graphical freeze-frame effects like how a character called Jimmy Nine♥♥♥♥♥ would be introduced in a Guy Ritchie film, and then every single one proceeds to stand around doing bugger-all except explain that you're going to have to raid another bandit camp. Usually it's because the bandits nicked some component you need for the story mission. Yes, bandits snuck into someone's house while the occupant was presumably off doing something wacky and hilarious, and made off with a single dubiously resellable piece of highly technical equipment rather than any, say, money.
Perhaps everyone should rethink the standard home security policy of letting every random thug wander in and ransack every box with a green light on the front. It's like bandits are the local equivalent of Oompah-Loompahs whose job is to contrivedly pad out the gameplay before too many interesting things happen in quick enough succession to actually start engaging me. Strip off that quirky wallpaper and we're left with dull repetitive shooting where every gun somehow manages to be slightly worse than the previous one.
Borderlands is a game in which the central mechanic is the maniacal gathering of random objects, like a fat ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who suspects he's about to be thrown out of the buffet, and proudly self-identifies as a shoot-and-loot game. Personally though, I call it stop-and-start. It's like riding a rollercoaster that just won't build up a decent speed because it comes to a lurching halt every ten feet so you can pick some flowers. You clear an area of baddies (perhaps you might even enjoy doing so, you monster), but then you have to rummage around opening the empty boxes and lockers, holding down X to pick up the ammo and money, checking every weapon against all your current weapons to make sure they wouldn't make things 0.1% more dead. Why make us open five ajoining lockers one by one when we could have dumped all their contents into one convenient trough? It's like the game takes perverse pride in flowing like a string of three-inch beads into a virgin ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
And why can't I track more than one quest at a time? Is it so maddening that I might want to take care of a few issues in the same general area at once rather than adhere rigidly to the to-do list like a passive-aggressive beaurocrat? Believe me, Borderlands, it would work in your favour to let me spend as little time as possible in the company of your user interface. Me and that guy, we don't get along too well. He got drunk at a party once and started asking women to sort his tabs. I can't remember, did I mention that the vehicles in Borderlands handle like♥♥♥♥♥ Well, they do, as in they literally handle like someone stuck a steering column into a giant pair of twitching buttocks that slide along the ground leaving a trail of ball sweat.
The best way to review a game I find is to start with the broad overall gut opinion about it and then work backwards to explain those feelings, and in the case of Borderlands, my broad analysis is that it bores me to ♥♥♥♥ing tears, and in fine analysis, there are lots of little reasons for that: the quest system, the item grind, the fact that I spent several hours stuck using an assault rifle with a ten bullet clip and a four second reload time. But at the end of the day, all you need to take is that after a while, I was greeting each new swarm of baddies as a data entry clerc would treat a fresh stack of forms plopping into their in-tray at four in the afternoon.
I don't even have the enthusiasm to hate it that much. Well, I used to, but then some bandits nicked it!

Play as Batman during the events when Batman became famous.  Batman Arkham Origins is a prequel to Batman Arkham Asylum and Batman Arkham City.

Although Arkham Origins is a great game it does not quite live up to the high standards of the previous two Batman games.
The good:
1. Great action.  The best yet.  It is super smooth and the new shock gloves are awesome.  Also new types of enemies.
2. I really like the design.  It looks and feels like a real city unlike the previous versions that where more cartoonish.  Note the spaces between buildings, much more like a real city.
The bad:
3. Snow, snow and freaking more snow.  Not very exciting.
4. The story line is not as exciting as the previous versions.  Very straight forward.
5. Some in game achievements are down right crazy.  I will not waste time trying to achieve them.
6. I miss the scanning for Riddler achievements from the previous two games.
7. Joker did not sound like the previous games.  Not aweful, it just takes some getting used to.
The ugly:
8. Bugs.  Bugs?  How do they manage to deliver two games without a single problem and then in the third a lot of stuff crops up?  Falling through the city model, game progress the does not register properly and achievements that randomly register.  The bugs are not so common, don't let this diatribe dissuade you from playing the game.
9. Some of the boss fights are unexciting and unnecessarily drawn out.

Another good game in the series but still lacking in the story department.
The game has good gameplay with good graphics and no bugs (so nothing changes much between games). However, you have less of the city to work with than in Arkham City which is kinda dissapointing, there are a lot of extra fluff missions if you want to fast travel and the story is still scattered. You have 8 assasins and each one needs to be set up, executed, and taken care of. You also have side characters like Enigma (riddler), the Mad Hatter, Anarchy, and a corrupt swat team. It's a big mess and ultimately what matters is *SPOILERS* the Joker. His story is very well put together with twists and turns and actual substance. Also, you get to see why he is obsessed with Batman and it devolops very well.
Overall, play this game for the Joker. He provides the backbone of the game. Otherwise, it seems like jumping from one assasin to another without having any set up to them and just seems like a chore.

Arkham Origins is a fun addition of the "Arkham" franchise.  It lacks much of the polish, and some of the charm of the Rocksteady games, but has an interesting story and nicely varied boss fights that fans of the series will be able to appreciate.  They do a decent job of keeping things in line chronologically, and there are only a few noticable anachronisms that break the illusion of a story that takes place before Arkham Asylum.
Unfortunately, there are a few bugs that persist even now, and some of them are game-breaking.  However, in my playthrough of the main story, i managed to avoid every one of them (the My Alibi Bug is easily avoided).  "Cold, Cold Heart" (the story DLC) is the only place where I ran into game-breaking and unavoidable bugs.  That said, I was able to retain the fidelity of my save file by simply quitting after the bug had triggered (not trying to save again), and everything loaded fine.  The only thing that is still in error, is that two of the Steam Achievements have not triggered appropriately for me during "Cold, Cold, Heart".
At the end of the day, I strongly recommend Arkham Origins for fans of the previous two Arkham games, especially if you get it cheap (A Holiday sale would be best, since the story takes place on Christmas Eve).  It's not one of the Rocksteady games, but it's a fun way to spend a bit more time in their world, especially while we wait for Arkham Knight.

This game offers one of the most touching stories I have ever seen / heard / read. However, the story is pretty straightforward and simple, so it does not require too much thinking about what is going on and the player can fully focus on the fairy-tale-like atmosphere, astounding graphic design and breathtaking soundtrack. I can almost guarantee you will want to cry during some passages of the game, especially towards the end.
The graphic design of the environment and the effects your character produces (lightning bolts etc.) are very well made. The soundtrack is brilliant and touching as well. Some people could complain there are too many colours everywhere and everything is a bit too much flamboyant, but hell, this is what we expect of a game like this one! The game is neither long nor short. It does not get to the phase where playing it feels like doing school homework. On the other hand, you are not finished with it after 3 hours if you really explore the whole world (oh, forest) and don't rush it.
In comparison with the original edition of the game, here you can choose the difficulty, which is a step forward, because some players (like me) want the game to be a challenge. Here you can choose the difficulty higher than the default one (only one) in the original edition of the game. On the other hand, you can also choose an easy one, but who would do that? :) The hard one is challenging enough but not too frustruting if you have some skill.
One of the things that disappointed me was the very end of the game. To put it clearly, story-wise it is incredibly beautiful but game-wise, so to say, it ends somehow abruptly and early. The game is thrilling towards the end, very vivid and intense, but in that moment when you expect one more, final sequence in the encounter with the "boss", the game ends with a (beautiful) cinematic and bye bye, credits, etc.
Another thing a find slightly troubling is the skill-tree. It does not really matter which skills you improve, it does not really influnce the play style too much. You know that next time you play the game again, you can't really play it a different way. This phenomenon appears in more games, e.g. FarCry 4 or Wolfenstein: New Order.
To sum up, this game has almost everything you expect of a game of this genre. In many aspects it exceeded my expectations, despite them being very high. Of course it has a few flaws. No game is perfect. But this one is damn close.

This game is the best game I've ever played. The controls are tight and responsive, yet Ori's movement remains fluid and swift. The art is incredible; every area hints at a hidden history that you can only wonder about. The music fits perfectly with the mystical forest Ori journeys through, and makes the story all the more memorable. One thing about this story (I won't spoil anything): As simple as it is, the story of this game is one of the most evocative stories I've ever experienced. I almost cried at the end, and I'm not the type who cries at the end of movies (let alone games).
The puzzles were fairly intuitive, but still were challenging. Simply figuring out how the puzzles work is half the challenge. You also have to figure out how to get through them without dying or dropping something.
The combat is brilliantly designed; it gives the player several ways of defeating their foes and lets them discover ways to use them. I frequently found myself using dash and bash in combination with Sein to defeat enemies quickly, and often felt like my skills were superhuman, even when I barely got by.
The game is practically open-world. The only things keeping you away from the more difficult areas are deadly enemies and locked abilities. Every area is revisitable, except for the escape sequence from the wind temple (which is partially revisitable). The save system is very unique. It allows you to venture wherever you want, and set up checkpoints almost anywhere, at a cost. If you checkpoint too often, you'll find yourself low on energy when you really need those checkpoints (which can be very devastating). If you don't checkpoint enough, eventually you're going to die to something minor and have to go through all the stuff you did since you last saved, including story clips.
The only issue I had was some minor difficulty spikes at a couple places, mostly due to bad checkpoint decisions on my part. I highly recommend it to...anyone. The gameplay is flawless. The level design is clever and always interesting. The story is evocative and memorable. The art and soundtrack are fantastic. It's an incredible platformer for all gamers, new and veteran. Ori and the Blind Forest is a masterpiece.

All Points Bulletin: Reloaded is a game that invokes many feelings. Off the top of my head, I can name relentless rage, grueling dissapointment, and cocky pride worthy of a guy that just ♥♥♥♥ed Ariana Grande.
APB is a great concept. The backstory behind it is very deep, and the entire caracterization of the city of San Paro(however unoriginal that name might be) is very detailed and well done. It doesn't draw black and white lines: it's all a thick mist of grey, and it certainly asks you a question: are the oftentimes corrupt, control-obsessed vigilantes right? Or is it ethically correct to leave the city to the self-proclaimed renegades and anarchists, however chaotic and destructive they might be?
Remember, I'm talking about the CONCEPT here.
Because the realization of said concept is about as clear as a snowstorm in the deep ocean. The backstory and personality of the contacts and city is only presented by tedious text, mainly in the form of emails that most people just delete, or don't even bother to open. I even asked a friend, that has 20 hours clocked in the game, what the Enforcers were: he thought they were just straight-up police officers. That's just how bad the story is brought to the player.
Now for the gameplay. The core is good: Reloaded Productions managed to deliver a good third-person shooter, with interesting weapons and playstyles. The smart player that uses tactics will more often than not have an advantage over the kid that has spent countless dark nights crouched in front of his PC playing Call Of Duty, while perfecting his aim and surviving on Red Bull and Cheetos. However, like almost everything in this King Kong-sized dissapointment, this is ruined by two reasons:
1: The lag. Oh god, the lag. Unless the monthly cost for the servers is 3 bucks plus a cute picture of a cat, I cannot possibly wrap my head around how bad they are. Driving feels like standing on one foot. On a stick. Which is balancing on a banana held by a blind monkey with Parkinson.
Often, during a unexpected encounter with a hostile player in the back alleys of the Financial District, I have either died because half of my shots didn't register, or I have won because my opponent's gun wasn't raised-which is a clear indication that some serious lags are going on.
2: The players. Sadly, the smart tactician is a long extinct species in San Paro, and the streets are now ruled by people such as "Pu$$ySlayer69", "lole_u_got_butt♥♥♥♥ed" and "UMAD BRAH??11?". I am seriously not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you right now, I have seen all three of these names ingame.
Dare to be good, and you'll be called a dirty hacker. Dare to be even slightly worse than either your teammates or your opponents, or equip a weapon they dislike, and you'll be called n00b,♥♥♥♥♥ and come to the realization that most of these people have had sexual intercourse with your mother, or that they wish you to do the same.
There are quite some topics I haven't covered, such as the hackers, which constitute, based on other people's calculations, 9,7% of the players. An alarming number, but hard to confirm, so I will leave it there. There is also the company known as GamersFirst. Sadly, these people seem to identify 'Gamer' as 'Man with a lot of money and no need for a honorable fight'. For excruciating prices, you can buy certain weapons that will shred through any average player. (Note that I'm not saying all of them are OP: a decent chunk are either reskins, or equally powerful as the in-game weapons.) The excuse 'you can get it in game too' is true, because you DO unlock modifications and bonuses as you go, but I myself have clocked over a hundred hours and all I got was a useless magazine mod and a slight increase to marksman zoom.
The customization is unrivalled, though. I have tried to find a game, ANY game, that has better character creation or vehicle customization, but to no avail. Shame, because this pearl just had to be incrusted in the (mostly) dried up turd that is APB.
TL;DR: APB: Reloaded is a great concept, that was insufficiently realized by Reloaded Productions, and completely♥♥♥♥♥♥on by GamersFirst, after they took over the game. You could of course take a look, because, hey, it's free, but greedy business ideals have screwed over the concept so bad that the game is now singing it's dying song.

Interesting third-person shooter game, with lots of take-cover action a la Gears of War.
Pros:
- Fun to play if you like 3rd person shooters
- Great graphics for a 4-year-old game
- While somewhat predictable, the plot is still above average for a game; certain parts are quite intense in terms of action
- Ability to command your other team members to focus their fire on specific enemies
- More realistic than average game in terms of damage
- More realistic with ammo management (it's not as widely available as other shooters tend to be, and often times you will be forced into using various weapons simply because your favorite gun ran out of ammo)
Cons:
- Commanding teammates is a bit limited, would've loved to see more control in this regard
- No character or skill building / development
- No weapons customization
- Aiming with a controller can be difficult
- Linear gameplay
- Take cover navigation can be a tad wonky in sticky situations
- About half-way through the story line, you can guess the plot twist because of the heavy amount of clues
The game is definitely worth checking out if you're a fan of games like Gears of War.

This may just be my settings, but this was my experience:
Do story mode for a bit, on one chapter try and improve a prison to the maximum but run out of money halfway through. Quit until I can figure out how to do everything correctly. Decide to try out Sandbox mode to get myself more familiar with the game.
Start sandbox mode, barely enough money to make a basic detention center.
Halfway through construction, delivery area becomes full without me knowing and for 13 in-game hours the workers are wandering around doing nothing.
Barely finish Holding Cell as prisoners arrive.
Accept a few grants, spend it all just to be able to assign the holding cell to the canteen and assign guards to their correct rooms.
Find out prisoners still don't go to the canteen even though I've assigned them it. Neither do they go to the showers.
Am told by another player I need a perimeter wall around the entire prison in order for prisoners to leave holding cell.
Place about 1/4 of the perimeter wall before my entire 50k left is depleted. Find out I could've just used a fence instead.
Too late to cancel because all the money is gone and the leftover perimeter wall material has already been canceled.
Before I can make anymore money, prisoners riot and 50% of the prisoners die, 50% escape, and everyone else is dead. Why'd they kill the cooks? They didn't do anything to you, criminals.
Besides the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ sandbox mode that's almost impossible to play unless you know every detail about the game, Story mode is still fun but how are you supposed to make enough money to do anything?
The only sure, fast way you can make more money is by accepting new prisoners. But to accept new prisoners you need more cells. For more cells you need more money. Basically, all the money you've gotten accepting prisoners is immediately spent on their cells, then you run out of space. it leaves you with no profit to spend on improving the prison. Grants are alright, but usually don't give you enough money to make decent improvements. It seems like all you're capable of doing is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t stuff like you're just trying to pass a C on your test, then costs waaay too much money to tear something down and build something better in it's place.
basically, I have these suggestions:
*Size of your lot should be able to be increased with money
*Ability to sell back building materials you don't need anymore
*Please, for the love of god, put more in-game support in. Trying to figure out how to assign my prisoners to a canteen; First, I was told to unlock Finance. Then it was Security. Then I was told to unlock Prison Labour. Finally I unlocked Prison Policy to assign my prisoners to the canteen, which I could've done without having to unlock the Maintenance tree at all.
And then I had to look up how to actually get my prisoners to leave the holding cell.
*Ability to assign prisoners to a shower. Gave prisoners a huge shower room for their prison block--and they still use the tiny shower attached to the Holding Cell on the other side of the road. Why!?!?
*More control over workers. Seriously, most of the time only 50% of your workers are doing what they're supposed to--and I don't believe they are able to "slack off" because there are no ways to punish them besides firing them, and I'm pretty sure that doesn't make a difference. Sometimes they don't even rest when they're tired, even if you have a Staff Room. Like, I told you to slack off and you didn't even do that right.
*Metal detectors are useless because of my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ workers. They frisk a prisoner, throw their weapon on the ground, then leave it there for any prisoner to pick up again. I tried putting bins next to the metal detector but it doesn't work and my workers neglect to throw out the trash.
Even with all this frustration I can't lie about the fact I still love the "controlled chaos" feel of this game. It's just frustrating when you're actually trying to build a healthy prison.

At 27 hours.
This game is a RPG brawler driving game. Here's how it's components rate.
**edit it has more of a story than I initially gave credit for. It's a well paced , in the end gripping, story
but well crafted.
1. RPG elements - there are a lot of options available and 3 seperate upgradable catagories.
But you'll have so many points to use that it won't feel like you are driving down your own road(metaphor for asigning points). The car category offers some variety.
I'd call this a bit more of an RPG than shadow of morder - less than Farc Cry (which gave you more playstyle options).
It's not really RPG - It's another GTA clone at heart.
RPG 3/10.
2.Brawling -
Easy so far but very well executed. Similar to sleeping dogs but improved.  It's some of the best (most fun) brawling in an open world game to date.
Batman or Morder is more of a challange but this system stays as fresh (maybe fresher) as the other 2 throughout the game.  Maybe it's because combat is spaced between other activities. I always look forward to brawling.
Brawling 8/10.
3. Driving/Racing
Some iffy physics and can survice a lot of cliff diving.  It's not GTA. The driving is fun though. The different cars have wildly different weight and speeds. You'l likely only drive your main car through most of the missions. It's not GTA(again).
Not even sleeping dogs , mafia or saints row. The driving stays fun though. And there are plenty of fast travel points.
The races are fun but easy. You can beat most of them in 3 or 4 trys. But again, it stays fun  - and I'm someone who races every race in GTA and it's many clones.
Driving/racing 6/10
Driving Combat:
This is where the game shines. I don't know a better open world combat driving game. GTA is great driving and has the best cars, best maps, and most creative race routes but the combat is limited.
This game offers so many enjoyable options to car combat. My favorite thing to do in this game is something called "caravans" where you have to chase down the caravan leader all the while trying to pick off the 5 or 6 armoured cars protecting it. It's a rush and very well designed.
Driving Combat 10/10
Story/Art ...
It's Mad Max - more than this last movie. This game conveys the feel of the barren waste with crazy cult groups who worship
gas, machines/cars. The lack of water , eating maggots etc are all good touches - better than the last movie.
But, again, it's not really an RPG so the star of the game is the driving and brawling. You don't care about the characters - youself included. There are no memorable villians like FarCry3(and primal actually). The side stories are just "go get this" tasks.  It  is barely a story. It's much much better than Morder(which had horrible writing) but similar in it's "lets get this out of the way" approach to plot/story.

This is a good game all around. A good brawler and a very good car combat game.
The racing is fun as well except it's pretty easy.
8/10.

I bought this game during a summer sale I believe, I bought it as a joke. I thought, "Hey, this game looks stupid, but I'll buy it since it's cheap and I can say I've got a truck simulator!" Little did I know this would sortly lead to a spiral that nearly had my family and friends write me off as dead. It certainly doesn't look it, but this game is highly addictive.
You boot up the game, make your profile, then you start doing little "Quick Jobs" using another companies trucks to move around cargo, but eventually you will decide you want your own truck, knowing it'll lead to more cash. A while later you will be buying a new garage, a truck, and hiring a driver for that truck. After that you just keep buying more trucks, hiring more drivers, and buying more garages across Europe, creating a trucking empire.
What makes this game addictive is the grind. It is a grind really, you keep doing the same thing, progressively longer and better, making progress in the game. You may be bored with the game, but once you finish a delivery you'll want to do another one, why? Because that truck you want is only another €3000 away and you really want it.
I'd say that if you like driving simulators you should definitely give it a shot. But if you don't, maybe you should look into the game more, do research, maybe even play the demo, give it a chance, you may actually like it. I honestly hated the idea of playing a truck simulator before I played it, but now I love it.

After the embarrassment that was Hitman: Absolution, it’s great that IO Interactive learned from their mistakes and decided to bring back what originally made the series so revolutionary. Welcome back, our bald headed friend.
Hitman suffered a seriously rocky launch period, with the controversial episodic content, performance issues and general lack of polish. For those newcomers arriving now that the game is complete with additional features, I congratulate you: you get to experience the finished product now that the game is out of
. Yes, I said it.
The visual department can’t seem to make their mind up on how they want their game to look. The modelling, texture work and level design are second to none. Sadly, the game is washed out in a dull blurry post-processing filter, as if simulating how a dog’s colour spectrum is like – with Vaseline all over his face. Additional graphical artefacts like trails left behind after rotating the camera and motion blur on some moving objects spoil the visuals.
My advice is to use Reshade/SweetFX to add some colour into the game and Lumasharpening so you can actually see a damn thing. After that, the game looks stunningly gorgeous like in the promotional screenshots.
Lastly and more of a personal note is that many of the rooms are just too clean and sterile looking. I have never seen such clean public toilets in my entire life and having worked 9 years in the catering industry, witnessing such pristine and sparkling kitchen environments means I must have died and gone to heaven as they simply don’t exist.
Like the graphics, the audio in the game is a mixed bag, and a troubled one at that.
The absence of Jepser Kyd makes an impact, more-so with the return to classic Hitman format. While more of a spy-style undertone to the soundtrack is good and dandy for what the game represents, it’s not a Hitman-esque soundtrack. It starts to grate after a while especially with all the annoying sound cues, to the point I just muted the soundtrack and let a Youtube playlist run in the background. Muting music in a Hitman game is blasphemy, but what to do without Mr. Kyd behind the scenes? Well, at least you don’t get loud trumpets blasting up your♥♥♥♥♥♥ I’m looking at you, Absolution.
As for sound effects, they’re pretty much hit and miss. Many guns just lack that oomph and appear tinny. Silenced pistols sound like a can of coke being opened, the Fusil sounds like someone beating a metal bucket, and the Jaeger 7 sounds like a gunshot recorded from an 80’s movie. Thankfully though, the ambient sound is fairly decent and helps immerse you in the already insanely detailed missions.
Voice acting is so-so, but every… single… guard sounds the same. Doesn’t matter if you’re perusing in Paris, moving through Marrakech, or hiking around Hokkaido: all the enemies are solely voiced by a single person, who doesn’t even bother to attempt regional accents. I can understand a low budget for voice acting, but this is really embarrassing and not even funny enough to become a running gag.
Hitman™ may lack in polish, but where it truly revels in is in its gameplay, and begs to be played, played, and played again. Each 6 locations steal the show here, and are possibly the most detailed levels seen in video game history. Each map is gigantic teeming with different NPCs, full of lived-in areas, mini scenarios, storerooms and service areas. The developers truly did their research to breathe life into each level, great work!
There are countless ways to go about your missions and with so much room for experimenting and exploring, playing through each level a clean virgin will leave you giddy with delight and foaming at the mouth with just what you can do.
You can utilise different disguises to get closer to your targets, arrange “accidents” to take people out, do stealth-only runs solely in your suit, go postal, go lethal or non-lethal, only use hand-to-hand combat, snipe, use poison, explosives, distractions, silencers only, pistols only… the list goes on and on.
The game feels well balanced and organic, with NPCs not having split second reactions that no longer go ape♥♥♥♥♥♥if you trespass, warning you to get lost and even personally escorting you off the premises. Disguises actually work too, unlike in Absolution. Still, enemies are unfairly accurate aimbots, terminating your existence in a quick burst from halfway across the map. Mass shootouts are difficult but not impossible, but the emphasis on stealth is strong here.
Challenges with unlockable rewards make an appearance here, which I have mixed feelings about. On one hand, they’re a great way to test your mettle and finesse. On the other hand, locking specific gear behind a paywall system made me frustrated and I ended up mirroring Youtube walkthroughs just so I could unlocked all the gear as quickly as possible, rather than figure them out myself.
I personally would prefer a currency system (how about your end of level score?) that lets you buy the gear, rather than a forced on “Simon says do xyz and here’s your shiny new toy”. Were it not for the rewards, the challenges are quickly forgettable, and the game truly shines when you orchestrate your very own assassination rather than a developer made one.
Lastly, you get Elusive Targets, Escalations and user-created Contracts to sink your teeth into. Again fairly forgettable, but nice to dive into every now and then.
Arguably the best feature of the last two games, weapon customisation is sadly omitted in this latest iteration. On the subject, most of the guns just aren’t that interesting and asides from looks and sounds, seem to function identical to each other. Plus who the hell thought it would be a smashing idea to paint most of the unlocked guns a baby blue colour like they were two-tone Airsoft toys??? Seriously, fire the person who came up with that idea.
Having sniped, stabbed and garrotted drug lords, mafia bosses and child molesters in previous Hitman games, I found all the targets in this new title lifeless and uninspiring. Most are rich snobby c*nts living lavish lifestyles who probably stepped on the wrong shoes at one point or another, so I never felt like I was snuffing out evil from the world. A handful of other targets include an ex-assassin, Yakuza crime lord and an army general who are hyped up to be extremely dangerous targets, yet never retaliate and flee on sight, making them just as boring and generic as every other target in the game.
Furthermore, all the targets are high-profile subjects, meaning they’re usually always surrounded by people and traversing open locations. I long to play a level where someone is so paranoid of assassination, they barricade themselves in a room and I had to use my guile and wit to get to him. Shogun Showdown anyone?
It’s great to have 47 back and despite a controversial launch period, Hitman™ has improved and evolved into the second best game to Hitman: Blood Money, and a fantastic stealth/espionage game in its own right. I can’t stress enough how much replayability is on offer, you will definitely be getting your bang for your buck.

For me, this is the most underrated game in 2016. If you're the one who likes to solve puzzles on your own, has a photographic memory and a good sense of direction, and also has Achievement OCD, this is your game.
Every time you open a new door, you have to remember everything. Where the wrench is, where the screwdriver is, where the NPCs are, which way they move, what's behind this room, how they work. Replan your assassination route based on those objects, people, barriers, shortcuts, different smuggling locations, different gadgets, clothes. It won't work as you planned at first. There will be restrictions, floors you can't go with your current disguise, it would be hard to get certain tools cause it's too far or there are too many guards, so you'll have to replan your assassination route from the start. The score varies from 50k to 250k, and you can get better scores as your kills become faster, more precise, and more quite. That's how this game should be played. Quality of the game really depends on how you play it. I bet those people on the leaderboard might have spent their best time with the game.
But beware, The game might become repetitive and boring if you don't have any clues, can't remember where they are, how the targets should be killed, or just rely on Youtube guides. if you're an impatient person and just want to shoot and kill, this is not your game.

Do you try for rehabilitation, or cram each one of your charges into the tiniest space possible to maximise your fiscal intake?  I'm already counting the cash.
Prison Architect does exactly what it says on the tin, and then some.  You start off the game with an empty field and a few workers, and your job is to build a prison.  You have a limited amount of upfront capital and a small monthly income and there are eight medium security prisoners on the way.  You don't even have a shower built to hide the soap.  Time to get to work.
This game is obviously a labour of love (forget about the soap for a second).  The developers have done a tremendous job in making this game as polished as they can.  The graphics are clean and consistent, and the characters are surprisingly unique given their size and lack of real adornment.  Play it enough and you start to pick out specific inmates, at which point you start thinking about permanent cell incarceration, and withholding food just to♥♥♥♥♥♥them off.  Then you assign a security guard to their wing with a taser.  Fried prisoner?  Yes please.
The UI is easy and familiar, though sometimes I find it difficult to pick out room names on the list;  a minor quibble, I'm a skim reader so it's probably my own fault.  Building a wing and allocating rooms is straightforward, drag and click basically.  Fill the rooms with the required items (essentials are highlighted, a nice touch) and, before you can say two days in solitary, you've got a fully functioning canteen and a healthy supply of accidental weapons for your inmates.  And they will steal them.  A lot.  My advice, for what it's worth?  Every few days, lock the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s down and search their cells.  They're crafty buggers and they will try to dig their way out of your facility, and there's nothing worse than wandering off for a coffee to find four of them have dug a korean bunker complex worth of tunnels under your nose.
Trial and error makes up a good portion of the replayability. You find yourself pushing for efficiency, trying to remove human interference in your system to reduce the entropy that is constantly hovering behind your monitor, desperate to reduce your highly ordered complex into a raging inferno of dead bodies and broken furniture.  Remote doors and security cameras become a neccesity once you go over a certain size.
The game is complex but the learning curve is graceful.  The community has built some wonderful prisons, and the developers have made the game accessible for all.  Want to play stock?  Go for it, you'll have a blast.  If you're looking to complicate it with some circuitry, you can do that too, it's all there, and the developers push regular updates, with content on the agenda.
There are bugs, nothing game breaking; small irritations at best, like the time all of my cast for some reason got stuck at one particular point due to a dropped item.  I forgave the game though, it was trying to process around four hundred different tasks at the same time.  I just restarted and everything went back to normal.
The best part of the game for me was the first time I authorised an execution.  Strangely, the gravitas of the situation wasn't lost in the translation to gaming fun.  It mattered.  I found myself pleased whenever one of my doomed inmates received a repeal.  I made their cell comfortable and large.  I was more Green Mile than Shawshank Redemption.  That took me by surprise.  As I said, the game is a test in morality.  It turns out I'm a liberal.  Who knew?
* nice simple appealing graphics
* Straightforward UI
* replayable
* graceful learning curve
* funny in a  horrible way
* death row
What's not:
* small writing (opinion)
* the bloody tunnels
* the occasional bug
