This game offers one of the most touching stories I have ever seen / heard / read. However, the story is pretty straightforward and simple, so it does not require too much thinking about what is going on and the player can fully focus on the fairy-tale-like atmosphere, astounding graphic design and breathtaking soundtrack. I can almost guarantee you will want to cry during some passages of the game, especially towards the end.
The graphic design of the environment and the effects your character produces (lightning bolts etc.) are very well made. The soundtrack is brilliant and touching as well. Some people could complain there are too many colours everywhere and everything is a bit too much flamboyant, but hell, this is what we expect of a game like this one! The game is neither long nor short. It does not get to the phase where playing it feels like doing school homework. On the other hand, you are not finished with it after 3 hours if you really explore the whole world (oh, forest) and don't rush it.
In comparison with the original edition of the game, here you can choose the difficulty, which is a step forward, because some players (like me) want the game to be a challenge. Here you can choose the difficulty higher than the default one (only one) in the original edition of the game. On the other hand, you can also choose an easy one, but who would do that? :) The hard one is challenging enough but not too frustruting if you have some skill.
One of the things that disappointed me was the very end of the game. To put it clearly, story-wise it is incredibly beautiful but game-wise, so to say, it ends somehow abruptly and early. The game is thrilling towards the end, very vivid and intense, but in that moment when you expect one more, final sequence in the encounter with the "boss", the game ends with a (beautiful) cinematic and bye bye, credits, etc.
Another thing a find slightly troubling is the skill-tree. It does not really matter which skills you improve, it does not really influnce the play style too much. You know that next time you play the game again, you can't really play it a different way. This phenomenon appears in more games, e.g. FarCry 4 or Wolfenstein: New Order.
To sum up, this game has almost everything you expect of a game of this genre. In many aspects it exceeded my expectations, despite them being very high. Of course it has a few flaws. No game is perfect. But this one is damn close.

Adams and Lugo are very helpful most of the time but there will be times they go out in the open to engage the enemy and sit there reloading while they get pummeled and eventually go down, leaving you to make the decision to go help them yourself, or send your other guy in and hope he doesnt go down too. Voice acting was top notch, yet another title on Nolan Norths resume, and the soundtrack was fantastic. I absolutely loved the radio chatter, music during specific gun fights, and the overall ambience in the environments you go thru. I will leave multiplayer out of this review until i can try it as my whole experience was in the single player campaign. I would give this an 8/10 only for the fact that its relatively short, as most shorters single campaign are, but it was definitely worth the play thru and i will probably go back thru it again just for fun. Highly recommended!

Yes, when you start playing, you'll see a different, slightly more cartoonish batman, you'll eventually get over it. The first few hours will feel very empty and pretty much dissapointing, if you have played the other 2 games of this series. The overworld feels empty, geometry detail is very simplified even with DX11 effects enabled. Overall the mood was pretty badly executed as far as the city itself goes. You will only see impressive visual and level design once you go indoors, where lights are elaborate, cinematic and colorful. Colour is much more abundant this time.
The combat system, both predator (stealth) and close up combat, remain pretty much identical to previous versions, aside from a few superficial changes like sounds. There is however a new mechanic that increases your damage output towards the second half of the story, but I don't want to spoil that for you. I found that close up combat felt more satisfying than stealth, simply because the stealth rooms were not designed for you to be creative, really. Rocksteady made extremely enjoyable stealth challenges, and WB basically was not capable of getting anywheres near that level of intricate design. All you really have to do in these sections is grapple around, wait for an enemy to seclude himself from the others, and take him down by gliding behind him and performing a silent takedown, rinse and repeat. So basically, this time close up completely trumps stealth, where as I found in City and Assylum, the stealth was more enjoyable than close up.
Gadgets remain from the previous games, some replaced by something similar, essentially reskinning previous ideas.
The main thing that WB really did right this time, is the storytelling, and the way you progress through the game. Arkham City's progression was fairly short, focused and let's face it, not very complex. Origins obviously tells the story of Batman's beginning, when he was considered a criminal just like the Joker, or Black Mask. Although Batman remains fairly emotionally flat, he lets out a lot of steam, and even interrogates many enemies through semi-torture, something that was rarely adressed before. Batman seems weaker in this game, he is actually a real, relatable person, in some ways. There is a sense of character progression that was completely absent in the other games. Hell, you even finally see some sort of relation between Batman and Joker that actually makes some sense, and let me tell you that relation becomes extremely interesting, and at times it almost seemed that Joker admired Batman, or even loved him.
TL:DR: Origins is a narrative experience, lacking the immersion of the previous 2 games but replacing that with a cohesive, understandable story with much more variety. Is it better than the others? No. but is it worse? I can't really say that, either.
It is definitely worth the price that I got it at, during the summer sale.

Please bear in mind that I only recommend this game under certain circumstances. Purchase it if it's on sale, I picked it up on the summer sale for $7.50 so it was hard to go wrong with that.
First off, the question that many will obviously have is, is it better or at least on par with its predecessors? No, not at all. Remember, both Arkham Asylum and Arkham City earned the prestigious Game of the Year award, and this title did not. Of course there are many great games that did not earn such an award, and one might even argue that the award is just a PR kind of thing, but you can't help but notice that this game failed to keep up the trend.
In terms of core gameplay, this game shares many similarities with Arkham City. The combat is the same, it has the same open world feel (except this time you prowl the streets of Gotham City, not the massive prison that is Arkham City), and the navigation and gadgets are pretty much the same as well (save for a couple new gadgets, but that was the least they could do). Now, many may be pleased to hear that they maintained the same kind of gameplay that made Arkham City so great, but I couldn't shake the feeling that this game lacked any kind of innovation. I was hoping that Warner Bros Games would take what Rocksteady did and expand upon it, incorporating their own sense of creativity and imagination, for better or worse. But instead, we simply got a continuation of Arkham City. It was almost as if Warner Bros was too afraid to alter anything that Rocksteady had done, and as a result, we ended up with new features that felt like add-ons from a DLC.
As for the story, well, I unfortunately found that to be quite disappointing too. In the advertisements that preceded the launch of this game, it leads us to believe that Batman is now going to be confronted with a new villain, that villain of course being the Black Mask. The Black Mask has hired a multitude of daunting assassins who's primary goal is to dispose of the Batman, and in return, they will be handsomely rewarded with a whopping 50 million dollars. So the stage is set, right? Batman's mission is to challenge each and every one of these assassins, and after defeating each one of them, he will finally be able to approach Black Mask and finish him off as well. Seems intriguing enough, and after two games where the main villain was the Joker, it's refreshing to finally face a new opponent. However, (spoiler alert) that doesn't turn out to be the case at all. As usual, the Joker is actually behind all this, masquerading about as the Black Mask when he's really not the Black Mask at all. Batman, being the skilled detective that he is, is quick to discover this, and doesn't hesitate to set his sights on the Joker, like always. So long story short, we embark on yet another Joker witch hunt, and one that feels markedly lackluster without Mark Hamill portraying the iconic character this time around. And on a final wistful note regarding the story, you don't even get to square off against two assassins that are mentioned early on, Lady Shiva and Deadshot, although I'm sure you get the opportunity to face them on a side mission, I wouldn't know because I only defeated the campaign, but nontheless, why would they refer to them in the main story, only for them to not actually be a part of it?
At this point, many of you may be wondering why I would still recommend this game after all this. Well, it's tough to deny the fact that this is still a part of the Arkham series, however underwhelming it may be. It maintains the core gameplay of the previous games as I stated before, and there's plenty of additional content to sift through, if you're into that sort of thing (again, I only played the main campaign, I frankly had no desire to continue playing beyond that). I wouldn't spend more than $10 on this game to be honest, I was fortunate enough to score a great deal for even less. Hope this helps, but if you're more interested in every aspect of the game, I would peruse some reviews that perhaps spend more time focusing on all the content that this game has to offer outside of the main story.

It's certainly unique. So the basic mechanics are: jet around in space from planet to planet, planting trees to restore them. Once a planet is restored, it dispenses a random treasure and heals you. While this is going on you will be assaulted RELENTLESSLY by enemy aliens, which gets pretty frustrating. I was having Spore flashbacks for a while. After X time has passed, a massive boss monster will spawn, which necessitates jetting through space while managing your fuel and hopefully hopping between restored planets for healing. This is the phase where you'll usually die horribly and start over -- and if you don't, you plod on until the next boss spawns.
From treasure chests you'll either get some gems (for postgame upgrades), bombs, bricks (build largely ineffective towers with), or artifacts. Artifacts can be traded in for mutators accessible from the main menu, such as disallowing towers, more enemies, less enemies, "no eggs" (???) and the like. Most of these are also largely ineffectual, as I've noticed no difference even playing with fewer enemies and lower enemy health. Each time you start a new game the galaxy will be mostly randomized, including planetoids, what types of enemies will appear, and whether or not weapon powerups (which are crucial, as you can't buy weapon upgrades) will actually appear. The RNG swing is kind of ridiculous, I've had games where apparently every chest has contained an artifact, and others where they don't seem to exist. I've repeatedly gotten duplicate artifacts, and sometimes I've been unable to trade a new artifact in for no apparent reason. I somehow collected a pickup from a boss after the game was over despite dying to it, which gave me a white screen and a weird three-minute musical number.
It's really hard to tell how much of this game is actually functioning as intended, what's glitching out and what's just plain dickish design, and much like Rogue Legacy the necessitation of perishing repeatedly to grind upgrades is starting to rub me the wrong way, but to a certain extent I'm still quite enjoying it anyway. I'm just not sure if it's more fun or frustrating yet.

This is a game in which you drive a truck around Europe whilst delivering cargo to various places… kinda sounds boring doesn’t it? That’s what I thought at first, but instead it’s been 170+ hours of fun driving and learning.
Once you turn up those settings to the max, you get to see the absolutely gorgeous details the game shows. Whether it be a bright sunrise or a small patch of grass, it will look really nice. They really showed how beautiful the game looks, even in lower settings the game still looks lovely. The graphics in this game is the best I’ve seen out of the simulator genre.
However, not quite the word “storyline” as this game offers none of it. It’s more of a progression system which is implemented as the player drives and delivers cargo throughout the entire game. There is no actual storyline that affects the game. It is mainly just a simulator for experience and pure immersion.
The engine noises, the wipers, the indicator light sound…they have been perfected for each truck which is pleasing to hear. The only compliant that I have is the truck horn and the traffic noise. The truck horn and the traffic noise sounds too quiet compared to the rest of the sounds.
Smooth and refined. From driving the truck out of the compound to parking the truck in the designated spot, it will feel satisfyingly smooth and refined. I’ve yet to play a driving simulator which offers the same quality of immersion.
This receives full marks and I would give it a higher score if you got this from a sale. Even playing this for 5 hours is enough for what the price is asking for. This is the most immersive driving simulator I’ve ever played and it is sure to please you with its realistic controls, beautiful details and refined gameplay. It is worth the price you pay for.

I have been enjoying this game massively since the Early Access. This was one of my first Early Access games besides Don't Starve and it hasn't let me down. The developer has provided the community with regular updates and the community itself isn't getting tired of providing mods.
I really enjoy starting new every once again, just to create a new layout for my prison. I feel like the UI is quite intuitive, creating a prison with the necessary rooms is easy. Tools like "Cloning" make it even easier to add already created rooms to your prison layout later on, if you need.
There are a lot of different rooms like cells, holding cell, family cells (only for female prisons) and dormitories to "store" your prisoners, showers to fullfill their hygiene need, kitchen and dining halls to feed them.
You can unlock more rooms later on by unlocking different perks by your staff members like Prison labour. This gives you the opportunity to let your prisoners work as janitors (cleaning the facility) or in a workshop or laundry to clean clothes and make licensing plates which can be sold. This way you can earn some extra money.
Of course there are additional rooms just to make your prisoners happy and make sure they are not starting a riot quickly like a library, common rooms, visitor rooms or a shop.
This game has a lot to it and if I would have to compare it to another game, it would be Dungeon Keeper. Of course, you are not luring monsters with your rooms, and your are not preparing to fight some white knight. But still creating the rooms and keeping your inmates happy somehow reminds me of the good old dungeon keeper times.
I would full-heartedly recommend this game, if you are into building/management stuff.

The good:
Wanted to build your own prison and micromanage everyone! Well, now you can! (Sort of.) Prison Architect is a 2D top-down management game with many different modes to choose from. Play in Campaign to experience the rich plotline, or start a fresh in Unlimited Funds mode, or even attempt to escape from your own prison!
The bad:
This game lags on my main gaming PC with a quad-core i5 and GTX 1070. With a prison with only around 200 prisoners. Some serious optimization is needed.
The ugly:
Nothing major.
Overall rating: Positive.

I loved absolutely every minute of playing this game. Artistically, it's one of the most stunning games I've ever played and there were many scenes where I just stopped to look at it. Ori and the Blind Forest possibly has some of the best art I've ever seen in a game, so it's even better that it also has extremely tight gameplay mechanics as well. At its most basic, Ori and the Blind Forest is a "Metroidvania" with a large world map, where progress is gated by acquiring different abilities allowing you to traverse (or enter) inaccessible areas. In addition to this, there is also an experience and leveling up system in place, where you can improve Ori's attacks, ability to see secrets and eventually gain the ability to triple jump (I found this incredibly useful in the final section).
All of these mechanics are implemented and used immensely soundly. Challenge, in terms of platforming, puzzle solving (which is generally fairly light) and enemy encounters are slowly ramped up over the course of the game. Enemies in Ori and the Blind Forest are generally used for solving puzzles, getting to higher areas or avoided. There are only a handful of times in the entire game that where being forced to fight enemies was particularly relevant or important for progress. I only encountered a few barriers that only open when everything was dead, but in these cases they were more often like small puzzles than a pure combat encounter. Where Ori and the Blind Forest is most tricky, is in several difficult platforming sections that occur after each major world event begins.
Essentially, Ori and the Blind Forest eschews traditional boss fights and instead has these extremely challenging platforming sections. Some of these take some time to master and learn, but once pulled off successfully they are an absolute joy to do. On the other hand, they are extremely difficult and don't feature any checkpoints whatsoever along their length: So if you're not very good at quick reactions and platforming, I can easily see these becoming very frustrating very quickly. In particular, the first one and the last of these platforming challenges are very difficult - especially if you didn't go all the way to upgrading to the triple jump.
None the less, some issues with the platforming aside this is a beautiful, deep and compelling game. Definitely one of the best metroidvania style games released in recent years IMO. Additionally, the Definitive Edition avoids a problem I heard about with the original game, where you couldn't go back to several areas after you'd finished them to search for secrets and items. You can return to and get all the items/secrets you missed from each area of the game in this edition - reducing the frustration for those who want to 100% all the secrets/map areas.

The introduction teaches you about the world
extensive voiceover, and makes you care about two characters in less than two minutes. It also introduces the game's major villain with a plausible explanation for the villain's actions. The first stages teach you all the basics of how to play by adding new elements one-by-one, ensuring you're never challenged beyond what you're capable of doing, but aren't bored with too-easy tasks.
The middle section of the story focuses on exploration and the changes happening in the world because of your character's actions, which gives the player time to enjoy being exposed to all of the wonderful level art and musical themes. These changes are told through the dramas of minor characters in the story, fleshing out the world for the player to appreciate. Mechanically, players are given more and more powers and puzzles that require combining them, requiring a demonstration of mastery of the game's basic concepts. Each level typically focuses on twisting or changing one of those basic concepts (gravity, ability to double-jump, etc.) which means you're kept on your toes and continue learning new techniques in a challenging environment.
The last section of the story focuses on the relationship between the villian, the villain's objective and motivations, and the consequences for the world and the characters in it. Levels become stricter, as players have had several hours with the game at this point and are skilled in most of the basic concepts and their combinations. Happily, challenge ramps up just as the motive drive of the story pushes a player to want to complete the game and see the narrative through to the end.
The ending and epilogue make sense, are emotionally charged, provide closure to the story, and will absolutely leave you saying 'Well... that was one of the best games I've ever played."
The story is perfectly paced. The music perfectly supports the action of the world. The art direction is phenomenal throughout. Animation and creature design is top notch. The characters are believable, likable, relatable, and unique. The mechanics are ridiculously well designed. In short, measure all other platformers by standards gleaned from Ori's story, design, art direction, and philosophy.
Also, write a thank-you note to Moon Studios for spending their lives making this masterpiece.

I've finished this game twice so far and let me tell you this; if you're a fan of good and fluid platforming like Super Meat Boy (or the old days of 2D Super Mario on the SNES or NES), this game deserves a spot in your library without a doubt. It has one of the best platforming in years I'd wager. Along with level designs that make great use of Ori's abilities (and how well animated Ori is), moving around and exploring have never felt more satisfying.
However, and this is entirely my opinion, if you're feeling for a more Metroidvania game with a fleshed out combat system or deeper RPG mechanics, this game does neither of those. The combat mechanics still fulfill their purpose, but it can be somewhat mindless as your means of offense is to only repeatedly press a button to kill your enemies with little to no strategy as your projectiles automatically homes onto an enemy and pulling off a charged attack from time to time.
The great piece of a golden nugget that this game can offer is a variety of ways to finish off your enemies by using the environment to your advantage. Additionally, you'll unlock more abilities to maneuver around the gorgeous world, allowing exploration to be fun, rewarding and less repetitive. The light RPG mechanic, albeit simplistic, works wondefully well as the abilities and upgrades you unlock have a great synergy with one another and are well balanced, making it so that there's no ability or upgrade that is outright useless or overpowered. This game's story is the weakest link, but if anything, it gives you just the right amount of motivation to continue playing while you're engrossed by the beautiful soundtrack, only to realize that you've already reached the end.
All in all, it's a wonderful game (with slightly lacking combat) and I enjoyed it thoroughly so play it now, you dork.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a beautiful Metroidvania style platformer. The story is very concise and focused with a small cast of characters. The art in the game has a wonderful painted picture feel and the character designs feel like something out of a Studio Ghibli film. The soundtrack is awesome and very evocative and was my first real introduction to the game and contains a memorable melody that keeps it in your head.
Gameplay involves having a small set of abilities that slowly grows the further you explore the game. Unfortunately, some directions to progress are not fully clear and I had to consult a guide early on to learn what I *could* climb onto. The player is free to explore regions once they have the minimum abilities necessary to get past the initial obstacles and in some cases you will feel like you completed puzzles earlier than the game intended. This is especially the case if you acquire the new abilities that were introduced in the Definitive Edition, which can trivialize some puzzles which would be much more challenging without them (or by playing the original version.)
Sometimes the platforming and puzzles can be absolutely brutal with several traps intended to kill you immeidately or allowing for only a few mistakes. This can be frustrating as death can come swiftly and send you to the last place you saved. Fortunately, you can create save points every few minutes provided you have energy resources and are standing on a non-moving platform. Forgetting to save regularly can result in the loss of significant progress, especially if you are out looking for collectibles and secrets.
While there are sometimes enemy rooms where you have to defeat all the enemies before you can progress, there aren't any true bosses per se. Progress is centred around gathering abilities and then using them in the three 'dungeons' in the game which require you to apply things you've learned in the overworld map and then adds an additional twist - like teleporters or gravity shifts. These culminate in an escape sequence, which is a timed obstacle course with the presurre of a deadly hazard forcing you to move. These sequences are the bosses of the game and there will be some situations where the game with through an unfamiliar concept at you and expect you to manage it. Often these screwballs are instant death and require you to restart the escape from the very start. This results in several near controller throwing moments and several expletives and "What am I supposed to do?" moments. There is a One Life mode where you are not permitted to die at all and I cannot imagine the task of completing all three dungeons on one life.
In spite of the frustration of some of the sections, Ori and the Blind Forest is a very enjoyable platformer with beautiful artwork, music, and a sweet, short story.

I haven't finished this game yet, I'm only on night four. However, that's technically enough of it for me to be able to do a review... or so, I'd like to think. Anyway, this isn't a bad game. I personally enjoy it for what it is and would even reccomend it to anyone who is a fan of "Five Nights at Freddy's", or anyone who wants to play it. With that being said, this game (at least, with me) is not excluded from a few "gripes" that I have with it. My "problems", if you would like to call them that, are as follows:
1. Thank you Scott for implementing a quote on quote "checkpoint system", so us players don't have to restart the night (unless you quit and exit the game) whenever we fail at something. Unfortunately, here's where the first issue is. Playing the game (and putting up with it for this long), I feel as if there maybe isn't enough of these "checkpoints" and that they are not placed in a more "appropriate" place and/or manner. In example, you'll get through a long trek through the vents, only to end up with a somewhat difficult task (Funtime Freddy, night two, anyone?), fail it, and then have to go through the simple, but, excruciatingly long trek all over again. In fact, you'll probably end up doing the same two things, over and over again, until you get it right.
2. Speaking of the long treks through the vents... yes, these "minigames" are extremely simple and I had barely any issue with them. It's not these sections of the game themselves that bother me, it's how long and how overtly tedious they are. Crawling through the vents in this game takes a long time, a lot of time, and a lot of patience. And as I stated in point NO.1, having to go through these multiple times is kind of agonizing, This, yet again, is why point NO.1 exists. I'm not trying to make myself sound impatient but, hopefully, you all catch my drift. I also found (might of been just me) that sometimes, when I would try out these sections, the "rules" the game gave you just wouldn't work. I started the vent crawl with Funtime Foxy, immediately flashed the beacon, and... immediate death. Yeah... Funtime Foxy is only supposed to "get" you whenever you move, which I didn't...Moving on.
3. After completing your gruelling trek thorugh a vent, you'll end up in a room which features the main minigame that you are supposed to complete. *Sigh* Just like the vent crawls, these games are easy to understand and by all means aren't (and/or shouldn't) be hard. Yet again, the "problem" is that they are more "tedious" and somewhat complicated, then they are outright "difficult". Night two and night three come to mind and funnily enough, my most rage inducing moments were with Funtime Freddy. I am not the only one who has had difficulty with these and I continue to not be the only one.
4. There is no "surefire way" to do things and/or complete your tasks. I've already breifly explained this in point NO.2 but, I'll of course, explain it further. What I mean is that, your given a simple set of instructions, the game literally tells you what to do, and sometimes... that's wrong. You'll figure out a "method", something that works and gets you close to vitory, and then, BOOM! You fail. You'll try the method again, since it worked the last time, only for it to suddenly stop working on your second time around. So, basically, everything is inconsistent and downright unpredictable... which I guess "works", especially with this being a horror game, but, it does make everything rage inducing. You can have unpredictable A.I. or whatever it is, but, there has to be somewhat of a "pattern". Otherwise, the player is not going to be able to progress. This made looking up a guide useless, as the methods I tried from said guide didn't work for me. It was literally a case of "what works for one person, does not or will not work for another". So, basically, you "win" by pure chance and luck, which feels awesome... but, it also makes me angry.
Regardless of these so called "flaws", I still intend to finish the game and I am very much willing to forgive said issues.

I had my doubts about this game after seeing a swapping of hands for developers and the metacritic scores, in comparison to the previous games (not that the metacritic was all that bad, its just lower than the previous titles.), but after picking this game up for $7.50, I can say that I got my money's worth and left satisfied. Although we saw the departure of Rockysteady on this title, presumably because Arkham Knight is quite resource consuming, WB Studios stepped in and did a fair job. They kept the good stuff (combat, open world, gadgets) and added a few nice features. Were you not aware of the change in studios, the only differences that might alert you to the fact would be the WB Studios logos and the new look interface. Otherwise, this game plays very much like the previous Arkham games. In my opinion, thats a good thing because it signals the developers knew what worked and didn't try to butcher it. For others, that is the inherit problem with this game; the fact that it is pretty much a clone of Arkham City. Were it not for a few changes, this game would be an exact clone. I really didn't have too much of a problem with this, seeing as its only the 3rd game in the installment and I'm not quite sick of doing the same thing over and over again yet. While its true that there isn't much innovation here, I'm glad that the new developers stuck with a route that worked and not one that tarnished the series. For that, we should all be proud.
The story in this game is fits well in the universe and unravels the beginnings of several overarching plot points in the series, mainly the beginning of the Batman-Joker conflict and early versions of Harley Quinn before she goes evil, for example. On that note, it was interesting to see the beginnings. Sure, they could have been fleshed out a bit more, but I'm not complaining. The story was good until the end, and I really didn't have any qualms about it. Like I said, gameplay is more or less the same, save for a few reskinned gadgets with slightly different (although still true to core functionality) uses, as well as some new enemies to fight. Combat is the same, with perhaps some new moves down the line when you level-up. The world is still open, and it plays very similar to Arkham City with a myriad of things to do. One thing I really liked, however, is they definitely fleshed out the detective mode here. While its still a very minor part of the game, you can analyze the crime scenes more by reanacting the crime and investigating more clues to solve the crime. Sure it holds your hand and it doesn't feel like it should, but its a welcomed addition that was missing from Arkham City that made me happy to see. In addition, the boss fights have been improved in my opinion, and overall, were a bit more satisfying than the previous game.
This game is not free of issues, however. I found that the counter key/button was only responsive 75%-80% of the time, causing large fights (10+ enemies) or counter heavy battles to be frustrating at times, as the counters would just not work at all some of the times. This also applied to ground takedowns. It just seemed like the key/button wasn't registering for me at times. There are also some combat bugs, such as enemies flying off the screen when hit or enemies clipping into buildings (still fightable even if you couldn't see them), but nothing gamebreaking here. A major issue, however, is the crashing. It shares a similar crashing issue with Arkham City. While this game crashing didn't seem to lock up my PC, it did seem to crash more often than the last game. I'd say it crashed once every 3-4 hours, and sometimes more often.
If you are looking for a new Batman game that innovates the series, you'll have to look elsewhere, but if you are looking for a solid and faithful prequel to the last two games, look no further. While this game is nowhere near perfect thanks to some bugs and such, it is a game worth playing and is enjoyable from start to finish. Recommened. 8.5/10

As a YouTuber, I have a love-hate relationship with this game. On one hand: it's new, unique, and definitely interesting, while also staying true to the Fnaf brand; on the other hand, this game is
for commentators, and is very difficult to go back and re-play when finished.
It's painfully obvious that the more games Scott makes, the better at everything he gets. The first four games were fantastically beautiful, but this game is on a whole new level of graphic fidelity. The models just seem to be more detailed and a higher-quality, and the 3d feels much more real and engaging than past games. Sound detail, as always, is fantastic, as well. There are small details placed throughout the game that just draw you into the game and convince you that much more that you are the protagonist.
The voices were also wonderfully recorded, and the actors were brilliant. I'm not sure how Scott found the people who voiced in this game, but he did a
good job at finding the right people for the job. It's clear to tell that it payed off, especially for a series that traditionally has very minimalistic speaking in it. The only downfall of the voices, which were necessary due to the sheer amount of tutorials necessary to learn to play properly, is that there was
too much talking. Too much time was spent trying to teach the player to play instead of letting them be by themselves and feel that aloneness that horror games are so famous for.
The speaking also hurts YouTubers like myself when trying to play the game. Naturally, we
to let the game say what it has to say, but whenever we're presented with something new or interesting, we're not really allowed to react because the game does it for us, and it doesn't give us a chance to speak for several minutes unless we talk over the game, which everyone hates. If you want to see what I'm talking about, you can check out my video on Sister Location linked below.
This not only hurts the replayability, because many people don't like to sit through the same-old-same-old multiple times, but it also hurts the game on YouTube viewership. One of the reasons the game became so popular was because of it's vast success on YouTube. The game was easy to watch, and many people watched from dozens of YouTuber's perspective because there was so much blank-space it allowed each YouTuber to be themselves and react how they were going to react, and that was the fun part. Now, with all the talking, no body wants to watch dozens of different people's perspectives because half, if not all, of the video is the game talking, and, like I said, nobody wants to listen to that multiple times.
Also, because half the game is spent with a voice alongside you, the game just seems less scary, and it doesn't help that they're cracking jokes and trying to be funny the whole time, either. It almost seems like Scott gave up on making it scary, and just decided they would be fun and whimsical. Personally, I'm not a fan of it, however because they were done so well, it isn't the worst thing the game could have done.
While Sister Location takes a brave new step in the right direction for Scott and the Fnaf series, it also takes a step backwards in a few ways. For one, Sister Location is based on a series of steps in order to beat a night, which is vastly different than the traditional "survive until 6am" that every other game in the series has adopted. While an interesting new idea, that is
by any means bad, I'm not sure it's the right approach for this kind of game. Maybe I'm a traditionalist who enjoys the original, but I honestly think that this removes a piece of the horror aspect out of it. For example, in the previous games sat huddled in a chair with nothing but a security monitor and a flashlight to fend off the demons coming your way. You were almost completely helpless, hoping with the very fiber of your being they stay away for just a few seconds longer. By adopting this new, task-based system, it gives the players more control over what's going on around them. They can leave the room and roam the building with the animatronics lurking in the darkness. It removes a large aspect of what makes games scary: helplessness, the feeling there is nothing they can do to fight the enemy.
Second, there are too many things to do in the game. Now, initially, this may not seem like a bad thing at all; most people
having more to do, but the essence is Fnaf is simple: here are two or three tools to help you -- don't die. The game was simple, easy, and still progressed in difficulty without adding
more mechanics. By adding in the extra mechanics,
changing them every night, it forces the game to hold your hand through countless tutorials so you understand what's going on
. Doing it for one night is ok, pushing it in some cases, but it's fine so long as we get the solice of perfecting our new-found skills throughout the other nights, but this game does do that. It's constantly changing on what you need to know and what you have to do to beat the night, and that hurts the game.
I loved having simple mechanics that progressed in difficulty, and I dislike the task-based system that's replaced every night. The old game was so fun, not because it was scary, I mean, after a while it got predictable and not very scary. It was fun because it was a
. It was nearly impossible to beat the game, especially the final night, and it was awesome trying to take on the challenge of beating it, and those who did were hailed as
and masters of the game that very few could accomplish. Now, it's just different. Not necessarily worse, but different. It removes almost every element that made the old games
and replaced them with something that was different and unique (which is good...sometimes). It's almost like it was systematically designed to be a
different type of game, and maybe that's what he was going for! Maybe he thought a complete overhaul of the game (besides the story, one of the best parts) was necessary to keep the momentum moving forward. Maybe that's why it's called Sister Location and not Fnaf 5.
It's hard to say what Scott's goal was in the development of this game, but all I can tell you is
! It has to be treated as a completely different game, because that's what it is. If you come in wanting another game that's
like the others, this is
where you'll find it. That is not a bad thing, in fact that can be a very good thing. This game is not bad at all, it's not phenomenal in my book, but I still had a ton of fun playing even with all the changes, good and bad.
While I have criticized this game fairly heavily, I hope you can see that I do actually care about this game, and the series as a whole. I
recommend this game to horror fans, and even Fnaf fans, because it really is a fantastic game. If you're looking for something interesting, something completely new and unique, you'll have a great time playing, I can promise you that. And even if you were looking forward to another copy-and-paste of the same old game with slightly different mechanics, this isn't the game you thought it would be, but it's
worth playing, and I know you'll have fun, too. The game keeps true to it's lore, and you'll like the fun minigames that are similar to some of the other games in the series. You'll have fun, maybe even get a few scares in, but just know: it's not the same as before.

The introduction teaches you about the world
extensive voiceover, and makes you care about two characters in less than two minutes. It also introduces the game's major villain with a plausible explanation for the villain's actions. The first stages teach you all the basics of how to play by adding new elements one-by-one, ensuring you're never challenged beyond what you're capable of doing, but aren't bored with too-easy tasks.
The middle section of the story focuses on exploration and the changes happening in the world because of your character's actions, which gives the player time to enjoy being exposed to all of the wonderful level art and musical themes. These changes are told through the dramas of minor characters in the story, fleshing out the world for the player to appreciate. Mechanically, players are given more and more powers and puzzles that require combining them, requiring a demonstration of mastery of the game's basic concepts. Each level typically focuses on twisting or changing one of those basic concepts (gravity, ability to double-jump, etc.) which means you're kept on your toes and continue learning new techniques in a challenging environment.
The last section of the story focuses on the relationship between the villian, the villain's objective and motivations, and the consequences for the world and the characters in it. Levels become stricter, as players have had several hours with the game at this point and are skilled in most of the basic concepts and their combinations. Happily, challenge ramps up just as the motive drive of the story pushes a player to want to complete the game and see the narrative through to the end.
The ending and epilogue make sense, are emotionally charged, provide closure to the story, and will absolutely leave you saying 'Well... that was one of the best games I've ever played."
The story is perfectly paced. The music perfectly supports the action of the world. The art direction is phenomenal throughout. Animation and creature design is top notch. The characters are believable, likable, relatable, and unique. The mechanics are ridiculously well designed. In short, measure all other platformers by standards gleaned from Ori's story, design, art direction, and philosophy.
Also, write a thank-you note to Moon Studios for spending their lives making this masterpiece.

One of the best and most beautiful 2D games ever made, expanded and with one of its only two notable faults fixed - namely you can now fully backtrack with no areas being permanently blocked off.  If you have even a passing interest in Metroidvanias and somehow didn't play Ori and the Blind Forest the first time it hit the market, you should pick this up.
For existing owners, I would say if you had any intention of replaying Ori at some point, it's certainly worth picking up the Definitive Edition at the discounted price.  Is it worth buying if you didn't already intend to replay the game?  Eh, probably not.  The new areas and abilities are cool, but the game isn't radically different - nor would I expect it to be.  If for some reason you weren't enthralled with the original release, this one won't change your opinion.  If, however, you loved the original, you'll find the Definitive Edition makes it even better without introducing any downsides whatsoever; improvements only.

I've finished this game twice so far and let me tell you this; if you're a fan of good and fluid platforming like Super Meat Boy (or the old days of 2D Super Mario on the SNES or NES), this game deserves a spot in your library without a doubt. It has one of the best platforming in years I'd wager. Along with level designs that make great use of Ori's abilities (and how well animated Ori is), moving around and exploring have never felt more satisfying.
However, and this is entirely my opinion, if you're feeling for a more Metroidvania game with a fleshed out combat system or deeper RPG mechanics, this game does neither of those. The combat mechanics still fulfill their purpose, but it can be somewhat mindless as your means of offense is to only repeatedly press a button to kill your enemies with little to no strategy as your projectiles automatically homes onto an enemy and pulling off a charged attack from time to time.
The great piece of a golden nugget that this game can offer is a variety of ways to finish off your enemies by using the environment to your advantage. Additionally, you'll unlock more abilities to maneuver around the gorgeous world, allowing exploration to be fun, rewarding and less repetitive. The light RPG mechanic, albeit simplistic, works wondefully well as the abilities and upgrades you unlock have a great synergy with one another and are well balanced, making it so that there's no ability or upgrade that is outright useless or overpowered. This game's story is the weakest link, but if anything, it gives you just the right amount of motivation to continue playing while you're engrossed by the beautiful soundtrack, only to realize that you've already reached the end.
All in all, it's a wonderful game (with slightly lacking combat) and I enjoyed it thoroughly so play it now, you dork.

Oddly enough, this game got me into the Metroidvania genre. It is seemingly punishing at times, and could really do with an option to continue playing after completing a story, but all in all you'll be hard pressed to find a game that achieves so much of what it set out to do.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a beautiful Metroidvania style platformer. The story is very concise and focused with a small cast of characters. The art in the game has a wonderful painted picture feel and the character designs feel like something out of a Studio Ghibli film. The soundtrack is awesome and very evocative and was my first real introduction to the game and contains a memorable melody that keeps it in your head.
Gameplay involves having a small set of abilities that slowly grows the further you explore the game. Unfortunately, some directions to progress are not fully clear and I had to consult a guide early on to learn what I *could* climb onto. The player is free to explore regions once they have the minimum abilities necessary to get past the initial obstacles and in some cases you will feel like you completed puzzles earlier than the game intended. This is especially the case if you acquire the new abilities that were introduced in the Definitive Edition, which can trivialize some puzzles which would be much more challenging without them (or by playing the original version.)
Sometimes the platforming and puzzles can be absolutely brutal with several traps intended to kill you immeidately or allowing for only a few mistakes. This can be frustrating as death can come swiftly and send you to the last place you saved. Fortunately, you can create save points every few minutes provided you have energy resources and are standing on a non-moving platform. Forgetting to save regularly can result in the loss of significant progress, especially if you are out looking for collectibles and secrets.
While there are sometimes enemy rooms where you have to defeat all the enemies before you can progress, there aren't any true bosses per se. Progress is centred around gathering abilities and then using them in the three 'dungeons' in the game which require you to apply things you've learned in the overworld map and then adds an additional twist - like teleporters or gravity shifts. These culminate in an escape sequence, which is a timed obstacle course with the presurre of a deadly hazard forcing you to move. These sequences are the bosses of the game and there will be some situations where the game with through an unfamiliar concept at you and expect you to manage it. Often these screwballs are instant death and require you to restart the escape from the very start. This results in several near controller throwing moments and several expletives and "What am I supposed to do?" moments. There is a One Life mode where you are not permitted to die at all and I cannot imagine the task of completing all three dungeons on one life.
In spite of the frustration of some of the sections, Ori and the Blind Forest is a very enjoyable platformer with beautiful artwork, music, and a sweet, short story.

Yes, there are unlockable levels and characters, but repeating levels gets monotonous pretty quickly (especially with how unvaryingly basic most of the gameplay is), and the game gives you a lot more incentive to play meatboy over anyone else, outright forcing you for many of the levels such as the warp zones, bosses, and extra world.
Additionally, this was designed with a gamepad in mind. You may want to avoid this if all you have accessible to you is a keyboard.
One of the best platformers in recent years. Don't let the much vaunted difficulty turn you off. This game is worth the time you put into it.

Twin Bros has this old school 8-bit style graphics that in someway takes you back to the old days. It is a puzzle platformer where you control 2 brothers at the same time. It is rather difficult at times but also fun. Some puzzles can be solved using different techniques (as far as I can tell). The puzzles include jumping from platforms to platforms, dodging turrets, passing through what seems to be electric fences, avoiding traps that disables the twins, and more.
The goal in each level is to allow the twins to enter a door at the same time which means you have to time everything so that they end up together. Take note that every puzzle has this time limit in the form of the twin's health bar that decreases over time or when you are damaged by electricity, turrets, etc.
Controlling the brothers is simple, W/Space/Up for jumping and A,D/Left,Right for moving sideways. When you move one of the brother the other also moves but the other one moves invertedly in respect to the other.
The music for the game fits the puzzle aspect of the game and also captures the challenge.
The game's presentation is good in my book.
The only draw back in this game is that sometimes when I press jump, the other brother doesn't jump or they both don't jump. This kinda messes things up especially when the game has a sort of time limit. Also, sometimes it feels like its becoming repetitive but after a few levels that feeling will be gone and in exchange becomes frustration due to not being able to finish a level but that is part of the charisma of a puzzle game.
In conclusion, The game is well made with only a few draw back (not even sure if it is a flaw or I just don't understand the mechanics that well yet.) For the price though, I think it could be lower so that more players can be enticed by the game but not too low though because the game is great and the developers deserve some kind of reward.
So In a scale of 1-5, I'll give TWIN BROS a 3/5.

Very well made! I've played several games in this genre (zachtronics games and more), but this is the first one I've played that is pure hardware and handles timing well. Most of the games invovling wiring hardware have the concept of calculation ticks (near instant) and state ticks (usually triggered by all chips waiting). But this game gets the division a little bit more realistic which is just enough to add a fun and interesting challenge.
Here you have long clock ticks corresponding to state, and then shorter calculation ticks. So not too different from other games on the surface, BUT different chips take different amounts of time to calculate and the clock tick is a variable number of calculation ticks. It feels like setting up a clock pin to be the maximum time for all signals to propagate from one latch to another in a processor (and it basically is!). It's not 100% realistic, but it was a lot of fun and more fufilling than some other games I've played in the past.
Highly Recommended :D

You also find jigsaw pieces throughout and piece some of your world back together on the title screen after each major area.
There are sliding, jigsaw and pipe puzzles and other minor brainteasers. The best thing I can say about the game is it looks very nice and is charming, the worst that it leaves you feeling you accomplished very little, if anything at all.

It's very pretty, and it starts out strong, but tedium and repetiition set in when each chapter repeats the theme of finding an array of hidden objects to first reassemble and then work your way through proper puzzles, with a few reflex tests thrown in on a few occasions. Each chapter ends with you literally putting the tiny world back together with twenty-five (!) puzzle pieces painstakingly found in the last world. Unfortunately a good third of the jigsaw is lightly cloudy or starry space, which makes many of the sky pieces nearly identical to a glance.
There's a built-in puzzle-spotter, which is obnoxious. To charge it for a single activation, you have to click thirty (30!) small, flying insects, which is simply punitive. There are also 'solutions' available for each puzzle, but be aware that many are reversed, incomplete, or actually wrong.
The game has maybe two hours worth of play. A tiny amount of time for a tiny bang, I suppose.

My initial impressions of this game were very positive. My current impressions of this game: still positive! This is a stylized, fun game, with very smooth controls, great artstyle, atmospheric music, ambiguous goals (I mean that in a positive way), and just enough addictive quality to keep you playing. The premise of this game is simple; relaxing, even. But what you'll soon fine is that this game can get quite hectic at times, making you go from "ahh" to "AHH!".
This game is still in development, and with the newest update, you can tell it's further along the lines of "completion" than "development". There are lots of great components to this game, that at first felt a bit disjointed, but as it's getting updated, everything is blending in together nicely. So I'm confident that the finished product will feel as cohesive as the dev intends.
So what is Cosmochoria? At a glance, you're a naked astronaut, terraforming - gliding from planet to planet, planting seeds and buildings and mapping out a very foreign universe. Baddies show up to stop you and you blast them away with your laser. However, as the game progresses, as you unlock more, you'll find that there's more depth to it than that. You're mapping out a universe. Dodging enemies while terraforming. And there's always the sense of an impending boss fight coming up. You have to balance offense and defensive tactics, depending on the situation. Sometimes enemies show up steadily, sometimes not at all, sometimes 4 pop up with no warning. Balancing that with what to build in that moment (plant or structure) keeps things fresh.
Overall, the game is fun as is, but coming together nicely!
My only minor gripes with the game, as of now, are that some of the power ups, feel a tad underpowered. And that sometimes getting hit will power down your gun.
[Sugggestions]
The power down aspect: I still think this is too punishing. Especially if it happens in the midst of a boss fight. I would suggest that the power down is timed to like... 30 seconds or so. This way, you're still punished for being hit, but you can also adapt to it. It makes fights more situational, and not as dire. Like, if I accidentally get powered down twice and a boss shows up, I know that I don't have much of a chance. However, if that happens but it's timed... I know I cna just run and hide for a bit or focus on dodging attacks and play more defensively until I'm back to full strength. It could add another layer to combat.
Compass/Map: I LOVE this very necessary addition. Although I suspect it was here, pre-update, and I just never thought to click the compass in order to open the map. For familiar design sake, maybe the map can benefit from being in the top right corner - only because that's where it is almost every game, and I'm just used to glancing up/right to get my bearings. But this is a very very loose suggestion because I got used to it almost immediately
Mapping: This is another loose suggestion. The ability to name planets, or mark certain ones, would be beneficial. That way you can look at the map and get your bearings, or if you have to escape from danger you know to go to planet X because you remember putting turrets down there and such. It could really flesh out the universe map mechanic, and help the player feel like they're contributing more to really discovering/fixing this universe.
Save feature: sometimes games go on longer than I'd like, but I'm really satisfied with my progress and don't want to suicide. On the other hand... that could be defeating the purpose behind the game concept. So take this suggestion lightly too.

Cosmochoria is a new action-adventure/strategy title with roguelike elements from developer Nate Schmold in which you, as the astronaut Cosmo, must breathe new life into a lifeless galaxy by planting seeds and fending off aliens.  Armed with nothing more than a laser blaster and a jetpack, (seriously, that's it, our little hero is buck naked) your task seems daunting at first, but all doubt washes away once you dive into the game and start shooting aliens and planting trees.
One of the first few things you'll notice is that Cosmochoria is by-and-large an homage to old-school games like Donkey Kong and Asteroids, complete with high scores and tons of pew-pew goodness.  The gameplay recalls a time when action games were one of the most popular games available.  To its credit, Cosmochoria goes a bit deeper than that.  Movement is done with the WSAD keys, you fire with the left mouse button and use your jetpack with the right button, and the S key brings up the action menu, from which you plant seeds and build structures.  When you start a new game, the first thing you'll see is the upgrade screen, where you can purchase things like bonuses and new equipment, as well as acquire new structures such as defense towers and force fields.  You make these purchases with crystals that are dropped by enemies, and they can come in real handy, as sometimes you will be faced with alien creatures and spaceships coming from all directions.  At some point, a boss creature will appear, with a big, red life bar as long as the screen.  These boss battles can be pretty tough, especially when you're first starting out and upgrades are sparse.  However, it's absolutely worth the struggle, as bosses tend to drop a plethora of crystals.
I mentioned earlier that Cosmochoria has rogue-lite elements.  The game is challenging, but not in a way that's really punishing.  When you die (and you will, a lot), you lose all of your progress, but keep your crystals to spend in the upgrade shop.  Some of the items in the shop include new equipment, extra health, and a mini-map.  The mini-map is a huge help, as it will help you keep track of what planets you have saved.  As you start to plant seeds and allow them to fully grow into trees and other plants, the color will return to the planet.  Your progress here is marked by a heart in the center of the planet.  Once the heart meter fills up, you have saved that planet and can move on to the next one.  As an added perk, saved planets can actually heal you as well, as long as the heart meter isn't empty.  More trees means more life to give.  I couldn't tell if the planet can regress once it's been saved, but I'd imagine that isn't a feature that's being considered as it would equal a ton of micromanaging.
Graphically, Cosmochoria is very cute and colorful.  The game is drawn with a hand-crafted 2D vector style of illustration, and while there isn't a lot of variety to the enemies at this stage, these creatures are at least presented in different color palettes to present a sense of variety, although some of them could also benefit from some added animation.  All in all, the game is very sharp and pretty, if simple.  The sound is excellent even this early in development.  Minimal sound design is employed, but the sounds of gunshots, revived planets, and your jetpack sound just right.  The music is electronic-based, and while it is quite catchy, it could also use more variety.
You could play this game until the cows come home, and far beyond that.  Unlocking every upgrade will take you hours upon hours, and since the world is randomly generated every time you start new, nothing is ever the same with each play.  Completing a "perfect" game will take you weeks, if not much longer.  For the high-score nerds, this game also features integrated leaderboards, so that you can compare your stats with other players as well as your friends.  There are a lot of updates being planned for this game, and it could take several months before it's even remotely complete.  However, what's already available is very much in a playable state.  I haven't really encountered any major bugs.  All in all, this game is pretty fun.  Progression starts out slow, but by slowly farming a few crystals with every playthrough, you'll be able to afford a nice upgrade in no time.  Once you do have a few upgrades under your non-existent belt, things will pick up.  Perhaps a bit of tweaking to make these upgrades more affordable could help, but it's not a huge deal.  Developer Nate Schmold is working very closely with the community to make this game as good as it can possibly be, and he's open to pretty much anything.  Overall, this game is enjoyable even in its current state, and it gets a big thumbs up from me.

There is a lack of story unfolding unfortunately, unlike Absolution - for example. The story remains completely unresolved at the end and focus will probably shift towards Season 2. I couldn't really make up what the story was, so I had to replay all of the cutscenes, which you can thankfully do. That, made more sense to me. It is really interesting and the way Season 2 will unfold makes me very excited! The story takes around 9 hours to beat, so it is quite short. However there is a lot of side stuff to do, which I will get onto.
If you were to shoot your way through the levels... good luck. Agent 47 barely takes a few hits until he dies, and therefore the gunner approach is quite numbed. I do wish there was an option to play things, a little less stealthy since you do pretty much do very similar things throughout the episodes. There certainly is replayability, which are both the Contracts - which are designed by players and where you need to perform and achieve certain requirements in order to complete the level. There are also other missions like some side sniper missions. However, I disliked how unappealing the menu was. It CERTAINLY takes some time to figure things out. From my point of view, I think it looks a little bit more user-friendly for a console. Not the worst, but could be better.
Is the PC port any good? Well, that is completely subjective. I am running the game at medium settings (MSI GTX 960 2GB, Intel Core i5 4590, 8gb RAM) and it runs in the mid 40s (average 47fps... see what I did there ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) for real though). You see, in this game, unless you take the completely stupid way of killing everyone with a loud♥♥♥♥♥gun like an idiot, the framerate will be of NO concern. Hell, even 30fps was fine in this game. Everything is just really slow paced, and you have to observe your environment a lot. High framerate is required in fast games, such as Counter Strike and Grand Theft Auto, and not in this one. Even if your game doesn't run at 60fps, believe me, don't worry. It works absolutely fine. However, 60fps would have been nice. I have definitely played better looking games at a higher framerate. However, the crowds are phenomenally large.
I haven't beaten it Escalation yet but I have taken a glimpse of the large and quite frustratingly rewarding world of Hitman. Yes, believe me, it is frustrating. However, the different approaches certainly add replay value, and the game is a heap-load better because of it. Just remember to feel like you are IN the world. And do things how you would... do them in real life. I definitely recommend this game, despite of the DRM - which hasn't troubled me (yet).

I am a bit shocked at the amount of recent negative reviews for HITMAN. When I first began playing it, I was uncertain what to feel, except that I didn't like the episodic nature of the game. I've changed my mind about that; it works well after all.
Most people are complaining about the DRM and need to be online to reap the benefits of the full experience, but this is absolutely nothing new in gaming. Ubisoft has been doing it since Splinter Cell: Conviction. EA has done it with its Origin, wanna-be Steam effort also. I have lost my connection a few times playing HITMAN, but have always gotten it back with no progress lost.
I might be one of the few people on planet Earth who actually liked Absolution, despite it's many annoyances (primarily the ridiculous disguise system which might as well not have existed at all). To me, however, it brought the cover system to the game, and that was a much needed feature for this type of experience.
There are definitely some problems, foremost of which, to me, is that the "optional" features in Contracts, featured missions, and Escalations, are really not optional at all; If you ignore these requirements, you get no points for completing the mission target(s) objective(s). I am not a guy to care much about points frankly, but I do think this would be very simple to fix, so why not do so.
You will need a solid rig to enjoy it fully; of that there is little doubt. The amount of NPCs and the huge nature of gorgeous locations simply requires a strong system. Anyone who has played Absolution will remember the first "level" in the game, with a billion NPCs around. Many levels in HITMAN are like that constantly, only more open. The Glacier engine was built for this purpose, and works well for it, provided you have a solid system.
The Contracts mode seems much better (aside from the aforementioned issue of "optional" requirements) than it was in Absolution. I wish more than anything that the Hitman franchise would add an online mode which is multiplayer. There are many ways to do this, so I find it interesting it hasn't found its way in to the game yet. However, I am happy to see the Contracts mode so improved.
Elusive Targets are an absolute treat! They spring up as new missions, and are incredibly different from anything else mission-wise. I can't believe I'm saying this, but perhaps it could be improved if they made it so exiting under pressure would kill the opportunity. Not sure though, since a drop out of the internet or other could really cause some anger!
This game is a very solid addition to the long loved Hitman series, and I can do nothing but recommend it. There are few things in gaming life better, for instance, than blowing up a person with a little rubber ducky.
Thumbs up!

I bought this game during a summer sale I believe, I bought it as a joke. I thought, "Hey, this game looks stupid, but I'll buy it since it's cheap and I can say I've got a truck simulator!" Little did I know this would sortly lead to a spiral that nearly had my family and friends write me off as dead. It certainly doesn't look it, but this game is highly addictive.
You boot up the game, make your profile, then you start doing little "Quick Jobs" using another companies trucks to move around cargo, but eventually you will decide you want your own truck, knowing it'll lead to more cash. A while later you will be buying a new garage, a truck, and hiring a driver for that truck. After that you just keep buying more trucks, hiring more drivers, and buying more garages across Europe, creating a trucking empire.
What makes this game addictive is the grind. It is a grind really, you keep doing the same thing, progressively longer and better, making progress in the game. You may be bored with the game, but once you finish a delivery you'll want to do another one, why? Because that truck you want is only another €3000 away and you really want it.
I'd say that if you like driving simulators you should definitely give it a shot. But if you don't, maybe you should look into the game more, do research, maybe even play the demo, give it a chance, you may actually like it. I honestly hated the idea of playing a truck simulator before I played it, but now I love it.

Arkham Origins is another valued contribution to the Arkham series.  It is set as a prequel to the prior two games.
However, it does suffer majorly from bugs.  This will show up with flying and some of the functionality of the downloadable content.  For instance, sometimes when I glide, Batman will shake and will glide up.  If using an alternate Batsuit, you cannot interrogate suspects.  There are a few other minor instances, but those are big ones.
Past that, I felt it was a great game.  It had elements of Batman: Year One and Knightfall in it.  The gameplay was fun.  The addition of the Batplane to transport me to checkpoints in the city really made things nicer.  Not having to fly everywhere like Arkham City was bliss.  The story was mostly straightforward, but it's hard to do twists for this game when we know what's coming from the prior games.
The combat system was modified slightly, adding characters that can counter your attacks.  A great contribution in my opinion.  Were we to presume that no one with any martial arts experience would be hired to fight Batman?
The Riddler is there in his usual likeable and annoying self.  Somehow he's managed to leave things everywhere for us to find.  Again.  A word of advice to those people who do get the game.  Don't run around in Detective Vision all the time.  You'll miss out on all the work they put into the game.
The boss fights take figuring out.  Don't be afraid to make backups and restart.
Have fun and knock yourself out.  Though I really recommend knocking villains out, it's up to you.

I recently finished Arkham Origins after purchasing it on the Steam sale and found that despite claims of game breaking bugs in the forums, I only encountered one major bug throughout my 15 hours of play, which did not stop me from beating the game or any of the side missions. Those who enjoyed Arkham City and would like more of the excellent combat and stealth mechanics from that game will be pleased to know that they'll get plenty of that here, but also that nothing significant has been added to either gameplay type. A couple new enemy types have been added, and players can unlock shock gloves that let you beat up foes more abley, while a new gadget can create a permanent tightrope in the environment, replacing the line launcher from the previous games. Both the gloves and the remote batclaw are fun new additions but those who value story canon in their games will almost certainly wonder why Batman would ever get rid of these upgrades once he found them.
Meanwhile the story is good with some surprising twists. This is NOT a Batman Origin story or an Akrham Asylum origin story though. You do get insight into the origins of some of the characters to an extent, but in most of those cases (like Joker or Gordon or Harly) they are origin stories that have been told countless times elsewhere. All told the story is fine and goes in some directions I didn't expect based on the marketing, but a lot of it feels like a retread of the recent Christopher Nolan films with many elements lifted almost directly from CW's Arrow TV show.
My main issue with Arkham Origins, though, is not the lack of new mechanics or the familiarity of the story, but how uninspired the missions are. In Arkham City there were certainly collectables but most side missions featured some sort of unqiue gameplay or at least a unique setup. Here all but a couple side missions are collectables. Enigma (not yet The Riddler) has you doing your normal collectathons, although you must now first take out a tower to unlock an area of the city similar to any of Ubisoft's open world games. There is a distinct lack of creative set-pieces in the side missions, though. The Mad Hatter makes a return but his level is more frustrating and confusing than disturbing and weird like his mission in the previous game or Scarecrow's levels in Asylum. At one point in Wonderland I spent 10 minutes trying to decipher a puzzle only to somehow solve it without doing anything differently than I had been doing the rest of the time. The Mad Hatter congratulated me on solving the puzzle, except if he hadn't said anything I wouldn't have even known I had solved it.
The main story missions have unique elements to them but they aren't nearly as interesting as missions in previous games. Penguin's hideout isn't guarded by a shark and you don't have to get around a freeze gun to take Penguin out at the end. Of the 8 assassins most are just standard enemies with more health. There is a reason you have likely never heard of Copperhead, Shiva, Electrocutioner or Firefly. They just aren't very interesting. And we've fought Bane, Killer Croc, and Deadshot in previous games. Deathstroke is the most interesting of the bunch but outside of that this rogue gallery pales in comparison with Batman's usual lineup who are mostly MIA in this game. Penguin and Joker are really the only two A listers on display, and Penguin has a very minor role. Black Mask, Anarky, and the others are bottom of the barrel villains who even Batman fans are likely unfamiliar with or only familiar with in passing. The whole game simply lacks the inspiration and creativity of previous entries.
Arkham Origins isn't broken like many would have you believe. Your mileage will vary but from my experience, while not super polished, the game works. There are visual glitches aplenty, as well as odd camera angles and the like. But as far as my experience went the game functioned. The core Arkham mechanics are all in place as well and working just as well as in previous games. If you are just looking for more thugs to beat up and terrorize then Arkham Origins will serve you well. Even the story was surprisingly good and threw in a few unexpected twists by the end. No, in the end Arkham Origins suffers from a real lack of creative situations. The set pieces are occasionally visually impressive, but they also lack the wacky flair that makes Batman such a great comic. In a sense Origins is closer to Nolan's films in its lack of the odd, magical, and over-the-top. These villains are all largely believable people and it makes their plots feel a bit to formulaic. Without your Poison Ivey's, Two-Faces, Scarecrows, Cat-Womans, Ra's, and so on, all you have are gangsters and mercs. Those make fine videogame villains, but this is Batman, and the setting here just lacks insipiration compared to the previous entires and that leaves a game that is good, but not masterful.
So for those who simply enjoy the gameplay of this series I do recommend it, but for those who want some of that patented Batman crazy, this entry is a bit lacking in that regard, with just the Joker to hold the fort.

It has one of the best platforming in years I'd wager.
