However, and this is entirely my opinion, if you're feeling for a more Metroidvania game with a fleshed out combat system or deeper RPG mechanics, this game does neither of those. The combat mechanics still fulfill their purpose, but it can be somewhat mindless as your means of offense is to only repeatedly press a button to kill your enemies with little to no strategy as your projectiles automatically homes onto an enemy and pulling off a charged attack from time to time.
The great piece of a golden nugget that this game can offer is a variety of ways to finish off your enemies by using the environment to your advantage. Additionally, you'll unlock more abilities to maneuver around the gorgeous world, allowing exploration to be fun, rewarding and less repetitive. The light RPG mechanic, albeit simplistic, works wondefully well as the abilities and upgrades you unlock have a great synergy with one another and are well balanced, making it so that there's no ability or upgrade that is outright useless or overpowered. This game's story is the weakest link, but if anything, it gives you just the right amount of motivation to continue playing while you're engrossed by the beautiful soundtrack, only to realize that you've already reached the end.
All in all, it's a wonderful game (with slightly lacking combat) and I enjoyed it thoroughly so play it now, you dork.

Oddly enough, this game got me into the Metroidvania genre. It is seemingly punishing at times, and could really do with an option to continue playing after completing a story, but all in all you'll be hard pressed to find a game that achieves so much of what it set out to do.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a beautiful Metroidvania style platformer. The story is very concise and focused with a small cast of characters. The art in the game has a wonderful painted picture feel and the character designs feel like something out of a Studio Ghibli film. The soundtrack is awesome and very evocative and was my first real introduction to the game and contains a memorable melody that keeps it in your head.
Gameplay involves having a small set of abilities that slowly grows the further you explore the game. Unfortunately, some directions to progress are not fully clear and I had to consult a guide early on to learn what I *could* climb onto. The player is free to explore regions once they have the minimum abilities necessary to get past the initial obstacles and in some cases you will feel like you completed puzzles earlier than the game intended. This is especially the case if you acquire the new abilities that were introduced in the Definitive Edition, which can trivialize some puzzles which would be much more challenging without them (or by playing the original version.)
Sometimes the platforming and puzzles can be absolutely brutal with several traps intended to kill you immeidately or allowing for only a few mistakes. This can be frustrating as death can come swiftly and send you to the last place you saved. Fortunately, you can create save points every few minutes provided you have energy resources and are standing on a non-moving platform. Forgetting to save regularly can result in the loss of significant progress, especially if you are out looking for collectibles and secrets.
While there are sometimes enemy rooms where you have to defeat all the enemies before you can progress, there aren't any true bosses per se. Progress is centred around gathering abilities and then using them in the three 'dungeons' in the game which require you to apply things you've learned in the overworld map and then adds an additional twist - like teleporters or gravity shifts. These culminate in an escape sequence, which is a timed obstacle course with the presurre of a deadly hazard forcing you to move. These sequences are the bosses of the game and there will be some situations where the game with through an unfamiliar concept at you and expect you to manage it. Often these screwballs are instant death and require you to restart the escape from the very start. This results in several near controller throwing moments and several expletives and "What am I supposed to do?" moments. There is a One Life mode where you are not permitted to die at all and I cannot imagine the task of completing all three dungeons on one life.
In spite of the frustration of some of the sections, Ori and the Blind Forest is a very enjoyable platformer with beautiful artwork, music, and a sweet, short story.

The classic edition Ori and Blind Forest is just astonishingly perfect and I almost find no shortcoming in its every respect. Admittedly, this new definitive edition is still a great expansion. However I have to say it decreases my rating of this game from previous 10/10 to current 9.8/10 .
Definitive edition basically add two maps and two abilities to the original game. One of the new maps which requires player temporally explore the world in the darknesss is my least liked map personnally in the whole series. The original Ori provides me a smooth and fluent gaming experience however in this map players have no choice but to move step by step carefully in order to avoid potential fails. This fact, regretfully, does not fit the whole pace of this game very well.
The two new abilities are well designed. Especially the animation of grenade throwing makes the main charactor much more adorable:) But when I move on to other chapters thereafter, I find no practial use of these two new abilities. You can still finish the game by using all the abilities in the original edition. Worse still, trying to use the new acquired abilities does not even facilitate the game progress. It's like an abrupt interruption in the middle of the game and force you to learn another two abilities and then just let you continue on. In other words, the new abilities are not well integrated to the whole game overall.
Changes I do like in Definitive Edition:
1.One of the new maps. (The one other than I just mentioned.)

3.Difficulty settings. Great improvement for all the players from different skill levels.

Amazing game; equal in quality and depth to Zachtronics games. It feels like a small game, but in reality it's 15-25 hours of fun. Would recommend to anyone interested in dabbling / learning programming.
It's a little harder to pick up - the levels after the end of the game are definitely geared for programmers. It does a very good job at going step by step and introducing concepts slowly, but it doesn't hold your hand at all.
It's also a lot more true to real-life than most Zachtronics games. You could actually teach a class using this. And the final prize, if you manage to pull it off, is REALLY impressive.
My only complaint is is that the last 3 puzzles after the end of the game are very inconsistent about branch delay slots, and it's never mentioned in the instructions. Perhaps I'm missing something, but the 2nd to last level requires delay slots (and the title hints at it), while in the last level they are an error.
It can be hard to find these programming games. If you like this, look up Zachtronics (SpaceChem, Opum Magnus, Shanzen IO) and [The Sequence].

I am not a huge fan of visual programming, but this game really does it well. There's only two things I didn't really like about it: 1) it lacks the ability to compare your scores to other players (friends and global) that most other programming games provide, and 2) I feel that the palette feature would've been better if it could've worked more like a function in a traditional programming language and less like a copy/paste feature (I didn't have much interest in returning to older puzzles to improve designs, and I found that I was getting worse scores in later puzzles because I opted to copy/paste designs that included unnecessary features because it was easier than trying to Frankenstein them every step of the way and had no way to refine them across the board like what a reusable function would provide).
With that said, it is still a very challenging game that slowly eases you into logic concepts and works its way up to you building an entire CPU. You are still using low-level components provided instead of building them yourself, but as far as concepts go, you can still learn a lot along the way.

Once upon a time, there was an Ancient Great Black Wyrm who ate the Earth.  However, a little baby in a rocket-propelled basket, and some other generally forgettable NPCs escaped the calamity!  Somehow, everyone - except the baby - learned how to breathe atmospheres with lower pressure than the Armstrong limit, in order to facilitate the baby's future revenge.
No, this is not D&D; this is Cosmochoria, a simple and refreshing action-roguelike.  In this game, the goal is to reinvigorate as many worlds with life as you can!  However, enemies - who shoot lasers, for good measure - intend to stop you.  There are also gems that you need to pick up, so that when you inevitably die, you can buy supplies and important upgrades so that the next time takes a little longer to kill you.
First, each planet has its own gravity, which makes the shooter gameplay really interesting, because you have to learn to aim around the planet you're on.  Also, the gravity serves a more important purpose - being anchors for the deep space, Asteroids-esque travel you do through the title.  On a planet, you can move and jump as you'd expect.  In space, however, gravity goes away, and all of a sudden it's up to the supplies in your jetpack to nudge your velocity such that you intercept other planets.
There's a neat TD mechanic in this game, in the form of the things that bricks can create.  You can fortify a planet with towers of various kinds, which is oh-so-necessary, because every third planet you revive invariably leads to a boss fight, against at least one big, nasty Chinese dragon, who spews projectiles the way you spew...well, never mind.  Moving along.
The first parts of the game allow you to progress really fast, but for me after getting the Laser Pistol - an exceptionally useful upgrade - the game slows to a crawl for me, probably because I'm having difficulty beating the Fire Dragon.  It seems that beating bosses unlocks some upgrades, which leads to a slight balance problem between a boss standing between you and an upgrade you need to more easiliy defeat it, instead of the game giving you tools that actually help you defeat the boss.
I'd absolutely say it's worth $4.99.  I think the normal price is high for the game that you're actually getting.

I have tried to get into this game, multiple times on multiple platforms. The issue is not the plot or the characters, persay, as I have played far more immature and hilarious games. The issue is that this is a first person shooter desperately trying to be an rpg. Resource management is practically non-existant, and the weapons system is based on a number of slots that can be upgraded over time. This system requires minimal effort, and though it appears to be a central point of the game, it just seems to be a clunky, poorly-built weapons wheel. The plot takes forever to move forward, and the side missions consist purely of kill and/or collect. Pardon me, but I'll stick with my bethesda rpgs.
Still, not to grossly underrate the game, it is still a fairly fun shooter, with a few elements of an rpg that are well done, for example the skill trees and character creation systems are well made, and offer a variety of specializations and appearances. Still, I would not recommend this game, at least not to someone with similar tastes to myself.

Okay, I think it's about time I review this game again, now that it's in a more playable position. As I said before, I know I should have probably placed my last review in the form of a post on the Forum Discussions on SL, but it doesn't matter now, let's get this right under way.
I will say this right now, I think this is one of the best games Mr. Cawthon has made for quite a while, and is definitely an improvement over his last horror game; FNaF4. Actually, I don't think the word improvement is a the best way to describe this game, I believe the best way to describe it is that it's a big change. Sure, simpler words, but that's exactly how this game is, as this game is COMPLETELY different from any of the other FNaF games.
This game went beyond my expectations with what it's gameplay and overall story was going to be like. I always thought this game was going to follow the same gameplay that the original games had, then when I saw the trailer I thought it was going to be similar to a point and click adventure horror game, allowing you to look through the different areas. Not like free-roam, but something similar. But once I sat down and actually played the game, I was actually surprised with what I got. While the game still has it's point and click style roots from the previous games, it also tries it's best to imitate a linear style story, similar to Outlast, Amnesia, and Slender the Arrival. It's more like Slender, as it does rely on levels, and each one has their own objective. Without giving away gameplay, Night 1 simply gets you started, Night 2 picks things up, Night 3 frustrates you, Night 4 makes Night 3 look like a cakewalk, and Night 5 is barely challenging at all, only to serve as a way to end this game's story.
Speaking of which, I can easily say that that story-wise, this game absolutely s***s on the previous FNaF games. It's a lot more clear as to what's going on, we're being told the whole story of things, rather than it all being hidden in minigames appearing upon death (although minigames are in this game, we'll get back to that later). And for Scott's first horror game to incorporate this style of storytelling, it's really damn good. Yeah I know FNaF4 was the first game to have storytelling, but that game was very simple in what it wanted to tell, while the rest of the full details were behind our backs. The production values for this game were very good (with the exception of the fact that Scott is still using Clickteam), all the voice actors do their jobs well expressing the characters, all the scenes are very dark and creepy with the ambiance, the animatronic models are very well done (though that isn't surprising, seeing how Scott has been doing this for years), and overall the story is good... *sigh* We'll get to that in a moment.
As mentioned before, Sister Location goes by a linear storytelling experience, with each level having their own objectives, spicing up the variety. Some of my favorites were on Night 2 at Freddy's section, and Night 3 with Foxy's section. Every other level does their job well, including Night 4. Yes, I know this level is hard, but by going by the right strategy, you should be able to complete it in due time. Night 5, as I mentioned before, has no challenge whatsoever, but I think that was only because it was a filler level to end the game's story.
AND SPEAKING OF STORY
I'm going to probably get a lot of hate for this, but as much as I like this game's story, it's production values, voice actors, everything... this game's story was ruined for me by it's ending. I'm not going to spoil the ending here, that's what the internet is for. But in terms of the ending, it was just so confusing, made no sense, all with so many questions regarding what it even means, what happens after it, as well as how it effects the timeline. If you're confused by what I mean, the best I can say is to look at the ending yourself, either on the internet, or by playing the actual game itself.
Speaking of endings, that's another thing that kinda ticked me off about the game.
For those who don't know, there is an alternate ending you can acquire by going through certain procedures. And THIS is where the death minigame comes into play. At certain instances when you die, you'll end up in a minigame, playing as Baby as she feeds cupcakes to children. To gain access to the secret ending, you'll need to beat the minigame... which can take a long time to figure out, and with how many times you die on the minigame, be prepared to count the amount of times you die in the actual game before coming across the minigame again.
Now you're probably wondering, well if there's a secret ending of the game, why did you complain about the ending you get on your regular run not making sense?
Because
Now, let me clarify something. Just because I think the ending is confusing, doesn't mean I think this is a bad game, far from it. Again, I think this is one of the best games so far from Scott. But is it the best FNaF game out there? Well, I can't answer that, because in actuality, this game isn't really called FNaF: Sister Location, it's just Sister Location. Sure, Steam may say that the game is called that, but it's only to establish that it's part of the franchise, not part of the actual series. It differentiates itself from the original series, in a huge way in fact.
But yes, I still think this is a good game. Is it something I'd recommend to newcomers? Yes, and no. Yes, because as a game, it's something that players may find interesting. But in terms of story, I have to recommend the original 4 games, because no one will really understand what everything means, not even the ending. Any of them to be exact. If you plan on getting this game and are new to the franchise, start with the original 4 for the story, then continue to Sister Location. Don't be turned off by the gameplay of the originals, this game is completely different from the others. To fans, I definitely believe this is something you'll enjoy. Just hope you guys don't get triggered over the ending.

I have had the game for just over a year and this review is from a solo player who plays community servers.
The first 10 mins or so of playing.
You tend to spawn near a coastline.
You start with a rock, with the rock you gather wood from whacking trees and stone from nodes (basic example). From there you can then craft better gathering tools. Just with wood at the start you can craft a map of the island you are on, a building plan for when your ready to build, a spear for defending or for hunting, as you move around the map you are able to pick up various ground items, ore, stone, wood and food. Also pick hemp for cloth.
If you plan to start of as a solo player, it is a good idea to know how much time you can commit to the game. This will then point you in the direction of the right server for you!.
You will see many people saying its tough as a solo player, personaly I find it nice and relaxing. However i do agree that it can be tough, yet that can be down to the server you join. I only play solo servers, there are not any offical solo servers, yet there are plenty of community servers which are aimed for solo, solo/duo or trio. Community servers are owned by other Rust players, their server their rules!.
The game has offical updates on the 1st Thursday of the month, Which is known as wipe day and when the servers wipe everything you have built up has been lost. Which brings us to how much time you can commit. Again this is detail about community servers, some wipe every week, some wipe every 2 weeks and some only wipe when forced/monthly on the 1st Thursday of the month.
I always choose the monthly wipe servers as it gives me more time to enjoy the game, to build a nice base and progress at a steady pace.
If you are a new player and wish to learn the basics there are a few low population servers in the community section which will be ideal for you. From there you can always step up to a higher populated server if you wish.
The community in Rust: As a whole I find the community to be fine, again it depends on the server you are on. You can be on a high pop or low pop server and the chat/voice can be toxic or it can be chilled with banter.

A very entertaining puzzle game, especially if you're into logic puzzles. The game strikes a good balance between being a feast of recognition for those familiar with computer logic while at the same time properly explaining every concept to the player (without being condescending) and introducing everything at a pleasant pace. This allows you to always focus on the puzzle at hand, without feeling overwhelmed by the new tools you've just been handed.
There are multiple solutions to many of the puzzles and an option to try to achieve a perfect score if you're so inclined. Scores are measured in the number of modules used and in later puzzles also in the time taken to generate the desired output. Sometimes there's a fast solution with few modules, other times however you will need different solutions to achieve fewest modules and best performance separately.
The only downside is the background music, it's simplistic and on a very short loop, so it gets monotonous almost instantly. Honestly though that is the only flaw I could find with this game.
The graphics look polished and have a nice retro feel to them. And because it's 'just' a puzzle game, it will run on pretty much any system. I've even tried it on a 10 year old laptop with a 2.0 GHz Core2Duo, 4 GB RAM and GeForce 8600M GT and the game ran just fine.
After having played the demo I bought the game during the Halloween sale for € 13,49 (full price at that time was € 14,99). But if it hadn't been on sale I would have bought it as well, it's definitely worth the money!

Why buy this game?
Well, "game" is a bit of an odd word for Silicon Zeroes. If I were to describe it, I'd say it's more a series of puzzles, tied together by a loose narrative. The puzzles are based on the workings of computer / electronic hardware. If you're interested in computers from that perspective, of course the game will be of value to you.
The puzzles start out easy ("Here's how to connect components!") but then quickly ramp up in difficulty. For me, this has really been a "Stare at the problem for a while, leave it alone for a day or two, come back and make some progress, leave it alone again for a day or two" sort of process. It's a nice to have these little puzzles sitting in the back of your mind, something to ponder on the bus ride or on a coffee break. Then, when you finally solve the problem you get that "Ah ha!" moment that's so tremendously enjoyable.
Note that you don't have to be a computer genius to enjoy Silicon Zeroes. I've never taken a computer course in my life, and I come from a non-science profession. For me, this game is really a set of logic problems, with the added dimension of time (clicks). Some of the reviews suggest the game helps explain how computer hardware works - if so, fantastic! But rest assured, you can easily approach these problems with a bit of plain old critical thinking and wit.
Probably not for impatient audiences. This is not a game of instant gratification. But for the more intellectually inclined, Silicon Zeroes really provides a satisfying, fun experience.

This is a delightful game, that does quite a bit right, for an early access title it is incredibly polished. The gameplay and mechanics on show all work, and in its current state it could be a full game in itself, and shows great promise of what is to come.
This is the state I wish more EA games were in when they hit.
First of all, and the thing that made me purchase this, is the art style, which is downright lovely. Its bright, poppy, full of character and consistent aross the entire game. A lot of hard work has gone into this presentation, from the menus through to the variety of plants and alien critters.
It really looks great, very charming. I really love the way the planets change colours as you rejuvenate them, as if theyve been terraformed.
The controls are simple(WASD and two buttons, fire/jump), but hard to master, and for a while you will be reeling round in zero-g with the jetpack. That said, there is a real nice weight, and the controls are very tight.
The AI is likewise simple, but diverse in type. You will often be juggling several enemy types, whilst trying to reform a planet, it can get hectic.
Then you have tower defense thrown in there, to start with I hardly ever built towers, then the game opened up and started to make sense, and you realise they are really necessary as you progress.
The planets are basically your health packs/defense/offense. You cant take on the later enemies without flitting around using planets youve set up.
This all comes together very naturally as you progress, with a lot of 'ahhh!' moments. Nothing needs to be blatantly pointed out, because the design has been well thought out. Buy this game. Do it now!

Literally beat it within 30 min of writing this.... my take away.
Graphics:  Absolutely beautiful.  This is the apocalyptic wasteland.
Sound:  Great.  Although I wish the music was more robust and harder.
Gameplay:.......   gameplay......    game.....  play?
I bought this two years ago (just finished mind you).  I had to FORCE myself to finish it.  Because:
1.  The story was uninvolving. Your car was stolen... you then make a faster, stronger, supercar... just to get the first one back.  (Why do I want it back again?)  No real twist and turns...Everyone you meet is one dimensional & forgettable.  There's no story arc.  The last handful of missions trying to throw in some emotional relevancy was misplaced.... It should have been there at the beginning.  As it stands, it's forced and hollow.... I can't care for characters that were only in two or three missions & had no relevancy to the story.
2.  Repeat, repeat, repeat....  everything... EVERYTHING is repeated ad nauseum.
3.  Combat system is like the Arkham Batman series... except extremely simple with no strategy or skill required.
4.  Leveling up and upgrading is unbalanced... I spent the entire game OP.  And the really cool stuff you don't get until you beat the game.  WTF?  Too much stick, not enough carrot.
5.  BORING.  When it's beautiful... it's amazing.... but the majority of ... pretty much everything... just runs together into one gigantic MMMMMMEEEEEEEEEHHHHHHH.
Yes, I'd recommend it.  Just because Steam doesn't have an apathetic button.

I first played this game when it was still in development and it was still very rough.  I only played maybe a half-hour because there were so many bugs.  But I picked it up again about 2 weeks ago and absolutely loved it.  The developers really came thru with this.  The story mode is a lot of fun and gives you the skills and understanding you will need to build sucessful prisons, so I suggest doing that first.  Then the sandbox part of the game lets you build as big a prison as you like.  The one flaw I have found so far with this game is that every time they have a patch, it seems to break all my current prisons and I have to start from scratch in order to play the game.  One example is that the cooks will suddenly stop cooking and all the prisoners will die.  Regardless of how many cookers, fridges, or sinks I put in the kitchen.  Pre-patch the prison was working just fine, then all of a sudden, post-patch that same prison is just broken.  Other than this one glaring flaw, the game is extremely fun and has a lot of re-play value.  It has been a while since I found a game which could draw me in so much.  I found myself thinking of different prison ideas to build on my days off from work.  Overall I definitely suggest you give this game a go if you like sandbox games or like city builders like sim city.

Silicon Zeroes is like getting smacked in the shoulder with a keisaku stick by some fastidious programming monk; until you reach enlightment in the great challenges of computer organization theory, or leave the retreat in frustration. Meanwhile, some of your fellow attendees are also worried that they accidentally signed up for some sort of 1960's alt-history SJW LARP weekend, but no way are you going to touch that subject with a 10-foot pole. So sit straight, don't relax, and silently fume about how you (yet again) fell short of the clock cycle constraint.
(About the play time: I have completed past the first ending and started on the next chapter focused on parallelism, but boy is it whipping me hard. Reminds me why I didn't major in electrical engineering. ^_^;;
Also out of impatience, I piped the game's executable through the strings unix utility and read the rest of the plot in plain text. Consider it "research" for the plot discussion in this review. @_@;;)
To add some context to the top rated reviews, it may be helpful to start with the potential turnoffs:
The game is not about building a CPU from low level components, such as NAND gates. Your parts list starts off at a very high level of abstraction (addition is already solved for you), and you don't need to worry about binary math. To its credit, this game covers entirely different ground from the typical NAND2Tetris recommendation.
I'm cool with the intentions of the author, but the story is easily the weirdest part of the game. I'm just not sure how much of my consternation was from being already familiar with the real history of Silicon Valley, even though there are some creative, playful ideas in how some underrepresented demographics were represented in the characters (minority fab workers, female programmers, etc). But when contrasted to the actual history, the progressive feel-good story of a bunch of underdogs enduring against all odds was ironically and unintentionally sad. The extra history commentary after you beat the first ending helps explain the author's creative choices, but boy was it kind of wierd working for an alt-history, non-eugenicist, nice version of William Shockley without that narrative context.
The common invocation of Zach-likes is warranted, but I think it falls short for 2 reasons:
(1) Zachtronics games in my mind are very tolerant of silly and unexpected solutions, while Silicon Zeroes holds you to very strict contraints where the suboptimal solutions are not tolerated. SZ is very puzzlely, and the hand of the designer is felt very heavily for better and worse. For better, the progression of challenges work to test you on insights that you'll need in later levels.  For worse, oh come on, why can't I use parts I know the company has and had let me play with minutes ago???
(2) I find the writing in Zachtronics games to be witty and funny, and an incentive to keep pushing through. SZ's plot didn't quite resonate with me in that way. It think part of it is that Zach-like characters, say in Shenzhen I/O or Infinifactory, get the freedom to be cynical, optimistic, fearful, all-business, gross, cosmopolitan, culturally-ignorant, etc, while the majority of characters in SZ seem like... uh, very positive and politically-correct ideals of their respective minority archtypes? To put in another way, there are "good" guys in Shenzhen I/O or Infinifactory or Spacechem who may actually be disagreeable to certain players, while it's pretty obnoxiously clear at each step who you should be rooting for/against in Silicon Zeroes.
With all that said, I highly recommend Silicon Zeroes for its treatment of the topics involving high-speed and parallelized hardware design. The puzzle-like design of the levels is often annoying, but there are many flashing moments of satori when you find that kernel of understanding the designer had in mind. It's actually kind of clever how you rediscover challenges such as pipelining, caching, and data/control hazards, without some long lecture on those same issues. If you somehow find yourself trying to understand the design tradeoffs inherent in computer organization and design,  SZ is a great active learning introduction to the topic.

Sister Location. Where do I begin? Well, how about correcting the mistakes I made in my LAST review of this game (which has since been deleted).
Previously, I had said that this was the best game in the series but now, I'm not too sure how I feel about that. I think I understand why I said that so blindly. It was because it was a new game, gave us new things to do, and changed up the lore. I thought it was the best thing ever; but now that the game has been out for more than a  year now, I think it's time to give this game its proper dues.
Sister Location is the 5th game in the franchise (6th if you count FNaF World) and tried to do something different; which it succeeded. Instead of being stuck in an office all night, you move around (but not much because all you're doing is pressing W on your keyboard, which affects the gameplay in no way). You also have different jobs every night, as you are a mechanic this time; rather than being a night guard. Your various jobs are to make sure the robots are intact by "motivating" them with a controlled shock, restore the power to the place when it goes out, don't get caught by the animatronics, to send them off to be scooped, and to remove their power modules.
To be honest, I thought these were all great ideas but they should've worked together a bit more. I must say, though, that this game at least brought us a little variety with the gameplay (although it's still mainly point and click).
There are some ups to the new mechanics and some downs as well. First of all, the ups. This game tried to be different and it kept gamers interested in playing to hopefully do something new (well, most of us gamers, that is); which don't get me wrong, the correct amount of variety is great.
Now are the downs. There was TOO much variety in the game. All the ideas were great but they all seemed disjointed; just like I brought up earlier.
Although gameplay is important, it's not too important in the FNaF games because the main focus is the lore.
Now this brings us to the lore.
This game was more of a lore driven success. It seemed like there were secrets and hints everywhere you looked; which is great for an avid theorist like me; but not too great for those who are new and don't really follow the lore.
Basically, what I'm saying is that this is pretty much a game all about the lore and nothing else. If you're new, try the other ones. Besides, you would have to follow EVERY SINGLE bit of info and lore on this series to fully understand the game.
This game requires you to have played the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and FNaF World (or at least watched these) and to read both books to get the lore (and/or theories by Game Theory or others).
In the end, it's a pretty solid game. However, it focuses more on lore than gameplay. When it does focus on gameplay, it can go too far. For example, Night 4 is a rage-inducing mess that only serves as filler for the last night. Sometimes, however, the gameplay can have pros. The custom night is pretty cool but yet again focuses on the lore in the end.
8.5/10 Great game but it requires WAY TOO much research and play time from the other games to understand this one. So, if you're a follower of FNaF and you want to learn more about the twisted universe it's set in, pick this one up and play it 'til the jumpscares don't affect you anymore!

This game is mad fun. You are just one tiny little guy in the galaxy on your own saving each planet one at at time. All the while, aliens and dragons spawn and try to ruin your day. Go along and plant tree all over the place restoring the natural order only armed with a single gun.
But don't let the gun throw you off, its far from an action game. This is probably more along the lines of casual with mild pressure.  I think it is meant to be challenge and impossible to do on your first time playing. You will have to sink a few hours into it before you make it really far, but believe me, you won't regret it.
It's got subtle jokes to lighten the mood and the art is cartoony and playful. The achievements are written in lymerick which is another bonus that has a sinister taste of challenging the riddle solving for the regular achievement hunter. But don't worry, they are TOO hard if you are looking for them.
The physics for the planets and space are nice and subtle but make a lot of sense; you have to escape the gravity of the planet and using the jetpack causes exponential accerlation. (I don't know why but I really like that part... it's cool)
Oo! and the best part is the upgrades! the more and more you play and longer you survive, the more upgrades you can afford and rewards you can collect. Buy new guns, upgrade your suit and add perks to your character all with a currency you collect from beating the ever-loving crap out of your enemies.
Line you score up against fellow players and discover the mysterious bearded owner of the 8-ball in Cosmochoria. I can't wait to see this game grow!

A great concept but fundamentally flawed. The combat has been stifled by unnecessarily nerfing the evade function, lowering the priority of the counter ability, and dramatically lengthening the time it takes to complete an aerial attack. The boss fights are a mess, especially all of Bane's (let's not even start on the trash that is the final fight, which is simply a hackneyed copy of the Mr. Freeze fight in AC). The claw gun is one of the few bright spots of the game, but even it is marred by being too easily exploitable in predator encounters. The leveling system is horrible, shoehorning the player into getting health before skills that would negate the need for more health - it feels as if the designers knew Batman would get his♥♥♥♥♥handed to him early on, and instead of fixing the broken mechanics that render skill at the core gameplay useless they simply made Batman slightly harder to knockout.
What makes it worse, paradoxically, is that for the most part the story is halfway decent. Yes, it lacks any semblance of structure starting out, and goes too long in the end, but it's a fascinating look at early Batman. Little things like thugs shouting, "Holy crap, did he just summon bats?!" mid fight are awesome accoutrements to an otherwise flagging game.
Play it if it's on sale (at least 75% off) and you're a completionist for the series, but expect controller breaking frustration if you're even halfway skilled at the other games in the series. Otherwise, don't even bother.

DISCLAIMER: This is going to be a long review so if you don't like reading you can skip this one, and SPOILERS!!!!!!!!!
Let me start off by saying I loved this series. I read the book, collected the merchandise, and consumed every theory video on Youtube like it was another clue to finding the Holy Grail. The story and the lore surrounding these games have been the focal point of my attention since the name "Purple Guy" was spoken into existence. I also have a tremendous amount of respect and admiration for Scott Cawthon. He has created one of the most successful independent game franchises to date, and it is in no small part to the hard work and dedication he has put into each FNaF game. Even after raising exactly $0 on Kickstarter for the original Five Nights at Freddy's he didn't give up, and his commitment has paid off. I truly think you would be hard pressed to find someone who is more devoted to their work than he is. His games have brought me more joy and entertainment than most AAA games that I own, and for that I say thank you Scott.
Now we come to the reason I am writing this review, and I take no pleasure in writing these words. I genuinely hope that I am being naive and can look back at this review and say that I had no clue what I was talking about.
Let me start by addressing the STORY of FNaF so far:
It all started with the box at the end of FNaF 4. In it, Scott said were the pieces of the story put together. The box represented what the FNaF community had been longing for; closure. What happened next acted as the catalyst for my departure from the FNaF world. Scott decided that he didn't want to open the box because he wasn't sure if "the community would accept it that way". As the creator of the series I have to respect that decision, but I disagree with it wholeheartedly. It shows me one of two things. Either Scott didn't have confidence in how he ended the story up to that point, or he didn't think the FNaF community could handle the truth. Either way I feel like this was the wrong thing to do. To bring a fan base as dedicated and passionate as this one so close to having the answers they have spent countless hours trying to find is no way to repay them for making this franchise what it is. Again, Scott is the only one who knows the masterplan and I hope I can look back and say I was wrong.
When I heard that Sister Location was being released, I was thrilled. I thought this might be the chance to finally have the answers to all of the questions we have been asking for so long. I couldn't have been more wrong. Instead what we received was a convoluted story that would take more of a stretch to connect to past FNaF games than even MatPat of Game Theory is capable of, and that's not even addressing how it answers almost none of the questions left behind by the past 4 FNaF games. Even if you took what this game did provide in the way of story for what it is and ignored the other 4 games, it still left me completely unsatisfied. Please Scott, I understand that you have more books coming and a potential FNaF movie being made, but if you keep overcomplicating the lore the way this game did you will be left with a fan base devoid of any motivation or energy to devote to this series. I know because I have reached that point.
Now let's address the GAMEPLAY:
Ask yourself this question. If you had no idea that this game was, in any way, related to the FNaF series would you enjoy playing it? Better yet, would you recommend it to someone else? I suggest you let your answers to those questions be your guide as you form your opinion about this game. Also, I am addressing Sister Location as a stand-alone game and will not compare it to the other FNaF games.
The BAD:
From a gameplay perspective, I didn't enjoy this game at all. The first night is literally following directions. That's it. For a game that consists of only five nights (If you count the hidden ending then you could say 5.5) to have 20% consist of clicking buttons when you're told to is disapointing from a player's point of view and poor design from a game making perspective. The rest of the game is, for lack of better terms, boring and frustrating. Night 2 is a glorified reskin of red light/green light and an exercise in holding down the mouse button to keep a door shut. Even the jump scares seem half-hearted. Night 3 consists of more "clicking where the narrator tells you to" and the most frustrating game of peek-a-boo I have ever played. Night 4 is essentially a game of "pay attention to me" with spring locks while shaking things off of your body, and is also one of the most frustrating things I have ever had to do in a video game.  I understand wanting the player to discover solutions organically and on their own, but when the gameplay is as frustrating as this it quickly becomes disheartening and an exercies in frustration. Night 5 is unfortunately more of the same, and is criminally short lived. When I was done, the only thing I said was "That's it?". The final scene of the game was also equally disapointing. Needless to say, this was one of the most disapointing endings to a game I have ever experienced. And those soap opera clips at the end of every night?? I pray that they are there to serve as clues to the story or some other purpose because they were hard to watch. Before I move on to the good, I know that there is a secret "fake" ending that utilizes gameplay from the previous FNaF games. Because those games have been reviewed to death and the mechanics are well known and already established I didn't factor them in to this review. Yes, it was a nice throwback and evoked a warm feeling of nostalgia, but if you have to lean on those feelings to make up for the lack of meaningful gameplay mechanics in the main game there is a problem.
The GOOD:
The voice acting was fantastic. The voice of Baby (or Ennard, depending on what camp you are in) was comforting, helpful, and unsettling all at the same time. That is a very difficult thing to accomplish in voice acting and the voice actor did it wonderfully. The rest of the voice acting was equally impressive and played an invaluable part in creating the unsettling atmosphere of the game.
The writing was also very funny and made me laugh on more than one occasion (except for the soap opera clips, those were terrible). It was also unnerving, in a good way, at certain points. The highlight for me was the monologue Baby gives about the scooper and her musing about how a pint of ice cream would feel about a scooper. I thought that analogy for comparing seemingly lifeless animatronics to ice cream was well done in the given context.
The 8-bit mini game was also enjoyable. Trying to solve the puzzle on how to feed all the kids was done very well and was an excellent example of testing the skill of the player and rewarding them for their accomplishments. I also liked that this mini game was the key to unlocking the secret ending (that we know of at this point).
To (finally) conclude this review, I can sum up my feelings towards this game in two words (then why didn't I just do that at the beginning you ask). Missed Opportunity. I honestly thought we would be getting much more than what this game gave us. Scott worked on this game for almost a year, and given what he was able to accomplish in the past in a much smaller amount of time, it was hard not to get my hopes up. I want more than anything to say that I enjoyed this game and what it contributed to the lore and the overall story Scott has been telling for so long. I even tried to convince myself that it wasn't as bad as I thought by watching other people enjoy it. I just can't. The only hope I have now is that some amazing easter egg will be discovered that will finally satisfy the masses, including myself.

Game about designing basic CPUs from basic components such as adders, (de)multiplexers, latches... Starts slow (counters, memory access) and builds up quickly (instructions, clocking, pipelining)
Pros:
- Pretty rewarding, especially if your solution is more optimal than developer's (yes, it is possible!)

- Good choices of puzzles, relevant to actual CPU architecture, not just pointless challenges
Cons:
- A bit short, expecting more puzzles to be added in updates
- Some lower level components would be nice (e.g. logic gates would be useful in some puzzles)

TL;DR: Great puzzle game. Extremely fun on its own and happens to teach very real computer science concepts.
Summary:
Silicon Zeros is a highly accessible story about a tiny Silicon Valley company at the dawn of the computer age, building digital devices and trying to swim rather than sink in the ocean of the tech industry. The plot is funny and relatively compelling, and the gameplay - building digital devices with an easy-to-use, beautiful editor - is tight, interesting, and never too easy nor too hard.
The core mechanic is this: Given a restricted set of fundamental digital devices, produce the desired output within the given part and time limit. You can also compare your solutions with those of other players.
The game leads you gently between the various challenges, introducing the you to real, useful computer science concepts as you need them to solve puzzles. It is never confusing, though it is often challenging.
I absolutely recommend that everyone play this game. The developer is extremely responsive and highly active. I'm a Linux user, and it works great on Linux, after users asked for it to be ported.

This game just keeps getting better and better as new mechanics are introduced.  Developer has done good job adding ease of life features for automating boring parts like automatic trace routing, clock speed calculation, being able to reusabe blocks between levels.
The levels have no limitations on board size or part count that allows focusing on creating a  solution that works instead of playing tetris game of squeezing your solution in board. Silicon Zeroes is a delightful computational puzzle game that made me go back and review the principles of CPU design. Though it never mentions any of them by name, the overarching concept of pipelining, details of hazard avoidance and a number of other very low level concepts are introduced and the player is made to understand them.
Though I have some complaints about the puzzles' arbitrary limits (how can I run out of time? Why won't you let me make an inefficient monstrosity?) and a few missing features (sandbox, solution import/export/saving/loading), for the pricetag and the obvious passion that went into the game, I can wholeheartedly recommend this title.
Though the story came off as heavy handed to start with, by the final ending, I was genuinely invested in the little illustrated heads that told me what to do in each puzzle.

If I didn't know this wasn't made by Zachtronics, I'd probably be willing to bet money that it was. There is a lot in the theme of this game that reminds of the super fulfilling puzzles that Zach had been creating over the years. These type of games, which allow building complex systems through a set of a few simple rules that are quite well defined, are my cup of tea. I also love the mystery of trying out new parts of the system as they are introduced, some defined, some not -- and those that are not, are left for you to discover.
The style of puzzles and testing system is quite similar to Zach's game, and those familiar with the "cram it in the least cycles and least parts as possible challange" will feel right at home here. The story is kind of meh, though to be fair , while Zach's story telling is much more intriguing than Silicon Zero's, I don't really play these games for the story, IYKWIM.
Those with some background with logic components (eg. Latches, Registers, CPUs, ALUs, Muxes, Demuxes, etc), will immediately recognize many of the parts available in the base game. But the best part is -- you don't need to know how these actually work to play!
So give the game a go, I think it's quite fun and challenging! Thanks for a great game, guys!

TL:DR - For fans of the Hitman series I'd recommend purchasing the complete first season, when it is on sale. For people who aren't sure whether or not they would like the game, try out the Intro Pack that has the prologue + episode 1.
With a recent sale (half price) I purchased the complete first season. I have Bangkok, Colorado, and Hakkaido yet to finish. So I am about half way through the game, at about 14 hours, and I have been going back to fulfill different challenges along the way. I've played about four other Hitman and this one is really well down. Nice open world to explore, with lots of ways of taking out a contract. Of course, one of the key features of any Hitman series are disguises and there are a truckload of them, ranging from the iconic cook and security guard to a pompous fashion model or masseuse.
The overall gameplay is what you've come to love about any Hitman game. When you first start off, you're limited with what equipement you can choose to bring with you, or your starting place/starting disguise, but as you progress and unlock more challenges these options will increase. Be stealthy and electrocute or poison someone or shoot it out with a sub-machine gun, the choice is left up to you.
There are weekly contracts and this is an interesting twist to the game. Word of caution though, don't screw it up. If you do, you'll have to wait for the next contract to come out. From what I've read, this particular feature of the game is only included in the complete first season and not the intro pack, which makes sense because contracts can range over any one of the settings of the 6 episodes. Don't expect to kill Gary Busey, either. I was looking forward to that, but that weekly contract is long gone...
Sometimes the game can be tedius, trying to chase down and set up a trap for a contract. and waiting...there can be lots of waiting... So, if you aren't the patient type this may not be your type of game, unless you go in guns blazing, but ironically, that takes out a lot of the subtlety from the game. There is some replay value too, but this can also be tedius at times, because it involves revisiting the same mission, say episode one's contract, and in order to fulfill the challenges, you have to complete a new way of executing a contract. For example, one challenge may have you electrocute a target and another may have you use poison. Essentially, you're killing the same target in multiple ways, in order to unlock different items and starting settings...It's a rinse and repeat kind of a deal.
It's not my favorite Hitman out of the series, that might go to Bloodmoney or Absolution, but it is a really pretty and fun game. So if your, jonesing for more play time as Agent 47, check this out (get the complete edition when it is on sale).  If you're new to the game, get a taste for it with the intro pack. If you enjoy it, then wait for a sale and purchase the complete first season. I would not recommend purchasing each individual game episode.

I'll admit I was skeptical about Batman: Arkham Origins when it was first announced. 1) It was not developed by Rocksteady. This made me immediately think that WB was attempting to cash in on Rocksteady's great franchise. 2) Based on the trailers and gameplay videos it seemed too much like a rehash of Arkham City. Arkham Knight looks like it is expanding on the foundation laid down in the previous two games in the series, but Origins looked like more of the same.
In a way it is more of the same. In fact some parts of the map are directly lifted from Arkham City, which makes sense in the context of the story. However, this more of the same isn't really a bad thing here. It actually helps alleviate my first concern (the one about this not being developed by Rocksteady) because the game plays mostly just like it did in Akham City. This is not a bad thing. While it does add to some repetition, the gameplay created by Rocksteady was very solid and it stays solid here - WB Montreal does a very capable job recreating the gameplay Rocksteady introduced originally.
While the game does redo some things (the Enigma Datapacks are Riddler Tophies, different in name only) that appeared before, I found that my concern was unfounded. I really wanted more of the great gameplay from Akham City and it can be found in Arkham Origins.
I won't spoil the story, but the Origins of the title are most definitely plural in nature as the game delves into the origins of many characters and/or relationships between characters.
The game is not without flaws and bugs, though. There were a few times early one (within the first 2-3 hours) the game would crash after about 20 minutes of play time. My computer is strong enough to run this game on high settings, yet this would still happen. For some reason once I had put in over 5 hours the crashing problem completely disappeared. However from about 15-30 hours the game would just lose my controller input (using a wired 360 controller to play this) and I wouldn't be able to move or do anything with the controller. I would restart the game and my controller would work again. After roughly 30 hours of playtime though, this bug stopped happening.
As for flaws, well the voice acting for Batman and Joker are good, but they aren't Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill. There are some AI issues here and there. Sometimes the controls aren't as tight as they are in the Rocksteady games, which can result in hitting an unintended target which may break a combo, or ending a glide because for some reason a graple point just will not appear unless you manually point the camera directly at the point.
Also, I wish the crime scene investigations did not hold the player's hand as much as they do and would actually allow for some more puzzle solving as opposed to essentially pointing you in the direction of solving the crime.
These flaws and bugs don't really break the game though. If you enjoyed Batman: Arkham Asylum or Batman: Arkham City. You'll enjoy Batman: Arkham Origins. I recommend it.

Observations and other musings...
Be it Wings over Israel, or First Eagles, or Wings over Europe, or Wings over Vietnam, or Strike Fighters... it's all pretty much the same game. Each just has a major theme change and setting for a different era, or a different war.
I agree with one comment that Wings over Europe is pretty much Strike Fighters, but I would have preferred Wings over Israel or Wings over Vietnam to depict wars that actually happened, rather than the hypothetical cold war campaigns.
In fact, I don't know why Third Wire and/or Strategy First didn't reissue all the versions on Steam. It would have been great to collect and replay these titles, or better yet have them in a bundle.
Anyway, I give this game the thumbs up for being a great simulation for its time...10 years ago. Also, it is fairly accurate in its depiction of air warfare, including air combat and strike. Another element is that there is something about how they have crafted it with mission background, situation briefings, mission planning, etc.; along with the flight dynamics and real world limitations that make it feel authentic.
Authentic to me feels like everytime I play a campaign, and I'm planning and executing a mission, I get a glimpse of what it as like back then flying over the jungle in Vietnam to ripple off a load of 500lb Snakeyes...and completely miss; or erratically jinking over the Suez Canal desperately trying to avoid SA-2 SAMS...and having the stabilizer blow off...
It just feels authentic...and doesn't need a lot of glitz and glam that other air combat games have.
Totally worth it in the $15-20 range (undiscounted), and $20-30 bundle of Wings over Israel, Vietnam, and Strike would be sweet too.
I haven't tried any of the titles with Windows 10. I don't see the point in an OS change when Windows 7 is so awesome. I should point out that I had no end of technical issues with all the versions of this flight series under Windows 7 using retail disk...I was glad to see the Steam version of WoE had no such issues, which is another reason why I would like the other games on Steam.
I would expect to see compatibility issue with Windows 10, regardless.

+ Decently long. I finished the game after 10 hours, having done a fair few of the otpional extras along the way. I would guess maybe 4-5 hours for a minimal completion and probably 20 hours or more for 100%.
The bad:
- The story and writing are not good. Cliches, uninteresting/unlikable characters, telling instead of showing, and so on. The game designer clearly isn't a writer and it shows. Happily, the story is fairly minor and easy to ignore.
- The niche that this sort of game occupies is fairly narrow, and is already fairly crowded. It's hard to say that there's anything here that particularly stands out from the crowd.
Overall:
A decent game, and I certainly feel that I've got my money's worth, but nothing that's going to set the world alight.

TL:DR - For fans of the Hitman series I'd recommend purchasing the complete first season, when it is on sale. For people who aren't sure whether or not they would like the game, try out the Intro Pack that has the prologue + episode 1.
With a recent sale (half price) I purchased the complete first season. I have Bangkok, Colorado, and Hakkaido yet to finish. So I am about half way through the game, at about 14 hours, and I have been going back to fulfill different challenges along the way. I've played about four other Hitman and this one is really well down. Nice open world to explore, with lots of ways of taking out a contract. Of course, one of the key features of any Hitman series are disguises and there are a truckload of them, ranging from the iconic cook and security guard to a pompous fashion model or masseuse.
The overall gameplay is what you've come to love about any Hitman game. When you first start off, you're limited with what equipement you can choose to bring with you, or your starting place/starting disguise, but as you progress and unlock more challenges these options will increase. Be stealthy and electrocute or poison someone or shoot it out with a sub-machine gun, the choice is left up to you.
There are weekly contracts and this is an interesting twist to the game. Word of caution though, don't screw it up. If you do, you'll have to wait for the next contract to come out. From what I've read, this particular feature of the game is only included in the complete first season and not the intro pack, which makes sense because contracts can range over any one of the settings of the 6 episodes. Don't expect to kill Gary Busey, either. I was looking forward to that, but that weekly contract is long gone...
Sometimes the game can be tedius, trying to chase down and set up a trap for a contract. and waiting...there can be lots of waiting... So, if you aren't the patient type this may not be your type of game, unless you go in guns blazing, but ironically, that takes out a lot of the subtlety from the game. There is some replay value too, but this can also be tedius at times, because it involves revisiting the same mission, say episode one's contract, and in order to fulfill the challenges, you have to complete a new way of executing a contract. For example, one challenge may have you electrocute a target and another may have you use poison. Essentially, you're killing the same target in multiple ways, in order to unlock different items and starting settings...It's a rinse and repeat kind of a deal.
It's not my favorite Hitman out of the series, that might go to Bloodmoney or Absolution, but it is a really pretty and fun game. So if your, jonesing for more play time as Agent 47, check this out (get the complete edition when it is on sale).  If you're new to the game, get a taste for it with the intro pack. If you enjoy it, then wait for a sale and purchase the complete first season. I would not recommend purchasing each individual game episode.

I was hesitant to buy this when it was first released after the abomination that was Absolution, but I now realize what a mistake that was, given that this is, in my opinion, the greatest Hitman game ever released. Yes, better than Blood Money.
As of this review, I have put in over 9 hours of playtime, and have only really played the opening tutorial and first location, Paris. The Paris location alone has kept me busy longer than most games released today, and I still haven't scratched the surface. The levels aren't linear at all, and are fantastically designed, full of little details that help make the locations seem real and full of life.
In most games, you are given the illusion of choice when it comes to dealing with a situation which usually boils down to either 'perform X stealth action' or 'perform Y loud action'. Not in Hitman though. There are dozens upon dozens of ways to eliminate your target. From the not so subtle planting a round into your targets dome, to feeding them rat poison, forcing them to go to the bathroom to vomit, then drowning your target in his/her own vomit. Forcing a target to believe his dead mother is haunting him, making him collapse, then breaking his neck, crushing fools under pianos, killing someone via an ejection seat and many many more.
Not all targets are so simple either, a lot require the extraction and acquisition of intel to determain how best to accomplish the hit.
The graphics are fantastic and it runs effortlessly on my rig, as is the sound design, with most npcs having their own conversations that are either irrelevent to the mission at hand, or offer hints.
Then you have the time based contracts where you are given just one chance to kill your mark. Fail, and you lose the chance for good, making these contracts very tense and fun!
There is an XP system in place for each location, where upon completing challenges, you are rewarded with even more equipment and ways to play. Instead of starting a mission from the front gate, maybe this time you start in the kitchen as a member of kitchen staff.
This game is worth it just if you want to throw hammers at peoples faces and laugh as they fall down the stairs, which has become my new guilty pleasure.

Online DRM aside this is easily the best Hitman to date.  I understand peoples issue with the DRM so this review is mostly based on the gameplay.
Hitman 2016 is everything people wanted in a Hitman game.  Going back to its roots in Blood Money and removing the cancerous features from Absolution. I think they really took into account peoples major gripes with Absolution and did a great job of removing every terrible "feature" from their previous game. My only issue with the game is that missions taking place in non-english speaking countries, has no affect on the dialogue between NPCs and the player. I think most people would like hearing their own language but me personally would perfer subtitles as the foriegn dialogue would add to the immersion. Overall this is a great game and worth the purchase in my opinion.

The attention to detail in each level (and the varying gameplay dynamics added to the last two released levels) has given me faith in their next season. My internet connection rarely goes down so I have never experienced the problems people are having the the DRM, but I do not support their online only DRM in any way as it makes it really hard for people, who don't have a consistent internet connection, to enjoy the game to its fullest. I've read other reviews of people saying the Hitman servers go down regularly and I can assure you that is not true as I've never once seen the servers down. The people having this problem may be experiencing their own personal internet connection issues.
Gameplay/Graphics/Audio: 9/10 (based on comparison between their previous games and other games in the stealth genre)
DRM: 5/10 (I gave it a 5 because, although cancerous, it is still functional to most online gamers.)

While I personally prefer the gameplay style of previous instalments; learning what to do and then perfecting your craft over the course of several nights while the difficulty increases, there is no saying this game is inferior without those elements. It does things differently and provides a much more story driven experience than before, but still keeps the classic elements you've come to expect.
The game has the same five night structure as the others, but every night is different from the last, so it's very difficult to know what to expect. It keeps things fresh and really keeps you engaged. Gameplay elements are wildly different from the FNAFs of old, but are familiar enough to not feel completely jarring.
The voice acting is very professional, and serves the mood quite nicely. Whether its the incompetence/shenanigans of your handheld assistant or the cryptic instructions from certain other robots, when the game wants you to laugh, you laugh, and when it wants you to be scared, by gum you're scared. The voice acting gives the game a very "Portal 2" feel, and it's a refreshing change of pace. The jokes are clever, and actually add to the atmosphere.
Overall, not the game I expected to play, but a really really good one nonetheless. I'm excited to see what comes next.

This game was pretty true to the details. I could tell the devs were instructed to do their homework and watch the movies. You can just picture them studiously taking notes from each scene. But like most students, they entirely missed the forrest for the trees. They didn't 'get' Max.
Having lost his family, Max's salvation has always been found in sacrificing himself to save those who would have otherwise been victims. It's not a tale of revenge or fame seeking. Nor is it about racing. It's about the last speck of his humanity reappearing and screwing up his otherwise selfish plans. The way they have this game play out would be a living nightmare for someone with a complex like Max's.
Something I really disliked was when you beat the crap out of a boss and... cutscene boss escapes, for the third freaking time. Give me a break. I hate being forced to chase a carrot. It's been said that a work isn't too long if nothing can be removed from it. Max started feeling very long. I hacked the scrap in the first few hours of playing and I'm so freaking glad that I did. One less stupid little scavenger hunt to deal with. I wish I could have just skipped the races. I like cars but I hate races.
In short, the story sucked really bad but the game itself was pretty awesome. A few things needed some tweaking:  For example, every boss has the same move and is beat the same way. I was fine with that because it made getting what I wanted quick and easy. Also, the V8 should have come at about the 10 hour mark, not at the end of th game. I randomly found a 12 cylinder hot-rod before I earned the v8.
Anyway, disappointed in the story but you'll be hard-pressed to find a better post-apocalyptic Mad-Max styled game. I'd play it again. One of the very few games that was worth the $7 I spent on it.

Being a prequel to the Arkham franchise, the game stars a younger Bruce Wayne trying to find solid footing as the Bat. This comes through in his interactions with criminals: he's much fiercer and almost homicidal in tone and actions. He lacks the distinct calm that he perpetually exudes; his actions are brasher and more impulsive. Although Batman supposedly never kills, he comes damn close in this game due to his rage, which has obviously settled in later titles. His anger is subliminally hidden in his tone of voice and the excessive use of force in cut scenes when giving beat-downs, so you might miss it if you don't understand that Batman is supposed to be calm, meticulous, and in control of his emotions.
The problem is that this is the only shot of Batman's inexperience for 60% of the game. Towards the end of the title you get a substantially larger view at a young Batman's doubts and worries. For almost half the game there is absolutely nothing to point at Batman's inexperience, nothing to tell you that he is just starting out as Gotham's knight. There's his anger, and it was done in a sublime manner, but given that there's suddenly an entire game's worth of development at the end you end up wondering what the ♥♥♥♥ you were doing for the first half. Suddenly Alfred is yelling at Batman for being reckless; Batman is having doubts about his effectiveness at saving his city; the gamer delves into the Joker's psychological profile. Yet half the game you're just doing some boring♥♥♥♥♥shit that doesn't amount to the development in character and story that we get at the end.
And don't get me started on the much hyped 'assassins'. They're introduced at the beginning and made to look as if they will be a significant element to the plot, but what you get is random drop-ins from people along your investigation. The drop-ins aren't even all that good: One guy you never fight, two are optional and are forgettable, and one fight is a golrified QTE where the only inputs needed are ''Attack'' and ''Counter''. The fight with the 8th assassin doesn't even make sense, as the bounty on your head (which they are all after) is completely gone. There must have been a better way to integrate the assassins into the main storyline. As it stands they seem to be an afterthought conjured up to give you a boss fight every few hours. And the boss fight's aren't even all that interesting.
'Gameplay'-wise the-ahahahahahahahaha. Why bother talking about game mechanics: it's exactly the same as the other titles. There is absolutely nothing different here, other than akward pacing. You get all of the same weapons and moves, with a few new ones that all wind up being more or less useless save for two or three. Hell, they imported Arkham City into this game, with the only addition to the overworld being a long bridge that leads to a new section of Gotham to mess around in. Granted, it's not the SAME exact area as before, as they had to downsize it to create new areas, but it's still pretty familiar territory. I'd argue that it was a change for the worse, as one of the shinning aspects of Arkham City was the character that each area had, signifying the leader of the place. That's gone, and now it's just gothic architecture.
Riddler is still there, but the quality of the trophy placement has degraded. Just like in the last title there are a bunch of trophies scattered throughout, this time in the form of 'data packs'. The odd thing is that you can actually solve a LOT of these from the very beginning, so it all feels underwhelming. That and the fact that some of them are just out in the open, waiting to be grabbed.
There are no Riddles for you to solve this time around, sadly. That means that you don't get the Batman references throughout the world, waiting to be scanned. Which means that the overworld feels more barren, because instead of:
-Harvey Dent's office in a corner
-Catwoman's home to the side of a building with graffitti sprayed on the wall
-a movie poster referencing a shape-shifting villain
-a jailcell with calendars strewn about in a peculiar manner
-a casino with a cool, Greek looking neon sign referencing a villain
you get:
-an office building
-an apartment building
-a movie poster
-regular looking jail cell after jail cell
-a generic casino
People need to understand that one of the cool things about the Arkham titles was the amount of references they tried putting into the games in the environment, which means that you got a really unique looking world with character instead of blank building after blank building. I don't even read Batman comics, but everytime I saw something unique in the overworld, which was almost always, I would scan it cause it stood out enough for me to wonder what it was. Now it's just gothic architecture that looks nice. Instead of Riddler's Riddles you get some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥'Anarky' tags, that are just leftist socialist dribble about the banks. I read four of those tags. Four. When he got to ♥♥♥♥ing collectivism I was like ''oh God I can't stand the ♥♥♥♥er I'm not gonna read any more of this propaganda'. Cause it's propaganda. I know for a ♥♥♥♥ing fact that some writer was typing it all up, assured that he would 'enlighten' the masses reading his garbage. Also, the villain behind the tags winds up being some 'Anonymous' inspired ♥♥♥♥♥♥ who goes on a LONG ♥♥♥♥ING SPEECH after you beat him. He's just really annoying, really political, and really really gay.
TL;DR it's like all the other games with nothing new to offer. The one thing it could have done, which was a showcase of a younger Batman, wasn't present for over half the title. When it emerges it doesn't save this from still being an otherwise plain affair. Something tells me to hit the 'no' button in the recommendation, but it's still an alright game. It's just a disappointment. Also, it wasn't made by Rocksteady, so that might explain why it doesn't try anything new. This is like a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥game released before the REAL sequel to Arkham City: Arkham Knight.
And yes, I focus on a lot of the bad in the review and yet still recommend it. Mainly because despite it's flaws, I'm not regretting the purchase and it was like a C+ summer film: I could've spent my money watching a better movie, but I don't regret the experience and am fine with it.

As much as it would shorten things to say that if you liked or are at least familiar with previous arkham games, you won't find much new here. You have virtually the same gadgets, same fighting system, same UI, similar city, the only thing that really changed was the voice actors and storyline and for the most part, that’s totally fine if all you wanted was more batman and the DLC for arkham city just wasn't enough, and for the most part, that was me. As of writing, I haven't actually completed the game, but I feel like I got a pretty good impression as to where everything is headed. Because this is a prequel to the other arkham games, it can't really throw too much at you in terms of story as to not mess with the canon, and this kind of permeates the entire game. Everything feels like its playing it safe, and no real effort has been put in to expanding on the previous games in any light, though again, this isn't really a bad thing, it's just something that will constantly be nagging at you in the back of your head as you play.
The gameplay mechanics are virtually untouched except for a few minor things relating to the upgrade path. And again, not really bad, because the previous mechanics it uses, are probably some of the best brawler mechanics in recent time. One thing I can do without though is the often clunky PC controls, half of my deaths could be attributed to the weird key presses required to dodge and preform special moves. This was a problem in the previous titles, and I feel like there really isn't anything that can be done about it, so I feel like some sort of "360 pad required" tag would be nice.
The story isn't really anything special so far, and I’m not sure whether it really will be either, since again, it can't really do a whole lot due to its prequel nature. The thing that stood out to me the most though was the replacement of two of the main characters, Batman and The Joker. In the previous arkham games, they were voiced by their cartoon counterparts. The joker epically was made by Mark Hamill, who is absent in this game. The Joker replacement isn't bad, but Batman, instead of sounding level headed yet very, what’s the word I’m looking for, stern? Now sounds like he is constantly angry and thinks half yelling makes him sound scary. It’s just something that got on my nerves slowly over time. This could have been explained by Batman not being as controlled or weathered by the years, but it’s never brought up and Batman is just as, or oddly if not more capable in this game that in the future games, it just made less sense the more I pondered it. Another thing is the city, while it seems to be bigger, it has less nooks and crannies, and is missing the hidden riddler riddles of previous games to seem "better" in any sense, and it just feels like arkham city all over again since its still all cordoned off and populated only by thugs, I don't ever recall seeing one civilian in the game outside of a few scripted cutscenes and segments. Again, this is sort of explained by there being a storm on Christmas Eve, but I really just found it odd.
Now, as much as I griped, I still find the game very enjoyable, and would definitely recommend it to anyone looking for more batman, or even just getting into the series, since playing them out of order probably doesn't help.
