is a 2015 indie title funded from a small kickstarter.
At first, it looks and sounds like an RPG from the mid-80s, with its
turn-based combat, upbeat tunes and level design of the era.
However, as you progress through the game, you'll discover
the game is more than what it seems on its 8-bit surface.
You play as a small child trapped in an an underground city
of monsters. Your objective? Escape and reach the surface.
Along the way, you'll face many enemies and meet new friends.
The game has a huge roster of memorable characters that you'll
see along your journey. But you'll face many enemies too that will
kill you
The boss-battles are one of the many highlights of the game,
each with unique and different attack styles, all with their own
musical theme. We'll get to the music later on ...
How you face your enemies will influence on the outcome of the
game and shape the world around you. As you progress onwards,
you'll solve many puzzles, collect special items and complete
intereting sidequests that span from the mundane to the bizzare.
The smaller things in Undertale add for richer detail that's nice to
see.
Now, the music is one of its other highlights. At times it can be
chill and calming, intense and bombastic, crazy and downright funky,
and at other times it can get pretty heavy with overwhelmingly sad
and uplifting music. There are tunes for every occasion, and some you
probably won't hear unless you play the game on a second playthrough.
It does a great job of setting the mood and tone as you travel through
the world, talking to local residents or getting you pumped for an
upcoming battle. It's easy to see why so many love the game for it.
I won't go into detail of the story, but I'll say it's good. That's it.
You're better off playing the game than reading about it since that's
where the fun lies. Not only that, it has great replay value, which is hard
to come by in single-player games now a days.
This game as a package is full of surprises, easter eggs, meta-humor,
and refrences galore, and much more. Ever since it came out, it's remained
on Steams top list for
reviewed games, and
it's easy to see why. It hits all the marks and ticks all the boxes for a fun
and memorable game. If you're late to the party and weren't in on the
kickstarter at the time, like me, then that shouldn't deter you.
For 10$ you're getting your moneys worth, and over.
is a must play for anyone. If you don't like 8-bit games,
you will after this.

What to say about Super Meat Boy? You play as a boy, who is super and made out of meat. One day, your bitter rival, Dr. Fetus, captures your girlfriend, Bandage Girl. Determined to be the hero of the day, Super Meat Boy accepts the responsibility of becoming the hero and sets off. Through forests and abandoned hospitals, will Super Meat Boy make it? That up to you to decide. You are joined by 'Super Tight-Controls Boy', 'Super Quick-Respawn Boy' and ' Super Never-The-Game's-Fault Boy' to aid in your quest.
Super Meat Boy is by far the BEST platformer out there. From different characters to custom levels made by the community, Super Meat Boy has it all. Some levels have secrets (that you'll have to find on your own) which unlock characters which can do an absolute plethora of amazing abilities. There are 7 ingame worlds for you to discover which really flows with the storyline. It is very replayable and along with that fact, the ENTIRE game can be played again in a more difficult alternate set of worlds. The only way to accomplish this though is to race your best and complete each level under a time limit. This becomes increasingly difficult as within one hour you already find yourself questioning the difficulty settings of the game; ranging from 'I'm too young to die' - 'Hurt me plenty' - 'Nightmare'.
Edmund McMillen (the creater of 'The Binding of Isaac' and 'The Basement Collection') really pushes himself in the all-round platformer classic, Super Meat Boy.
I give the game 10/10. Super Meat Boy is a great game and if you like platformers or notoriously difficult games, pick this game up!

I have zero friends who play Rust, and play 100% as a solo. I’m not aggressive, I’m overly friendly, and I have the belief that all people are morally good. Boy has that changed. I picked up for like two quid in a sale a while back. It's a pretty minimal effort conversion, with nothing to make you hate the UI, but certainly nothing impressive either. The real issue is that the underlying game itself is pretty pants.
Now, I knew this was a risk which is why I bought it so cheap. Lots of reviews, especially of the board game, talking about its flaws. They're all pretty spot on. It's one of those multi-player solitaire games. Interaction between players is virtually non-existent, and even if you pull a card which affects other people, you weren't making a choice, it was just random chance.
The other major issue is you will spend 50% of the game just healing. The game is brutal when it comes to punishing you, especially early on. Monster in your area? Probably too strong for you early on. Fate card? Well you better pray to the RNG gods because there's ♥♥♥♥ all you can do about that. And then when a card punishes you you're using one of your precious two actions to heal the damage. In fact one card might do enough damage to cause you to spend multiple turns using half your actions to heal. Once you've developed enough to handle things you're still going to be caught in a repetitive loop of the same two actions turn after turn.
There's no real arc to the game either. You complete quests for VPs, which consist of running to locations, picking up coloured tokens, and then exchanging them for other coloured tokens. It doesn't matter which locations you're at, only which tokens they provide. And when you've done one quest you go on another pulled from the deck. The game doesn't build a story, it just stops when someone did enough quests.
Perhaps there's something to be said if you were playing this on a tablet where you just want to kill some time, but it feels like there's so little going on in terms of meaningful decision making. Certainly there's no reason to play this multiplayer because you have nothing to do with the other players.

Game is good by itself. I wish there would be more interaction between players, because right now you can just complete support quests for other players, Dandelion recieves some victory points (after he is developed) based on the other players actions and finally, some Bad Fortune cards affects all players, and that's all. It feels like you play the game just by your own. Game mechanics is decent and your victory is based on your decisions + some luck. I found Tris to be stronger than other characters due to the fact she can collect investigations twice faster than anyone else, means she completes side and main quests faster. This is especially felt in the games for three, and even more so, for five main tasks.
I do recommend this game if you would like to spend some evenings with friends and you are not able to buy original board game. It is hard to find multiplayer games due to the lack of players. I have had only two multiplayer games, both of them with the same person.

I am not particularly interested in Simulator games, and I haven't played one in 10 years. I got a sudden craving to, and I bought ETS 1 on sale, and I loved it. Lo and behold, ETS 2 goes on sale a week later, so of course I purchased it, and WOW. The difference is astonishing. Graphics, detail, variety, sounds, available jobs/missions, HUD (rearview mirrors, GPS, etc), and not to mention MUSIC. Yes this game has a radio that doesn't require you to manually put music into the game folder, but rather it streams music from the internet and there are a bunch of different stations to choose from. Plus, in this game, you can make your own company, have your own garage, hire drivers, and all that which is awesome. The driving and parking trailers in this game is more difficult than in the original, because it has more realistic physics, but that doesn't bother me much. It motivates me to get better. Anyway, BUY IT NOW while it's on sale for $9! Absolutely recommend.
PS. Oh, and I can't forget to mention, the modding scene for this game is amazing.

I'm sure a narrow audience will enjoy this, but by that I mean fans of old Hitman games who are also willing to pay an unjustified amount of money. The levels are very well made, there is a ton of freedom and multiple ways to eliminate your targets and the audiovisuals do a good job, so I don't have any problem with those parts.
The problem, however, is that the solid level design is expected to carry the game alone, while terrible decisions regarding other aspects weigh it down almost every step of the way.
It feels like yet another skeleton of a great game that had the engine stripped down to work on consoles and then dumbed down for a "wider audience", hereby alienating both core Hitman fans and PC gamers. And here I thought these two were your primary demographic.
Here are some bullet points off the top of my head:
It's not a bad game by any stretch of the imagination, don't get me wrong. The levels are great. Everything else about it, however, is sub-par. I loved the little things, but the big picture is a mess.
The potential is there, but they absolutely have to solve some of the issues I mentioned above. Just introduce difficulty options, fix the scoring system and wait for the price to drop. How hard is that? I won't even mention the sales strategy.
Until they address these points, I'll reluctantly say that Hitman: Absolution was more enjoyable, though I'm sure 90% of you will disagree with me. If you are looking for good a stealth game, I would recommend you get Hitman: Blood Money, MGS5: Phantom Pain or the Batman games. All of them bundled together are likely to cost around the same as this title alone.

Let's start with the improvements.
Moon Studios has added an extra area that can be explored at any time. It gives us a little more backstory on the character
. The location's design is not only beautiful but also clever in the way it becomes partially explorable at the start but story-acquired abilities are required to progress further.
While I'm not a huge fan of the newly added abilities to Ori's skillset (more on that later) I can't deny that they've been implemented professionally. The animations are smooth, a select few pickups scattered across the map require you to utilize those abilities well in order to obtain said pickups and most impressively they're
It's easy for developers to make a small mistake and accidentally introduce a new ability that actually allows players to sequence break the game to their desire, but in Ori this is thankfully not the case.
(Sequence breaking means progressing through locations and parts of the story in a way that developers did not intend to happen, such as expertly leaping over gaps that were meant to be uncrossable.)
For those completionists out there, Moon Studios has added the ability to fast travel through the map using
. Additionally, areas that were previously sealed off after completion are now still open in Definitive Edition and after completing the main story you can still open your save to explore Nibel or reach 100% completion.
It's a great improvement over the original Ori where you better made sure you didn't miss anything before heading to the exit of a dungeon.
Having trouble with some of the game's famous escape sequences? Simply crank that difficulty up to
so there'll be a few checkpoints along the way. There's no shame in that.
Already completed the game once? It feels like a breeze now, doesn't it? Then perhaps try playing the game on
or even
difficulty. The difference is rather noticeable and even the most diehard Ori fans will have to admit that it was a lot harder than they expected.
Allow me to bring up that extra area again,
.
It's well designed and feels like a natural part of Nibel's map.
However it's also
. 1 hour of extra content? Not even that. It takes around 30 minutes to breeze through this entire extra location.
And finally to top it all off, where's the backstory again?
To quote the Steam Store description:
The game promised and the game delivered exactly that. But players surely expected more, right? I won't spoil the whole thing for you here but I can confidently conclude that at the end of Black Root Burrows, the player is left with more questions than answers. There is no emotional reveal. No sad shocker. No twist.
Nothing. The player gets exactly what he started expecting to happen at about halfway through the area and the emotional value to be experienced is
. No surprises.
Ori and the Blind Forest was already close to the edge of turning its great gameplay into frustrating gameplay, and I'm afraid Definitive Edition succesfully leaped over said ledge.
The original game had no rebindable keys. This is a huge problem for PC gamers. I will admit to finding the default control scheme just fine but I reckon there's also a huge amount of players who aren't comfortable with it at all. Left handed gamers, people who prefer ESDF over WASD, etc.
Ori and the Blind Forest: Definitive Edition has made no effort to fix this. Even in this version you cannot rebind your keys (you can edit your KeyRebindings.txt file but I fear for those unfortunate many who will not discover this method).
This is already bad on its own, but it gets even worse due to Definitive Edition introducing 2 new abilities to the game. BOTH of which require their own key on the keyboard.
So yeah. This game that was once considered by many a "simple platformer" now forces you to utilize half your keyboard with no way of rebinding keys. (Again - I'm not considering the KeyRebindings.txt method as an actual part of the game)
SHIFT to glide.
E to create a soul link.
CTRL to Dash horizontally.
Hold UP to charge your HORIZONTAL dash. (definitely doesn't feel counterintuitive at all)
R to use Light Burst. (which you can aim with the ARROW KEYS if you use the full-keyboard control scheme without the mouse, something that is never explained in-game)
It becomes such a frustrating mess at times. I'm sorry but it really does. In tense moments where you're expected to react quickly it's an infuriating experience to rely on the far too many keys you now require.
To sum this problem up:
The addition of a harder difficulty is nice, but it's implemented in such a dull way that it only makes the game more frustrating.
If
difficulty at all alters the escape sequences in any way, I have
noticed it.
As far as I could tell it did absolutely nothing to those scenes (which I consider the highlights of Ori).
Instead, the only thing
difficulty did was add more difficulty to the normal, calmer parts inbetween those sequences that seem a little dull and repetitive in comparison.
It's the usual difficulty slider like in every other game. All it does is increase the damage taken by enemies.
It did a good job at making the biggest part of the game relatively difficult for me but that only made the rare few escape sequences even more disappointing, as these supposedly "hard" sequences were now easier than the rest of the game due to not being affected by the higher difficulty setting at all.
From the short Black Root Burrows to the difficulty slider, none of this feels impressive enough to condone the developers saying
Stuff like the revisiting areas to reach 100% completion should've been part of the core game all along. Definitely not something a player needs to pay for.
The extra abilities, extra area and difficulty slider... Well, they're nice additions but even when all of them put together I just don't see the reason why this had to become a new game.
A free update would've been far more appropiate for this amount of new content.
Or even a cheap DLC, perhaps.
Not a full game.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a wonderful game. An INCREDIBLE game, in almost every way. Satisfying, enjoyable, astounding, dazzling in both graphics, style, gameplay, story and even music, it's no wonder Moon Studios has won so many awards for their beautiful game.
There are several ways you could describe Ori, if you'd dare. You could call it awesome. You could call it unbelievable. Some might call it frustrating. What ever you may call it, it deserves all the recognition it gets.
Put into the role of an orphaned Guardian Spirit, you must face the merciless and fateful forest of Nibel in its terrifying blindness, to which you must restore the weakened light to. A series of unfortunate events prior to the forest's decay sets Ori on a dangerous path, causing the Spirit Tree, the reason to all Nibel's life, to lose his power. With the guidance of the mystical creature Sein and the bravery to outmaneuver the antagonist Kuro, Ori is Nibel's last hope, a hope that must shine above all else, or the world will never live again.
What I've given you is a mere taste of this inspiring tale of hope and self-discovery; the longer version is something you will have to find for yourself. It probably has one of the best plots I have ever come across in a video game especially, and it only continues to compliment every other attribute of Ori and the Blind Forest. I found the story to be bittersweet, filled with action, thought-provoking, and beautiful in more than one way.
The artwork in Ori and the Blind Forest is altogether breathtaking. I knew, as soon as I saw it, I wanted to immerse myself in the world this game presented. And when once I did... well, let's just say it took forever to get myself out of it. The painted style of Ori and the Blind Forest is something I rarely see in such games, or if I have, it isn't executed nearly as well. The graphics in this game are what initially sold it for me, and as I played, they just complimented everything else even more.
However, Ori isn't just a pretty face- that is important in many cases, but what I'm about to talk about is the GAMEPLAY. Oh, my gosh. Where do I even begin? The mechanics in this game are genius, especially with such a spry and lithe being such as Ori. Everything from the jumps, to the dashing, to the wall climb... they are all fluid, just meant for Ori's agile form. It never once felt too slow or too laggy, and none of the mechanics felt out of place (even the newer ones, which I thoroughly enjoyed).
Am I done? NOPE. There is more still, and that is the MUSIC. The score in this game has enchanted me for the longest time. Sometimes, I'll just put my controller down, slap on my headset and listen for minutes at a time. The effort Moon Studios put into making the music a fantastical experience clearly showed in this fantastic score. The music could go from soft, to loud, to tense, to sad, all with excellent transitions. The music always felt right, and that's the best anybody can do.
I've played the original Ori and the Blind Forest before the Definitive Edition was released, but I will also be reviewing the DE as well. I loved every second of Ori and the Blind Forest, and hearing about the expansion made me buzz with excitement. The thought of returning to the world I loved so much, with even more content and artwork, was like a dream come true. After playing it through again with the DE installed, I realized I had almost forgotten how incredible this game really is. The additional areas and the added backstory with Naru made me appreciate her character perhaps even more so than I did before, and I loved leaping and flipping through the newly painted areas.
The areas, nor the added story, nor the new mechanics seemed out of place to me. That was one of my main concerns when I started playing, that it wouldn't fit with the overall game and dampen my opinion on it. But no, this was not the case even a little. In fact, I think it made me appreciate it MORE.
I'd like to mention quickly that there are a few small things; when I played Ori originally, I would encounter a few bugs, and I have found some here and there in the DE as well. But they haven't really changed anything for me; I understand that a game isn't without its few imperfections. There will be bugs.
So, am I recommending this game to you? YES. YA. SI. If you haven't noticed already, I have a high opinion of Ori and the Blind Forest. 9.8/10, I believe should be fitting. Thank you, Moon Studios, for sharing this incredible creation with us. And thank you, person reading this review, for clicking "Add to Cart". ^^

So I've received the game as a gift. Back then I thought "woah dreams do come true!" because I've been watching Rust gameplays on Youtube for months, I really wanted to try the game myself and I've finally got it from someone.
Pros:
1. OUTSTANDING atmosphere. Sounds, animations, graphics. I still got to find a game that would be even close to Rust in those aspects. The game is expressive, it makes you feel as if you are really there. Every sound and animation are thoroughtly thought-of. Opening a bottle of water, grabbing a sword and watching how the character spins it in the air while at the same time enjoying the crisp sound the metal blade produces when unfolding... dang, even mining a stone with a pickaxe is a show on its own. In brief, the game is immersive, even when played on lowest settings on a non-HD monitor. All of this made me fall in love with the game from first glance. Every sound and animation feels like a sort of reward. However, that's sadly all I can list as a pro.
Cons:
1. Optimization. There was a time Rust could run on a mid-end PC without any issues. Some months ago something changed and the game became almost unplayable for me. It runs smooth and cool when I farm or build, but any gunshot makes my FPS drop to 3-4. The framerate is gone when you need it the most. It's been months and the FPS lag is getting worse for me and for people I know.
2. Lag. Same as before - Rust used to run smoothly with my internet connection, but not anymore. Maybe the FPS issue is what makes the lag pop out so badly, but I can barely kill anyone when using firearms. Which sucks, because even when I get my hands on an AK, I still got to use a shotgun, since it requires little aim. I've been playing First Person Shooters for the past 10 years or so, and it frustrates me that I'm being rekt like a noob because of poor optimization of the game.
3. Community. Last, but definitely not least, Rust community is the illustration of the Theory of Evolution... but backwards. Yeah, you can call it 'degradation'. Rust community is now composed mostly of 12 years old who are bored to death and will be mean to you with no apparent reason. Big servers are plagued with big clans. Small servers always have that handful of permanent dwellers who are farming at least 20 hours a day. Therefore, they have everything and again, they seem to be bored to death. So they will be bullying you just for the "fun" of it.
In conclusion: If you've got no life and at the same time you've got a beefy PC with a GTX 1080Ti, then Rust is definitely a great place to be. Unless, of course, you don't enjoy bullying others for the sake of bullying.
Now, if you want a challenging gameplay with relatively equal conditions, then I'd suggest you to look elsewhere.
Personally, I might get back to Rust from time to time, but on low-pop servers simply to enjoy the atmosphere, the graphics and the sounds of the game. Might gather some resources, enjoy the evolution from stone hatchet to iron pickaxe, build a little cozy base and then quit.

I remeber when this game released. I thought it was just another silly shooter game that was pooped out by a low budget team of devs. I wasn't necessarily wrong though. The game itself is pretty straightforward. Point, shoot, kill. Nothing fancy about it. The cover system was pretty smooth, and it provided a challenge here and there, but mostly the game isn't there for the gameplay aspect as you will soon find out. To me, the game was a pretty big shocker, but it didn't affect me like it has a lot of the other people who have played this game. You won't lose sleep. You won't think that you're a terrible person. This game is just a dramatization of what war is and the things that can go wrong during war. The problem I do have with this game is the fact that I beat it in four ♥♥♥♥ing hours. Seriously. This game is marketed at $30 without a sale and usually it's only around $15 with a sale. Do I think you should buy it? No. Does that mean the game is bad? No. It's just not worth the money to play 4 hours of story mode and then hop into a dead multiplayer. I do recommend this game to someone who can blow money, but to the general gaming community, wait until they drop the price. I don't care how emotional the game may make you feel, 4 hours of gameplay is nowhere near worth $30.

How have I not written a review for this game yet? In a way, this game actually changed my life a little bit. Before you stop reading and write me off as just another obsessed fangirl (I mean... you wouldn't be COMPLETELY wrong there...), here's what I mean by that: This game has impacted my daily life. I give it my time willingly. I listen to fan made songs/remixes when I play games with friends, read comics, talk to friends about it, draw/trace fanart, learn songs (either fan made or from the OST) on piano, and I also fight the hardest boss in the game daily as a streak challenge. If you're looking for something to love, this is the game for you.
Before I talk about the game itself, let me talk about what happens AFTER you finish it. There's SO MUCH beyond the game after you've completed all its major endings. This is one of the most creative and passionate fanbases I've ever seen. AMAZING ideas and things have came out of this game. Hours upon hours I've spent watching dubs, animations, theory videos, listening to music, reading comics. There's always MORE.
The game itself is timeless. It'll hook you within the first half hour. Once you get in this game, it's pretty hard to get out of it. It impacts me emotionally and never fails to make me laugh. It's so complex, you think you know a lot about the game, but you learn something new about it every day. There's SO much replay value. You can find ways to challenge yourself as I have. You'll fall in love with the game design, story, and characters. I can't reccomend this game enough. Every person I've reccomended it to loved it.
This game means the world to me right now, because it's a great thing to love. Meeting people who love it just as much as I do sparks a great friendship. I've met people through the fanbase who are amazing as they are talented. I don't see my love for this game dying any time in the near future. Sure, I go through phases, but this one is going to last for a long time. Thanks for reading this review, now go play the game if you haven't already!

Hitman is what happens when you devote your entire staff to one game. The decision to release this game in episodes was a divisive choice to the consumers, but ended up benefitting both sides tremendously. The obvious cash flow benefits and focus allowed the developers to respond to the issues noted and the gameplay seen within the first episode. Consequently, every episode that followed seemed to tighten the systems in place, or experiment with different ways to use them.
Players will find that this edition caters to what feels like all the different splinter factions of Hitman fans. For those that love open gameplay and replayability this, of course, gives you that in spades. Its contracts mode and elusive targets, along with the myriad ways to eliminate your normal targets, insure this. For those that want to play Absolution style, with no costumes, the maps offer routes and opportunities that will let you do it this way. Sniper Assassins can always get their fix within this game, though the offerrings on weaponry is a bit sparse. Finally, to the die-hard fans who have been around since the beginning, the game offers so many callbacks that you leave smiling every level.
That's not to say it doesnt have its issues. AI can sometimes be super alert, keying in on your activities through a wall. Also, things like overflowing a sink can sometimes glitch, causing it to not be able to be turned off. And cheesing the systems breaks immersion. For example, you can (most times) nudge the bodyguard repeatedly until they are far from your target, and deal with the guard alone. Or in a firefight, you can usually find a bottleneck and kill copious amounts of guards who seem confused as to how to deal with you. This feels wrong. And while it is possible to complete every map with a "kill everyone" personal challenge, the shooting still feels less responsive than you would expect. This has always been a small issue with the hitman games, but hopefully it can be addressed in the upcoming sequel. The most annoying of the problems has to be when you try to execute a choke out, only for the system to register it as face to face combat. This can lead to an entire session, such as stalking an elusive target, needing to be scrapped.
While not without issues, Hitman stands as a shining example of how the episodic business model can allow you to address issues and feedback quickly, improving your game as it goes on and extending the positive exposure. By the final episode, you sense the developers have mastered the technical and creative aspects of their game, and are primed to take it to the next level for season 2.

I already reviewed the original game and much of what I had to say about that still holds true. However, there are a few important things the DE does that I feel improve the original in several welcome ways. And this game always deserves my thumbs up.
* 2 new areas that expand a bit of backstory for a certian character. These areas a beautifully well done and fit right in where they are placed. They also feel unique and have their own mechanics and puzzles built around them in addition to weaving in the new abilities.
* 2 new abilities, a dash and a "grenade"-like orb, with new skills on the skill tree to improve them. Very fun to use and usefull outside of their obligitory use to get certian collectables. I found that when upgrading the dash to be useable in the air, it was immensely helpful in the escape segments which in turn improved them overall for me. It made them more fluid and fun. I did play the origional nearly 9 months ago so maybe the muscle memory hasnt worn off yet but still, they were welcome additions to further expand the already fun gameplay. The upgrade to make the air-dash an attack was simply ♥♥♥♥ing awesome. My inner Mass Effect Vanguard was giddy as hell using it. A ton of fun and super impactful.
* Spirit wells are now fast travel points. Allowing you to teleport to any previously used well. Some may complain this takes away some of the backtracking that made the original "feel". But I think it improves the pacing of the game. Exploration fans like me still take time to traverse the scenery and unless you are going for 100% completion from the get go, you arent using these wells terribly often. If you are adverse to fast travel, simply use them as save points and nothing else, it is still possible to beat the game without using the feature.
* You can now revisit areas that would previously be locked after exploring. A huge plus for me, and made 100% completion more enjoyable. Plus being able to revisit the Ginso Tree was a huge delight.
* Difficulty options are available. Playing through 3 out of the 4 (the 4th being permadeath); completing the game on normal, I think "Hard" best caputres what the original was all about. But for those more interested in the sights and soundscapees the game provides, the first two difficulties suitably allow others to complete the game with maybe a bit less frustration. You might still snap your keyboard at the escape sections however.
To adress the cons I had for the original game:
* Escape sections I feel are more fluid provided you have the new dash ability, more so if you can use it in the air by unlocking the skill from the green skill tree. However they can still be quite trial and error. Even with the difficulty turned onto easy, the following hazards will instant kill you regardless: rising waters, giant falling rocks, lava, large fire balls, lasers, and
. That said, the non-lethal hazards are more forgiving and allow more mistakes on these sections. But still be mentally prepared for it. Overall I had a much more enjoyable time with them than the first time, but muscle memory might have stayed with me over the past 9 months.
* The droning old narrator grew on me. So subjective is still subjective.
* You can revisit areas previously locked off after exploring.
* I still think that (Story Spoilers)
Despite this, I still really enjoyed the emotionally charged storybook narrative the game had.
Overall however, this game has definately improved from the tweeks and additions it had. For 5$ as an owner of the original, it was a no brainer. For new comers, 20$ is still a great price for what you get.

So I've received the game as a gift. Back then I thought "woah dreams do come true!" because I've been watching Rust gameplays on Youtube for months, I really wanted to try the game myself and I've finally got it from someone.
Pros:
1. OUTSTANDING atmosphere. Sounds, animations, graphics. I still got to find a game that would be even close to Rust in those aspects. The game is expressive, it makes you feel as if you are really there. Every sound and animation are thoroughtly thought-of. Opening a bottle of water, grabbing a sword and watching how the character spins it in the air while at the same time enjoying the crisp sound the metal blade produces when unfolding... dang, even mining a stone with a pickaxe is a show on its own. In brief, the game is immersive, even when played on lowest settings on a non-HD monitor. All of this made me fall in love with the game from first glance. Every sound and animation feels like a sort of reward. However, that's sadly all I can list as a pro.
Cons:
1. Optimization. There was a time Rust could run on a mid-end PC without any issues. Some months ago something changed and the game became almost unplayable for me. It runs smooth and cool when I farm or build, but any gunshot makes my FPS drop to 3-4. The framerate is gone when you need it the most. It's been months and the FPS lag is getting worse for me and for people I know.
2. Lag. Same as before - Rust used to run smoothly with my internet connection, but not anymore. Maybe the FPS issue is what makes the lag pop out so badly, but I can barely kill anyone when using firearms. Which sucks, because even when I get my hands on an AK, I still got to use a shotgun, since it requires little aim. I've been playing First Person Shooters for the past 10 years or so, and it frustrates me that I'm being rekt like a noob because of poor optimization of the game.
3. Community. Last, but definitely not least, Rust community is the illustration of the Theory of Evolution... but backwards. Yeah, you can call it 'degradation'. Rust community is now composed mostly of 12 years old who are bored to death and will be mean to you with no apparent reason. Big servers are plagued with big clans. Small servers always have that handful of permanent dwellers who are farming at least 20 hours a day. Therefore, they have everything and again, they seem to be bored to death. So they will be bullying you just for the "fun" of it.
In conclusion: If you've got no life and at the same time you've got a beefy PC with a GTX 1080Ti, then Rust is definitely a great place to be. Unless, of course, you don't enjoy bullying others for the sake of bullying.
Now, if you want a challenging gameplay with relatively equal conditions, then I'd suggest you to look elsewhere.
Personally, I might get back to Rust from time to time, but on low-pop servers simply to enjoy the atmosphere, the graphics and the sounds of the game. Might gather some resources, enjoy the evolution from stone hatchet to iron pickaxe, build a little cozy base and then quit.

On the other hand the Game lets you decide on some occasions and thats what it does good, you dont have to press a key to nod yes or go right instead of left... no no it just lets you work out your own solution. These Situations are also very rare.
It does a great Job in showing you how bad War can and will be, but then again most of the time you are just playing a generic cover shooter and everything almost feels the same and you are just wondering how can 3 ppl kill so many guys (but hey it is a game). I am glad that there were atleast some nice Weapons along the way to maybe test out a different playstyle. ( i just like to snipe everybody). I also have to add that this game is quite bloody and gory, i also like that kind of stuff.
All in all i recommend this game because it is a cover shooter and it kinda makes fun, tho i cant imagine playing this game in one go, i had like 4-5, because you die stupid deaths and the fights are exhausting. This game is basically Arkham City all over again.
If you liked collecting riddler trophies, you will be collecting datadiscs now (but the buttons and switches are alot easier to figure out).
If you liked beating up riddler's snitches, you will be beating snitches up again (and guess who's snitches they are).
If you liked AR challenges, you will be doing those again (but at least they are alot easier now).
the list goes on...
only the riddler secrets are missing. argueably they are replaced by different symbols that you have to scan (one of them only visible in detective vision, given you yet another reason to keep it permenently on...), but the difficult part is discovering the locations now instead of riddling which is kind of a loss of depth too.
the problem is not that the game reuses old materials and play elements. The problem is that it does nothing else.
The city has a few more areas than in Arkham City. But you will find yourself gliding over the same buildings as in Arkham City most of the time.
Indoors you will find the same interiors as in Arkham City as well. There are few but very scarce new elements.
Story-wise you will see a few new faces that havent been featured before, but most of them desolve a bit too quickly or have very brief screentime.
What annoys me most though is the inconsistency of the story, which is supposed to be a prequel to Arkham Asylum. It does a steady job on preparing the setting for it, but in doing that it takes a few too many liberties:
A very early stage of Batman, the hero, is being shown. He is still emotionally unsteady and kind of a loner. He is supposed to meet, struggle with and grow on the Joker.
Given that awesome scenario, i simply cannot grasp what is made out of it.
Why does Joker know Batman already?
Why does Blackmask know Batman well enough to hire other villians to assassinate him (who also seem to know Batman already)?
Why does Batman know Joker? Batman: "that name sounds familiar" Familiar? How can you not remember joker once you meet him?!)
How can he ask Alfred for more information about a "certain Joker" and immediately get a reply?
Why does Bane already have a personal vendetta against Batman?
The list goes on.
The story would have proved countless opportunities to introduce all those conflicts in Arkham, yet it is very ambivalent and far too brief in it's presentation.
The only real highlight of this part of the franchise is the extended Crime Scene inspection. In the old parts you simply had to scan a few objects on the crime scene location and get a bit of dialog between batman and some of his allies. Now you are doing the same, but you are also reconstructing the crime and have to replay it back in forth to find even more points of interest. Unfortunately this highlight is not extended to its full potential yet, but it is a step into the right direction.
As negative as my review sounds i would have prefered a neutral rating, since this would have been a solid large DLC or Addon (Developed by the studio WB Games Montreal that took over from Rocksteady). Not more.
I can recommend grabbing this on a sale, as long you can live with the technical redundancies.

Undeserved hate!  People seem to dog this game for falling short of the first two.  I would argue that it only falls short in terms of the little loving details and riddles of the first games: A Ras Al Ghul toe tag on a corpse in the morgue, an ad for the Flying Graysons, those little additions that Batman fans (like me) appreciate.  But this game makes up for those missing details in a few meaningful ways, completing what I will argue is the COMPLETE BATMAN EXPERIENCE:
*Big Gotham: It has a very large Gotham City (although there is more on the horizon) compared with Arkham City, which put you in a moody, but smaller walled-off portion of Gotham.  The additions to the AC Gotham are really noteworthy.  The new neighborhoods are nicer, higher class, and have a neat feel.  I really like the big Hotel.
*Batcave: Finally we get to go back and forth between Gotham and the cave.  The cave's design is very nice, with good details that give a wink to the prior games (plans for the zipline from AA which has not been fully built yet).
* Batwing: You use it to quick travel only, but it's cool.  It would be pain, and unrealistic (within the story/universe) for Batman to jog across the city when he needs to get somewhere.  This is a nice addition.
* Nice suit: It's  across between comics and the Christian Bale/Nolan suit.  Love it or hate it... for me, video game adaptions of movies are usually bad, but I always wanted an open world Batman game.  The ways that this Batman looks a little Nolan-y, growls at bad guys, and drives (pilots?) his Batwing through the waterfall into the Cave, all remind me of Nolan stuff (which is a positive for me).
* More side missions: It has more than the last game.  They are pretty basic but it adds to the overall Batman experience.
* Story: This story is as good as the last two.  It takes you through cool locations and setpieces (like the awesome Gotham hotel)
* Characters: This game has some of the corrupt cops from Frank Miller's Batman Year One (my favorite) which was a huge plus for me.
The only things it lacks in terms of the complete Batman experience are other playable characters like Robin and Catwoman, but those don't fit the prequel timeframe.
Overall, I rate the trilogy (so far) like this:
Arkham Asylum A+++ (overall atmosphere, the original)
Arkham City A+++ (perfectly brought AA into an open world, great story, just awesome)
Arkham Origins A+ (see above)
I will continue to play all 3 games for a long time.  I would describe this game as a love letter to fans of Batman Year One, Batman Nolan movies, Batman comics, and Tim Burton's Batman Returns (in appearance only, snowy Christmas theme).
If someone told me they were making a Batman game that was an open-world blend of Nolan, Burton, comics, and Miller, I would have been really excited... and I am really happy with this game.

The only game I've ever stopped watching a Let's Play of with the intent to buy and play myself, and I've watched ALOT of games.
Definitive Edition:
The definitive edition is better than the original but not totally without its flaws.
Pros:
+New Difficulty settings, so newbs don't get destroyed and pros don't fly through it.
+New Warp System, saves a lot of backtracking. Especially when you want to bypass a convoluted area.
+Adds a New Area, very pretty (as per usual) with unique puzzles.
+Two new abilities, found inside the new area.
+Lots of behind the scenes movies and concept art.
Cons:
-The new area isn’t integrated into the plot, as in it is optional to go to it. As such you can get into too early and die or wait too long and it isn’t a challenge.
-The two new abilities while interesting aren’t highly useful, compared to double jump. On the final level you have use all the abilities you’ve gained thus far however the new abilities feel extraneous.
-Reorganized upgrade tree, almost everything costs more points and additionally they padded out the utility tree with upgrades for abilities you probably won’t get for a while, so getting to triple jump, one of the most useful abilities, is far harder to get. Additonaly water breathing is now so far up the upgrade tree that in the instance in the game that it is the most useful it is impossble to get as you can't get enough xp to get it by that point.
-This expansion STILL didn't add the ability to rebind keys, which causes difficutly when using a mouse and keyboard. Doubly so when you factor in the new abilities one of which I would have used far more if it wasnt all the way on Ctrl. Who the hell puts Dash on Ctrl? You can't hit that quickly. As such I never used a useful ability due to keybinding.
While I am put off by some of the new stuff I still think the Definitive Edition is an improvement on the base game. As I love the base game then by the transitive property of equivalence I highly recommend Ori and the Blind Forest, Definitive Edition. Now that that is over with I am now eagerly waiting for Ori 2.
Beat the Defintiive Edtion in 7 hours and with about 225 deaths. I don't have the self confidence to look up what a speed/no hit/no upgrade run would look like...
Original Ori Review:
A beautiful platforming game which took me about 11 hours and I think around 500 deaths to complete the first time. The sounds and visuals are the best part about this game and the character you play as is adorable. The game is a bit hard for non-pro-platformers like me, particularly the escape sequences. While some of them you could theoretically get on your first try, one stands out as being totally trial and error on where you needed to go which meant you needed to die in order to know how to beat it, something I think it a bit unfair. As a Hitman series veteran with more than a hundred hours spent on every game in the series (except absolution) i thought it would be appropriate to share my oppinion on the game with the community. I have made a detailed list of pros and cons , and for the impatient i have written a quick summary at the bottom of this review.
(Hitman : Absolution doesnot even deserve to be on the list for obvious reasons)
A worthy addition to the hitman series that every hitman veteran gamer should get his/hers hands on, the devs really tried to get us an experience as close to the original quadrilogy as possible even exceeding expectations in some aspects although some minor improvements could have made this experience the ultimate hitman game.
Now is the best time to start! Elusive target reset.

If you like replayability, easter eggs and funny AI, this is the assassin simulator for you.
Growing up on Hitman 2, Contracts, Blood Money; I've had my fair share of hitman games. I enjoyed the open world, go where you want, do what you want. The older games offered very little in improvisation but IOI took the critique of Hitman Absolution and made something close to a master piece this year.
I'll start with the cons of the game so I can top of the with the pros. I had to scrap my HD 6970 that has been faithful for 6 years in order to play this game. The game uses Denuvo and heavy CPU dependencies so the game always ran at close to 100% on a quad core, making the game fall back in performance. Even the lowest graphic settings that looked worse than Hitman Blood Money could not make the game run on a rig that runs Arma 3 with long view distance. If you slow down the game to 70% using an external program, you can get it to run more smoothly, which indicates that there's CPU optimizations to be done on the game.
After getting the R9 390X the game ran at more than 60fps on highest detail settings. Playing the game was achievable and the graphics are very nice on each level.
Elusive targets provide a hard core roguelike experience as you are only allowed to do them once and once you started killing your targets, the "restart mission" button fades to black. The elusive target missions however are a little quirky because there's little to no information on what zones you are allowed to go to and what disguises work. In order to play these missions, you must know the original level by heart and be a master assassin, so that you can assassinate your targets with the information you have gathered over the multiple times you've played the level. Something that puts me at disadvantage because I did not play levels more than twice per mission.
Equipment loadouts provide very few objects compared to the old games. You get 2 items + a gun, 1 item to be smuggled and that's it. In Hitman Blood Money the coins were infinite which provided more freedom, but Hitman™ forces you to find and pick up coins. The problem was further solved by making any object throwable so there's more things to throw that you can keep in the inventory (e.g pasta cans)
No quick save and quick load buttons. Hitman Absolution used checkpoints saves but they would respawn all the enemies in an area. Now Hitman™ uses a proper save system but failed to put a quick save feature in.
The pros of the game are plenty. Interesting AI dialog, but gets tedious to listen to the 5th time you forgot to save. Weapon handling is smooth and quick with 60fps and with practice you can Leon a whole room of bad guys with 7 bullets without sounding the alarm. They removed the sniper rifle suit case and used a rifle on back system instead, which makes the game a little harder. On top of that, they didn't provide the missions with good sniper spots like in HBM so it balances out.
There's also plenty of accidental kills that allows for absolute joy in killing. Exploding barrels, overheating saunas, poisoning of both food and drinks, it gives humorous events in the game.
I give this game 7.5/10.
Minus for performance craving Denuvo.
Minus for the 7 missions for 50 USD game.
Plus for creativity and opportunities.

I like Sister Location, a lot. The production values are a lot higher, the voice acting is good, and the story is the most intriguing that FNAF has produced since the first game. Scott deserves a lot of credit for his hard work on the title.
That said, as many other players and reviewers have noted, this game's difficulty is very poorly balanced. It's like all five levels were put together into a basket, shaken up, and then arranged in whatever order they were plucked out of. The first night, the tutorial, is obviously a no-brainer. The second night took me over an hour to complete. The third night I beat on my first try, and the fourth level, as with many others, is breaking my balls.
Scott, please consider rebalancing the game a bit so that the difficulty is incremental, not schizophrenic. I want to like and continue the game but its levels are all over the place.

A game reminiscent of Mario Party with board game mechanics.
A board game themed witcher game, which features characters from the witcher series in the game. Basically, it plays like a board game on the pc. If you ever played any of the Mario Party games, this game is similiar. Each player takes good or bad card hits on their turn and can move spaces or do certain actions on each turn. Note that it seems that negative cards usually are more in the game then positive cards, but that what makes it interesting, what you do with the negative effects and play a round with them. Anyways, here is my pro/con list as usual:
PROs:
`Featuring characters in the Witcher series
`Board game mechanics
`Interesting playing cards randomized to give good or bad fates
`Quests that you need to do
`Online Multiplayer
`Local Co-op up to 4 players
CONs:
`Repitition. Every turn, you do something, kill a monster (or fail), and then end turn. Every turn is similiar.
`Getting killed by same monster every turn can happen to you, thus making you fail the game
MY final thoughts: If your a fan of the witcher series, i recommend it. Also, there is multiplayer online play. Other than that, this game can become repitive if you play it too much. Be careful of that.

After a good 200+ hours, the first thing I have to say is: "this is not Minecraft." I don't even know why anyone would think that this is a copy, and if it is, it is unrecognisible. Minecraft doesn't have nearly as many different items, blocks, weapons, armor choices, bosses, ores, somewhat-fleshed-out-beyond-trading NPCs, the list goes on. And it's 2d, adding (or removing?!) a dimension that makes this an even more unique game. This is one of the best survival games out there (in my humble opinion), and a must-buy for fans of survival games focused around boss fights. Terarria even has a set course of action, somewhat like an RPG. You don't have to follow these patterns, but you can't access the entirety of the game without beating certain bosses (The wall of flesh is a good example. A good 3/4 of the game is locked behind that wall, and you need to destroy it to get it), and you may need to fight a boss to get the weapons required to fight the bigger boss. (Like the Eye of Cuthlulu, the first boss. He drops materials that allow you to build a sword that is strong enough for the upcoming pre-hardmode bosses, like the Brain of Cuthlulu (if you have a Crimson-infested world), or the Eater of Worlds (if you have a Corruption-infested world.)). Overall, Terraria is NOT Minecraft, and is all the better of a game for it. It still keeps the core concepts, but adds in a lot more to the mix.

* 2 new areas that expand a bit of backstory for a certian character. These areas a beautifully well done and fit right in where they are placed. They also feel unique and have their own mechanics and puzzles built around them in addition to weaving in the new abilities.
* 2 new abilities, a dash and a "grenade"-like orb, with new skills on the skill tree to improve them. Very fun to use and usefull outside of their obligitory use to get certian collectables. I found that when upgrading the dash to be useable in the air, it was immensely helpful in the escape segments which in turn improved them overall for me. It made them more fluid and fun. I did play the origional nearly 9 months ago so maybe the muscle memory hasnt worn off yet but still, they were welcome additions to further expand the already fun gameplay. The upgrade to make the air-dash an attack was simply ♥♥♥♥ing awesome. My inner Mass Effect Vanguard was giddy as hell using it. A ton of fun and super impactful.
* Spirit wells are now fast travel points. Allowing you to teleport to any previously used well. Some may complain this takes away some of the backtracking that made the original "feel". But I think it improves the pacing of the game. Exploration fans like me still take time to traverse the scenery and unless you are going for 100% completion from the get go, you arent using these wells terribly often. If you are adverse to fast travel, simply use them as save points and nothing else, it is still possible to beat the game without using the feature.
* You can now revisit areas that would previously be locked after exploring. A huge plus for me, and made 100% completion more enjoyable. Plus being able to revisit the Ginso Tree was a huge delight.
* Difficulty options are available. Playing through 3 out of the 4 (the 4th being permadeath); completing the game on normal, I think "Hard" best caputres what the original was all about. But for those more interested in the sights and soundscapees the game provides, the first two difficulties suitably allow others to complete the game with maybe a bit less frustration. You might still snap your keyboard at the escape sections however.
To adress the cons I had for the original game:
* Escape sections I feel are more fluid provided you have the new dash ability, more so if you can use it in the air by unlocking the skill from the green skill tree. However they can still be quite trial and error. Even with the difficulty turned onto easy, the following hazards will instant kill you regardless: rising waters, giant falling rocks, lava, large fire balls, lasers, and
. That said, the non-lethal hazards are more forgiving and allow more mistakes on these sections. But still be mentally prepared for it. Overall I had a much more enjoyable time with them than the first time, but muscle memory might have stayed with me over the past 9 months.
* The droning old narrator grew on me. So subjective is still subjective.
* You can revisit areas previously locked off after exploring.
* I still think that (Story Spoilers)
Despite this, I still really enjoyed the emotionally charged storybook narrative the game had.
Overall however, this game has definately improved from the tweeks and additions it had. For 5$ as an owner of the original, it was a no brainer. For new comers, 20$ is still a great price for what you get.

Definitive Edition:
The definitive edition is better than the original but not totally without its flaws.
Pros:
+New Difficulty settings, so newbs don't get destroyed and pros don't fly through it.
+New Warp System, saves a lot of backtracking. Especially when you want to bypass a convoluted area.
+Adds a New Area, very pretty (as per usual) with unique puzzles.
+Two new abilities, found inside the new area.
+Lots of behind the scenes movies and concept art.
Cons:
-The new area isn’t integrated into the plot, as in it is optional to go to it. As such you can get into too early and die or wait too long and it isn’t a challenge.
-The two new abilities while interesting aren’t highly useful, compared to double jump. On the final level you have use all the abilities you’ve gained thus far however the new abilities feel extraneous.
-Reorganized upgrade tree, almost everything costs more points and additionally they padded out the utility tree with upgrades for abilities you probably won’t get for a while, so getting to triple jump, one of the most useful abilities, is far harder to get. Additonaly water breathing is now so far up the upgrade tree that in the instance in the game that it is the most useful it is impossble to get as you can't get enough xp to get it by that point.
-This expansion STILL didn't add the ability to rebind keys, which causes difficutly when using a mouse and keyboard. Doubly so when you factor in the new abilities one of which I would have used far more if it wasnt all the way on Ctrl. Who the hell puts Dash on Ctrl? You can't hit that quickly. As such I never used a useful ability due to keybinding.
While I am put off by some of the new stuff I still think the Definitive Edition is an improvement on the base game. As I love the base game then by the transitive property of equivalence I highly recommend Ori and the Blind Forest, Definitive Edition. Now that that is over with I am now eagerly waiting for Ori 2.
Beat the Defintiive Edtion in 7 hours and with about 225 deaths. I don't have the self confidence to look up what a speed/no hit/no upgrade run would look like...

Although this opinion may not be popular, i'm tempted to consider arkham origins the best one of the trilogy.
The gameplay is obviously similar to the previous titles, but it added some changes i really liked. First, i think it's graphically better, it has a darker atmosphere, nice physx and lighting effects and, at least on my rig, it runs smoother than City. A lot are complaining about the bugs, but so far i had to restart the game only once, unlike city, where i had to restart it twice.
However, what i appreciated the most is the inspiration taken from Nolan's trilogy. Origins depicts a younger batman, a batman filled with anger that shows some pretty brute manners. I think that only origins portrays batman for what he should be: fear, a detterent against criminals, and you'll fell this from the first scenes. Plus, this time, the military Nolan's style suit is just sweet. Never liked the comic ones. It's a pity they didn't add a way to repair it visiting the batcave, considering that we'll come back there several times during the game.
Bought it for 16€, and i'm not regretting it. If it's your first batman, this may be the one for you, it has no backstory and you won't need the previous titles to understand what's going on.

I did Undertale after finishing 120h of Witcher 3 and I'm so glad I did. It's a very refreshing game to play after so many hours of pointlessly slaughtering bandits just for asking directions... That sounds boring, I know, but it's actually REALLY HARD. To actually succeed the True Pacifist route, you have to be bloody determined not to kill anyone, even if everything in the game encourages you to do so.
And because it IS a possible thing, killing becomes... much more significant. And horrifying.
If you're a fan of RPGs, please play this game. It puts all the genre clichés into perspective and really shows that you don't have to stick to them to make something amazing.

This game has by far some of the most frustrating mechanics of any game I have ever played.
Let's start with the basics: it's a cover-based, squad-based third-person shooter.  Well, except for the fact that there is one magical button for sprinting/cover/rotating out of cover/healing your teammates.  Roll a dice to figure-out which one the game will pick to do this time!  Want to heal your squad member?  Sorry, you're rushing into the meat grinder like a maggot straight out of basic!  Want to sprint to that cover?  No dice chief, it's at a slight angle so instead you're sprinting next to the cover until you mash the button enough that your character decides to commit suicide.  But there is cover, so I guess you could call it "cover-based."  Don't even get me started on the grenades.
Oh, and did I mention your squad?  Your two helpful teammates with minds of their own, who love to run out of cover and get shot and bleed out and force you to replay the same section over and over because they are too stupid to just stay put and keep their heads down.  I don't know whether I spent more time replaying chapters because they died or replaying chapters because I kept shooting them in the face.
Thankfully the third person mechanic saves everything.  As long as everything you need to shoot is on your right.  If it's on your left you're out of luck.
Issues aside, my favorite part of the game are the setpieces.  Those wonderful scripted moments where something completely out of your control happens in a masterful stroke of storytelling and you have to play the same thirty-second section again and again for over an hour because the scripted event accidentally kills you.  Whoops.
The story is well-told, the atmosphere is perfect, the music is fitting, and the characters' development is superb.  It's a great Heart of Darkness adaptation and a nice parallel of the modern problems with US jingoistic foreign policy and military hero worship.  Even with all of its problems, I'd still recommend playing through it for the story alone.  Just make sure you choose the cake-walk difficulty to avoid tearing your hair out.

Ignore playtime, I have a couple hours offline due to Internet being dead at one point. Video review:
Eaten Alive is an interesting concept in RPG Maker games, but ultimately falls flat due to being unfinished and horribly empty. It's a perma-death zombie survival game that has many things going for it potentially. You play as Mia, a dark, edgy heroine I can only imagine as someone's self-insert into a zombie apocalypse. She can't kill the zombies and she dies in one hit (Unless you avoid damage via a very bland quicktime event). I like the idea of not being able to kill zombies but you can't honestly tell me there isn't some way our useless heroine Mia can't pick up some of the odds and ends lying around to attack the slowest moving zombies ever created.
Speaking of which, the zombies are more of an arbitrary obstacle that more or less serve the purpose to slow you down. They move in a pattern that leads them closer to you, but they move like they're walking in molasses in the middle of the quicksand. The fact that they are so spread out doesn't help at all either. They're not intimidating. They're not scary. They're not even threatening. They're just a mild annoyance. It's the equivalent of Megaman X7's 3D level design.
And on the subject of level design, doors. You like locked doors? Boy do I hope so, because almost every door in this game is locked! In my few hours of playing and researching, I could only find ONE key, and it led me to Jim Sterling's apartment with his terribly bland and lame minigames. I'd like to point out that Jim Sterling's cameo is a selling point for this game. Thank GOD for that, right? Because that'll save a game whose original focus was zombies, when it was early access.
The areas do look nice in places. The city shows signs of destruction, as one would expect when military intervention occurs. However, the park and the cemetery areas have some of the most nonsensical layouts I've ever seen. They look more like they belong on a Final Fantasy overworld than an actual level map.
Perhaps the biggest flaw in the game is the lack of content and the lack of direction. You are free to roam wherever. There's nothing wrong with that, except when you don't give the player access to damn near anything. All those locked doors? There's no key. There's no way to get in to almost ANY of them. And you're telling me Mia can't take a trash can and smash a window to break into the building? Seriously?
This game was early access at one point. It's now released. It isn't finished. You can't complete it. There is virtually NO story. I'd find it easier to recommend dining at an Olive Garden dumpster than spending a dollar on this trash.

This RPG maker is a good attempt at trying to create a functional game however it just fails at all the important points.
Eaten alive is an RPG where you play as a character called Mia, probably the most lifeless character i have seen in a while. your goal is well, there is no goal you just decide to leave without reason and run around outside between "zombies" that are slower then a bike with triangular wheels.
The story of this game is the woman Mia staying in a warehouse with possibly her brother or friend Mac, he has locked them in that warehouse to protect them from the zombie horde outside. for no reason Mia debates with Mac that she wants to leave. All the points that she makes make no sense and are no reason for her to leave at all. After she "escapes" from the warehouse she ends up on the street where a massive horde of about 3 zombies slowly waddles around. After this i eventually got so sick of the game that i couldn't play any more.
By this i mean that the most prominent character, Mia, is so unbelievable i could not even be immersed by the slightest. The story of her family is cliche, unoriginal and mostly very boring. There are no reasons to like her, only to not like her because of her ridicilous amount of swear in unnesecary places; which the developers probably thought was cool but it's really not.

The game itsself has a lot of problems, i have not experienced many of these but the ones i did made it very annoying. For example, i cannot open the settings screen; every time i try the game gives an error and crashes. The mouse is a seperate mouse that doesnt follow your own cursor, to reveal it you have to move your cursor up far enough until you see the game cursor; i think this is ridicilous.
And most imporantly, objects you need to interact with have incredibly small zones in which the neccesary icon needed for intteracting with them shows up; which in a game about interracting with objects is really gamebreaking. Not only did this frustrate me it also ruined any immersion i had left for the game as i continously wondered if i had missed anything and if certain things were supposed to happen.
According to the steam page this game has an amazing soundtrack, and it does! the only problem is that you only hear it in the main menu and for the rest of the game you hear the same annoying 7 second mp3 which made me turn off the sound. The soundtrack on the main menu is amazing, it's very catchy fast paced and it sounds very nice; i just wonder why they didn't put it in the actual game.
Eaten Alive is a fun attempt at an oversaturated genre, but like many other games it fails at it's main purpose. The gameplay is repetitive. The game doesnt function well due to many technical flaws. The immersion is absolutely horrendous. And the story is incredibly lame and cliche. I would recommend you spend your dollar on a different product then this one.

Sister Location had me hooked the entire way through. Everything from the art, voice acting, puzzles, characters and gameplay were on point, and its easy to see just how much hard work went into this game. You are getting 100% what you paid for, and even more content exclusive to this partivular game in the series.
However, the pacing in this game is much different from the prevoius games. Instead of staying in one room with a monitor, you get to explore the entire underground facility.  Exploring each room gives a legit feeling of free-roam gameplay, and offers a new challenge wherever you go.
But I must rant about something that had me stuck for HOURS.
Throughout the game, you are given the instructions to press "W" for forward, and "S" for back.
There comes a moment in the game where you are told to go different directions, however it is never explained how to do so. I spent countless hours trying over, and over again moving my mouse to whichever part of the screen the direction is, but no luck. I kept dying and having to go all the way back to the point I was at, because the checkpoint was so far back.
The solution is to use "A" and "D", even though you were NEVER tought to use those keys. But, things werent adding up. Sometimes using my original method of moving the mouse, I would make some progress just before getting killed, leaving me clueless of what to do.
I think that this part of the game should be fixed, and additional onscreen instructions for "A" and "D" must be added.
Besides that, the game was FANTASTIC! I can't wait for what could happen in the future for the series!

Hey, how's it going, Guys? Heroe here. I wrote a review of this game the day it came out, and in it I'll admit, I was salty and cynnical. That's not who I am. I got frustrated with MANY things going on in my life and I kinda took it out on Scott.

No matter how much I said I didn't like the game, I really enjoyed the game. I gave it time for consideration, reconsideration, ecaluation, etc. I'd call that a big LIKE.

The game is chocked full with story, scares, and adrenaline. The constant feeling to survive each animatronic was thrilling and very enjoyable. It takes a stance on how well one person can make something and how far it can go.
The only cons I have for the game (aside from Night 4's difficulty. Scott patched it so I'll leave it alone) is the intructions. Baby/Ennard will tell you one thing, which indicates a game mechanic. Ex: Baby tells you not to move in the Springlock suit. A and D will move you. Baby says "Don't touch those buttons." but touching those buttons is key to survival. There are a few times that happens in the game, and all it needs to fix the confusion, is something like the instructions in FNAF 4. There was the transparent grey box telling you how to fend of the animatronics and how to manuever around the room. This game really does need that.

It does seem like the story changes with every game. This one explains William Afton's secret plan on how he plans on killing the kids: Cute kid friendly pizzaria filled with cute robots secretly designed to kill. But that's not my problem. William Afton planted a walkie talkie in the Fredbear plush and managed to move it around and whisper things to the boy. This is concluded by the secret Ennard room on Night 5. 3 Security cameras were placed in his house, watching him as he faced off against his nightmares. Or did he? There is a hidden map placement linking Sister Location's rooms to FNAF 4's rooms. It's deep underground from this boy's house. This boy was nothing more than an expierement/test. On these floor plans, animatronic locations are marked. There are 5 plushtraps, meaning there wasn't just one. It was a case of the Tortoise and the Hare, how the Tortoise's brothers tricked the Hare into thinking he was ahead of him. When one plushtrap moves and hides, another one becomes active and runs to the next room, and so on. Nightmare animatronic locations are placed on the map as well, so were they actually nightmares, or were they real robots desgined to terrify. That would explain why we explode into a splatter of blood when we die in FNAF 4. But then what about the halloween update, when Scott said that Nightmare Balloon Boy fits into the lore and isn't there just for fun. The boy saw a tubby child holding his balloon, then proceeded to have nightmares of him. But Sister Location said these are real robots. But Scott said they were Nightmares.
The story isn't adding up correctly and we need some clarification. And so I ask, Scott. Can we know more? Can you give some hints like you did for solving FNAF 4? And will there be a continuation of Sister Location's story? (SL 2 or SL book, etc.)

I love Ori and the Blind Forest. The art is beautiful, the music is charming and enjoyable and the gameplay is fun. The definitive edition makes some good steps forward, removing all the points of no return that existed in the original, and even added the unnecessary ability to teleport between spirit wells.
If you're new to Ori, then I can't recommend picking this up enough. It's fantastic and more than worth the investment. I personally recommend starting with the original, as I feel it paces itself better and is all around a more enjoyable experience despite the points of no return.
If you're a prior owner of Ori, I would say that the new content is probably worth $5 for most of you, though I can definitely understand why some people would be disappointed. There are 2 new abilities for Ori (ignoring the passive skill tree), 1 new environment where you learn about Naru's past, and the above mentioned spirit well teleport and removal of points of no return. It's not insignificant, but perhaps not as much as the description might lead you to believe.
Highly recommended if you've never played, hesitant recommendation for prior owners until the discount expires.

Ori and the Blind Forest is one of the best platforming titles that I've had the fortune to play.  The game features simple but deep gameplay mechanics, a stellar artstyle, and a soundtrack moving enough to bring a man to tears.  If you have not played this game yet, I cannot recommend it enough.  My review, however, mostly regards the Definitive Edition.
For the time being, owners of the older version have the option to upgrade to the D.E. for five dollars.  The additions include a new area that offers up to an hour of gameplay, a couple new abilities, and a lot of minor tweaks and improvements.  The new area was enjoyable to play through, and was quite diverse as the tone of the game would change as you progress.  I also found the two new abilities to be very useful and made a substantial impact on how I played through the game.
One downside to these new abilities is that with my increased range of movement, some of the later abilities were less needed when it came to reaching difficult places.  Some of the existing "puzzles" were also changed to incorporate one of the new abilities.  Getting this new powerup, however, is not required to progress through the main story, so those that do not get this ability will have a less enjoyable experience.  I personally liked that there was a substantial reward for exploring and going off the beaten path.  These changes to the puzzles made the game a bit more interesting, as you had to keep an eye out for certain background objects and did something other than pounding on a pole to open a gate.
Another big change is that the player now has the ability to teleport between spirit portals.  One may think that this breaks up the pace of the game, since you no longer would have to walk through the areas when traversing the map.  However, at most points in the game there were many new collectibles to get when moving between areas.  Additionally, the portals are spaced far enough away that it was often easier just to manually move through the map.  This new feature saved time at a few points where I did not have to backtrack, but did not have any major effect on the way I played the game, so I would say it is an overall positive addition.  The game also now lets you return to areas previously locked off after leaving and lets you return to your save after completing the game, making 100% completions a lot more tolerable to do.
All-in-all, I thoroughly enjoyed playing through this masterpiece again with the new gameplay and features.  I do wish the D.E. provided more content, considering that upgrading costs money when there are other games that provide more substantial additions for free.  However, I felt the original game was very cheap given the amount of time and enjoyment I got out of it, and the new additions meet the bare minimum required to justify a five dollar cost.
The Definitive Edition is absolutely an improvement over what was already a phenomenal game, and I would recommend upgrading for those that really enjoyed the original.

So when it came out on Steam, I immediately bought it. I got a discount because of owning the original game, so it was a lot cheaper than I expected, but it was worth every penny and more. New powers, new areas, new skills to play with and new achievements, new story, new music, new art assets. So yes, if you haven't already got Ori and the Blind Forest, get this one. If you have, get this version anyway as well. You won't regret it.

That beign said, the game is wonderuflly replayable with heaps and heaps of content, unlockables and alternate missions. I just wish that you could add a weapon to your permenant arsenal by leaving the mission with it, like in some other entries. Theres a mission in the game though which i think is weak, which, without going into spoilers, has no civilians on the map, everyone is a soldier and everything is a drab boring millitary theme. On the whole though, wonderful, wonderful game for anyone who appreciates the stealth genre at all, this is Hitman at its very best.
