Attractio is one of those cases where I would have liked a middle-ground option or a real rating system rather than a "Recommended" or "Not recommended".
It is a first-person puzzle platformer that takes inspiration from games like Q.U.B.E. (most reviews compare it to Portal but both games are vastly different in terms of mechanics, in my opinion), and while it is not a terrible game, I thought the experience could have been improved from what it is now.
The game starts off as a very enjoyable puzzle game with a smooth difficulty curve that introduces you to several interesting mechanics to solve each room:
- Gravity boots that allow you to turn upside down to basically switch from the floor to the ceiling.
- A gravity gun which changes how items (mostly cubes of various sizes) in the room are affected by gravity when you shoot at them.
- A time slowing mechanic which allows for precision shooting and grabbing (useless in movement as time is slowed for you as well).
Add to this real time physics which takes into account the weight of your character and the objects around you to determine what moves at which speed, and from what height you can fall before dying.
And if it would have kept at that premise until the end, I would have been perfectly fine.
My biggest issue with the game is that half-way through most of the puzzles take more from the platformer genre than from the puzzle genre, and end up being awfully punishing if you can't keep on the very tight timing to perform a specific course of actions the game is expecting you to do.
There were a couple rooms near the end where I figured out the puzzle pretty much instantly, but kept dying over and over again on the platforming sequence required to solve it, and I ended up being really frustrated.
(Guess I mistakenly thought "hard" from the "solve hard deadly puzzles" in the description was for the puzzles, while it was more for the "deadly" part.)
Otherwise, the puzzles themselves were challenging without being overcomplicated, and there were some surprises near the end that would be spoiler-worthy if I was to talk about them here.
The story is a nice addition for this kind of game, but I honestly didn't care that much about it, nor for any of the characters which didn't have much of a personality and relatively forgettable voiceovers.
I also had many crashes and graphical glitches, as well as a couple of bugs that forced me to restart some puzzles, like the game somehow quicksaving when I was falling to my death (which is theoretically impossible with the checkpoint system in this game).
Bottom line:
If your favorite parts in Portal were the ones with the turrets, you will probably enjoy this game.
If like me, you preferred the regular test chambers, you might end up being very frustrated in several rooms from the second half of the game.
I wouldn't recommend it at the full price point, but it might be worth it on sale if you're out of other games of the same genre to play.
It's a good game, but as it exists in a world that has Portal and Talos, it feels lacking, somehow, without a fault of its owm.

I cannot highly recommend Ori and the Blind Forest enough. However, I would recommend the original over the definitive edition. It is my understanding that you get the original when you purchase this version. The original is comparable to Super Metroid in terms of gameplay, collectibles, and backtracking. However, some of this gets lost in translation with the ability to teleport between areas but at the very least you still have to walk between the areas to gather all the collectibles.
The biggest letdown as the original owner of the first game is having to purchase the definitive edition for $5 for only ~1 hour of bonus content which is just added off to the beaten path and absolutely not required to beat the game. However, to extend the game longer, they "artificially" add length by placing a power up in the game in the new area and changed puzzles to require this powerup to gather collectibles that did not need it prior to the definitive edition.  This breaks the game's pace from the original as there is no reason why it has to have this other than to find something to do with the new powerups.
I would say that this game has the "Other M" syndrome in which the new area requires you to go through the darkness thinking at first I need a powerup to do so. No, you have to suffer walking through the darkness to find this ledge that leads to a ball that gives you light to find the hidden platforms required to beat the area. The issue with this is that typically when I fall down to a pit full of spikes countless times, I would think not to go there until later. Well, you are more than welcome... just a tad bit too the left and a little higher would solve my issue. And then when finishing the new section I almost felt like I did it backwards... but can't really figure out if I did.
In the end, the new area completely breaks the game's pace at collecting all the collectibles by requiring the player to go off the beaten path to collect an ability that otherwise was not required. Sure the new edition lets you replay certain areas that were not repeatable in the original and lets you teleport between areas, but again, at the cost of breaking the games pace. Piror to the definitive edition everything could be collected before the end of the game without going off the beaten path, however the same puzzles are changed to be solved by collecting a powerup which (again) breaks the game's pace.
I would not recommend getting this if you have the original Ori and the Blind Forest. Divinity: Original Sin added a definitive edition that more than doubled the content of the game for free to all original owners while Ori and the Blind Forest only added ~1 hour of content and hid it away and artificially lengthen the game.
With that said, I would recommend this game to all new players of Ori and the Blind Forest, but I would recommend playing the original over the Definitive Edition (that is, if you still get the original with the new one). The old one had that "feel" that the Definitive Edition fails to offer with some unnecessary changes.

If you need a reason to buy this game, it is $10 when it is not on sale and it has an incredible amount of content and replayability.
And if you still need more convincing--
+ The gameplay is fluid
+ You can progress using your own methods at your own pace
+ Different classes of weapons, accessories, and armor add variety (magic, melee...)
+ Two different gameplay modes: normal for a standard experience and expert for a more challenging and awarding experience.
+ You can play multiplayer with your friends, adding more methods of playing
+ Terraria can be modded, and some mods add tons of content
+ It's fun to play
The only bad comment I can make about this game is the amount of learning you may need to do when you start the game (I will recommend the Terraria Wiki for this part), but worry not, once you do get a good grip on the game mechanics and recipes, this game will keep you entertained for a long time.

Video review:
Mad Max is a third person action game based off the film series where you get to drive around in a car, upgrade your abilities by collecting scrap, and complete seemingly endless tasks. I say seemingly endless, because Mad Max is a pretty big game depending on how much you’re willing to actually do. The main story itself is pretty short, but very impressive as a storytelling device. Then there’s a vast array of side objectives you can do, scrap locations you can loot, and races you can challenge yourself with. It’s a huge ♥♥♥♥ing game. There’s a lot to do. Not all of it is fun though, like deactivating mines to reduce the threat of your enemy in the region. That’s boring and takes like 20 minutes per region. The fact that I made some mistakes might have lengthened that though. But to preface the rest of this, the story is absolutely fantastic. If you like Mad Max and want an intense story with the craziest plot twists I’ve seen all year, then this is the game for you.
In terms of gameplay expect combat similar to assassin’s creed on foot and car combat similar to….I don’t even know what it’s similar to. Imagine a demolition derby where you also get a harpoon to rip things off cars and mini bazookas to fire at them called thunder sticks. It’s all very intense and a whole lot of fun. You’ll spend your time driving and fighting, clearing bases, collecting scrap and parts, tearing down giant metal scarecrows, and maybe even doing a race or two. All of the mechanics behind everything you can do in this game are solid.
I have four complaints about the gameplay however. There’s not really any stealth, so if you move into a certain radius around enemies they can see you through walls. There’s a lot of metal platforms during some objectives, and the metal platforms are always on uneven ground. If you fall off, it’s sort of annoying to get back on since the jump key is left control for some reason and they don’t actually teach you that. Parrying on uneven ground doesn’t work. If you’re fighting on uneven ground you’re going to get beat up badly. The parries just don’t trigger. And finally, the third person view is annoying as all hell because the game likes to put you in close spaces and make you drive cars that makes it so that you literally cannot see what’s in front of you. I hate third person views. I always have and always will.
The graphics of this game are top notch, It’s beautiful, it really is. I’d love to say the audio is good too but it just glitches out too much. There’s so many sound effects that break when you run around. And occasionally there’s sound effects that just don’t work at all. The game’s graphics and sounds though can really help make the game immersive. There’s this one point where they try to go for a scary effect that’s really interesting. I didn’t get scared, but I certainly got immersed into the story more.
There are some broken animations, especially when executing people. Collision detection with walls just sort of seems to die. And speaking of collision there’s a lot of spots in this game where the game seems to think there’s a giant rock or something? I’m not quite sure, but one second you’ll be driving and the next hit an invisible something and you’re now flying through the air.
To keep the world alive and dangerous the game also has these crazy storms that roll in. They’re very dangerous if you don’t have a well armored car and fast repair tools, but you can venture into them to find mutha loot boxes which contain a LOT of scrap. One time I actually had an entire storm disappear because I ran through an interior in an attempt to get back to my car. Unfortunately that footage broke or else I’d show you. These storms are intense and deadly and help give the game a more dangerous dynamic. Though later in the game they become a little routine once your car is upgraded to all hell.
And finally it’s good to remember Mad Max is an Australian franchise. That means the steering wheel is on the right side of the car. The game likes to insult you if you don’t remember that.
Overall Mad Max was a simple game. There’s not too much to actually say about it, but it was fun. There was a lot to do. I didn’t do everything, but I did plenty and I had fun doing it. Sure it had a lot of bugs. Some of them were really frustrating, but it doesn’t take too much away from the value of the game. Mad Max gets an 8/10 from me. Those two points are missing literally just due to all the crazy bugs, and there were a lot more than I talked about in this review. It’s a really fun game if you enjoy this genre or this IP. I’d recommend it, even to someone that has never watched a Mad Max movie. I haven’t, and I enjoyed the game just fine. You’re getting your money’s worth if you are willing to venture off and do the open-world objectives. If you only want it for the main story then pick it up on a sale.

ETS2 is a zen game more than anything else.  No twitch gameplay here.  Just the mechanics of driving a tractor-trailor long-haul across the nation.  Is it uber realistic?  No, not really.  The scenery is abbreviated, the distances severely compressed and many of the systems are simplistic in their representation.
But it works for me.  Why?  Because I used to drive long-haul in the lower 48.  I wouldn't want to spend several hours to get from one town to the next.  The distances in ETS2 are appropriate for a representation of what it is like.  But at the start and end of the journey the mechanics of picking up and dropping off the trailer remind me of my trucking days.  There's something satisfying in cutting the perfect corner, of figuring out how to approach that tricky dock and then just doing it.
Colored by nastalgia?  Maybe.  But if the game is evoking nastalgia in this former trucker then clearly SCS is doing something right.
A well constructed game, with excellent control customization, beautiful trucks, and decent landscape. Also, plenty of excellent mods are available.

While APB is not without its own set of issues, GamersFirst's dedication and continual, weekly patching makes APB an enjoyable PvP based open world GTA clone that is always fresh and vibrant.  The vibrance of this game also stems from the community, as  ever complex and new artistic designs of clothes, cars and symbols are being made with the in-game photoshop client. If you can dream it, you can have it in game (and if you cant make it yourself, many individuals would be more than happy to be contracted out to do so).
GamersFirst strives for a truly free-to play experience where nothing is pay-to-win or pay-to-play.  All real world cash bought weapons can be bought from within the game, and the starting weapons given are considered to be above aveage in terms of usability and reliability.  The only real money exclusives are cosmetic items for clothing, weapon skins or car kits, give nothing in terms of game advantage.  When Realtime Worlds went bankrupt in 2010, APB reopened up under GamersFirst with a premise of creating a better user experience.  And within the last year alone, patches for elective spawning, multiple new weapons, level-cap increases/contacts, UI optimization, Server and Client side optimization, new open world maps, new character/weapon/car modifications have all greatly improved the content and expereince within APB.  And in Q1 of 2014, the complete overhaul of game engine from Unreal 2008 to Unreal 2013 will breathe new life into this game, allowing it to compete against games such as GTA V Online in terms of massive content, graphics and playerbase options.
The gameplay itself tends to present itself as a steep learning curve for most new players, but new tutorials and an active community allow for even the most inexpereinced players to enjoy the game. After putting in enough dedication to declare myself a Golden God (100% completion) here's what I have to say about Super Meat Boy:
This game is the only one that I've played that has made me question why I am playing it, dying over and over for hours.  It's the only one that's left my thumbs bruised and callused from playing so hard.  It is the only gave that has given me a headache because of a certain level to unlock The Kid from IWBTG.
BUT!  All that aside, it is the only game I own that made me want to stride to get that 100% completion.  There is an addictive charm in this game, and the feeling of intense satisfaction when you finally triumph over a level you have been grinding away at is nothing short of exhillerating.  Once you get those controls down pat, and can make those insane saw-dodging jumps that you thought impossible when they were first presented to you, you realize that this game manages to capture what made all those tough-as-nails SNES titles so gripping: the feeling of progressing and knowing that you are
getting better at the game.
There is no one to blame for your own deaths in Super Meat Boy, but there is also no one else to congratulate but yourself when you get through it.  It's unforgiving, but oh so satisfying.

For an adaptation from a board game, this is a far cry from poor. The game's replay value is very high, and is a lot of fun to play with friends both locally and online. This game is very easy to learn, and introducing someone to the game is very quick, as short instructional videos are included in the game itself. If watching videos to learn isn't much your fancy, the game can be learned fairly easily through gameplay. The game successfully captures the darkness and the bad-to-worse story development of the Witcher literature and games, making the experience familiar and fulfilling to those familiar to the franchise while also fun to those who are not so familiar with the Witcher world. It also includes a feature allowing players to vary the length of the game by changing the number of requirements to be filled in order to achieve victory, making the game last anywhere between a twenty minute spree to a night-long affair depending upon what is desired.
There are occasional bugs that crop up, such as results from dice rolls momentarily disappearing from the screen or development cards not glowing when they are usable, but such glitches are so few and far between that they do not hinder the experience much. The only other complaint worth mentioning about the game is that, to some, the experience may grow repetitive after successive playthroughs, as the gameplay is much the same from game to game. As such, many tend to take breaks in between playthroughs.
I would rate this game an 8.5/10 for its fulfilling play yet repetitive nature.

Overall, given the cost, this is pretty worth it. It's fairly short, and there's really just one part that gave me some significant annoyance.
There's a "challenge" you can do at one of the first villages and due to the controls being just a little flimpy at times it can be kinda maddening. Sometimes if you hit jump again too soon before hitting the ground, or even right as you hit the ground, you won't jump. Sometimes you'll land and hit the D-pad but won't turn. If you hit jump again near the ground before quite landing you'll "glide" for a split second and that seems to wonk up your ability to swing. Similarly, some state transitions, such as gliding to landing and whatnot, kinda muck up your ability to attack in weird ways. I also don't particularly like that one button is jump as well as wall-grab as well as glide while in air.. BUT despite these nitpicks, none of them were a real source of frustration during the normal gameplay, it was just the challenge that it really stood out.
With that out of the way, the music and aesthetic are solid. The story is cute, I kinda got into the little bit of the world we got to see and wanted to run about sword-chopping all the jerk enemies and it was generally pretty satisfying doing so. There seems to be a couple endings based on a pretty obvious set of choices throughout the game, and there was a good bit of platforming, fighting, a decent variety of enemies, etc. - it all kinda came together nicely for the duration that the game lasts for.
For an afternoon or evening of fun it's worth a couple bucks, in my opinion, if you like the aesthetic and want to see a birdman through his quest for revenge and (ideally) the freedom of his people.

It is an absolute pleasure to be able to hop quickly from one narrow platform to another and stick the landing without having to "adjust" to the game's controls or physics. Combat feels good as well. The way you are able to string together combos and kills is very flashy and satisfying.
Way of the Red is shorter than the standard metroidvania platformer. Honestly, I look on this as a pro. I think the game is priced well for the experience I got from it. I don't always want to play an 80 hour epic (in fact, I want that less and less as I get older). I got a satisfying experience that I actually want to revist in the future. I didn't find every power-up, and I look forward to my next playthrough so I can find more.
There is one thing missing from the game: credits. I want to know who the creators are so I can follow thier future work. Fast paced, fun, fluid combat, with just the right amount of challenge. A steady ability based progression, a-la Metroid, with platforming that is familiar yet inventive. All packed into an 8-Bit retro package, that doesn't overstay its welcome.
After playing through Hyper Light Drifter I was looking for a good fast paced action game. Way of the Red came up on my suggested games list. I was immediately drawn to the retro style. It definitely invokes a classic NES 8-Bit style. And not the "clearly couldn't be done on the old hardware" way, this truly looks like a NES Game. It borrows designs from Metroid /  Castlevania, gating progress by abilities that you learn. The platforming is well done, allbeit a bit stiff at first, but I warmed up to it nicely. The swordplay is where the game shines, it is fluid and fun, and you certainly feel like a badass when you can get the combos right. It does a good job of making things feel really difficult but in a fair way. Though  the checkpoint system could be a little better. I will often find myself just close enough to the next checkpoint that having to redo all the previous encounters is a bit of a chore. The story is simple, but I think that works to its benefit. The fact that it was made all by one guy is also really impressive. I am curious to see what he makes next. Highly recommended!

Way of the Red was an enjoyable experience from start to finish for me. I enjoyed everything about it, from the story, the platforming, the fighting, and even dying multiple times didn't deter me from playing. Special kudos to the graphics and music direction too- it's all just stellar.
It's definitely an under-the-radar game that is just an excellent example of what a single game developer is capable of! I really hope to see more from this developer in the future!
Also, thanks for making an awesome game about birds as well.  <3
For more in-depth commentary about the game, check out my podcast where my cohost and I talk all about our experiences playing Way of the Red.

Very fun and $8 is the perfect price for this type of game. It's developed by Avalanche Studios the same studio which makes the Just Cause games. I would not call Mad Max a Just Cause reskin but it does have some bit and pieces which remind me of it. Like the threat level, take over hostile bases and destroy Scarecrows to lower it; It can get repetitive.
Lots of cars and your Magnum Opus is very customizable. Enemy vehicles are very interesting with one which chuckes mines out the back while another has a flamethrower attached to it. Vehicular combat is solid and crashing/ramming is very satisfying. Pulling up alongside a car and blowing up its gas tank with a shotgun and then watch it flip in slow-mo will never get old.
Hand-to-hand combat is quite fun and well developed. When you've got punches flowing Max can go into Fury mode which makes his hits much more powerful and things start to get cinematic. Kill moves aren't once in a blue moon occurrence and you can do them a lot. All of them are brutal as can be and will make you go: "Damn!!"
Max can be customized with new jackets, facial hair styles, and upgraded with new kill moves, ammo capacity, knuckledusters, and forearm guards.
Story so far isn't special but then again that's not what you'll be playing this game for. Like I said it can get repetitive but for me the driving, fighting skirmishes, occasionally taking over a base is fun and stays interesting even though there's not something brand new around every corner.
Graphics are amazing and the optimization is on the same level as the Witcher 3 is. The map is a wasteland but the graphics give it a sort of beauty.
You start off in the Great White which was once the ocean floor and at one point you'll go up to the area which was once the coast among a couple other landscapes. I like how the devs made a number of different regions but they still tie into the whole wasteland theme. Finding old, rusted ship hulls, containers, and other stuctures adds a lot to the scenery.
Very few bugs, something you don't see with many games these days. Looks like someone actually gave a damn with QA instead of throwing all the money into DLCs.
There's a first person mode for the cars only but the interiors are blurred. The devs wanted some depth of focus going on but it's not dynamic, if I look around in the car it doesn't come into focus and the only place unblurred is where the windscreen would be. Honestly, no blur would have been perfectly fine even if the interiors had low resolution textures. But then again there's mip-mapping in the game so isn't that technique also applied to the interior textures?
The lack of a speedometer and RPM gauge is annoying, I know in Mad Max's universe you floor it 24/7 but still. Seeing your vehicles rev up and then the speedometer needle fly forward would be nice.
There's no option to disable the HUD. Every game has it but it's just not in here, it's such a simple thing.
There's no option to load a save file while you're in-game. You can in the main menu but then you would have to exist out to the main menu and then load. Why there's no option to do it in-game is anyone's guess.
Fast travel--why it's in a game which is all about driving and traveling makes no sense and what makes even less sense is you can "fast" travel while on foot.
Surprising a solid game since it is based on the movies and those types of games usually aren't well done. Vehicular warfare in a post-apocalypse setting--it's as fun as it sounds.
It doesnt have an amazing story, but is a good game. Nice graphics and effects.

Best hitman game. Period.

Through the years Hitman has gone through constant revisions, flip-flopping between story driven action adventure, and sandbox murder simulator.  Blood Money felt like the correct blend of every ingredient,  a snapshot in time where IO managed to create a nearly perfect sandbox assassination sim.  Then Absolution came along and shook everything up again, pushing the series away from the sandbox and into highly scripted 'cinematic' take on Hitman that felt entirely at odds with what attracted me to the series to begin with.  Remember that part where you spent an entire mission carefully sneaking through a building only to have a pre rendered cutscene totally undermine what your character just did?  Yeah.   Not great.
With the taste of Absolution still in my mouth when I started playing, I wasn't expecting much.  And that makes it all the sweeter to say that this new Episodic Hitman might actually be a better game than Blood Money was. At least, I'm enjoying it more.   The stealth mechanics finally feel *fair* with only certain NPCs being able to see through your disguise.  Y'know, ones that could plausibly tell you apart from the man who's clothes you're wearing?  i.e  That guy's boss, or people who worked close to him.  This is a HUGE step up from the previous games where NPCs were either 100% oblivious to the fact that their co-worker had gone from being short and hairy to tall and bald, or, (as was the case in Absolution) preternaturally aware of your disguises.
I will say that I followed some advice before I started playing and disabled two of the newer Hitman features which seem to have been introduced to smooth out the difficulty curve for newcomers to the series.  These are "Opportunities" and "Instinct", both of which, I feel, do not add anything to the game and actually remove some of the feeling of exploration that is an integral part of the Hitman experience.  It's not for me to tell you how to play your game, but I would advise you at least consider disabling these features if you are finding the experience too hand-holdy.
Well, that's about all I can say.  They did it.  This is the Blood Money sequel we all deserved.  It feels great to finally be invested in the Hitman franchise again, and I can't wait to see what they do with Season 2!
P.S.
A lot of the negative reviews on here mention the "online singleplayer" feature of the game.  While I can't say I'm a fan of the concept,  in practice I have found it works fine and has not disconnected me at any time thus far.  I am not discounting other people's experiences, but it may not be as large of an issue as you would assume from the reviews.  Bear that in mind.

76 hours later, I can safely say that this is the best installment of Hitman, ever. And yes, IMO it even exceeds Blood Money. Each & and every level was a genuine pleasure to play through. But the best episodes  (for any episodic buyers) are Sapienza, Bangkok and Hokkaido.
And I know a lot of people will disagree with this,  but I think the episodic structure suits Hitman. Especially with the frequent ET's, Escalations and Contracts etc. And the always online component didn't bother me either.
For me, after Season 1, Season 2 of Hitman has become a must buy...

If there is one game I have  consistantly come back to over  and over again its Prison Archetect.
Prison Archetect is a game that consistantly punishes you to get it right. It's challenge isn't in the campaign mode, or even the sandbox, the challenge is consistently fighting with and against the games well implemented and thought out systems.
Gameplay:: Prison Archetect plays like any good simulator should. It doesn't hold your hand, it simply gives you some prisoners, sets some goals in the form of grants, and lets you attack it however you want. Prisoners have a set of needs, from bladder, to hunger, to spiruality and excercise. How you choose to fulfill or not to, is entirely up to you and where this game shines.
Do you create a state of the art detention center? Where prisoners are given a bed, a toilet, two meals a day and an hour to excersize? Along side this supermax housing unit, you may want to put in a medium security section, where medium risk prisoners work, excersize, trade goods and fight, before you deem them too dangerous and upgrade them to supermax. Over the road, you can have a low security section, where you may want to hold some of your less desireables, such as ex police, and prison guards.
You'll be in charge of every facet of these prisoners lives (each individually named with a background written by kickstarter backers).
Graphics:: The game has a simple 2D art style, the animations are well done, and works well overall.
Sound:: Sound plays an important part in the game, not only adding to the ambience of a prison simulation with cries of terror and the sound of clanking doors but is important to tell when something is about to kick off, or already has based on how your prisoners sound. When treated well, you won't hear much from your prisoners, but forget to hire cooks or cleaners for a few days, and you will begin to hear your prisoners rumble and yell before eventually they will riot.
Overall:: Prison Archetect lets you go as deep and as complicated as you want. Giving you full control on how you want to play, it is a true sandbox of creativity with a whole miriad of systems that simply work. Whether it be the water and electricity system, the smuggling system the prisoners use to sneak in weapons and drugs, or simply just how staff combat this with the steps you put in place to control contraband. Prison archetect is not only a deep simulator, it is constantly updated even after release, by a developer who goes above and beyond for their customers long after they've received your money.

Prison Architect is a game about planning and building a prison from a 2D top down view.  You have to manage finances, your prisoners needs such as food, cleanliness, toilets, beds, entertainment, visitation, medical, religion, execution, etc.  You start with a very limited budget and eventually work your way up on either a small, medium, or large map.  You can make everything free and also have access to the Steam workshop for even more fun.
As you build, your prisoners will let you know the general consensus based on the top bar.  If you have a phsycologist on hand, you can break own their needs even further via the reports. If you prisoners get out of hand they end up hurting each other and possible your guards.  Sometimes they will even riot if it gets too out of control.  I settle things the old fashioned way, all of my guards have body armor, tasers, and guns.  The occasional sniper is in the towers in case they think they can make a run for it.  Hasn't worked out to well for them yet.  I have even went as far as to set them up and leave a door open only to have a firing squad on the other side ready.  Not my fault they made the mistake of coming to MY prison.
You also are responsible for hiring other staff like cooks, foremen, workers, more guards, a chief of police, and a myriad of other people not forgetting the warden himself.  You need to run electrical and water to everything that requires it and also make sure ou got sprinklers for those fires.  The game is actually quite challenging if you don't play in free mode.  I'd say pick it up when it's on sale.  It's been out for a bit now and the last sale just ended.  If you want to dump full price, by all means.  I don't think it isn't worth it but I also don't like to spend tons of cash on games.  Either way, Prison Architect needs to be in your Steam Library.

In short, Attractio is an excellent Portal-style puzzler based around gravity manipulation.
A brief anecdote: On one of the later levels of the game, I encountered an issue where the exact action I had taken successfully the first few tries of the level (only to die later) suddenly resulted in my death the next few times I tried it - this, mind you, fairly far along in a complex level. I was prepared to call it quits there and began to leave a tentative recommendation, relaying the story of how an action you had to take to complete a level sometimes inexplicably resulted in your death. And then I thought about it a bit more carefully, glanced at a guide, realized it was a miracle my strategy had ever worked at all, and completed the level with a decidedly different approach.
That's how Attractio works - even when you think you know what you're doing, you don't know what you're doing. Though the mechanics behind the puzzles are fairly simple (depending on the character you're controlling at a given time, you can flip your own gravity, shoot boxes to change their gravity, or both), the puzzles themselves are anything but. Every now and then, there's a shift from "Wait, you can do that?" to "Wait, why can you do that?" - the physics, while well done, are less than smooth at times - but on the whole there's plenty of variety to keep you guessing, pondering, and pulling off a wide array of gravitational stunts.
This solid gameplay is backed by an intriguing (if a bit generic) sci-fi-Hunger-Games-esque plot, and there are some nice stylistic touches to match the backstory. Alongside the main story (my playtime essentially reflects the time that took me
), there are challenge levels if your hunger for puzzles isn't sufficiently sated.
Whether you're pining for another Portal installment or just a fan of puzzles in general, Attractio will pull you in.

After buying the other two Arkham Games during the Summer Sale last year and enjoying both of them immensely, I knew Origins was a game I had absolutely no choice but to purchase. I, regrettably, did not purchase it until I believe the Winter Sale, a little after it came out. For financial reasons.
Enough about that, I didn't get into the game until about a few weeks ago because of time contraints but I remember up until I played it, I had heard an odd reivew every now and again from any number of sources that said Origins didn't really add anything to the series, that it was boring, that it was hardly discernable from the first two. Opinions are subjective but I sincerely disagree.
Origins is by far and away, the best game in the series as far as I'm concerned. The gameplay is roughly on par with the previous two games, but I find a couple of the additional mechanics that come with the updated gadgets is quite entertaining. Combat, to me, feels more fluid and precise than it did in the previous titles. I'm not sure if Gotham in Origins is much bigger than it is in City, but it feels significantly more massive. I played the game through on normal mode (because I'm lame like that) and I have to say Origins challenged me a great deal more than the previous two. And finally, the story is just... phenomenal, for lack of a better word. I think people would argue that's because it's an origin game, but regardless, the story is just amazing. So much so that I would hazard an opinion that Origins also has the highest replay value.
All in all, I stand by my opinion that Origin is the best in the series, though I am looking forward to Arkham Knight. I wouldn't give the game a perfect review, I'd say 8.5/10, but overall, I would recomend this game to anyone who's played the series or a fan of Batman in general. If you can't afford it, for the love of god, pick it up during a sale. It's beyond worth every cent.

Short n' sweet hack-em-up metroidvania-lite. The trailer and description don't lie: the combat is the core of the game and easily makes up for the limited length and simple, somewhat repetitive assets. BUT: the music is cool, the story is engaging enough and the right level of self-aware besides, and the character animations in particular punch way above their weight.
You have 100% air control when you jump and the wide joystick deadzone means you're only ever speeding left or right. It's nigh impossible to make subtle movements while falling to avoid spikes or land on a floating block. This remains frustrating thru-out. BUT: once learned, this tradeoff allows for mid-combat acrobatics that quickly become necessary in the more enemy-dense later levels. The game does not hand you hit combos on a silver platter, instead forcing you to intelligently string together uppercuts, air glides, invulnerability frames, Nidhogg-esque weapon throws, etc etc etc. Every combat perk you unlock smartly reinforces the central flow, and by the end you're using a focused arsenal of moves to dance around a madhouse of telegraphed sword swings, projectiles, infuriating Castlevania Medusa Head-inspired environment-clipping bobbers, and one-hit kill pitfalls, and it's effin' great. I wish it went on longer.
V good, I hope this dev makes more games of this ilk in the future.

Oooh. I played it for about an hour and a half and it was off to such a good start. Very satisfying puzzles with some of those same sorts of kinetic elements like Portal. But three strikes killed my interest in playing it any further:
1. This game is guilty of "Quantum Conundrum" syndrome. It starts off great, but then the puzzles start to veer more and more into a type of puzzle where you have to execute a very specific sequence of action-oriented events in a very specific order, timed perfectly, or else you instantly die. Why is it that every game that tries to imitate Portal is full of these timing-based death gauntlets? Anyway, every time you insta-die, you  have to go back and position all the blocks into all of the right places over and over again, which gets pretty tedious. This sort of thing really grates away my patience at an extreme rate. Maybe you are more patient than me.
2. The VO. First of all, it's terrible and constant. Second of all, you absolutely can't turn it off or turn the volume down. Third, this is one of those games that thinks it's really cool/funny to taunt and make fun of the player every time they die or fall for some cheap trap. Much like grading jokes are only funny to teachers, player death jokes are only funny to designers. Don't do it. Finally, the VO that plays when you first enter a chamber will play over again every time you die, so you get to listen to the same terrible VO making fun of you for experimenting over and over again like a broken record.
3. Some jank. For example: If you put a cube in a doorway and then let the door close, the falling door will destroy the cube. But sometimes if a cube just touches a door as its moving past, the door will "destroy" the cube through the power of EXISTING NEARBY.
I fully admit that as a player I am extremely impatient. While I like being challenged, I have a pretty low tolerance (no tolerance?) for being harrassed and/or hassled. While this game does have some really satisfying challenge in the puzzle department, the harassment and hassle kinda killed it for me.

Attractio is a game where you play as three contestants in a controversial reality show. As you progress through the levels (spaceship) you are faced with many puzzles and death situations in which you must use your brains to escape/pass the puzzle.
Positives:
+ Graphics are really nice
+ Cut scenes are really in-depth and have great detail behind them
+ Audio really adds to the atmosphere
+ Challenge mode to test your skill
+ Beautiful lighting effects
Negatives:
- Controller does not seem to work on the main menu
- Sometimes I could get stuck on a puzzle and it would get me a little annoyed. (Maybe there could be a hint system in future for the easier modes?)
- Game can take a long time to load
I had a lot of fun on Attractio. Fans of Portal would definitely love this game too. I happened to get stuck often though and it really did challenge me to use my brain (what I have left of it) – I would most definitely recommend this to gamers seeking a challenge and a game which is pretty in-depth with the cutscenes and story. The game also has a challenge mode in which you can go over the levels you completed and try to beat the times for Gold, Silver or Bronze respectively.
I feel the price is fair but it may sway a few individuals. For the majority I recommend a purchase. If you feel the price may be too steep then I would definitely recommend waiting for a sale. This game is definitely worth a purchase down the line though.

The DRM (Although I personally have never been kicked offline by crappy servers)
The not-so-clear package titles
Optimization could be better
The fear I'll need to fork over another 60 dollars everytime they decide to start off another "season".
But from what I've played, the game as a GAME is just fine. I very much enjoy it.
Now, for context. Take this from someone who has over 300 hours in Hitman: Blood Money. This game as far as gameplay is concerned is like something out of a wet dream. Gun play is fun, stealth works fine, levels are well designed and there is a good variety of locations (however I could do without anymore "mansion" levels).
I especially like the different restrictions that some levels put on you. Episode 5 is a hostile zone, similar to some levels in Hitman 2: Silent Assassin where you are not a "grey man". If you're discovered in your starting outfit, you will be shot on sight. Episode 6 prohibits you from smuggling in items on your person. Making you think twice about actions you may take knowing that you don't have your handgun, or any other tools to fall back on.
The episodic release system works well for this game in my opinion. The levels are given enough depth that a dedicated player could spend entire evenings finishing every task, finding every secret, unlocking every upgrade. Even puting your own restrictions on yourself, or creating your own goals, which is something I still enjoy doing in Blood Money.
Bottom line, there is plenty I could tell you about this game. Some things good, some things bad. But if the DRM doesn't spook you too bad, you're okay with episodic releases and all this season business, I recommend it. If you like the challenge of discovering everything in a level, if you like sandboxes, if you like Silent Assassin and Blood Money, hell if you like puzzle games. Give it a shot. I recommend.

When it's working it's probably the best Hitman game to date.
It combines the sandbox nature of Blood Money with the challenges / leaderboards of Absolution.
---
I say, 'When it's working.' because it not only uses Steam, but also requires you to be always online.
This game is entirely single player so not being able to play when you have no internet is a kick in the♥♥♥♥♥♥
Also, when I first purchased the game I had the recommended hardware to a T. The exact CPU and Videocard suggested.
It defaulted to Low graphics and crashed randomly and constantly. I never figued out why exactly it crashed so badly, even on all low settings at low res as a test.
The solution for me was to buy a new graphics card. Now it runs fine with no issues.
---
The gameplay seems to be a iteration of Absolutions attempt at making the game easier for everyone with hitman vision and HUD elements that let you know about opportunities and dangers. But the level design is an iteration of the Blood Money philosophy of crating a clockwork level with AI routines and let the player loose. There are authored specialty assassinations like past titles but also allows for and even encourages experimentation.
There is an experience bar for each level of the game, which unlocks more loadout options and starting locations (along with disguises) within a level. You gain level XP but completing a long list of specialty kills like 'Dress as X Character to kill Y Target with Z' but also with feats such as making it look like an accident or completing a level without alerting anyone.
It encourages replayability and I found myself wanting to jump right back into the same mission again to discover all the secrets.
On top of that you can play, create and share custom contracts within the levels much like Absolution.
You begin the level and kill any NPC with as many stipulations as you want to add on to it and then publish it to the contracts available for other players. This creates a leaderboard for that contract.
On top of that there are elusive targets, which are unique targets that you only have one try to kill, if you fail you fail forever, if you succeed you gain a level XP and bragging rights. There have been a lot this season and Io have confirmed they will continue into Season 2, even for the Season 1 maps.
On top of that there are escalations. Sort of like the player contracts but created by Io. Its the same contract you complete 5 times, each time they add a new twist to it. These are interesting but I found a lot of them beatable using the same tactic every time, except for some where the last time they do something totally off the wall.
The levels are pretty sizable. Some are so large that even after playing through it multiple times I was still finding new areas, and disguises. The very intricate kills are usually hinted at via the challenges or opportunities system. Opportunities give you checkpoints and a vague idea of how to get a high level disguise or how to set up one of the flashier kills, but not all of them so again, potential for exploration and replayability are very high. And it has to be because of the business model.
You can buy the intro pack which includes 2 training levels and the first main level. From there you can purchase each level seperately if you want. But honestly I think they're all worth playing. This is a great introduction to a classic franchise whose older titles are hard to go back to.

Super Meat Boy is hard. Delightfully hard. It's difficult to exaggerate or, on the other hand, put cleanly into words the violent sinewave of emotion you'll feel as you appreciate a level's intriguing challenge, get frustrated when you realize you've died 20 times with nothing to show for it, finally beat it with your self-confidence taking a leap, and get thrusted into the next level. It all makes for a much richer and more meaningful experience when you're done (or have decided to take a break). Super Meat Boy is an acclaimed challenge, a rite of bash-age for self-respecting modern gamers, and it deserves in every way to be.
I first tried this game at a meeting with a team with which I'm developing a game right now, while one member had walked away from his computer for a few minutes. I wasn't too impressed initially; the floaty platforming physics and slapstick, adult-cartoon aesthetics called to mind the unfortunate epithet "one of THOSE indie games." I didn't think much more about it until I happened to pick up a Steam card a couple months later. (As a helpless college student, the closest thing I have to a credit card is unconfirmed and unusable.) At that point, I figured, sure, why not, I'd give it a second chance. After all, I needed distractions from the more pressing issues over break, like getting a job.
The bloody mess grew on me. Like Meat Boy leaping vulnerably over a mesh of squealing gears, caked in the congealing bodily fluids of his unlucky clones, I narrowly averted the tragedy of letting my experience end at mediocrity by actually investing time in the game. As I learned, it's not a product you can touch once for a short time and claim to have experienced; like a young pet, it just needs more time and love. You will grow as a player as you, with fractions of fractions of seconds standing in your way, let countless Meat Boys be ground up, crushed, or burned to death. Even as a seasoned platforming player, you will be in for a long battle.
Hopefully you won't bleed too hard yourself.

Still the best open-world game to date.
You play as Carl Johnson, an ex-gangbanger that moved to Liberty City to live the good life. After years away from his old mates, he goes back to Los Santos to attent to his mother's, only to find himself back into the life he desperately wanted to get away from.
Unlike Grand Theft Auto III and Vice City, the gameplay hasn't aged at all. Anyone who played IV or V will know what to expect, as it is the basis for every new GTA title. You can climb anything you want, look anywhere you want without the camera bothering you, interact with pedestrians, climb a mountain with a bike and much, much more. It's not about what you
do, it's about what you
do.
As this is the first 3D open-world game ever to have multiple cities, it leaves a lot to be expected. Fortunately, it does not disappoint. The cities (Los Santos, San Fierro and Las Venturas) are incredibly huge and detailed, fiddled with minigames, side-activities and crazy characters to spice up the formula. All accompanied by a large countryside for you to
explore.
When you attach all that with an awesome licensed soundtrack that takes cues from dozens of different genres with the voice of Samuel L. Jackson himself, you realize that this is a game like no other. The world that Rockstar created using this engine feels like a living charicature of 90's USA, even if it's held back by the game's primitive visuals. It's just one of those rare videogames that everyone just needs to experience atleast once in their lifetime. I still find myself in awe from time-to-time with the outstanding atmosphere the state of San Andreas provides.

I used to play this game ages ago on gog and i wanted to get into it again, so i bought it on steam. I really think this is one of the most fun games in the sandbox category, but playing it again made me realise just how difficult it has to be to figure the game out on your own without looking anything up. It's a load of fun and i think many people who play it will enjoy it, but i dont anymore. I played through the game many times and i think that the early part of the game is a little stale, barely changing at all since 1.1. The late game is where it's at though. And here is in my opinion the biggest flaw of this game. The game just kind of cuts off after you defeat all the bosses and events. It's not like you can "beat" terraria, i mean it just keeps going forever, but after you get the best gear there really isn't any point in it. The only reason why you need better gear is to beat the next thing, but after you beat it all, all that the better gear does is make things easier and not really more fun. I mean you can still do whatever you want and have all sorts of fun with the game, but it's just kind of  pointless. The big thing about this game for me though is the mods, they are a pure 10/10, especially calamity mod. At least with mods when you finish the game you get to just start a new game with a mod for a different experience, instead of doing the same thing differently (class specific letsplays). If you don't care about the mods and you just want to do something fun with the base game i recommend the engineer let's play. You just do whatever the hell works the best. Abuse glitches, traps and just automatise everything, it can be rather challenging at times, but there is some seriously fun things you can do if you put your imagination to the task. Here is something fun you can do if you want. At the start of the game go to the jungle as quickly as you can and glitch your way into the temple with the hammer (there is a guide on youtube, but it really isn't that hard to figure it out on your own) take the traps, and destroy apsolutely everything for quite the long time. When I heard about this game being developed by a different company, I thought it would be a refreshing experience. I am not opposed to change, if that change is good. But then, when I played it, I immediately realized that I was wrong. This game is not a change. Let me explain why:
• In terms of gameplay, Arkham Origins is identical to Arkham City. It even has the same map. The environments are different, but that difference is merely superficial. The devs made the easiest decision: don't innovate, just recycle. Even the gadgets are the same. Most of them we've already seen before, and the "new" ones are just different versions of the same thing (remote claw=line launcher, though the claw is a bit of an improved version; glue grenade=freeze cluster). The shock gloves are a very nice addition though, but because of its usefulness, every fight after you get them is a joke. Except boss fights of course, in which you will be screaming to your monitor the word "bull****" several times.
• In terms of story telling, it follows their predecessors with extreme accuracy. The story itself is different, of course. It includes several villains that weren't present in previous installments, but it also includes several that were, and without the need to do so. But there are no plot holes, and the story shapes out well as a prequel to Arkham Asylum. I recommend staying through the credits (despite the fact that credits are extremely long).
• In the graphical aspect, don't even get me started on the bugs. Man this game is buggy as hell, considering it's been released some time ago. Consider yourself extremely lucky if you get past your first boss fight without issues. And pray that enemies don't get stuck behind walls forcing you to start a fight all over again, and this applies to boss fights as well. I wouldn't say this feels like a beta, but it's certainly close. When it's not bugging out, it's the same as Arkham City. Don't expect anything new here.
It has its epic moments, don't get me wrong, but it all feels the same to Arkham City, and that's where the game fails: originality. Still, I would recommend any fan of the franchise to get this game, but only when it's on sale, it's not worth the full price.
Final score: 3.25/5

I cannot highly recommend Ori and the Blind Forest enough. However, I would recommend the original over the definitive edition. It is my understanding that you get the original when you purchase this version. The original is comparable to Super Metroid in terms of gameplay, collectibles, and backtracking. However, some of this gets lost in translation with the ability to teleport between areas but at the very least you still have to walk between the areas to gather all the collectibles.
The biggest letdown as the original owner of the first game is having to purchase the definitive edition for $5 for only ~1 hour of bonus content which is just added off to the beaten path and absolutely not required to beat the game. However, to extend the game longer, they "artificially" add length by placing a power up in the game in the new area and changed puzzles to require this powerup to gather collectibles that did not need it prior to the definitive edition.  This breaks the game's pace from the original as there is no reason why it has to have this other than to find something to do with the new powerups.
I would say that this game has the "Other M" syndrome in which the new area requires you to go through the darkness thinking at first I need a powerup to do so. No, you have to suffer walking through the darkness to find this ledge that leads to a ball that gives you light to find the hidden platforms required to beat the area. The issue with this is that typically when I fall down to a pit full of spikes countless times, I would think not to go there until later. Well, you are more than welcome... just a tad bit too the left and a little higher would solve my issue. And then when finishing the new section I almost felt like I did it backwards... but can't really figure out if I did.
In the end, the new area completely breaks the game's pace at collecting all the collectibles by requiring the player to go off the beaten path to collect an ability that otherwise was not required. Sure the new edition lets you replay certain areas that were not repeatable in the original and lets you teleport between areas, but again, at the cost of breaking the games pace. Piror to the definitive edition everything could be collected before the end of the game without going off the beaten path, however the same puzzles are changed to be solved by collecting a powerup which (again) breaks the game's pace.
I would not recommend getting this if you have the original Ori and the Blind Forest. Divinity: Original Sin added a definitive edition that more than doubled the content of the game for free to all original owners while Ori and the Blind Forest only added ~1 hour of content and hid it away and artificially lengthen the game.
With that said, I would recommend this game to all new players of Ori and the Blind Forest, but I would recommend playing the original over the Definitive Edition (that is, if you still get the original with the new one). The old one had that "feel" that the Definitive Edition fails to offer with some unnecessary changes.

Super Meat Boy is hard. Delightfully hard. It's difficult to exaggerate or, on the other hand, put cleanly into words the violent sinewave of emotion you'll feel as you appreciate a level's intriguing challenge, get frustrated when you realize you've died 20 times with nothing to show for it, finally beat it with your self-confidence taking a leap, and get thrusted into the next level. It all makes for a much richer and more meaningful experience when you're done (or have decided to take a break). Super Meat Boy is an acclaimed challenge, a rite of bash-age for self-respecting modern gamers, and it deserves in every way to be.
I first tried this game at a meeting with a team with which I'm developing a game right now, while one member had walked away from his computer for a few minutes. I wasn't too impressed initially; the floaty platforming physics and slapstick, adult-cartoon aesthetics called to mind the unfortunate epithet "one of THOSE indie games." I didn't think much more about it until I happened to pick up a Steam card a couple months later. (As a helpless college student, the closest thing I have to a credit card is unconfirmed and unusable.) At that point, I figured, sure, why not, I'd give it a second chance. After all, I needed distractions from the more pressing issues over break, like getting a job.
The bloody mess grew on me. Like Meat Boy leaping vulnerably over a mesh of squealing gears, caked in the congealing bodily fluids of his unlucky clones, I narrowly averted the tragedy of letting my experience end at mediocrity by actually investing time in the game. As I learned, it's not a product you can touch once for a short time and claim to have experienced; like a young pet, it just needs more time and love. You will grow as a player as you, with fractions of fractions of seconds standing in your way, let countless Meat Boys be ground up, crushed, or burned to death. Even as a seasoned platforming player, you will be in for a long battle.
Hopefully you won't bleed too hard yourself.
Worth trying if you like speedruns

Hitman is back!
I was reluctant to get this after much scrutiny over some features, but missing that classic hitman gameplay I decided to take a gamble and give it a spin.
So after trying a few hours,  I came out with a few pros and cons
Pros:
Classic Hitman Versatility: Like any proper hitman game, there are dozens of different ways to approach each hit. This time, there are normally at least 8 ways that can be revealed to execute a hit, on top of whatever you want to do.
Graphics: They're good; It won't blow your mind, but they are sufficiently modern that the game will still look great years from now
Levels: These missions are HUGE, it will take you a while to explore each map, and each is jam packed with things to fool around with and such
Cons:
Online: so as many people say,  to get the full experience you should be online. During an online playthrough if you lose connection, it will pause the game. UNLIKE what other people say, you dont get kicked to the main menu and you don't lose all your progress: The game pauses, and asks you if you want to try reconnect or go offline.  If you reconnect, carry on. If you go offline, you go back to the menus. If you get bumped, dont worry too much, there is a decent autosave during playthrough that you can get back to murdering quick.
Offline mode is like having a different profile, the missions are still available but online and offline saves are separate. The elusive contracts and other features are only available online though.
Voice acting: Big immersion breaker here; wherever you are, the voice acting is the same. British or American. Slightly annoying, but I'm sure they will make a better attempt in the later seasons
I defintely reccomend this game to any fan of the hitman franchise, and the quality of gameplay definitely outweighs any of the funky always online features.

To be completely honest, there are plenty of things that I do not like about this game.
The DRM (Although I personally have never been kicked offline by crappy servers)
The not-so-clear package titles
Optimization could be better
The fear I'll need to fork over another 60 dollars everytime they decide to start off another "season".
But from what I've played, the game as a GAME is just fine. I very much enjoy it.
Now, for context. Take this from someone who has over 300 hours in Hitman: Blood Money. This game as far as gameplay is concerned is like something out of a wet dream. Gun play is fun, stealth works fine, levels are well designed and there is a good variety of locations (however I could do without anymore "mansion" levels).
I especially like the different restrictions that some levels put on you. Episode 5 is a hostile zone, similar to some levels in Hitman 2: Silent Assassin where you are not a "grey man". If you're discovered in your starting outfit, you will be shot on sight. Episode 6 prohibits you from smuggling in items on your person. Making you think twice about actions you may take knowing that you don't have your handgun, or any other tools to fall back on.
The episodic release system works well for this game in my opinion. The levels are given enough depth that a dedicated player could spend entire evenings finishing every task, finding every secret, unlocking every upgrade. Even puting your own restrictions on yourself, or creating your own goals, which is something I still enjoy doing in Blood Money.
Bottom line, there is plenty I could tell you about this game. Some things good, some things bad. But if the DRM doesn't spook you too bad, you're okay with episodic releases and all this season business, I recommend it. If you like the challenge of discovering everything in a level, if you like sandboxes, if you like Silent Assassin and Blood Money, hell if you like puzzle games. Give it a shot. I recommend.

When it's working it's probably the best Hitman game to date.
It combines the sandbox nature of Blood Money with the challenges / leaderboards of Absolution.
---
I say, 'When it's working.' because it not only uses Steam, but also requires you to be always online.
This game is entirely single player so not being able to play when you have no internet is a kick in the♥♥♥♥♥♥
Also, when I first purchased the game I had the recommended hardware to a T. The exact CPU and Videocard suggested.
It defaulted to Low graphics and crashed randomly and constantly. I never figued out why exactly it crashed so badly, even on all low settings at low res as a test.
The solution for me was to buy a new graphics card. Now it runs fine with no issues.
---
The gameplay seems to be a iteration of Absolutions attempt at making the game easier for everyone with hitman vision and HUD elements that let you know about opportunities and dangers. But the level design is an iteration of the Blood Money philosophy of crating a clockwork level with AI routines and let the player loose. There are authored specialty assassinations like past titles but also allows for and even encourages experimentation.
There is an experience bar for each level of the game, which unlocks more loadout options and starting locations (along with disguises) within a level. You gain level XP but completing a long list of specialty kills like 'Dress as X Character to kill Y Target with Z' but also with feats such as making it look like an accident or completing a level without alerting anyone.
It encourages replayability and I found myself wanting to jump right back into the same mission again to discover all the secrets.
On top of that you can play, create and share custom contracts within the levels much like Absolution.
You begin the level and kill any NPC with as many stipulations as you want to add on to it and then publish it to the contracts available for other players. This creates a leaderboard for that contract.
On top of that there are elusive targets, which are unique targets that you only have one try to kill, if you fail you fail forever, if you succeed you gain a level XP and bragging rights. There have been a lot this season and Io have confirmed they will continue into Season 2, even for the Season 1 maps.
On top of that there are escalations. Sort of like the player contracts but created by Io. Its the same contract you complete 5 times, each time they add a new twist to it. These are interesting but I found a lot of them beatable using the same tactic every time, except for some where the last time they do something totally off the wall.
The levels are pretty sizable. Some are so large that even after playing through it multiple times I was still finding new areas, and disguises. The very intricate kills are usually hinted at via the challenges or opportunities system. Opportunities give you checkpoints and a vague idea of how to get a high level disguise or how to set up one of the flashier kills, but not all of them so again, potential for exploration and replayability are very high. And it has to be because of the business model.
You can buy the intro pack which includes 2 training levels and the first main level. From there you can purchase each level seperately if you want. But honestly I think they're all worth playing. This is a great introduction to a classic franchise whose older titles are hard to go back to.

It's nice to finally see some new and interesting concepts after 4 games that didn't change the formula too much; even though that didn't mean the other games were bad.
This time you're not a security guard anymore: you're a technician whose job is to repair the animatronics and make sure that the place they're in for the night is going as it should. The problem is, the robots are not happy about *something* and they will try to -you guessed it- murder you. Instead of surviving from 12 AM to 6 AM, you'll be required to perform certain tasks that change every night. Thanks to this, the game isn't just a "learn the mechanics and then repeat them until the end while they become progressively harder", and it feels much more organic than before. However, what almost ruined the game for me, is the 4th night. The difficulty suddenly increases and unfortunately it even becomes frustrating; which is a shame, 'cause the 4th night's mechanics are creepy and original. Other than that, the voice actors are really good, especially for the spooky animatronics, the atmosphere is top-notch and the game even delivers quite a lot of black humor, which to some extent resembles Portal's.
In layman's terms, I absolutely recommend this game.
P.S.: have fun playing with *them* in the dark. ;)

-Always the same, with no content change between different runs, not justifying having to restart from scratch over and over. Not to mention, the first sequence is extremely annoying to do over and over.
-As stated above, imprecise in controls and inaccurate tiling in a game where the main survival mechanic is avoiding visible enemies
-Expressed in dialogues that you really don't want to experience twice
-Very vague in what exactly triggered you being where you were, so if you do even something seemingly menial (or that you might have forgotten at that point) differently, you might get stuck.
Basically, this isn't a game with one or two glaring flaws: it's a trip to unfun land that you're forced to relive over and over while fighting with the UI. I don't only think it's not worth your money, even if it was free, I think it wouldn't be worth your time.

Attractio is a puzzle-platformer in the same vein as games like Q.U.B.E. and Magrunner.

If you like puzzle, you will probably like this one.
Pros:
Actual puzzles, The game wants you to think, and most puzzles have more than one way to actually get to the finish.
Mechanics are explained right when they come into play. The game uses smaller layers throughout to slowly make things more and more advance.
Check points. Not only can you quit and start rooms, a lot of rooms also have save points within them allowing you to save your progress in that current puzzle. Moved that box? Well you can save it there, then kill yourself in every random way you could imagine to try and figure stuff out.
Cons:
Graphics. Not sure what causes it, but at maxed out settings the lighting is a bit harsh. Staring anywhere near a light source can be a bit blinding and a lot of things give off light.
Dialog/story.  It is suppose to be a reality show, but, it gets pretty cringe worthy. I guess this shoudl be a middle ground thing since you could like a bad story/dialog mix.
Load times. Even on an SSD it takes it a few minutes just to load up every stage. If in windowed mode you could just do other stuff while loading though!
The last two stages, I'm not sure if I did the second to last stage correctly, but it just kind of enforced a trial and error until you get it right, with a very small window of success. And the finale is a "boss" which gives you no hints how to beat it.
Over all I would say they could have done a lot more with this game if they had ditched the ending and just kept making more puzzles, after all one of the last things you get to play around with is Zero-G, but it was really only used for the boss, and one or two other puzzle rooms.
Final words on the game and TLDR If you have twenty bucks, want a puzzle game. I would suggest it.

Imagine if QUBE & Portal had a baby. Now imagine that it grew up to be a conniving, sadistic, evil Gameshow Host. Then you have Attractio. These puzzles get HARD, in most games I dance through chambers with ease, but no, not in Attractio.
"Here, have a cube" says Attractio, "Cube press buttons"
"Okay, easy"
"Coloured buttons affect all things of that colour"
"Waaaaay ahead of you Atrractio"
"Oh, really?" Attractio sneers, with an evil glint in it's eye. "Try this on for size!"
And from there you're hit with a barrage of absolutely brilliant puzzles that will have you scratching your head (or banging it against the desk in my case) for hours.
Just when you think you've got the hang of it, Attractio mixes it up once again, and back to the headscratching we go. Was that puzzle really suppossed to be so complicated? Probably.
Things couldn't get much better for puzzle lovers, but they do.
Attractio features a story that will have you hooked. I am currently still making my way through some tough chambers, so I am unsure of how much there is, but with each chamber that goes by, the story unravels, and that half hour it took me is worth it.
Quick Pros & Cons:
Pros:
*Intuative Puzzles
*Clear graphics
*Challenging & lacks repetiton
*Many Puzzle-Solving Gadgets
*Great graphics
*Pick ups adding to the story, found in challenging locations.
*I can't think of a "Cons" list
Notes:
This game requires a LOT of patience & thought
You WILL (probably) get stuck for a while on at least one puzzle.
Remember to look up.
I would expect, and more than happily pay, a price tag of at least £25 for this game.
Buy this game; it's an absolute bargain.
Buy this game; support these incredible devs.
Buy this game; so that, one day, there may sequels.

Essentially, this is a board game RPG based on The Witcher series of games, utilizing cards and dice to determine outcomes.  The implementation is fairly simple to understand, particularly since you can play a game without any opponents.  This allows one to get a feel for the game goals, mechanics, and character abilities.  Overall, it is a fairly simple game, but for the price, is a unique game implementation.
Playing against the AI tends to get old quickly, but this is a great game to play with one's children if one is an older gamer with children such as myself.  The rules are relatively easy to understand, and the implementation of cards can be a useful tool to help children with their reading abilities.  The game encourages them to think ahead, and consider the probable outcomes.  Playing alone gets old, but given the price and nature of the game, I highly recommend it as a "family game" to play with the kids.

Pros:
The gameplay is fanatastic. Between story, contract, escalations, and elusive targets to do, this game has a lot to do. You complete those missions however you want. Wnat to use a .50 caliber machine gun to lay waste to your target? Go for it. Want to sneak in as a janitor to kill someone with a machete? Do it!

Cons
The story is pretty much nonexistant. If you get this game, get it for the gameplay. The story isn't as bad as Absolution, but that's because it barely exists in this game.
The music and sound effects. You will hear the same track of music over and over again. In a game that's meant to be replayed, it gets old VERY quickly. The sound effects also sound like they game from a sample pack.
Bugs. While it has vastly improved from when it orginally released, it still has quite a few bugs. Bodies falling through the floor, randomly dying when picking up an object, NPC paths not working, etc. Hopefully now that the full release is here they can work on them, but don't get your hopes up.
Overall:
I enjoyed this game a lot. The gameplay is excellant with an incredible amount of ways to kill your targets. Experimenting is the name of the game. Unforgentally, due to the bugs and story, it makes it difficult to recommend it but the gameplay is so good that I almost have to.

*INTRODUCTION*
Batman arkham origins is a prequel of the original trilogy of the batman games (made by: Rocksteady). The game focuses on the story of Bruce Wayne who has recently taken the mantle as the ''Batman'' to fight crime and serve justice.
*THE STORY*
It is christmas eave, and several blackgate prisioners have escaped from their cells and are now on the streets of gotham to spread terror, not only that but ''Black Mask'', a notorious mob boss, has put a bounty on the Batman for 1,000,000$ Dollars, attracting several mercenaries to fulfill Black Mask's task. Now it's up to Batman to stop Black Mask and save Gotham.
*THE GAME*
The game has several ways to be played, sometimes the player is ambushed by several thugs and then engaged in a fight, or, the player enters a room and then is faced with lots of armed gunmen. Those are the ways which you will face the several enemies in Arkham Origins, However there are boss fights, the real golden moments of the game are the boss fights, fighting several Batman comicbook enemies you will struggle to win most boss fights, but will occasionally come out victorious.
PS: The graphics are awesome, now go play the game

I actually really enjoyed Arkham Origins, including the ending. Although I don't believe that the quality of the overall game quite matches Asylum or City, I thought Arkham Origins was a great addition to the series. The game is quite a bit longer than City, which was a plus, and I felt more absorbed in the game-play. The ending sequences were also much more satisfying than Arkham Asylum.
There were a few unanswered questions in the story (which presumably are answered in the massive amounts of additional game-play) and some problems in the game that took away from the overall feel. (For example: Why the hell was the battle with Deathstroke so difficult when it was the first battle in the game? And am I really expected to believe that the 'mandatory curfew' actually kept all of Gotham's citizens from the street?) There are a few of congruency issues regarding puzzle solving and map design, such as the 'Find the Button' goal, which didn't make much sense contextually and blended in enough that it didn't appear as part of the actual game.  They made a few improvements to the series, though. (That final fight with Bane was the most fun/intense boss battle in any Arkham Game and seeing Joker meet Harley and Batman was really awesome to watch.)
Overall, the gameplay, the atmosphere, and the character development all were awesome. The game doesn't advance the series, but it surely uses all of the tools that the other games brought to the table and in some case, it uses them more effectively.

Gameplay: 10.5/15 ................. Machanics: 9/10

Overall: 85%

Essentially, this is a board game RPG based on The Witcher series of games, utilizing cards and dice to determine outcomes.  The implementation is fairly simple to understand, particularly since you can play a game without any opponents.  This allows one to get a feel for the game goals, mechanics, and character abilities.  Overall, it is a fairly simple game, but for the price, is a unique game implementation.
Playing against the AI tends to get old quickly, but this is a great game to play with one's children if one is an older gamer with children such as myself.  The rules are relatively easy to understand, and the implementation of cards can be a useful tool to help children with their reading abilities.  The game encourages them to think ahead, and consider the probable outcomes.  Playing alone gets old, but given the price and nature of the game, I highly recommend it as a "family game" to play with the kids.
