This game is quite literally a work of art. It's beautiful to look at, it's invigorating to play, and I guarantee you it will be one of the best - if not THE best - platformers you'll ever play with a heart warming story to boot.
The jumps in this game just FEEL right. The air time feels good, and can be slightly controlled by how long you hold the jump button. The travel distance in each jump also feels accurate and fair, and even though some of the levels will take time to adjust to you can look at the scene and just tell what needs to be done most of the time, it just takes timing.
Abilities, and the ability tree also are interesting and fun. I'd like to talk about them more but I don't want to spoil anything, but I will say that one in particular was extremely satisfying to use throughout the entire game. The ability tree feels impactful, but not so much that you feel like you miss out by going down one path too much, plus exp points can kind of be farmed if you really want every thing unlocked.
Pacing of this game did feel like it sped up a bit much at times, like it would be fairly casual going through a level with a bit of tension on landing on certain platforms and then all of a sudden there's just a rushing, climactic moment that occurs, but it luckily saves the game before each of these scenes so all is good. For the most part you can easily predict when the speed-run moments are about to occur, and with a little preperation -and a few retries for me- your gold.
The story is what really keeps you playing though. The stunning drawn backgrounds, sprites, effects, sounds, and characters on top of the gameplay will make you WANT to get through this game so badly to see what happens next, and it definitely has replay value if only to relive those warm moments. I can definitely see now why this was deemed a "new classic".

The latest installation of the Five Nights series is a complete turnaround from the original formula. No longer are you chained to a single room looking through cameras at still, eerie animatronics as a nightguard. Rather you are a technichian at one of Fazbear's sister locations (hence the name of the game) and you have the privilege of getting up close and personal to the robotic menaces.
Your task is to perform nighttime maintenance to the animatronics after their days are done, but not always will they cooperate. Each night functions differently from the last, and you won't know what to expect (this is ironic, since past FNaF games had identical nights). The suspension is built up pretty well, as you're forced into locations that make tensions rise as you expect a jumpscare or some sudden occurrence, yet jumpsacres are not all this game has to offer.
This game is much more story-driven than past installments. It's not so much a game of trying to survive a night to try and unlock more of the story, it's more about experiencing the story as it's told to you in little bits.
In my honest opinion, I like the direction Scott took in changing up the game altogether. It made things fresh, yet it's still similar enough to the original games to not feel too different.
-ORIGINAL REVIEW-
I get the sense that this game, out of all the FNaF games Scott has produced... is by far the best. Although I have not played as long as most people have on the game (just made it to night 5), I am still intrigued and want to play it more! I want to, unlike other FNaF games I've played, keep going with it.

Usually when I make a review of a FNAF game I make a joke, today I am going to do an actual review.
This game is not what you would expect, it doesn't follow the same formula as the previous games. It allows a limited free-roam system (the game is still 2D) that adds this extra dimension to the game. This game's nights don't have the "Survive till' 6AM!" Theme of the previous game, it instead focuses on one or two characters and/or a plot point. Instead of sitting in an office, checking cameras and keeping the Animatronics at bay, you have to run around and fix the animatronics. That may sound weird, but it actually is a really effective horror tactic in this game. A good example of this tactic in-game is the Breaker Room area, you have to hold down some buttons while also keeping an Animatronic at bay. The thing is, the animatronic is in the room with you and you can only see him on certain light flashes. He also says some spooky stuff in a spooky voice, that I am able to compare to dialog from Splicers in Bioshock.
Honestly I thought I would regret purchasing another FNAF game after the experience I had with FNAF World, but this is the best experience that I have had in a FNAF game since the first game.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PROS
- Doesn't have the same formula as the previous games; its a new experience.
- Chocked-full of secrets.
- Comes with a free Soap Opera.
CONS
- Short
- Some nights are almost too hard
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TL;DR: Sister Location is a refreshing experience for the FNAF series, and I do not regret purchasing it.

Undertale is a really enjoyable game. I went into it as blind as possible, having not seen any playthroughs or anything and managing to avoid most of the insane hype stuff the fandom did a while ago. The only things I knew going in was who Papyrus and Sans were, but even then I knew nothing about their characters.
The characters are fun to get to know, and there's plenty of them to get to know. I enjoyed seeing different types of personalities throughout the game. Many of the characters had a bit of "lol so random" type humor, but I didn't think that was overly done. The dialogue didn't get old, even after playing and seeing some of the same jokes after 8 hours of playing. Even the combat dialogue is fun, and it switches up a lot of the time, which kept it from getting old. The atmosphere was also very pretty. I expected a lot of dark, cave-like environments considering you're supposed to be in the Underground, but the variety in what you see keeps the game from getting boring to look at.
Based on how you're "supposed" to play the game, the combat itself can get repetitive, and even just old sometimes. Performing the same actions on most every monster will start to wear pretty quickly. The boss fights kept things more interesting, since they had some better dialogues and action options.
Also... the art style. Some of the environments looked really good, and I even thought some of them looked great, but the 8-bit style is very overused now, especially in indie games. I don't think the art really takes away or adds to the game, it's just kind of there, but later and in the end of the game, there were some art choices that I personally would have liked to see more of throughout the ENTIRE game. As far as character design and atmosphere design, I feel like there were some good creative choices made, but I feel as though the variety in the art used at the endings in the game could have made the rest of it even more great, and it would help this one stand out quite a bit more from other indie 8-bit games.
Overall, I would recommend Undertale to anyone interested, but I suggest going in without looking into the characters, endings, or choices first. I would also warn that this is probably not the greatest game ever, like the hype train would try to make it seem. Just go in with an open mind and play how you want!

What nobody told me about Spec Ops that would have sold me on it instantly?
It's essentially the gameplay Gears of War meets a story heavily influenced by Apocalypse Now/Heart of Darkness set in a semi-apocalyptic Dubai.
Let's get this out of the way: The gameplay is mediocre at best. It's a 3PS with your standard cover-based combat. There's nothing interesting about it, and plenty of games have done it better. All that said, it's functional, it's visceral, and it feels good when you finally manage to break through a particularly difficult corridor.
Now, I'd heard people talk about the story and the "twist," and I'd been wary. Most media involving critiques of modern American military involvement still seems to either have the characters "go native" (like Pochahontas or Avatar) or has the character portrayed as some kind of hero (Hurt Locker or American Sniper) despite their violent and harmful actions.
What Spec Ops did was very clever, though not entirely novel. People familiar with Apocalypse Now and/or Heart of Darkness will recognize right away the ambiguity of the introduction. You are DELTA SQUAD, from America, and you're here to ... do something? Save people? Look for survivors? It's never really made entirely clear what you're doing in the wreckage of sandswept, arid Dubai. You know that you're supposed to be rescuing somebody, but the game is ambiguous.
The villains also seem to be mysterious and ambiguous. The first group you fight are survivors of whatever happened to Dubai, but soon you're fighting an American detachment called the 33rd, led by a shadowy figure named "Konrad" (a very unsubtle nod to to author of HoD, Joseph Conrad, as well as the main 'antagonist,' Kurtz). Very soon, and very quickly, you seem to abandon your mission in order to take vengeance upon Konrad.
This is where the story gets interesting. This is where the twist begins.
Despite some awkward pacing around the middle, I felt that the reveal was slow enough that I had about an hour or two of wondering and trying to piece things together before I was shown what was actually happening. Your character is suddenly forced to make unpleasant choices, and you have to wonder whether or not that says anything about you. Probably my favourite detail is that a little past the halfway point, the load screens stop giving tips and start making accusatory statements.
"This is all your fault."
"How many Americans have you killed today?"
As this is happening, the player character (voiced by Nolan North) becomes increasingly strained. Instead of saying "Tango neutralized!" or "Heavy target down!" he starts garbling in an exhausted rasp "THE ♥♥♥♥ER'S BEEN KILLED" or "ONE LESS ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ TO WORRY ABOUT." Combined with the wear and tear of his clothes and a fresh wound after every cutscene, you really feel the character's mental state start to decline.
Noticing this for the first time made me realize that this was a game that was very much trying to push away from other games in the military shooter genre. It wasn't the run and gun propaganda of CoD MW, and it wasn't the batshit insane conspiracy theory garbage of CoD Blops. This was a game that was trying to ask you what YOU thought was right, by giving you a certain amount of power and encouraging you to abuse it as you saw fit.
The ending was satisfying. Not as satisfying as Brando staring into the distance and repeating the famous lines "The horror... The horror!" but it was still satisfying to see the game play out in a way that you almost expected, but didn't really want to see.
Anyways, 7/10. The gameplay is a 6, the story is a solid 8.5.
Must play if you're into third person shooters, military games, games that make you question your own code of ethics.

Despite having an entire year to implement "full backtracking support" and fix any and all glitches, plus an additional month and half delay for the PC version, this supposedly "Definitive Edition" somehow still ended up with a glitch where I passed through a gate I wasn't supposed to go through yet, which as a result permanently locked me out of both the area I accidentally skipped and the items located there, as well as map percentage.
After treating those who purchased the original game as mere beta testers, I had expected this paid update to be polished to the point where such glitches simply don't happen anymore during normal play. As it turns out, however, this release is still neither "Definitive" nor a proper Metroidvania, as backtracking support is still incomplete.

The Definitive Edition is exactly what I needed to get back into this game. It still remains one of the few games I can almost always go back to and get lost in. Absolutely beautiful, remarkably fun, and the new content is definitely worth the additional $5 for anyone wondering if they should upgrade.
For folks new to the game, unless this kind of game is a complete and total turnoff to you, there's next to absolutely no reason not to experience it. Especially for the ridiculously fair price they're asking for. Don't wait for it to go on sale, support this amazing piece of work at face value. It's a purchase you wont regret, I can assure you.
One of the defining factors behind what makes the game so fun is the level of trust it has in you to grasp concepts and quickly. You'll very quickly be given new abilities which rapidly ramp up how quickly and creatively you can navigate the world, but the game is fully aware of your new capabilities and almost instantly puts them to the test. There's no hand holding. Once you get out of an area with a new ability, you've basically reassured the game that you understand the mechanics and are effectively forced to become adept at it. In a very good, rewarding way.
Throw into this the traditional "metrovania" style of exploring and you'll find yourself actively revisiting locations to test out your new abilities and find new secrets. At the same time, you'll feel the strength of your new abilities as you soar through areas once tricky to navigate. It's a rewarding sense of progress that isn't measured in purely in numbers, but by your ability to build upon what you knew before, with entirely new powers.
You'll also figure out just how layered your powers can be as you experiment with them. While there's no explicit chaining, you'll find yourself pulling of combinations of moves that have a certain degree of synergy about them. It's fun, but above all, it's satisfying.

Given that this was a point and click game, I thought it'd be an interesting, fun game to play.  I did see there were a lot of negative reviews, but I still wanted to give it a chance.  To be blunt, this is a terrible game.  My first complaint was the default volume of the music.  At least for me, the music got annoying pretty fast, and I ended up just turning the music off completely.  I really wish developers would set the music volume at half instead of setting it at max so it just blares in your ear.    The game starts off with two people arguing, and that's your introduction.  As you progress, you realize just how bad this story is. It even got to a point where I almost just gave up on the game and put it on my 'uninstall' list.
Lets move on with the most common thing that happens.  When you die, the game over screen seems to last forever, and then you have to start over from the very beginning.  If you're going to make us sit through a very long game over screen, at least give us check points.   As if that's not bad enough, nothing changes when you die.  It's the exact same process over and over.
One of my biggest issues is that you seem to have only 1hp.  If a zombie so much as spits on you you're dead.  I get zombie mucus is goss and all, but really?  You're going to make our death instant?  You can't even defend yourself, you just have to accept it.  That is a really, really poor mechanic.
At cetain spots I noticed you could walk onto the wall as if it wasn't there.  I'm not sure if this is intentional or an unintentional bug.  If it's intentional, why?
To my surprise, you can't alt tab.  You can't even use the Steam overlay.  I'm sorry, but how hard is it to allow us to use Steam overlay? It's a vital part of all Steam games, and it's incredibly disappointing when the option is not there.
Something that I did like was that you can use the arrow keys to move, and space to click things.  Sure, it's a point and click, you're supposed to use the mouse, but I ended up just using the arrow keys.  Always nice when you're given option to choose how you want to play/control your character.
As a final note, I do not recommend this game at all.  The only way I could see myself recommending it is if it was free.

Mad Max makes good use of the Batman and Shadow of Mordor formula: huge map with a lot to explore, fluid combat, upgrades. It also adds a new system, cars! Driving is a bit clunky at first, especially because your car is terrible and you need to improve it. Max upgrades won't make it feel like a racing game, but it does enough of its job.
Not only that, the game is amazing presentation-wise. You have sounds matching stuff you hear in the movies, astounding graphics, good VA.
What could go wrong, you ask? Everything else. This game is boring, plain and simple. Couple that with a story that doesn't even try to make sense, and you have zero motivation to get to the end.
The idea is that the map is divided into areas, and each area has some stuff the enemy uses to show its power over that place (settlements, totems, minefields). Imagine that and multiply it by 15.
Exploration feels good for the first hours, but after some point, you will be fighting the same enemies at similar places over and over and over again.
It's worth mentioning that a lot of the hard-earned currency comes from liberating settlements, and the story also locks you until you lower the enemy presence in certain areas.
The game is worth a shot for a low price, but its lack of variety certainly damages what could be another amazing game from WB

Five Nights at Freddy's: Sister Location really changes up the gameplay in comparison to the first four games. Instead of getting your nights down to a routine as you did in FNAF 1-4, in this game, you need to complete different task each night in order to progress to the next level. Be warned though: Night 4 is a real challenge and will take time and concentration. This game is also much more story-driven than the other four games, and reveals key parts of the new but familiar storyline as you progress through each night. Another thing that makes this game so different than the other games is the use of voice actors. We have always wanted to hear what certain animatronics/people sounded like, and in this game you do for many characters. Overall, this is my favorite game in the Five Nights at Freddy's franchise!
Custom night update: Wow... This game got 100 times better than it already was with the addition of the custom night. There is much more replay value in the game now, and the custom night is like a whole new game within the original game. Plus, a new key part to the storyline is revealed after beating all the nights on very hard. The best part about this update, though, is the fact that you can finally beep Fredbear's nose in any of the custom night stages! :D

The Hitman game I've been waiting years for.
Pros:
-It dumped a lot of immature baggage after Absolution. Less women with giant fake♥♥♥♥♥♥hanging out for horny teenagers,  and a more mature atmosphere really helps the feeling of being a hired killer mixing into his backgrounds to close in on his target. It makes the gameplay more immersive and less goofy than having one of the Carradine brothers going on about breeding Agent 47 while I infiltrate a super-secret base of pornstar nuns or some garbage.
-Missions are about assassinations. There are no infiltration missions like in Hitman 2 or Absolution. All 6-ish missions (there are two open-ended training missions I'm not counting that are simple and fun) revolve entirely around assassinating one or more targets with the occasional side objective. There are tons of ways to achieve objectives, and they can get really fun.
-The way the DLC is set up suits the game well. It was fairly obvious in Absolution that it was becoming difficult to create a large amount of traditional Hitman maps in modern-gen, and I feel this is a decent compromise to give the team extra time and opportunities to create well-crafted missions and extra content. All of the first season missions are out now, but each mission is large with lots of stuff to do and completion boxes to check. Add in that each map has a multitude of separate challenges to assassinate/steal different targets under different circumstances, and there is a lot a of replayability here. I'm not dismissing peoples' complaints about the DLC system, but I think the choice was made with the game in mind and IO handled it well.
-The mechanics feel incredibly solid for once. They've been getting better since 2, but now I feel like any time I get caught, it's because of my own fault for not checking around, noting which people can see through my disguise (they're marked with a circle over their heads in this game, or using tools at my disposal, versus randomized nonsense like ninjas only attacking you if you looked directly at them in H2 or something.
Cons:
-I'm kind of tired of how strict the ratings get in the series as a whole. You know how Metal Gear Solid will give you like eight trillion guns and a ton of ways to lethally take out targets but punishes you when you do it? Hitman still kind of does that. I kind of want to do an assassin-y thing of sitting up in a perch, sniping my target, and making a clean getaway without having to game the system to get a decent rating.
-A lot of old equipment is useless. There's a "subdue" move now that lets you either quickly knockout or kill someone while you're unarmed, and it breaks the game in certain spots. I don't think I've used the fiber wire once yet to get Silent Assassin rankings, which feels wrong in a Hitman game.
The only Hitman game I haven't played is Contracts, and I would honestly rate this just above Blood Money as my favorite in the series. It's well crafted and designed from a gameplay standpoint, and I can see myself easily putting over a hundred hours in this trying to complete side missions. If you can get over the weird DLC system and just buy the bunch when it's at a good price for you, I can recommend it to anyone who's interested in what the game has to offer.

I've had nothing but good times with Hitman. As a long-time fan of the series, IO's recent take on the game has been refreshing, and - honestly - nearly perfect. The polish on each scenario, the magnitude of ways any solution can be achieved... It is all just staggering. I think this is the best Hitman game in the series, by far.

Great game by Io-Interactive, going back to their Hitman: Blood Money roots, allowing the player to approach missions through one of virtually countless ways of completion. A new "Opportunities" system has been added, allowing the player to take advantage of certain situations in missions. The maps are quite large, and interactable, rendering it possible for the player initiate whatever their hitman intuition is thinking about. There is a story to the game, however the game is not driven by the story unlike Hitman: Absolution (which was not liked by many players due to it being too story-driven, linear, and not presenting a lot of freedom for the player unlike its predecessors). The graphics are quite appealing, and the flaws stated by the community for Hitman: Absolution have been taken care of (kudos to Io-Interactive for listening to the community). Additionally, for the completionist, there are hard to achieve optional challenges for each mission, and the Contracts mode from Hitman: Absolution is still there. Overall, it is a great game for both newcomers and Hitman fans.
The only problem of the game is the strictly-enforced DRM, which requires you to be online to save the game. If the game is saved offline, the progress is not carried over to the online profile. This might cause problems, however as long as you stay online it should be alright.

Playing this game is rather like watching the proverbial train wreck: you'll be horrified, but you can't look away. This is in no way a bad thing. Spec Ops wants to tell a story about soldiers in war. But unlike games such as Call of Duty, it doesn't want you to feel like an awesome, unstoppable killing machine that's fighting terrorism FOR 'MERICA!!! or whatever; it wants you to see that war is not glamorous, awesome, fun, or desirable. It wants you to see the terrible toll that combat can exact on those who experience it. And above all, it wants you to see that in real conflict, there are no "good guys" and "bad guys," and the world is full of gray areas. War is hell, and anyone who goes in will either join the fortunate dead...or have to live with what they've done to survive.
Spec Ops is a third-person cover-based shooter that alternates between desert environments and crumbling urban ruin. You have two squadmates who can be directed to attack specific targets or heal a fallen comrade; they're pretty good at following orders in a timely fashion and, unlike some other AI partners, they're not highly prone to getting themselves shot constantly or hung up on the level geometry. Enemies are decently clever, more than willing to flank you, toss grenades to get you out of cover, or trick you into walking right into a Heavy Trooper's line of fire.
The game also offers the clever idea of having drifts of sand piled up on fragile surfaces like windows, which you can shoot out to bury your enemies. It doesn't show up that often, but it's kind of neat when it's there.
There's the usual shooter stable of weapons: pistols, heavy pistols, shotguns, sniper rifles, etc. They sound good and feel decently punchy, and aiming is never a problem. Most weapons also have an alternate fire mode, which does add a little depth to the combat.
I didn't play the multiplayer, so I can't honestly review it. I will say the developers originally didn't even want multiplayer, and the campaign is designed well enough to stand on its own, so make of that what you will.
I highly recommend this game. It is a breath of fresh air in an over-crowded genre that's becoming increasingly generic. This game is also visually stunning, with exceptional voice acting, and sound. It is definitely worth the money and the effort to play the game from the beginning to the end.
Final Decision: 8/10

This game is one of the few new games I can call "Nintendo Hard" with a straight face
Yes, this game can invoke a lot of trial and error, but that's almost half the fun in figuring out the correct jumping.
This game, while difficult really respects your abilities more than almost any other platformer (especially indies) i've played in recent history. This is not something you'll breeze through on the first try.
The controls are very fluid and tight. Which are very useful since you only have one hit-point without the possibility of powerups. There are no non-boss enimies (at least through Ch2-1), but the saws, needles, and salt will give you a hard time.
Speaking of bosses, they are difficult, but play cleanly and are far from luck-based. I have heard that Ch4's boss is rather cheap, but I can't say anything as I haven't made it that far yet.
The courses are rather short, but there are a lot of them (at least 20 per chapter+Boss Fight). and with 10 chapters between the light and dark worlds, as well as a ton of user-generated content. You will be hard pressed to be at a loss for content.
This game really respects your abilities.
Not for people who game for the story, there's a plot, but it's about as deep as SMB's story. However, if you (like me) play for gameplay and want a challengeing but fair platformer, this would be a great game to try

So, I love zombie games. A lot. This seemed pretty interesting at first glance. Not to mention super cheap. However, there are some pretty major flaws in the game itself.
-For starters, it took a LOT of player nagging for the developers to even a save function for people not wanting to play for however many hours straight.
-Additionally, there's no such thing as health or anything in this game. If you happen to accidentally bump into a zombie (whether due to actual accident or due to the shoddy pathing) you have to immediately manage to succeed in clicking at the right time or... suffer permadeath. I mean, I get that it's a hardcore permadeath game, but come on.
-To expand on the previous point, yeah. The pathing for the character is extremely shoddy at best. It'll often take the dumbest route to the clicked location, often passing right through a horde... or even a single zombie for that matter.
-Putting mechanics aside, the main character in the only available story is a piece of crap. There is no possible way to actually empathize with this character in the slightest. I get that the game is more focused on the survival component, but seriously? If you're going to put in a story, at least try to make a character that has redeeming factors. She's akin to a soulless raider or something similar.
-Another point I should add is that the fullscreen mode is rather broken. The in-game mouse cursor and out-game mouse cursor are constantly in conflict, depending on where you have your mouse on the screen.
All-in-all, I'd give this game a 5/10 at absolute best. The sprites are nice, even though they look like they are just the base sprites from the zombie pack for RPG Maker or similar, at least. The idea of the game is also alright. But that's about it for the redeeming qualities. I honestly thought for a little bit that the game was early access, but there is no early access label on the page. This feels like an alpha at best. Not a full game in the slightest.

Great game, definitely one of the best in the series.  Its a shame that its getting such a bad rap because of the always online nonsense.
Some notable improvements from previous games:
- Absolution disguise system is gone.  Now instead of everyone dressed the same as you being able to immediately recognize you, only a handful will recognize you.  They are easily distinguishable from people who won't notice you, so avoiding them becomes a fun challenge.
- Enemy responses are more realistic.  For example guards will now attempt to escort you out of a restricted area and not just start shooting immediately.
- Mission planning is great, letting you choose where to start, what equipment to bring, and even offers the possibility to start the mission with a disguise.
- Mission replayability: Every mission has challenges, and completing these challenges unlocks new planning options for the next time you play the mission, ie new starting spots and new equiptment.
- Challenges: you can choose to play through the levels your own way, but looking through the challenges will give you some fun ideas for stuff to try, especially on subsequent playthroughs.
- Opportunities: These give you a more structured way to achieve certain mission goals, such as giving you several objectives which will lead to you meeting one of your targets in private.  These are totally optional and purists can easily avoid using them, but I think they add to the experience because they give you some cool pointers/ideas without having to revert to using online walkthroughs.
- A 'Pro' for me: I haven't beaten the story yet, but from what I've seen so far, it seems like this game virtually ignores the events of Absolution.  We're right back to doing missions for the ICA as if nothing ever happened.
- It feels a lot more like Blood Money than Absolution, with some small features returning from Blood Money like the ability to distract guards with dropped guns and bodies being taken away in body bags, etc
Cons (I'll be ignoring the online issue, since apparently the game is fully playable offline, it just uses a different save than your online game, so either always play offline or always play online)
- The only con I've really noticed is that there is no sniper rifle case anymore.  You can, however, have a sniper rifle smuggled into the level, but it can only be carried around if you have a disguise that makes it seem appropriate, or if you hide with it.

IO understood the huge mistake they made with their 5th Hitman game: Absolution.
Keeping the engine and the few good gameplay ideas they added at the time, they actually have come back to what made Blood Money the (not anymore) best Hitman game: many opportunities, non linearity, replay value... YOU are the hunter, not the hunted.
After completing the whole 1st season, I can say it: the game is awesome. Some levels are better than others, but my 170+ hours of gameplay are here to testify that the fun is genuinely here.
The bad thing I have to say about it:
Elusive Target: WHY CAN'T WE TRY IT MULTIPLE TIMES? IO answered the question, I disregard that anwser, way too stupid. There is content, I want to be able to play it as much as I want and when I want to. Who cares about stupid leaderboard?
That being said, here comes the new best Hitman game. Buy it.

Turn-based tactical board game with fascinating art and the story, based on the (finally) world-famous fantasy universe written by Andrzej Sapkowski. You have four playable characters, each with own strong and weak points. And you've got some quests to do, by travelling in the dangerous world, fighting and tricking monsters and politicians, helping and betraying other good guys around, to make a better final score for yourself.
Surely, card game is looking better when you have 3 pals around, free evening and cozy place to gather. And maybe pizza to fill the list... But! Funny thing is that this Adventuring Witcher game is more suitable to the PC, than to such gatherings as a gaming party of good friends. It's a bit more on the digits side, than I'd really loved to see in my basement (or garage), when I meet my people.
On the other hand, for the multiplayer little session, game feels quite alright: fast, challenging... If only a bit too cold, though, during a little amount of real interactions between players. Still, for its current price, this game is must-have - if you ever were about turn-based games where you gotta think and calculate your steps miles ahead.
My mark is 8/10. Not the thing I'd take with me on the space flight to Alpha Centauri... But quite fine as a card game, a gem among many others there on Steam. And - yeah, I'm biased, as I'm really love the setting.

Over the shoulder view, shooting mechanics, movement, team tactics - all decently implemented.

Sister Location is a prety damn good game, and was well on its way to being the second best FNAF game behind the original, or maybe even *the* best in the series.
And then Night 4 happens.
Now, Night 4 starts out AWESOME with some great things never before seen or heard through the entirety of the FNAF series, but then immediately falls off a cliff in the sharpest, most sudden downward 90-degree angle in FNAF history when, for lack of a better way to put it, you need to start doing stuff. Of course, it starts with some confusion - a feeling out process to see how everything works, like with any other thing in any game you're exposed to and must react to in any other game, so no problem here - and then simply, time after time after time at this point, erodes into pure frustration, easily killing any motivation to dig deeper in this otherwise stellar chapter in the ever-intriguing FNAF series. Easily, in my opinion, the worst part of any FNAF game on several planes.
With that out of the way now, I can turn back to this game's strengths.
Sister Location is a kick to the balls of the regular FNAF formula, and that is a good thing, especially since it works beautifully. Going into the game not knowing what to expect, the game seemed to be going into the same direction and going with the same formula of the other games of the series by introducing what appeared to be the recurring tools used to keep the animatronics at bay, but goes into a totally different direction. The emerging uncertainty factor in this deviance from the known formula helps maintain a lingering sensation of tension (which actually gets completely cut off thanks to N4 unless you manage to beat it before frustration sets in), and simply does not let go.
With that said, as gripping as the game could be, it only lasts as slowly or as quickly as you allow it to. Once again barring Night 4, a slower, more conservative player can get 2, maybe 2.5 hours out of this game, but it's a hell of a 2-2.5 hours for the "main" storyline. Past that, Sister Location is all about barely (and I mean BARELY) squeaking by a few situations.
I do very much recommend this game, but with all of the game's content that I do know of at the time of this writing, I don't think this game should be bought at the full price of $7.50 or whatever it would be, but that's just me. Definitely go for it while the 15% off launch sale is going on, or perhaps wait for any sort of sale in the future. I really wish there was a little bit more length in this game to justify going for it at full price, but the experience is still among the coolest I've ever had playing any video game, so it's still probably going to be well worth it for you to drop those few extra pennies.

Five Nights at Freddy's: Sister Location is a new entry in the "Five Nights" franchise. To begin with, I can already say that you'll be playing in a more story-driven environment, so if you're a fan of replayability or overall the structure of the previous games, you may need to rethink if you're going to buy this one.
Okay, so, with that out of the way, I like this one. I mean, don't get me wrong, I liked the older ones, but I felt like they were really repetitive and seemed to go on for a little too long. Anyway, this one ditches most of the aspects from the previous entries and focuses more on something new every night, although it's not as straight-forward or even in the same pattern rather from a few similar places in the building. I can say, for sure, that there's more lore in this game like the others and it explains a lot, but also raises a few questions.
To start, Five Nights at Freddy's: Sister Location is a trip for any FNaF fan. If you're like me and stuck with the series when its first entry crawled its way into the Youtube industry, you probably know this series by heart. If you don't, however, this game will probably not be easy to follow in any circumstance, at least primarily in the "story" aspect. You should obviously start with the first "Five Nights at Freddy's" and work you way up here. Well, anyway, if you're a fan of FNaF, buy this. It's a great new entry and feels truly different than the usual treatment we're used to. There is, however, a gigantic problem that now has risen from the repetitive grave that I consider the older games to pertain to. Due to Scott Cawthon, the developer of this game and series, attempting to ditch the very foundation the series was built on, there are more issues with this formula in itself. Starting with the fact that the game relies heavily on the first play-through and a minor search for easter eggs, rather than a continuous nightly pattern, results in a short, detailed experience that is very much shorter in theory than the previous FNaF games.
In short, this is a very different game. I can say, however, that I think most of the FNaF fans will enjoy it, but I can't say anything else. It's a good game at heart, but to truly understand and to grasp all of its concepts, I recommend you tackle the originals.
If you aren't a FNaF fan and didn't like the original games, I think you shouldn't buy this one, or at least watch a few videos online about it first.

Prior to buying this game, or more precisely upgrading from the Original version of this game, I wondered if it was worth it. And while on paper it looks all so nice and shiny, reality is slightly different.
So, what improvements have I noticed?
1. New logo in main menu. Yet the desktop shortcut is the same.
2. Fast travel between fountains! That is handy if you'd like to skip some backtraking.
3. Difficulty levels. Yes, they're there, but do they make any difference gameplay-wise? In some degree: the higher the difficulty -- the more damage player receives. But don't expect the game to be easy on Easy  -- it is still nearly-dark-souls-difficult with manual & limited saves.
4. One new area and slightly re-designed sections of the main map. Um, that is a tricky one. A new area is there, it's very cool, quite large and brings two new abilities. Re-designed sections however are not quite "re"-designed -- more like a few extra interactive objects to be activated with the new abilities. Nothing really mind blowing to be honest.
Overall all I've seen so far should have been a free patch + a dlc. A few save points during escapes for noobs, fast travel and improved stability (i.e. bug fixes)? Not quite worth of a separate game, besides the original Ori still needs a patch or two to fix crashes. Or is it abandoned now?
By the way, that new level is totally missable and is not required to be explored in order to progress. I found it only thanks to the achievements and google. Located
.
If you have played the Original Ori and the Blind Forest and either completed it once and for all or dropped because it was too-damn-difficult for you -- no, don't upgrade. You most likely won't be happy with your investment. Also keep in mind that save files from the original game are not transferable. Actually it reminded me of many other definitive/redux/director's cut paid upgrades..
However if you are a new player or want to replay it from the very beginning -- sure, go get it. Because it's still visually astonishing and well desined game. Just a little more polished and patched.

First for those who are trying to decide whether to buy the orignal version of Ori or the Definitive Edition:  buy the Definitive Edition.  Both are the same game, but this version comes with two new areas to explore and two new skills to play with.
For those who have the original and are trying to decide whether to buy the Definitive Edition:  It's the same game, aside from those two afore mentioned additions, so it depends on how much you love Ori.  For me, I REALLY love Ori, and so paying the sale price of 5$ was absolutely worth it.
For those who are trying to decide whether to buy any version at all, here's my review copied from the original:
Ori and the Blind Forest is an excellent game with scenes that will definitely tug on your heart strings. The visuals are breathtaking, and the level designs are quite good.
It's a metroidvania with a heavy emphasis on platforming action rather than combat, although fighting enemies is still a significant part of the game as well. How does it emphasize platforming, then? The biggest example of this is that there are no boss fights, but rather boss quality platforming challenges that require quick reflexes, good timing, and will absolutely get your heart pumping! I mean this literally. After the first of these, my heart was racing at twice its resting rate.
The story is short, as is to be expected of this type of game, but the depth and emotional impact is solid. It's very rarely that I've felt an antagonist to be fully justified in everything they have done to our hero, yet still known that I must stop them anyway.
Truly an excellent game. I highly recommmend it to you, and everyone else!

This is a fun little game to play with your friends, or against yourself if you are good at shifting from one personality to another at the click of a mouse.
The flavour text of the cards, the music and the look of the game board and the unique abilities of each of the characters make for good immersion that makes you feel like you are THEM and THERE.
While some characters might seem totally imbalanced and unbeatable in one game, this is ultimately a game where a lot depends on luck, so you might find that that darned OP dwarf that totally pwned your poor sorceress in the last game is faring a lot less well when hordes of legendary monsters are eating his face as he is only capable of shooting (or rolling, really) blanks.
One feature that would make this game more multiplayer-friendly would be a combination of local and online gameplay - say I have a friend at my house and one in another city, the two of us could play my copy of the game locally while the third person joins in online. But I'm guessing not a lot of people will be in this situation so it's a minor issue.
Overall, it's a fun way to make friendships end, akin to a fantasy Monopoly.

This what it? This was the cult classic shooter every video game hipster this side of the solar system ranted and raved about? Really?  Okay, where to begin...
First and foremost, the game was four hours on the normal difficulty.  Four.  That's about a dollar an hour for what I paid this game for on Steam, so whatever,  But definitely not worth the $30 it's worth normally.  Beyond that, the game doesn't really successfullly subvert the shooter genre like a lot of people like to say it does.  Why?  Because you, as the player, never have any real decisions to make.  The game tries to make you feel bad for doing things, except you have no choice but to do them.  If I could choose not to do bad things but I did them anyway, mistakeningly or otherwise, I might feel bad about the bad things my character does in the game.  But I can't, so I don't.  Beyond that, the story was pretty convoluted.  Some of the crap the characters do is overtly sabotaging their mission and they don't seem to notice until after the fact.
The rest of the narrative is pretty much "find this guy, so you can find that guy, so you can find THAT guy", and that's pretty much  it.  It's a quest to find a bunch of different dudes who are in the game for fewer than thirty minutes so you can find the next guy who will be in the game for fewer than thirty minutes and that's pretty much it.  On top of that, the suppossed delta operators act like anything but.  None of them seem like they've ever held a weapon before in their respective lives.  The player character inexplicably has two rear iron sights on his rifle and fires it with the stock under his armpit.  The dialogue is also horrible.  Additionally, there are military inaccuracies out the wazoo.  There are two officers in your "squad", but delta doesn't recruit officers.  A fireteam is at least four guys, but your team has three.  The 33rd Battalion has way too many guys to actually be a battalion, and the guy leading them is also a delta officer (again, even though there's no such thing).  Why is a spec ops guy leading an infantry unit?  Who knows.  This game makes zero sense.  Moreoever, you carry about half the actual combat load of an actual soldier, so have fun constantly scrounging for ammo after you burn through your whopping 120 rounds in your primary weapon.
Your teammates are also completely useless.  They can't do anything unless you tell them to, otherwise they just get in your way.  Ocasionally, they'll even get downed and you'll have to revive them, even though there is no such system in place for your character.  If you go down, you die.  Which is horribly frustrating, considering you'll sprint when you mean to slide into cover and vice versa due to the bad controls.  All in all, this game is just bad.  It doesn't really succeed in anything it tries to do.  The only part of the game that really got to me was one of the endings that you can affect, and even then, the game couldn't fight its compulsion to be lame and cut the awesome pan-out and the music just as the full effect of the scene was setting in.
The game's cutscenes are abrupt with rapid transitions and violent cut-outs of music.  There are fewer than ten commonly-encountered weapons in the whole game, and none of them can be customized.  Which, is kinda ridiculous, considering delta guys get absolute autonomy over their gear.  Your companions are noisey and incompetent tag-alongs who constantly shout at you, giving away your position.  Even the gunplay is mediorce at best.  Buy the game and give it a go if it's on sale.  Otherwise, avoid it like it's the plague.  This game was atrociously bad.

It's a good game and I'd recommend it.
First of all, it's not a 2D ripoff of Minecraft; it's far from that, I'd even go to say Minecraft is worse than Terraria, but I'm neutral. Some examples of Terraria not being a "2D ripoff of Minecraft" are: It has guns. It has magic weapons. It has more tool grades than just: Wood, Stone, Gold, Iron, Diamond. It has mechanical things that actually occur in the real world, it has mythical creatures and biomes.
Second of all, if you get bored, that's not the end, there's mods and challenges which will keep you playing for much longer than just after your beat the game. The community is active, and (from what I've seen) are willing to help you if you're stuck. Sure there's the occasional troll, but you find those in pretty much EVERY game. I won't spoil too much, I'd rather not ruin the experience for you.
In short: There's mythical creatures, items and biomes, with things which are found in the real world, the game proves to be fun, challenging and always has something new for you to discover. You can even play friends and it's as simple as making a world, character, and clicking a few buttons! Terraria is a great game, sure it has it's flaws like the 2D aspect, and the limited worlds, but you learn to get over them and even make them benefits! You can use the same character in different worlds, you can increase your stats and fight amazing bosses and discover what's strong against them. You can cheat if you want to, (by using mods, or item servers) and it's a really great sandbox game. Discovery. - 9.99/10 rinzor

The online requirement is destroying this otherwise fantastic-seeming game. Video version of this review:
I love this game. I love everything ABOUT this game. The characters are adorable, the backgrounds and colors are absolutely beautiful, and the villain is frigging awesome! But the soundtrack. I can’t even put into words how much I love this music. Gareth Coker, I take my hat off to you.
The story of this game revolves around Ori, obviously. Kuro, a ginormous, and might I add, majestic owl, steals the source of the Spirit Tree’s light, causing the forest to slowly die. You can find it at the beginning of the game. The light of the Spirit Tree is apparently it’s own living thing, named Sein.
You’re main objective is to restore the light back to Nibel, if that’s how you pronounce that. But to do this, you have to restore three different elements at three different locations: the Element of Waters at the top of the Ginso Tree, the Element of Winds in the Forlorn Ruins, and the Element of Warmth at Mount Horu. Kinda funny that a ton of water just flows through a giant tree.
Each of those three locations are chock full of puzzles. The puzzles in the Ginso Tree consist mainly of portals and the use of your Bash ability, which you actually get inside the Ginso Tree. The Forlorn Ruins gives you a light orb thing to protect yourself from the heated areas of the ruins, as well as alter gravity. I actually really like this puzzle mechanic. And Mount Horu gives you several different rooms that you have to solve in different ways in order to stop the lava from flowing so you can move forward.
But the biggest challenge of these areas are the escape sequences. You can choose whatever difficulty you want before you start the game, so the challenge of these sequences may depend on your choice of difficulty. I went with Normal, so I did end up having a bit of trouble with each escape, especially when trying to collect all the items along the way. But even if you don’t manage to get them all, at least they allow you to go back inside.
There is a lot of combat in this game as well. That’s where Sein comes in. Ori, being the pacifist that he is, has to rely on Sein to fight off the creatures that attack you in the game. Also, it only just dawned on me that you are controlling two characters at the same time.
After you defeat each enemy, you pick up Spirit Light. These can also be obtained from exploring the entire forest. There are even secret areas where you can find stuff, not just Spirit Light, but other items, like Life Cells and Energy Cells, which are essential to your survival. You can also find Map Stone Fragments to make more of the area visible on your map. If you collect enough Spirit Light, you gain an Ability Cell, with which you can upgrade some of the abilities you get throughout the game.
There are a total of 11 different abilities in this game, which you get from some dead Ori guys who turn into trees apparently. The first ability you actually get is Spirit Flame, a.k.a. your attack ability, which you get the moment you pick up Sein. I’m not gonna go over all the rest of the abilities. Most of them are pretty self-explanatory.
There is one problem I have with The Dash Ability. The only place you actually need to use it is in Black Root Burrows, the place where you get the ability in the first place. It’s pretty much unnecessary everywhere else. You would think they would add more situations that require you to use it. I mean, sure, you could use it to get around faster. But Ori already moves at a fast enough speed, that you don’t need to use the Dash at all. Plus, you can warp with the spirit wells. How much faster do you need to be?
I have had some moments of unresponsive controls, likely caused by spamming the buttons, and some camera glitches. These problems don’t happen too often for me, but they are annoying when they do happen.
But honestly, I don’t think I could recommend this game more. It’s fun, it’s pretty, it’s cute, and I’ve left out a bunch of stuff, because this is the kind of game I do not want to spoil.

This isn't an appraisal of the game for new players (it's very good, get it now) but me sharing my 2 cents with those who have already finished the original and are wondering if the new content justifies another purchase...
The new levels (with the new abilities) are accessible early, but do require some later abilities to complete. It's also possible to finish the game without seeing the new content, which is what I initially did. This actually frustrated me, because the only changes I initially saw involved blocking off originally accessible areas with walls that can only be opened using the new abilities. The game now includes full backtracking so if you are like me and finish it first you can still use the same save to go back and visit the new levels. They are actually really enjoyable (and very pretty), but not lengthy - I only took about an hour to see all the new stuff. New abilities are fun to use but nothing special. (bash is still by far the best!)
The new hard difficulty just makes enemies more powerful and increases environmental damage. You can now warp between spirit wells, personally I think it cheapens the game a bit as the interlocking level design is so superb.
There are some new videos/concept arts; some of the videos are fascinating, some (like the promo one with the music being recorded) are really quite uninteresting.
All in all? It's basically some glorified DLC levels, and extra goodies that *should* have been a free update. The only brilliant new stuff is the new level, and I guess the one life mode is cool. I suppose this gets a totally new release so that the original is left "pure" for speedruns and whatnot, but it is not very different from the original. If you want some pretty new levels I guess it's  worth $5USD, but once the promo ends it's not worth a re-purchase. Would have been nice to have the Soundtrack in FLAC included in the bundle too, one can dream... :)

Because of the last 2 cons, I can only give it an 8 out of 10.

An expanded version of one of the best platformers out there.
The Ori-ginal is great by itself. It has some of the most fluid, fun controls and challenges of any game I've played, and it's clear from the start that the people of Moon Studios perfectly understood what they were doing, because everything works masterfully! Simply moving around feels great, and combined with creative environments and obstacles, it adds up to a kind of platforming brilliance that you don't see very often. Despite the structure of the game, I'd argue that it's more Rayman than Metroid, though I strongly recommend it to pretty much anyone who enjoy sidescrollers. It's a game that keeps getting better with every new challenge and every new ability, most of which only enhance the platforming (the bash ability changes everything). It also has the best quicksaving system I've ever seen.
All of it is wrapped up in a fantastic presentation. The art is detailed and gorgeous, the soundtrack is dramatic and unforgettable, and both compliment each other perfectly, as well as the grand, poetic storytelling that goes all out to make the world feel gigantic and ancient. It seems like the developers only took lessons from the best of the best, and nothing feels underwhelming, cut short or left out in any way. It's all extremely polished.
It's pretty weird that this Definitive Edition isn't just an update to the original version, because now that game is just taking up space on the store and in my library. There doesn't seem to be any reason to buy it when the DE is the same thing + new levels, new abilities, difficulty settings, fast travel options and full backtracking support (although more graphical options would've been nice as well). Having beaten the old version, all these additions were very notable, very early on, and they only serve to make the game more exciting than ever.
If you like magic, fun, challenge and feeling emotions, you should pick this up. There has never been a better time to do so.

Undertale is, at its core, a fantastic game. The game just doesn't feel enjoyable to play, playing the game normally is incredibly boring as the combat sections are easy so that you can finish them with the pacifist amount of HP (20), while the genocide run is able to be balanced around your current level, as the game knows exactly how much HP you have at individual points.
Yes, I think that this game about how being aggressive is bad is actually
if you play it as a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥
The only problem with this is that the genocide run takes at least 3 hours to complete, with almost all of that time spent grinding. This is supposed to push the purpose of the game as "violence is bad and pacifism is good" by simply taking away the fun in playing one half of the game, but it results in an empty feeling experience where the main, pacifist route is boring due to the lack of challenge, and the fun, side route is boring because you have to spend about two and a half hours grinding.

Now that the first season of HITMAN has ended, I feel that I can give my views on the game. I was sceptical about the episodic approach to begin with, but after sticking with it for a few months I can honestly say that it really suits the game. The maps included are probably the biggest in the entire Hitman series and are full of detail and challenges to complete, and the wait between episodes gave me enough time to master each mission and discover many different ways of eliminating my targets. In fact, on your first playthrough of a mission, I recommend ignoring your objectives completely and just exploring the map for a bit to become familiar with it, as these levels are huge.
The gameplay feels a lot like Hitman: Blood Money with the improved controls and mechanics from Hitman: Absolution. It's pretty easy to get the hang of it while the game still offers a good challenge. You really need to use strategy when playing this game, as going into missions guns blazing will not only get you a lower rating at the end of levels but also get you killed very fast, as the amount of health that you're given is minimal.
In terms of graphics, the game often looks beautiful, and locations like Paris and Marrakesh have massive crowds of people which help to make the game world feel alive. I rarely encountered lag in these locations and when I did it was minor. I found the music in the game to be decent but forgettable. Sadly, None of the tracks come close to Jesper Kyd's work on previous Hitman titles.
I don't really play Hitman games for their story, but the one that is included in this game is quite weak and disappointing, with the stakes never really getting that high. Another negative aspect is that parts of the game are online-only, and although I never disconnected from the servers while playing, it seems ridiculous for a single-player only game to require this.
However, I really do recommend this game, even if you're not a fan of Hitman. It's a brilliant stealth game where you can get very creative with how you accomplish your goals. At the time of this review, I've just hit 50 hours in-game and I still haven't completed many of the challenges, not to mention the many contracts that are created by the community. There is lots of content on offer here, and overall I would say that it justifies the price tag.
tl;dr - this game is brilliant and if you're a fan of stealth games then I really suggest that you get it.

I know that a lot of people accuse this game of its awful bugs and instability and as well as what they say are true, I still love this and dare to suggest that you try, either as a Bat-fan or a game user.
Its graphic, sounds, and actions are amazing, obviously improved from the former Arkham series (even though those bugs might take away some of the admiration). Story is rather short and less elaborate than Arkham City, and yet strong and impressive enough. It's actually cool that it starts off with Batman vs. all the hired supervillain assassins in town over one night, on should-be-merry-and-happy Christmas, and wraps up with the origins of Arkham, literally. The detective mode and Wayne tech got more detailed and richer (which is ironical as this is the Batman in far earlier years than in Asylum and City). Though gadgets have not advanced very much from those of City, compared to the drastic evolution between Asylum and City, the variations were enjoyable. The serious bugs have been generally fixed by now, so small ones may disturb a bit of fun, but they won't keep you from playing the game.
As a Bat fanboy or girl, you should really check this younger Batman out, with him Jim Gordon, Barbara, and Alfred. You wouldn't want to miss Bruce and Alfred talking with jokes, humor, sarcasm, and sometimes even sharp observations in every word they say. Younger Gordons are just brilliant, that I wish I could see them more in the game. New and old villains are great too; Deathstroke on the top of the list like everyone says, and the always-spotlighted-clown, needless to say.
So basically, yes this game did not get a high score from both fans and critics, mainly due to the bugs, and also because, I assume, the former works in this series, particularly City, were too remarkable. Definitely Arkham Origins is not the worst game; it is somewhat well-made game, yet its brothers were beyond comparison. I pre-ordered this game and for me this deserves the price, but if you are reluctant, try this when it's at a discount--and they are offering large discounts quite often these days.

Mad Max is very close to being a fantastic game but a number of design flaws fundamentally knee-cap the experience, leaving it as only an "above average" licensed game. You'll play it for X number of hours, have a decent time, and then never feel the urge to touch it again. If you're dying to play a light Mad-Max simulator that feels like a diet Arkham series game, go for it. I'd suggest saving your dollarydoos for other titles.
Everything outside of Max's car and the car combat are largely forgettable and fairly shallow; locations, enemies, and combat all blend together as mechanics are recycled and stretched out. This problem is consistent across story missions and generic overworld "collectathon" type progression mechanics. Even the spectacular sandstorms largely turn into forgettable experiences.
There's just too much filler content in the game for an experience that just isn't that deep or satisfying. The highlight of the game are the convoy assaults but they rarely ever fall into a sweet-spot of difficulty or challenge. You'll either be frustrated at your lack of stamina early on, or find dismantling them to be all too easy. Often the only things really moderating your progression are whatever artificial barriers block your way: Maybe a part you need won't unlock yet even though you have the scrap, or you haven't done enough requisite side-missions for a given faction (who do nothing but sit around their crummy forts anyway).
The game makes passing attempts at adding depth to the game, such as letting you collect enemy cars, and letting you discover secret routes into fortresses that allow you to bypass the defenses... but ultimately why would you bother? You've never a good reason (that I've discovered) to drive enemy vehicles as you lose access to several vital weapons and mechanics, and you can always just customize your car to match their capabilities if you feel like it. Likewise, sneaking around might seem novel at first but a direct assault winds up being simpler, and faster. Max's "collectathon" trinkets and commentary are equally forgettable, with the odd comments to nobody at all a sure sign that he truly isn't right in the head.
I'm glad the game was attempted, and had a decent bit of fun at first... it's just not a game for anyone who wants something a little more substantial.

This isn't an appraisal of the game for new players (it's very good, get it now) but me sharing my 2 cents with those who have already finished the original and are wondering if the new content justifies another purchase...
The new levels (with the new abilities) are accessible early, but do require some later abilities to complete. It's also possible to finish the game without seeing the new content, which is what I initially did. This actually frustrated me, because the only changes I initially saw involved blocking off originally accessible areas with walls that can only be opened using the new abilities. The game now includes full backtracking so if you are like me and finish it first you can still use the same save to go back and visit the new levels. They are actually really enjoyable (and very pretty), but not lengthy - I only took about an hour to see all the new stuff. New abilities are fun to use but nothing special. (bash is still by far the best!)
The new hard difficulty just makes enemies more powerful and increases environmental damage. You can now warp between spirit wells, personally I think it cheapens the game a bit as the interlocking level design is so superb.
There are some new videos/concept arts; some of the videos are fascinating, some (like the promo one with the music being recorded) are really quite uninteresting.
All in all? It's basically some glorified DLC levels, and extra goodies that *should* have been a free update. The only brilliant new stuff is the new level, and I guess the one life mode is cool. I suppose this gets a totally new release so that the original is left "pure" for speedruns and whatnot, but it is not very different from the original. If you want some pretty new levels I guess it's  worth $5USD, but once the promo ends it's not worth a re-purchase. Would have been nice to have the Soundtrack in FLAC included in the bundle too, one can dream... :)

An expanded version of one of the best platformers out there.
The Ori-ginal is great by itself. It has some of the most fluid, fun controls and challenges of any game I've played, and it's clear from the start that the people of Moon Studios perfectly understood what they were doing, because everything works masterfully! Simply moving around feels great, and combined with creative environments and obstacles, it adds up to a kind of platforming brilliance that you don't see very often. Despite the structure of the game, I'd argue that it's more Rayman than Metroid, though I strongly recommend it to pretty much anyone who enjoy sidescrollers. It's a game that keeps getting better with every new challenge and every new ability, most of which only enhance the platforming (the bash ability changes everything). It also has the best quicksaving system I've ever seen.
All of it is wrapped up in a fantastic presentation. The art is detailed and gorgeous, the soundtrack is dramatic and unforgettable, and both compliment each other perfectly, as well as the grand, poetic storytelling that goes all out to make the world feel gigantic and ancient. It seems like the developers only took lessons from the best of the best, and nothing feels underwhelming, cut short or left out in any way. It's all extremely polished.
It's pretty weird that this Definitive Edition isn't just an update to the original version, because now that game is just taking up space on the store and in my library. There doesn't seem to be any reason to buy it when the DE is the same thing + new levels, new abilities, difficulty settings, fast travel options and full backtracking support (although more graphical options would've been nice as well). Having beaten the old version, all these additions were very notable, very early on, and they only serve to make the game more exciting than ever.
If you like magic, fun, challenge and feeling emotions, you should pick this up. There has never been a better time to do so.

I love the way they have gone about this game and tried to be a little different.  I love the fact that you don't create your character and you are forced to learn to live with what they give you. I love my black guy with a smaller than everage endowment, and anybody who tries to make fun will get my mace over their head in the night while they are sleeping!
I love the newer art style... a really nice (slightly cartoon) style that allows the game to look both mean and gritty at times, and yet still a bit soft.  Fantastic job!

Community around any game is going to be fickle, and I think sometimes with this game some people got too used to a good thing and got thoroughly spoilt!  Anytime they feel like the game isn't so good they should try playing any of the other survival games... The Forest, Conan Exiles, Osiris New Dawn, 7 Days to die, or H1Z1 just survive... which will remind them just how spoilt they are.
Don't get me wrong, all those games I have mentioned are brilliant games, and it would be a little unfair to compare them as they are different. But I can compare them based upon polish and attention to detail and I just don't think they are as good. Rust's sheer imagination and detail can only have been created through real effort, time, and talent on behalf of the dev team. A wonderfully, terrible third person shooter that you can finish in a weekend. Spec Ops: The Line will draw you in with its generic box art and derivative gameplay, and then flip you on your head and stomp on your gut because you're a terrible person.
The game opens in medias res with (all together now) a helicopter chase scene wherein you mow down other helicopters with an infinite ammo minigun, until one of them crashes into you. flash back to the beginning where our protangonists are on a mission to find out what happened in Dubai after a record sandstorm hit. You fight some local insurgents, explore some interesting sand infested buildings, and slowly learn about a CIA operation and a rogue American Infantry unit.
After about an hour of run-of-the-mill shooter story, things start to get a little strange. First you start killing other American soldiers in self-defense. Then you're trying to figure out if you can trust the CIA agents or not. pretty soon you're raining down white phosphorus on an entire platoon of your fellow soldiers and innocent civilians!
Wait what?
Yeah, it only gets better from there, and the best part is the story ramps up so smoothly and the gameplay is integrated into that story so well. The loading screens start off with helpful hints about gameplay then slowly shift to unnerving messages directed at the player in real life. The animations of the characters even change over time! The early game will see Cpt. Walker punch or rifle butt a downed enemy to finish him off, but later on he starts getting more viscious by shooting them in the face while they beg for mercy. Even the mission objectives are integrated into this mad scheme. They start off like any other game: go here, defend this, eliminate that. But then they change: obey, murder, and so on.
Often in games we see a sort of cognitive dissonance between what the game is telling us about a character and what the character actually does in the game when we're controlling them (see the Tomb Raider reboot). Spec Ops is both a great example of how to not have that problem AND is the greatest display of cognitive dissonance AT THE SAME TIME!
I could go on, but the Extra Credits team has already articulated my thoughts better than I can. I do have a few closing thoughts though. First and foremost, yes the gameplay isn't very good. You run. Your gun. You take cover. Enemies spawn in obvious spots. It's all very early 2000s shooter. However, that's all done on purpose to highlight and critique those very same generic shooters. Second, this is strictly a single player game. There is no multiplayer, nor should there have ever been (although maybe they also tacked it on just to show a point).
Finally, and most importantly, I'd like you all to remember: you choose to play this game. You choose to do all those horrible things. Really, the only way to win this game is to stop playing it. But even then, you'd still be losing.

I never leave game reviews. In fact, I think this is my first. It's important I dispel the negativity I've seen in regards to this game.
If you love Hitman, you will be so very happy with this game. As a big 47 fanboy, I've always just wanted to play this character doing what he does best, in as many open ended situations as I can. This rendition of Hitman is heavily inspired by Skyfall (one repeated shot taken directly from the film) and for good reason. This game marks a shift in tone very similar to the introduction of Daniel Craig as bond; where old bond films were campy, niavely sexist, new bond takes a shift towards realism while keeping what was good about the classics. And it is clear that Hitman 2016 is attempting the same shift, and from what I can tell so far, succeeding.
Old Hitman classics were great, slow paced and made you feel like you were a secret hitman and that was all they needed to do. But they had their flaws; poor controls, abhorrent depictions of women, forgettable stories, and a mix of comedy and brutality that did not always mix. However new Hitman is here to do what Craig did. The silliness has been almost completely dropped and the rampant sexism turned down a few notches (and this isn't just me over analyzing, there is a bit of dialogue in Episode 2 that directly references the infamous "not in the mood" scene from Blood Money), and in their place is crisp settings, tight controls, and better dialogue. All while keeping the relaxed pace and expansive maps that made Blood Money a classic.
However with this change Hitman looses some amount of flavor; the new pseudo mission guides telling you exactly where to go to complete tasks feels like pondering to more contemporary audiences, and the change in tone somewhat makes this game feel somewhat standard; however Hitman 2016 certianly has enough design sharpness to it that I feel it outweighs this feeling. This has been the first time in the entire series that I have ever cared about the plot, and it is not because it's novel or smart (along with the other Skyfall references a key plot device is also taken from that movie), but because of how crisply the story is being told.
All in all it's fantastic and I would highly recommend it.

Mad Max is very close to being a fantastic game but a number of design flaws fundamentally knee-cap the experience, leaving it as only an "above average" licensed game. You'll play it for X number of hours, have a decent time, and then never feel the urge to touch it again. If you're dying to play a light Mad-Max simulator that feels like a diet Arkham series game, go for it. I'd suggest saving your dollarydoos for other titles.
Everything outside of Max's car and the car combat are largely forgettable and fairly shallow; locations, enemies, and combat all blend together as mechanics are recycled and stretched out. This problem is consistent across story missions and generic overworld "collectathon" type progression mechanics. Even the spectacular sandstorms largely turn into forgettable experiences.
There's just too much filler content in the game for an experience that just isn't that deep or satisfying. The highlight of the game are the convoy assaults but they rarely ever fall into a sweet-spot of difficulty or challenge. You'll either be frustrated at your lack of stamina early on, or find dismantling them to be all too easy. Often the only things really moderating your progression are whatever artificial barriers block your way: Maybe a part you need won't unlock yet even though you have the scrap, or you haven't done enough requisite side-missions for a given faction (who do nothing but sit around their crummy forts anyway).
The game makes passing attempts at adding depth to the game, such as letting you collect enemy cars, and letting you discover secret routes into fortresses that allow you to bypass the defenses... but ultimately why would you bother? You've never a good reason (that I've discovered) to drive enemy vehicles as you lose access to several vital weapons and mechanics, and you can always just customize your car to match their capabilities if you feel like it. Likewise, sneaking around might seem novel at first but a direct assault winds up being simpler, and faster. Max's "collectathon" trinkets and commentary are equally forgettable, with the odd comments to nobody at all a sure sign that he truly isn't right in the head.
I'm glad the game was attempted, and had a decent bit of fun at first... it's just not a game for anyone who wants something a little more substantial.

I own all of the Batman Games. In order of best to worse I would rank them as follows: Batman Arkham City, Batman Arkham Origins, Batman Arkham Asylum. Don't get me wrong they are ALL good, some just more so than others.
The campaign of this game is shorter than Arkham City, which was disappointing, but better than Arkham Asylum. The extra challenges are just as fun as the were in the last game. Can you get 3 stars on all the Riddler Challenges? Now you have a multiplayer mode for the challenges too!
Glitchy? Some people have said it is. I don't think so. I think it was more system issues than anything else.  This is a very resource demanding game, especially in the video department. When I bought this game I had and HD5850 with 1GB of GDDR5. I encounter a few errors and crashes. Later (about 4 months to be exact), I built a new computer which had a R9 270X with 4GB of GDDR5. Game runs VERY smooth on highest settings, with no errors or crashes.
Always determine if your computer can run a game based on the RECOMMENDED settings. IF you don't meet those and you try to run it, don't complain about the game having issues! Minimum requirements normally mean if you put all settings on low if should work, but not great. Recommended settings is what is needed for the game to operate how it was intended.
