I've always been a fan of the Arkham series. When it was announced that Rocksteady will not be making the new installment for the game, everyone suddenly became skeptical of this new studio WB Montreal but many of them did not know that the same studio had already worked on the Arkham series before (Arkham City Armored Edition for Wii U). So if there was any suitable alternative for keeping the people busy while Rocksteady invest their time on a next-gen Batman tilte (which has come to be known now as Arkham Knight), it was WB Montreal. The inital trailers of the game were pretty impressive and addition of Deathstroke as a playable character sounded exciting. So, I brushed aside any doubts and bought the game. After having completing the orignal story, here are my impressions:
Pros:
1. The game carries forward the same gameplay mechanics from the previous titles in the series with addition of new types of gadgets, villians and expanding the game world to 5x than in Arkham City.
(Note: Some people may argue that simply replicating the gameplay mechanics is the biggest flaw of the game, but is a deviation really warranted ? Why reinvent the wheel ? Why make the players get used to an entirely new gameplay style when everyone knows that the game is just a makeshift till the actual developer comes out with their next-gen title.)
2. The story is really gripping and voice actors, even though new, tried their best to do justice to their roles. Troy Baker (Joker) was especially outstanding.
3. The game looks really beautiful. The occasion Christmas night has been drawn really well by the artists and animators have done a fine job with all the light-studded conifers and sparkling snowflakes.
4. The boss fights are, even though not groundbreaking, offer a pretty good challenge to occasional gamers and are well spaced in the storyline.
5. The multiplayer, developed by Splash damage, tries to give a new perspective to the series and satisfies many of demanded the same from previous games of the series, atleast to some extent.
6. The Cold Cold Heart DLC is really good and gives a good insight into the origin of one of the greatest comic book villians, Mr. Freeze.
Cons:
1. Yes, its true, the game is buggy. The occassional glitches like enemies getting stuck at odd positions in the environment, unable to save progress, achievements not unlocking, some parts being not navigable do bring down the overall experience of the game substantially. Moreover, the game developers decided to ignore such critical bugs in favour of the new DLC which just shows how much they care for the community.
2. The new detective mode, which showed so much promise, turned out to be just a point-and-click adventure at the end. Some more effort into more innovations in this mode could have set the benchmark for forthcoming titles in detective genres.
3. The replay value of the game is really low. There is nothing that forces you to play "The New Game Plus Mode" or "I Am The Knight" mode. They even withrew the "Worst Knightmare" skin which could have been a good incentive to complete the last game mode.
All and all, the game was a hurried attempt to keep the players busy while the "Real Masters" Rocksteady were preparing their magic potion. If you play the game without any prior expectations, it is really a worthwhile adventure which gives a peek into early life of Batman with a riveting story. I mean, common, we have had bigger letdowns. *Cough* Alien Colonial Marines *Cough*

$3.15, an okay price for the game. This is an unfair review as I am slightly partial to CD Projekt Red's Witcher series. There are some flaws with the game design, such as multiplayer solitaire. I tried using Triss Merigold and she seemed fine. However, after playing multiple games, I've decided to vote it down, mainly due to the insane random events from dice rolling and card drawing.
PROS
1. Follows the Witcher Series
Very accurate, all the main characters are inside. I was actually looking forward to using the Scoia'tael (Elves), Philippa Eilhart (Mage ♥♥♥♥♥) or Saskia (Dragoness) in the game.
2. Intuitive
It's easy to learn. I didn't play a single tutorial to be able to understand the game.
CONS
1. Multiplayer Solitaire *****
You don't really care about any other player as none of actions matter to you. There is hardly any player interaction.
2. Advanced Snakes and Ladders *****
It is just personal racing like advanced Snakes and Ladders. You just roll dice and play the game on your own.
3. Random Monsters and Combat
This is so boring. The random monster generation doesn't capture the fantastic monsters that I experienced playing the Witcher 2. To defeat SINGLE monsters, you roll Swords and Shields. If you roll a sufficient amount of Swords, you kill the monster. If you roll a sufficient amount of Shields, you block its negative effect.
It lacks the skilled planning and excitement that the normal Witcher game brings since it all boils down to Sword and Shield.
4. Random Bad Fortune and Investigation Cards
Some just make you lose 2 VP just for drawing them and some just do nothing. The randomness is horrendous. The investigation cards are also full of negative cards called Setbacks which have no redeeming value. If you draw badly, you are screwed.
SUGGESTIONS
1. Traps
If you arrive in a location, you can play a card that leaves a surprise for the next player who crosses (not land) its path. It might be a nasty surprise or a simple challenge. That way players will look at where other players are moving to.
2. Learning Other Player's Abilities
Currently, each player has their own unique development deck. No one will care about what another player develops.
Based on the abolve design, one deck will likely be superior to the others. It would be interesting to take 2-3 developments that belong to other players as your own. This could create crazy combos and make player's more interested in what the others are doing.
3. Global Quests
This will give something that everyone will fight over for VP. E.g. Save Ciri. Pay 3 Blue Leads, 3 Purple Leads and 3 Red Leads for 12 VP. Only completable once.

I just had my first long review nuked by Steam's interference, so I'm going to be short here.
This is a very entertaining game.  The car combat and melee/ranged combat fit very well into this thematic open world setting.   The game runs very smoothly, has loads of in-game help, has a solid tutorial system, allows you to upgrade your custom car and Mad Max the fighter as you want.   You can use hijacked enemy cars.   There are at least 40 different standard cars, there are 3 factions.  Cars of a smilar "class" for each of the 3 factions do vary.  Likewise the enemy footmen for each faction can have several similar classes for each faction, but they also vary slightly from one faction to another.
You could easily play 100 hours to finish the game once.   There are no difficulty level options, which some worry can limit replayability.  But you can always do things in a different order, can ignore most missions most of the time, use different cars, upgrade your character and also his custom car differently, and so on.   So it is easy, if you choose to do so, to change your experience each play-thru.
Your overall objective in this game is to push back, undermine, and eventually take away control of this entire region from the violent barbarians who control it currently.  That their "king"  has brutally stolen and scrapped your car simply makes these actions fit any personnel vendetta you may now feel and with your need to rebuild the means to your survival in this violent world -- namely a car good enough to take down this evil horde.  His is the key faction, but there are two other basically evil factions as well.   You aim to both take vengeance and take back this region for the good of civilization.  You do this by basically slowly whittling his power down, by direct resistance, and other methods.   You'll be attacking convoys, looting sites, finding new strongholds, commandeering enemy vehicles to add to your stable of options, perfecting your custom car, learning new skills for on foot combat, resisting the plague of evil and providing thru your acts of vengeance and subterfuge an opportunity for more civil society to reassert itself in this violent wasteland.  Basically, you are going to Mad Max their sorry little behinds and enjoy every moment of it.
Since the game relies heavily on combat, you might find it eventually repetitive.  But unlike most games, here you have an elaborate car combat system, while also having an elaborate melee system with some ranged weapon combat thrown in but with highly limited ammo.   You have lots of skills you can use and types of attacks in the human fighting, and you have lots of special attacks due to upgrades and gear in the car combat.   So, you can find a way to revisit the game and play it again.  The story will be the same, so you can't modify that on another play-thru, but although the story fits a Mad Max theme, you don't play this game for the story alone.
The game is simply smooth, it works, it is fun, there is lots to do, the strategic map makes sense, the help is solid, you will enjoy yourself, and finally the game is heavily discounted often to $5 or so.
There are very few bugs if any.   Sound volume is low at times and seems to happen often when you switch from the car to the map and back, but repeating that usually fixes it immediately  (volume is low though for this game compared to others).   It can be annoying that when you leave the car to go on foot and return , the game will often override your harpoon weapon and reset you back to the shotgun, but one scroll of the mouse wheel and you are back on track, just remember that it likes to reset it when you do things like that.   The interface is a bit too console like at times, but it works and it works well.   There just are no real complaints that can detract from the quality and enjoyable experience.
There are storms in this game and they can be a dousy.   One part that irritated me is that I'm fighting and trying to follow the tutorial, trying not to die, and then while all this is going on in a semi-tough early fight, a storm hits.  This also happened when I tried to take down one of Stank Gum's cars.   A storm hit then as well.   These storms are incredible.  They act like hurricanes and make it hard to see.  They make sense, are thematic, and very impressive.  But the timing of them during a tutorial and some major fights seems hard to take early on as a beginner.   Later, it just adds to the excitement.
The game never punishes you unfairly for exploration or adventure.   If you die, you just start over at your current allied stronghold and have one more death in the stats screen.  No big deal.  So you can enjoy every approach and every bit of the game.
Fun.  That's what this game is all about.   Highly recommended.  It is often on sale.   Get it then and you will probably enjoy it for many years when in the mood to play it.  It ran very smoothly and easily on my Nvidia Geforce GTX 750 Ti with a 3.4 GHz i5 CPu and 16 GB of RAM on Windows 7-64 bit OS.

I am rewriting my review, my old review was "Not Recommended" based mostly on not wanting to support Square Enix's business practices and the way they had been gouging IOI over the course of this games development and release, showing in the always online DRM they had been implementing in their games, and the corners cut in the final product due to a clear lack of budget and/or time, along with the episodic release so Square could try to recoup development costs faster than waiting for the entire game to be completed. (Its also worth noting I got this game for free from a AMD promotional deal, despite being a massive hitman fan, I was originally going to wait until the game was complete and released, and on sale.)
As of now IOI is a independant studio, so if you had been waiting on buying this game, now is the time to help support them.
The game features some of the best gameplay and levels in the series, its heavily based on the success of Blood Money, leaving the linear level design of Absolution behind entirely. Every level is a huge sandbox, every target has many ways you can take them out, scripted or not. While the game can sometimes feel a bit too much like it holds your hand with some of the more scripted ways to take out your target, you can of course ignore the "opportunities" system, or, if you really want a challenge, play on Professional difficulty. Even after mastering every level, professional difficulty is very challenging, even for veteran hitman players.
The main drawback of the game, is the low quantity of levels, seven levels and two tutorial missions, I greatly wish the tutorial missions would be remade into full-fledged missions (Remove the "training facility" set dressings, add planning options.) Especially since the game really lacks in smaller missions. They do try to remedy this by having things like escelations and contracts mode, but while they can be enjoyable, they feel like what they are, filler.
Of that note is also the "Elusive Targets" missions that IOI releases for a short period of time, you get one chance to complete the mission, or fail it forever. I get the idea behind it, but I will say, I dont like it in practice. Outside of getting every unlockable outfit from the missions, I hardly play them anymore. Playing them blind I mostly wind up resorting to "old reliable" tactics, using either a explosive duck, or just shooting the target. And it just bothers me that a lot of the more fun elusive targets, can never be replayed again, even if they were incredibly well done and unique.
Equipment is a mixed bag, this time around, 47 has a ungodly amount of toys you can unlock and play with, and they are fun. The gun variety leaves a lot to be desired, however the melee weapon system in this game...I adore it. Every melee weapon that can be used to kill or knock out someone, can be thrown, either as a distraction when you lack coins, or at someones head. Throwing crowbars at peoples heads, will never get old.
The voice work is probably my second biggest problem with the game, every level has you globetrotting across the world, however the budget clearly didnt allow for many voice actors, so you will hear the same voices everywhere, all with british and american accents, whether you are in paris, bangkok, or japan.
However, there is one thing this game does, that no other Hitman game comes close to. The AI is amazing. When someone sees through your disguise, they immediately tell everyone they can, your identity will spread like a virus through the world. Guards will call for backup, and the more mayhem you cause, the more cautious they act. Jimmy ran through the door and got shot in the head? His buddy who watched it wont just run into the meat blender after him, he will wait for backup, and go in with a team to try and overwhelm you, maybe even try to flank you through a side door. Gunfights are long, protracted, and deadly, unlike absolution where the game was filled with mechanics clearly designed around making running and gunning feel like a shooter game, these are here to make you feel like a cornered rat and encourage you to use stealth. Novel concept for a stealth game, I know.
All of these pieces come together to form a overall great experience, at its core, Hitman games are puzzle games with stealth mechanics. The levels always play out exactly the same, the only wild card, is you. You have the wrench, and its up to you to decide where and when to throw it into the works, and this game emphasizes that extremely well.
I could go on for hours about the pros and cons of the game, the ins and outs of every level, the design brilliance and design flaws, but its simple, if you like Hitman games, stealth games, games that make you think, or just good games in general, this game is worth your time and money.
As a final note, and this is more for IOI than anyone else, I greatly hope they consider removing the always-online DRM from the game entirely. DRM like this is only one things for games: a death sentence. These servers wont be on forever, one day, whether its a year from now, or twenty years from now, they will be shut down. This results in games like this being either killed entirely, lost to time forever, or left crippled with only a less feature rich "offline mode" still around.
Its happened before, it will happen again. To quote Ross Scott "Stop Killing Games"

Now that the first season of Hitman is fully completed, I am re-editing this review to include the latest updates. First let's see the positive aspects that we encountered throughout the 1st season:
+ Excellent Graphics that offer a unique experience and a feeling of realism at maximum settings. (Note that this might also be a double-edged sword for users that have lower-end PCs, as they will find themselves lagging by having low frames per second even at the lowest graphic options). The landscapes are really well-designed and each mission provides you with a unique experience: From the glamorous Italy and Paris to the cold Hokkaido of Japan, every mission has something unique to offer so from time to time try to take a break from killing the targets of your mission and cherish the beauty of your surroundings. For example, don't miss the chance in Hokkaido to go in the balcony of your suite and enjoy the fireworks from the nearby town.
+ Plethora of ways to complete your missions: The missions are designed in such a way to offer replayability and many different opportunities to execute your targets. If you like non-linear missions in which you are the one that decides whom to kill, when and in what way instead of having the developer directing your every step or forcing you to a specific pattern, then this is definitely the game for you.
+ You will encounter a great variety of high quality disguises in every mission and plenty other features such as places to blend in and avoid detection, clues about your missions, even discussions from NPCs that add more pieces to the story puzzle.
+ Overall, I am happy to see that the game implemented many positive elements from the previous succsessful Hitamn titles.
Despite the good impressions, there are many negative aspects that made me very skeptical not only about this new title, but also the future direction of the whole Hitman franchise.
- The Terms of Service and the DRM model of the game are a "crime": You basically pay 60€ for renting a game and a place in their server, you DO NOT own it. In other words, publishers have legal ownership of the copy/service you bought while you have only beneficial ownership for the services you pay for (similar to MMO games). Expect to lose even your beneficial ownership once the legal owner (publisher) decides to shut down the servers in a year or two from now (similar to when MMO servers close down).
- Requirement to be online to get the full experience: In order for your missions, achievments and mastery points to be recorded so you can unlock new mission features (e.g. weapons, disguises, locations) you must be online all the time because the game records everything you do to an online server. If you are not connected you lose so many privileges and, as a result, the point of replayability is nulled. While this is a meassure to prevent piracy, it backfires and makes you wonder what's the point of having a single-player game that you can only enjoy in places where you have access to internet. Not to mention that the Hitman servers go offline at random times and you might end up losing your progress if you are unlucky enough to be in the middle of a mission when that happens.
- Dumb AI: While IOI promised they will give much emphasis on improving the AI, they failed by a long shot: It is very bad and dumb and once you learn the patterns/loopholes it is really easy to abuse it. Honestly, the bad design of AI take away a lot of credibility and realism from a game based on infiltration, espionage and assassination. For instance, a guard might see you acting suspiciously but if you manage to hide behind a wall or obstacle before his suspiciousness bar is filled, then you are safe. Or the fact that nobody suspects you when you stand nearby staring at them while you listen to confidential discussions about the 'opportunities' you can use to kill your targets.
- No difficulty levels: Fans will argue that you can disable certain helpful functions of the game to purposely make it harder for you. But what is the point of giving a handicap to yourself instead of the game itself becomig realistically more difficult? This goes in accordance with my previous point about AI: Even if you disable certain functions that help you navigate around the map in an easier way, that alone does not improve the intelligence of the NPCs or anything. It simply makes the game more time-consuming instead of more difficult. It is like playing a soccer game with no difficulties and deciding to score a few own goals to give yourself a handicap before playing against a dumb AI.
- Mediocre story: While Hitman Absolution had many obvious weaknesses as a game, one thing it did right was the story. In this new Hitman the story is very unappealing and random. It is not until you reach the last mission that the dots start to connect but even then you are left with disappointment because it is an open-ended story (if you can even call that an ending) and, of course, if you want to find out more you will have to wait, pay again and buy the future sequels of the game (as it is confirmed by the developers that there will be more seasons).
- While the design of each map is marvelous, sometimes you will find yourself utilizing only a very small portion of the map to complete your mission which makes you wonder whether that sandbox-like environment they created really serves a purpose or if it is there for the sake of simply being there since the targets in your mission will never step to certain areas of the map. It appears that the sandbox design is mostly an illusion (fallacy) that you have the freedom of roaming around the map, when in reality your mission might utilize only one third or one forth of the map. For example Bangkok mission takes place in a hotel. The areas/rooms of the hotel are very well designed but your targets will never step in the majority of them, so what is the purpose of them being there in first place? Same story with the mission in Morocco. The problem I am trying to point out here is not that creating big areas is a bad thing necessarily, but not utilizing these areas and simply creating for the looks is an issue.
- The episodic release of an action-based game such as Hitman ruined the experience for many people including die-hard fans of the franchise. Don't get me wrong, episodic release is not the worst thing to happen and I totally see where the publishers/developers are coming from: They want to offer replayability to the game instead of simply finishing the campaign and abandoning the game in your library after that. I can understand that move. However, the problem with the episodic release is that it took a very long time to release each episode which makes you wonder why did you initially have to pay for a full game when it was obviously still under development? If the episodes were released weekly (like anime episodes) it would have been really great and it would have kept people more anxious about what is going to happen next in the story.
- The number of missions is only 6 which is a very small number for a single-player game. This is not Battlefield or Call of Duty, which you play mainly for multiplayer. Paying such a hefty price for a single-player game that has only 6 missions is quite unfair. One can argue that there are a lot of features in each mission that you can only unlock by replaying each part of the story, hence spending more time in each respective mission than your average game. However, not everyone is a fan of replaying the mission you completed. Not to mention that out of the 6 missions, only 3 of them were interesting enough to justify replayability.
Verdict: The game is decent but drastic changes are needed. Vote with your wallet and send a message to both publishers and developers by not supporting that crappy business model they try to enforce and by not becoming part of this big fraud of ownership.

Moai Better Blues is probably the strangest episode of the season with its backwards solutions and disjointed puzzle setups, but it also has ridiculous amounts of entertainingly crazy dialogues.
Sam & Max arrive home from the North Pole—where they may have caused some irreparable damages to the spirit of Christmas in the last episode—in time to get entangled in a strange series of events involving Bermuda triangles (yes, plural) and the Eastern Isle.
Therefore, the special setting of the second episode is a nice tropical island, where we meet quite a few new characters, including several historical figures (and not just Abraham Lincoln, who spends a nice picnic there with his girlfriend).
Their banter is the high point of this episode, because the puzzles are strangely bland and really insanely difficult at the same time. Bland, because most of the subtasks feel like a random series of puzzles with little cohesion (for example, the C.O.P.S. minigame here makes no sense, and not in a good Sam & Max crazy way). And difficult, because the lack of a clear theme means there is very little to go on besides some of the hints hidden in dialogues. It is also the first time in this series where time becomes a part of the puzzles, setting off the insofar laid back, casual nature.
I couldn’t say Moai Better Blues is bad, since it has the true essence of these characters, down to the sometimes almost cruel comedy bits and the really wonky banter and situations. If for nothing else, it should be played for its script.

Ori and the Blind Forest Definitive Edition Review
What is it?
Ori and the Blind Forest is a 2D puzzle-solving platformer at it's heart. With an atmospheric world, fantastic gameplay, tight controls, emotional story-line, and sweeping soundtrack - it's sure to blow away many gamers. Developed by Moon Studios, Ori has back-tracking, puzzles, fast paced combat, and a story-line keeping you from putting down the game.
Similar Games?
Metroid Series (Open World and back-tracking elements)
Castlevania Series (Back-tracking elements and combat)
The Legend of Zelda Series (For story-telling and Puzzle Solving)
Plot
Ori and the Blind Forest's story-line is one of the most emotional in 2015's gaming year. With laughs, heart-aches, sadness, fear, and happiness all rolled up into one 2D game, it's one to treasure for awhile. Ori, the last light spirit must go out and return the light lost from a great tree to restore the life of a dying forest and home. Kuro, the main antagonist, keeps Ori at bay as she tries to keep the forst blind and dark. I can't say too much without spoiling the game, but one of Ori's strongest elements is it's story-line.
Gameplay & Combat
**This game is best played with a controller!**
Ori and the Blind Forest has fast paced gameplay and combat. SImilar to Super Metroid's gameplay, you will have Ori jumping around the map as you explore the giant world, Nibel. Gracefully jumping and wall climbing, Ori is a very fast and flexible character.
Fast gameplay and movement requires fast combat as-well - Ori is occompanied by Sein, the light needed to bring back life to the forest of Nibel. Sein follows Ori and discharges light that act as attacks - get near an enemy and rapidly tap the attack button and it will damage the foe. It's not just repeated tapping to defeat an enemy, you can charge up Sein, dash through enemies, and even smash into the ground as Ori. Combat is fast, satisfying, and addictive - though it's repetitive, you'll be gliding by enemies and still want to take them down.
Ori and the Blind Forest also includes a level-up system in which you pick up light orbs that act as experience points. Gather enough and you level up and get to unlock a new ability off of your skill tree. The skill tree comes in three different categories; combat, efficiency, and utility. Each unlocks a brand new ability that greatly improves (and changes) your gameplay and the way you handle enemies and the world around you.
Visuals & Sound
By far the most impressive and best qualities of this game are the Visuals and Soundtrack. The art direction and graphics put into this game are outstanding. Each area, each screen, and each "dungeon" are created in such a gorgeous and creative way that will leave you awe-struck. Made with Unity, this game is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played.
Being the most beautiful game ever, it's also one of the most pleasureable games to hear. It's soundtrack has memorable tunes and sweeping large action songs that will make you want to download the soundtrack once you are done playing. The soundtrack is my favorite aspect of this game and while you won't hear grand orchestra music, you'll hear wonderful simplicity that stems from the theme of the game and the area/situation you find yourself in.
Verdict
Ori and the Blind Forest was my favorite game of 2015 and the Definitive Edition breathes in new skills and light into the wonderful game. After playing through the story-line multiple times, downloaded and listened to the soundtrack countless of times, and achieved every achievement, I can say that this is a must own game. Beautifully crafted, wonderfully sounding, fantastic gameplay and combat, and an impresive story-line makes for a game that you need in your library. While it is a short game (first playthrough will run you about 5 hours or less), it's a must own for any gamer that enjoys exploration, fast paced action, beautiful story telling and visuals, and a fantastic score. The game is not perfect, as it does suffer from some uneven difficulty (the game can get pretty difficult pretty fast), it's still a wonderful game. It has a unique save system as-well as you get to save at any point, anywhere in the map with the expense of some of your "energy". This allows for unique strategies and save points depending on what you feel is going to happen or what you may have failed at.
Overall, you should get this game. Fantastic game and one of my favorites for a long time to come.
Pros
+ Fast Paced Gameplay
+ Addictive Combat
+ Lots of exploration/back-tracking
+ Fantastic Visuals and Sound
+ Emotional Story-Line
Cons
- Can get difficult fast
- Short Game
9.8/10

This game could have been way better. I'm sorry scott, but when I saw the trailer, I was so hyped for the game. this btw is the first fnaf i played all the way through. I liked how everything was layed out, but there were so many things that were missing from this game. I get the first night was to get our bearings, but everything we learned didn't even end up mattering, and where's that feeling of being left to do our thing from the rest of the game? Everything was scripted from beginning to end, with little to no element of surprise, the voice on the intercom really should've just told us what to do instead of holding our hand the whole way. checking the stages didn't change anything when we'd actually go through the rooms, crawling through the vents gave no feeling of endangerment. Ballora, to me at least, had no effect against the player, i'd be surprised if she killed anyone. and the 5th night gave no challenge whatsoever. So there were really only three nights of real gameplay, aside from the easter egg ending. Now on the topic of NIGHT 4, I though that part was really what this game was about, I was really generally afraid of what was going on compared to the rest of the game, it was just too difficult like everyone was saying. Night 5 was really just like a long cutscene, almost no effort is required to finish it, and it's Night 5.  *SPOILER ALERT* The whole security office with Ennard was really the only main enjoyable part of this game, but the point of this game was to go another way with this game than the other games, so why is this the best part of the game? So to end this review, I feel this game was WAY WAY WAY more rich in story aspects compared to gameplay. If you were willing to remake or continue this game, but put more time into it to really bring out it's potential, maybe even use a different engine, i would recommend this game, but not for the time being.

This game obviously has effort put into it, but it's just no fun to play. You start out in a four-room warehouse (trust me you'll be seeing this place a lot) where you angst at your adopted father. You need to go from room to room and interact with various objects and eventually get out. Once you're outside, you'll meet zombies. If you touch them and fail a quick time event, you're dead. Totally dead. Permadead.
This is the most "controversial" aspect of the game. It definitely gives the game a unique feel and differentiates it from other RPGmaker games, but my major issue with it is how the game starts. It's extremely tedious to go through the uneventful initial cutscene and puzzle over and over when you die. I get that it's supposed to be punishingly difficult, but I wish there was a way to skip to when you get out.
Once you are out, there's not much I've figured out how to do. You can head north and find Jim Sterling, a game critic, for some reason and play minigames. You can find a group of soldiers, one of whom may or may not be a stereotypical Brony. And lastly, there's a mother who wants a medkit for her hurt child. No matter how hard I've tried, I can not find any way to fight off the zombies, the medkit, or the horse that the Brony guy wants.
I really want to enjoy this game, but it's far too cryptic and tedious for my tastes.
Update: 5/14/10
The developer has made it so that when you die, you respawn in front of the initial building as I suggested! Unfortunately, once you're outside, there's still very little to do. The outside world has expanded a bit, but the game feels empty. Almost all the doors are locked, you can't pick anything up, you can't fight the zombies, and the few quests that there are can't be finished due to the necessary items being absent. While I still feel that this could become a good game, I don't think it was ready for Steam when it was posted or even now.

As a hitman fan that has played all Hitman games, this one is definitely one of the best! You can really feel the effort that has been put into this game by IO Interactive. From top quality cinematics to much improved mechanisms and constant tweaking, this game allows me to live the ultimate hitman fantasy.
As long as you don't aim to exploit the AI behavior and just play it according to your common sense, overall the AI is quite satisfactory.
If you want it to be more realistic and challenging, turn off opportunities (hand holding guidance to complete your hit), mini map, suspicion indicators, and improvise whenever you face a difficult situation, plan ahead what to do when things go wrong. This way you'll feel the thrill and a sense of satisfaction when you completed the mission without dying.
Each map is BIG and with much more contents compared to other hitman games, different ways of executing your target makes each episode a lot more replayable and fun, you can be a sniper assassin, always bring in the accidents, or be a ghost and nobody notices what has happened.
Elusive targets give you only one shot, which adds up the tension and thrill.
Now the downsides:
1. you need to be online at all times when playing it, but normally if your internet functions well, it won't be much of a problem, so far in my near 200 hours of gameplay I only experienced connection issue once and it's back online in 10 minutes.
2. Episodic release pisses a lot people off, but now that all episodes are out, this problem is no more.
3. voice actors, voice actors are good, but since the game takes you to different places like Paris, Morocco, Thailand, Italy. The locals having American and British accents makes it feel out of place. Though they did improve it a bit by putting in local accents for elusive targets and the last episode Japan.
Overall highly recommended for hitman fans and those who wants to live the hitman fantasy.

The games item shop has alot of items which you can buy permanently for both only characters and account wide ranging from unique weapons, pre set cars, car kits and some unique clothing.
Even though customization is very restricted without premium you can still buy uniqeue clothing, cars and alot of other stuff from players with in game cash that can help your character look cool and stand out.

I love board games, and I love video games -- so I should love this, right? I mean, I loved Talisman... and this looks even cooler! Sadly, no. This game PRETENDS to have three equal mechanics to it (diplomacy, magic, and combat) but the only thing that really matters is combat. Game ends when any player completes a pre-set number of quests, but the person who finishes the most quests isn't the winner -- the winner is the person with the most victory points. What's the most reliable way of making victory points you ask? Why in combat of course! Every turn there is likely to be a combat, and many of the combats give VP... because of this, it is possible for the combat characters (really just Geralt, because he's the best fighter) to lap all adversaries on VP even if he doesn't come CLOSE to finishing as many quests. This game is like going to a dance contest and realizing you're also going to be judged on your attire, which is okay I guess BUT WAIT... you're ALSO going to be judged on a juggling routine... and somebody else is an expert juggler. Seriously? Keep walking.

A genuinely hard, but fair, platformer. It's a timeless genre that will never, and probably can never, die or get old fashioned. Super Meat Boy is a super simplistic game that does one thing, and that is provide a fun, and fair, platforming experience through a lot of different mediums, ranging from modern to old school.
The game has a nice sense of humor, but for those just looking to have a blast going through it, there are no roadblocks that take up valuable time and space.

Arkham series on-foot combat (left-mouse attack/right-mouse defend), vehicular combat, and things to collect which go toward persistent upgrades. I loved that kinda stuff in games, a lot of the time. Based on these individual qualifiers, Mad Max should be a clear candidate for being a game I love, if not one of my favorite games. Instead, it was an exercise in repetition to the extreme, with clunky on-foot combat, rarely exciting car combat sections that are on a track, no interesting lore, and few interesting events in a region making up ~25% or more of the game's playable space that I fully explored. I'd like to detail each of these to explain the issues.
These weren't any of the aforementioned subject matters, but I would be remiss not to mention the great graphical work, well-designed post-apocalyptic scrap constructions, and other good-looking stuff. The game looks great, and I want to give credit where it's due. The same goes for the sound effects, which include voice acting. I liked what I heard. As for music, I couldn't hum a single tune, but none of the music rubbed me the wrong way or annoyed me, either. It was just fine, and nothing was tonally off.
I did not get very far into the game's storyline. Of what I saw, the plot is as follows: Max's car gets stolen and broken down for parts, Max goes to get new parts to build a car, then Max wants to upgrade the car to kick more butt. This would be great in a silly game that lasts a couple of hours where the gameplay is all that matters, and it's so fun that I literally do not care about the storyline. However, when I'm playing a game that has moments (or hours) of time feeling like
instead of fun, I need a plot to care about to compell me to keep playing, and this game did not do this for me. I did not get far enough in (story-wise...I definitely played longer than I should have, time-wise, though) to say if the story gets more interesting, but what I did saw did not impress, interest, or even remotely satisfy me.
Grand Theft Auto is probably not the best comparison...perhaps True Crime, based on the shooting mechanics while driving? In any case, being able to hop in a vehicle in a game and drive around, then hop out, has enthralled me ever since Blaster Master on the NES. My mind was blown that you could enter and exit the vehicle in a game, and that there was reason to do so! Granted, I hate that game to this day because it was so difficult and there are no passwords or saves, but being able to use a vehicle or not for different objectives was fun there. It's a bit more mundane today, but I still like that. Also, the importance of cars in Mad Max games ideal for this gameplay element. However, I wasn't entertained by it for more than half an hour or so, which was just me enjoying the harpoon time-slow to aim while driving.
In a game where a phenomenal amount of your time will be spent driving, it had
be fun to drive in it; as much or more fun than in other games, but I didn't really enjoy it at all. Just driving should be fun. That Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands game was so much more fun for me to drive in than this, and it took longer to drive from A to be in that game, and I can get impatient, which means it would make more sense for me to prefer Mad Max's driving, but I don't. It just never felt right for me.
When I play as Batman, or Talion in Arkham games or Shadow of Mordor, respectively, the system always felt receptive. In Mad Max, however, right clicking when I should be able to parry a blackable attack sometimes simply does not defend against it, despite pressing the button more than a second before the attack connected. One challenge I was supposed to complete was taking out 8 guys while on foot, without getting hit. Sure, I suck, but I had 100+ combos and was taking out swarms of guys in those other two franchises without getting hit. If they want to make the game more difficult, they can, but making controls less responsive is a pathetic way of doing that. Just add more bad guys, or give them more unblockable attacks or something else. Unresponsive controls are just plain frustrating.
I don't know if I can adequately describe just how terrible this aspect of the game is. It has to be the absolute worst part, in my opinion. You might suspect that I don't like collecting stuff/taking care of stuff marked on a map in large numbers, etc. However, I loved collecting the Riddler Trophies in the first two Arkham games, and the various collectibles in the Tomb Raider reboot, as well as Metroid Prime 3 and other games with collectibles marked on the map. Heck, even Far Cry 3 and 4's collectibles didn't phase me! I got them all and had a pretty good time. I actually
that sort of thing, and I enjoyed completing the map-marked missions on Shadow of Mordor and various other games using similar systems.
The problem in Mad Max, however, is that although the locations are well-designed, they did not create enough interesting main story or side quest objectives to send you to many of them. Instead, it's as if the developers realized they made the area too big with nothing to do in it, and overcompensated by just bloating the area with tons of bases to clear of raiders, scrap/upgrade gear to collect, etc. These things would have been perfectly fine, if there was perhaps 25% of it in the game. Instead, it is everywhere. They didn't seem to know how to give the player something fun to do, and rather than put any real effort into making the large area fun to explore and complete tasks in, they lazily did what feels like the game developer equivalent of 52-card-pick-up: just dump out a mess of stuff and have players clean it up. This game is "something to do." All games are, but many transcend that. They are either very deep and amazing, or they're fun for me to play (or both). This one is a slog of a to-do list. This is coming from someone who actually enjoyed the recent Fallout games' and Skyrim's maps being cluttered with places to check out that were completely optional.
One might say "Well then, don't do the extra stuff!" The problem is that this is an overwhelming majority of the game. Also, I'm not great at games, so I'm going to need better gear for Max and his car. The only way to get this is to complete objectives to lower "threat" in each region to unlock vehicular upgrades, and collect items to build structures at bases that help with replenishing Max's resources and getting you extra scrap to buy more upgrades. There is little else here, with story and side missions making up a tiny, tiny fraction of the entire first region. There appear to be 3-4 major regions, and the first one was almost completely barren except for the collect-a-thon stuff. I cleared 100%' of the first major region, which took me dozens of grueling, boring hours, forcing myself to keep playing, telling myself it would be worth it and that completing a couple of main objectives and actual side quests might make it better. It didn't. I was then faced with putting myself through that again 2-3 more times, and I like myself way too much to do that to me.

Prison Architect, much like Theme Hospital or Rollercoaster Tycoon, is a very addicting prison simulation building game. Recently released out of Alpha and into full version, it still gets regular content updates from the development team at introvision. These regular updates bring new content to the game, which is usually enough to bring you crawling back for a few more days while you build a new prison.
Unfotunatly every great game also comes with its draw backs. For me, the draw backs are major and I debated for a while on weather or not I wanted to reccommend this game. While the game developers update the game constantly with new content, renewing the interest in the game, the updates that come out usually come included with bugs that, for some people, break the game until the next update a month or two away. While the development team is usually good at addressing these bugs in the next update, ultimitly new bugs are introduced with every update as new content gets added.
FInally, a major draw back for me is the apparent lack of attention to detail the development team has. Minor things that would make sense, just don't get done. The development team of Prison Architect have brought us an amazing game, unfortunatly it appears they lack the attention to detail to polish it up into the best it could be.
All in all, I highly recommend prison architect. The pure level of addictiveness is amazing. I however do not reccommend purchasing this game at its full price until the development team starts putting more focus on fine polishing the game. However, if this game goes on sale, you should absolutly pick it up.

As a hitman fan that has played all Hitman games, this one is definitely one of the best! You can really feel the effort that has been put into this game by IO Interactive. From top quality cinematics to much improved mechanisms and constant tweaking, this game allows me to live the ultimate hitman fantasy.
As long as you don't aim to exploit the AI behavior and just play it according to your common sense, overall the AI is quite satisfactory.
If you want it to be more realistic and challenging, turn off opportunities (hand holding guidance to complete your hit), mini map, suspicion indicators, and improvise whenever you face a difficult situation, plan ahead what to do when things go wrong. This way you'll feel the thrill and a sense of satisfaction when you completed the mission without dying.
Each map is BIG and with much more contents compared to other hitman games, different ways of executing your target makes each episode a lot more replayable and fun, you can be a sniper assassin, always bring in the accidents, or be a ghost and nobody notices what has happened.
Elusive targets give you only one shot, which adds up the tension and thrill.
Now the downsides:
1. you need to be online at all times when playing it, but normally if your internet functions well, it won't be much of a problem, so far in my near 200 hours of gameplay I only experienced connection issue once and it's back online in 10 minutes.
2. Episodic release pisses a lot people off, but now that all episodes are out, this problem is no more.
3. voice actors, voice actors are good, but since the game takes you to different places like Paris, Morocco, Thailand, Italy. The locals having American and British accents makes it feel out of place. Though they did improve it a bit by putting in local accents for elusive targets and the last episode Japan.
Overall highly recommended for hitman fans and those who wants to live the hitman fantasy.

A game where others teaches you to be just like them, or die and give up on the game.
Toxicity is the buzzword: The game tells you to survive. People are free to do whatever they want.
The issue is not the game itself.
The issue is that players *Want* to destroy everyone else, no matter who, no matter what they're doing.
There's no instruction manual on how this should be played. It doesn't say that you have to kill anyone. You could do much, the tools are there: But all you will get is the equivalent of a singleplayer game with an AI trying to kill you.
There is no real interaction aside being shot, or being swindled by someone who feels smart enough by pretending to be friendly so they can steal your stuff.
The few and far between who want to interact with others in any other way are killed on sight and, eventually, either give up, or learn that they have to kill others on sight to keep playing the game.
If you want this game for an FPS shooter multiplayer with elements of crafting, get it. That's all it is.
If you want it for any other reason, you're better off looking elsewhere.

The Definitive Edition makes an already great game even greater!
With the Definitive Edition, 2 brand new areas are added to the game, with 2 new abilities to go along with them. Each new area makes use of the new ability and teaches you how to use them. The new Dash skill will also change the speedrun game in its entirety, allowing Ori to speed through areas once this skill is mastered. Players can also now warp between the save point wells.
For those of you having trouble with the original game, the DE adds a brand new easy difficulty. Enemies will fall over and merely tickle you, and checkpoints will be added to some of the escapes. Those of you seeking a challenge can try the new Hard difficulty, where enemies will takes less damage and kill you in 2-3 hits no matter how much health you have, and the brand new One Life mode. As the name implies, you get one life to beat the game.
Finally, there is a new story element to the game! With the addition of two new areas, players gain a bit of insight into Naru's past.
Those of you femiliar with the original version of the game will notice that althought many of the secrets remain the same, the way to access them has change. Areas that previously required the Ground Pound may now require a different ability to access them, so things have changed for even those who think they know everything just because they completed the original.
If you have the original, there's plenty new to justify the $5 purchase! If you haven't played the original, well, now you can play a superior version of Ori!

Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CSGO) is a pretty good game. That being said, there are some shortcoming as well. From a casual players perspective, here is my list of pros and cons.
Pros:
- Takes skill, you can't just buy the game and master it in a few hours, you really need to practice and put in many hours to be even somewhat decent. That makes it challenging and thus fun and rewarding, it feels good to win.
- Large community. A lot of it is cancer but with such a large community you have great maps, a large comp scene, and many people to play with.
- It can run on ANYTHING. It ran on my 2012 Macbook Air at 40-60 FPS on lowest settings at native 1440 * 900 res.
Cons:
- Being an online team based game it is full of hackers, smurfs, and people who just don't care and make the experience of playing the game just bad.
- Valve does not care about this game. As long as they make loads money from skins they are fine. From what I have heard they never test anything before putting it into the game and you have loads of broken (OP) weapons.
- It is repetitive at times, same maps, same weapons. Can get boring and there is not much motivation to play expect for ranking up. Valve needs to add more to the game.
Verdict: CSGO is a very challenging team based game that is very satisfying. The community makes it all the better, as long as you can deal with the cancer and Valve not really caring about this game anymore. If you can deal with that, go ahead and buy it.

Prison Architect is a simulator/builder game akin to Rollercoaster Tycoon or SimCity but with the novel setting of a prison/correctional facility. Overall the game is rather great, if not lacking in any additions since Early Access through to release.
Weirdly one of the biggest issues with the game is the actual building part of the game as workers can often become stuck behind a variety of doors and the process slows down rapidly as they run back and forth across the entire facility or as orders become bugged and are never completed for no discernable reason, despite there being some pipes NEXT to the order to lay pipe and you keep buying workmen between the two tiles and yet they just refuse to ever lay that final piece of pipe or cable.
The actual maintenance and concepts that are unique to the prison setting are quite enjoyable though as you can specify guard patrol routes and what rooms and areas are restricted to what level of security prisoner. Although, that's about all you'll ever need in order to maintain order in your prison, guard dogs, CCTV and even armed guards seem rather redundant when the biggest issue you'll face is your prisoners NOT taking up any of the many classes you've presented them with... or just failing them.
The only level of chaos you'll come across is that which you're 90% sure you'd set up to avoid as no matter how many metal detectors and guards and room searches you'll have, somehow people will still have a trowel or knife on them, which just becomes frustrating more than anything.

For a digitized board game, The Witcher Adventure Game is pretty fun. It's a great mix of strategy and luck where you will essentially battle the game itself more than the opposing players. The object of the game is to complete objectives in as few turns as possible to collect Victory Points. Whoever has the most VP at the end of the game wins.
The mechanics of the game are handled well. Battles, random events, and consequences of cards make the game tense without making it a chore. My only complaints are 1) that the computer AI is too easy overall, often seeming clueless as to what they should be doing and falling behind rapidly and 2) AI opponent turns can take forever (wait-fest). Since both of my complaints are leveled at AI opponents, you can avoid these hassles by having friends. Otherewise, 1v1 with an AI opponent is not too bad.
This is a really fun game, i'm glad they made a board game out of this because it is not only mechanically sound, it is an original concept! 10/10

The music is exceptional, and the graphics quite vibrant; if you zoom in a bit then you can see various animations such as weather effects on the board. The game itself is a bit hard to wrap your mind around, at first; "Leads" and "Proofs" and "War Track" are rather abstract concepts. In addition, it lacks the direct player interaction (PvP, really) of Talisman, for example. Then again, the characters are not antagonistic.
Overall, I think that as far as a digital version of a board game goes, this is a very good buy. Actually, I can't really see myself playing the tabletop version because having the computer manage all the tokens, keep track of when quests are eligible for completion etc. is just so convenient!

Whilst I like the feel of the game, think the whole thing is presented well, and believe this is one of the better board game type offerings currently available, I'd suggest it's only really suitable to be played in online mode. First full game I completed, I won with a score of 64 to the AIs 21 and 2. I'd never played this board game before, so had no particular strategic approach to it (beyond the basics), so to me this is a sign of bad AI, the huge gap between my ability and theirs.
Additionally, the character balance seems off. I'll probably play the game a bit more as other characters to see, but for now it seems as though the strengths of Geralt far outweigh those of any other character.
So while it's a no to recommend this game, it's not an outright no... it's more a 'be aware' of what you are getting. If you want it for the online mode only, then fair enough, you'll probably enjoy it.

Arkham series on-foot combat (left-mouse attack/right-mouse defend), vehicular combat, and things to collect which go toward persistent upgrades. I loved that kinda stuff in games, a lot of the time. Based on these individual qualifiers, Mad Max should be a clear candidate for being a game I love, if not one of my favorite games. Instead, it was an exercise in repetition to the extreme, with clunky on-foot combat, rarely exciting car combat sections that are on a track, no interesting lore, and few interesting events in a region making up ~25% or more of the game's playable space that I fully explored. I'd like to detail each of these to explain the issues.
These weren't any of the aforementioned subject matters, but I would be remiss not to mention the great graphical work, well-designed post-apocalyptic scrap constructions, and other good-looking stuff. The game looks great, and I want to give credit where it's due. The same goes for the sound effects, which include voice acting. I liked what I heard. As for music, I couldn't hum a single tune, but none of the music rubbed me the wrong way or annoyed me, either. It was just fine, and nothing was tonally off.
I did not get very far into the game's storyline. Of what I saw, the plot is as follows: Max's car gets stolen and broken down for parts, Max goes to get new parts to build a car, then Max wants to upgrade the car to kick more butt. This would be great in a silly game that lasts a couple of hours where the gameplay is all that matters, and it's so fun that I literally do not care about the storyline. However, when I'm playing a game that has moments (or hours) of time feeling like
instead of fun, I need a plot to care about to compell me to keep playing, and this game did not do this for me. I did not get far enough in (story-wise...I definitely played longer than I should have, time-wise, though) to say if the story gets more interesting, but what I did saw did not impress, interest, or even remotely satisfy me.
Grand Theft Auto is probably not the best comparison...perhaps True Crime, based on the shooting mechanics while driving? In any case, being able to hop in a vehicle in a game and drive around, then hop out, has enthralled me ever since Blaster Master on the NES. My mind was blown that you could enter and exit the vehicle in a game, and that there was reason to do so! Granted, I hate that game to this day because it was so difficult and there are no passwords or saves, but being able to use a vehicle or not for different objectives was fun there. It's a bit more mundane today, but I still like that. Also, the importance of cars in Mad Max games ideal for this gameplay element. However, I wasn't entertained by it for more than half an hour or so, which was just me enjoying the harpoon time-slow to aim while driving.
In a game where a phenomenal amount of your time will be spent driving, it had
be fun to drive in it; as much or more fun than in other games, but I didn't really enjoy it at all. Just driving should be fun. That Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands game was so much more fun for me to drive in than this, and it took longer to drive from A to be in that game, and I can get impatient, which means it would make more sense for me to prefer Mad Max's driving, but I don't. It just never felt right for me.
When I play as Batman, or Talion in Arkham games or Shadow of Mordor, respectively, the system always felt receptive. In Mad Max, however, right clicking when I should be able to parry a blackable attack sometimes simply does not defend against it, despite pressing the button more than a second before the attack connected. One challenge I was supposed to complete was taking out 8 guys while on foot, without getting hit. Sure, I suck, but I had 100+ combos and was taking out swarms of guys in those other two franchises without getting hit. If they want to make the game more difficult, they can, but making controls less responsive is a pathetic way of doing that. Just add more bad guys, or give them more unblockable attacks or something else. Unresponsive controls are just plain frustrating.
I don't know if I can adequately describe just how terrible this aspect of the game is. It has to be the absolute worst part, in my opinion. You might suspect that I don't like collecting stuff/taking care of stuff marked on a map in large numbers, etc. However, I loved collecting the Riddler Trophies in the first two Arkham games, and the various collectibles in the Tomb Raider reboot, as well as Metroid Prime 3 and other games with collectibles marked on the map. Heck, even Far Cry 3 and 4's collectibles didn't phase me! I got them all and had a pretty good time. I actually
that sort of thing, and I enjoyed completing the map-marked missions on Shadow of Mordor and various other games using similar systems.
The problem in Mad Max, however, is that although the locations are well-designed, they did not create enough interesting main story or side quest objectives to send you to many of them. Instead, it's as if the developers realized they made the area too big with nothing to do in it, and overcompensated by just bloating the area with tons of bases to clear of raiders, scrap/upgrade gear to collect, etc. These things would have been perfectly fine, if there was perhaps 25% of it in the game. Instead, it is everywhere. They didn't seem to know how to give the player something fun to do, and rather than put any real effort into making the large area fun to explore and complete tasks in, they lazily did what feels like the game developer equivalent of 52-card-pick-up: just dump out a mess of stuff and have players clean it up. This game is "something to do." All games are, but many transcend that. They are either very deep and amazing, or they're fun for me to play (or both). This one is a slog of a to-do list. This is coming from someone who actually enjoyed the recent Fallout games' and Skyrim's maps being cluttered with places to check out that were completely optional.
One might say "Well then, don't do the extra stuff!" The problem is that this is an overwhelming majority of the game. Also, I'm not great at games, so I'm going to need better gear for Max and his car. The only way to get this is to complete objectives to lower "threat" in each region to unlock vehicular upgrades, and collect items to build structures at bases that help with replenishing Max's resources and getting you extra scrap to buy more upgrades. There is little else here, with story and side missions making up a tiny, tiny fraction of the entire first region. There appear to be 3-4 major regions, and the first one was almost completely barren except for the collect-a-thon stuff. I cleared 100%' of the first major region, which took me dozens of grueling, boring hours, forcing myself to keep playing, telling myself it would be worth it and that completing a couple of main objectives and actual side quests might make it better. It didn't. I was then faced with putting myself through that again 2-3 more times, and I like myself way too much to do that to me.

Caveat: If you're into CoD-zombies or CoD-multiplayer, this is not the review for you.
While Modern Warfare series is roughly sixteen shades of fun, Black Ops is more or less the opposide. Cod-blops 2 does improve on the original in many ways, but still suffers from many of the same issues.
There's still a lot of railroading and fake freedom of movement, and there are still a ton of QtE's. The enemy grunts still act like they were cut from a Bond movie for beeing too suicidal and ridiculously evil, and the story is still not really up there. There's also too many Deus Ex Machina moments betraying a sudden lapse in the writers' imaginations. If you absolutely hated Black Ops, you're most likely not going to enjoy the sequel either.
However, as said, there are improvements. This time, there are actually a few characters in the game, as opposed to the mil-speaking cardboard cut-outs from the original. They have some sort of motivation for doing some of the things they do, and some are even a little relatable. The guy with the gigantic love-stick for "realistic military speak" seems to have been fired as well; so in Blops 2 you can actually figure out what you're supposed to be doing most of the time.
So yeah, it's better. But that's hardly an achievement.

Like snow or Christmas decorations, Call of Duty shows itself by the end of the year. Like every year since Modern Warfare. This time, it's the turn of Call of Duty: Black Ops 2, developed by Treyarch. Unlike its predecessor, the story sets in two distinct eras, the 80's and the year 2025. Two viewpoints which allow the game to offer many side roads in the story, and 8 different endings. This is a first for such a mainstream series. Of course the game's core remains the same on the basics: cinematic action, epic scenes and a percussive score. Even if Black Ops 2 reuses old recipes, it does it really well and remains a great experience.

The Definitive Edition makes an already great game even greater!
With the Definitive Edition, 2 brand new areas are added to the game, with 2 new abilities to go along with them. Each new area makes use of the new ability and teaches you how to use them. The new Dash skill will also change the speedrun game in its entirety, allowing Ori to speed through areas once this skill is mastered. Players can also now warp between the save point wells.
For those of you having trouble with the original game, the DE adds a brand new easy difficulty. Enemies will fall over and merely tickle you, and checkpoints will be added to some of the escapes. Those of you seeking a challenge can try the new Hard difficulty, where enemies will takes less damage and kill you in 2-3 hits no matter how much health you have, and the brand new One Life mode. As the name implies, you get one life to beat the game.
Finally, there is a new story element to the game! With the addition of two new areas, players gain a bit of insight into Naru's past.
Those of you femiliar with the original version of the game will notice that althought many of the secrets remain the same, the way to access them has change. Areas that previously required the Ground Pound may now require a different ability to access them, so things have changed for even those who think they know everything just because they completed the original.
If you have the original, there's plenty new to justify the $5 purchase! If you haven't played the original, well, now you can play a superior version of Ori!

+ The basic mechanic of a tycoon/sim game is given a glorious shakeup by making your "sims" hate you.  While your prisoners will act against your interests, you must always act to benefit them, making for an asymmetrical relationship that works well in this type of game.
+ With the latest patch adding snipers and guard towers, most of the major subsystems you expect in a prison are available in some form.
+ Simple aesthetic that works well and keeps everything easy to see.
+ Very smart NG+ feature lets you sell your prison, letting you build bigger and better things from the start while making you still earn the progress.
+ Due to the nature of the game, running a prison is just as fun as building it, avoiding a major pitfall of many building games.
+ Escape mode lets you play from the other side of things, adding even more life to the game and a whole new building goal (making a fun prison to escape from).
- The big one: pathing is sometimes awful.  Prisoners path well enough most of the time, but guards regularly get hung up on concrete walls, and doctors require frequent babysitting.  This results in the occasional completely BS death as well as untold gnashing of teeth as you micromanage large prisons.
- Punishments are one dimensional.  Prisoners can be given lockup or solitary time for infractions, but all this does is suppress them temporarily (make them obedient), and some are immune.  Meanwhile their needs build up, making them more likely to offend again.  There are no tiers of long-term punishment/privilege, the AI cannot learn to behave better to receive better privileges, nor can you assign increased security protocol such as requiring shackles when outside their cell at all times, or shackling before removing from cell, etc.
- There are some gaps in available staff.  You have basic guards with batons and tasers, armed guards with shotguns, K9 guards, and now snipers.  There are riot guards available as *temporary* emergency units, when most maximum security facilities would keep such personnel on staff at all times.  Likewise, you can't set protocol for handling situations; you might like guards to wait for backup before opening cells, but you can't make them do that, and they will die as a result.
- Gangs need balancing.  They're an optional feature, but an extremely cool one, so it's a shame that there's not much to help deal with the challenge they present.
- Lots of rooms are superfluous.  There's no need at all to have such basic things as a yard, a common room, etc.  Contracts require them but a prison without them can function exactly as well as one with them.
All in all, 9/10 would recommend to fans of the genre, of any experience level.

Despite some flaws in the execution this FPS came along with a strong and deep narrative that stirs you up to think about ethics of war. This game blurs the line between everyday morals and the cold reality soldiers have to face at times of war. Throughout the game you are forced to make choices in a warzone as the commanding officer of a 3 man troup. You make none of these very lightly and they leave a foul afterthought behind, getting you to think about the harsh reality of war.
This game brought a well needed breath of fresh air as the first FPS where paying attention to the narrative/story is actually mandatory and you don't want to immediately skip every cutscene like in other modern day shooters and their sloppy SP campaigns. Looking at you CoD.
Along the compelling storyline comes some solid shooter gameplay we all know too well. The gameplay in Spec Ops: The Line doesn't revolutionise the genre but with many different weapons, some different enemy types it brings enough variety so that you can mold your own style of play throughout the short 6-7h of gameplay.
I played on the highest difficulty from the get-go and even tho some chapters had their frustrating parts if you play smart every level is manageable without feeling like a total breeze. War shouldn't be a breeze, right? What irked me was that you sometimes where forced to stray from your current playstyle or weapon preferences.
The AI of your 2 comrades is refreshingly smart and with the ability to command them to focus fire targets or throw stun grenades they are actually very helpful on higher difficulties.
Overall, this game was a nice experience with a surpisingly good narrative given the genre. Gameplay is fine but nothing innovative. Graphics aren't on the highest end of spectrum but totally suffice. I played the game with my surround sound speakers enabled and the sound/music are bombastic, at times a bit over the top but thats expected.
Entertainment for the weekend is assured with this game. Would recommend.

This game is technically solid. There's good music, there's a nice atmosphere, the encounters are cool and the interaction is nearly well excecuted. It's a very well thought out board game, with minor flaws and weird 'fast travel' systems that just robs you of your money.
With nearly well, I mean that the AI is A) dumb as hell, B) cheats.
As for the dumbness - the AI tends to just spend all their development cards for 1 fight, while s/he should only need 1. Then there's the endless 'fast travelling' that they're doing and making things harder for themselves.
Then there's the fact that they simply refuse to complete their main quest. Dandelion for example, had 6 purple proof items and kept spending gold on 1 more every time he could, while avoiding the main quest area.
This didn't happen once or twice, this happens nearly every game I'm playing.
As for the cheating, I'm convinced that they don't cheat with the dice rolls, but there are cards like Dijkstra's thugs, that makes you have to cash in 2 investigation tokens. Or, if they lose a fight, to hand over 1 or 2 tokens. The AI doesn't have to do this for some unexplained reason. I've also seen instances where they become 'delayed' and still perform 2 actions, while not having a good fortune card to ignore the delay.
All in all, it's not a masterpiece, but deffinatly worth spending 1 hour per day for a round of fun and the price tag isn't too bad either.
Here's to hoping that the patch removes these weird AI issues.

Not a bad game at all, though I feel it lacks a little polish and content.
Pros:
It's fun. It's challenging.
And in all, a great game if you're into boardgames.
Multiplayer both online and as hotseat.
Cons:
Needs a proper tutorial - even though there are short videos to explain the basics, it doesn't cover everything, which eventually will send you to the rules section for tedious reading.
And even those rules are taken directly from the hardcopy boardgame, with instructions to place your playing piece on the side, and stuff like that.
You'll pick it up as you play, but a proper tutorial would have been better.
Needs more cards, especially for battle encounters.
Playing a 4 player game with a 5 quest goal, with have you battling the same few handfuls of monsters over and over.
And quests are pretty much all the same - strip the description and you're down to 'collect X tokens of type Y' and go to place Z.
Game mechanics are a bit shoddy.
You can pretty much spend the first ten turns drawing development cards to OP your character.
And often rewards  are penalties to the leading player, which kinda blows if you pick a reward that actually penalizes you.
Character balance is off, with Geralt with a severe lead on the others, by having 2 more dice to roll for combat encounters.
Yeah, the others have other advantages, but bashing monsters is a good way to rack up victory points, which makes a free skill for Triss to run away without penalty kinda bleak and useless in comparison.
In a long game, I don't see how you can lose with Geralt.
Conclusion:
It's decent enough to recommend, but wouldn't say it's worth the full asking price of 10€.
Picked it up on a deal for 6€, which I think is a more appropriate pricerange, all considered.
You will have a good few hours of fun with it, but I'm imagining it gets kind of pointless once you've played all the characters and handful of times, simply because the character balance is totally off, the game mechanics have obvious exploits and are somewhat poorly designed, and it lacks diversity and content for longer games.
But that's just my opinion. I'm a boardgame geek, and I have been designing games since I was a 10 year old kid back in the 80's, so I spot the flaws immediately.
You could end up having a fantastic time with this game, regardless of what I think.

Very underrated game from the Arkham franchise. People usually complain about this title not coming from Rocksteady and constantly ♥♥♥♥♥ing about how bad it is when in reality it's not that bad at all. The story is actually pretty good considering Warner Bros. Montreal made it and not Rocksteady. The feel of the game and the atmosphere is good because it is an open-world Batman game and fans of the series will realize the familiarity of the map to Arkham City (because it's a prequel to Asylum). The world is beautiful but feels a bit limited in the free roam after about 15+ hours of gameplay. When you glide from building to building you there's a point when you go like, "I should be able to grapple that but I can't". The gameplay itself is well clunky compared to the Rocksteady titles if you put enough time in it. Combos and free flow combat are smooth but later you'll feel that sort of miss that refined finish Asylum and City had. Side missions are a blast in this one as they were in Arkham City but I find myself finishing them quicker and easier than in previous games. The boss battle are the usual cape-stun battles but there are a few that stand out that are amazing (Deathstroke, Shiva, Joker, etc). Overall Arkham Origins isn't a masterpiece or a real upgrade from Arkham City, but it indeeds fulfills the roll of entertaining levels and the player feeling like a BAMF when playing Batman. Fans of the series will definitely enjoy Arkham Origins and others might.
