So none of the reviews in the store page give any sort of indication of what the game is. So I'm gonna do that.
HITMAN is an episodic game that was released over the course of several months. One could buy any combo of the first level and the prologue, as well as the remaining episodes, or all together with a standard $60 USD pricetag. The game is, at its core, a full game that was just split up to space out content and allow them to add small content (Elusive Targets, Contracts, etc) in between episodes.
The base game starts off with two tutorial missions that form the prologue, as well as the first episode, Paris. Each episode includes: one location/map (sometimes an alternate version of the location is included), a story mission that takes place on the map, access to all the developer contracts (mini missions) in that mission, the ability to use the location to create your own contracts as well as being able to play other's contracts made on that map, and the ability to use the unlockables earned in that location on any other episode.
The maps themselves vary in structure and size, but all of them feel complete, packed with a multitude of hidden areas, secrets, side missions, and things to do. The first episode's map, as an example, is a large mansion with a guest area, fashion show area, back stage area, museum, hidden auction and clandestine operations area, a cellar and kitchen, the entrance expanse, a large parking lot filled with access points to various levels, a construction area with similar access, an outside party area, a helicopter landing spot, and a guard only garden area. That's a lot, and currently there are 4 other maps released with that same level of content.
Gameplay wise, for those who are fans of the series, it calls back to many inspirations found in Blood Money. Maps are open and non-linear, AI reacts in relatively intelligent ways (including picking up weapons found, bagging bodies laying around, etc), which were things sadly missing in Absolution. It does bring back Absolution's smoothness in execution, and  thankfully leaves out its arcade-y "Point Shooting" ability.
The game does have notable flaws, however. The game is not well optimized, and can cause performance issues on medium level builds. The AI can be dumb at times, which can cause frustration in your meticulous planning. To reduce client-side tampering, the game does have separate inventories and achievements for offline and online play, which can cause issues if you regularly switch between the two. Despite the comments of others, the game is still fully playable offline, you just have a separate inventory.
In conclusion, the game is a mix between Absolution and Blood Money, and I feel like the developers really tried to take the best of both. It fails sometimes, but the effort is there. I highly recommend the game for anyone who was a fan of Blood Money as long as they aren't expecting the exact same game.

Prison Architect: The most effort you'll spend to get a tiny ounce of fun in your lifetime.
It has a lot in the game and it would be very fun, but the bugs, obvious DLC scam, unforgiving gameplay, and terrible pathfinding just ruin the game outright.
I really,
want to like this game. I got it when it was in early access about a year before its release. It's unique and has a lot of depth. It's one of those games you see on steam and watch a youtube tutorial of and you can't stop thinking about how much you want it. Unfortunately, it doesn't live up to your expectations.
I'll start off with the good.
Prison Architect is exactly what you'd expect. You make a prison. The game has a tutorial and neat little introduction. It helps you learn the basics of playing with the grant system. It has a variety of ingame features: lots of types of rooms, contrabands, prisoner mentality, fighting, death, Shawshank Redemption toilet escapes, the whole nine yards. From when I first bought the game, the developers have added even more. The electronics have been expanded, logic gates and whatnot. I don't really know how all that works, but it's a nice feature. There's also logistics. Have your guards travel certain routes to attain maximum security. It's all very mathematical and interesting. The game has a lot of depth. However, for the type of game it is, this depth is expected; no part of the game makes you go "wow, they really went above and beyond! Nevertheless, it still is refreshing to have a plethora of in game details to customize your prison.  Players who enjoy games like Banished will thoroughly enjoy this title.
Unfortunately, the game is ruined by some of the most irritating defects that I have ever seen. I'll start with the minor ones. The first being the developers. This game has been 'finished' but I feel like a lot is missing. The developers never really tried to polish anything in game. They just made sure their features worked and didn't bother to improve them. Take, for example, the God mode (I can't remember what they call it in game). Basically, you can set it so that you have unlimited money. But rather than have 999,999,999 money, the game just starts you out exactly the same, but you can just go into the negatives. It's this type of lazy developing that is upsetting as a player to see. Also, the game is so 'pass fail.' When I first played this game, it made it very hard to pick up. Essentially, you have a certain income based on the number of prisoners you have, which increases every day. You need money, obviously, to do everything. When you run out of money, you're screwed. They try to make it easier by including financial grants, but get the wrong one and you're SOL. A lot of the grants give you some money in advance to accomplish the goal, but some grants don't give you anything and end up costing you money in the longrun, making it really hard. What the game should have is a 'life system' where a limited number of times where the player can get additional funding as a failsafe. Instead, any instance where you don't have enough money is detrimental, as more prisoners arrive daily. In addition, the game is RIDICULOUSLY overpriced. I got it on sale when it was like 12 bucks, and that was for the 'Name in Game' edition. Now they expect people to pay FIFTY DOLLARS? It is worth 20 dollars, tops. If a game like Banished costs only 15 dollars -- and it's essentially the same concept but you build a town instead of a prison -- there is no logic behind the high cost other than developer greed. By the way, the name in game is lame. You don't ever get to see your person other than by luck. You just go on their website and submit their name and bio and they tell you 'It's been added!" I just wish i could specifically insert my custom character into the game.
But the absolute WORST part of the game?
THE PATHFINDING AND WORKER AI. It's awful. It ruins the game. If you build a large structure that covers up most of your land by the road, good luck building anything else. The workers will always be unable to build something because their path is blocked off, despite multiple clear paths available. This problem is exacerbated by the terrible worker AI. Instead of assigning a certain amount of workers to work on a certain project, the developers decided to program the game so that specific workers are assigned to do specific things on a project. That means that each worker only finishes certain tiles of the building. How does this translate into the game? Trying to build a foundation in the back of your land will result in the entire foundation being laid, but
of cement will be missing because one worker will be 'blocked' due to the terrible pathfinding. I have played a game where, upon trying to build a building for a classroom for my prisoners, this same scenario happened and it took 4 days to finish the building.
. It is so frustrating when this happens, because your game gets ruined. If this simple error were fixed, the entire game would be vastly better. Just typing this makes me angry.
This game could be great, but it's overpriced and has one game ruining glitch. Could be 7/10, instead I give it a 3.5/10. Don't buy it unless it's on sale.

Moreover, they tweaked many existing puzzles that you had to solve in order to gain bonus pick ups so they now involve two new abilities you can learn and thus rekindle the originial content with a bit more variety and a few new things to see.
All in all, DE is a sound incentive for another playthrough and thus well worth the money.

Ori lables itself a metroidvania, and unlike some other games that make that claim (Cave Story, looking at you. You aren't a metroidvania) this one really does fit the genre.
Right away you're gonna notice how god damn beautiful this game looks. It's really pretty, and the animations on Ori and some of the other characters just add to the overall amazing aesthetics. I don't think I've played a game that looks prettier than this. Sure, some games might have better graphics, but they don't look this vibrant and alive.
Okay, anyway. So I said it's a metroidvania, right? It is, but the vast majority of Ori's powers that you will gain as you go through the game are movement based powers. You're not going to find various laser beams like Samus or anything. The gameplay is designed with this in mind, and while there are enemies in the game (they're all pushovers), your real adversary is the environment.
You'll get real familiar with double jumping up walls, going from side to side avoiding spikes or fireballs, then launching yourself off of enemy projectiles with another movement skill.  They even go as far as to not have actual bosses in the game, at least like you are expecting. What function as bosses are elaborate escape sequences from various areas that will really put your platforming skills to the test.
Aside from these new powers you'll find, you can also find the standard things like items that boost your max hp or energy, or give you a free skill point. Yeah, Ori has a skill tree. Well, it's not really a tree. He has three linear paths, each with a different theme. You have to progress down each path in order, but you can hop back and forth between the three as you like. If you put your first point in the combat path, you aren't stuck with that branch only until you complete it. Protip: do the path that ups your movement abilities first. This is much more helpful than combat upgrades. Triple jump anyone? Yes please.
I'm a huge fan of this genre, when it's done right, and this is done pretty damn right. It's not quite on the level of Super Metroid, Symphony of the Night, or Axiom Verge, but it is really close.
Oh, did I mention how pretty and cute Ori is? Buy this just to look at him. He's adorable.

Not a bad game at all, though I feel it lacks a little polish and content.
Pros:
It's fun. It's challenging.
And in all, a great game if you're into boardgames.
Multiplayer both online and as hotseat.
Cons:
Needs a proper tutorial - even though there are short videos to explain the basics, it doesn't cover everything, which eventually will send you to the rules section for tedious reading.
And even those rules are taken directly from the hardcopy boardgame, with instructions to place your playing piece on the side, and stuff like that.
You'll pick it up as you play, but a proper tutorial would have been better.
Needs more cards, especially for battle encounters.
Playing a 4 player game with a 5 quest goal, with have you battling the same few handfuls of monsters over and over.
And quests are pretty much all the same - strip the description and you're down to 'collect X tokens of type Y' and go to place Z.
Game mechanics are a bit shoddy.
You can pretty much spend the first ten turns drawing development cards to OP your character.
And often rewards  are penalties to the leading player, which kinda blows if you pick a reward that actually penalizes you.
Character balance is off, with Geralt with a severe lead on the others, by having 2 more dice to roll for combat encounters.
Yeah, the others have other advantages, but bashing monsters is a good way to rack up victory points, which makes a free skill for Triss to run away without penalty kinda bleak and useless in comparison.
In a long game, I don't see how you can lose with Geralt.
Conclusion:
It's decent enough to recommend, but wouldn't say it's worth the full asking price of 10€.
Picked it up on a deal for 6€, which I think is a more appropriate pricerange, all considered.
You will have a good few hours of fun with it, but I'm imagining it gets kind of pointless once you've played all the characters and handful of times, simply because the character balance is totally off, the game mechanics have obvious exploits and are somewhat poorly designed, and it lacks diversity and content for longer games.
But that's just my opinion. I'm a boardgame geek, and I have been designing games since I was a 10 year old kid back in the 80's, so I spot the flaws immediately.
You could end up having a fantastic time with this game, regardless of what I think.

Not as good as Arkham City, but a worthy entry in the series, which sheds some light on how the relationships between Batman and his rogues' gallery were formed in the Arkhamverse, prior to Arkham Asylum.
Great graphics, (mostly) excellent voice acting and one of the most gripping Batman stories I have personally experienced, in any media. It's like playing through the game version of a good Batman comic book (on a side note, if Rocksteady were to make a video game adaptation of The Dark Knight Returns, my head would probably combust).
However, the gameplay is mostly rehashed from Arkham City and, though still thoroughly enjoyable, it inevitably becomes repetitive. Nevertheless, some of the new gadgets integrate pretty well with the rest of the game and are fun to play with; also, I noticed the combat received an update in terms of difficulty and responsiveness, which I definitely appreciate.
Around Half of the game world is copy-pasted from City, in terms of most of its composing areas - still, they received enough of a visual improvement to not seem too same-y and the new areas are definitely some of the most memorable you've seen in an Arkham game.
All in all, a solid, if a bit underwhelming, Batman title. If you loved Asylum and City, it's easy to recommend.
P.S.: Troy Baker as the Joker just rocks.

If you haven't skimmed/read it already,
is my review of the previous edition before this expansion.
As for the new version (Edit: I completed the game, this is more relaible)
Think of this as an addition to my other review.
After completing the game, profiles no longer show as "Completed", but instead now allow you to play again (It saves before the last part) and get more items. That's a great pro.
Other than that, the new abilities added to the game are absolutely amazing, though it's unfortunate that the new areas are so small. It upsets me.

There is not a crazy amount of new content (as in they didn't double it or anything) but the new areas are super high quality, perhaps even higher than the original areas (or perhaps it's just my personal preference of the new themes). You can access the new zones right away but you may have to turn back at some point until you've unlocked the necessary abilities to proceed. Luckily, they made sure you never turn back empty-handed even if it's the first thing you do in a new game!
Moreover, they tweaked many existing puzzles that you had to solve in order to gain bonus pick ups so they now involve two new abilities you can learn and thus rekindle the originial content with a bit more variety and a few new things to see.
All in all, DE is a sound incentive for another playthrough and thus well worth the money.

Terraria is quite a great game, and I would say it certainly doesn't get enough attention for how good it is. I'd say that it really doesn't do everything, nor does it need to do everything. As for what it does do, it somewhat combines a JRPG with a sandbox game, all in 2d. Surprisingly, it merges these different genres very well. When it comes to the game, it starts off with a calm, more slow paced, but fun feeling. Often, you can go out into the many biomes in a given world, and explore through said biomes, along with enemies to challenge the player, many different blocks and tiles to explore around, and often times a boss accesible within the biome. Personally, this is a very good system to me, and it all works well. Also, the whole 2d graphical style really makes it a lot less resource intensive, which is very good for computers that can't handle the game extremely well. The different areas make progression fall into a style of first, go to said biome, two, fight off enemies and mine ores or obtain resources you may need, three, create new equipment using resources you obtained, four, make your way to or defeat the boss ahead of you, and finally, upgrade again to better equipment and repeat the process. This simple system is one I think works great, and makes getting lost or not knowing what to do a near impossibility, especially when NPCs may help you with some tasks. The only few issues I found were that sometimes, the pace of gameplay slows, or if you aren't good enough at the game, it becomes hard to progress, but I personally don't think they are too big of issues. Overall, i'd say Terraria is a 98 out of 100 game, and I would easily recommend this to anyone who likes sandbox or JRPG games.

Super Meat Boy is the perfection of the 2D platforming formula created nearly 30 years ago. Everything about the game suggests that the developers knew exactly what they were doing. From little design quirks to more noticeable ones. For instance, every level is specifically tailored to be able to be speed ran. Time Trials are implemented as a test of definitive skill. Different characters are thrown in as unlockables for you to experiment with their different gameplay/physics/controls. Hidden bandages and warp zones add an element of exploration to the game. Ect.
The controls are spot on and really compliment the obstacles. Without the precise controls and creative traps/obstacles, this game would fall apart. The difficulty is perfect, despite what some may say. In fact I find the difficulty much overhyped, the game isn't nearly as hard as a lot of NES games were. This is how a game is supposed to be. Games are supposed to challenge you, not every game is meant to be beaten by everyone who plays it, that's not a "game". People who grew up with modern "games" that coddle you with a safety net and hold your hand with interlaced fingers while frolicking through a field of flowers need not apply.
I absolutely love this game! It's a simple platformer that also adds a challenge in the latter levels.

Characters are interesting but you never really get to know any of them in any degree of detail.  There is no bonding between characters, thought-provoking dialog or llikable characters.  There is no inventory system or trading which could have vastly expanded upon scrap collecting.
The missions were the most compelling part of the game but they seem short in number, artifically lengthened and don't provide enough reward for the effort.  Customizing your vehicle and upgrading Max are the best parts of the game but at the end of the game it seems like its all for nothing.  The ending was underwhelming, too easy and logically inconsistent.  A situation of life and death is presented and you are not given the opportunity to choose the outcome, breaking immersion and making it all seem trivial.
I enjoyed the game as I played it but once I realized how much time I was wasting doing tasks that the game wasn't even sufficiently rewarding me for I just focused on finishing the story missions.  Tasks like clearing landmines, destroying scarecrows, talking to people outside bases, destroying insignias, doing races, taking down convoys all equate to wasted time.  Even collecting scrap in every area is a waste of time as scrap is eventually just acquired automatically while online and off.  Its not until you look at the requirements for car upgrades that you realize most of them don't require you doing any of that.
I got the game for 5 dollars and for that price the price is right but for anything else it is not worth the cost.  There is simply too much busy work, too few actual characters, a lack of narrative depth, an ending that defies logic and an overall sense of pointlessness with the majority of the in-game tasks.  Some mechanics like gasoline never even come into play.  I didn't once run out of gas for my primary vehicle.
I give the game a 6/10.  I don't recommend it unless you can get it dirt cheap and you focus on only the main missions.

Now that I finished Mad Max, it's time for a review.
There is almost so much about this game I don't know where to start. It's obviously an open world game, that follows a lot of standard formats of the genre. However, in one of the major places it deviates is car combat, which makes a lot of sense. The car combat in the game is fun, however once  you get a weapon called the 'Thunderpoon', it gets really easy to destroy cars, however, it's really useful in assaulting bases so it's kind of a trade off. The convoy missions where you have to destroy an enemy truck surrounded by escorting cars though, is definitley the most fun.
The game mechanics honestly, overall are really enjoyable even though the combat mirrors the Batman: Arkham series of games. (Less dodging though, I found myself going more of a brutal route and blocking and taking hits to get damage on the enemies.) The graphical violence is way up there, which honestly, can get pretty cathartic, especially after you take down one of the sub-bosses in the game. The main boss hand to hand fight, it was most refreshing to pummel him when I was all maxed out (no pun intended).
I won't go into too many story spoilers, especially since it's a bit light on story, the theme however, is all Mad Max. The whole story and game just oozes the universe of Mad Max. My one complaint was not enough Aussie voice actors. Quite a number were American and... it just felt off in that one particular area.
The gameplay mechanics, sidequests, and making your vehicle more upgraded just makes the game overall a blast. The fact at the end, you get some fun unlockables just made me smile too. Some reviewers out there found the sidequests though to be just 'busy work'. To that, I'd say, I'd rather pick and choose to do them if I want to, rather than not have them there at all. They're sidequests so they're purely optional of course.
I have to agree with a few reviews I saw out there that said this game needs a sequel. It really does.  I got this game on a sale, however 20 bucks at this point is well worth the time and fun you'd get out of it. No extra DLC, no extra microtransactions... a full, great game for a fair price.

Mad Max is a good example of a tried a true formula for games that achieves your expectations, but doesn't go that far out of its way to be exceptional.
The game itself is a open world single player game, with combat directly from the arkham series. If you haven't played any of those its a combination of button mashing and blocking enemies attacks. You spend the other part of the game driving around in your car. There is a leveling system which you learn new combat moves, and upgrade your car . Car combat is quite fun as it comebines ramming, harpooning, and shooting other bandit cars. It gets old after awhile but this isn't a game you replay unless you really like this style of game.
That said the setting was quite a suprise. Knowing the world of Mad Max you would think that the majority of the world would be flat desert. But while it was almost all covered in sand, theres quite the variety between the regions. For example one area is covered by dried up coral. Another is full of tight canyons. Its quite impressive actually how the devolpers made all the locations stand out and feel unique in this monotone world.
That said the game is full of those open world activities including vantage points, races, outposts, and all the other stuff we have already exprienced in other games like far cry for example. Its the major problem this game has for me, it feels like just another open world game without anything really new or innovative. Theres a good amount of content in this game and I've completed the story and done most of the side objectives for a total playtime of almost 32 hours. While its not bad, its makes me feel that the game is just mediocre.
Theres a story here (NO SPOLIERS) that is pretty basic and lackluster. Max is the strong silent loner type going through the whole I just need a V8 thing and a bunch of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of war boys trying to kill him for revenge or something. Its just dull and predictable and goes how you would expect when you see things happen.
Overall Mad Max is a decent game, that follows industry trends without doing that much to set itself far apart from its compitition. For twenty dollars its worth picking up if you have the time, just don't expect something incredable or amazing here.

Rust is a multiplayer survival game that can be compared fairly to similar games, such as The Forest. The game is pretty solid, I've experienced no glitches in my (as of writing this review) 5 hours of play. As for the graphics, the game looks amazing, even when using the defaults for the 'potato graphics' launch setting. The game has a nice menu interface that makes it extremely easy to find and join a server. The only downside I see to this game is that there's no choice to play the game in singleplayer. Such is to be expected with a specifically multiplayer game but the online community is harsh. Building and keeping something in this game is near impossible, someone will always want to destroy what you've done, loot your base while you're offline or even kill you when you aren't there. Granted, it could be argued that the game is a multiplayer sandbox and again, such is to be expected but for people who want to have a similar singleplayer experience, you're going to want to look elsewhere.
Overall it's a stunning game but be prepared to be treated harshly.

INGREDIENTS :
1 egg
3⁄4 cup milk
2 tablespoons butter or 2 tablespoons margarine, melted
1 cup flour
1 tablespoon sugar

DIRECTIONS :
Beat egg until fluffy.
Add milk and melted margarine.
Add dry ingredients and mix well.
Heat a heavy griddle or fry pan which is greased with a little butter on a paper towel.

The Witcher Adventure Game is a fun little digital board game which has a resemblance to Elder Sign.
While it may look difficult and at the start also feel difficult, it's easy to learn and once you get into it you barely feel the difficulty any longer.
The game has a multiplayer mode. Although it needs a lot of work.
The multiplayer mode lacks a lot of key features you would connect with multiplayer. For instance, you cannot start a public multiplayer game and then invite your friends. This is a huge minus. Same goes for creating a private game. There is no way to create a private and invite a friend and then open it up to the public. So playing with friends abroad is often a challenge just to get the game started.
It's a very interactive game in terms of collecting items, quests and spells and spending gold. Along the way you will face obstacles, evil monsters and other nasty things out for blood. These can at times be a little challenging and make it feel like you're being set back a little. As the game progresses, you will become stronger and stronger.
The game is based around questing. Currently you can pick between doing 1, 3 or 5 quests in order to finish the game. Who ever has the most Victory Points (VP) at the end wins.
The game lacks character player interacting. With the extreme weak AI it is often more beneficial to play against or with other real people, but even so it still feel like you're playing against the a slightly stronger version of the AI. It lacks some interaction elements with other players instead of an action tab where you can see their roles. While you get to see what monster they're fighting, you don't get to see the monsters strenght and benefits. This makes it a little tedious and most players just sit around and wait for their turn without really having to pay attention to what the other 1-3 players are doing.
The community is a little dead and it can sometimes take a while to find other players.
There's a HUGE lack of information on the forums in terms of what direction the game is going to such an extant that there's not even any sticky posts from the developers. It makes the game feel dead and when I take a look at other digital board games forums (on steam) their forums usually thrives of activity.
The 4 classes you can pick between are all different in terms of play style, which is a great thing. Downside is, there's just these 4 and there are no news about them adding more.
As much as I want to recommend this game to people I just simply can't.
It feels dead and tedious to play and I regret not only buying a copy for myself but also gifted a copy to a friend before I knew what hassle the multiplayer would be. Along we're having random disconnect issues to deal with as well, which is not making all the bad things look any better.
This is a game that you can acquire on most platforms but without cross platform, it should probably just have stayed on tablets.

As great as this game can look and as cool as building your own war machine in the Mad Max universe sounds on paper, this game really does not live up to that potential. It's a lot of grinding for basically no payoff. You'd be better off getting your post-apocalyptic fix elsewhere.
So as much as I love Mad Max and this setting, the entire game was just one big swing and a miss. The bulk of the gameplay is grinding the same five or six objectives over and over again trying to reduce threat levels to unlock different parts for the Magnum Opus. Max needs to build a new car for his journey to the plains of silence, and that's about as deep as this story goes. Your one motiviation is to try to find the Big Chief V8, and there are only hints of characterization here and there. To top it off story-wise, the ending makes everything you do throughout the story completely worthless. None of your actions mattered in the continuity of the universe. It basically throws out everything and hits the reset button to be able to say it was connected to the movies. The game would have been so much better if they would've actually focused on making a story and stopped worrying about how it tied into the main series.
If you can ignore the lackluster story, the gameplay is basically one giant grind. The most exciting thing in the game is to take outposts and take down the convoys, and basically every single one of them is exactly the same. Even the top dogs have no variety in their fighting style. While the fighting in the game is fluid, it's completely barebones and shallow. Despite being a completionist with most other games, I had absolutely no desire to get through any more of Mad Max. All it was going to be was the same things over and over again just to make a better car to do the same things over and over again. Drive for five minutes, stop, pick up scrap, drive for five more minutes, stop, shoot sniper, etc. into infinity. There's just no depth in this massive world when they could have done so much more for the franchise.
I'm typically the kind of person that doesn't mind collectathons, and even I got tired of playing this game. Unless you just want to look at the post-apocalyptic landscapes and really don't mind grinding for eternity with an unsatisfying payoff, you should probably spend your money elsewhere.

Ok, so im not good at writing reviews, but here you have a brownie recipie.
Step 1: Choose a brownie recipe
When searching for the best brownie recipe, first consider the texture you hope to achieve: Do you like fudgy brownies or cakey brownies? In many brownie recipes, the proportion of flour to other ingredients is significantly less than in other baked goods. Reduce the amount of flour to make your brownies dense, fudgy, or rich. If you prefer brownies with a cakelike texture, look for brownie recipes with more flour. Some cakelike brownies contain milk or buttermilk, making their texture more like rich, fluffy chocolate cake.
Step 2: Chop chocolate
Of course, you can't make chocolate brownies without chocolate. Using a chef's knife, coarsely chop chocolate bars or squares on a cutting board. Chopped chocolate melts smoothly and evenly, and it won't scorch. Some recipes call for making brownies with cocoa powder. Both are delicious and easy ways to make chocolate brownies.
Step 3: Melt chocolate and butter
Place the chopped chocolate in a saucepan.
Cut up the butter and add it to the saucepan with the chocolate.
Heat and stir over low heat until all of the chocolate and butter is melted and the mixture is smooth.
Remove the saucepan from the heat, and let the chocolate mixture cool. This mixture will serve as the chocolate base for your brownie recipe.
Step 4: Stir in sugar
Add the sugar to the melted chocolate and butter. Stir with a wooden spoon until the sugar is completely mixed into the chocolate and butter.
Step 5: Add eggs
Add the eggs one at a time. Stir vigorously with a wooden spoon after each addition until the egg is completely incorporated into the chocolate mixture.
Beat in the vanilla with the wooden spoon.
Step 6: Add flour
In a separate bowl stir together the flour and baking soda.
Add the flour mixture all at once to the chocolate mixture.
Step 7: Mix batter
Gently stir the brownie batter until the flour is moistened.
Use a heavy-duty rubber spatula to scrape the sides and bottom of the saucepan.
If desired, stir in chocolate pieces or chopped nuts.
Step 8: Bake, cool, and frost brownies
Grease your baking pan or, if desired, line it with foil for easy removal. Spread the brownie batter in the prepared pan.
Bake brownies as directed in the recipe. Most brownies bake at 350 degrees F for 25 to 35 minutes.
Let the brownies cool completely in the pan on a wire rack.
If you want frosted brownies, wait at least an hour after baking to be sure the brownies have completely cooled.
Prepare the frosting. Chocolate-lovers may enjoy brownies with chocolate frosting, but we also recommend a simple vanilla frosting, cream cheese frosting, or even rich peanut butter frosting. Use an offset metal spatula to frost the brownies while they are still in the pan. Cut the finished dessert into bars, serve, and enjoy!

The permadeath sounds like a good idea...until touch a zombie, die, have to watch a game over screen that takes far too long to get through, and then start over right back at the beginning. Starting over means doing the exact same things you already did in the same order you already did them.
If there were randomized elements or at least some sort of checkpoint system it would make the game enjoyable. Think of it like the movie Groundhog Day, where Bill Murray can alter the rest of the day just by making a different choice. There will be none of that in Eaten Alive, as it's straight forward mirroring what you've done and hoping you don't get within spitting distance of a zombie before you can get to that point (and a little further) all over again.
As far as death, you only have to graze a zombie and it is INSTANT death. There's no trying to push it away, no kicks to topple them over - you're just 100% done.
I like the idea of RPG Maker games that aren't the standard RPG, such as horror or mystery/adventure. So, with that being the point of interest for me, I went ahead and played this long enough to get a feel for it. I'll play it some more later, but I just hope the repetitiveness isn't going to keep me from getting at least a little fun.
So, if you don't care about doing♥♥♥♥♥♥over, and over, and over, and over, buy it, it's otherwise decent. But my final verdict is that some changes need to be made by the developer before it's going to be a recommendable game.

Never wrote a review on steam... and to think this game brought me to that, means a lot - to me anyway.
i don't have a great deal of hours into this game, and yet, here's my 2 cent:
this game offers you Everything, and nothing.
you can have it all, own your game, own the server.. or you can be the one being owned.
i suppose dying in Rust is not something you should be ashamed of, since every time i died, every time someone stole 5 hours of work (and even a lot more than that), was paid back with game experience.
Rust is a Thrill i didn't feel for a very very long time (since the days of WoW - as much as they are on different catagories).
the Graphics is amazing (to me anyway - playing with Asus ROG Strix 1080 Ti 11GB makes this game looks like its the best Graphics Engine there is, and i played a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of Triple A Games through the course or my life).
the game play is catchable. it takes a bit of practice and muscle memory to start clicking fast / quick when situation presents itself (as any game i guess)
you might not agree but i can compare Rust's Early stages of the game to the same Principle of Starcraft:
you join a server, you decide you wanna stick to this one and start surviving.
you have to gather wood, stone, cloth, and as fast as you can so you can establish your first house - and this is just the beginning.
creating a house doesn't just ends up with having a Foundation, walls, roof and a door.
it requires a lock, which without metal, its a lock that requires a key, a key that can be stolen upon dying and everything you gather in the past 2 hours (each and his own experience and therefor progress - can be faster and can be slower, alone, or with groups of friends / allies)
and basically, the faster you acquire the materials you need to defend yourself along side with arming yourself with your first bow (to hunt animals ..or.. humans.. i guess) - the faster you get to the point where you might be able to protect yourself from the Zerg coming to you (sooner or later, they will come).
just like Starcraft. the longer you delay your defenses, the higher the possibility you'll get zergged without being able to defend.
since i am not sure how well is my review (certainly not a professional - but indeed a review that comes from the heart of a gamer who never knew how hungry he was for a Survival game such as  Rust) i will end this review by saying this.
i bought this game about 2-3 months ago (maybe even more).
this game was lying in my Library all that time without playing this game for 1 single hour.
this last Thursday, i logged into Rust starting my adventure without realizing i am about to play this game from Thursday night till saturday (or should i say Sunday early morning) at 4:30 AM (2 hours and i gotta get up for work).
i played almost 35-37 hours of Rust, Basically, with almost no downtime other than sleep, shower, eat. (wife and kids were on vacation).
i am a father for 2, 33 years old... and i feel like 16 again.
if anyone actually have read this review all the way to the end, and was able to get the sensation of how i felt during this  crazy weekend (how much of a Nerd can i possibly be..) that you'll turn back the moment you see this because i am giving you a warm warning...
THIS GAME IS FRIGGING ADDICTING AS ♥♥♥♥.

Ok, so im not good at writing reviews, but here you have a brownie recipie.
Step 1: Choose a brownie recipe
When searching for the best brownie recipe, first consider the texture you hope to achieve: Do you like fudgy brownies or cakey brownies? In many brownie recipes, the proportion of flour to other ingredients is significantly less than in other baked goods. Reduce the amount of flour to make your brownies dense, fudgy, or rich. If you prefer brownies with a cakelike texture, look for brownie recipes with more flour. Some cakelike brownies contain milk or buttermilk, making their texture more like rich, fluffy chocolate cake.
Step 2: Chop chocolate
Of course, you can't make chocolate brownies without chocolate. Using a chef's knife, coarsely chop chocolate bars or squares on a cutting board. Chopped chocolate melts smoothly and evenly, and it won't scorch. Some recipes call for making brownies with cocoa powder. Both are delicious and easy ways to make chocolate brownies.
Step 3: Melt chocolate and butter
Place the chopped chocolate in a saucepan.
Cut up the butter and add it to the saucepan with the chocolate.
Heat and stir over low heat until all of the chocolate and butter is melted and the mixture is smooth.
Remove the saucepan from the heat, and let the chocolate mixture cool. This mixture will serve as the chocolate base for your brownie recipe.
Step 4: Stir in sugar
Add the sugar to the melted chocolate and butter. Stir with a wooden spoon until the sugar is completely mixed into the chocolate and butter.
Step 5: Add eggs
Add the eggs one at a time. Stir vigorously with a wooden spoon after each addition until the egg is completely incorporated into the chocolate mixture.
Beat in the vanilla with the wooden spoon.
Step 6: Add flour
In a separate bowl stir together the flour and baking soda.
Add the flour mixture all at once to the chocolate mixture.
Step 7: Mix batter
Gently stir the brownie batter until the flour is moistened.
Use a heavy-duty rubber spatula to scrape the sides and bottom of the saucepan.
If desired, stir in chocolate pieces or chopped nuts.
Step 8: Bake, cool, and frost brownies
Grease your baking pan or, if desired, line it with foil for easy removal. Spread the brownie batter in the prepared pan.
Bake brownies as directed in the recipe. Most brownies bake at 350 degrees F for 25 to 35 minutes.
Let the brownies cool completely in the pan on a wire rack.
If you want frosted brownies, wait at least an hour after baking to be sure the brownies have completely cooled.
Prepare the frosting. Chocolate-lovers may enjoy brownies with chocolate frosting, but we also recommend a simple vanilla frosting, cream cheese frosting, or even rich peanut butter frosting. Use an offset metal spatula to frost the brownies while they are still in the pan. Cut the finished dessert into bars, serve, and enjoy!

This is a good realization of the board game. It is playable as hot-seat or online and may give you many hours of enjoyable experience.
But there are some flaws that need to be fixed to make the game perfect:
1. When a player have to do a choice, he/she can't access to the game map and/or any player hero sheet and resources including his/her own. This may easily lead to wrong decisions and waste fun. The board game is obviously free from this limitation. So, the possibility to "minimize" the choice and take look at the game state will make the game much comfortable.
2. Some choices are not clearly described. For example, Triss Merigold has a spell to look at the two top investigation cards then put one on the bottom of the deck and the other back on top. When this spell is used, the game show two cards and say to the player just "choose one of them". What will be happen next with the chosen card is unclear.
3. The rules of the game says that proofs can't be exchanged back to leads. So, the investigation successes of a hero converted to proofs must me "protected" from any bad events that force the hero to spend leads. But in the computer version proofs ARE exchanged back to leads every time a hero must spend more leads than he/she have.
4. The AI is wery weak, so the single-player games are dull and not enjoyable at all.
5. There is no russian language, sadly to many and many russian-speaking Witcher fans.
6. In network games, when a player quits at the characters selecting stage, all other players are forced to quit and try to start network game again. That allows one player to abuse many other.
7. Triss "Teleport" spell is mightly overpowered. It allows Triss to collect two leads in a turn without any risk. I think, this is not the board game disbalance but the wrong implementation in computer game. Some other abilities with the text "when you perform [stated action] {do something in addition}" also work weird in the computer game.
I understood the game to be more Role Playey... it's just a digital boardgame. Still fun, but no character progression or anything. You just start over each time. Still fun.

Where to begin?
The game does an excellent job of creating the theme to The Witcher games. Characters, environments and monsters all give it that excellent feel that the games have. Detailed and impressive art work can be found from it's map to the monster cards. It has the look and feel of an actual board game.
I've invested a few hours of the game and have played a few of the "Complete 3 Quests" games. The pacing of the game is alright, though a bit of downtime between turns towards the late game. Be prepared to do something in the background while you wait your turn. A signal to anounce that your turn has come would be very helpful.
One major complaint I have with this game is it seems you are penialized for doing practically everything. I understand that the universe of The Witcher is a very unforgiving thing, but having to draw a fate card for almost every action (while having a fate token on an action) seems excessive. Most games I have played I have spent either trying to remove Fate tokens from my actions, or healing from wounds. I don't know if this is a major part of the game, dealing with Fate tokens, but it became more of an annoyance.
The quest system works well. Having to do investigations to gain resources works well and having side quests helps along the way to acheieving your quests. Side quests can give a bit more flavour to the game and is a great way to earn some extra Victory Points.
The battle system is alright, though it reminds me more of Elder Sign than anything else. Roll dice, match symbols, if you have enough, you win! If you don't! Bad stuff happens (if you don't defend).
The game has a lack of save system, which I find odd. So if you're wanting to play a long game but don't have the time to invest, prepare to be disapointed or to have the game run in the background.
For me, the game does a very good job of emulating a board game, but the mechanics are either ones I've played from other games, and does much better or just flat out annoy me for existing. I cannot really recommend this game.

This game seems like a top-notch digital conversion of the boardgame, so if you enjoy the physical game and want an online copy, don't hesitate to buy this.  The price is right.
TLDR: The game isn't terrible but also isn't great.  There's no meaningful interaction between the various players.  Constant status ailments can become frustrating.  3/5 stars.
My negative review is of the game itself.  It's a simple four-player "collect various resources until you have the right combination to cash them in for victory points" type of game, coupled with basic dice-based combat (versus the environment, not versus the other players).  The main problem I have with this game is that there really isn't any interaction between the different players.  For example, I might draw a card that affects all of the players, but it happens automatically, whether I want it to or not.  At no time in the game was I able to choose to influence the other players in any way, either to help them or to hurt them.  So basically it boiled down to four players, each playing a single player game on the same board.  It wasn't terrible, but it wasn't very enjoyable either.  I originally bought the game in the hopes that multiplayer would be fun, but considering the lack of meaningful interaction, it kind of seems pointless now.
And this game is dark.  You will be negatively afflicted with status ailments every freaking turn.  Because of this, the game becomes a long, grim slog to complete your quests.  This is all very true to the witcher universe, I just don't know that it lends itself toward making a game fun.
On the plus side, the artwork is fantastic.  Having read the various Witcher stories and played the excellent RPGs allowed me to appreciate the lore that is depicted in this game.

This is a simple but suprisingly entertaining game, made for fans of the Witcher series and who also enjoy casual board games.
I'll start off by saying this: don't expect too much from this game; the system has been developed competently enough so that it offers more than an average amount of replayability, with gameplay duration lasting somewhere between 70-120mins depending on how many main quests are necessary to win the game - the number of quests to determine the victor can be chosen at the beginning of the game. However, if you are expecting the next X-Wing or Arkham Horror, you'd better look elsewhere. But if you can put such hype aside and play it for what it is: a decent board game that, if played with friends either online with this digital version, or face-to-face with the physical copy (the way I believe all board game SHOULD be played if you're able to do so) is worth your consideration.
The Witcher Adventure Game is, in certain aspects, similar to Arkham Horror and Talisman - in fact to me it feels somewhat like a mish-mash of the two. Is it as good as Arkham Horror? In my opinion, no; Is it better than Talisman - if judging Talisman without all the expansions and basing the comparison simply on the base game itself - yes, to me at least it made for a more enjoyable experience, both online and face-to-face with the physical copy.
In terms of gameplay; it's kind of a mish-mash of Arkham Horror and Talisman, so, like I said, this game has a level of spontaneity, with random spikes of difficulty throughout the game - but it makes for an interesting story as you're playing. Taking into consideration all the different events (foul events and good fortune), monsters (leveled as bronze - easy, silver - medium, and gold - hard) and the war track, it really isn't suprising how you might find yourself at the bottom of the pack if hit with too many unlucky cards a few turns in a row; but if you play it smart you generally defy the odds and hold out for these few 'bad' turns and bring yourself back into contention for first place.
The characters are pretty well balanced. Having played with all but Triss, I've yet to find anything overpowering or game-breaking with any of the four playable characters. Each have their own pros and cons - not that I'll spoil their abilities; learning the playstyle of each character for the first time was half the fun!
Last but now least, the artwork is pretty topnotch - and it should be, considering CDPR and FFG have sourced most of their material from the concepts done for the three witcher games.
Overall I reckon it's worth a grab for witcher fans who also enjoy BOARD GAMES. This isn't a hard game to wrap your head around; you can learn the system within the first 10minutes; but it is enjoyable, and that, at least for me, makes it worth the buy.

I can't recommend this game for several reasons. Square released this as "episodic", meaning you have to wait until they release each chapter of the game. Okay, I guess. I mean, I've pre-ordered and done "Early Access" stuff before. This, however, wasn't labelled technically as early access but rather a full game. The story is uncompelling and the missions feel rather forgetable compared to the others. Sure, there's lots of replayability stuff, but this has 6 missions and they're short. After Episode 5 I'm at 17 hours, and that's having done several missions multiple ways. They tried to do some stuff with "Elusive Targets", all it is is putting NPCs in places that already were setup. It's still not hard, and after you've gone through a mission once, it's pretty easy to complete the next one on the same level in like 30 minutes tops. The difficulty just isn't there for me and the size of the maps doesn't feel like it's something that was worth waiting for in the end, it's not really any bigger than any other Hitman game. It just doesn't feel fresh and even after Episode 5, the game just feels way too short. I feel like I paid to wait, and as of Episode 5, I'm still waiting on something interesting to come out of this game.
Also, mod-locked and online only, for what? It has player generated missions and leaderboards, all of which are pretty underwhelming for the average player and for me didn't add any value to my experience.

This review is going to ignore the business practice of distributing the game episodically.  Personally I find it distastful, but if that was the only way they were going to green light hitman to keep going then I guess I'll live with it.
Each and every hitman game has been getting better with every iteration.  While I am aware many would argue the move from Blood Money to Absolution was like slipping in a puddle of liquid♥♥♥♥♥♥ at least it did move the mechanics and graphics forword even if Keith Carradine was the highlight of the game in my opinion.
That being said Hitman has moved back to its native setting of a large open area with lots of people and a few you need to murder.  The graphics and animations are solid with a few random bugs like womens legs clipping in their dresses.  killing people is as enjoyable as ever.  While you can use the camera to your advantage you cannot go ham and kill everyone with ease like in Absolution.  Enemies kill you in a few hits and if your trying to kill everyone your best bet is to hit and run all around the map.  Although luring 20 people into the same bathroom and drowning them in the toilet seems a bit broken yet hillarious.
Sadly I have found the first 2 missions to be the most expansive and enjoyable.  While missions 3 and 4 are by no means bad or small they do not really hold up to the first 2 in terms of quality in my opinion.  Perhaps its because mission one had me killing a character voiced by Mary Elizabeth McGLynn who voices the Major in Ghost in the Shell.  That was a cool revelation.  Colorado is certainly interesting but I feel like the developers decided to add more targets to make up for a smaller map that is not really all that interesting compared to the rest.  The story is giving me flashbacks of Hitman 2, but its well acted and has me interested on what Japan has in store for 47.
The game is definately a move in the right direction, but as mentioned above the buisiness model is another story that wont be factored in this.  The addition of escalation, challenges, and elusive targets bring great replayability.  The maps are just really well made.  Although I do wish some of the silly escalation challenges like hide all bodies or facify nobody would be replaced with less arcady challenges.  Maybe have a target with body guards, change up the patrols, or do something besides having me walking with a remote control to keep the lasers that only I can trigger murder me.
I also think that elusive targets while interesting in concept suck for a person who isnt on IO interactives schedule.  Oh you didnt own the game or have time to play when Gary Busey was the target?  Well you can go ♥♥♥♥ yourself.  Even making them a one time thing seems like your giving and then taking away content.  Some of the stuff Busey says is funny and panicking and killing him in a stupid way only to never get another shot is just dumb.
If you have not bought the game yet I am not sure if I can recommend it or not.  They might come out with an ultimate edition that is a good deal.  Or it might be an awful deal.  But it is a good game.  Its just a shame the business model makes you feel like you have 3 doors in front of you and 2 have a clown behind them who is going to molest your wallet.

While I love playing this game, and I have spent tons of time playing it, I can't honestly recommend you spend 60 dollars buying it.
When the game was announced, they said they would release an episode every month for a year. I assumed 12 episodes because of this, but was extremely skeptical that they could maintain this timeline and so I was prepared to be disappointed. You heard nothing on the number of episodes until well after the game had released, and we were informed of this by the developer randomly changing it on the store page.
The game is extremely thin for what you pay, and although it has extra content like elusive targets, these are entirely useless if you travel, have a life, or did not buy this game on day one. as they are only available for 48 hours after release and only appear once every few weeks. The story is almost non-existent in the game, effectively making it a 7 mission Hitman tech demo. They have announced an additional 2 seasons, at an additional 60 bucks a pop, so to see this barely coherent story flesh out, you'll have to pay a total of 180 dollars and wait two additional years. None of this information was available on release, and was not announced until well after Episode 5.
They knew the fans wanted a return to blood money style missions, but they have absolutely no clue how to flesh out a story over this format and thus, have turned the game the game into nothing but a money grabbing tech demo intent on exploiting the nostalgia from the last time they made a decent hitman game. Wait until this is extremely discounted to buy or you'll be disappointed.

As far as a digital implementation of a board game, this is fairly good. It's a nice PC interface. Everything works fairly well. (The dice are a little funky, but eh... whatever).
I love the Witcher series. I was excited when this game was announced. I was excited to see this game hit the store.
If you you love The Witcher Adventure Game, and want a digital implementation, then stop reading and just buy it.
If you haven't played The Witcher Adventure Game, let me stop you right there and say "Don't". Go buy Merchants of Venus, Xia: Legend of a Drift System, Steam, Merchants & Marauders, Istanbul, or even Firefly: The Game. Those are all vastly superior Pick-Up and Deliver games - which is all this is. An unnessessarily complicated, frustrating, painful, lengthy Pick-Up and Deliver game.
It's a mean game. And I don't mean that in the way that Diplomacy or even Munchkin is a "mean game". Or even how "Ghost Stories is brutally difficult". I mean this game stabs you in the liver, and then deducts points from you because you're bleeding like a wimp.
The designer is a wonderful designer. He also owns the game publisher "Portal Games". Go check out all of his other games (Robinson Crusoe, Imperial Settlers, 51st State, The New Era, Pret-a-Porter). This doesn't even measure up to the worst game I've played from Fantasy Flight.
The interaction between players is awful. It's mostly a solitare experience. Which doesn't help when the game points how you don't have any friends.
The turns are very repetative. Especially when the game finally gets you into the fetal position, and all it leaves you to do is to rock back and forth as you bleed from your severed ankles.
Ever played Bunco? Where you just roll the dice, hoping to roll three of a kind? No agency. No decision making. Just luck of the RNG. This game wants you to roll a 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, or 10 of a kind with 3-4 dice - and that's not really an exaggeration.
When when you fail, because - well - math, you take damage.
Nothing good really happens to you. And when it does, like finally completing one of your quests, you STILL get punished. For a good ol' fashioned "Good job. ♥♥♥♥ you." - like mom use to say.
The monsters seem incredibly out of balance. Rolling the dice usually seems like a wasted effort. There ARE things you HAVE to get in order to over come the dice, but those dont' seem well balanced either.
This is easily one of the worst board game experiences I've had in the last few years.
The only value this game has had for me is that I only spent $8 on this before foolishly spending $60 at my local game store. And for that, I'll look very favorably at it.
10/10.

Here are my pros and cons for the game so far (from what I have played)
Pros:
- Enjoyable music that sets the mood nicely for the game
- Easy to pick up on
- Nice tutorials
- Graphics are quite nice as well for a board game
- Auto save games for later plays
- Based on The Witcher
- Different from majority of other board games
- A little bit of The Witcher story is told through the cards etc.
Cons:
- Daunting at first
- Games take forever although this is too be expected for a board game so not really a con
- If you are unlucky, you're going to have a bad time
I will update my review later.

I'm a huge Mad Max fan, and count Fury Road as one of my favorite all-time films.  I say that so you know i'm a fanboy.  I expected a decent game, that would scratch that post-apocalyptic itch for me.  This game is actually pretty good on its own merits.  Game of the Year it is not, but it is still a very, very good game.  I take some issue with the story, but don't worry, that's not really an issue for the vast majority of the game.  Most of it is spent roaming the wasteland, and that the developers did amazingly well.  The vehicular combat feels right, and some of the chases you get into look and feel amazing.  Challenging convoys, in particular, felt exactly like something out of the climactic chase of the Road Warrior.  Graphically, the game is rock solid, if not absolutely mind-blowing.  The world looks great, and feels like it stepped right out of the films, as it should.  The gameplay can feel somewhat repetitive, as you roam about, attack raider settlements, and upgrade your vehicle.  But, as a testament to the combat, it never sucks.  There's enough variety in the terrain, and the sheer multitude of ways to approach a situation, that you will not regret playing this game.
So if you're a fan of the films, definitely give it a go.  If you want a really great example of vehicular combat, give it a go.  Its not perfect, but this is a very good game that never got its due.

A simple review of why this game is worth the asking price:
this is about as good as it will ever get for a platform exploration game of the current generation, you will not find another title that can rival the sheer playability, graphical prowess or the mindblowing background music.  I own the original "Ori" and did not hesitate to acquire the "Definitive Version", I now have two variations of this legendary game.  Make no mistake, this is a future classic and it will take years for any studio to surpass the love that has gone into making Ori what it is, something very special indeed.
Graphics, sound, playability, those are the magic ingredients that make a computer game, but Ori has more than just those things, Ori is filled with a "unique something" that words cannot or ever would define. I don't think I've ever been emotionally involved in a game more than in Ori and the Blind Forest, and it's been a real pleasure to play it again in the Definitive Edition, the feels are still there.
This game has everything for it, from gorgeous graphics, to insanely good music and addictive gameplay with a great difficulty curve as well as clever level design, and a nice story with adorable characters.
The new features in the Definite Edition are really nice, the difficulty settings let everyone enjoy the game the way they want, teleporting made me more motivated to find all secrets, the two new zones are really fun to explore, the new music is really pleasant to listen to, and being able to come back to the Ginso Tree and Forlorn Ruins if we forgot to get some collectibles is awesome, as well as being able to keep playing on a save file even after completing the game.
I'd also like to mention how the game runs way better than the original Ori and the Blind Forest, the problem of visuals and sound not being in sync during cutscenes isn't there anymore in the Definitive Edition, and some laggy areas of the original doesn't anymore, which is perfect if you don't have a beast of a computer.
So yeah, I really love this game, and I HIGHLY recommend anyone to play it.
Unless you really have a passionate hate towards Metroidvanias, I'm pretty sure you'll love Ori and the Blind Forest: Definitive Edition.

There's so much to explore and discover (especially in the earlier episodes) that you'll probably spend hours just scoping out all the possibilities, eavesdropping the brilliantly funny conversations and trying to find all the strange weapons and disguises at your disposal.
What really makes this a game you'll keep coming back to, is that even after you're familiar with the game and have finished the main missions, there's a load of extra escalation missions, hidden challenges and player-created contracts to complete too.
It looks great, feels great and I hope this is what all future Hitman games strive to be.

While a bit rough around the edges, Arkham Origins is great addition to the Arkham franchise. I found the story to be the best of the series with much more emphasis on how Batman is the catalyst for all of these super criminals springing up in Gotham along with telling a bit about the origin of the Joker. Gameplay is still as fluid as ever with a few new elements including the enemy martial artists that can counter your attacks. The Riddler challenges are simply a chore in this game, basically a dumbed-down version of what we got in Arkham City. New Game Plus tells you that your gadgets are all unlocked from the start but a few of them are withheld, which was dissapointing. The level design leaves a lot to be desired, especially if the game insists you return there to collect a riddler item. God help you if you need to go back to collect that riddler item at the final area of the Gotham Royal Hotel, it will be a good half and hour round trip.
The progression system is a little different. Most upgrades are unlockable via the old XP/Leveling system, but some have a new system requiring you to complete challenges --in a specific order-- to unlock certain abilities and gadgets. For instance, clear a predator encounter without using detective vision. The only thing is, that must be your next available challenge for it to be completed, do any of the challenges out of order and you will not get credit. Frustrating.

You know, sometimes I wonder if I just have something inherently against sequels. I liked Half-Life 2 a little less than Half-Life, which still means I enjoyed it more than I'm probably going to end up enjoying sex. My opinions of Fallout 2 vs. its predecessor have been well-documented, and even Fallout 3 and New Vegas I like a bit less than the original. Portal 2 I've declared not a part of my little head-canon. I haven't played Just Cause 1, Team Fortress Classic, or the first half-hour of System Shock (in keeping with how much I've played of its sequel), but I've heard that they're objectively worse than their successors, and that's a hard thing for a bias to compete against. Anyway, now we have Borderlands 2. A ♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game.
In keeping with my review of the original, I'm going to name a bunch of tiny, petty things and then come up with an overall opinion. So, without further ado, let the complaints begin.
The GUI, rather than being streamlined like would have been a good idea, has just been made all cool and transparent and intangible, making it even harder to use. And also somehow pretentious.
The weapon type proficiency system has been replaced with "Badass Tokens", a fun little exercise in pointlessness that I wouldn't mind were it not for the fact that they replaced the ability to increase stats with certain weapons by using them a lot.
Iteration times after dying have been increased using pointless cinematics, which any competent game designer will tell you is one of the cardinal sins of game design. THIS IS NOT HARD
Picking up of money, ammo, and health has been made automatic, which is an objectively good decision but subjectively I dislike because it takes away from the janky, Deus Ex-style RPG feel of the original that gave it a lot of its charm.
It's good to see a game that recognizes that battle rifles are things that are fun to have and includes them, especially ones with explosive rounds. I kept my one of my original ones of these throughout the entire game for how helpful it was for the first few levels.
I played with Salvatore, hoping to recapture memories of playing Brick in Borderlands 1, and for all his faults (to be detailed later), his melee attack punch was understated enough to be funny when it killed an enemy who just took several shotgun blasts to the face. I upgraded it as soon as possible.
Cars were an instakill in the last game, which I made light of in my review, and they nerfed that this game. However, they've done so a bit too much, as cars now do barely any damage. This makes even less sense than enemies dying on collision with a car's stationary tires, and kind of removes the point of cars.
The NPCs carried over from the last game, with the exception of the ever-stoic Marcus  (who I'm fairly sure actually died in the last Borderlands DLC), have all become caricatures of their former selves. The main victims are Scooter, who now devotes his time exclusively to pointless romantic interests (you can have several quests from him trying to woo women simultaneously); Dr. Zed, who actually gets a lot less screen time but is generally even less subtle about how bad at his job he is when he is on; Moxxi, who is now an explosives expert for some reason (but only in one side quest); and Tannis, who I now hate with a passion even though I was genuinely interested and amused by her story in the last game. The worst of all, though, is that mysterious helper from the first game, the Guardian Angel, who now has a personality, a backstory, and some running jokes, none of which I will spoil because they're too stupid and predictable. It's really a shame, because these were pretty good characters in the first game.
The new player characters, on the other hand, are incredibly bland, especially when the old members of the crew show up again and steal every scene they're in. On the other hand, the continuation of their story may be worth the price of admission alone if you idolize them more than the rest of us idolize Gordon Freeman.
The talking and idle animations have become frightfully inane. It's hard to concentrate on what people are saying, or the genuinely well-written dialogue, when they look like f*ckin' Food Fight.
I don't remember if unlocking portions of the map of each area as you discovered them was in the last game, but it's really fiddly here.
The graphics are better but who cares.
It's substantially less silly-gory, in a way that makes enemy death less cathartic. It's not worth it  to shoot a bandit 10 levels lower than you with your rocket shotgun if you don't know that his arm will fly off for your trouble.
Gunzerking is not as fun as Berzerking, because as anyone who's played the Heavy knows sometimes you just want to throw caution to the wind and punch things, but it becomes necessary later on when the game gets insipid.
Revival stations now give you ammo, which I'm not sure how I feel about.
The story is...I'm not going to say better, but it certainly is...fuller. Yeah. Fuller.
Handsome Jack is really interesting and really good, and he has a really good arc. He's the one standout thing in the entire game.
Tiny Tina is annoying. I don't care what everyone else says.
CLAPTRAP'S BIRTHDAY IS NOT FUNNY. IT'S REALLY SAD.
Battles often become particle effect maelstroms to the point that you can't actually see the enemies, or indeed the gun you're holding right in front of your face.
You can have a Borderlands game, and then you can have the heartfelt scene where you go around telling people that Roland has been killed. You can't have both. (I still think the guy respawned on the other side of the planet.)
Here's one of my main problems. It's okay for games to be kind of easy. Half-Life 2, Fallout: New Vegas, and Borderlands 1 showed us that. Not every game needs to have a meaty challenge, not even at the end. Sometimes the experience and the world are what matters. Borderlands 2 does not realize this, and thinks it has to ramp up the difficulty. It decides that the best way to do this is to have SO many enemies with SO many pointless gimmicks and SOOOOO much health that I'm getting tired and resigned just writing this sentence. Second Winds help, but only to a point because the gameplay is fairly shallow with little opportunity for variation and therefore doesn't bear repeating. Ammo practically rains from the skies because the enemies become so pointlessly bullet-spongy. It doesn't help that the infinite respawning of enemies is so blatant that there's no sense of progression after you kill yet another one, because odds are his identical clone is being produced in front of your eyes this very second. It's just so pointlessly insipid that I almost gave up on the game at one point after chipping away at a miniboss's health for half an hour because at that point all the minor enemies with way too much health respawned behind me and squashed me into lunchmeat. The only reason I pushed forward was for closure, and to write this review with authority.
Borderlands was a really good game. This game tries to recreate that glory for commercial gain, and clearly has fan service stamped all over it. The returns of the characters. The backstories for everyone. The jokes at all costs, even character consistency. The pop-culture references kicked up to 11. The "difficulty". The hero-worship of whoever happens to be around. You know what it is? Death by focus group. Not making a choice for yourself based on what you want to make, but just asking the person you're selling it to so that you can make whatever they want, with no regard for whether that's a good idea. Fans were obviously consulted for every single element, and they chose what they wanted, not what was good for the series as a whole. As usual, I haven't played the DLC yet, but I don't think I'm going to. And neither should you. Just go play Borderlands again.

I'm a huge Mad Max fan, and count Fury Road as one of my favorite all-time films.  I say that so you know i'm a fanboy.  I expected a decent game, that would scratch that post-apocalyptic itch for me.  This game is actually pretty good on its own merits.  Game of the Year it is not, but it is still a very, very good game.  I take some issue with the story, but don't worry, that's not really an issue for the vast majority of the game.  Most of it is spent roaming the wasteland, and that the developers did amazingly well.  The vehicular combat feels right, and some of the chases you get into look and feel amazing.  Challenging convoys, in particular, felt exactly like something out of the climactic chase of the Road Warrior.  Graphically, the game is rock solid, if not absolutely mind-blowing.  The world looks great, and feels like it stepped right out of the films, as it should.  The gameplay can feel somewhat repetitive, as you roam about, attack raider settlements, and upgrade your vehicle.  But, as a testament to the combat, it never sucks.  There's enough variety in the terrain, and the sheer multitude of ways to approach a situation, that you will not regret playing this game.
So if you're a fan of the films, definitely give it a go.  If you want a really great example of vehicular combat, give it a go.  Its not perfect, but this is a very good game that never got its due.

… Where do I start?
So, here we are, the oh-so-hyped Sister Location. What people have been waiting for so long, after a moderately commendable trailer. New faces, more advanced movement mechanics, familiar yet different setting. A good show of promise...
Too bad you aren’t free to taste them out properly.
I was always skeptical about SL being a good fifth game in the series (counting out World which doesn’t really adhere to the horror formula).
In fact, I was absolutely happy with FNAF 4 being the last chapter. It was clear enough there was no more space for new content, and it was right and legit that way.
Now, I’ll be as fair as possible: it could’ve been much worse than how it turned out to be. The voice acting is a fine addition, one that I’m sure would’ve worked out nicely in the classics as well. The graphics have definitely improved, and the fact there’s a certain degree of additional player/animatronic animation makes the game feel more alive and immersive at times. The new story content also helps up clear out some lore matters and doesn’t just clutter it with more questions like some of the others did.
The problem is: as a player you aren’t given the chance to really enjoy what’s new. Sister Location takes a different turn compared to the classics, and decides to focus on a narrative playstyle, telling the player a story, making them win against some challenges, and then treating them to an ending. It’d be nice, if the game didn’t basically become an interactive short movie with no further reason to play it but to “rewatch”.
Aside from two challenges the game imposed, one of them being optional even, the rest of the game felt led and granted. As I found out later, there were many more ways to die than I experienced for myself, and that fact is kind of baffling by itself, because the game was practically playing itself in those phases. I technically shouldn’t even worry about spoiling anything because I’m pretty sure everybody already spoiled all by themselves, but anyway...
All in all, I felt great disappointment in playing this game, which had such a promising start, only to wear you out with boring
, only to give you an actual challenge in the end, just to realize you’ve come this far for a downer ending
Now uhm... I’ve been harsh, but you’ll notice I haven’t called the game “crap”. No, it’s yet far from that. Sister Location is a smart product that lends itself to be listened to at the very least. From Sister Location we do see that there’s been a good effort to explain several doubts imposed by previous titles, without revealing much in a clear way, to leave the typical aura of mystery the series has been known for, without becoming excessively illogical.
And that said: It’s sad there’s only the Thumbs Up or Down choice in this case. I can’t really say Yes or No, at least as a long time fan of the series, because what this game lacks in gameplay, it has in storytelling.
Sister Location unlocks the potential the classics had and never used, and loses the potential used by them. We could say it’s almost the polar opposite, barring out the creepiness factor.
TL;DR:
Pros:
-	Great Voice Acting
-	Decent full HD rendering, with better animation level.
-	Allows for a decent immersion
-	Not just jumpscares
-	Story. Story, story, story
Cons:
-	Poor gameplay, with what’s good being either too short and frustrating
-	Even more of a Youtube game than ever before
-	Movement is an unnecessary illusion, acts as filler (vents) and boring challenge (Auditoriums)
-	Degradation of humour level.
7/10: Enjoyable (6/10: Passable before Custom Night Edit)
Exceptional potential, mostly wasted in attempting to become a mashup of a puzzleless Amnesia, Outlast and FNAF. Full interactivity was the base of the sense of freedom FNAF granted. Sister Location’s content is sadly limited by unskippable dialogues, frustrating failure punishment, and Exotic Butters. Much more could’ve been done, but this cow has been milked dry long ago, apparently.
Pity. However, Peace.
