I highly recommend this addition to the Hitman series.
It captures the same feel as previous titles to the series namely Blood Money which was one of everyone's favourites adding to that in almost every way but giving the same overall feel which everyone came to like so much about the Hitman games.
It started out as a bit of a mess with all kinds of issues and the onslaught of bad reviews mostly pertaining to the fact the game was being released episodic which really upset a lot of people but to date the game is totally worth it's money giving you tons of hours of playability - ofcoarse you will be probably playing the same missions over and over again that having been said however the options as to how you go about each mission are quite extensive offering you the ability to really get a feel for the mechanics and AI of a mission and how best to navigate through those missions usually doing your best to do so completely undetected.
The gameplay and controls for the game are sharp, accurate and most of all feel fluid. You die extremely fast so getting caught is not a good idea but thankfully the controls are not clunky or anything like that allowing you to feel better in control of your overall movement.
Some of the accents of locals and such that you find in maps is unrealistic to say the least as everyone seems to have American or British accents only.
One of the funnest parts of the game and not a permanent feature is the elusive targets which only come once a life time giving you just one shot to kill a target and escape one of those having been a celebrity, Gary Busey himself was quite funny. Hearing about an upcoming elusive contract is exciting too giving you a feel as if you are an assassin getting ready for a serious contract with no replayability like in real life - it feels crucial or something that you succeed which is quite immersive in itself.
Graphically the game really is something to behold visually. The way light reflects off marble floors and such is truly a work of art and I highly commend the team behind this game because they are really trying to be immaculate and it shows unlike a lot of other titles out there where they just kinda throw clunky controls and bugs at you and then begins a slow couple months progress trying to iron out the game. Hitman felt like it had been looked over by a perfectionist and when they realised some of the GPU tweak problems they were not at all slow to ammend and fix the problem.
Now with the finale episode just around the corner there are rumours that they are taking the game for at least another season which means another bunch of world location and targets may be around the corner extending on the storyline even further and I am excited.
I highly recommend this game especially if you got into the earlier Hitman titles not including Abosolution which was a bit of a different direction in itself. This is more like the old school Blood Money feel but much better.

This is basically a assassination simulator, which is not a bad thing for a HITMAN game, yet the story content is heavily lacking. Each location you visit will have a briefing video of the targets you have to assassinate as well as short information on what they did bad and who wants them dead. After that you're on your own, with many ways you can play out the job.
You will encounter "opportunities", when you basically eavesdrop on people and game gives you objectives on how you can eliminate the targets. Some opportunities are more amusing than others, and award you points if successfully eliminating target without witnesses. That said every location is a one mission job, be it for example Paris, you just kill two targets and that's it, get briefing and go to next location.
However you can revisit the location and do more challenging opportunities, replay the mission with different set of targets, kill targets with a specific weapon or dressed in specific disguise and get awarded score based on how good you did, with leaderboards and other challenges. And that's pretty much the meat of the game, killing how you want it, with whatever weapon you want, in a disguise you want, unless mission specifies otherwise. You can also create your own contracts and/or play contracts created by other players.
Every location is unique and has many ways you can get to your targets, and ways you can deal with them. Levels are somewhat large, with a lot of NPC's and rich scenery, that will stress out any modern computer. Don't dream about reaching 60 fps even on recommended specs, even though game looks beautiful on highest settings, it won't run well because it's not as optimized as you would expect from a well known developer. However they are always tuning and fixing stuff, and you get better performance as time goes on.
At launch game had only tutorial and Paris level which was very bad practice as you still (at the writing of the review) don't have the full game content available. Last mission update will only be out on Halloween. For me personally it was a big deal, as you pay full price for a game, and then must wait nearly half year for all the content. This would have been a more enjoyable experience for me if they included more story, and optimized it more because even on 980Ti this does not run well at all.
So here's my conclusion, if you like Hitman contracts and replaying same thing just in different ways, it's what the game is in nutshell, if you want a more story driven experience, try the older Hitman titles or buy first location mission to test it out, check some YouTube videos or streams. Personally I had way more fun in Hitman: Absolution and older titles as they were a bit more story driven than this, however, being a Hitman fan you want to try out the new games as you believe in developer making something good, which they sure tried, maybe focusing more on the contracts for my taste, but not a bad game overall, had my share of cool moments and laughs with it.
Enjoy.

My first review on Steam, and it's a negative.
Don't misunderstand me: Ori and the Blind Forest: DE is a great game (Buy it if you don't own the Original). However, having played the original Ori, and having had to pay 5€ on top, I was disappointed by this re-release. If I could rate the upgrade separately from the game, I would. But this isn't possible since they decided to re-release the old game, with some content on top, and I mean literally on top:  They just found a location on the map that was still empty, and added the new content there. The devs claim they wanted to integrate the new content in the world we already knew. Nonsense! I completed the game without even touching the new content, and IF I DIDN'T KNOW THERE WAS ADDITIONAL CONTENT, I'D NEVER HAVE SEEN IT. I had to search for it on the map for a while. When they say "integration into the 'old' world" they mean "we also changed 2 puzzles to make use of the new abilities". And that's it. I was completely disappointed by this upgrade, I was expecting way more for a Definitive Edition that is also a new game on Steam. If they just made it DLC, I would have been fine with it, but this way? No. (Also, the month delay with no communication Microsoft and the devs helped form this review.)

This version takes everything that made the original Ori and the Blind Forest the best game of 2015 and takes it up to 11.  The new areas are a lot of fun, and they add even more to the already sad/tragic story.  This game finally dethrones Super Metroid as the best 2D Metroidvania game.  It is definitely on the difficult side, if you aren't very good at platform games this may not be your thing.  Unlike similar games like Guacamelee though, this game is exploration/platforming focused and not combat focused, so there aren't lots of combos...attacking things is one button and very simple (which is the way I like it in a Metroidvania).  The new easy difficulty for beginners should help with the issue the original game had of being very difficult if you aren't basically an expert at Metroidvania/platform games, so...even if you aren't an expert at platform games it's still worth a try.  All in all, this makes an already amazing game even better, and I can't recommend it enough.  I think this game is worth easily double what they are asking for it, and it already has my vote for GOTY 2016.

Mad Max is an action-adventure video game based on the Mad Max franchise. Developed by Avalanche Studios and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment, it was released for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One in September 2015. Feral Interactive published the game's OS X and Linux versions.
It is set in an open post-apocalyptic wasteland consisting of deserts, canyons, and caves. Players control Max Rockatansky as he progresses through the wasteland to seek revenge on a gang of raiders, led by Scabrous Scrotus, who robbed him of his possessions, and along with his assistant Chumbucket, he aims to build the ultimate car: the Magnum Opus. Mad Max emphasizes vehicular combat, in which the player uses weapon and armor upgrades on their car to fight enemies, while on-foot combat combines professional wrestling attacks and boxing techniques. The game features extensive car and character customization, and soft boundaries, also known as the "Big Nothing."
Two other Mad Max games, developed by Cory Barlog and Interplay Entertainment respectively, were in production before the announcement of this game, but neither of them were successfully released. Although Mad Max is not based on the film series, it was inspired by its universe, and franchise creator George Miller was consulted during the game's pre-production. Avalanche Studios found developing a vehicular-combat video game a challenge because of their inexperience with creating that type of game. Announced at the 2013 Electronic Entertainment Expo, the game was re-tooled during development and the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 versions were canceled.
Originally planned for release in 2014, it was released in September the following year, several months after the theatrical release of Mad Max: Fury Road, the fourth film in the series. Mad Max received mixed-to-positive reviews from critics. Although the game's environment, direction, vehicular combat, and graphics were praised, its quest design and story were criticized. The game became the eighth best-selling retail game in the US in September 2015.
Gameplay:
Mad Max is a post-apocalyptic action-adventure game emphasizing vehicular combat, in which the player is the eponymous Mad Max (Bren Foster). According to its publisher, up to 60 percent of the game focuses on driving. Some weapons and tools, including flamethrowers and turbo boosts, are mounted directly onto the Magnum Opus, while others, such as a grappling hook and sniper rifle, are used in conjunction with the vehicle by Chumbucket, Max's assistant, or Max himself. Max's Magnum Opus, with its V8 engine and powerful ramming ability, can destroy enemies' vehicles and weaponry. When simultaneously driving and aiming, the game changes to slow motion to allow the player to toggle between targets. Although Mad Max primarily uses a third-person perspective, the player can switch to first-person view when fighting enemies while driving the Magnum Opus. Chumbucket repairs the car when instructed to do so or when the player exits.
To encourage exploration, the Magnum Opus can be upgraded with materials scavenged from the desert, by hijacking enemies' cars or collecting their car parts. An enemy can jump on top of the Magnum Opus to make it explode, but the player can avoid that by surrounding the car with hazards such as spikes. The player can access the garage screen throughout the game, allowing them to customize the Magnum Opus. Max's garage can change and modify the car's engine, chassis, wheels, body work, paint job, and its "shell". Upgrading one aspect of the car will negatively affect other aspects; upgrading the engine will allow Max to drive faster, but handling will be more difficult. The sound produced by the engine changes when players change, add, or remove parts of the Magnum Opus. Max, his armor, and weapons are customizable; the player can unlock new skills and upgrades for him as he progresses through the game and earns experience points. Max is also customizable, with his clothing, appearance, fighting skills, and weapons being modifiable. Griffa, a wasteland wanderer, also offers Max tokens which can be used to upgrade his abilities.
Although the game has many choices (such as playing stealthily or aggressively), it emphasizes action over stealth. Mad Max features a variety of weapons, including Max's iconic shotgun, but ammunition is scarce and the game emphasizes melee combat over firearms. One weapon is the explosive Thunderstick, which can be lanced into an enemy's chest. The game has a free-flow combat system combining professional wrestling attacks and boxing techniques, similar to Warner Bros.' previous Batman: Arkham video-game series (in which indicators on enemies' heads remind the player when to strike, counter or make finishing moves). Attacks by Max during his "frenzied" state are more powerful than usual.
Mad Max's landscape consists of canyons, caves, deserts, and abandoned wastelands. The game's world is divided into several regions, with each having its own backstory and landscape. Unique landmarks and ruins can be discovered in each region. Side activities such as races, time trials, invading enemy fortresses, and eliminating enemy convoys can be found in each region. A region's threat level is lowered by completing these activities, facilitating its navigation. Each region has a boss, who can be found and defeated in their base. Some of the game's strongholds are friendly, and eliminating hostile strongholds gives Max additional quests and rewards. These strongholds can be upgraded, offering Max different benefits such as helping Max to collect scraps when the game is turned off, or restoring Max's health and shotgun ammo upon visits. Max can ascend in a hot-air balloon (permanently attached to the ground) to look for new objectives and locations. After seeing the objectives through binoculars, they are highlighted on the map. Max can be guided by Chumbucket in strategically completing his objectives. Max is accompanied by a dog companion called Dinki-Di, who can help players detect land mines. Max has limited climbing abilities, and objects that he can climb are highlighted in yellow.
Most resources in the game are scarce except for gasoline, which is needed for driving. The player can collect one jerrycan at a time, storing it in the back of the Magnum Opus, and can find collectibles (history relics) throughout the game. The relics are primarily photos and notes of the wasteland before the apocalypse. Food and water are vital to Max's survival; the player can collect them in the wasteland and use them to replenish their health. Max can also eat small animals, such as rodents, and maggots from decomposing corpses, to replenish his health, and areas where he can find food and supplies have crows flying around them. The player can venture into the Big Nothing, an uncharted, volatile area of the wasteland with dangerous sandstorms and no food or water in which rare parts for the Magnum Opus can be found. According to Avalanche, due to the "Big Nothing", the game's map is infinite. A dynamic day-night cycle, a weather system and a variety of environmental hazards are included in the game, whose terrain is affected by weather and natural disasters.

Sister location was announced around, 6 months ago, I believe, and has been hyped up so much that the fanbase has suddenly become a lot more active than it was before the release of the game. This review will probably get a lot of dislikes but its my honest opinion.
Sister location seems to carry over from one of the biggest critisisms from the 4th fnaf game - its just too darn difficult. Unlike the other games, this one is more of a linear story with lots of different types of puzzles in it that you have to complete, but these puzzles aren't really explained very well. For example, the night 3 puzzle of climbing through the "Funtime Foxy" room dosent really explain how to actually complete the puzzle, only that "the animationic is motion sensored", and that the flash beacon you have "Should be used as less as possible". They don't tell you that you actually have to use it too see if the animatronic is in front of you,
I actually had to look up youtube videos of the nights to understand how to complete them.
Another problem is checkpoints. If you do manage to get past one of the really hard puzzles, the checkpoints are just not very good and very scarcely placed. When I was playing through the second night, the
part was pretty easy but it took a long time, and once you got through it to the breaker room, which is actually really difficult, if you die it places you back before the room, meaning you need to slowly play through it again just because you died on some bullsh*t puzzle.
I originally intended to play through the game properly, but up untill I completely gave up at night 4, I just kept going into the games save text file and changing the night I was on because I didn't want to continue trying the same bullsh*t puzzle over and over again.
Sure, call me stupid, that im in-patient and that im just a re*ard for not being able to complete even a part of this game, but being a very long supporter of the franchise (Ive been here since fnaf 1) and, out of all my friends that also played it, was able to complete night 6 on fnaf 1 and 2, and complete fnaf 3 normally long before all of my freinds that also played, I think I would say that I am, in fact, "Smart" enough that I should be able to progress in even a small part of the game.
Not to mention the games terrible... whats the word... "steam verification"? Thats it. Most steam games would require steam to be open and logged in to play, while this game, as well as all the other fnaf games, is literally just a single .exe file that can be copied and played by anyone who dosent actually own the game. Its like the creator wanted the game to be easily pirated.
That concluded one of my first ever "Proper" Steam reviews. I hope the infomation here has helped you, and hopefully Scott, if by the slim chance he is actually reading this. If you honestly dissagree with my opinion, hit the "this didn't help me" button and tell me what I said wrong. Please don't press the button just because you don't agree with my opinion.

I took my sweet time before coming out with this review, but as we approach the end of the episodic 'season' I feel it's a good time to get my thoughts down, in preperation for the season finale.
Hitman 2016, is a source of great indecisiveness from me.
I don't want to make the biased judgement of recommending it purely because it's better than Absolution (because mark my words, it's certainly much better than Absolution).
Hitman 2016 goes back to the old Hitman franchise format, with self-contained sandbox missions. While there is an overall story, it's not pivotal to the gameplay, with only one level of the current 5 being truly influenced by the plot (although this may change in the season finale).
And in the return to the original format, with modern systems, is where Hitman 2016 shines and shines brightly:
Each mission map is expansive, varied, and busy. Packed with content and options and versatile mechanics.
The maps are larger and busier than any Hitman game prior, and they feel truly alive and breathing, taking advantage of the modern engine and processing to really fill each square inch of the maps with activity.
The combat is a compromise between the original Hitman games, and Absolution, but it does it smoothly.
It makes for an excellent assassination game, with hours and hours of replayability to occur. I'm STILL finding myself in buildings and rooms I didn't even know existed.
There are a few cons, however.
Many people have commented on the soundtrack, and I'd have to agree. The soundtrack doesn't feel as immersive or powerful as previous Hitman games, and often seems repetitive.
Also the voice cast; while I'm always ecstatically happy to hear David Bateson once again as Agent 47, NPC voice acting was often out of place, with a constant presence of American accents even as 47 travelled the globe, while it wasn't game-breaking it often kept me from fully immersing.
And I deeply miss the weapon customization options of Blood Money, although I will admit and accept that the weapon unlock system in Hitman 2016 aids a large amount of replayability to the game, and is honestly one of the main reasons I keep playing the game between episodes.
All in all, it's a solid game, and a promising return to the format we know and love.
Absolution has been forgiven for its shortcomings but it hasn't been forgotten, and the developers are making it pretty clear that they're willing to learn from mistakes.
I anticipate the season finale, and look forward to (hopefully) a second season of missions.

I'm going to reccomend this game, because:
- It excels at being a "classic hitman" game. Knock out a random waiter, grab his clothes, drop some laxatives in your target's fois gras, then sneak into his bathroom and drown him in his own faeces. Job done. Much fun.
- The level design is epic.
- The engine is very smooth.
- You can finally save whenever you want.
I do have quite a few quibbles with it, though:
- The storyline is weaker than a pornstar's sphincter. If you're expecting to rip Lenny's head off with a lawnmower in this game, look elsewhere.
- There's the occasional glitch that prevents you from quickly hiding some poor guy you just stabbed in the throat. So his mates show up, spot you hovering awkwardly above the dead body, and promptly proceed to pump you full of 9mm slugs.
- You have to be online to play!!! While it's not normally an issue, my ISP modem started crapping its pants last night while I was playing, and my gameplay was interrupted by a big, red splash screen until my internet connection was resumed. After the 4th interruption, I rage quit and made a sandwich.
- While the levels themselves are amazingly beautiful and detailed to hell and back, they aren't very original. I feel like I've played all of these before. Rich dude's mansion? Check. Crowded Maroccan market? Check. Beautiful Italian coasline? Check.
- Same story with the missions. Kill rich dude (+ model/evil mastermind wife), destroy vile of virus thingy, etc. There's nothing here that feels new and exciting.
- Where's my damn Silver Ballers?!
Yes, Absolution had its problems with regards to level design. Some were super linear and felt useless and unconnected to the storyline, while others were very open and "hitmany". But at least it had a story! And I felt involved playing it. I had fun killing all the crazy characters and having a shooting contest with the biggest pair of 3D boobs this side of anime.
Absolution was an incredibly fun and memorable game. Silent Assassin redux, if you will. This, sadly, isn't. This is more like Blood Money redux.

Okay, this is my first real review. Go easy on me
Now I really wanted this game to be good. At first I had my doubts about the episodic nature of the series, but I decided to try it out. I understand that this game has some issues, one of the being the DRM features and it was initially a ♥♥♥♥♥ to run. At least one of those issues has been solved now, and in my opinion those were the only issues of the game. Even after completing the fantastic gameplay of each episode, I crave for more, and thats why I love the replayability aspect, theres so much creativity involved with killing your targets and so many ways to do it. In addition to this I love the eposodic nature of Hitman, it's like a tv-series, it keeps my hyped for the next release, and when I get it. Oh, it is so much more special. The story although a bit fragmented by the episode format is fantastic, interesting and thought provoking. The most recent episode excited me so much for the upcoming Japan release, because it opened up so many interesting possibilities and avenues. You can really tell the developers actually put time into creating the story, to make it seem real, alive even. The story even make 47 even more mysterious, which I didn't think possible. It's like an intricate puzzle, but the puzzle pieces are given to us ever so slowly, meaning that as we get more puzzle pieces the story starts to concrete itself. Rust will never be forgotten, and it will never be at peace. I told myself I would wait to do this review, that I would let it settle, that it would one day be finished and then I could write my thoughts. Well, too much time has passed for me to wait any longer, and for some reason, today seems to be the day.
I'm not even sure now how I discovered this, "new game with a cool idea". A friend, DayZ-exploring, a flashing Steam store page, who knows. But once I installed it, and loaded it up, I had found a new, exciting video game. The music when loading was incredible, eerie and atmospheric; and this was 'alpha' music? Once I loaded into the world, an island of apparently great size, I enjoyed the experience from the start. Nature, trees, vast distances, animals, ruins, and...people.
For that is what makes Rust tick, people. The first moment, not knowing whether to hide, fight, or try to communicate, is telling, and this is a common thread. And with these first moments, come the first deaths, both expected and not. And so comes the first rule of Rust, don't trust anyone. And with this rule comes the choice you have to make, do you strive to live a solo life? Do you have Steam friends that play and can band together? Or do you try to find some team to take you in? Be ready, you are going to die, a lot.
I made a shelter, and built, and harvested, and hunted. I ventured into dangerous places and survived. Or died. In the end, it was a great experience. Then came the version changes, at first it was good, bugs were fixed. Then, they started over from scratch, and things started getting different from what made it good in the first place. It was good, then bad, then good, then bad.
The game today is worse than it was, a new thing we are seeing in games when they are made to be a service. A game with a golden age, something we used to only see in MMOs. That is why I can no longer recommend this game. I am going to give it a thumbs up, because of my experiences, and that it was worth the money I paid, but now is a different time. Rust is over for me.
Graphics:
Apart from certain updates and small periods, Rust has always looked fantastic. As they moved into Beta and the modern Rust era, the game both looks great, and takes a great system to run. It's one of the games that gets my PC as hot as it can get. Beware!
Sound:
Great music and sounds at first, but inconsistent sound production. Seemed like the staff never settled on consistant sounds/music during the process. To me, this shows a lack of focus, which has been clear from every player since the beta started. This developmental blurriness seems to coincide with when Rust had already made huge sales. Pretty much the team had success, and just went in slow-patch mode. It was less about a work of art, a work that could have defined the team of producers and developers for the rest of their lives, and more about making the project akin to updating the software in automatically flushing toilets.
Community:
It's a multiplayer game, and the community can be tight-knit if you're in good, but overall it's as toxic as it gets. The sadness with Rust comes from both the community and the developers. Nobody is happy, ever. This has bred conflict between players I've never witnessed before. In short, Rust has the worst community of players I have ever seen, and the clear lack of maturity in most players is almost depressing.

Do you like platformers?  Then you should buy Super Meat Boy, full-stop.
The controls are quite responsive and precise.  The level design is also really great, with plenty of variation.  Mechanics are added to keep things fresh-ish, and the length of each level feels tuned just right. The time-trial and item hunting increases replayability considerably; 100%'ing this game is no easy feat.
This game can induce old-school controller throwing with how frustrating it can be to miss a jump for the umpteenth time.  However, when you do manage to cleanly clear a level, you feel like a platforming badass.  It's great.
The only major gripe is that the game seems pretty dependent on the sprint function (at least for the first character), which can lead to finger fatigue from death-gripping the trigger button.
And yes, I'd agree with the warning sign the game gives you on start-up -- a controller is a necessity to enjoy this game fully.

This game is really _really_ hard and unforgiving. You die at least 20-50 times before you manage to complete a single level. There's instant death everywhere. Unlike it might seen at the first glance, this game is not about ultra-human reflexes. This game is about die countless times, slowly finding an optimized way of overcoming the obstacles, and imprinting that into your _muscle_ memory. If you buy this, prepare some strong language in advanced and a lot of free time. But hey, it's so much fun.

A server is a system (software and suitable computer hardware) that responds to requests across a computer network to provide, or help to provide, a network service. Servers can be run on a dedicated computer, which is also often referred to as "the server", but many networked computers are capable of hosting servers. In many cases, a computer can provide several services and have several servers running.
Servers operate within a client-server architecture, servers are computer programs running to serve the requests of other programs, the clients. Thus, the server performs some task on behalf of clients. The clients typically connect to the server through the network but may run on the same computer. In the context of Internet Protocol (IP) networking, a server is a program that operates as a socket listener.[1]
Servers often provide essential services across a network, either to private users inside a large organization or to public users via the Internet. Typical computing servers are database server, file server, mail server, print server, web server, gaming server, application server, or some other kind of server.[2]
Numerous systems use this client / server networking model including Web sites and email services. An alternative model, peer-to-peer networking enables all computers to act as either a server or client as needed.
The term server is used quite broadly in information technology. Despite the many server-branded products available (such as server versions of hardware, software or operating systems), in theory any computerised process that shares a resource to one or more client processes is a server. To illustrate this, take the common example of file sharing. While the existence of files on a machine does not classify it as a server, the mechanism which shares these files to clients by the operating system is the server.
Similarly, consider a web server application (such as the multiplatform "Apache HTTP Server"). This web server software can be run on any capable computer. For example, while a laptop or personal computer is not typically known as a server, they can in these situations fulfill the role of one, and hence be labelled as one. It is, in this case, the machine's role that places it in the category of server.
In the hardware sense, the word server typically designates computer models intended for hosting software applications under the heavy demand of a network environment. In this client–server configuration one or more machines, either a computer or a computer appliance, share information with each other with one acting as a host for the other[s].

Which means everybody will experience something different but it makes it also replayable to see what you missed out and what would off happened if you would off choosed something else, a little bit like the Tell Tale Games.
Another new thing which was new introduced into the Call of Duty Campaign Series was that before each Mission Starts you can choose your own class almost like you do it in Multiplayer, which makes the game more fun and leaves you more choices.
The Multiplayer is one of the best games that got released and is so far one of the last call of dutys that is still playable. The Settings have a native FOV Slider that goes up to 90 and also have Borderless Fullscreen Mode which is for me personally important with 2 screens. There is also a ping filter where you can decide to what kind of people you would like to connect for example would you rather play with 300 ping or with 30? Its up to you. Also this game is one of the only games that has dedicated servers.
There are 5 standard classes already unlocked and with each prestige you can get another one (up to 10 classes). With each Prestige comes also a permanent unlock tocken, which means if you prestige and your favourite weapon is for example going to be unlocked at level 50, you can permanently unlock it right away. Everytime you prestige your guns stay the same level, keep their cammos and attachments unlike Moderen Warfare 3 where you lose everything. Which makes it easier to get gold cammos or diamond cammos.
You can get diamond Cammo which is another first for the Call of Duty Series, if you want to get diamond guns you have to go through all the challenges for one class for example the smgs, once you got all gold, the diamond cammo will be unlocked. Those Challenges are alot of fun to do. So if you ever get bored of just brainlessly killing people or you like games where you can work towards something than you should try this out.
The Zombie Mode comes by default with 1 Map the Bus Depot you can buy more maps by purchasing the DLC or the Season Pass. The Zombie Mode itself is fair and has good graphics, sometimes it can be a bit glitchy but 99,9% of the time you won't find anything wrong with it. The Graphics are amazing and there is as well as in Number 1 always a hidden Song. You can complete the Bus Depot Map on your own or together with a friend (I recommend 2 people). The Story is really facinating and I hope it is going to continue in Number 3.
But you do not have to play the Story on Zombies, you also can play turned, where you fight as a zombie against your friends and Survival where you are just in one spot and can see how many rounds you will make it until the zombies finally got you.
The Singleplayer should be easy to complete.
The Multiplayer is also easy to complete as long as you have a good team to play in the League Mode.
The Zombie Mode will require alot of work and is rather hard to do. Mostly you won't be able to do it on your own, so for some maps you will need up to 4 people with good communication possibilitys.
All in all, this game is wonderful. Yes I know there is a few cheaters in the multiplayer, but unlike other games you can record or even make pictures and send your proof + steam id of the cheater, to the actuall developers and they will ban the cheater.
See also my Guide:
Due to the fact that this is one of the only games that have dedicated servers and Developers that still banning people it is playable and can be still alot of fun. Another important thing I forgot to say is, that it is very well optimised and I had no problems running it whatsoever on max graphics. It also supports 120fps screens. Personally this is my favourite Call of Duty so far.

Sister Location is very different from other FNaF games; it's a lot better. It puts in even more atmosphere, which is a must for me in a horror game. If I'm not twitchy out of fear about what is going to jump out of the dark at the calmest part, then it isn't all that fun. And I was, I am. Crawling through each room was TERRIFYING. The breaker reset was a freaking anxiety attack ready to happen. Fixing the bots could make you a nervous wreck.
And Baby talking to you through the whole thing? Creepy. Creepy, creepy, creepy.
One big Pro for me is there is no longer a timer each night. You're given a task and once you complete it, the night is over. So there wasn't any undue pressure which allows you to get more into what you're doing and what's going on.
The comedy bits were gold. It was nice to have a bit of a comedic edge here and there to take the edge off, haha.
Considering I have played horrendous horror games at a MUCH higher price tag, FNaF: SL is getting a thumbs up from me; FNaF has always been a gem and it's only getting better.

Of the 11 hours I have currently spent on this game, I'd say I enjoyed myself for about 8 of those hours.  I'll get to why in a bit.  I will be spoiling one of the endings.
I will say this to start off:  This is very unlike all of the other core-series FNaF Games.  It does not follow the standard "defend your little room from 12 AM to 6 AM without leaving" gameplay style.  It is very story driven, and, as I'm sure, not what anyone was expecting.  Each night, you are assigned a different task.  There are very few occasions where you can branch off from the route that takes you to where the task is meant to be completed.  When you do explore these areas you aren't supposed to, however, there are some interesting secrets to be found.  There are only two times it reverts back to the room-defense style.  The first time (and the reason why I only consider 8 of the 11 hours worthwhile,) is on night 4.  The second time is
There are plenty of hidden bits of lore and easter eggs to keep you searching for a while if you're the kind of person who likes to do that.
There are three gripes I have with this game, though.  The first being that it is almost too linear.  The two times I listed that you could explore off the beaten path are, as far as I know, the only times you can do this.  When you die, you have to start over from a certain point earlier in the night (usually before the the parts where you have to avoid the animatronics,) and do it all over again.  As I said, the game is very story driven, so there wasn't much of a way around this with a 2D Engine.  The second flaw is night 4.  It requires lightning-fast reflexes (even post 1.02 patch,) and is a little harsh.  I understand that it's near the end, but it still seems a bit much, especially because of the general ease of night 5 (if you're not exploring.)  The third and final gripe is the comedy.  Don't get me wrong, I loved some of the jokes, but as someone on the forums said, it makes it seem like a better Portal game than a FNaF game.  It takes away from the creepy, ramshackle, malfunctioning vibe to the place.
In conclusion, if you can handle the linearity, are willing to explore, and feel that you can bull through night 4, I'd recommend this.  It has an engaging plot and brings more interesting mysteries to the table.  If you want to introduce youself to the FNaF series, I recommend the first game.  It's got the best atmosphere, it's the cheapest out of all the core-series, and, if it were left as a single game, the story could've still stood on its own very well.

There are a few reasons to recommend this game (It's novel and fun at first, if you're into planning and optimizing) and many reasons not to (Bugs, poor design decisions, it's far too easy/lacks complexity, it's not yet finished but "released" from EA, balancing issues, ...).
I originally planned to write a detailed review, expanding on each issue, but decided against it as to not steal focus from the one big reason I'm writing this non-recommendation:
Prison Architect produces a heavy CPU load to calculate its simulations, or the AI decisions of the game's agents. Unfortunately, it isn't multi-core capable and will only use two threads. This results in significant FPS and simulation speed decreases as the number of agents increases.
My current prison - which I'm stubbornly completing despite it having become a major chore - holds 300 prisoners, employs around 350 staff, has slowed down to around 12-15 FPS and a proportional simulation speed decrease while idle, and a nigh unplayable 5-6 FPS while building my next cell block of 100 cells. System: i7 5930k, @2800MHz RAM.
To put things into perspective: There are achievements for holding 500 and 1'000 prisoners respectively. The achievement here being patience and a tolerance for slideshows, of course.
Which brings me to my next, and final point. As other games have proven, it's perfectly possible to have an agent based simulation maintain a smooth, stable simulation speed for most of the game's situations even without multi-core capabilities. The trick is to have a difficulty-induced softcap on the total number of agents the system has to handle. In PA, it's ridiculously easy to keep hundreds (or thousands) of prisoners' needs fulfilled. Once you have the money to build all the necessary facilities, you would need to purposely mismanage your prison for anything "interesting" like riots to have a chance of happening. If it weren't for the need to occasionally and manually check for and remove tunnels, or watch out for tagged snitches among new arrivals, you could run the game on full autopilot for days and the only thing that would have changed once you return would be your account balance.
Prison Architect has (had) a lot of potential, but sadly, I cannot recommend it in its current state (A sentiment that should be reserved for Early Access reviews). Stay away from this (for now) unless you plan on only building tiny prisons, have a lot of patience, don't mind slideshows and screen tears, or have hypothreaded your CPU down to two virtual cores.

This is wordy, but I'm hoping to win you over, dear reader. There are experiences worth having in this game. Both good and bad. This game will evoke emotion, thought, and more than a little introspection if you dig into it. I struggle to think of what else I can say to emphasize that this game is worth sticking with. So I'm going to try to tell my own tale of disinterest, in the hopes that maybe you'll relate and choose to press on anyway. Spoiler free.
I lost interest before the second "real" boss the first time I picked this up. It just didn't really grab me. The humor was a little cheesy, but it had it's moments. I enjoyed the combat, but it turned into a chore thanks to the random encounters. I'd discover the "solution" to the fight but end up forced to repeat it over and over as I pressed forward. It was a charming game, but ultimately kinda easy and repetitive. It just felt like a slog between often overly cutesy character moments. So I put it down shortly after the first "real" boss.
Some time later, I gave it another shot for a lark. I pushed onward and made it to the second major boss. And got my♥♥♥♥♥destroyed. The kitten mittens were off and the game felt like it had hit it's stride. From that point onward the game had me. And it also slowly took on more depth. I didn't stop until I hit the true "good" ending that day. That experience alone made this game something special. But it wasn't done yet. Later on I came back to check out the "bad" ending. That was not a single sitting affair. That might have been one of the hardest things I've ever done in gaming. In multiple ways. But again, that experience is incredible.
So yeah. Almost off handedly dismissed one of the most memorable games I've ever played. Your mileage may vary, but I implore you to stick with it. Get that "true" ending. And, if you've got the determination, make it through the "bad" ending. If only so you can see what a real hero looks like.

If you are here, then it's because you REALLY like simulators, like this one. Well, the word "simulator" is very deep, actually: and I'm not sure, since I've never driven a truck in real life, whether this can actually be considered a simulator.
So, the main goal in this game is driving a truck with a trailer, earn money, buy new trucks, give them to your hired drivers and earn a lot of money that you can't possibly spend even if you change truck every in-game day at a certain point. So, that's it: then why have I more than 500 hours on record? Well, the idea of being in a truck, being on the streets, is actually awesome. You can drive a monster Volvo FH with a 750 HP engine, or a very little Mercedes Benz 1519 with a cute 140 HP engine. You have thousands of kilometers of streets, a good part of Europe indeed.
And then there are mods. With mods you can literally change this game. In fact, I am currently running this a realistic physics simulator, some sound mods, some custom trucks, some custom maps: in fact, it is a custom game.
One thing to notice though: map is heavily scaled down, with a ratio of about 1:19 for streets outisde cities and 1:3 for streets inside cities. That is, when you have driven 1 km from a real life point of view (time and space), you have actually done 19 kilometres in the game.
I like very much the idea that is behind this game; I love it so much that I am planning to build a new simulator from scratch, more realistic, more... well, more like I would like it.
The main things I don't like in this game are in fact the scaled maps, the unrealistic physics and the fact that there are little buttons/switches/sticks with which you can interact inside the vehicle. You can use your wipers, your blinkers, switch on and off the lights, use the retarder, use the brake engine, check the board computer, the parking brake and of course brake, accelerate and steer... but what about all those tiny switches on the dashboard, like the air conditioner settings, and all those typical truck stuffs?
For many aspects you can, indeed, use mods to provide a lot of things. Full-scale maps are an example, but it takes months of works, and I still don't like the result. The graphics looks old and the game engine is not so optimized, so you really have to be careful about how many objects you place in a map.
For the rest, I really strongly recommend you this game. One advice, though: stay away from American Truck Simulator. It is, in fact, a copy of ETS2 made in America, with american trucks, with even smaller maps, that really look ridiculous compared to real places. And another advice: be sure to have a very powerful computer if you want to enjoy this game in the best way possible.

After 100% achievements:
If you are like me and have played your fair share of tower defenses then maybe you have played Creobit's earlier games: "Royal Defense" and "Fort Defense"? Those predecessors were mediocre games with crappy mobile phone UI with no keyboard shortcuts, tedious star grinding and absolutely no new ideas at all. The games weren't awful mind you, just very generic.
This time around the UI and graphics looks good, great even. It's very stylish, colorful and follows a nice theme. But except for the nice assets you'll very soon realize that it's actually the very same ♥♥♥♥♥♥ UI all over again, only re-skinned. The mostly uninspired upgrades are identical to previous games and even the achievements are the same. Doesn't bode well but what the heck, as long as the gameplay is decent right?
The first few minutes had me really worried. The first thing you'll notice is that tower-range has been thrown out the bloody window(!!). Instead there nothing but floor-plates that the creeps walk over and take damage. In my mind, this takes away tons of complexity and leave you with very choice as for what tower should go where. This is especially true since towers can only be mounted on pre-defined locations.
The second thing that boggled my mind was the damage abstraction. You now have 4 color towers (or elements) where each color beats another color. There's even a small diagram visible at all time for you to look at. It seems convoluted. It also doesn't help strategy that you don't know what waves will come ahead of time.
But to my surprise it actually works out pretty good. It definitively has a focus on action over strategy. The tower balance feels pretty good and the timing on some waves can make things turn rough and interesting. It's truly a shame they did nothing about UI, progression and upgrades. But all in all the game is an original.
It's a much, much better game than it's predecessors. It's shorter, not only fewer campaigns but also less grindy. The game is still far from great (I like strategy over click-frenzy), but this time I'm left intrigued with what kind of tower-defense Creobit can come up with next.
I would recommend this game at half price.

So far so good.  I only have an hour of playtime and I like it so I'm posting a tentative positive review (subject to change).
Elemental combat.  I've never seen that in a tower defense game before.  It's an interesting twist.  And instead of a long line of the same enemy type followed by a line of a different enemy type, as all the other TD games I've played do, this game has mixed groups of different enemy types attacking at the same time.   That means you have to have a variety of traps from the beginning, instead of just a basic type first then add different types later as you get more money from kills.  So far I have not seen anywhere that it tells you what enemies are coming up, which is unforunate since I have had to quickly sell traps in order to buy ones I need for an enemy.
Fire, Ice, Earth, and Shadow (no Air element underground, I guess).  Some enemies can be defeated by two different elements and they have defense against their own element (you see a shield icon appear when they pass over it).  For instance, skeletons take more damage from ice traps but less from earth ones.  Ice enemies are defeated by fire traps, obviously.  There's also a money trap which gives you more money and damages a little (it's a shadow trap).
Magic spells.  In addition to traps there are also recharging magic spells, like a rock fall or a time freeze.  These recharge over time or you can pay to get them instantly.
In between battles you can upgrade your skills.  You can choose what you want to upgrade, the trap damage, trap cost, income from kills, initial gold upon start, magic spells.  Each trap has two aspects you can upgrade.  Obviously in the mobile version they want you to pay real money to upgrade faster.  In the Steam version you don't have that option (and I wouldn't even if I could!) so you might have to grind a little or just play smarter.
Graphics style is okay.  I like it, but you can see screenshots and decide for yourself.
Music and sound effects are not the best but okay.  So far there's only been one background track during battle.  I hope there are more otherwise it will get repetitive and annoying.
More later...

This game really tickles my Hitman fancy in a big way.
I've been in love with the franchise since the first game, and while not every game has been great, this one absolutely is.
Voice acting is superb, pacing is great, guard AI is competent and missions are relatively varied.
The episodic format is absolutely perfect for this game, as the overall story arc isn't needed to carry the game. The missions are pretty much self-contained.
The graphics are superbly done. Artfully understated, with excellent texture work and very good models.
Runs smooth as butter on my rig, and I haven't really heard any complaints from any of my friends either.
Considering the market in Marrakesh, for example, has thousands of simulated people, this is a monumental achievement. It feels like a part of a city, not a game level. The attention to detail in the level design is simply staggering.
For an entry fee of €13 to give it a try on Episode 1, it's almost silly value for money, and once you get your feet wet, as it were, you will have no qualms about the €8 missions.
It's a gigantic harddrive hog, though. Holy moly does it spread out! It eats disk space like a poorly optimized MMO, for crying out loud!
My guess is that this is because the thousands of hours of NPC dialog. There is so much to learn from guards chatting, random passers by discussing what is going on and, of course, multiple sets of reactions to what you're doing.
For example, in Sapienza, I took out one of two human targets, which caused his bodyguards to search for their employer throughout the mansion, talking to other staff to see if they had seen him.
It's always well voiced, and as with the rest of the sound in this game it's always appropriate for the setting.
For example, there is an intern in the Swedish consulate on the phone with a furniture manufacturer, trying to get help assembling a chair. It's hilarious, without detracting even a little bit from the seriousness of the game.
Things like that elevates this from a pretty good game to an excellent one. The episodic thing had me on the fence for a bit, but now I'm a firm believer.
I'm currently only about 10 hours in, but I have a feeling this game will keep me coming back for *months*.
"Do you recommend this game?", Steam asks. Oh, absolutely.

This may very well be the best game in the Hitman series. The levels are huge, and each one is filled with myriad intertwining stories, so many that you can't possibly observe all of them in a single playthrough.
For example, just the first mission we see: a fashion designer who's blackmailed into working a corporate gig against his will; a journalist who compromises her values and puts herself and her friend in great danger to save her website and take down a corrupt businessman; a reporter who's ready to make her big break, but only if she can get a new camera; and all of this is in addition to and intertwined with the main plot of the level, which features a fashion show that's really a cover for an illegal auction held by an international spy ring.
Each of the game's huge levels is filled with stories like this, and enough branching gameplay paths to make your head spin. There are five full missions (and two smaller but still free-form training missions) released as I write this, and each of those missions could easily give you 10 hours of gameplay if you want to really see an experience it all, completing all the challenges.  If you take into account the player created contracts the replay value becomes essentially endless.
This is all put in a package with some of the best graphics I've ever seen on PC. I've read some users complaining about performance problems, but with graphics this good, it makes sense that you need a high powered PC to get the most out of the game.   Another complaint I've seen is about the episodic release structure.  I was put off by this at first too, but in truth, it actually works fairly well with the game. The wait in between levels encourages players to really dive in and explore everything the levels have to offer, and so far Eidos has done an excellent job of following its release schedule, so the full game should be ready in no time, but the levels released already have enough content on their own to make this experience worth the price of admission.

With the episodic release method I was worried for awhile the game wouldn't measure up, but now that most of the levels are released I can say it's a totally worthy addition to a great franchise. In fact, it's one of the best of the series.

Overall I personally find the game has more positive than it does negative going for it. Ultimately what pushed me to easily recommend this game is the amount of satisfaction I have from playing it.
What struck me the most is that I was able to play this game and just have fun!  It’s nice to have a game that isn’t about grinding something out and is just enjoyable.
There are a few negatives however, and I will list them for completeness as for some people it may be a deal breaker. But whole-heartedly, these issues I think are overshadowed by the fun to be found.
############
The only technical issue I experienced with the game was a bit of weak support for GSync. A lot of gamers don’t bother with this, but I do not like screen tearing so I do use this in all my games!
Basically, I found that VSync was not applied at all using “Exclusive Fullscreen” (thousands of FPS in menus). However in just “Fullscreen” (which really is borderless windowed mode), it was fine but uses whatever HZ you set for your desktop.
This one is hard to explain. It’s a rather specific issue; many people might not care, but this was something that I noticed and for me it broke the immersion a little. I ignore it as best as I can but I wish they did it better.
I am specifically referring to the hit-scanning and view angles when you have a weapon drawn; an issue that is specific to 3rd person. I will try to use an example to explain the issue:
Imagine having a perfectly central over the head view from behind your character who is standing directly behind a pillar. On the other side of the pillar there are 2 objects that you CANNOT see from this view. You draw out your pistol in your right hand and the view shifts slightly to the right onto a centralized crosshair. Because of this shift you can now see the object to the right (but not the left) and shoot it. Now, without moving your character you switch the view to over the left shoulder, but the weapon remains in the right hand. Suddenly you are able to see the left object which was previously invisible AS WELL as shoot it, while the object on the right is hidden again.
I think this inconsistency could be easily resolved by having Agent 47 shift the gun from one hand to the other depending on which shoulder your view is over. This could then be passed as ‘peaking that side’ and would not (at least for me) break immersion by what I could only characterise as a rather magical bullet.
While this is not really a big deal, I did feel like it was missing for some reason. Perhaps I have been playing too much MGS?
For me this is not really an issue as I did not buy the game on release, so as of now there are plenty of story missions, challenges, contracts and online content to keep me occupied until the last several missions become released.
For some people, not having the complete game from the get-go is a deal breaker, so do be warned.
Honestly, it’s not really an “issue”, perhaps just a personal peeve.
Specifically, when dumping bodies, it is a, admittedly very short, ‘cinematic’ experience, reminiscent of Deus Ex: HR melee. It’s really toned down which is great, and the melee is completely unaffected by this thankfully! But I just wish they would do away with it from all their games. I am not a fan of the camera shift and game state pause.
Unfortuantely, there's a couple here.
You may “occasionally” come across a situation that makes you realise there’s really no rush. While I do not intend to suggest that missions should be timed, I want to point out that unless interrupted specifically, your targets will take set ‘circular’ paths… Forever.
Only noticeable if you take an extended period of time to complete a mission though.
Additionally, there are situations that can make you go "huh?". The targets and guards can be a little TOO non-chalant sometimes. If you kill 1 target publicly, the other target isn't always automatically taken into lock-down.
And while NPC's do react to public deaths, their reactions are sadly only temporary, and they are right back to their routine... Cops, SWAT, etc, never arrive after a gun fight for example. The map 'state' is not permanently changed after a public event, like you might expect in real life. REALLY unfortunate.
############
############
Each map is rather alive. There are many NPCs floating around, all with seemingly individual personalities rather than “copy/paste”. At least the illusion is thus even if it is not true.
You will experience this mostly by way of opportunities. Listen in and take steps to start and propagate a chain of events that may or may not be in your favour. Fantastic, inventive and fun ways to divert your targets from their ‘predefined patrol’ with a LOT of flavour.
There is definitely plenty of NPC dialogue, chatter and animation to keep it feeling immersive. You would be hard pressed to find solitary, upright, motionless guard.
This is only made more awesome by the sheer size of the maps. While if measured by a ruler they might not be that impressive on paper, when played, the amount of content and DETAIL crammed in there really adds to the scope and depth.
I play with a stock 6700K and a 980Ti from an SSD @1440p. The load times are quite decent and the game runs quite smoothly. I have NOT experienced a single crash and I have not noticed any significant glitches either.
Plus, the game looks fantastic. The art, lighting and colours are spot on. The surround sound is done well, I never found that voices were too soft at specific angles like some other games.
To me this is important. The difficulty isn’t just a choice between “easy, normal, hard”. You are given the option to manipulate each specific game mechanic that can affect difficulty. An example is the mini-map, have it on, off, or on without NPC blips, show only targets, etc.
So you can give yourself the challenge you want without sacrificing things you would consider “quality of life”.
I think the challenges are fantastic. For me at least, being new to the game, they are a great way to help me along my way and add content. They are split up quite nicely from very specific to rather general and open-ended.
Each challenge guides you to a new way to complete the mission and experience a whole new amount of fun by giving you ideas on how to eliminate your targets in ways you may not have come up with on your own.
############
What more can I say?
I think the game speaks for itself. I really do think it’s a well built and most importantly, really fun game. Perhaps the genre might not be for everyone, and sure there are things that I would personally like to have seen improved or changed… but when you look at the picture as a whole there’s definitely a little gem here.
I bought it at full price and I would do it again if needed.

If you love open world games you'll most likely enjoy the unique environment and gameplay of this game. It's both fun and unique to have a car (that you can upgrade) as a one of the primary forms of combat. The game is a bit short compared to most other open world games. I have ~35 hours as of this review and cleared everything except for the challenges (I have all but 1 achievement). But, the shorter game is probably for the best since the desert does get a little bit old after a while, no shock there, right? I think the game is just the right length that the visuals don't lose their appeal. Any longer and it probably would have gotten pretty old, pretty fast. There isn't much to say for the story. If you've watched the first Mad Max movie, there are some homages to it, but there isn't much of a story otherwise.
Overall, it's a very fun game as far as gameplay goes, but with a story that lacks much depth. I personally found the comments on the relics the be more interesting than the main story because they give you the backstory of the game in a way that lets you imagine how events unfolded.
So, to sum up:
1) Fun gameplay
2) You get to beef up your car to make combat more effective
3) Short, shallow story
4) Shorter game, but probably for the best
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game to a friend, especially if it was on sale, but even at the current full price of $20 I think it's worth it.

I will echo what so many have already said: This game deserves so much more than it got.
One thing I'm surprised I haven't seen more of is a comparison between the game and Apocalypse Now.  Some might say Heart of Darkness is where the comparison lies, and that's true too.  But I also think that Conrad's novella works best as a premise or setup.  I don't know anyone who actually enjoys the writing.  It's the story.  It's the events that transpire that are so captivating and haunting.  (I personally don't find Conrad's writing very good.  Maybe I'm too American, because I'll take Melville or McCarthy any day.)  And that's how Coppola approached Apocalypse Now.  It's not an adaptation of the book, it's a recontextualizing of its premise.  And that's exactly what Yager and Darkside did with Spec Ops.
And I should give a nod to the voice talent who performed it all: Nolan North, Jake Busey, Christopher Reid, and Omid Abtahi really shine.
I picked up on the Heart of Darkness/Apocalypse Now thing right away with a primary military character being named Konrad and his connection to a deposed, somehow boundaryless warzone.  If you're at all familiar with the source material you can figure out where it goes from there.  You've got to find Konrad, and fight your way through a lot of ambiguous situations.
There's no question about it.  You do ♥♥♥♥ed up things in Spec Ops.  And for me, it wasn't exactly fun.  Every time another fire fight started I thought "I don't want to kill a bunch more men."  There's plenty of dialogue and simple situations to hit home the humanity of these people your mowing down, like one of them reluctantly taking his friend's last piece of gum, just before you silently murder them.
I have never seen a videogame so effectively and honestly capture the completely non-standard experience many veterans have in combat, and the fog of war that exists in every single violent political conflict.  I understand the game has four potential endings.  The one I got wasn't very pretty.  But it felt completely reasonable, if not inevitable.  So impactful, in fact, I can't see myself going back to this game any time soon.  I know I will eventually, but the emotional impact of it is still too strong to try and repeat it, or even mimic it, or even attempt to try something different.  In fact, I'll probably never play a military shooter again, least of all this game's antithesis: Call of Duty.  Spec Ops achieves such a brilliant balance between narrative and shooting.  It's not just a story.  It's certainly not just a game.
This game has actually revitalized a part of my interest in games.  We need more games like Spec Ops: The Line

I could forgive someone for thinking Undertale was Game of the Century if they knew nothing else except what they read online. Based on the overwhelmingly positive feedback, I too was ready to accept this game in my Pantheon of Favorite Games of All Time. After all, I was a huge Earthbound fan, I enjoy old school RPG's, I enjoy retro art... everything seemed to point in the direction I would love this game. Oh boy, was I wrong.
Let's get the most obvious thing out of the way, there is no exploration in this game at all. If Call of Duty is a byword for linear rollercoaster experiences full of bombastic Michael Bay set pieces, then Undertale is the Call of Duty of facepalm-inducing "lollool so random" humor. Most of the time you will walk from the left side of the screen to the right. The game doesn't need you to think, to experiment, or use strategy or anything. It simply requires you to keep walking forward and press 'A' as you scroll through endless jokes. If that's the game you want, you're in luck. For people who enjoy using their brain during gaming, this will be a boring game.
The big twist that everyone keeps hinting about "omg! If I talk about it, it will ruin the game for you!" Yeah.... it's not that big of a deal. It's clever for maybe... 5 seconds? But if you play the game with the "good" ending in mind, then you will forsake every meaningful RPG mechanic in this barebone game and you will simply play Bullet Hell... over and over.
The music was passable, the art style was wildly inconsistent and grating. In the realm of Earthbound-inspired games I honestly enjoyed Lisa 10x more than this game.
This last bit had no impact on my review whatsoever buuuut.... ♥♥♥♥ the hardcore fanbase. That is all.

Hitman™ is a return from Absolution to a different type of approach and in turn, makes the game feel very Blood Moneyish. By this, I mean, the levels feel a lot more sandboxy - there's tonnes of different ways in order to take down your targets (or whoever you want, really) and you're given additional choices to approach the level again with the introduction of "mastery", which allows you to chose where you spawn, what with, where drops are, etc. You gain mastery via completing challenges, which means whilst a single level can be completed in an hour, to truely "complete" it, you're talking about hours on hours..
Whilst instinct is back, it's tweaked a little and you can just turn it off to make the game more like the traditional games if you don't need your hand held, or you can tweak it to fit how you'd like.
There's not a lot of levels by themselves, but, as I said, the levels that are here are densely packed with♥♥♥♥♥♥to do. I like this. I might have paid too much at retail, but, I'm getting enjoyment out of it.

This episodes format does not work for me. I want a game with a (connected) story like Blood Money.
Having said that. This objectively is a good stealth game. There is a background story but it isn't as prominent as in previous Hitman games.
The quality of the episodes is alternating but on a somewhat high level. I like them - even though the only one that really stands out is the second one.
However, the controls (e.g. the inventory) still feel kind of odd. Way worse than in Blood Money. It feels like a bad console port in this regard.
tl;dr: Better than Absolution but still not great. If you like Hitman this is a viable choice though.

It's a fun game, and I got a lot of hours out of it, as you can see. The world that it takes place in is interesting. There is a lot of history to this world that is mostly revealed in bits and pieces as you explore, but I feel like they could have pushed it further.
This is supposed to be apocalyptic... wastelands... hunger... death... and so on. We're talking about people living in a world in which they dig below the sand to find old cans of dog food in the ruins to eat because they're starving, and they have never seen a body of water. It does not rain. There are no lakes, or ponds, or puddles, and there are only
, but I didn't feel that at all. It feels like a game that was made primarily for fans of the latest Mad Max movie, and not made for gamers.
The game is far too easy, particularly the melee combat after you get used to it. Melee combat is like the latest series of Batman games except with less gadgets (although the variety of enemy types is pretty good). I didn't feel threatened even when surrounded by 20 underground mole men in a dark train tunnel. It's still fun combat, but not challenging enough in most areas.
The car combat is much more interesting and intense, even dangerous, and there are a lot of upgrades you can buy for your car. There are a lot of races you can do in different cars, but that didn't interest me much. Again, this is where a higher difficulty setting would help, because the enemy racers just aren't very good.
This probably seems like a negative review, but I'm mainly just going over what I thought could be improved. I hope they make a sequel, and I hope they concentrate more on the survival aspect (or at least add higher difficulty levels).

I have been a fan of the HITMAN franchise since the PS2 era of gaming. I first played the Hitman 2: Silent Assassin demo on a demo disc my friend brought over one night to show me the game. I was astonished at how the game used a subtle approach to dispatch your target, but you also had the complete freedom to go guns blazing if you wanted.
After playing the demo I was hooked on the enigmatic Hitman, Agent 47, and I couldn't get enough. To this day, he is my top video game character and will continue to be as long as he keeps his style.
So in light of all that nostalgia, let's get to the review of the new game...
CONS:
The two main gripes most people have with this game so far is the requirement for a constant internet connection in order to play the game, and the game comes out episodically. Now, it depends on your perspective on this, but I always consider a constant online connection for a single player game a hassle for the most part. However, this game does have good online features, considering it's not a multiplayer game. As for the episodes, I personally bought the game at full price (which I RARELY do nowadays), so I just wait for the next episode to be released as I play through the past ones more and more to unlock all the weapons, disguises, starting locations, etc.
Also, as with all the Hitman games, there is a lot of trial and error within the game. Stealth is definitely encouraged and the shooting mechanics have been toned down from Absolution quite a bit. So even though you can run 'n gun, you are at a huge disadvantage in most cases.
There are many features from previous games that aren't included. They should implement the sniper briefcase back into the game for sure, along with the ability to go into First Person View mode. That was one of my favorite features in the classic games. It first showed up in Silent Assassin and lasted until Absolution.
The game runs well for the most part. I'm playing it on PC and when the first map was released, it kept crashing, but the developers seemed to have fixed this problem for the most part.
So, honestly, the two main gripes don't bother me since the development and publishing team are doing a good job actually utilizing the online features and creating some great content, even in the old maps that were released already. They are also updating the game to run better as the maps are released.
PROS:
As for the good things in the game, they are plentiful. First off, the game returns the franchise to good form, bringing back large open maps to explore with multiple targets usually. What's nice is that it seems like the developers have taken some of the great things from the previous games and brought them to this one. The Contracts mode is back from Absolution, as are many good gameplay mechanics. The "accident" kills from Blood Money make a return as well, among many other features from previous games.
The developers have added many more "common" ways to take out the targets in this new game. I say "common" because there is usually an opportunity to kill the target in this manner in every map. These common ways include gas explosions from cannisters, fire burning from oil drums, drowning, electricution, among many more. Then there are the exlcusive "accidents" that each map employs as well, which is a nice touch. I do like the new opportunity system that is used to give you hints and tips on dispatching the targets. You can turn these hints off, set it to minimal, or have the feature on full. Usually, these hints and tips are given through conversations with NPCs and a quick briefing from your handler, Diana. This feature opens the game up to many people who do not have the time or patience to play with the feature turned off, which would force you to explore the level very carefully and diligently to figure out how to truly take down the targets.
The graphics are the best I've seen so far for a Hitman game. The game is running on the Glacier 2 Engine, as was the previous game, Absolution. Where Absolution went for a more stylistic/cinematic approach in its visuals, the new game definitely goes for realism in its art design. Gone are the "glare" effects of Absolution, and the game looks more closer to Blood Money but with a huge visual upgrade, making it look great! The sound design is very well done, too. Firearms have some punch and heft to them. The voices and ambient noises within the game are very well done and if you listen to some NPC conversations, they can be quite interesting, and sometimes give you information about a target or place on the map. 47 is voiced by the returning David Bateson, which I am very pleased about. He will always be 47's voice. As for the soundtrack, I have to say I do miss Jesper Kyd. I liked Absolutions soundtrack, as it fit the story and missions very well. Also, in this game, the soundtrack fits the settings very well and has the action triggered tracks just like previous Hitman games. This soundtrack has an almost spy or James Bond feel to it in some ways, but it still does a great job changing it up map to map.
OVERALL:
The game feels like a Hitman game, pure and simple. It has many new features that work well within the gameplay, and some that should've been brought back from previous games. However, it all makes you feel like the legendary 47, and that's what it should be about. A new narrative is in place, but seems little lacking compared to the heavily story driven Absolution. However, Hitman should feel like an open experience with multiple pathways, allowing for replayability and challenge. This game has delivered that so far and I am excited to see where it goes from here.
4/5
