what most is impressive about this game is that it includes every element that the past fnafs had and some that did not, the game even being shorter than the other 4 has its own science and let me explain you why it is such a big concept for the game.
starting with the elements that were included in the last games:
the intersting part is that the game is including  all past game mechanics in difrent parts of it:
the first aspect is on night 2 where you have to sneak up on the ballora gallery to pass to the other side, the aspect in this part is listening, most likely from FNAF 4, you have to hear if its safe to advance due to hearing how close and loud her sound is, similar to fnaf 4 again.
next is the breaker room, in this place the challenge is to restart the power on all rooms in the map and at the same time control fun time freddy not to murder you by USING sound, not listening, this part is similar to FNAF 3`s mechanic of maintaning the facility and distracting springtrap with sounds but in a much easier way, it also includes a little reference of the camera function on the first 2 games, witch is nice.
next is on night 3 on the funtime auditorium you again have to pass trough the room with a flash beacon and pass to the next room, with that you need to use your flashlight to make foxy go away, very similar to the FNAF 2`s mechanic of keeping (not so coincidentaly) foxy away with your flashlight, but now you have no other light sources and you have no ♥♥♥♥ing idea what you are doing.
next part witch is probably my favourite is the mantenance room beacause it gets most of players, it first tells you to press an amount of buttons on freddy`s face to open it (sounds really weird) and when less expected a jumpscare comes out when freddy`s face opens rapidly, it uses FNAF 3`s way of jumpscaring the player without killing them, after you have to open his chest witch leads to another weaker jumpscare, you then remove some type of power template (im not sure) to deactivate him, it then tells you to do the same on the bonnie hand puppet but when you look to the left, its gone, this is my favourite moment beacause it always get people off guard and lead them in confusion and panic as they desesperatly search for bonnie, to catch him you have to point your flash to a corner of the screen and slowly raise it to the opposite side and WAIT for bonnie to slowly move up and catch him, this type of mechanic does not look familiar to any of the 4 games but if you think about it it is the FUN WITH PLUSHTRAP mechanic of waiting for your target to then catch it on the spot!
and then night 4 where you have to defend yourself against the minireenas and unluck the spring locks to escape the suit  but you also have to check both sides and keep the minirinas (those freaks) away by wiggling when they are crawling on the left or right side, sounds familiar? if it doesnt, know that this is the  FNAF 1 AND 2`s mechanic of checking and clearing two sides at the same time as you take care of important chores for your survival.
those are the only recognised game mechanics so far, now onto the aspects that were NOT present in the past games and were included in this one:
first is the humor, that is a great plus that has been lacking in the previous games and actually got a lot of people including me with ironic sitituations
another important thing that was included in this game is not having any time objective (with exeption of night 4), you can stay on the same spot forever that either you will die or nothing will happen, that way the player doesnt need to have a stress about the time left beacause they dont know when the shift will end.
next and probably the most important aspect is PATIENCE. Something that was needed for a game like fnaf. In the past 4 games, it could be noted that the played is being overwhelmed beacause they had to do things as fast as possible, if you try to rush on this game, you`ll die.
onto the downsides:
-game is too short and should be charged for a smaller amount of money
-the popcorn stuff between nights is not just badly animated but weird and desnecessary too.
-again the game is too short, maybe there could be a 6th night or somehow a chapter selection so you dont need to restart the whole game just to play that one part you wanted to.
-please make achievments for this and other fna games, they feel much more rewarding.

is a game that starts out with a lot of promise. Though the weak plot, forgettable characters, boring gameplay and repetitive ‘content’ quickly wears thin. The graphics are beautiful and it has a great art style, though it’s too busy to be atmospheric. Overall if you are looking for a shallow and repetitive open world game that you ‘could’ spend a lot of time in then
is probably pretty good but I’m mostly sick of this type of open world game.
takes place in the post apocalyptic world of the film series and set after the events of Fury Road, so it’s good to see a ‘continuation’ of the same narrative of the recent movie though I don’t think it’s the same Max. Anyway, in
your goal is to free yourself from the torment of your past and to do that Max seeks some sort of paradise or serenity at the Plains of Silence. To get there though you will need to upgrade your car so it can handle the journey, and that is basically driving force of the narrative. Along the way you meet a slew of one dimensional boring side characters and weak villains. You can complete quests for the side characters, though they are incredibly dull and have absolutely no incentive other than the limited in-game rewards. The main questline is thankfully not very long, and I completed it in ~14 hours, and with the exception of a couple of interesting missions it’s completely forgettable full of boring and uninspired tropes.
Time in
is split roughly equal between vehicle and on-foot combat. In the beginning the vehicle combat is very enjoyable, and in general the game starts off quite strong. You have a couple of interesting tools to deal damage when in the car, of which the most interesting is the harpoon gun. You can use the harpoon gun to rip parts off other cars such as wheels, doors or drivers and it’s quite fun to use, however later in the game it’s effectiveness against other vehicles is very limited because their shielding becomes ridiculous, the same applies to ramming. One of the main objectives is the upgrading of your car, and there is a lot of practical customisation here, however gathering the scrap you need to purchase the parts is a mind-numbing chore.
The on-foot combat is a lot worse than the vehicle combat. It uses an
style melee combat system with very spongy enemies. C-) While I am glad I picked up Super Meat Boy, if not just so I can say I tried it given its relatively low price, I can not recommend it to just about anyone. While there is a lot there for the makings of a good game- fun but simple music, a wacky (slightly offensive) plot, simple game design and the enjoyable feature of a simultaneously replay ( watching an army of Super Meat Boys getting destroyed simultaneously only for one to survive is certainly fascinating) the game is simple not fun. It is not fun for one single reason- it is too damn difficult. Some people might get off on a game that is punishingly difficult. I, on the other hand, can not ever see myself having fun playing the same 10-20 second level for an hour. Over and over and over and over and over again. Even with the funny replay feature it is simple not enough of a jem at the end of this agonizing trial to make it worth it. While the game does avoid long waiting times between replays (no watching the same cut scene again and again here) this is really only a bandage on a far more systemic problem. The human mind can only enjoy anything, even the must fun activity, after only so many repetitions. So for the few of you who enjoy this kind of self punishment I would maybe recommend this a try. For the rest of us  I would recommend you avoid this game.

Alright, alot of people seem to be saying this game is pay to play, which is in no way true. In fact, the ONLY things you have the OPTION of paying money for are premium(which doubles XP and money gain, which is common free game fare, and by no means required) and aesthetic items, currently colors and trails. Even without premium, it doesnt take all that long to get the money for things, a few matches, which if you do well, and the game lasts long enough(It's based off the points you get in a match) gives ~10~15k of the in game currency each, and that's without premium, which is plenty. Now, if you're not doing well enough, it can feel a bit like you're not making much, but... that's true regardless of if you paid for premium or not. not to mention you can log off for a while and come back to an idle game style money generator, which generates money even while offline till it hits 15k, at which point it stops until you collect it.
It's an interesting concept you should try, the game's graphics are really good for a free, early access game, the controls are customizeable and handles rather smoothly. I'm honestly astounded that one person managed this much for an alpha release.
Only downsides would be bugs, a wierd "matchmaking" system, the low player count(Though that may be an illusion caused by the matchmaking being wierd)
Overall, it's a free game I recommend to anyone who wants to be part of an early access game that has a good bit of potential in my opinion.

Undertale is a beautifully written masterpiece that combines Earth Bounds combat mechanics with vibrant storytelling. You play as an androgynous child who’s fallen into a unknown world of monsters that have been thought to be extinct. You must make your way through their kingdom facing many challenges along the way but the real question is how you’ll deal with the foes who lay before you? Will you kill them in self defense or because you can? Run, or try to befriend them and find more diplomatic solutions? The choice is entirely up to you.
Things I liked:
=====================
+ Brilliant soundtrack
+ Excellent storytelling and world building
+ Fun and unique battle system
+ Replayability
+ Going well beyond it’s simplistic style
+ The love the developer put into this game
+ Gave me the feels and almost made me cry. (Only two other games have done this)
+ Loveable cast of characters
+ Dogs >w>
Things I disliked:
=====================
- Genocide
- The fan base is really cringy. (Community is important, but unfortunately you’ll see a lot of weird stuff if you delve too far.)
- You’ve probably seen the game on Youtube and if you haven’t, stop reading this and buy it already!
Final Result:
=========
I’d give the game a solid 9 / 10. Easily worth your money and was a experience that will forever stick with me. I’m just grateful I went into it completely fresh without spoilers.

Hitman has always been a fantastic franchise, although I had my doubts about the high price tag when I bought the latest version.
I have to admit though, even though I only opted for the basic version that only included Paris, I've been completely blown away and have spent countless hours so far, with still more to go!
The wealth of different kills for each target are amazing, but it's the mechanics that have won this over for me.
Instead of having to kill certain enemies to obtain their gun to use, this one is based on achievements. The more you do, the higher your level, the more you unlock to use... it's that simple, and it keeps making you want to retry the mission to get the next unlock. It's a great, great way of doing things.
I think it's exceptionally clever how they're releasing the missions in stages instead of all as one game too, because it makes you focus on one particular mission before going on to the next which could be up to a month later! I've played each of the missions to death, and they're so massive that I wouldn't hesitate to play them all again.
Lastly, the two "beginner" missions are very cleverly done as well. I've spent hours on the army base one alone, just working out if I can wipe out the entire map without getting detected. Needless to say I have ;) That doesn't stop me retrying it though.
By far the best Hitman ever released, and I've owned every single one since Hitman 2. Wouldn't hesitate to recommend.

Arkham Origins is, unfortunately, sort of the black sheep of the Arkham Games. What with it not being made by Rocksteady while they worked on Arkham Knight, Origins was put out by Splash Damage Studios instead. And it is, to some degree, underrated. While Arkham Asylum was excellent and Arkham City was good, Origins falls further behind and winds up in the realm of "Better than average", but it is still decent. Everything you liked about Arkham Asylum or Arkham City is still here, mostly. The problem is that Origins somewhat coasts off the success of the Asylum and City, and suffers from a lack of any new cards to throw down.
On the gameplay front, combat has been improved once again, but it's gotten around to where it has inevitably become repetitive. And the entire map does feel somewhat lazily designed, as no less than half of it is copied over from Arkham City, right down to the Steel Mill section. Side missions are also making their return, although not quite as much of a spectacle. What is new is the crime scene missions, which are a welcome addition using Batman's crime reconstruction technology, although the number of them makes them go on a bit too long and a bit too short each to be truly entertaining. Boss fights haven't been copied, but as a result they're worse than City or Asylum and fail to do anything as impressive as the Mr. Freeze fight from City. Hunting down Deadshot and Riddler are also almost exactly the same from the previous games. Really, on the gameplay side, there isn't much to talk up. It's basically an expansion for Arkham City.
The story is where Arkham Origins finds a good place. Asylum played much more like a comic book and did quite well in its niche, but City tried to take a darker turn without changing Asylum's formula of "Villain X is doing Y. Go to location Z and beat them up", and therefore suffered for anyone who tried to take it seriously. While Origins doesn't do much to shake that up that formula, it actually explores the relationships of both Batman and one of his biggest enemies, which both its predecessors failed to do. The character arcs affect the plot much more than they did in the previous games, and so with that, Origins takes that successful dark step up that City tried to take but misstepped somewhat. The main plot thread does hop back and forth between side stories a bit too much, but it's not that noticable, and its enjoyable while it lasts. The voice actors also do a very good job filling the shoes of their predecessors, and one villain's VA who I won't mention did such a fantastic job that I didn't realize until halfway through the game that the character's actor had changed.
If you liked the previous Arkham games, you'll find pretty much everything you liked here, and maybe something you haven't seen before as well. That being said, while Origins doesn't do anything that made me want to punch the developers in the face, it didn't make me want to sing their praises either. There's nothing really new it can bring to the table, although it does make better developments in the story department by making characters more three-dimensional and making them more important to the plot. I'd pick it up on a sale if you aren't 100% convinced, but Origins isn't not worth your time, and it does no dishonor to the name of the Arkham franchise.

I love this game for its complexity. So many mechanics are thought through, and it is challenging to master them all. You have to feed, teach, punish, organise and give work to your prisoners, all while avoiding the occasional stabbing between each other or of the guards. You have to manage the architecture to get the links between the buildings right, plan the prison cells and get them a shower room.
All that without any real tutorial. You only realize that stuff is thrown over the wall from outside when your prisoners are suddenly super well stocked with tools to dig tunnels. Then they start stealing tools from elsewhere and so on. It is super rewarding to identify a problem and then get rid of it.
Only big downside is: The problems are finite, and messing up real bad is not that easy. After several hours you know the drill of setting everything up fool proof, so the discovery and solving part fades out. Then the prisoners don't really get super angry. I starved them locked in their cells in the dark without water. Two out of two hundred started beating their stuff up in the room, the rest endured it for several days.
It is still a nice build your own prison game, with good mechanics and a challenging to master system.

This game is absolutely amazing!  BEST HITMAN TO DATE!!
The game itself has gorgeous graphics, huge detailed maps, loading times and framerates are decent.
I would dare to say it's even better than Hitman: Blood Money.
Apart from the improved graphics, the controls are better.  No more dropdown selection menus to perform actions.  You can drag bodies faster.  There are more spots to hide bodies.
The AI has also been considerably improved.  This time, when a guard is alerted, all other guards aren't instantly alerted as well as in H:BM.  The other guards have to be informed about the situation first which makes it more realistic.
The world feels more alive because there are so many NPC's to interact with who have independent storylines.  So many different approaches to eliminate your targets.  So many secrets to discover in each map (some of which you may never even find).
You have "instinct" but it's nowhere near as lame as in Hitman: Absolution where you had a limited talent-meter to "blend in" for a few seconds. As if it's exhausting to hold your hand in front of your face to camouflage yourself.
This time "instinct" allows you to see people through walls and targets are marked in red which is extremely helpful to plan your next move.
There's also a professional mode you can unlock in which everything is more realistic and difficult to beat.
Yes... this season of Hitman only has 7 maps while other Hitman games have 11-20 maps each but the maps here are so much larger than any that came before.
The replayability is also very high because there are so many targets to kill and so many ways to do it in order for you to earn new unlockables to use on your next mission.
I do have some suggestions for the developers if they read this:
1) It would be interesting to have upgrades to weapons (laser, flashlight, explosive bullets, anti-recoil grip, extra unlockable inventory startup slots,...
2) Allow some weapons to shoot through doors, wooden crates, some even through concrete.
3) Maybe implement a system where bullets can ricochet off walls in order to calculate hitting your target behind the corner?
4) I would love to see a Hitman game where just about every structure is completely destructible by explosives.
5) Add multiplayer?
6) We NEED sleeping gas grenades! PLEASE!!
Anyway... please release season 2 soon and TAKE MY MONEY!!!

With game playability, realism and in-game management, I'm very pleased.
It's fun to drive, fun to deliver the goods on time, take the money, invest in better trucks and bigger garages... plenty of fun  moments to deal with.
But, if you find ETS2 world rather narrow (especially if you read the title "Euro..." and put some effort to find good mods with wider map coverage or some truck equipment mods, you can end up (as I had) with complete career loss.
When the game updates itself (and you can't do nothing about that), there's pretty high possibility that mods will not be compatible with that new version. This phenomenon is not problematic by itself. It's acceptable to some point, because mods are created by people not related to SCS and their mods behaviour isn't something that SCS should deal with. We can discuss if the editor should allow incompatibility issues with minor updates, but this is something for separate topic.
BUT, if the game itself allows you to install mods, it should allow you to fix old savegames (profiles) so you don't lose everything you gained so far, just because new game version can't work with old mod and at the same time. So, when new version can't work with old mod, it's not the worst one - you  can't load old savegame at all, because game warns you that your savegame contains some data which depending on these very mods, so you're on your own. You can play it from scratch or to give up for good, as you have no option to postpone update or downgrade if something goes wrong.
I just can't understand why SCS is unable to offer savegame update or at least clound profile data with we can import in freshly created savegame, to continue where we stopped?
OK, I'm ready to lose my beloved mods, wider coverage and better equipment, but some of them are stock and should be working.
So, I'm sorry, but this is a big dealbreaker for me.

I enjoy huge RPGs. I want to see loads of dialogue and exposition from characters around me. I like picking a class and building it in massive skilltrees. And the Ultima games are some of my favourites.
And yet Avadon falls totally flat for me. I'm finding it hard to put into words why, it's more of a build up of lots of little things.
Some of it is how utterly static the backgrounds are. There's things lying on the floor but you don't interact with them. You just press your inventory and they show up in an area called "on the ground". Chests and barrels are occasionally available for you to open and you can touch those, but that's it.
When you equip items they don't show up at all on your character either. Not even on their paperdoll.
There's huge amounts of totally useless items too. Mops. Weights. Bones. Limbs! I understand that they're there to add character to the world but when everything else is so static it doesn't "fit".
The dialogue trees are extremely annoying as well. I don't feel like I have choice. To find out about a quest I often have to ask everything available even if it doesn't feel like something I'd want my character to say. If I say the wrong thing there's times i've had to repeat the ENTIRE dialogue again until I get back to the point I was at.
This isn't for specific story stuff either, just random normal quests. A quest where a character wants me to find a gift for his betrothed and because I asked a question at the end of the dialogue I had to re-do the whole thing to get the quest.
And a big thing for me - if you've already done a quest you can't say that during the picking up of the quest. If I've cleared the quarry you're asking me to clear I cannot say "I did that already!". I have to finish the dialogue and then speak to the person again.
This often meant getting the quest, going to where it said and realising that I'd already done it a few hours ago. That's extremely frustrating for me.
It also autosaves extremely rarely. It's my own fault for not saving, but it's still quite annoying.

Many, many years and probably about 20 games later, Vogel releases his finest game to date. A lot of people who look at Spiderweb's titles as being the same over and over again most likely haven't played enough of them to see the subtle differences. There are a couple things that set Avadon 3: The Warborn apart from previous titles. One, it's slightly more accessible than previous entries. The character leveling and skill trees aren't quite as involved. This may offend some of the most hardcore RPG fanatics, but may help newer players get into the characters a bit more without feeling overwhelmed. Also, while still being a fairly open game, progression feels a bit more pointed, and less "all over the place" like the earlier Avernum games. I can appreciate both of Vogel's styles completely, the mass chaos of the Avernum sytling and the simplified, slightly more streamlined Avadon entries. Without ruining the story, I'd say by the end I'm completely satisfied with the way Vogel ended the Avadon series. Lots of twists and turns, and plenty of choice and consequence, and certainly multiple endings, depending on how you handle certain events. The game took a bit less time to complete than Avadon 2: The Corruption, and that's okay. Finishing it never felt like a chore, and makes me look forward to playing whatever he comes up with next. Highly recommended to older gamers and younger players who prefer substance over flash.

is a thirdperson cover shooter with an interesting setting. The game looks and sounds appealing, but it falls flat on its face when you actually play it.
The gameplay is so generic that it hurts. The most unique mechanics are the sandstorms and commands and even those don't offer much to the gameplay. Most of the weapons (especially the assault rifles) feel identical with the only real differences being lightly modified stats and a different mesh. There is almost no enemy variety. You will play the whole game only encountering reskinned versions of the same enemy. However, the game will occasionally throw a heavy or charger at you. Even then, they do not add enough to the combat to bother.
On the topic of gameplay, the controls are weak. I found myself pressing spacebar or shift on accident and quickly dying because of it. By default, spacebar is sprint, cover and revive. Shift is for your melee attack (which is completely useless) and leaping over cover. Even after rebinding them, I still do not believe they work very well.
One of the most praised aspects of this game is the story. It's certainly better than the gameplay, but that isn't saying much. I will admit that the darker perspective is refreshing but I never felt interested or involved in the story at any point.
In the end, you are supposed to feel bad for the things that "you" did. However, you are forced to make the majority of these bad choices to progress with the game. There were only a couple choices you can actually make and none of them have any real effect on the story.

(This is a pre-access title, so my opinion on the game may change as time goes on)
THE GOOD STUFF
1.  Two Vehicle Classes:  You've got the lightly armored, highly agile buggy.  And you've got the heavily armored, lumbering tank.  So simple varity.
2.  The Gameplay:  So far, I've only seen Capture the Flag.  But I assume there will be more in the future.  The gameplay's pretty solid for a game that's 2 days old.
3.  Wait times don't take longer than...  A half a minute.  So not too long.
4.  The base generates currency even while you're offline.  You literally never have to play after the tutorial.  Just leave your base, come back, and collect the currency every day.  And you can have a tricked out ride in about a week!  Or you could play the game and get it in about...  No time flat.
5.  It's Russian.  And I only put this reason so I don't go to Gulag.
THE BAD STUFF
1.  Early access:  Bound to be glitches.  None encountered but don't hold your breath.
2. Special Ability takes too long to regen.  For the Buggy, it's a booster that literally just thrusts you up for about 8 seconds.  And then it takes 8 YEARS to regen.
3.  In game payment.  Don't think this is a downside?  They said that in World of Warships, until the Tirpitz came out.  No, don't try and argue the point, it's a downside.
4.  The sounds need a little work.  They aren't terrible, but they aren't great either.  The engine sounds like it's mumbling, even at full speed, and there's a lack of inertia when you go up a ramp, because the sound is so mediorcre.
5.  Some of the effects seem a little unrealistic.  Like I imagined when I slammed into a rock that I'd be crush.  Nope, I ricocheted off of it and bounced about for a moment like a ball.
However, despite everything I've said, I recommend supporting this game.  It's free, it's actually decent, and it's only a few days old.  Plus you get a bonus 1500 GC, (Premium Currency), for just downloading the game.  You have to go through the tutorial, of course.  But it's still worth it.  I think this game can me something really special.  Just add some more content, improve on some vehicle and landscape characteristics, and you've got a starter game bound to turn heads.

Undertale is not good!
The Metacritics gives it a stunning 92. But take a look at the user ratings...
I know it's a difficult subject, but Undertale is the very definition of overrated. First things first, it's not a bad game but not very good either.
1. Story
The story, for what it is, is simple but effective however never shows up in the game ;) Instead you just walk from point A to point B. Pretty tedious. What saves the entire product is the fact that there are some goofy characters but that's it. THE JOKES HOWEVER ARE JUST BAD!
2. Gameplay
Gameplaywise it's got problems: It's pretty much hit or miss. Some fights are well made, other e.g. the normal "monsters" are just bland and repetitive. It only has one mediocre gameplay style which is used with lots of innovation but also to its limit of credability.
3. Music
6 / 10: This may shock you, but it's also very hit or miss: Here the great songs: Megalovania, Toriel's Theme, Asgore's Theme, Papyrus' Theme, Undyne the Undying, Undyne's Main Theme, #Bergentrückung and last but not least Spider Dance. These are so GOOD. I loved them! The rest is just musical grabage. Especially Lava World just sucks.
By the way: The OST costs as much as the game itsself. That's just too much! Just buy it if you're a fan and leave others alone with it.
4. Design
The Design is bad! Undertale has a great sense of innovating and reinventing its only gameplay style but fails in execution. Random encounters are annoying and a thing of the late 90s. But that's what this game wants to emulate, so I guess it's alright...
5. Open World
Just kidding, the world is boring, dark and hostile....
6. Art Style
Dark and colorless. This really makes me sad because I like colors. But the Game is called "Undertale" so there you go. The art style is mediocre, nothing more nothing less.
SUMMARY
It's a miracle how this game got the praise it recieved. I would give it 7/10 maximum score. There are much better Indie Title. Try Stardew Valley or Hyper Light Drifter! For 10 Bugs this game should have been so much more. It's fan service of the old days. Love or hate this review. I never said Undertale is bad, just disappointing for 92 Metacritics. I recommend a pass on this product, buy it on Steam Sales. And one word on itsself: Don't always believe what Reviewers or hyped Fanbases say. I made this mistake twice with this game and now Sonic Forces.
If I find enough time, I'll discuss this topic in a video on my Youtube Channel in an adequat manner. (This means not using clickbait like lots of others do)

Honest Review: Black Screen Simulator
Don't get me wrong I love FNaF as a whole. I've been on the band wagon for awhile and the hype for this game was real for me. There are also things about this game that is awesome but as far as this being a "game" is held a little too high, it's more of a experience.
Looks like Scott wanted a more streamline experience for Sister Location, the game has little to no random elements to it as the other 4 games did. My playthrough and watching YouTubers play through have been exactly the same with the exact same jumpscares. So, the feeling of tension and fear of not knowing when a jump scare will happen is completely gone cause the only jump scare is when you fail a objective, which when you fail, you expect the jumpscares making everything just expected.
The dialogue is a nice touch to the game, though it is very overused with a AI voice that explains every, damn, thing to a T so you don't even have to think or figure out anything on your own. Though, Baby says that he lies and not to listen to him, just do the opposite, I only found maybe 2 or three times where I had to do opposite of what he said.
As a example, when you go through Foxie's room, all you have to do is tap W 4 times, flash your light then rinse and repeat and you'll never get hit by Foxie's jump scare. When he says to "go slow and use your light sparingly" I just ran and flashed my light like crazy and I constantly made it through without a jumpscares... Plain and simple.
My biggest complaint is that the game is filled with areas that are nothing but complete black screens where you have to just hold the W key with absolutely nothing to see or be afraid of. At one point a voice(I won't say who's (;) literally tells you when to stop, when to turn left and when to stop.... Word for word in pitch darkness.
Honestly, if you love FNaF it's worth playing for the elements that are there but don't get this expecting a long and scary experience like the other games. There is little to no replay value. Watching it on YouTube is the same as playing it on this one I promise.

I bought this recently on Green Man for about £3.99 and what a bargain that was, I'd been watching how it was recieved since release and it never really seemed like it had much a good standing with the gaming community, nobody really 'talked' about it like it was something special or notable BUT after playing for some time I really love this game.
Mad Max as a franchise I really liked it, the Mel Gibson movies are my favorite, I thought Fury Road was a terrible movie but that's just my opinion, the game on the other hand is awesome given the fact I can run it on Max settings and the game has a hell of a ton of stuff to do like search wastelands for wrecked car bodies, scavange for food, scrap, water, historic relics all to upgrade the cars you find/steal and upgrade Max's abilities and loadouts.
The cars upgrade system is pretty in depth with upgrading wheels, engine, suspension, body, paint, weapons, etc which gives so much customisation, for Max himself you unlock new features as you gain notoriety from missions and races in the wastes which lead to better attacks, combos, weapons, clothing, counter attacks tools, etc.
The missions themselves can be pretty standard by taking over bases to collect items for strongholds or even special parts for specific features within the strongholds which benefit you each time you visit or can help you gain more scrap from the strongholds scrap crew which is automaticlly added to your own scrap heap which then all add towardds vehicle/Max upgrades through the game.
Graphically the game looks pretty impressive, obviously there could be improvement but when you're travelling through a desert wasteland at 100mph there really isn't much to see that needs to be improved on. The game also has a fantasic photo mode built in so if you love playing around and creating art within a game like I do you'll spend hours playing with all of the filters, effect and features that provides.
The combat in the game is ver similar to the Batman and Shadow of Mordor combat systems which is pretty much the same for all Warner games which is instantly memorable and has great fluidity in combat situations as well as fury mode with is acticated after a certain hit streak and then Max let's out a completely different set of attack moves compared to the regular attacks.
All in all after all that I've said, I'd give this game a solid 9/10. If the game is on sale for less than £15 I'd say definitely get it, if it's on sale for less than £10 that's a no-brainer. I could see myself going for the 100% completion.

Driving around the huge open world wasteland in your custom death machine is pretty enjoyable, but one unavoidable issue with this game is that it pads way too much of its gameplay with fetch-quests and trying to make you into a completionist. I find it annoying that you have to do a bajillion side quests and hours of grinding just to unlock the really good parts for your car.
Combat on the ground is ok, works pretty much the same as the Arkham games but with more gore, explosions and shotguns to the face. Combat with cars is very fun and can get pretty intense once you get to the harder areas.
The story is self-contained and fits well for the series, with some likable original characters. I'm not a fan of how 90% of the game's progression is going back and forth on fetch-quests, turning Max into a wasteland errand boy.

A decent story and brilliant voice acting aren't enough to stop this game from feeling like Arkham City 1.5, but given the strength of the Arkham franchise, it's a hard game not to enjoy. The combat system is as refined and enjoyable as ever, and new investigation sequences do a great job of making Batman feel like the detective he's meant to be. Plus, the game looks stunning and runs brilliantly.
Just be sure to ignore the game's boring and unnecessary multiplayer, and start work on the single player campaign's Dark Knight challenges early. Some sloppy game design on the part of the developers means it's possible to get locked out of finishing challenges and unlocking goodies if you don't complete them by the time you finish the campaign.
Definitely worth a purchase if you were a fan of previous Batman outings.

There’s a great scene in the first Star Wars film where Han Solo boasts that the Millennium Falcon made the Kessel run in less than twelve parsecs. Disregarding the fact that a parsec is a unit of distance, not time (something that has been retroactively explained with black holes (of course)), Han continues to explain how fast and badass his ship is. He comes off as cool, cocky, and like a damn smooth criminal. SmuggleCraft is a game about that feeling. It’s a game about building and managing your ship, shipping contraband and feeling like a chaotic neutral smuggler. Unlike Han Solo, however, the player runs his or her business on a barren, rocky planet full of the kind of empty space for which people would build really fast vehicles. It’s all designed with this pastel low-poly aesthetic, with just enough detail as you speed through the environment to an excellent chill synth soundtrack.
SmuggleCraft starts you out indebted to a local merchant, who helps you off the ground with your hovercraft. With that, you need to get to work, because he’ll be needing payment by tomorrow. Of course, you could refuse to pay him, if you’re willing to deal with the bounty hunters he’ll sic on you while you work. So you run odd jobs for the locals, of varying legality. They’ll reward you with credits or parts, both of which are used to upgrade your ship. These jobs are usually some form of A-to-B drive, sometimes A to B to A, or even the occasional race. With some of these, you can return the goods you were sent with, or grift your employer and sell them to someone else if they offer a good deal. You might also start to get the heat on your tail if you take too many less-than-legal jobs. All of these little quirks fill out the roleplay to a great extent. You start thinking like a smuggler. On the quest screen, you can talk to locals (who, I will be frank, look pretty bad aesthetically), who range from young kids telling you they look up to you to people who just straight up tell you, “You’re a bad person.” For a game with little-to-no “actual” world, it’s filled with flavor.
But when you’re out of the quest screen, you’re on the road. And there is a lot of road in SmuggleCraft. A lot of empty road. The game is randomly generated, as many games are now, and this is probably SmuggleCraft’s biggest flaw: the maps generated are boring. The racing itself is highly simplistic, too. There are customizable ship parts, but they don’t seem to change much mechanically. There’s fast, and faster; the upgrades are really linear, as well. The majority of the gameplay is spent holding down accelerate and guiding the control stick a little to the left or a little to the right so you can hit a boost or grab some energy for your ship. Within thirty minutes, I was already bored with the driving. The maps are big and barren and have a large set of little sections recurring in different orders. Occasionally, I would encounter a new segment, but they all played the same.  Honestly, I wanted the bounty hunters or the police to get on my tail so it would give me something to actually do on these maps. The core gameplay is so boring and so nothing that it totally took me out of my wonderful Giraud-style fantasy world and reminded me I was using a controller.
SmuggleCraft is a good start. It feels like it’s in Early Access. I was more than ready to get wrapped up in its fantasy fulfillment, but it took me right out of it with its bland maps and simplistic gameplay. I seriously believe the game would have benefited from a set of handcrafted levels, a dedicated campaign, or maybe some form of combat, or just anything to give this driving more depth than it has right now. Because right now, there’s a lot of road, and not enough rubber to hit it with.

I attempted to play this longer, but SmuggleCraft just couldn't hold my attention. While SmuggleCraft is not for me, I still think there is an audience out there who would like it, for that reason I'll give it a thumbs up on Steam.
The concept of SmuggleCraft sounds exciting: take on different mission types to earn credits and materials to then build various body parts for your hovercraft, altering how it handles for future missions. However, while the low poly visual aesthetic is fantastic, the gameplay couldn't hold my attention.
I really wanted to create rad hovercrafts. Unfortunately, I found it difficult to grind the bland, repetitive, and sometimes boring missions in order to get the materials/cash needed to craft. Sure, some missions were more exciting than others, but I found them few and far between.
Look, SmuggleCraft isn't a bad game, it's just not a game for me. You may get more mileage out of it, especially if you're looking for a more serene, casual racer with the ability to create super-rad looking hovercrafts via a neat little crafting mechanic.

This is a big step up from Hitman: Absolution, which I did not recommend.  Though I do recommend this one it's hard to quantify super cleanly so I'll get to the list;
Good
-Big, involved missions
-Lots of ways to solve things
-Unlockable starting areas
-Unlockable gear
-Challenging
-Feels like the classic Hitman games
-Atmosphere feels consistent, areas are varied
-Progression initially feels great and story-driven
-Production values are good
Weird
-After you do a handful of missions, you're now redoing the same missions with the same targets in the same location because there's nowhere else to go anymore.  In its current state, this leaves story feeling like it just jumped out a window.  Nothing new past that aside from kiling different NPCs with specific weaponry while wearing specific clothing in the same levels.
-There's no satisfying overall "ending" or any ending at all (aside from the endings of certain missions which had me hooked at first)
-Waiting for another installment to the game's areas/story seems to take months which can kill all momentum
Not as good
-There's no "quick" sorts of missions due to the scale of each area, so newer players will have to commit a good half hour at least if they want to complete something to keep their progress.
-Doing a mission the loud and sloppy way seems to go against it all now due to the sheer number of guards in the level and the punishments you incur for each person shot.  You'll be fighting what feels like 25 guards with machineguns if you get in a gunfight in just about anywhere.  There's lots of equipment for being loud but I can't really seem to get away with using any of it at all.
Overall, if you miss the classic Hitman games (my favorite was Blood Money) then this might scratch that itch.  The content delivery system is an odd business choice, but it's nice to know they're still updating the game.  I'm sure if I come back in half a year there might be a couple more levels for me to try -- though the game punishes you by waving what you permanently missed during that timeslot in front of your face in a permanent list.

Technical problems aside, Hitman 2016 is an incredible videogame.
The narrative is fresh, catchy and truly well written. You can undoubtedly feel the spy/hidden assassin feel from Blood Money, with a new Agent  47, which seems like a refreshed, younger and more stylish version of the Absolution hitman; makes sense, since the ambient tends to be modern, polished and more civilized. The game shows us the darkest side of the human nature: greed, apathy, arrogance and madness,; most of the targets will present this characteristic, so, even when the new Agent 47 seems more dehumanized than the previous, you won't have moral dilemmas when trying to eliminate your target, you may even call it justice; but there is still a balance. The targets are  well written; they seem real, which is crucial when creating a character; you can feel hatred towards the ambitious and arrogant Strandberg, and sorrow for the troubled Caruso. And common subjects will be treated: Corruption, Coups and terrorism. The cinematics, are the best I've seen in any video game, they are, pardon me, ♥♥♥♥ing astounding. Something I wanted to add, personal, I can definitely feel a James Bond nimbus; there is a Dr. No reference, which in my humble opinion, is one of the best Hitman kills
As I mentioned before, the ambient of the game is pleasant. The places are alive; in each corner of the world you will find minor conversations between the NPCs, which will give us (the player)  brief amounts of information about the storyline, targets and surroundings; there are laughs, shouts, natural sounds plus innumerable amounts of places to enter, so the immersive feeling is guaranteed. I will add, that, contrary to the general opinion, I find the design satisfactory, because it fits the, we may call it, Hitman "reboot" scenery. Pristine and elegant. My personal favorite, Sapienza (Vernazza).
The score is adequate. It won't be diverse, but it will surely make the playthrough more enveloping and interesting.  This is personal, but I can feel, after finishing the missions, an ominous sensation, something like pride and amusement, all due to the theatrical background melody. I hope you feel it too, it's nice
My problems with this game are the lack of identity and the silliness. Apart from the design of each map I can't really appreciate the culture of each nation; English language being the universal dialect allows this to happen. The way the NPCs behave and the incidents will sometimes seem incredibly dull and childish, along with sims graphics, which make the look sillier.
I don't advise you to buy the game now, due to the outrageous price and the technical problems, but, when fixed, this games will be a must on every single person list, because, guys, the game is funny. You will have hours of entertainment, finding new and hilarious ways to kill your targets. I wouldn't call it a Blood Money 2.0 (since there are more seasons to come and each game has it's own identity), but I think it will surpass it.

is an old-school turn-based rpg with exploration and combat as it’s primary focus, well balanced by character interactions, vivid and constant world-building through descriptions and textlogs, and the occasional equipment upgrading. The option in classes and a wide array of abilities helps keep the encounters engaging and allows light tactical planning on medium-to-large scale battles (especially on higher difficulty levels).
Following the well-established molds of the Geneforge and Avadon sagas, Avadon offers a huge world and interesting characters to populate it. This game’s particularity comes in the form of a more focused storytelling that takes precedence over the free-form exploration. The story itself revolves around the player as a lowly Pact soldier that gets elevated to the status of Hand of Avadon, being given the power and the responsibility to end the war with the Farlands. How this is brought about is up to you: crush your enemies mercilessly, or subdue them by aiding in your common struggles. The sum of your positioning towards your superiors and companions determines  later-game outcomes.
Between all the aspects that come out upon hours of gameplay, some excel.
:

Avadon 3 is a great game. Small things, like choosing which companions will be by your side, learning their backstories, ideals and motivations and coming to expect their input in a given situation is one of the highlights of the experience. Likewise, defeating hordes and bosses and tracking down your antagonist step by step gives a real sense of progression to your campaign of liberation. The fact that story events are the direct outcome of the previous games’ plots should be enough incentive to get through the previous games first, even though it’s not strictly necessary. All around, the positives of the game far outweigh the weak spot that are almost inherent to this type of indie, like graphics and sound (On regards to which, by the way, you can always improve your experience by having your favorite dungeon synth/dark ambient playlist at hand, it makes the wandering around far more enjoyable).
Spoderweb quality right there. If you prize story over graphics, but think choose-your-own-adventure books don't have enough gameplay, this game is for you.

This game is absolutly phenominal and really makes me proud to have stuck with the series from the start. The horror element is completly different from the previous four games, while the jumpscares aren't as loud and they are still scary and in your face, but the real horror is the general atmosphere of the game, having to go through pitch black rooms with the possibility of death with every move. Another thing that makes this game completly unique to the series is that you are taking part in completly different tasks each night. While in the previous four games you could pick up a rythum after the first few nights, this has you confused from start to finish about what you're doing each time, and the consntant inconsistency of the tasks makes the horror a lot more scary because you never get the chance to learn how to avoid it.
As far as how this game fits into the series lore wise, it is packed full of easter eggs and hiddle clues that point to it being set at the same time as 'Five Nights at Freddys 4'. The links to the book 'The Silver Eyes' are very prominant with the precense of Mr (william) Afton. I would also hazard a guess at saying the child we hear at the beginning of each chapter is Aftons child, and if thats true we now have a reason as to who Afton (revealed as Purple Guy in the book) would go after Henry's (the design side of the buisness) children in animatronic suits. If Henrys animatronics caused his daughter to die, thats a fairly good motive for revenge.
I feel like Sister Location is going to have a series of its own, i think it needs to after all the new things they were revealed and unanswered, and completing the 'fake' ending takes you back to your home where you see the TV show say 'to be continued' which i think applies not only to that ingame tv show but to the game series as well.
Over all, a fantastic game, fasinating new mechanics, tones more lore to think about, and the start of something completly new for the franchice. I cant wait to see whats next!

You really can't go wrong with Borderlands 2. I really don't have to sing its praises for it. In my opinion, the Borderlands games are one of the few games that are the go-to game for 4-player online action. It's got a nice variety of enemies, it's got plenty of quests, the enviornments are fun, and you get to make the class you choose your own. I love this game, played it on the Xbox 360 and PC, and it's very fun. There's a lot of good to it, and there's no way I'm giving this game a negative review! But for the sake of writing a review I think I should just name a few things that I don't like personally and in my opinion bring the game down for me a bit. I'll throw the *SPOILER WARNING* here so if you're new to it and don't want any hints on the story, don't continue reading! Also might be a little long and wordy, so my apologies. Firstoff, the game still lacks an engaging story. Borderlands 1 didn't have much of a story either, which a lot of players complained about. Trailers and information from the creators of the game stated that a new story with more complexity would be added. But in all honesty, I didn't see it. Throughout the game I didn't feel a sense of urgency or see how oppressive Handsome Jack was, I was getting it all second-hand from everyone else. Sure you go to Opportunity and you can listen to the distorted history of Pandora and Jack's propaganda, but I don't find all that meaty in terms of story telling. You can find some audio logs along the way too showing how much of a murderous tyrant Jack was, but again, it's second-hand, not experienced. It's not that profound or engaging. I also felt awkward when I was built up as the person who faced Handsome Jack and survived--when in the intro cutscene all you did was find a dynamite riddled dummy of him. The stakes never feel high enough to make me feel engaged. Obviously there were a few parts that shocked me, such as the deaths of Bloodwing and Roland, but those were over so quick and you spend so much time out in the wastelands you barely see them, so it's not that disheartening. And you might say, "Well, this is a self-identified shoot and loot game, we're here for the shooting and the looting!" And I would say yes, we are, that's why I'm here too, but the game creators said there'd be a story, and I wanted a story, so where's my dang story? It wouldn't be that much of a issue if they had trumed storytelling as a selling point. The majority of characters are not engaging; even the player characters are reduced to one-liners after you listening to about four dialogs halfway into the game, plus the one you start with. That is NOT character development. They're all bland, and the most engaging characters I'd have to say are Tiny Tina because she has a personality that is enjoyable and funny. Moxxi's a runner up because she's a fun toss up between some relatively funny quips, violence-loving, and actually being kind of compassionate. Other than that, gameplay is my next biggest topic. In RPGs, because this game is under the classification of an RPG by my standards, as you level up, you meet harder enemies that give you more XP. Your XP bar is bigger so you need more, so naturally game offers new, more challenging enemies. Enemies you fought previously still exist, and still give you the same amount of XP, but because your XP bar is bigger they don't fill it up as much. And because you've fought them for a long time, they're easier because you know how to handle them. Borderlands takes that concept and throws it out the window. As you level up, enemies don't level up with you until certain parts of the game, then it just stops altogether. Since your XP bar gets bigger, it takes so much longer to level up because enemies barely give you any XP. What's more, enemies's XP output doesn't stay the same, it goes DOWN. What!? That's asinine! Challenging enemies are still really difficult to fight, especially on True or Ultimate Vault Hunter modes, even when they're extremely lower leveled, and they barely give you any XP! The difficulty to reward ratio is nonexistant. You can complete dozens of quests and kill thousands of difficult enemies, and barely register a couple slides on your XP bar. That's ridiculous, and leveling up becomes a bigger chore instead of being fun because you can't even grind. Grinding can be a good or bad thing, but it's not rewarding at all. The game boasts about all the cool abilties you can unlock but you won't be seeing them for a longtime. And when you do get them, they're not exciting or rewarding because you won't be doing anything relatively new with them. As well, the loot you get isn't that profitable nor do they possess good stats. You'll probably end up using a gun you don't like only because of its high damage output, which is a real bummer. And the game punishing you for dying is probably the most insulting--you can have a million bucks and after a couple deaths you'll be down in the ten thousands. I don't understand the lesson the game is teaching you by taking away MORE money when you start to accumulate MORE money! The lack of story I can live with but after so many hours of gameplay I have to stop playing because the game becomes much harder and your rewards are puny, taking away the fun and the overall point of the game. But as I said, I don't hate this game and it's still a very enjoyable game. That might seem back handed, but if you round up your buddies and start a new game, you'll have a grand time, and ultimately, that's what this game is about. Get your pals together, fight hordes of baddies, and get frigging rich. With your friends, the gameplay and story negatives I've listed are nulled because you're having fun with them in a game that gives you some simply objectives and tools.

The Apparent P2W guns are obtainable for rent without paying but require Joker Tickets which you can obtain from fight club. Honestly I feel like this game is not P2W more like you need Skill2Win I would recommend APB to any other gamer out there.
People also forget the positive parts about APB: Reloaded which includes the games detailed character design. The customization in APB is by far one of the best due to the ability to make individual symbols and then place those symbols anywhere on a piece of owned clothing, car or graffiti. Regarding the Symbol editor you have amazing artwork for purchase from other players with in game money that could be tattoos, clothing details, car logos, anime characters, nsfw, guns, and other things.
Positives:
- Great customization
- Fun
- Mailbox at Social District
- That nice tingling sensation when you beat a maxed rank gold
- Combat is more strategic then a point and click to kill shooter
- GM's hold events occasionally and distribute GM Joker Boxes
- Fight club for those who like instant action
- Variety of guns in which each gun counters another just got to be smart on what you choose
Negatives:
- About 1/3 of the cool clothing is armas
- The fastest car in game with nitro is as fast as a potatoe (Feels like the max speed is 100kmph)
- Occasional server lag
- In game 13 yr olds that teabag
- occasional hacker

Let's be clear, Hitman has some issues lying under the surface. The always online DRM, while it has never been a problem for me is a serious bummer, the pricing structure is confusing and can cause you to miss content, and preformance can be an issue, but in my opinion all of these issues have been over exaggerated and are sadly keeping many people from playing a fantastic game.
Hitman 2016 takes everything that was great about Blood Money (sans the money system, which I do miss, although gear unlocks do return, more on that later) and combines it with the more intuitive and frankly better controls of absolution.
Always online DRM is plenty annoying, however I haven't personally had any server issues or latency issues with the game, so it's hard for me to dock it any points here. Game worked as intended, never once got kicked out of a mission or couldn't play.
Pricing actually worked in my favor. I decided to try the intro pack because I was a bit strapped for cash and then was able to upgrade to the full experience. I did end up paying 5 dollars more this way, which seems like such a small amount of moeny that it's more of an insult, but it let me give the game a try on my system to see if performance was an issue.
For me (GTX 980ti, i5 3570k @ 4.2 ghz, 16 GB RAM) performance is fine. There are some dips in the Paris level due to large crowds but since most of the time in those areas is spent walking around and not doing anything too intensive it doesn't really interrupt gameplay, although it is annoying.
The best thing I can say about this game is how open and expansive the levels are. These missions beg to be replayed. At the time of writing I have ten hours in the game just in the first three missions alone (and the first two are training missions that take about 10 minutes to complete on the first try)
I never replayed any missions in Blood Money, but Hitman 2016 has such large and expansive levels that you want to go back and try things. The challenge system hints at all the different ways you can assassinate your targets without giving those things away. You can finish a mission, check the challenges, and then try it again with a different approach. They still force you to be creative but they help nudge you in the right direction. By completeing these challenges you also unlock new gear and starting locations/disguises for the missions, which keeps the levels fresh. Even though the Paris level is technically "one" level, starting with a certain disguise in a different location can show off portions you've never even seen before.
While I wish Blood Money's economy had come back, with challenges giving you money to spend rather than linear upgrades, this is still a decent system.
All in all, even in just the intro pack, there is a lot of content here. Contracts mode returns, although I haven't really dabbled in it yet but I can only imagine the possibilities in the more sandbox style levels.
Don't let the negative reviews talk you out of this one. I recommend purchasing the intro pack and playing the Paris level before the refund window closes, if performance on AODRM don't bother you in that time, you've got yourself a winner.

APB: Reloaded has one of the coolest premises ever. Cops and Crooks, simple right? It is.
OVERVIEW
The game takes place inb San Paro, a city with crime unparalel to anything else. So much so that the City Security Act (CSA) was passed. Allowing any citizen to walk the streets with a liscense to practice Vigilantism.
When you start the game you make your biggest decision, Do I want to be a good guy or a bad guy? Once you make your decision, you get to make a character with a very good, high detailed  creator.
STARTING OUT
Once your character is situated, you're basically set free, the tutorial system is very poor. In the city you'll simply be dispatched to start or stop crimes. The game usually does a great job to match you with even teams.
CUSTOMIZATION
The game does although have great customization. Most clothes in the game are relatively cheap, so if you have the time, you can have an awesome character. Same with vehicles, customization is a big deal in this game.
The game allows you to create custom symbols as well. To paste onto your clothes and cars.
COMABT
There's lots of variables in combat. Combat can either be very fast and fun. or slow and boring. It all depends on the players, and enviroment.
The game kinda influences camping, with lots of defense objectives simply being, guard this choke point on this conveinient rooftop.
DRIVING
Ugh, driving is a mess. There's always a delay, you'll press "d" to steer right. Then after half a second to three seconds later your character will steer the car. This cuases very awkward and slippery driving.
FINAL VERDICT
APB: Reloaded is a fun hectic expirience, especially with friends. But poor tutorials and slippery driving kind of ruin it.
~ 7/10 Worth Trying.

Let me start with taking away the illusion of the pay2win aspect. APB is a free2play game and gives you a slightly "limited" version if you're not willing to upgrade your account with "Premium". So what is this Premium Membership actually giving you?
A Premium Membership for APB can be bought through the Armas Marketplace, and sometimes can be received free through Redeem Codes and joker boxes, this gives players several advantages in the field.

Premium Benefits
Up to a 90% bonus to all Contact Standing (XP) Gains.
125% bonus to all APB$ gains.
20% discount in the Armas Marketplace.
50% reduced cooldown on activated abilities (e.g., Field Supplier, Nitro Booster).
Advanced access to Customization Suites (50 Symbols per Vehicle / Clothing item. 100 layers per Symbol).
Extended duration for Armas Trials for Weapon and Vehicle Trials.
The rest of the Armas Marketplace offers weapons, vehicles/kits and clothing. These available so called "pay2win" weapons are merely re-skins and have the same statistics as already existing in-game weapons. Some might have slightly different statistics, but can still easily be beaten by the standard weapons. Also some of these Armas weapons, vehicles and kits are also available at the in-game Joker Store for a period of time by the use of Joker Tickets earned in Fight Club or with Daily Activities. If anything this game is "pay2pretty". ALL weapons ingame are available either in the joker store for JT, on the player market APB$, or on ARMAS for free trial.

Prison Architect has the potential to be a fantastic game.
The gameplay is incredibly addicting. You will experience the same urge that something like the Civ series will give you, except "just one more turn" becomes "just one more room/building". Once I had begun the third iteration of my prison with $500k in funds, the fun was really getting started as I had the ability to build what I wanted instead of what I had to do to get by.
Or so I thought.
Once my budding prison complex reached ~175 prisoners, I noticed something; the frame rate had begun to drop.. Surely this game with its 2D sprites wasn't slowing my gaming rig down...or was it? By 250 prisoners I was down below 30 FPS.
Upon further inspection, it wasn't just the FPS that had dropped; the actual pace of the game seemed to be tied to the frame rate. What was 3x game speed had now slowed to a stuttering 1x game speed. A quick search of the internet revealed the root cause of the issue (and that I was far from alone).
Prison Architect is a processor-heavy game. This is expected and normally not a problem; there are a lot of things happening at once when you reach the point where 500 entities are "thinking" and moving simultaneously in your game world. However, what IS a problem is the fact that Prison Architect only runs on one of your processor's cores, with no hyperthreading. The 3.0 GHz eight core beast sitting in the case next to me might is about as useful as the Celeron in grandma's laptop. This means that EVERYONE who plays this game, regardless of their rig's power, is going to experience the same slowdown once they get to ~200 prisoners - which is RIGHT when the game has sucked you in and you are ready for the long haul.
Prison Architect is insanely fun. I spent roughly 16 of the last 48 hours playing it. Unfortunately, it's so poorly optimized that it will eventually become virtually unplayable if I continue to feed my new addiction.
I cannot recommend Prison Architect to anyone in its current state. The developers should be ashamed of themselves for letting this issue exist for so long. If things change in the future, I will edit my review.
Edit: After 4 months and 4 more updates to the game, this is still unfixed.

It's likely that anyone reading reviews for Avadon 3 has likely played the first two, and perhaps some other games by Spiderware Software too. "More of the same" is an accurate description, since there haven't been any huge changes to the game, and it's a continuation of the story that began and progressed in the first and second games. This time round, Avadon finds itself in the awkward situation of having two keepers, as well as fighting a prolonged, fractured war on several different fronts from enemies both within and without the Pact. You're a young Hand who's been dropped into the middle of this confusing situation and - as with any other Spiderweb game - you're supposed to navigate through the events of the game via combat and intrigue while deciding which of several imperfect factions deserves your support the most.
The UI is mostly the same, with a few cosmetic changes here and there (nothing that'll confuse anyone who's played the first two games). The mechanics feel very similar too. The only major changed I noticed was that you now recover all mana after a fight, instead of some of it (in my opinion it makes the game easier, seeing as now no longer have to "hold back" your most powerful spells, since all your spell energy will recover after a fight anyway, except for a tiny slither in the event that you get knocked unconscious). The skill trees have been changed slightly, but it's nothing too major. There's some new spells for mages, although I feel like one AoE one in particular is a little OP.
Although I get the impression I'm only about a quarter of the way into the game, I can already feel my loyalties being tugged in at least three different directions. In between trying to end both a civil and a foreign war, there are plenty of opportunities to make money,♥♥♥♥♥♥people off and gather potted plants for your lovelorn enemies. There are several new companions to get to know, along with some returning faces, and following in the style of the previous games, they all seem to have their own niggling problems that they'll pester you with
Overall, I've enjoyed it, but that's not too surprising considering that I also enjoyed the first two games.
List of cons I've found so far:
- Usual Spiderweb problem of minimal sound and perhaps too few sprites for the game.
- Suffers from lack of proof-reading (at least 7 or 8 spelling mistakes that I've found so far, along with a bit of strange grammar at times)
- Khalida

Dream Daddy is a novel game (get it? it's novel as in the adjective AND a visual novel).
Dad jokes aside, it's a game with genuine charm and heart in its storytelling. In short, you play as a recently single dad who moves with his daughter into a cul-de-sac that happens to be teeming with eligible dads. After a prologue introduces you to all of them, you get to decide who to pursue. Each Daddy has a sequence of three dates that you have to complete in order to reach their ending. You can plow straight through to an ending right away, or you can take your time and work through the first couple dates with each daddy before making your final choice.
Pros:
- You can customize your "Dadsona" to look however you want, and fill in his name and backstory accordingly
- Minigames help break up the monotony of dialog trees
- Having a more modular format for the dates means you don't have to start a new playthrough just to romance a different guy. Each storyline can happen independently.
- Very nice soundtrack, although it is used somewhat sparsely.
- Lots of dad jokes. That's all.
Cons:
- The writing style feels a little forced sometimes (obviously the Game Grumps helped produce it, and it's sort of a parody of dating sims anyway, but sometimes it leans too much on current internet humor)
- Characters are on the underdeveloped side.
- It's completely SFW. Which, given the wholesome nature of the game, is probably for the best. But c'mon, a patch with NSFW pinups wouldn't kill anyone, would it?
- Honestly one run could be finished in an hour. I finished the first two dates with every daddy and still had only logged eight hours.
Overall, I'd totally recommend it. It has a nice story (that gives you all the fuzzy feelings inside), a very memorable soundtrack, and a collection of very fine daddies. Just know that it bends the rules of the visual sim genre, which may or may not be your cup of tea.

Ok... I was about to write a
review for this game - it was a really hard way for me to play through it, but I finally managed to, after completely uninstalling the game
.
Why I, despite that,
recommend this game and why I had so much difficulty getting it done I will tell you soon.
You might be able to tell from this short overview, otherwise, you just have all the points clearly visible.
A three-headed Delta squad led by yourself is sent on a rescue mission to the once beautiful city of Dubai - now a wasteland covered in sand. In this hostile environment you are to find survivors of the 33rd Infantry Battalion who volunteered to evacuate the civilians of the city, afterwards received orders to abandon them and leave but disobeyed and broke contact since.
Throughout the game, you will see what happened in the five and a half months and how the order of command in the city turned around.
As it is, I think it's not a great story but it is beeing told in a unique way that shows a perspective you are normally not shown by the media. At the end of it, you will be able to emphasize with everybody but yourself - you might hate yourself, you might want to kill yourself (not in real life, mind you, but as the character you are playing) and you will regret everything.
Dubai is beautiful - it has always been and even all those sandstorms couldn't take the beauty of the city away.
What however takes aways it's beauty are the tributes of war and the things that have long left the definition of 'war' and go into the fields of mutilation and violation.
There is quite a lot of detail - many posters and grafiti with different messages - some from the old face of Dubai like expensive cars and then the messages of the survivors, sometimes written in bloody red.
The textures are ok for the age of the game I guess and they are not your main focus anyway, they are pretty mushy at places, though.
It plays as a third-person shooter with quite a lot of tactical elements.
, there is a big problem with all this: the movement.
I used to play this game with mouse and keyboard, but just couldn't navigate really well from cover to cover like this and soon found a lot of bullets in my belly, so I switched to my XBOX360 controller which made moving easier but aiming all the harder. Therefore, I could only play on the lowest difficulty and still died quite a lot.
Enhanced was this problem by the fact, that the damage you take is quite 'realistic', meaning you can endure some 3 shots at most. There is a regeneration system but it takes so much time to recover from just one graze that it makes the firefights feel like walking through instant glue.
This resulted in me quitting the game so many times - I could play through it, after all, mind you, but it was no fun at the beginning.
You will get to enjoy quite nice and atmospheric music while you play - provided by Robert Darden - the Radioman of Dubai.
The voice acting is good but not all too good in my opinion, at times it just wasn't matching the situation however at others it perfectly did.
I experienced a lot of sound bugs such as hearing my own steps behind me, noise while inside of a sandstorm - which was
resulting from it and the like. This often hurt the atmosphere and, therefor, decreased immersion.
At the end of the day, the game has a great anti-war attitude which is shown directly through the eyes of a high-ranking soldier suffering  and losing himself in what started as a rescue mission and ended as a suicide commando.
, it's being held back a lot by the gameplay, which feels poorly ported.
If you can live with the problems it has and manage to maneuver your squad safely through the sandy wasteland you are in for good a story.

Prison Architect has the potential to be a fantastic game.
The gameplay is incredibly addicting. You will experience the same urge that something like the Civ series will give you, except "just one more turn" becomes "just one more room/building". Once I had begun the third iteration of my prison with $500k in funds, the fun was really getting started as I had the ability to build what I wanted instead of what I had to do to get by.
Or so I thought.
Once my budding prison complex reached ~175 prisoners, I noticed something; the frame rate had begun to drop.. Surely this game with its 2D sprites wasn't slowing my gaming rig down...or was it? By 250 prisoners I was down below 30 FPS.
Upon further inspection, it wasn't just the FPS that had dropped; the actual pace of the game seemed to be tied to the frame rate. What was 3x game speed had now slowed to a stuttering 1x game speed. A quick search of the internet revealed the root cause of the issue (and that I was far from alone).
Prison Architect is a processor-heavy game. This is expected and normally not a problem; there are a lot of things happening at once when you reach the point where 500 entities are "thinking" and moving simultaneously in your game world. However, what IS a problem is the fact that Prison Architect only runs on one of your processor's cores, with no hyperthreading. The 3.0 GHz eight core beast sitting in the case next to me might is about as useful as the Celeron in grandma's laptop. This means that EVERYONE who plays this game, regardless of their rig's power, is going to experience the same slowdown once they get to ~200 prisoners - which is RIGHT when the game has sucked you in and you are ready for the long haul.
Prison Architect is insanely fun. I spent roughly 16 of the last 48 hours playing it. Unfortunately, it's so poorly optimized that it will eventually become virtually unplayable if I continue to feed my new addiction.
I cannot recommend Prison Architect to anyone in its current state. The developers should be ashamed of themselves for letting this issue exist for so long. If things change in the future, I will edit my review.
Edit: After 4 months and 4 more updates to the game, this is still unfixed.

. A visual dating sim novella in which you become a Dad. Not a dad, but a Dad.
Heavily story-driven, Dream Daddy allows you to portray a Dad, in a series of events you choose to let happen. At its foundation, Dad (you) and his daughter Amanda are in the process of moving out of the old house previously purchased alongside his late partner Alex. The two of them move into a house located in a cul-de-sac in Maple Bay, where they find themselves greeted by new, pretty faces in the area.
What's the objective of the game? That's for you to decide. Moving around, you get to interact with seven Daddies and their immediate families, as you begin to adjust to your new life among them.
Even if it was created as a joke in the office, Dream Daddy provides content that has not been populated much in games; most notably, it fixates its central story on predominantly gay romance and feature queer characters and characters of color without feeling forced or stereotypical. The game has many delightful scenes and dynamics that, upon replaying, add to the overall experience. It also gives the player a choice in how they choose to interact with their daughter Amanda, often giving out many, somewhat, serious situations in their teen's life during her final moments in school.
Alongside Amanda, the game gives players loveable (and hateable) characters that, even presently, will live on in their hearts (and fanfictions).
