I am a strategy gamer, so games like this are usually my thing. Not this one though.
The game has the basic mechanics of a strategy game (e.g. some units are better in some areas than others) but the word basic is already exaggerating things in this case... there is no experience, there is no building defenses or bases, there are only thrre unit types and three terrain types and most dramatically: There is a limit to 4 armies, no matter how many resources you have, it's four armies with limited strengt and no special abilities.
Did I mention that the game is also real time? In this case this is a problem since there are the limitations mentioned above. Just imagine: You are fightin 3 enemies on a map. Your lands have no defenses, only your armies and every one of them has 4 armies... all armies can only be brought up to a certain stength which is quiet easily achieved even early in the game... and then the manouvering starts... I capture province X, then on to province Y, computer B captures X... pfff... so I turn around and recaputer X, while player C caputres Y from me again... and this continues and continues until all you do is frantically sending out your 4 armies and clicking on the armies after a battle to refill their ranks. As I said: Resources are not a problem usually... and should you manage to get into the vicinity of an enemy castle... forget capturing that even with a maxed out army! You will be able to destroy two or three defensive walls of the castle, which cost about as much as your cheapest soldier unit and in 5 seconds the computer will have rebuilt that while you are still clicking on your army and buying replacement soldiers for the second attack...
The game is "Whoever clicks the fastest wins!"
Oh well, it had potentiall but what is there now is just the bare bones of a strategy game.

- The campaign is more or less a tutorial and series of "challenges" that get boring quickly
- The story is pretty poor, and the game does a pretty low-end job of keeping the story interesting or relevent to what is happening.

Finally, a simple RTS for people like me who cannot into macro/micro.

This is a summary of my review video, which I encourage you to watch if you are looking for a more in-depth review.
Tenshu General is a casual simple real time strategy game set in feudal  Japan where you play as a General of an army defending your own territory and expanding and battling to conquer other territories. There is music that plays for the opening menu that is of that time in history and culture. I believe that it would have been beneficial to have that music continue during the actual gameplay, as it would have added to the atmosphere and immersion to the game, instead of the silence or marching of troops that is the games only sounds during gameplay. The graphics are simple, but it fits to the gameplay and mechanics that the game promotes. There have been a few crashes in my gameplay, but the progress I lost was minimal, and the devs are active in trying to fix any issues. It is clear from their activity on Steam and personally that they care about this game.
The game has a fair bit of content for the price they are asking, Each campaign is fast paced, and is centered around strategic, military and money management. You can upgrade tools, farming, and livestock to increase your resources.  You have a max of four armies that you can upgrade, each of which need to be replenished after you engage in battle. It would have been nice to be able to replenish entire armies instead of individual troops as a lot of my time was spent micro-managing each army, as it pulled me out of the enjoyment of the game. It becomes a delicate balance between grabbing up available land in the beginning, then harassing enemies in a give and take scenario to keep them from expanding their territories into yours. You are fighting on different fronts, and you are at the mercy of the slow map movement before you can assess how you have progressed.
The game is simplistic, but overall it works out fairly well. I felt that it respected my time, and was enjoyable. The slow reaction time did pull me out of immersion a bit, but overall the game was fairly balanced. This is an easy recommend.

Tenshu General fills a very specific niche. It's a real time strategy game for those who aren't all the good at real time strategy games. This is a category I find myself firmly sitting in. A decent amount of the first PC games that I played (and were good enough to still remember) were real time strategies and my favourite game for a long time was Age of Mythology. With all that being said however I'm pretty rubbish at them. I'm honestly not sure how many of these games I only beat because I used cheats or how many I must have given up half way through the campaigns because it got difficult. The problem I think is that you need to manage so many different things in real time; troops, resources, upgrades. It can be very easy to forget about this or that.
Tenshu General is something of a devolution of the genre in much the same way as DiveKick is of the fighting genre. The amount of things you need to think about is very limited. You have one single base and can have up to four separate armies that all move as one. Resource Management is stripped down to a single resource, rice, and upgrading towns to collect more is a simple process. That isn't however to say that Tenshu General is simple. The troops you buy for each army, which upgrades you buy and when, where you place your ambassador etc etc. There's still a large amount of choice and complexity.
There are also elements taken from grand strategy, namely the provinces. Each section of land is a separate province, of your army is the only one on it you claim it gaining any resources collected there to you. But not only this you move slower through unclaimed territories and you cannot pass through them meaning that spending the time to capture a province with no rice production may be worth it. Each province also has a different terrain which can impart bonuses or negatives on a particular troop type meaning that army composition is important.
However Tenshu General has it's limitations. Whilst there aren't enough small factors to consider such that it overloads you they also perhaps don't have enough effect. The way to win almost any map feels exactly the same; capture as much as early as possible and crush your opponents main army before they are able to build it up then simply take out whatever small forces they can muster until you have control of the whole area and have four fully powered armies with which to storm their castle. It hardly matters about positioning and terrain advantage when you have a fully stocked army and almost every game plays out in the same way. The only real difference for this is if you include more players.
As I said right at the start Tenshu General fills a niche and it does it very well. It's simple on the surface but has just enough depth to it to allow for more interesting play. It's certainly not for a hardcore RTS fan but for those who maybe missed the bandwagon of the early to mid 2000's RTS it's a small and cheap game that would be a great introduction to the genre.

Don't let the simple graphical interface, and simplified aesthetics fool you, Tenshu General is a fun entertaining strategy title at a very low price point. It's real-time RISK style gameplay is catchy, and its AI does adapt to your style of play. While it's depth may not be miles deep, there is enough there to entertain for hours. Solid campaign, fun AI skirmishes. In spurts this title was much more entertaining than expected.

Writing a review about a game that is part of an established series is always hard. That's why whenever I consume any kind of media I like to evaluate them based on their own merits, as standalone experiences. But it's undoubtable that if you are a long time fan of the Hitman franchise there will be things here that you will love, and things that you will miss.
The first time you play a level you will be lost. You won't know the rules, you won't know the layout, guard positions, area restrictions and you will feel like a stumbling idiot. But the more you play the better you'll get. As a lot of people said already, this game is about repetition. But the good kind. Because you will get better and better, you'll take on harder and harder challenges and you will become a true hitman. BUT after a while it gets old. The game desperately needs a harder difficulty setting where enemy positions, weapon placements, tool placements, etc. are randomised too keep the game spiced up. Escalations and contracts help the matter somewhat as they tend to introduce new challenges. But after a certain number of replays there doesn't remain any reason to continue on a certain level simply because you've experienced everything and unlocked everything.
There are some intricate scenarios that will play out here, some are a bit absurd for some people's taste, but I feel like it's a perfect match for a Hitman game (they've always been a bit over the top). It has a morbid sense of humour that I apreciate very much, as a game about killing people should.
Now, the things that you might miss. There are some intricate details that are missing. Like how there's no carrying case for sniper rifles, no weapon costumisation, no double silverballers (although something tells me we might just see them later on), but overall I don't really miss any of these things. The game is great if you are willing to invest your time in it.
Best Hitman game by a far.

Lemon cakes - Time to make 3hrs
- 3 cups cake flour
- 1 tsp baking soda
- 1/4 teaspoon salt
- 6 eggs
- 2 cups white sugar
- 1 cup butter, softened
- 2 tsp grated lemon zest
- 2 tbsp lemon juice
- 1 cup plain yoghurt
1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). Grease one 10 inch tube pan.
2. Sift the flour, baking soda, and salt together. Set mixture aside.
3. Separate the eggs. In a large bowl beat the egg whites until soft peaks form. Gradually add 1/2 cup of the sugar, beating until stiff glossy peaks form. Set aside.
4. Cream butter or margarine, 1 1/2 cups sugar, egg yolks, lemon zest, and lemon juice together until fluffy. Add flour mixture alternately with the yogurt to the egg yolk mixture. Gently fold in the egg whites and pour the batter into the prepared pan.
5. Bake at 350 degrees F (175 degrees C) for 50 to 60 minutes. Let cake cool in pan for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a rack to finish cooling. Serves 12.

Let's be clear here. I still haven't beaten the game, and part of the reason for that will be included in this. I have watched people finish the whole game.
So, let's get into this.
Sister Location is a weird departure from the main formula for a Five Nights at Freddy's game. It seems like it knows that the previous two games in the series(FNaF World and FNaF 4) did something wrong, and it really, really wants to try to fix that, but it kind of fails. It does a fantastic job of bringing in elements of the previous games. FNaF World's humor, the insane talent for listening you needed for FNaF 4, FNaF 3's audio, FNaF 2's music box, and the power mechanic from FNaF 1, although I can't tell you where for fear of spoilers.
The vampire soap opera inbetween nights is fantastic, from the voice acting to the animation. The story and the jumpscares feel like a typical FNaF game, but turned up to 11. There's an intense amount of focus that has to go into this game, if you want to even get past a night. You need different skills for each night, too, so I'd reccomend brushing up on the rest of your main series FNaF games.
The main thing about SL is that it feels like a spiritual recreation of the scrapped One Week at Flumpty's. It reeks of the game. Everything from the concept of only facing a couple enemies every night to the scrapped blind character in One Night at Flumpty's 2 shows up at some point in SL. I would be unsurprised if someone made a mod to make it as close as possible to OWaF. The other thing is the glitches. While they're minor, they're still annoying. There's a point early on in Night 2 where you should only be somewhere for a few minutes, then that section is done, but it often gets dragged out to ten minutes before you realize, "Hey, wait a second, nothing's happened for about five minutes. Shouldn't I be done?"
There's also Night 4. This is the worst part of the game. There are people that have already put hours of work into this night, and haven't beaten it. It doesn't work. It's incredibly difficult, to the point that you'll be sinking the kind of hours into it that you've put into the 20 modes in the other games. Practice the Golden Freddy Challenge in FNaF 2, if you're really looking to practice this part before buying the game. Night 4 is like doing that, but having ten music boxes to wind up while the animatronics in the center hallway don't actually do anything.
The secondary ending is also a pain. You have to go to extreme lengths to find it, and it's not even the real ending.
Overall, if you're looking for a good scare or incredibly confusing story, it's a good game. If you're looking for a true FNaF-styled game that goes by the formula, or for a generally good game, then you might want to avoid it. So, I do reccomend it, but only for die-hard fans of the series like myself.

A mainstay of gaming since the early days of the form, the visual novel has become somewhat synonymous with "dating simulators."  For the most part, these don't touch on very many real-world issues, concenred as they are with the idea of "you chasing after and dating" some perceived beau.  While this isn't a problem, of course, this particular game type is a great place to look at real-world issues in a slow, methodical way that few other game types can manage.
In that vein, the big, overarching concept for Dream Daddy is quite simple:  you're a father moving into a cul-de-sac that happens to have seven other fathers all living there too.  And since you're single, you decide to get to know the other men.  Perhaps there will be a man here that you can settle down with.
To begin, you meet your daughter, create your Dad - the person you will be playing throughout the game - and then proceed to move house.  Once here, you get acquainted with the surroundings and the other people who own the other lots in the buildings surrounding yours.  Many of these meetings are simple - enough so that you understand the basic gist of each character but not enough to ruin their stories.
That done, you create an online dating profile and this, then, becomes the hub from which you venture forth.
At specified times during the story, you can pick a Dad to go on a date with, make choices that affect the date and then get scored based on what you did.  Your rank [A, S, etc] determines "how well" you did with that particular person and based on those, there's either a fail state or a fine little image celebrating that particular Dad up for grabs [plus, of course, the notion that you are then dating that person for the long haul.]
For the most part, Dream Daddy is great and fires on all cylinders.  The writing - and that's really why you're here if you like visual novels at all, varies wildly from good to great with the occasional stinker or two of a line for good measure.  The choices you make are generally consistent and generally well-handled.  Heck, the whole thing is - for a visual novel - quite tasteful, fading to black when it has to, but showing the emotions of a scene when those crop up.  [Since the form runs the gamut - especially with dating simulators.]
By and large, the gameplay consists of picking choices from a list of three items, occasionally playing mini-games and getting to know the characters a little better with each passing date.
It is here - as each little story is unveiled - that I had perhaps my biggest issue.  While I
the small stakes - really, most of these stories involve you talking to someone else, learning a bit about them and helping them come to terms with some sort of internal demon, I do have to take umberage at the fact that - as a dating simulator - this game sets you up with seven dates, but only allows you to actually win the hearts of six of the men.  The seventh, the developers have decided, is morally off-bounds because of his situation.  While I "generally agree" with this sentiment in the real world, the trouble here is that this is a game world with an "advertised" list of people to woo and win.  That you cannot follow through with this - especially since folks will be roped into the game based on what they see - having, beforehand, decided which Dad to date, I feel that it is a mite underhanded of the developers to stymie that one route for the sake of some sort of moral high ground.
Related to this issue, you CANNOT [at present, anyway] get all the achievements.  There's one that is walled off because the developers have not issued a fix for the game to allow that particular route to be pursued.  [Of interest, too, to achievement hunters:  there are a pair of VERY arcade-reflex-intense minigame based achievements.  These are a bit unfun to complete.]
With those two somewhat bad points out the way, I do want to praise this particular game.  The backgrounds are pleasantly done, the build-a-dad character designer is great and while the minigames are somewhat more miss than hit [in the same way To the Moon should never have had minigames], they make for a pleasant diversion from "pick an option and run with it and hope for the best."  The writing is - as I say, quite pleasant, and the twists and turns of each character are neat to see.  There are some
pleasant little small stakes stories that I greatly adored - a thing I wish more games would do.  Then, of course, there's the great, diverse cast of men - while they're
steretypical in their presentation, they all come across as people and not gay caricatures, which is FANTASTIC.
I mentioned, up top, that the grand idea here was a dating simulator where Dads date other Dads, but this slots into something especially pleasant about this game:  it portrays homosexual men as "just people."  People with worries and doubts and children and demons of their own.  If I can endorse it for no other reason, then I endorse it for this.
If you're a straight person, I feel this is worth playing.  No, it's not exactly real-world, but it might help you see homosexual men in a very different light.
If you're a young homosexual male, I feel this is ABSOLUTELY worth playing.  If nothing else, this will show you that homosexual men come in all kinds of shapes and sizes, with all kinds of hobbies and worries and joys of their own.

Spec Ops the Line is an interesting game. On one hand its a refreshingly different from other shooters but on the other hand it is frustratingly the same and often feels its missing out on its full potential.
Spec Ops the Line is a 3rd person shooter that is inspired by Joseph Conrad's novel "Heart of Darkness" which also servered as the inspiration for the film "Apocoalypse Now." You play as Captain Walker as him and his troops Lugo and Adams work their way through the ruins of Dubai  which has been ravaged by sand storms, and there is lots of speculation as to why the U.S. Army's attempted evacuation of Dubai failed. The plot to the game is filled with interesting insights into the characters of the game and it has some surprises in store for the player.
Let's start with the games strengths. Spec Ops the Line does for sure succeed in most of the aspects. The gameplay is good, if a little generic for a 3rd person shooter. The story is great for sure, it delves into the mind of Captain Walker as these horrors occur and the game presents moral choices which are genuinly really difficult to decide. I'll talk more about this later in the review. The voice acting in the game is top notch (Walker is voiced by the always excellent Nolan North) and the character writing is great here. The game features a great soundtrack and solid sound design. The graphics are good and surprisingly despite the whole taking place in the same desert destroyed city the setting is never boring and actually one of the games strongest points. The game also features some more sureal moments that are some of my favourite parts of the game. The work effectivly and are a smart way to mix things up.
Now, Spec Ops the Line does have some slip ups for sure. The game first of all is short, I beat it on normal in 5 hours which ever for shooter standards is pretty short. It features options for stealth gameplay but i found my AI team mates would often screw up my attempts at stealth by running around like they're in open combat as well as sometimes even opening fire with unsilenced weapons. I also found it a little ridiculous that an entire infantry batallion would stay behind in a ruined No Mans Land of a city without trying to get any kind of help when they started running into trouble. But that's mostly just me nitpicking, it probably won't bother most people. There's also a plot point involving Walker that I can't get into due to spoiler reasons but it really makes some things that happen in the game make no sense.
One thing with the game that lowered my opinion of it the most is actually how in a lot of ways I feel it didn't live up to its potential. First off is the interaction's with your AI team mates during combat, you can give them a couple orders but with the exception of telling Lugo to snipe somebody i rarely used these which didn't make me feel like much of a team. I found they also were kind of idiots in combat occasionally, i saw Adams and Lugo shooting walls sometimes and running in an open area with heavy enemy fire which didn't really make me feel that they were well trained soldiers. I mentioned earlier in the review that the sound design is solid and that's true, but that's it. It's just solid sound design. It feels so cookie cutter and generic, modern military shooters have extremely high standards for sound design in my opinion because so much of the sounds in this game feel artificial and soft. Battlefield is the best reference point i can think of for amazing sound design in a military shooter game, Battlefield sound design really highlights what's possible for shooters like this.
So, I saved my favourite thing about this game for last. Spec Ops the Line has some choices you have to make in the game. The way these choices are presented to the player is possibly the most well done I have ever seen in a video game. This isn't like a Bioware game where your choices are clearly laid out for you and you have to chose. In Spec Ops you simply find yourself in a situation and it leaves it up to you what to do. It doesn't give you any hints and it doesn't tell you your options, you simply have to actually think about it and make a choice. You also have a time limit on all these choices which adds to the tention but you have no idea how much time you have left. You have to look at the situation and see if you think time is running out or not. It's realistic and it makes some of these situations really intense. It also shows how easy it can be for things to go bad when you have to make a tough choice in the heat of the moment. In my opinion this is the absolute best way a game can present the player with complicated choices and I really hope more developers use this design philosophy.
Overall its a pretty solid game that I can recommend for sure, especially if its on sale. 7/10

Tenshu Generals is a neat Indie Samurai Civ Game.
If you can't quite afford Civilization, are looking for a lighter game for your lower end pc or just want something that isn't so triple AAA this is the game for you.
Gameplay:
The game plays like a risk board game in which income is added over time with the addition of being able to upgrade certain terrain tiles that contain villages. These villages provide rice income which is used to buy everything within the game, you then must raise an army and compete against opposing empires for domination of the map.
Unlike Civ there is no diplomacy victory that I've encountered, it all about the combat conquest which is fun in itself. (And perhaps leaves room for expansion?)
Verdict:
Definitely not on the 2016 must buy top ign of the year list, but I enjoyed playing the game and will probably come back to it from time to time until completion as I did enjoy it. If you need a cheap fun compact civilization conquest game this is the game for you and at 5.99 can't really complain to much.

A very thin RTS.  Repetitous with little to do except to build up your villages and armies as swiftly as possible.
Typically you build a strong defensive line, wait until your economy can quickly replace any battle loses, then rapidly move forward in an offensive.
Rinse and repeat.
You do have different units and village improvements that you can choose from,  But unlike good RTS games where careful selection and planning is necessary, the units and improvements in this game are so vanilla that it makes little difference what you choose.  Just fill up your army and village slots and get moving.
It all feels more or less like some kind of a weird race or puzzle game.  I guess there may be some satisfaction in winning a particular scenario in record time.  But I found the whole exercise tedious and boring.

If you stay on top of the game, and make the right decisions, you'll win for sure! But if you don't have a strategy, or just do random moves, you'll get rekt!
Looks deceivingly easy, but there is more to it than meets the eye!

I am a huge Hitman series fan.  I really was very let down with Absolution, seeing them basically garrote all the key aspects out of the series and leave it for dead in a laundy bin in a dark secluded corner.
Then came Hitman.  It looked great if the episodic bits scared me.  Turns out it was pretty damn great and somehow the episodic format actually fits this game better than it has maybe any episodic game I have played, despite not being story focused.
Mechancially this is hands down the best Hitman game.  It gives you a lot of cool options around the environment, like areas to conceal weapons, lots of little opportunities for sabotage, and a wide variety of improvised weapons you can toss into anyone's head like a true assassin would.  There's also some really cool things going on with the AI and suspicion, where witnesses see you act and have to spread knowledge of your deeds to their allies.  Meanwhile guards on the other side of the map are unaware.
The level design has been solid to great.  Blood Money to me is a masterpiece as far as level design and this Hitman game is a bit uneven in comparison.  Paris and particularly Sapienza are really strong levels in comparison to the series as a whole, while Morrocco and Bangkok were pretty limiting and straightforward, without the kind of crazy kill options that I really come to Hitman for.  However, none are bad and there's still fun to be had.
The Elusive Targets are a brilliant addition.  Yes, the execution of them isn't always amazing but just the one off tension in a Hitman game is brilliant.
Hopefully the last two levels are great and more is on the way.  I really thought this series was done for and I am so happy to say that is not the case.  Highly reccomended.

Summary:
Buy this game. Period. IOI has created a masterpiece and has tuned this game perfectly in my opinion. 10/10.
Breakdown:
I am a very casual gamer but I have racked up over 170hrs on this title at the point of this review. This is more than any other game I own. The main missions have an expansive array of methods in which to play the game, but for me the real fun comes from the variety of challenges and escalation missions. These force you to become more creative in order to obtain the SA rating.
Unlike absolution, I find this game does a great job of incentivising the player to obtain a higher rating, and I am extremely happy that they have done away with the points counter that annoyingly told you to stop killing non-targets in absolution.
In addition, the option for a harder difficulty is great. I like that it boils down to just two options (normal or proffessional), although I would love to see escalations that are tailored to the proffesional mode.

No longer seems to have connection issues like in the beginning. Although I think always-online is still quite unnecessary.
Everything else is perfect.

It's an open-world rhythm brawler, much in the vein of Assassin's Creed and the Batman Arkham games (and apparently Shadow of Mordor, but I can't verify that one, myself).
Some folks have complained about it being repetitive, so let me try and shine a light on that. The game primarily consists of you raiding camps and killing everyone to take them over, and there isn't a lot of variation in the enemies. This is what people consider to be repetitive about it. Normally, a lack of enemy variation is a red flag to me, but I found myself not bothered by it since there was variation in the designs and defenses of the camps, forcing you to change up your approach and infiltration styles. That, plus the shocking variation of the wasteland scenery (who would've thought areas of a wasteland could look so different to each other) which was absolutely breathtaking for me. Also, for whatever reason, the idea of slowly conquering a map by replacing existing gangs with your own, I'm finding has a very strong appeal for me. Assassin's Creed: Syndicate had missions that felt more repetitive than the ones in Mad Max, and I didn't even mind those.
There's still other things to do in the game. I just thought I'd address that since that seems to be the element that potentially breaks the game for some people.
The combat system is fantastic. It uses the WB combat system that we see in the Batman Arkham games (and pretty much the same thing as the Assassin's Creed games). But my god, they do a great job of making those strikes feel like they're hitting hard. It's very satisfying. There's also a lot of use of shallow depth of field, which I'm finding that I'm loving in games these days (Doom 2016 comes to mind for that as well). It gives a richness and cinematic feel.

Of course, I’m still in the throes of enthusiasm of a new special interest, so perhaps I’m over-hyping now. And maybe this isn’t for everyone, but it challenged me. It still does, even when I’m not playing it. I’m very happy even writing this. I hope I can share the happiness.

I finally got all of the game's Steam achievements so I think I am now qualified to rate this game.
In short. I have mixed feelings about this game, but I'd still definitely recommend it to everyone except people who are low on patience. For the most part, Mad Max is a thrilling adrenaline fueled ride with some incredibly awesome in-game mechanics (pun intended).
First and foremost Mad Max sports one of the most awesome and feature rich car customisation systems. You Max, are tasked with attaining a car powerful enough to defeat the numerous and powerful enemies that roam "The Wasteland". To do this, you form a grudging alliance with a hunchback and master blackfinger (mecahnic). Together you set off through the wasteland, laying waste to your enemies and gradually upgrading your car with what you find littered around the game.
Driving is the main thing that you do in this massive open-world game and in that, the game does it very well. Controls are pretty responsive, driving is for-the-most-part smooth and enemies in other vehicles are not
I just wish you could take the dog with you in the Magnum Opus (your main car) and that you could use ALL your weapons in the other vehicles. Even though some vehicles have really awesome perks like insane speed or even the ability to drop mines. There is little incentive to use them because the Harpoon, Thunderpoon and Burners are just so good on your main car (not to mention the part upgrades).
Taking into account all of the tasks both optional and part of the story that are in this game, there is an absolutely huge amount of things that need doing. Realistically in order to unlock all of the game's upgrades and get all of the achievements, you will be playing for about 40 hours or so. This is because certain upgrades are locked behind large and repeitive "time sinks" that need doing. I'd spent 30 hours completing tasks before even getting to the final area "Gastown".
For me, at times I felt that with all of the tiny areas filled with just a few scrap (literally 1 or 2) that are just strewn out in seemingly over one hundred locations. I had a monumental task of scouring through every single little side area and hole in order to get the rarest achievement [Looked Everywhere]. The thing is, not only are there just so many areas where the scrap is, MOST of the areas have the scrap placed in such insanely frustrating places. They're either so well hidden or they are located at the end of a massive one-way hike. If I had not gotten something like 88% of all of them whilst going through the game I wouldn't have even attempted it.
__________________________

Ever since I purchased Euro Truck Simulator 2 it has been one of my all time favourite games, with myself playing over 75 hours, all of which helped be grow and expand my company. Although the game never ends, once you are earning more money than you could ever need, and you don't really know what to do next.
The Performance of this game is incredible! I could run smoothly on my old laptop on medium settings and on my desktop I play on elevated high settings smoothly. The graphics are very realistic in high settings but sometimes out of place. Most motorways in the UK in the game look the same but none the less the experience in terms of graphics is amazingly realistic. Definitely see the performance for youself and do youself a favour and download the demo!
When I first purchased the game I owned a Thrustmaster 458 italia racing wheel, which as the market goes is near the bottom. The wheel worked with the games like Insane 2 very well, but for Euro Truck Simulator 2, since it only had a 90 degree turning radius in each direction the sensetivity was insanely high. I changed the controller imput from 'wheel' to 'gamepad' and the sensetivity issue was fixed, but nothing felt real, as when holding the wheel still in real life, the wheel kept turing in the game, it took getting used to and did work but I didn't really like it and it caused coutless MVAs.
Once I was hooked properly on the game I invested in a Logitech G920 racing wheel which has a 900 degrees turning radius. All my problems were fixed, the driving force shifter felt realistic and worked perfectly, the amount I turned the wheel in real life was mirrored in the game.
The scenery in the game is very good and HD but is out of places in a lot of the game, my fix for this is to either go with a scenery mod like ProMods, which is a bit of a hassle to get working or try the Scandinavia expansion. I bought the expansion and it looked really good, I've never been to Scandinavia but I got a feel for the place, it looked really good and was definitely woth buying.
Going East came with my version of the game, but didn't really click with me, the east side of the map felt just like the rest of it but the price reflects that I think.
I would recommend both Going East and definitely the Scandinavia expansion if you love to drive, but if you just want to mess around and are casual, don't bother.
As I got more into Euro Truck Simulator 2 I starting looking for ways to improve my experience, origionally I looked towards VR and the oculus rift which the game is compatible with, but the price put me off so I instead bought Track IR 5 with the standard head clip. The clip worked and fits onto any hat, and meant I could look around the environment as if I was in it. Although expensive, really cool and awesome.
One of the things that I love about Euro Truck Simulator 2 is the endless posibilities with customization of trucks, you can change everything... literally everything, the wheels, tyres, exausts, sun visors, interior trim, and loads more! There are endless posibilites and having played lots of the Truckers multiplayer have never seen anyone with a truck like mine.
One thing missing from the game I think is some realistic damage to the environment and your truck, which never happens, everything is clean and un-dented. Hopefully SCS can think about that one.
Overall Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a brilliant game, very much woth the money and heaps of fun to play if you are serious or want to mess around. I recomend this game to anyone with interested in driving games as it is in my oppinion the most realistic driving simulation on the market. There are plenty of mods to have fun with so is perfect for any player,
Thanks for reading and happy trucking,

I came to the Hitman games pretty late with my first being Blood Money. The things that I loved about that game were the 'hiding in plain sight' mechanics with sometimes ridiculous costumes and weapons. The other great part is that I could truly achieve my goal in any way that I wanted. I tend to play stealth games with a fetishistic dedication to not getting spotted and in Hitman you could save and reload to be as OCD as you needed on each run - aiming for Silent Assassin each time. The only issue with the game was that it had inconsistencies in AI and in its own rules that prevented the stealth/disguise mechanics from being 100% reliable.
Absolution sadly strayed from this and whilst I enjoyed the game, it became more pure stealth and suffered from a lack of imagination in its kills or gameplay.
I am extremely pleased to say that the new Hitman is a brilliant return to a more Blood Money style of game but with more consistently performing mechanics. The line of sight guard vision whilst trespassing is completely reliable and if it looks like you will be spotted, you will. Disguises now ping a white spot above people who will rumble you if you get too close. Poisoning drinks as a waiter is not conspicuous and people react predictably as in real life with distractions and events in the world. Full disclosure: I have been a fan of Game Grumps since the channel began, and am part of the LGBT community. By all standards, I should be part of the group who most heavily supported the game.
On the surface, it's a cute game. The basic premise is pretty standard for the genre, the art is appealing and colorful. There's a lot of diversity, and the game doesn't really lock you into anything short of having to play a gay/bisexual man with a daughter. The story, for what it is, is well-written and flows well enough. Some of the characters are quirky and memorable.
That's really all that can be said about this game's good features. Everything else is bad.
It was launched as an unfinished product... late. The devs made it pretty clear that this was a cash cow that they weren't to concerned about because they knew LGBT/GG fans would pay the $15 on launch. It's not worth $15, and even if they fixed everything (as of today, the game is still incomplete), I wouldn't give them $15. They simply haven't earned it, and their decision to "take mental health breaks" IMMEDIATELY upon launch screams suspicious to me. It's a shame, because some of the collaboraters did a fantastic job and their work was used to take advantage of people.
The game is ridiculously short for the price. The game has very little branching narrative, so most of the time it takes to play is repeating the same dialogue many times over. Also, as a result, there's basically no replayability once you've played all the routes. It's linear enough to be boring and tedious to complete, even by dating sim standards. There's too many free or cheaper dating sims that have more branches/content to forgive this laziness.
Some of the routes suffer heavily due to the limited length. The narrative becomes forced and awkward; it doesn't really feel like you get to know these characters. Some of these romances would barely work as friendships due to how limited your interaction with the characters are, and it makes the endings feel especially unsatisfying. You have to play every single possible route to even begin to feel like these characters aren't flat, boring archetypes.
The voice acting is minimal, which would be fine if they hadn't pushed how amazing and great the voice acting is. They acted as though it was fully voiced, but it is essentially the same 5 grunts for each character.
The music is fine at first, but obnoxiously loud and repetitive. You will get tired of it if you choose to play every route, and even more tired of it if you choose to do every (available) achievement. Turn it off; you'll be glad you did.
In short:
If you can get this game for dirt cheap, it might be worth it. However, the devs simply don't deserve your money, because they released a half-baked game without even ensuring that it was fully playable. It's short, it's bland, and it's gimmicky. If you're looking for a good dating sim, there are many better choices. Don't let the diversity or the financial backing from Game Grumps fool you into thinking they care at all about you, the genre, or being good developers.

If you are looking at the reviews because you are hesitating on buying this game, before i make a review i should say this:
1-If you don't have it already, go and buy ''FTL: Faster than Light'' (People say this game is similar to FTL but i really don't think so, just ideas on core game mechanics are similar, gameplay is different)
2-If you have FTL and you are looking something VERY similar, then go and buy ''Space Rogue'' (It is not a masterpiece like FTL, it is just an average game but it is closest thing to FTL you can currently find in here)
Now, my review on this game(No spoilers):
Story: It is pretty plain and basic, i am saying that because you can see very similar storylines at other similar games (like Homeworld), i didn't like it BUT devs of this game made a good lore for game itself, it covers its basic story and making you feel you are making real decisions through the game. You will feel a poor but solid RPGish feeling through the game. I really don't know if random dialogs/decisions to make pops up in random sectors or in pre-generated sectors yet. There are also some particular quests.
Gameplay: First of all it is rogue-like, you will have only one save and it will save&exit from the game. There are 4 different difficulty levels. Your ship crews will gain experience from events and combat but not as different individuals...it will actually look like your ship is leveling. You will pick 1 ability within 3 different abilities at each level of each ship. You will have 1 ship at the beginning of the game; as i understand you can't change that ship BUT you can purchase 4 more ships to command from different shipyards. Which means you can have a 5 ship small fleet to yourself as you progress. There are several ship classes so you have to make a good combination of classes to work. All ship classes have differents shapes, sizes, hull, shield and reactor powers. Their number of weapon/activated or passive ability slots are different as well. I think...variety of all these things are not sufficient for my taste but well, they will do; i have seen lots of worse examples afterall.
Space/Area map: Similar to FTL. Danger level increasing slightly at each sector jump in every solar system. (Because you are messing with everything you encounter and your enemies naturally don't like it.)
Event dialogs: There will be an event dialog in almost each jump, which will kinda change your current goal in that jump. You will decide what to do about whatever it is in that sector. As i said dialogs and its options are simplyfied but it is still ok.
Combat: Real time combat with holy pause button (space) No aiming, just selecting enemy to shoot at and selecting weapon and/or active ability to shoot with. There are also buffs&debuffs. As you will have more than 1 ship, also enemies are almost always striking in small or large packs. I have a feeling it will become boring after a while. There are some defend etc. type of missions at some of the sectors. Not just shoot your way out.
Controls: Really good.
Music: Good and fitting but repeating same thing over and over.
In game dialogs: You are playing a human looking race with an alien language....it is (speech) VERY ANNOYING.
Overall: 6.5 or 7 out of 10.
**Review edited after making it to last boss on 3rd run at easiest difficulty level.

How did they go so wrong?
Setting:
I have three main issues with the setting of Arkham Origins. First, the map is pointlessly huge. It's at least twice as large as the map or Arkham City for absolutely no reason. Riddler trophies and riddles are gone, the amount of sidequests hasn't increased, and the plot could have been easily condensed to North Gotham, where most of the game takes place anyways.
Second, Gotham City itself is poorly designed. Everything is just too big. You can't even see the ground most of the time, and the cityscape is littered with buildings that are so huge the game won't let you climb them. The architecture of the city ranges from ugly to bizarre, but it mostly comes across of bland. And don't get me started on the bridge, which seems to exist for no other reason than to incentivize you to use the fast-travel system you wouldn't need if the bridge wasn't there.
Finally, why does a game set years before Arkham City seem more modern than its predecessor? An easter egg in Arkham City revealed that the game is set prior to 2000 (presumably in the late 90s), and yet Origins is full of the technological and cultural hallmarks of the 2010s: drones, the Internet, even Occupy-style political strife. The game is littered with anachronisms--even Batman's gear seems more advanced than it did. It's plain that the developers didn't want to make a prequel, and only set the game in the past to get around the Joker's inconvient demise at the end of Arkham City.
Characters:
Batman is nothing without his Rogues Gallery. It's the strongest of any comic universe, and full of colorful characters like Two-Face, the Scarecrow, Catwoman and Mr. Freeze. None of whom appear in this game.*
Instead, the developers chose to saturate Origins with weak, second-string antagonists like Firefly, Deadshot, Copperhead and *groan* Anarky. Even the game's faux antagonist, Black Mask, isn't a "classic" Batman villain. The presence of characters like Branden, Calendar Man and Alberto Falcone shows that the developers have, at least, read Year One and The Long Halloween. So where's Two-Face? Where's Catwoman? Where are Poison Ivy and Scarecrow? Or, to fit with setting, where's District Attorney Harvey Dent? Where's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-turned-thief Selina Kyle? Where's psychologist Dr. Jonathan Crane, who bother to sign himself in to Blackgate at the beginning of the game but never makes an appeareance?
The four classic villains who do appear--Joker, Bane, Riddler, and Penguin--feel pointlessly contemparized, adding to the anachronistic feel of the game. Bane, despie giving his strongest showing in the series, takes a few ill-advised constume cues from The Dark Knight Rises. Riddler, or Enigma, as the game annoyingly refers to him as, is a hacker, and has planted "extortion files" throughout Gotham City. It's about as boring as it sounds. Penguin, who made an excellent showing in Arkham City, goes over the top, getting not one, but two annoying eye-candy sidekicks (neither of whom are named Lark, Jay, or Raven). Then there's the Joker.
I remember that everyone was a little relieved by the Joker's death at the end of Arkham City. The relationship between the clown and the bat had been masterfully potrayed for two games in a row, and now, at its crescendo, the clown spectacularly met his demise. The death of the Joker was an fantastic tragedy, and opened the possibilty of focusing on new villains in the series' future (Arkham City set up Scarecrow as the antagonist of the next game). To top it all, Mark Hamill, who had lent his voice to the best performance of the clown prince for decades, announced that he was retiring the character. A bittersweet, but fitting end to Hamill's unparalleled run.
The developers of Arkham Origins didn't get the point. Instead of realizing that Hamill's parting performance as Joker couldn't be topped and it was time to move on, they set Origins in the past so they could bring the Joker back ONE MORE TIME. And it isn't worth it. Troy Baker's performance as Hamill's Joker is passable, and does occasionally shine (his first seduction of Harley Quin is his strongest moment), but it feels like Origins is trying to recapture something that wasn't meant to be. Instead of taking the opportunity to push the series forward, they fall back into their comfort zone and turn it up to 11. If anything, the Joker appears even more in Origins than in the rest of the series, mainly because characters like Poison Ivy, Two-Face, Scarecrow, even Victor Zsasz are given the boot.
Which leads into...
Plot:
The plot tries to be a lot of things: the origin of the strange relationship between Batman and the Joker, Alfred coming to terms with Bruce's double life as Batman, and the birth of the partnership between Batman and Gordon. It does none of these things very well. Alfred comes across as an annoying nagger whose feelings change at the drop of a hat, Gordon's faith in the GCPD despite evidence of corruption so overwhelming even his annoying daughter is yelling it in his face isn't believable, and the Joker feels like he's been dug up to go at it with the Batman one more time just to sell another entry in the Arkham series. Which is he has.
The sidequests, besides Mad Hatter, are forgettable.
Gameplay:
Compared to the other entries in the series, Origins is a very hard game. The game is balanced for the Electrocutioner's gloves (which are the only reason Electrocutioner appears in the game), so fights are too difficult for the first half of the game and too easy for the second half. Brawling, rather than stealth, is the focus of the game. However, enemies are equipped with an ever-growing arsenal of annoying weapons and abilities to ensure Batman's trademark free-flow combat is as choppy and useless unless the Electrocutioner's gloves are activated.
The boss fights range from incredibly frustrating (Bane) to annoyingly easy (Deathstroke), but they never fail to not be fun. Deathstroke is a not-very-cleverly disguised quicktime event, and Bane's various fights require you to charge up the Electrocutioner's gloves to inflict damage. Both are fairly representative of what you'll find in Origins, with the exception of the Mad Hatter, whose boss fight, or rather boss-adventure, is a welcome break from zapping your foes with your fists.
Conclusion:
I wanted to enjoy this game. But the more I played it, the more it became clear that Origins was ill-concieved on a fundamental level. If you're a huge fan of the Arkham Series, like I am, you'll probably enjoy some of it. But there are too many steps in the wrong direction, even for a game obviously playing it safe, for me to recommend it.
*Mr. Freeze appears in the suprisingly strong Cold, Cold Heart DLC, a retelling of Freeze's origin story from the Batman: The Animated Series episode "Heart of Ice."

tl;dr: Good base engine, but my recommendation varies based on the actual scenario you are looking to play. Some are worth it, some aren't.
Starting with the bad first: The devs have admitted to have blundered a bit in their pricing and DLC policy, which is true, but their admission goes to their credit. The scenarios are a bit uneven in quality, with some (e.g. Berlin) being pretty interesting from a tactical/strategic standpoint, while others (e.g. Waterloo) are rather broken. For example, playing Waterloo against the AI, all one has to do is turn Napoleon's main force against the Prussians rather than waiting for the British to assemble. Instant win, as the Prussians can't even score a hit on Napoleon's troops. The AI isn't equipped to handle this.
Why then, do I recommend this? It's quite simple: the game is still fun. The ruleset is simple enough to be pick-up-and-play if you've ever even remotely had any contact with wargames, but just in-depth enough to be interesting when used in the right scenario. This is what it comes down to: some scenarios are worth the asking price and more, while others aren't. I highly recommend checking the forum and reviews once more roll in for which scenarios are worthwhile.

I'm feeling a bit of whiplash.
--------------------PROS--------------------
-Level Design. The levels are massive, they vary, and they are most certainly fluid. VIP's, targets, and other important people will flee the area, security in toe, if any obvious murders or major crimes occur. There is a lot of things to interact with, interesting opportunities yielding unique ways of approaching and killing targets, accidents are back again, and crowds can make disappearing easier or harder depending on how you work. Besides actual gameplay, the levels are certainly good looking, beautiful even.It's like a pleasant mix between the beauty of Absolution's levels and the well designed and functional levels in Blood Money.
-Disguises. This was something that was massively improved over the last wreck of a game. Disguises are much more realistic, having only some guards or staff that are wary of infiltrators or simply ones that have seen you do some bad things.Targets that control an event or compound will know their staff members' faces and will become suspicious of new faces.
-Melee. Best in the series, by far. Melee isn't novelty. It's a very suitable way to knock out, sabotage, or just bludgeon your way into a new situation that works in your favor. Throwing blunt items knocks out annoying guards, sharp weapons instantly kill enemies leaving a "what just happened?" kind of reaction to any witnesses or large crowds. Your fiber wire can silently kill enemies and allow you to drag them away quickly.Thrown items have a nifty lock-on, as well, making it easier for you.
-Agency Drops. Weapons can be smuggled in on you or in drop-points around the level. Easy to use system lets you choose an area on the map for you to store an item for later pickup.
-47. Our favorite Psychopath returns. I'm not sure why he let a good-guy play him in the last game, but he's back to being our favorite feeling-less assassin. 47 no longer complains about killing people, doesn't save little girls, and certainly doesn't stop bad-guys from becoming world dominators. He kills people for money. That's it. He doesn't give a flying fuch (gottagetmahsoup) who he kills. And that's the way it always should have been. Honestly, his new look isn't my favorite (I preferred contract's face), but it looks good enough I suppose. Speaking of looks...
-Graphics. Best looking graphics I've ever seen.
--------------------CONS--------------------
-Online Requirement. Yeah yeah yeah, this kills the game for you. It makes it impossible to play sometimes, and I really do mean that. However, it's pretty avoidable. Just play online, and everything is fine. Honestly, I feel like this is exaggerated greatly.
-Episodic Releases.It's eh. Certainly makes it look like less instead of more, and it creates this sense of "oh crud I have to pay the whole price THEN wait for dlc." feeling.
-Guns. Literally no customization for our shooty-bangs and I'm not quite sure why. This was needed. Honestly, they could've copy and pasted Blood Money's and satisfied pretty much everyone.
-Voices. In mah head, everywhere, always the same. Americans have overtaken the world. We have murdered accents and language out of every man, woman, and child. Even Italian priests don't have an accent or even speak different languages. We are one. We are legion.
-Settings. I'm the ashamed owner of a desktop with an integrated graphics card. Do you know what that means? Just in case you don't, I'll explain. It means that I don't have a graphics card, just some mutated mess of inter-coital motherboard and graphics card combo. It basically means my computer is an obese laptop. Why am I telling you this? I'm telling you this because I can run this game on lowest settings at 10 fps. It's my fault right? Definitely, because I'm bad at picking a functioning desktop. But with a bit of elbow grease, I was able to kick out 30 frames through regedit (a tool used for opening registries and changing values, like settings). There are settings that help you get some good frames in, you just have to go through hoops to change them. They limited the ingame settings so drastically people can't even run the game. I know my computer sucks ♥♥♥♥ and I know it's my fault but why would they PURPOSELY LIMIT YOUR ABILITY TO RUN THE GAME?
-Contracts. No one gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥about these, just make one or two more levels instead.
--------------------TLDR--------------------
It's the worthy successor to Blood Money that we wanted, you just need to have a great computer or be a desperate mother-♥♥♥♥er like me.

HITMAN is a return to form for Agent 47, and I absolutely love it.
Whereas Absolution strayed away from the formula that made the game before it so great (Blood Money), HITMAN firmly throws you back into massive, open ended levels (no immersion breaking escapes through a loading screen to the next area), with an obscene amount of ways to approach the level and complete the objectives/kill the targets.
It's exciting and tense, crammed to the brim with interaction and NPC dialogue. The levels are beautiful, hand-crafted in every nook and cranny (the Himmapan Hotel in Bangkok being my favourite), and playing back through the levels has been a pleasure.
I write this review now, as I believe there is MORE than enough content to pick it up if you've been avoiding it until more bits came out. There's 5 levels at the moment, but 2 of them have Alternative Missions that completely change the way the level looks, feels, and plays. On top of that are Escalations, and on top of that you have Contracts if that's something that appeals to you. More than enough content.
Replayability is the big one here. You could spend hours on Blood Money, completing 'A New Life' a different way each time, and I really missed that on Absolution as for the most of the time, it felt like we were just progressing through the level to get to the end.
In HITMAN, you're left to your own devices from the start. Listen in on convos, gather Intel, take in the scenary, then go find your targets and kill them in the coolest way possible.
All in all, I am ecstatic that IO have taken Hitman to the next level. It's not a nostalgic feeling, it's a satisfied feeling that the Hitman series has progressed forward, and not just tried to recreate what made their games so great in the past. The AI are smarter, the details are more varied, the hits are creative.
And it's got an increasingly good story ticking away in the background, which reveals itself subtley as you play!
What a game, 5* and highly recommended.

A couple of tips:
1. This game is hard.  If you're only a casual Roguelike player like me, start the difficulty on Rookie, or you'll be lucky to make it to the second system.
2. Choose a support ship.  Pulsars are godsends in the early game.  The only reason I was finally able to get anywhere in the run I finished was thanks to my little pulsar.  After that, choose a light ship that appeals to you, and fill in the role of heavy later on.

I'm pretty sure that a lot of people who look at this game think "ah, it's like FTL - but you have several tiny ships that you fly around with instead". For the most part that turns out to be true, but desptite the many similarities to the great FTL, there are few things in this game that seem to click and come together for me.
It's the kind of game that I really want to work and succeed, but no matter how many times I've replayed it, things just never end up being fun. The battles, which I feel should be the main pull of this game, tend to play out as waiting games for me. Usually I just order my ships to target one opponent at a time and slowly grind down it's shield and hull, while simultaneously firing of skills, special weapons and other disapointingly ineffective abilities.
Then you move on to the next one, and the next, until the current wave is downed. After that you fly a little distance, a new wave spawns, and you start another waiting session. It's all rather uninspiring and uninteresting in the long run.
A few ideas and features attempt to mix things up a bit, such as fragile sniping ship(can't recall it's name) with a huge damage potential, but in the end my ships are mostly just sitting there, grinding. Ocassionally I'm forced to move them a bit in order to avoid a hostile ability or such, but too often I'd just let it hit me since the battle has already been won and I'm just waiting for it all to end anyway.
Progressing throughout the map and trying to reach the end goal also has it's issues. I can rarely afford anything interesting to buy for my ships, and once I finally gather up enough credits to do so, the effect is so marginal that I might just as well have skipped the purchase altogether.
To their credit though, the developers have been nibbling quite a lot at the balance and given it an honest effort. Sadly, I think the core design issues are too large to fix in a quick manner and this game will never work out and become the hit that I'd like it to be.

+ Clean, crisp art direction and UI lend much to this game's ease of play.
+ Common sense mechanics and application of said mechanics to the gameworld is simple, and comprehensive. Emergencies like fires can have obvious knock-on effects to the workings of a prison if not handled properly. Not having enough free time for prisoners can make them unruly. Too much and they may have time to prepare an escape.
+ Solid developer support during early access.
- Art direction may be a bit bare to some.
- One can argue the controversial nature of handling a prison, and its knock-on arguements about criminal correction, rights of prisoners, and the like.
- Took time to really develop during early access, leading to some early adopters burning out before it really flourished.

If you want a good example of how a game should be developed and launched, look at how the guys at Introversion have done it with Prison Architect. Monthly video updates from the guys with the new features outlined in detail, a good bug bash reporting system with entire months dedicated to streamlining the experience and a team that listen to it's fan base.
The result is a fantastic game with plenty to keep you occupied for hours, whether you are building your Prison or attempting to escape from it. Worth every penny.
Keep up the good work Introversion!!!

I think the game is pretty fun. It's like "RISK the Boardgame, Superdeluxe Edition" or something like this. This is NOT a big wargame and anyone who expects something deep like Gary Gigsby or the likes will be severly dissapointed.
The game plays very slow, each turn is in phases and because theres a (quick) animation between the phases the overall pace drops severely. This is added by the battles being in phases as well, also with both popups and watching the 10-sided dice go. A single battle doesnt take too long, but since you don't have any input, and there may be quite some battles per turn, this can drag on. The battles are actually quite weak I think, they look cool, kind of reminds me of "Victory and Glory Napoleon" or what it was called, but you have, besides maybe putting a card down in the beginning, not really any influence.
Now not having any influence might be OK, there's many games where you dont, but if I don't, I'd like the battles to speed up, because in Normandy for example, you might have 5 battles in a row with no input from your side whatsoever, each taking it's sweet time to role the dice and give you many many unnecessary popups.
This get's annoying over time, but for me personally, not a dealbraker. Do keep in mind that when you sit down to play this you really want a drink or something because you'll spend quite some time not giving any orders and just waiting and clicking away textboxes.
The game had a pretty rough start with a broken Scenario (Hastings), BUT I dont feel like this is representative of the overall quality of the game. When the first thing that happened was the game crashing multiple times I was shocked, but now that I played the other scenarios, I did not encounter more bugs and feel like the QA did a decent job, yes they missed a HUGE one, but **** happens, right? Also: The Devs were very quick in the Forum to respond to both bugs, Ideas and critique, so I feel that should be mentioned here.
Also: The pricing policy of the game changed right after release, and as someone who bought the "classic edition" because I wanted the smaller maps (It used to be that both packs only give 3 scenarios), I now feel kind of cheated, because the Expanded Edition now has all the scenarios of Classic + the other three for just 4 Euros more - while these would cost me 30 Euros in DLC! Now I know I shouldn't complain, just because someone got something for free... but still...
Also, I think even after the price changes the DLC are way too pricy. 10 Euro is enough for a decent game, asking this much for what is basically just a map is too much I feel.
But enough of my whining, to summarize, I think it's fun and depending on your personal value of money the game might be worth it.
So TLDR: I would probably get it again, I'd buy the Extended Edition now that you get so much more for the 4 Bucks (5 when the sale ends), but actually right now I would wait a tad, the developer mentioned a "complete pack" coming soon and depending on the price of that, it might be worth it since the single DLC are so increadibly expensive....
Hope this helps! :)

Having the played previous 2 titles on the XBOX 360 console, I decided to get Batman Arkham Origins too when I switched over to gaming on the PC. Like it's predecessors, Arkham Origins offer the same free flow combat and roaming experience. There isn't much of an improvement except for some newer gadgets. Players are also yet again challenged to complete side missions given by the entity commonly known as the Riddler.
However, although the gameplay may be somewhat repetitive(reminds me of Assassin's Creed as a money sapping franchise eh?) the storyline is entertaining enough to make users focused and engaged. Even on a harder difficulty, combat is seemingly easy but getting combos allows for Batman to use some spectacular moves that manages to make me the player want to challenge myself harder and get longer combos.
To sum it all up, Batman Arkham Origins isn't something I would get on release due to it being too generic and not really well worth the money. However I would certainly get it if it were on sale as players would get entertained for awhile before moving on to another game. In fact, somehow, as compared to Assassin's Creed, I would very much prefer AC due to the richer storyline. In addition, Batman is well just Batman. Gameplay, storytelling are basically almost the same as it's predecessors, there isn't really anything much new to the table thus all in all I would give Arkham Origins nothing more than a mere 7/10, 2 points above average just for the effort made, and the fact that it is on a much larger scale than it's previous titles.

This game is genuinely entertaining: I look forward to the episodes coming out each month, and even the elusive targets. For fans of the franchise, think Blood Money, but with a modern engine.
Whilst it has less of a sense of humour than Blood Money, with fewer ridiculous murder methods, the AI is mostly OK, the levels have a wonderful sense of scale and escapism and the levels have good replayability.
A few things need to be fixed, but thus far I'm hopeful that the final product will be worthwhile. For those who haven't bought the game yet, I suspect they'll miss out on the 'elusive targets'. These are missions which pop up every few weeks. You only really get one attempt at them, and if you screw it up, you permanently fail them.
I'm not sure how I feel about that: on the one hand, it really does add to the suspense. Where I'd drop a save before doing something stupid in the normal game, in ET's, every action has a sense of weight. On the other hand, I really don't like not being able to replay these things. It feels artificially constrained and I've failed one of the ET's because the game bugged out rather than a failure on my part.
The game has become more stable, and now does run far more acceptably than when I first bought it. The developers haven't done something as stupid as the Latex Murder Nuns of Absolution. It is a fun, entertaining Hitman game and I definitely recommend it - but with the caveat that there are still a few AI flaws, ET's are once only, and the final two missions are still unknowns.
------------
Edit: Somehow I've managed to sink 100hrs+ into this game. The ET's are getting more varied, but the escalations are a bit dull. Some mechanics (I'm looking at you headturning) can make the game's stealth a bit hit or miss, but ultimately I can strongly recommend this game for anyone who liked Blood Money.

Undertale is by far one of the best games on Steam. If you are unsure about getting it, DON'T BE. Undertale has ruined my life in the best way possible. I am now an eternal fangirl. Don't think twice for another SECOND. CLICK PURCHASE RIGHT NOW because your understanding of game mechanics and storylines is about to be flipped on its head. 20/10 rating. 15 stars. UNLIMITED THUMBS UP. Undertale is one of the best things I've ever stumbled across.
My friend bought Undertale for me, and I could not be more grateful to him. At the same time, I want to punch him in the face ten times more than usual because now I cry at the thought that I'll never get to eat spaghetti with Papyrus.
Not to mention, the MUSIC. Undertale's soundtrack BLEW ME AWAY. I have all of the songs downloaded on Spotify and I listen to them constantly. The track called "Undertale" (yes it was named after the game itself) makes me cry uncontrollably.

Undertale is an amazing game. It gets a lot of hate because of the fandom, which is understandable because the fandom is garbage. However, the game itself is great. The most important thing to do before you play is to shield yourself from spoilers. It's so much better to just play through it not knowing what to expect. This game was inspired by the classic and amazing SNES game Earthbound, and it lives up to it's inspiration. The music in Undertale is amazing. It's such a good soundtrack. The reason I started playing this game was because the soundtrack was so good. In fact, I think the soundtrack is actually better than the game. The game itself is good, but way too short. Undertale only takes a few hours to complete. However,  replay value is insane. I've played through this game a handful of times, and I've gotten multiple completely different endings. The battle system is simple. You can either talk your way through battles, or use brute force to destroy your enemies. This is what determines the outcome of the story. During your opponents turn, you have to dodge attacks by moving around in a small box.
The dialogue in Undertale is hilarious. Every time I play it I always find myself laughing. Undertale has a good story, but the game is too short and the story doesn't have time to develop. You don't really feel a very strong connection to the characters due to how short the game is. Earthbound is a 30-40 hour long game,  and it has time to develop characters. By the time the game is over you feel a very strong connection to the characters. Undertale tries to make those connections in a lot less amount of time, and makes up for this with emphasized humor. This works, but not as well as just having a longer game. That's Undertale's main flaw. It's too short. It was made by mainly one guy over the course of a few years, which is why it's short. This game would be so much better if more people worked on it, and if it would be longer. Undertale is still a good game despite its problems.  It's fun, funny, and the soundtrack is outstanding. I would definitely recommend this game. Just don't go near the fandom ;)

So there are two main components in this game - when you fight on foot and when you fight with your car.

Car combat - sweet stuff. Your main weapon is your own car which you will slam into opponenets after pressing turbo boost for extra damage. You can also use side flamethrower and grappling hook (and boring overpowered homing thrown explosives that will ruin the fun).
You are on a mission to liberate wasteland from bullies from Gastown to rightful owners - some dudes who don't even have a car. Story is very boring.
Repetiveness is great - none of the 4 area bosses is any different, each camp has different architecture but you do the same all the time - blow stuff up and beat all opponents.
As you go you gonna collect scrap and xp points that you will use to level up skills and upgrade car and personal gear.
Car mechanics are great although a little linear - each next item is just better than earlier, no alternative engine like (less speed but much better handling or acceleration).

+difficult enemies if you are not using thrown explosive spears all the time
Cons:
-foot combat
-repetiveness
-boring story
