In the end I would probably recommend this game. Not because it would be particularly delightful to play. Actually, at times, the cover shooting mechanics are totally infuriating, the hordes of enemies you encounter become dull very fast and your squad seems very, very useless.
It is quite obvious that this game is played for its story. I'm pretty sure it is quite well known at this point that this game is about war crimes, sanity, reality and morality. Most of the time the choices are forced on you, which might feel like cheating, but I think the narrative wouldn't work as it does if the player really had a freedom of choice. It is pretty damn obvious that clear majority of human kind would not commit war crimes or other atrocities, as normal reality permits our minds to stay intact. If the player really would get to make a clear-headed decision whether or not kill civilians or be an all-around bad guy, the choice would be robbed of its meanings. Either the player does the sensible thing (from normality's perspective) or roleplays a total psychopath, doing bad things only because they are evil, not because there is actually some "logical" reasoning behind the choice. Engaging in small digression, I actually think many choices in RPG-games are bereft of true meaning in this way: it just is pretty difficult to assume a role and stay consistent when you are sitting behind a screen.
The game attemps to shed some light on war crimes, PTSD and whatnot. It could be taken as giving jabs to violent entertainment in general, problematizing mindless violence that often serves as the greatest form of interaction games usually provide, especially in the genre of war-themed FPS games. I still would've wanted to see a game that takes a stronger stance on this. Even though the game puts you in an uncomfortable situation, massacring civilians and whatnot, the interaction it provides still revolves totally around killing endless hordes of faceless bad guys. Even though this could be taken as a part of the games morals, I believe a more sturdier anti-war sentiment could've been conveyed if developers would've attempted to mold the action scenes more elegantly. Possibly it wasn't the job for this game, but I certainly believe it is an important task for some game.
Story is pretty good, mechanics are a bit poopy, what else. The game looks good, but it contains surprisingly little pre-arranged scenic views and sights for the player to stumble upon. A war-wrecked Dubai could very well have room for vistas like this, but some technical limitations have probably prohibited them. The optional collection quests are well integrated into the story and gives you a real reason to hunt for them. The length of 5-7 hours on normal difficulty is compact and I enjoyed it. The story did not need any dragging on and the game itself wasn't so good that I would've wanted to play it any longer.

So far in my life I have only played two games with such moral complexity that I would say as a gamer, you HAVE to play them. One of those games is Shadow of the Colossus and the other one is.... Spec-Ops: The Line. I'm not going to spoil the big plot twists because this is a game that spoilers will ruin. I can't stress how much you need to play Spec-Ops: The Line. Anyway, over all Spec-Ops: The Line is a sophisticated deconstruction of the modern warfare genre and one of the most down right brilliant games I have ever played. So when you start Spec-Ops, the first hour is nothing special. You play as Captain Walker, a special forces operative on a mission to rescue civilians in Dubai because massive sandstorms have totaled the city. The game starts as your typical, generic, linear, modern-warfare shooter as you meaninglessly gun down "enemies". It's not until after the first hour when the game starts getting interesting. You quickly find that things are not as what they seem then plot twists unfold and by the end you are left thinking about who is really the bad guy. Usually I say that a good game connects gameplay, narrative, and design which Spec-Ops: The Line does this flawlessly. The design starts off very modern as the story and gameplay are utterly generic. But as the narrative starts to dive into the psyche of Captain Walker as he goes totally insane, the design of the dull environments seamlessly transitions into looking and feeling more vivid, colorful, and surreal. Gameplay isn't anything special, you just shoot tons of people like any other modern warfare game but it's amazing how the narrative contextualizes and comments on the gameplay by asking questions like who were those people, why are you shooting them, why does that make you the hero, and what is any of the killing even worth? The gameplay also feels clunky and stressful which these mechanics intentionally feel this way to serve as metaphors that help express some of the major themes of the narritive during gameplay. The narrative paints most of your actions in the game with a coat of moral ambiguity which makes Spec-Ops: The Line profound, brilliant, and complex. As for the plot, it is driven by Captain Walker's coherent character arc as he and his squad are isolated and thrown into a hostile environment and any humanity is stripped away along with compassion, reason, and rationality until only a monster remains. But it's brilliant how Spec-Ops questions the morality of the player by involving them in the gameplay because we essentially control Captain Walker. This raises some interesting questions about the relationship between player and player-character. Are Walker's actions merely our own? Or do we just represent the last thoughts of reason in his damaged mind as he railroads us into committing more war crimes. Even the gameplay starts reflecting the narrative as Walker goes more and more insane, his hallucinations slowly start becoming intertwined with gameplay until you aren't even sure what is real or not. This game is a masterpiece in storytelling and you just have to experience it.

I rather enjoy the overall atmosphere of Distant Star: Revenant Fleet. The story is interesting and the events that unfold are really cool to read (even if a few may repeat themselves during a run). The soundscape is great. The music very much reminds me of Homeworld while being its own. And I just love the sounds the ships make when you give them orders.
There are elements of this game that are reminicent of FTL. The way you jump from point to point, sector to sector, culminating in a final boss-like battle. How each point may have a random (or non-random) event. Each sector has an overaching theme (hostile/friendly/neutral in this case). All of this I really like, in both games.
Combat is enjoyable. Seems overly simplistic at first. Then you get into later battles and realize positioning and timing your skill activations become very important to survival.
My biggest knock against this game: not enough event variation. While there are a decent number, this title could use more. And there are some events that feel like they should happen only once, but I had occur multiple times (usually in different sectors).

This is a fun, tactical rogue space fleet combat game with light RPG elements.  For $10 it was well worth the 8 hours of enjoyment I got out of it.  I like that it is procedural, every "map" isn't the same.  You also get to make choices how you progress through a region.  The save game feature is limited, but really isn't a deal breaker (and I am normally a save-freak).  The most important advice:  always buy supplies!  This will make everything else easier.  I ended up bulding to a 3 Dreadnaught, one Carrier, One Assault fleet that worked really well.  While movement tactics are simple, you do need to keep moving to minimize damage.  I agree with others that all of it's elements are simpler than implementations in other games but for what it is...a simple, easy to just drop in and play a mission, game, it does all of the elements fine.  The only weakness I would say is the RPG element.  I only saw a couple of instances where my decision made a clear difference.  Most things ended in battle for me anyway.  it still adds a nice additional layer between the battle progression.  There is also obvious repetition in the types of missions (escort, protect bases, capture bases, just fight, etc).  But the maps always change so there is that.

A Mix of FTL and Homeworld, this game grabs much from both parent games, but can't really make the most out of it.
- The Combat is repetitive and the AI is pretty dumb.
- The graphic style is good, but seems to be blurry and unsharp.
- The Maps are very small and the missions on them are repetitive also. Fly there, cap that, destroy these, etc.
- Ships can shoot in any direction, fly in any direction etc. There is no maneuver, or allining the weapons toward the enemy, in other words, no tactic.
- The "RPG" Element is pretty flat aswell. Your Ships progress after a few battles and can pick one of three perks then.
Conclusion: This gmae literally lacks the depth it needs.

This game is genuinely entertaining: I look forward to the episodes coming out each month, and even the elusive targets. For fans of the franchise, think Blood Money, but with a modern engine.
Whilst it has less of a sense of humour than Blood Money, with fewer ridiculous murder methods, the AI is mostly OK, the levels have a wonderful sense of scale and escapism and the levels have good replayability.
A few things need to be fixed, but thus far I'm hopeful that the final product will be worthwhile. For those who haven't bought the game yet, I suspect they'll miss out on the 'elusive targets'. These are missions which pop up every few weeks. You only really get one attempt at them, and if you screw it up, you permanently fail them.
I'm not sure how I feel about that: on the one hand, it really does add to the suspense. Where I'd drop a save before doing something stupid in the normal game, in ET's, every action has a sense of weight. On the other hand, I really don't like not being able to replay these things. It feels artificially constrained and I've failed one of the ET's because the game bugged out rather than a failure on my part.
The game has become more stable, and now does run far more acceptably than when I first bought it. The developers haven't done something as stupid as the Latex Murder Nuns of Absolution. It is a fun, entertaining Hitman game and I definitely recommend it - but with the caveat that there are still a few AI flaws, ET's are once only, and the final two missions are still unknowns.
------------
Edit: Somehow I've managed to sink 100hrs+ into this game. The ET's are getting more varied, but the escalations are a bit dull. Some mechanics (I'm looking at you headturning) can make the game's stealth a bit hit or miss, but ultimately I can strongly recommend this game for anyone who liked Blood Money.

There are much longer reviews, that describe it in greater detail, so I'll keep it short.
Nice tactical spaceship combat game, with simple but effective mechanics, decently deep system of upgrades, ships you can recognize at a glance and, um, void-shattering explosions. Background story is told through mission briefings and such, with additional quests that you can follow but are not mandatory. Missions are pretty believable, as are the dialogs and the choices you need to make  - as in, if you're short with fuel, will you raid a neutral station. Travelling through sectors itself can become interesting - if you have sustained damage, do you travel toward a potential repair facility that can be an ambush or you leave the sector asap, risking an encounter with a stronger enemy...
Now, none of this is really new and nothing here is so mind-blowingly good that you'll write home about it. But all these aspects come together so nicely, they click so well that I am hard pressed to find a better example of  a game being better than the sum of its parts, or for the good old "less is more".
Well done, Blazing Griffin, well done!

Decided to finally review this game since the developers seem to have gotten it in the place that they want it to be, or close. And they did so through AMAZING and dedicated support, that every developer out there should take a page from to be frank. I want this at the top of my review because it's the most critical aspect to me--whether you like a game or not is subjective (aside from mechanical or design flaws), but whether the developers are worth their salt is not. These guys have done well to earn their place in the gaming industry, I think.
About the game itself and my thoughts. I grew up a multigamer, but my core has always been RTS. On that note, the closest gameplay I can associate it to would be something like Ground Control, stuffed into a roguelike progression system with scenario-based play/missions. Frankly, I loved the old Ground Control series as I tended towards a micro-focused RTS player for most of my time. And roguelikes are my favorite genre to play inbetween my mainstay titles.
Sure, this game has had issues upon release and things you can nitpick for a long time afterward. You can read other reviews to get pages upon pages about all of that. I soared through this game like 2-3 weeks after release and got my first win, after only 1-2 attempts on Elite difficulty. There were definitely challenges here and there. I tried to keep pausing to a minimum. But that was expected (imo) from someone with my background. However, the game was still FUN, and the game is even more enjoyable now. Seems more challenging now as well--and that's coming from someone who's played nearly every RTS since Warcraft 2 dropped. It's certainly worth sinking several runs into now, as you should in any roguelike. But bear in mind, I can only speak for Elite difficulty as it's all I've played.
I saw that the devs were initiating a massive campaign of overhauling the game back then, so I let it sit until now. Coming back to it, I can say it's now polished enough to be taken seriously by everyone. Give this title a purchase if you have any interest in squad size RTS at all. The pause feature makes it accessible for literally everyone. I feel like cramming RTS into a roguelike and making it a truly playable title was quite a feat, to be honest. I prefer this over the horde of twin stick shooter roguelikes that have been surfacing the past few years.
I'm hoping Blazing Griffin get enough support and have the desire to add more content to this title. I would love to see this type of game with the depth of replayability that most of the more well known roguelike titles have. How they should go about that, I'm not sure. But I feel like the potential is there. /end rant

Gameplay wise, if you liked Arkham City, then you'll find nothing wrong with Arkham Origins, so long as you can get past some of its bugs. The main selling point would be the story if you're heavily invested into the Arkham series.

Avoid this pile of crap!
Arkham Origins attempts to be what Arkham City was, only more of it.  It has twice the city area to cover, twice the crime scenes, lots of "crimes in progress" to rescue people from, and lots of cut scenes and scripted events.  It also has twice as many continuity errors and is twice as shallow.
It also has lots of bugs, many of them game wrecking.
Sometimes Batman randomly flickers, usually while flying.  Control is terrible, movement is very slow, and the game is very confused.  Usually, diving / crouching will fix the issue.  Usually.
You will find yourself unable to complete certain encounters and events, because you randomly can not interrogate foes.  This is especially problematic post-credits.  (And yes, the credits are 32 minutes long, and cannot be skipped.)
You will find the game randomly not working.  Freeze followed by crash to desktop; often at a check point, leaving your game stuck at that spot.  Really.  Search for Copperhead crash, you'll find many instances of it.
The main story is 10 to 16 hours of gameplay.  The sidequests are another 10 to 20 hours (including all of those dang riddler items).  Plus however long you take to play the challenge maps, and if you do any of the multi-player stuff.
Overall: Good concept, rushed out the door to make money; inadequately tested, and only partially patched.  Not worth the time or money.

This game is not perfect.  But the plot is amazing.  It made me feel like I was Batman more than any other Arkham game.
The plot is far better than in any prior Arkham game, the dialogue is better, and the characters are very good.  The voice acting is competitive with the Conrad\Hamel team we all know so well.
But, most importantly, at no point in playing this game did I start scraming at Batman during a cutscene.  The biggest problem with Arkham Asylum and Arkham City is simply that the Batman of the cutscenes is significantly more stupid\less intelligent than the Batman you have to be to beat the games.  In Arkham Origins, the Batman you have to be to beat the game is about as smart as the one in the cutscenes, and for this, it made me feel like I was Batman more than any other Arkham game.
There are tech issues, yes.  And I never got the game to run as well as I thought it should.  BUT forgive games like "Fallout 3" for these issues because the content is worth it, and the content of this game more than balances out the flaws in the code.
This is a prequel worthy of being a prequel that avoids all the other famous mistakes over prequels in the past.  If you love Batman, you have to get it...but if you can't ignore points where characters get stuck in walls or just run against them blindly, or one or two serious level design flaws that stand out just because the rest of the level design is consummate, you might want to pass.

One of the biggest problems with the other 4 games in the franchise is that they always failed to scare you after a while, because the game wasn't able to throw new things in to scare you. But besides that I loved the other games, and this game fixes that problem, but comes with so many more.
One of the minor problems, but is something definitely present, is the mixed tone.  It tries to be dark, gloomy, and scary, but also tries to be funny.  The TV show in the middle of each night is a great example of it feeling awkard.  After going through a scary and intense night, to sit down and watch a silly show just feels off in terms of tone.  And moments throughout the game where the AI(?) changes his voice are another example, just doesn't fit within the game, no matter how funny it may be.
Another huge problem is this game's "difficulty."  This has been present mainly in FNAF4, but it really shows here.  You are thrown into multiple situations not knowing what to do, they tell you about 10% of what you need to know, and leave the other 90% for you to figure out for yourself.  And they draw out each of these moments out for far too long, and are far too punishing if you fail.  The "puzzles" in this game are like trying to solve an invisible puzzle, and if you screw up once you have to start over, you don't know where you screwed up, but you better not do it again.  Its tedious to say the least.
However when the game is good, it's really, really good.  The voice acting is impressive, the plot is mysterious (although having to go over it again and again if you die or re-open the game is pretty annoying), and the gameplay, once you figure out what to do, is pretty good in some places.   And the game is very scary, and adreneline rushing, and unlike the other 4 games keeps this feel throughout the entire game.
If you liked the other FNAF games chances are you'll be able to overlook these problems, and find enjoyment,  however if not I really wouldn't recommend it.

Look! Even though I recommend this game, there are still some points you need to know.
This has to be if not the best but one of the best call of duty titles out there. Oh, I love the colors in this game. All 3 game modes are enjoyable, but as you can tell, the main thing we are going to focus is the multiplayer.
First of all, campaign. Black Ops II brought us a great campaign with a good story which continues Black Ops I's. If you played previous cod titles, this one will probably not look much different for you. However, it was a good idea that here you continue previous storyline and also play as a new character from future. Oh yes, about future. This futuristic cod had it right on its right level. Why? Because futuristic things did not affect gameplay, yet it was mainly for visual look. During the gameplay, you are given some options which only change cutscenes between levels and the ending only. I am not going to spoil storyline, but I definitely suggest you to pass it at least once.
Zombies. Well, even though the regular map "Green Run" frustrated for lots of reasons such as lava, denizens, large map size, worst wonder weapon and etc. The rest maps are really awesome. "Die Rise" is fun map but sucks when it comes to glitches, stupid perk and falling from the map. "Buried" is interesting when you setup and see how the map itself looks but it gets too repeating and boring if you camp which is the main strategy to play it. "Mob of the Dead" is the map which lots of fans loved and it is satisfying for reasons. It is unusual due to its "ghost" mode, awesome wonder weapon, nice setup system, cool atmosphere and great training spot. "Origins". Ok, this map is the best one ever created. Why? It finally brough us characters from WaW and the time of world war I. There are so many things to do, lots of training spots, many wonder weapons, puzzles, challenges with awards and so on. Forgot to mention, to play these maps you need to have dlcs, which of course sucks.
Now, multiplayer. I can talk about this all day, but I will try my best to explain as shortly as possible. BO2 awards you scorestreaks by killing and now also completing definite objectives.One of the best things about mutiplayer is that this is the most played cod multiplayer on pc. There are at least from 3K up to 10K people playing at one moment. There are many great maps like Nuketown 2025, Carrier, Raid, Hijacked, Studio. Oh no. By the way, if you are going to play only mutiplayer, do not bother buying any dlcs. They will not just make it better, no. Dlcs will make it even worse making it unplayable because only few players own them and there will be only 1 game mode playable and it is "team deathmatch". Personally, I had much fun playing this game, but now, it is not as much fun as it used to be at the beginning. Because you understand what is happening, how other people are playing. Eh... Let us talk about these "players". There are 3 types which probably will annoy the crap out of you: tryhards, campers and hackers. Do not get me wrong, it is still enjoyable enough to play bo2 even with these human species. It is not my excuse of calling them tryhards. I am pretty sure I am a good player. They are just insanely sweaty people always playing with the same overpowered weapons like an-94, scar-h, c4. Their game style is mostly either dropshooting or jumpshooting. I wish their pcs burnt somehow, but anyways now let us talk about campers. Camping is alternative option to play for sure. Yeah... I do not care if some machine gunner or sniper camps, but how cannot I rage if there is some autistic smg gunner, shotgunner or even assault rifler hiding in the corner waiting for someone to come and then these campers shoot their back? I cannot stand it. Also guess who also annoy more? Hackers! Where the hell is our VAC system? There are so many hackers in cod games in mw2 which it led to the point why most players quitted it because it is unplayable now. There are not as many hackers as in its predecessors, but anyways, it makes you either leave the game or keep dying because one or few people have "vsat hack". Let me clear this up for you. There is scorestreak "vsat" which you can activate after you earned it, but there is some hacking program or mod called "vsat hack" which activates in every hacker's game. It basically is a wallhack. There are so many challenges which award you more XP points, calling cards and title emblems. Oh my lord. The whole emblem system is so good in this game, because there is a big variety of forms. If you are a professional or just follow tutorials on youtube, you can make beautiful emblems so you can add them to your profile and weapons. Theatre mode is little glitchy with its hitboxes as always but it does not make it any worse due to its pros. It records any game you have played recently and what is more is that you can make montage right there even from different player's point of view or angle of map. Well, I was about to forget about game and lobby finding system in this game. Yeah there are no dedicated servers... It is not a big deal to be honest but it sucks when you keep getting into the same lobby over and over again. The weapons, perks and equipment are pretty balanced here. Although there are now some things that are overpowered. C4. Oh... Please do not run with scavenger, fast hands perks and keep c4ing everyone. I beg of you. An-94. Why is this overpowered? I will tell. It kills in 3 bullets in most of the time, has no recoil, yet has great iron sight, and main thing why I am mentioning this is that the speed of the first 2 bullets come as fast as the fire speed of average smg 950 rpm and then shoots as common fire speed for assault rifles 750 rpm. I may be made a little mistake with numbers, but I did not exagerrate anything! I could not say that community is bad. You will meet nice people as well as idiotic ones, too. Here is a tip for you. Mute everybody in your lobby and enjoy the game. However, there is a chat. Do not bother reading it. I wish you good luck if you are playing exclusive for pc game "Nukejacked". There people play only 2 maps: Nuketown 2025 and Hijacked but with all possible game modes in game. But the thing is that the maximum amount of players is higher than usual and most of the time you will play on hardcore which makes your health 30%, little regeneration, no HUD, no map, no killcam. Also mainly in Nuketown 2025 there is decent chance to get spawn trapped by some lmg spraying dumb across the map. So just keep that in mind.
The main reason why I love this game and franchise overall, is that there are many variations to play from only knife running class to a complete terminator with 2 lmgs. Yeah...
That is all I guess. I may edit this review few times. Sorry I do not know what to write for tl;dr people. I am really thankful for everyone who read my review!

This is a very, very tentative thumbs up for Distant Star: Revenant Fleet. A 6 or 6.5 out of 10, interesting and enjoyable with serious flaws, worth checking out but not necessarily a genre classic. It's better than FTL, although I have wrapped around to hating FTL so this may be damning DS:RF with faint praise.
I don't particularly like roguelikes but heard about DS:RF through the fine people at Extra Credits and was intrigued. Eventually getting an entire fleet and being able to kit out ships for specific roles, like the tank-y Dreadnought and Pulsar for healing is a nice step up from other roguelikes. The graphics are crisp and really work for the setting, although I got a lot of lag in the last few missions. There's much more of a game to DS:RF than FTL, and racing to capture an orbital factory or destroy a convey before reinforcements showed up was as tense at the end of the game as it was at the start.
On the other hand, I've only beaten the game once and I don't feel like trying again. One of the biggest problems with DS:RF is that there just isn't much variety, and by the end of my winning run I felt like I'd seen everything the game had to offer. All of the missions are either capture a point or destroy a fleet and the combat system isn't quite deep enough to sustain that. Maneuvering the fleet just comes down to shifting whatever ship still has shields to the front, and occasionally dodging an AOE attack. Manually triggered skills are mostly a chore to use. The small ships don't have enough health or shields to make them worthwhile, and the big ships are so expensive I don't see how you could get a full fleet of them by the end.
The economy overall is pretty screwed up. Everything, from ships to gear to fuel, is ludicrously expensive, while mission rewards are laughably small. One unit of fuel costs 1500 credits, while most in game missions offer 2000 or 2500 credits as reward, while the smallest ship costs 10K. This is not even counting better gear for the ships. I would have lost my winning game if I wasn't playing on easy mode, because I ran out of fuel 90% of the way in and of the 4 shops I found in the last level, none of them sold fuel.
I would have given this a thumbs down if I had paid $10 for it. At 50% off, $5 for an ambitious but deeply flawed experience was worth it.

I grew up watching the 'Mad Max' movies and love those movies with a passion. The new one is pretty good too. Then there is this game. This was one of the best games I have ever played, and that is saying a lot. The story is rich and so are all the characters, even Max. I didn't get 100% completion because I didn't want to do all the races with the cars you build. But to me, this game has replay value because I wanted to start over and play through it again. Simply put, I got to the end and didn't want it to end...(but you can continue after the end to get achievements that you missed, or that 100% completion).
You are Mad Max. Your main objective is to build an awesome car from parts you scavenge or win with the help of his sidekick Scumbucket, err I mean Chumbucket. There are different territories you can take over by doing objectives and quests for the certain person that rules over it. When you take over more and more of a territory by lowering the threat, (by taking over outposts, clearing minefields etc.), you can then add upgrades to the main base that territory holds. Doing this will give you perks when you enter that base (like say it will refill all your ammo or give you a full water canteen etc.) All of this to get revenge on Lord Scrotum, I mean Scrotus. Chum and Max call his new car that he builds the Magnum♥♥♥♥♥♥ uh.. I mean Opus. His old car he wrecked was called the Black on Black. (not sure where they get all these silly names.) The car combat gets really intense, as does the actual fighting on foot does too. I agree with some, it does seem like your character levels up fast but I just wanted to experience this game and make the most out of it and take my time. I also love throwing a good beat down on the bad guys.
Exploring and scavenging for water and supplies can get a bit repetative at times, even taking over areas and encampments too. But then again I always had fun with it because it is part of the game. You can stick to the main story line if you want, but it will make your life easier and a little more worthwhile if you experience all this game has to offer. Getting a new part for your car or gear and fighting skills for Max is always kind of exciting. If you love driving and fighting games and a good story line, pick this game up. I got it on sale so I felt like I got my money's worth and more. I would have easily bought it at full price if I knew what good a game it was.

A single dad moves to a town called Maple Bay with his only child, an 18 year old Amanda. As it turns out Maple Bay is full of dads who are ready to date. As Amanda prepares for her transition from high school to college, her dad prepares to enter the dating scene in a town full of handsome dads.
Dream Daddy is a visual novel game with a simple premise: to date a dad of your preference. In it the main protagonist, otherwise known as Dadsona which you can create yourself, joins a social media platform DadBook and messages dads he will want to date. There are 7 dateable dads altogether and they are all very different. After a few dates the last one leads to an ending, good or bad depending on your choices.
I'm not gay, I'm not a male either, I definitely don't have any kids (nor will I want any) and I'm also not a fan of visual novels. So by all accounts Dream Daddy is a game which isn't made for me. I admit I got it mostly because of all of the handsome men I saw on the store page and because it has one-of-a-kind storyline. I've played a couple visual novels despite not liking them much and Dream Daddy intrigued me to the point where I wanted to try it.
Unfortunately I was sorely disappointed and partially blinded by the beautiful hunks. The character artwork is beautiful and easily the hightlight of the game. Whoever designed them deserves a pat on the back. The rest of the artwork is quite the opposite. First of all the dad which you'll create via a character creator will always look ridiculous, no matter what you choose, to the point that I realistically can't see any of the other dads dating him. And the backgrounds, which put bluntly by another reviewer, look more like sketches than finished pieces. It's like two people on the opposite ends of the spectrum worked on the visuals: one who put as much passion as they could muster; and one who just lazily halfassed it all.
Then there's the writing which only makes me cringe and shake my head. The game tries so bad to be funny but more than often overdoes it. So many bad gags, puns, dad jokes and memes about everyone and everything. It's just too much. And the main protagonist is incredibly unfunny. He is socially inept, awkward and insecure and the only thing he's good at is making bad jokes at inappropiate times. Once again I can't understand what any of the dads see in him. And the relationship between the Dadsona and his adult daughter is so bizarre it leads me to believe they're actually robots disguised as humans. He can't function without Amanda: constantly asking for advice to many things, always waiting for her to come back home from school and even letting her write messages to his love interests. Relying on her help so much that I'm not sure which one's the parent and which one's the child.
There's not enough dates or time with the dads to really get to know them. One playthrough with one dad takes about 1-2 hours depending on how fast you can read. And you only get 3 dates with them in total. After the last date the game just ends abruptly. After my very first playthrough with my chosen dad all I really got to learn about him is that he is a youth minister who has a troubled marriage. The Dadsona jokes with the dads so much that you don't get a lot of mature discussion going on. You don't get to know them enough in such short and shallow dates to warrant a serious relationship. They barely scratch the surface.
Other cons? Quite a lot of typos which retract from the experience. The misleading store page which makes it seem like there's voice acting but it actually means some grunts or yells of shock and delight and one single line after every date. Boring and repetitive music. And lastly hastily done and terrible minigames which are trying to hide the fact that there's not enough gameplay because it's a visual novel.
I've played worse games than Dream Daddy but there was a huge missed opportunity when the idea was so unique yet the execution of it fell short. I wouldn't recommend the game to anyone as a good representation of a decent visual novel when something like Hatoful Boyfriend, a parody and April Day Fool's joke, manages to be more in-depth and entertaining.

First off I just want to say I was surprised by how well the campaign was written. I wasn't expecting much but it has quite some emotional impact.
The game itself is fun! There seems to be many possible ways to construct and run your prison, and I'd say the replayability is fairly high. It seems mostly bug-free and is functioning very well. It's mostly a very satisfying experience, if you like these kind of "build and manage"-games.
It has some problems though.
The most appearant is money balance. I'm not sure if I'm just playing it wrong, but I found it hard to earn money in a pace that allowed me to keep constructing and improving my prison without spending a lot of time waiting for money to tick in.
There are some small glitches, the most annoying one i encountered was that my doctors kept getting stuck in the walls of my infirmary for some reason. I could fix it by ordering them to move somewhere, but until I did that, they would not function as usual. And after a while they'd end up stuck again. Firing them an rehiring didn't fix it.
Some of the requirements for rooms are somewhat unclear. A couple of times I ended up rebuilding buildings because the room wouldn't function, only to later figure out I had made some stupid mistake like not tagging all squares in the building as part of the room.
There is a bit of information that is hard or impossible to access in-game, and you have to go look at a wiki or something to figure it out. For example, connecting CCTVs to a monitor only works if you connect from the monitor to the cctv. if you connect from the cctv to the monitor, it doesn't work. There is no tutorial for these things in the campaign and that limitation is so incredibly odd yet mentioned nowhere in the game.
It looks like I've listed a lot of negatives, but most of them are actually relatively minor complaints. I've had a lot of fun with this game and it was well worth the money spent.

Awesome game first off! Even though it wasn't done by the same guys who did Asylum and Arkham City, it still lives up to the Arkham name. The story was really well done in my opinion, they really balanced story and action perfectly. It's a fresh take on the Origin stories inb my opinion. The side-quests aren't too tedious, my only complaint is the amount of Enigma trophies and relays etc that you have to collect. The extortion files are fun, but having that many collectibles is a bit much. Other then that, the back stories are amazing. Seeing all the big name villains together is pretty cool too. This game is worth the current price, the season pass is also a good buy too if you like the combat in the Batman games. Initiation was a lot of fun, and I'm not far into Cold Heart, but so far its a blast.

If you have not played the previous two Batman Arkham games then do not miss them especially Asylum. Many complained of Arkham City's not reaching the same heights as Asylum. But City didn't not fall so far from that high bar as Origins. The real fault is the level design.
This game fails routinely on two design fronts. Ideas from the previous two games are frankly ripped off and reused which is fine, but often these mechanics such as riddler puzzles are misused. Even worse is during story missions the player is expected to find is own way quite often leaded to getting stuck. For a wide audience all skill level game, getting stuck is unforgivable.
Finally, they managed to mess up the combat system. Its still really solid, but lacks the sense of fairness seen in the previous two games. Only players competing with their friends on the challenge leaderboards will really have a problem with this. Overall, I say pass on this one unless you are a huge fan of the series so far. Then jump right in and be underwhelmed with the rest of us I guess. :P

Look! Even though I recommend this game, there are still some points you need to know.
This has to be if not the best but one of the best call of duty titles out there. Oh, I love the colors in this game. All 3 game modes are enjoyable, but as you can tell, the main thing we are going to focus is the multiplayer.
First of all, campaign. Black Ops II brought us a great campaign with a good story which continues Black Ops I's. If you played previous cod titles, this one will probably not look much different for you. However, it was a good idea that here you continue previous storyline and also play as a new character from future. Oh yes, about future. This futuristic cod had it right on its right level. Why? Because futuristic things did not affect gameplay, yet it was mainly for visual look. During the gameplay, you are given some options which only change cutscenes between levels and the ending only. I am not going to spoil storyline, but I definitely suggest you to pass it at least once.
Zombies. Well, even though the regular map "Green Run" frustrated for lots of reasons such as lava, denizens, large map size, worst wonder weapon and etc. The rest maps are really awesome. "Die Rise" is fun map but sucks when it comes to glitches, stupid perk and falling from the map. "Buried" is interesting when you setup and see how the map itself looks but it gets too repeating and boring if you camp which is the main strategy to play it. "Mob of the Dead" is the map which lots of fans loved and it is satisfying for reasons. It is unusual due to its "ghost" mode, awesome wonder weapon, nice setup system, cool atmosphere and great training spot. "Origins". Ok, this map is the best one ever created. Why? It finally brough us characters from WaW and the time of world war I. There are so many things to do, lots of training spots, many wonder weapons, puzzles, challenges with awards and so on. Forgot to mention, to play these maps you need to have dlcs, which of course sucks.
Now, multiplayer. I can talk about this all day, but I will try my best to explain as shortly as possible. BO2 awards you scorestreaks by killing and now also completing definite objectives.One of the best things about mutiplayer is that this is the most played cod multiplayer on pc. There are at least from 3K up to 10K people playing at one moment. There are many great maps like Nuketown 2025, Carrier, Raid, Hijacked, Studio. Oh no. By the way, if you are going to play only mutiplayer, do not bother buying any dlcs. They will not just make it better, no. Dlcs will make it even worse making it unplayable because only few players own them and there will be only 1 game mode playable and it is "team deathmatch". Personally, I had much fun playing this game, but now, it is not as much fun as it used to be at the beginning. Because you understand what is happening, how other people are playing. Eh... Let us talk about these "players". There are 3 types which probably will annoy the crap out of you: tryhards, campers and hackers. Do not get me wrong, it is still enjoyable enough to play bo2 even with these human species. It is not my excuse of calling them tryhards. I am pretty sure I am a good player. A challenge isn't "Here, throw 5 more ships at them, and give them all 50% more health." That isn't challenging, because the only thing I have to do is fly in circles THAT MUCH LONGER until I finally wear them down, or I randomly get a ship disabled because the AI is terrible.

Warning: This game has no meta-progression in any way. There is not a lot of ships or weapons and random events are pretty binary, so replayability may be very restricted for some players.
Otherwise the game is pretty decent. Nice 2d graphics, good audio and nice gameplay, even if a little hectic. Mechanics force you to use tactical pause a lot, maneuver each ship manually to dodge fire (there is no order queuing) and do a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job explaining it to you, so do yourself a favor and skim through some basic guide before your first playthrough (or in a middle of it).
Complains about difficulty are outdated: I've beaten the game in my first try on "regular". First hour was a little too easy but after it, game picked up a pace. I'm obviously played on wrong difficulty for me, but nonetheless it proves, that you can pick a difficulty suited for you.
Random events seemed to me a little dull. Almost every time you got three options: 1. fight, 2. don't fight, 3. read some story to see if you will fight or just get the resources. It shows that the game is mostly combat-orientated. If your fleet is built nicely you won't need to run away from enemies, and if it doesn't - well, you'll need to win some fights to get resources for upgrade.
Overall I've enjoyed my ~4 hours in first playthrough and I'll try it on next difficulty, but I doubt that I will play it a lot. If you will be satisfied with 3-5 hrs experience - this game is good. It may give your more, but don't count on it too heavily.

This is an awesome game that soars waaaay above most of the other 2D space shooter games.
The production quality is high.
Art in this game is simply beautiful. Space backgrounds with giant hulks and derelicts that could hold entire star systems bring Homeworld to mind.
The music also reminds me of Homeworld soundtrack, sort of tribal, very fitting for the "war of the two peoples" narrative.
I wish the soundtrack would be available as DLC to buy.
Spaceship upgrades are diverse and fun, no linear progress "more damage and ROF" but actual choices like "more damage but slower reload" or "less damage but you don't have to aim that lance manually any longer".
Spaceships themselves are diverse as well, you have ewar, support, carriers, dreadnaughts, assaults, snipers, brawlers, disruptors, all the whizzbang. Kinda like a flat EvE online ;P
The strategic map of travel through the sectors is similar to the strategic map in FTL.
Encounters are less humorous than FTL though, they carry the heavy seriousness apropriate for a Tribe Warfleet on a mission that you can not afford to fail.
The narrative is very pleasant, no traces of cheesiness, just a grim shadow of struggle against time to reach your home system in time to stop the enemy from deploying the planet killer, that is constantly looming over you.
I do recommend this game to anyone who likes space games.
I personally am not much into flat space games, but this one is a work of art executed with such mastery, that I do accept the lack of third dimension.

I like the concept and the execution of the story-writing. It feels like great lengths have been gone to capture the lore of the world the game attempts to build.
Sadly, for me this is brutally let-down by the in-game graphics and menus. It feels like this should have come out on PS1, Legacy of Kain springs to mind. For a game that spent millions on development, how can it look so unpolished? If you go retro, then go full retro, don't hover inbetween sprites and large textures like a modern Final Fantasy VIII port.
The menus are clunky but functional. You are given a lot of character decisions to start with which lock down for your playthrough, for a ditherer like myself this fear of locking in the 'wrong' trait without knowing my character yet was a little paralysing. I think the creators expect you to have a working knowledge of their universe mechanics going in, lore explanations are helpfully provided but combat-style mechanics and choices is very much click and guess.
The game starts with spoken dialogue, which is nice. This very quickly dips away leaving you with walls of text to read, I would have appreciated NPC's having all of their lines voiced, not just a part of them.
Perhaps I would have had a much more engaging experience if Torment: Tides of Numenera was not so massively hyped up by it's creators. Christ, I want to play the game in their trailers but the reality felt so different it was a massive turn-off.
TL;DR
Not one for me, but if you are a fan of old-school RPG Dungeons and Dragons and don't mind visuals so much, this could be a really interesting pick-up.

The last Paragraph of this review will contain a short "yay or ney" summarie for those of you who do not wish to read my wall of text. The review in general is a spoiler free as I could manage and should not infringe on your exploration of the game.
What are the consequences of unchecked ambitions and what is a life worth?
Those are two questions central to Tides of Numenera. A very story centered roleplaying game of a slightly unconventional sort. Questions which are, alongside others with equally deep and potentional sad answers, explored in depth through out the game, which leads to two very simple question you can ask yourself before reading any further:
Do you want to spent 26 to 30 hours exploring them, even though many of the answers you get might be sad, dramatic or maybe not even an answer at all?  Do you want to spent 26 to 30 hours with a story, several stories infact, and not so much with bashing peopls heads in?
You are still reading, good. Sadly there is another question you might want to ask yourself:
Is a mix of High Fantasy and Science Fiction something you would enjoy?
The world of Tides of Numenera is a world build on the remnants of at least 8 high cultures which have developed technology in the realms of reality and time manipulation, while the ninth world, the one you will be playing in, is sifting through the rubble, trying to understand the marbels of long lost engeneering. People fight with crossbows, swords, energy weapons, technology seems like magick to those who do not know how to use it and name giving Numenera: Remnants of the old worlds with many or maybe just one charge left in them.
This game lives through the setting and the way it is conveyed to you as the player. If the idea of such a world repells you, it will not be for you, since you will spent a lot of time reading through increadibly thoughtfull and detailed side storys, world building moments and much more.
The atmosphere of the game is developing over the course of the story and becomes a very dense creature, side quests, main story and just random bits and pieces of the world are written well at worst and thoughfull and detailed in a way I have rearly seen in other games. Most of thr world, the people in it, the events happening and already happened tie into each other in some minor or major way like a giant jigsaw puzzel spanning time and realitys and only once did I think: Hold on a minute. You just got cought up in your own writing and messed something up. A moment I would have to replay to be certain, but the point stands: Even though the story is complex, it does not stumble over itself. It remains coherent, at least once you have most of the puzzles pieces.
Comparison with other games is a difficult thing with tides. It is an RPG, you have a character generation tied in with the story, you have combat and non combat abilitys and skills, you have a persona to build (and change if you so please), experience and level ups, all what you would expect from an RPG, but something that has been lost to our world for about 20 years now makes it feel ..strange. The game does not follow along the lines of Baldurs Gate, Mass Effect, Witcher or other milestones in modern and not so modern  RPGs. Fighting is rarely your only option, combat encounters, unless you activly seek them, are few and far between, but danger is a constant part of your journey, since you yourself have to sift through the rubble of long forgotten technologys and who knows if those dancing cones are a weapon of mass destruction, ready to obliterate you and everyone around you at a wrong touch, or just a childs toy?
Most of the time you will talk, read, relive memories, walk and explore the world.
Sometimes you will enter a "crisis" the games version of a combat system, which by no means is restricted to combat. You can talk your way out of a hostile situation, you can avoid it before it becomes hostile in the first place, you can sneak by when your presence would be percieved as a threat. Alternativly you can opt for the brutes option and smash your way through, a choice the game hands you willingly.
A crisis is what the name suggests and not just combat. Most situations which put you into immenent danger but need more than 1 simple action to be resolved will activate it.
For example: Breaking into a guarded vault will trigger a crisis event which you have to resolve. You can fight, or complete several tasks (skill checks),  while beeing on a timer. All of this can (and throughout your journey will) fail at some point, which will sometimes lead to an undesired outcome, but sometimes to something you didn't forsee and might actually like.
Savescumming might be a good solution to some events, but other times it would be better to just flow with the events, it is a difficult descision you have to make and one that MIGHT break your enjoyment of the game if you chose wrong. I can't help you with that.
Skill checks are also a strange beast and their mechanic is used for combat and normal activities. Your character and party members have 3 stats: Might, Speed, Intelligence. Those can be increased or decreased through descisions you make or simply through level up (only increase here..) and form pools for your actions. Each action is on a 0 to 100% scale and the amount of "effort" you put into the action is represented through points you can put into the action, coming from your pools.
Those pools do not regenerate unless you sleep, or use certain consumables, so you can run out at inoppertune times, but can mostly be avoided by properly preparing yourself.
The system took some getting used to, especially because failure IS occasionally a valid option within the game, but it ended up beeing quite enjoyable but a tad rough around the edges.
What you end up with is a RPG that leans heavily on the story and RP elements of the genre and less so on combat as games like ice wind dale would, which is the reason why I asked you if you want to spent 26-30 hours in the world of Tides of Numenera. If you don't like the setting or the idea of gameplay beeing mostly descisions you make as well as exploration and not so much combat, than this game might not be for you.
If you like the ideas on the other hand, the game will most likely take you on a journy of wonder and bewilderment, deep questions, sorrow and joy.
What would you do to save a life or lifes? Would you try to save it or them at all?
Final Paragraph:
Story: Very well written and thought through, but also converluted. Mind bending is fun, right?
Worldbuilding: Incredible.
Setting: Difficult, but well done. (see Worldbuilding and the two questions paragraph at the beginning of this review.)
Very futuristic with multiple realitys at work, timelines crashing into each other, crossbows and laser weapons
side by side. A world build on the ruins of long forgotten civilisations trying to usethe creations of those world,
without understanding them fully.
Companions: Mostly well done, but also a case of to many colourfull birds in a cage. Your maincharacter, who is by all
means extraordinare, seems almost normal compared to a couple of your companions. Nothing new for you if
you played Planescape, but also something fitting into the world, since "unusual" is the normal of the 9th world.
Gameplay (Turn based crisis): Enjoyable, but rough at times . I may have missed it, but in case I didn't: The ability to delay
a characters turn during crisis events would have been nice.
Gameplay (Exploration through conversation): This is why you play the game. To explore the world and uncover the story
surrounding you and it. Fantastic, but you better like reading. Alot. Almost nothing is voice acted.
Stats, Skillchecks and Levelups:  Simple, functional, easy to comprehend but maybe difficult to get used to. Failure can be
desireable.

First of all, Super Meat Boy looks absolutely lovely! Even when being run at sub-native, it's still a pure treat for the eyes. The warm, bright crackling of a hell's fire was just as lovely as a decayed, post-apocalyptic rapture.
No doubt is that you've heard about Super Meat Boy's insane difficulty. Whilst it's true that the difficulty does get very difficult very quickly, you need to understand that the game doesn't want you to have an easy time. If you wanna get to the next level, you've got to work for it, buddy! There's no point in raging. Just get up, dust off your shoulders, and remember that every death is a learning experience. You are meant to die, just so that in the future you WILL become stronger and better. It's one of the most satisfying things to be able to breeze through a level you found difficult only hours ago!
This difficulty is complemented by what truly seals the deal. The controls. They really are pitch perfect, with being as responsive as they are powerful. Meat Boy (or whoever you're controlling on screen) really does only what you tell him to do, to whatever extent. This teaches you that every death is a misjudgement of your own; the game is in no way unfair.
One final thing to note are the lovingly crafted references to retro games, both mid-level and in cutscene, and last, but most definately not least is the insane ammount of unlockable characters you can get. They're all fun to use once you find out their special ability, but it would be nice if some levels complemented some of the unloackable characters, as I rarely used some of the characters.
All in all, if you love a challenge, if you love platformers, or if you love retro games, Super Meat Boy is a MUST!

This game..... where to start....
At first the game seems like just another shooter, and maybe not even a good one at that. Initially the controls are like funky/clunky and the game may be flat out frustrating. But then, things happen......
It's not long into the game before you're drawn into the story. And boy, it's one hell of a story. At times, this game will fill you with joy as you recognize how the good in humanity is as you listen to soliders talk of their loved ones and their lives, and then it will rip that feeling and lead you on a heartwrenching, and often times flat out depressing, journey. Without spoiling anything, there was one moment in particular that really got to me, and I clearly remember staring at my screen with a mix of emotions. I was disgusted by what had just happened, but at the same time I was in awe that a game such as this could evoke those kinds of emotions. But I picked myself up and continued the journey that is this game. By the end, I didn't know what to think or feel. Certain things happen that leave you questioning everything in not only the game, but your life and life in general. As most probably know, this game shows you the forgotten parts of war, but it also does so much more than that. I played this game right during the attacks in Paris (my heart goes out to all who suffered from that day), and I found myself dealing with real emotions. One night I found myself lying under the stars literally on the brink of tears as I thought about how horrible humans can be. I thought about all the suffering that we're capable of, even when we think we're right, and the often tragic results of our acts.
This game legitimately made me feel and think of things I never normally would have, and I am truly grateful for it. The gameplay itself is most definitely not top notch, but everything else makes up for numerous times over.
If you haven't played this game, you need do but one thing: Play. It. You won't regret it.

Five Nights at Freddy's: Sister Location is the fifth game in the Five Nights at Freddy's series (not counting FNaF World)
It's also the game with the longest development time of all games, and it released on time as well! And it's not for no reason, because, this is probably the scariest Five Nights at Freddy's game so far, and the most polished one as well.
The gameplay in Sister Location is absolutely, completely, different than from all other FNaF games. You still need to survive 5 nights, but you're not a security guard this time. In this game, you play as a technician, who needs to do maintenance on the animatronics.  This time you won't be trying to last 6 hours in the game, but you'll have to do all of your orders for the current night, and then are allowed to go home.
When you start the first night, you're starting up in an elevator, and are soon greeted with HandUnit, the "Phone Guy" for this game. He will tell you various things what you'll be needing to do, and will explain the mechanics. Unlike in the previous games, you're explained carefully what you need to do, so you won't be as lost as in the previous game if you couldn't figure out the mechanics. That doesn't make it easier though, the game's as challenging as ever.
During the nights, you'll be going through rooms (Yes, this means that this game has partial free roam) by such ways as travelling through vents. In the various rooms, you'll need to do various things, each with a different gameplay mechanic. You'll need to check if the animatronics are working correctly, and if they're not, you will need to "Shock" them to make them work again. You'll also be doing various things such as doing maintenance on animatronics. Where you'll need to do  specific orders in order to retrieve something from an animatronic, and such. It's not really easy to explain, but to put it simply: Each night is different from the previous one, and you'll have different gameplay mechanics each night. The main area where you'll be working at will be the same, but you'll be also going through new rooms, and will pretty much do different orders each night.
The jumpscares are also very different in this game. They're only your PUNISHMENT. Yeah, they can be scary the first time, but they aren't the main thing which makes you scared. The game has a ton of suspension and tension building, which makes you think "Oh, I'm gonna get jumpscared" sometimes, but you'll be way too distracted and stressed with all the other things going on, that you won't even think about them. They're just your game over in this game, nothing more. There's a single time where you'll get jumpscared, but that's for lore reasons, which makes me go to my next point:
The lore. The lore in this game is amazing, the game is absolutely filled with it, and doesn't make it subtle like the other games did. The story of the game is very well crafted, and gives lots of answers to the lore of the previous games, while still giving questions as well. The story is very dark as well, and you'll feel downright disturbed at certain points of the game, without it being forced in. In other words, the lore in this game is very good, and there's a lot of it as well.
Now we go to the "Scary" factor of this game. The game makes you feel constantly suspenseful, and terrified. When you hide under your desk, you'll see tiny robots peeking through holes in it, they'll be trying to open the hatch under which you hide, and you'll need to fight with it to try to close it back. You'll be opening up an animatronic's body, while its plates just spring out at you. You'll have to go through a corridor while trying to hear a music box, which means a Ballerina is just next you. The game manages to constantly keep your suspenseful, and feel nervous. The game mechanics are fair, yet still challenging, and while you try to complete them, you'll be full of suspense hoping for the best. Honesty, from the entire game, I've never felt as nervous and scared as I was ever before in a FNaF game. The game manages to make you feel dread constantly, without you being able to catch a breath, and when you finally managed to complete a shift, you feel a ton of satisfaction, just to be thrown into the next night, with the tension rising up again. There's even 2 "characters" who constantly tell you to do 2 different things, with one saying the other one's methods will cause your death. This invokes a ton of paranoia as well, making you unable to know who to trust. Sister Location is more than just jumpscares, and they're just the "Game Over" for this game. Jumpscares are simply put, the thing you'll be fearing the least in this game.
Now, let's go to the Voice Acting. The voice acting in Sister Location is very nicely done, and it's very high quality. From what I've gathered, the developer has hired professionals to do it, which was a very good choice, as they have done their job perfectly in my opinion. They managed to voice act in a way that fits the respective characters, making the voices feel perfectly fine in the game. For instance, Circus Baby's voice, is a balance between cold and emotionless, while also sounding affectionate toward the player, and making the player feel afraid. Her voice also sounds innocent, as well having a bit of sorrow in it. There's not a lot to say about this, but simply put, the voice acting is really high quality in this game, and is a really good, which is good since you'll hear voices for a ton of the game.
The game also features an original soundtrack, which is absolutely phenomenal, and fits the overall theme of the entire game. It fits the places you'll be at in the game, and it can be creepy as well. I really dig the Main Menu theme of the game, as it gives the vibe of this being a completely new experience.
Other things are such as the HandUnit, he's supposed to be your main "friend" in this game, while also providing you with a bit of humour, and information.
Pretty much every character speaks in this game, giving them all personality, and making them feel more than just "animatronics" They all are characters now, which you'll get to know, and learn about them. They all have different personalities, so you'll be able to be afraid of "them" as not lifeless robots, but as characters. You'll be afraid of characters in this game, characters with actual personalities.
In summary: The game is an entirely different experience than the other games from the series, with barely resembling the other ones. The game has different mechanics on each night, it has professional voice acting, as well as characters with personalities and a dark story and lore. The game is not too long in itself, taking me around 3 hours to complete it, but it has various easter eggs, as well as a different ending if you do some things in a different order. I honestly think the game is very much worth the money, and is a great horror game, with a completely new experience. I've enjoyed the entire game a ton, and felt dread the entire time. The game itself can be enjoyed without playing the other games as well, although it will feel a lot better if you played the previous games in the series first, as they explain various parts of the story.
Honesty, this has exceeded my expectations completely, and I might as well say that this is my GOTY. I give the game a 10/10, and I recommend it to everyone.

Batman: The Animated Series: Big Guy Edition

SINGLE PLAYER CAMPAIGN REVIEW ONLY.
Let's cut to the chase and face it - Batman: Arkham Origins is "more of the same", for the most part. It's basically more Batman: Arkham Asylum + Arkham City. If you were a fan of the two previous Arkham games and wanted basically more Batman: Arkham, then Origins certainly delivers just that. If that sounds good to you, great - you'll probably feel right at home with this title. If you wanted and expected more - well, prepare to be disappointed.
Arkham Origins' voice-acting is still pretty good, even with some of the changes in some of its cast members. Regardless - the cast delivers and does a great job on their performances. While the story does take a little bit for it to get rolling, once it does - it finally decide to get good. Eight assassins are basically coming for Batman's head, as there's a bounty of $50 million on Batman's head from Black Mask.
That's just the start of things, to say the least. There's certainly more to it than that. Because of such a huge cast of characters and some twists + turns in the plot and storyline, some characters - like some of the lesser known Batman villains to most non-fans of the series - never really get the time to get explored and shine here, which feels like a missed opportunity.  Some of Origins' story fills in the blanks of what happened to certain characters, how they become the character they become, or talk about some of their past - explaining some things that happened before events of the previous Arkham games. B/c this is an Origins story, it feels like some of this should've been explored a bit more.
If you loved the combat of Arkham Asylum + City, it's not really changed much here - and this definitely has always been one of the strengths of this series. Some of the combat feels tweaked, here and there. Plus, there are some new weapons and gadgets here. One of the best things here are the boss fights - which are always excellent here. There certainly are plenty of side missions and collect-a-thon's here, for fans to dive into - if they are digging the game. And if that isn't enough, there's a New Game Plus Mode, among other things to dive into.
After 23 hours approximately, Batman: Arkham Origins' single player campaign deliver basically more Batman: Arkham. Fans of the series wanting more Batman: Arkham, that's exactly what you receive here. If you were expecting more, innovations, and major improvements - don't! Origins is not that title. If you want more Batman: Arkham, you'll come away happy with this title. It's certainly a solid game and delivers such an experience. Origins certainly does not touch the greatness and freshness that came from the previous two titles developed by Rocksteady. Though, it can't be denied that WB Montreal has put forth a solid Batman: Arkham game.
Final Grade = C+.

I didn't like the game at first because of the fact that I played the previous two Arkham games to death. Origins is good, it's very good and if you're a Batman fan like me, you won't go wrong by buying it. The only thing missing is the "finishing touch" that Rocksteady has put to Asylum and City. Being that this one is not developed by the core team, it just feels off at times, gameplay wise. The story and the side-missions are amazing, there are glitches here and there but nothing game-breaking as far as I can tell. In short, this is a very good Batman game that suffers from the fact that previous two games set the bars a bit too high. Still, it's worth a playthrough, if only to experience the "origin" story of the Arkham universe.

It's almost like a whole different game since the 1.1 update, so I've had to completely redo my review as just editing it wouldn't cut it. The game is a lot more fun and buying new ships no longer causes encounter difficulty to instantly spike, instead the difficulty gradually increases as you move to new sectors, and hanging around in a sector with a high danger level will probably make you think twice about the wisdom of doing so unless you're playing on easy.
Speaking of difficulty, "Easy" now feels like a proper easy mode for people who just want to play through and try out different ships, gear, and skills without having every fight be a frantic battle to the death against a superior force. Normal is just that, not too easy, not too tough, most people should be able to at least reach the final sector on normal even if they've never played before. Veteran is still a challenge but without the hopeless feeling you'd get after having bad luck in a noncombat encounter or being forced into a "no retreat" battle while having a fleet of ships with multiple critical damage debuffs. Elite is like before, you feel like an underdog through the whole game facing very tough encounters that require constant micromanagement and having to know the proper times to use skills, with the game making you all too aware of it when you mess up. And you WILL mess up occasionally.
These two points were done in previous updates but I feel the need to address them again as they really shine with the rework of the game's difficulty in the 1.1 update.
The final stage as a whole is much more manageable on any difficulty, I remember playing through it on normal difficulty being stopped seemingly every half screen by a new group of enemies that felt like they were set to spawn at just the right places to almost force you to fly through a nearby minefield to avoid being penned in between them and a wall. The minefields are still there, but the enemy spawns have been reduced so you can actually make it to where the final boss appears before it actually warps in, meaning you'll likely have the full time limit to dedicate to fighting it and it's escorts instead of spending part of it finishing off the enemies that show up along the way.
Shops sell better quality gear as you progress instead of just being totally random, you're much more likely to find level 2 and 3 weapons, attachments, and skills as you move to new areas.
All in all a great update, and I'm more than happy to give the game a thumbs up now.

First off, reader, be aware that T:ToN has NOTHING to do with Planescape and has no ties whatsoever to the Planescape world - it only uses the name Torment as part of the hype to sell the game. It is not a sequel, and is not based on any of the Dungeons & Dragons rule sets or worlds. If you're considering buying this game believing that this is a continuation of the story of the Nameless One, you will be disappointed.
Second, this is a 40 to 45 Hour Which Way book. The amount of reading in this game grossly overshadows any real game content. There were, at most, 10 to 15 battles some of which the party didn't even have to fight and could teleport to safety. While the graphics were beautifully done, based on the Pillars of Eternity and the Unity engines, there was a lot more reading and a lot less actual gameplay.  This game barely scratches the surface of what an RPG is supposed to be.
Third, the romantic arc based on Tybil, was totally unnecessary and really was more "in-your-face". In other games, there are choices to accept a character in the party that the player might find personally objectionable, but in this game, Tybil is clearly a MacGuffin.
Fourth, with the three main areas in the game, gameplay requires the player to complete ALL the side quests before moving on (or they are unavailable) which makes the game decisions linear at best and pointless at worst.  The endings were generally anti-climatic and left the player wanting. The player doesn't even get to fight the boss at the end.
Fifth, with only three ability stats (might, will, speed), and with all the game arcs leaning on will predominately - not that building a fighter class was especially important for the lack of battles throughout the game, as mentioned earlier.
Overall, the game had the potential and drive behind it to be a nice sequel to Planescape, but with that principal let-down, all the reading, lack of defined gameplay, and linear story - the only Torment here was the game itself. (2 stars out of 5)

On the plus side: Choice & consequences, an interesting world, a story that manages to build on Planescape: Torment but be original enough to feel new. Great music and sound, interactive maps that are better looking than for instance Pillars of Eternity 1. Long - 60+ hrs easily.
Minus: A very sluggish interface, slow load times. Occasional bugs. Combat feels a bit half-baked. The main story does wrap up satisfactory, but some characters are not fully explored, it feels like they had planned the game to be 50% bigger than it was.
Recommended for those who like classic RPGs, adventure games, reading a lot, and have patience with bugs and and slow UI. Not recommended if you want challenging tactical combat, or a lot of action.
There has already been one big patch that restored a lot of planned content (like a few new companions). Hopefully one day there will be a directors cut like there was for Wasteland 2.
