Most of the positive reviews of this game praise the story, and rightfully so; it's based on a number of military novels containing similar themes and is written quite well. It sets the scene and atmosphere of the game: our protagonist is fighting with their own morality and mental strength in a nation plagued with disaster. It starts out averagely enough, but quickly spirals out of control as the story progresses. However, the story is all that's good in this game.
Before even starting the game, I tried to enable borderless fullscreen, but it's not supported. To someone with one monitor, this might be pretty trivial an issue, but it's still a legitimate one. For games that don't support it, it's easy enough to use thirdparty tools to fake it, but this was not the case here. When I tried to change the windowed resolution manually, it was automatically clamped, meaning that it was impossible for me to resize the window to fit my native resolution. While this isn't a problem the developers should be responsible for, they
be responsible for not including the feature in the first place.
In addition, the game is forcefully letterboxed, so it won't stretch to any aspect ratio it doesn't support, including over two monitors or on a super-wide monitor. While this can be hacked with tools like Flawless Widescreen, it's still annoying.
When attempting to edit the game's configuration files to see if there was anything I could do about my problems, I was greeted with encryption. As far as I know this was manually implimented and not a standard feature of the Unreal engine. Thankfully, more tools exist that can decrypt these files and allow the user to edit them. I learned later that there is forced mouse acceleration that cannot be disabled by normal means; I was able to turn off the acceleration, normalize the sensitivity, turn off the awful bloom, and fix a few other issues I was running into by editing and re-encrypting the files.
The controls are uninspired, and in some cases completely broken. The cover system was clearly designed for controllers, with the button to vault over cover the same as the melee button, causing you to often beat your cover with your gun before you're able to vault over it. The sprinting in this game works like the "roadie run" from Gears of War and similar games, meaning you can only run in a mostly straight line and can't sprint left, right, or backwards. I suppose the saving grace of this is that you can hold a direction and press sprint to quickly spin around and run in that direction, but the fact that it takes
to stop running without pressing a button like crouch feels incredibly awkward and got me killed a few times. Additionally, the sprint button is also the take cover button, and the cover snapping either works
well, causing you to snap into cover when you're trying to run away from enemies, or doesn't work
, causing you to stand there awkwardly as you try to take cover, or worse, make you sprint into the open and get shot to death. The sprint/cover button is also the "jump off of ledge" button, which makes no sense; shouldn't it be the vault button? To make matters worse,
. Clearly, the controls took some time to get used to. It doesn't help that there's no urgency to the game, save for a few sections, and the time-tested "sit back and snipe everything that moves and wait for your health to recharge" tactic works
, and is sometimes your only option on the harder difficulties.
Unsurprisingly, enemies are bullet sponges in this game, at least on the second hardest difficulty, which is the highest unlocked when first starting the game. Very few enemies take a single headshot to kill, and most later on in the game will take two from the lesser powerful rifles and pistols. The game also features "heavies" which see implementation in so many other games it's become average, and these in specific lack suitable tactics to taking them down. At least in other games there are gimmicks that can make fighting one easier, but no, not this time. It's shoot it in the same spot until it stops moving. It gets old very quickly and their resilience to bullets is uncanny.
The maps are incredibly linear, with little explorative value aside from finding the (usually very obviously placed) intel pickups. Lots of invisible walls and things that look safe that aren't. Map triggers sometimes fail to occur, causing hangups in gameplay and/or checkpoint restarts.
The game is... okay to look at, despite the graphics appearing dated in many places. However, where and when it was noticable, the drop in quality is very apparent, especially for the characters' faces. The scenery looks pretty low-res for a last-gen game. I will admit, the environment textures look pretty good with lots of detail, but this quickly falls off as you lower the settings. The game also runs horribly on my machine, even though I can run more modern games on higher settings without issue. Also, explosive container fireballs are garbage.
The voice acting is incredibly repetitve, with hordes of cookiecutter enemies all spouting the same selection of 10-20 lines every few seconds. The scripted sections are voiced very well, however, and add more emotion and depth to the story. The sound effects are pretty good, but are lacking for a few of the guns and explosions. Overall, very good sound design, though the constant blaring rock music got pretty old as well, especially with how frequently the background music was reused. The music really didn't add much to the game besides annoyance, and there's very little musical ambiance aside from it.
The game has an inspired story with great writing that honestly would have worked better as a book or a movie than a videogame. You're led around on a string as the story reads itself to you, helpless to the hell around you, despite being given a number of supposed choices in the game (and set up for a few more, but contrarily these aren't actually choices and the game will kill you if you don't play along
). There are four endings, which all take place in the same penultimate sequence of the game, and affect nothing but a short cutscene change. Your actions during the course of the story and your reaction to the moral choices proffered do not change the endings you can get.
Simply put, there's too much story to consider for what the game is. They tried to make a game around a story that was too ambituous, and it shows. There are a few sequences that offer moral choice, but either force you to choose one action, or the choice ends up being meaningless. Maybe they were trying to convey a message by doing that, but all it ends up doing is disappointing me with the thought of what could have been in a more polished game. To top it off, the ending is depressingly laid out, despite the thousands of lives that could have potentially been saved by your actions (even if you did just
and
). No matter what you try, the game forces you make it worse.
Overall, there were few times I actually had fun in this game, and that fun was quickly squandered by the horrible gameplay elements, repetitve voice acting, and negative story. I can barely recall myself smile, gasp, or show any kind of emotion at all at anything the game tried to do. The story is interesting, but even if that's your thing, the gameplay could likely ruin it for you.
Not worth full price.

To get into what made Spec Ops the Line one of the best games of the 7th generation I have to first shed a little background on the game.
Spec Ops the Line is a sequel to the Spec Ops games released in the 90s. It was originally planned to be a new IP but was made part of the Spec Ops brand for sequel bait. This is important because this ties into what Spec Ops the Line was advertised as. It was advertised as a big budget modern military shooter with an interesting setting but overly generic game mechanics and plot premise.
What we got was an elaborate satire of modern military shooters. Spec Ops the Line starts out similar to how you'd expect a big budget AAA game to start. You are a squad of soldiers, sent in to investigate a crisis, and you have to cowboy in and shoot some brown people.
However the game plays with this a lot. What was the exact nature of your mission? Why are the enemies so hostile to you? Why are your squadmates talking erratically about you? There are so many questions raised and the game delightfully gives you answers that you don't want to hear.
Spec Ops the Line's writing is very top notch. It satirizes the heroic power fantasy nature of modern military shooter plotlines and characters. And it plays with the idea of "how would killing hundreds of people change you as a person".
Beyond that the gameplay is sound, it has Mass Effect style squad combat and fairly generic multiplayer. The singleplayer is what you get Spec Ops for, and it remains one of my favorite games ever for its message and its post-modern view on the 7th generation of video games overall. The main gripes I have with it are due to the linear nature of the game, and due to how the plot is written it isn't as replayable as you might think. But it still is one of the most breathtaking games I have ever played, and one I dearly recommend to people who want to play a game that'll make you feel uncomfortable and uneasy with your objectives.

Before I provide my opinion, please do remember this is all respective of my own experience, as I do not think anyone else will have the exact experience I did. As for the purchase, got this for $10 off of humble bundle and bought the dlcs through steam.
I do not suggest this game due to several issues and qualms I had right off the bat (no pun intended), and after a few hours, I stand by my suggestion. The game is poorly ported over, as several major aspects of PC play are completely disregarded and difficult. I personally play on a wide screen monitor, so the fact this game has no ingame FOV or graphical setting to adjust quality to my choosing is deplorable. Furthermore, if you have dual or more monitors running, the game essentially overrides any resolution on these extra monitors despite resolution limitation (i.e. the rest of your screens will be blacked out, kind of pointless dont you think?). The initial graphical settings just consist of Normal and High, not much customization there. Additionally, for those playing on high res monitors, mouse smoothing and the sensitivity options make it extrememly difficult to play as you must manually adjust them through the ini files. This comes to my next problem, as adjusting any of these ini files shoot up the ctd and glitch frequencies beyond the normal buggy gameplay.
Of course, I have played the previous games as well, and can shed light on the experience to the plot and mechanics. The mechanics have relatively stayed the same, but imo, have been simplified right off the bat. The executions are far more limited than in previous games and I think the responsiveness of the movement suffers as a result of the above optimization issues. That being said, its pretty much the same thing as the previous game. Some new gadgets and detective methods have been added, but the balancing efforts disrupted much of the combat. I still say play the first two over this one as they were much better imo.
With the lack of optimization and subpar experience, save yourself the trouble and dont buy this, but if you must persist, get it during a sale. The skins are unavailable during the initial playthrough which is again a bummer as most of the dlc consists of skin packs, and replay is not an experience I wished to partake in. My advice for dlc's, get the campaign addons, avoid the season pass, you'll save cash.

For reference, this review is primarily concerning the DLC, Cold Cold Heart (as well as some of the Season Pass content).  My review for the original game is at
.
In my review for Arkham Origins, I noted a number of game-breaking bugs.  I am sorry to say that WB Montreal patched only a few of these, and actually made the Burnley Tower issue worse by making some of the buildings surrounding it physically intangible (as in, you literally fly straight through them).  They coupled their poor attitude towards releasing a very broken game with an announcement some months later that they would no longer be patching the main game and were focused on DLC.  I remember thinking, "So your plan is to build DLC on top of a broken game?  What could POSSIBLY go wrong?"
Oy vey.
As you might have guessed from the DLC title, the storyline DLC Cold Cold Heart (which is a lame lame title) is the origin story of Mister Freeze.  Minor spoilers ahead, but here's the short list of what I liked.
-Getting to navigate Wayne Manor is cool and those levels aren't poorly designed.  Plus Alfred regualrly smarms the goons who are holding him hostage.
-Thermal batarangs look pretty kickass and are actually used in a neat way.
Yep, that list was short.  Here's the bad stuff.
-The story is completely predicatable for anyone who is even remotely familiar with Mr. Freeze, even if your only familiarity comes from his appearance in Arkham City.
-The main story arc takes place in an artifically limited version of Gotham (two disctricts) and features new buildings and girders which happen to be installed over outdoor stealth sections.  For reference, this story also takes place EXACTLY one week after Arkham Origins... so in the week between Christmas and New Year's, which as we all know is the high point of activitiy for construction crews, Gotham City construction workers managed to put up (or at best, relabel) a new skyscraper for GothCorp, AND install girders that support no structural purpose over bad guy hangouts.  This is what happens when the DLC is concepted and sketched out AFTER Gotham City is designed and modeled.
-The first two guards you encounter (the ones with the codes) use the same model and skin.  This is especially sloppy considering there are other, uninteractable guards with different models later in the level.
-Whoever made the decision to zoom in during the initial dialogue sequence between Alfred and Bruce should be fired.  Both Alfred and Bruce's lips appear to come a good inch away from their faces while speaking, something which is not noticible in later dialogue sequences because they are further zoomed out.  It genuinely looks like a goofy Garry's Mod face.
-The DLC is noticibly padded in multiple places - first, with Anarky's "riots" (yes this is the same Anarky you appreheneded a week before in the main game).  By "riots," I mean five or six Anarky guys standing around chatting.  Then breaking up the parts of the Cryo Drill, which are very large but apparently fit well within his utility belt pouches, because why not?  There are another couple of instances, but I'm too bored to point them out.
Oh word, remember the part at the beginning of the review where I mentioned bugs?
-Don't land too near any frozen guard, or you will be caught in an infinite loop of hovering and attempting to land.
-Don't attempt to leave the game before completing a mission objective (especially clearing a room) unless you like having to start the DLC over from scratch - this causes the DLC to clear the room of baddies, and if you were required to interrogate any of them in order to progress, well eff you.
-Grappeling is just as buggy and weird as in the main game - you're going to say to yourself "Why can't I grappel there?" A LOT.  I particularly liked it when I grappel to a point just below an armed guard to perform a ledge takedown, only to have Batman hop the ledge and stand in front of the bad guy.  Nice stealth, bro.
-Especially on stairs, performing a stealth or ground takedown is buggy, will cause the body to glitch partially through the stairs, and occassionally bounce up wildly into the ceiling.
-You will still randomly drop combos, especially when most of the enemies are down but not unconscious.  I know someone will say this so let me go ahead and ask the question - "But y don't u use ground takdown!!1!"  Uh, because the animation is so long that by the time you are finished performing it, anyone else who was on the ground is up and already hitting you or about to.
-Using alternate suits in the main game can and will crash the game under random conditions.  This was particularly a problem with the Brightest Day suit.
The worst part of this, though, (read the latest patch note comments for reference) is that people are actively swearing off Batman video games because of how broken this game is.  A lot of them don't realize that this is the only Arkham game WB Montreal ever made, and the two previous (and upcoming Arkham Knight) were made by Rocksteady.  I mean, if I were Rocksteady, I would actually draft a press release concerning their disappointment with Arkham Origins, and clarifying that they didn't make it.  If Arkham Kinght underperforms because of this glitchy mess, that would be a real shame.
At the end of the day, I got the Season Pass on sale at Amazon for $8.  And I still feel like I got ripped off.  Don't buy either the DLC or the main game unless you don't have enough frustration in your life.  I wouldn't even recommend this to diehard Batman fans.

I read a lot of reviews before I bought this game. The negative reviews were almost all about the business model of the game, and not the game itself. I was tempted to buy just the first level to see if I liked it but so many reviewers complained about not being able to get all the bonus content when you upgrade from that point. I decided to take the plunge and buy the full experience and have not regretted it.
I really enjoy the gameplay. It's smooth and well done, the levels are beautiful and quite large. There are so many ways to accomplish the missions, and there are tons of challenges for each one that encourage you to try out different things. There are also a ton of additional contracts in each level which are also very fun.
I was worried that, only having a handful of levels, the game would not be able to hold my attention for very long. So far there are two tutorial levels and four full levels out (plus two bonus levels that take place in the full levels but take place at different times of day and are reworked.) At this point I have played 22.5 hours, and it has mostly been in the tutorial and first level. I have beaten the second level but haven't really dug into it beyond my additional runthrough. I haven't played the two other levels that are availible yet, and there are two more levels on their way.
If you like stealth games, this is a really good one and definately worth it, but buy the full experience. The publisher made a bad choice about how to market the game that made a lot of people feel ripped off. Don't let that stop you from enjoying an excellent game if this is your type of thing though.

Overall, I would recommend this game.

Even though Super Meat Boy is notorious for being infuriatingly difficult, I would actually say that the difficulty curve is quite pleasant. That said, I wouldn't recommend it to someone who's never played a platformer before. The first set of stages gives the player a nice space to get a feel for the physics and controls of the game before throwing any real challenges at them, but stages only get more difficult as the player progresses.
From my experience, I'd say that the main story levels are challenging but not impossibly difficult (others may or may not disagree). However, the true challenge (and furious cussing and fist-shaking) comes from the bonus stages and trying to unlock all the playable characters. I like me some platforming, but I don't have the kind of patience to try and complete this game 100%.
Other notable aspects are its arcade style of gameplay, an instant replay system (you get to watch all of your attempts simultaneously after you complete each level), its colorful artstyle, its catchy (albeit somewhat repetitive) soundtrack, and its morbid sense of humor. It has smooth controls and the flow and pacing of the game are near-perfect. Super Meat Boy is a pretty good game, and I'd say it's worth a purchase.
Note: It's best to play with a controller. Don't play with a keyboard unless you want an additional challenge.

I purchased this game about a year after it came out during one of the Steam sales, but unfortunately it's specs were just a little much for my PC at the time. Following an upgrade, I was not only able to play this game but do so on the best settings, and I have to say I enjoyed the experience.
The plot of the game is pretty straightforward and uncomplicated, and it's only really going to surprise anyone who hasn't seen at least one of the movies. It's not bad, but it's not brilliant either. It unfortunately has such a modest presence in the game that your own curiosity will be more of a driving force than it is.
The aesthetic of the game follows that of Fury Road - gritty, rusty and run down, with the over-the-top stylization of the various groups that have managed to band together in the post-apocalyptic wasteland. This world is the ruins we've come to expect after Road Warrior, and what we've seen in the Fallout series (but with less humor).
The controls of the game are solid - driving is responsive, and each vehicle feels unique. Considering the scope of the wasteland and the need for vehicles, this is good. No two vehicle designs feel identical, and the cars range from small, modified VW Beetle-type buggies to a handful of big, heavy trucks (although no proper semis/War Rigs). Your main mode of transportation, however, will be the highly-customizable Magnum Opus.
Fighting controls are good as well. As this was published by WB Interactive, anyone familiar with the Arkham Asylum games will feel right at home - though obvioiusly since this isn't Batman, the level of gadgetry is far lower, and the combat is a bit slower, heavier and feels more brutal than what you get from Batman. Of course, Batman doesn't have the option to use a shotgun, shiv opponents or just straight up smash their heads in with a crude club...
One legitimate complaint people have about this game is that it feels very samey and grindy after a while. Make no mistake - once you've done one region, you've pretty much seen the variety the game has to offer. Most scrap loot locations are the same and don't yield much, the historic relics and races are all option, and if you don't feel like giving yourself nice, safe bases that replenish your health, ammo and scrap (money) automatically, you can even skip those as well if you just want to plow through the main story on its own.
However, the game makes up for this by making each region unique compared to the others, and with one major, story-related exception you can effectively go anywhere from the beginning. If you want to explore, immerse and generally soak in the atmosphere, Mad Max won't disappoint there.
The characters are also decent. Max is more or less what we've come to expect since Road Warrior and is showing what he became in Fury Road, and the secondary characters are the motley sort we've come to expect in games like this. None will stand out strong after the game is over, but you'll know them well while you play.
Do I recommend this? Hard to say - I had fun, but I will admit that there were plenty of times the game became a grind. I ran into the same problem in Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag, and that game at least had a much more exotic locale and ship combat. If you want solid action, combat want to loot the barren wastes of Mad Max's world, give it a go! If you need something with more plot and the driving and exploration aren't enough, you may want to take a pass on it.
TL;DR - Better than Mediocre, but not quite Shiny and Chrome.

I wanted a spiritual successor the planescape:torment, the best game ever made. I got a pretentious, mismatched frankenstein's monster of mechanics and themes. At times, it all came together: the music, tone, voice acting, and visuals. Other times, it seemed like they were just trying to put random things together. In one part, you fight a karate master in a regular old 2017 martial arts gi. Frickin' innovation right here.
I thought the numenara system would fit perfectly with a dialogue focused system, but it just dumbed down the mechanic to such simplicity that there was no mechanical depth. You have three stats, and you can pump up your chance of success until it hits 100%, then rest and recover. Any story driven progress affecting your gameplay is lost in the simplicity of this system. Imagine D&D, but with 3 stats instead of 6, and the rolls boil down to difference in skill.
Dear lord, the dialogue is droning and pretentious. Torment: Planescape had an enormous amount of dialogue, but it was not so exhausting to read. No ♥♥♥♥ing joke: they describe things with prolonged metaphors like some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ creative writing class. "His cloak falls and crumples around him like two children chasing each other on a spring day" <-- this is how the stuff would read. I would read it and be like, "ok, is it just normal stuff?" Mechanically she was too accurate as a child: whiny and useless. In Planescape: Torment, your first companion is a talking taunting floating skull. In short, the mechanics hold this game back, and the writing is pedantic.

Without a doubt one of my favourite animes in recent memory, with an especially promising story if it continues.
If you are a person that enjoys military stories, with political intrigue, reasonably deep characters and an underlying theme of reason and logic then I can certainly recommend this anime. In similar lines would be Code Geass (though obviously different settings) and Arslan Senki.
The story itself contains what would be considered near post renaissance levels of technology (the transition from swords to guns is one of the concepts looked at) but obviously has some fantasy elements thrown in such as spirits but nothing that would allow the anime to escape from a reality that it delves into quite deeply. Additionally, it has what could be considered a love story underlying the whole plot, which leads to one of the main questions of how do you reconcile your duty with a conflicting world view.  The two main characters are actually awesome, you wont find a useless MC here and the supporting characters each carry themselves.
Additionally, It does not try to avoid some of the grim realities of war and generally, unlike a large number of animes, fall into the trap of being stupid for comedies sake or trying to be cute for no reason.
Thats not to say that it doesn't hit some of tropes found in anime, but it never loses sight of the bigger picture of what the show is, its setting and how characters should be.
Its greatest failing, in my opinion, was that it tried to do to much in its first two episodes which would have been better spread out over perhaps three, having read the source material. After that the story really does pick up and become quite memorable.
Overall I can only recommend this to anyone that is looking for an entertaining, action packed yet well reasoned show that builds on its characters. I would rate it a solid 8/10 and depending on if it gets further attention (as it hopefully will, even though Japan did not buy into it) it could honestly become of the best animes within its genre.

I honestly don't get all the hate for this game, Hitman is an excellent return to form after the somewhat dissapointing absolution.
The core mechanics, whilst a little limited, are solid, The level design is extremely detailed and the game looks great (requires some beefy specs to maintain 1080p, 60fps though).
They've ditched the linear level design and returned to the great sandbox enviorments we all know and love and whilst doing so have upped the ammount of stuff to interact with tenfold.
The new events system works well, if not a little dumbed down (Key events no longer happen at set times, they trigger when the player is in ear shot), and they've kept the instinct mode from absolution.
The escelation missions make the gave even more replayable by adding a simon says type feel, starting out as easy assasinations and gradualy increasing the difficulty by adding more targets and obstacles to the level, and after completing a few I felt that I had learned much more about the base map and could go back and master the main mission.
The game is always online, which I know an awful lot of people hate, however i've never had problems with the server and you can still play the main missions offline.
The main gripe I have is that by buying all the missions seperately you miss out on bonus content, so if you are going to pick this game up, buy the complete eddition as you'll save money and get the bonus missions, With each release of a new mission the maps keep getting better and better so theres nothing to worry about (as of yet).

The biggest thumbs down EVER, possibly.  They want you to connect to their "Online Server" during singleplayer, and since there isn't a multiplayer this is weird - but ok.  Then, to top it off, your "Connection" to their "Server" gets dropped multiple times per mission.  I'm not talking about once or twice, we're talking about every fifty feet you walk, you gotta "Attempt to reconnect".  I live in Germany, my internet is 1.5 terabyte..
US Connection: 5,000-15,000 Megabytes per second..
German Connection: 1,500,000 Megabytes per second...
I've never had this kind of issue anywhere, and this largely cannot be my connection.  This might be because they've had the hitman games pirated quite a bit before, but thats not a reason to punish the player, thats a reason to punish your developers who you're paying money to work on the game!
2/10 Score.

I'm really embarassed for the developer on this one, the mark was utterly missed.
Art Department: 10/10

Audio: 1/10
Technical Artists: 3/10
On a final note, the Hitman games earlier were about as absolutely rock solid as it gets in terms of content - with this game - seven levels?  Most hitman games have around 20 levels, its really embarassing.  I feel bad for them, but then again they've made their money and you have the power to poll your voices together and make them change for the better.

**Batman Arkham Origins**
A lot to live up to with Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. Super unsatisfying.

- Horrible gameplay. I mean, all they had to do was copy Arkham City, and I would have been happy. Instead they had to mess it up. Combat camera is the worst in the series, enemies attack waaaay to often that your most used ability is easily Counter (which is super boring when it's what you do 70% of the time). Those idiotic Shock gloves break the game, making it extremely easy, and destroys all variation in combat. Who needs counters, rock/paper/scissor gameplay when you can hit the "win button" of shock gloves. It literally does everything. unblockable, very powerful, and has priority over every damn attack in the game. Ruins every single combat arena, as you'll be getting almost twice as much score required for Gold status for basically mashing on one button.
- Bosses. Horrible bosses. They advertised Deathstroke to death as this awesome character, and pretty much the only one that can stand up to Batman in hand to hand combat. He was the second boss, and is beaten in less than a few minutes and never seen or heard from again. Other bosses like Bane are fought more than a few times. Also the difficulty. Difficulty for bosses range from boringly easy, to stupidly hard. When I say hard, I mean unblockable attacks coming at you from off screen. Attacks that can't be avoided if your too close, which is fun when you find yourself in a corner. Bosses with little henchmen everywhere, which if you saw my last comment, are actively attacking you 70% of the time. This takes out any satisfaction of actually pulling off a combo on a boss, as your constantly interrupted. If you counter henchmen, it takes too much time and the boss hits you. If your flipping over henchmen, it takes too much time and a boss hits you or you just spend most of the time flipping around.
- Combat equipment. This needs to be emphasized again. In previous Arkham games all your gadgets became battle viable battle options, each useful for certain playstyles or variation. In this game, most get eliminated as an option, based on how the next gadget just dwarfs it in usefulness and power. So less options and variability to break up the gameplay. Shock Glove in particular just straight up breaks the game. You will destroy bosses and huge groups of enemies, and feel no sense of accomplishment whatsoever. It's like flipping a "win" button, and just watching a CPU beat the game for you.
- Multiplayer. Unbalanced, broken, time sink. Just... Just... Don't even try it.
- Story. Without giving too much away, the game was decent first half, then terrible last half. It was also VERY unoriginal. If you pay close attention, the ENTIRE game will seem extremely familiar to you.
- General environment and focus. A lot of the actual map is just a repeat of Arkham City. Often times, there is no clear direction of where to go for story or side missions. Collectibles can be annoying to get (ANNOYING, not challenging). Heck, some of the collectibles are not even challenging at all when they want them to be. "Ooh, they want me to hit these 3 targets, set off a bomb, them jump on that pad... Or I'll just use my Bat Claw AGAIN to just get it in 2 seconds. Hmm, maybe I'll go for this challenge where I use bat claw 3 times at different locations within 8 seconds. Okay, flipping between these two targets, whips the camera around and makes it hard to see, and there is no auto target on the 3rd location so it makes targeting and hitting within the time just plain idiotically luck and frustration based! Yay!". Collectibles that you can never get an ability to locate on a map, and be standing right up against and not see it. A collectible that absolutely requires you look it up online... Not a good thing.
- DLC and unlockables - Oh hey, you like side missions? Spoiler, they suck. DLC you purchase or get for free with the game, are also the rewards for beating some of the long side-quest challenges. Which makes it super unsatisfying when you beat any side-quest. Side-Quest are kind of decent for a couple of them, but end with virtually no pay off at all. One of the hardest and most indepth side-quests ends literally with something written on a wall... Wow.
- Bugs. Lots of bugs. Required henchmen to defeat getting to unreachable areas, then not being able to advance as a result. Extreme common bugs for me, were flying through the city, then suddenly losing all impact detection with the environment. This means I just fly through buildings, and fall through floors. All textures disappearing, and everything becoming greyscale. Henchmen bodies warping and contorting when often times getting stuck in geometry (mostly when dead though, thankfully). There are too many to list. I experienced at least 1 bug each session I had, and more than a few times my session ended because of these stupid bugs. But, you may ask yourself "Hey ElvisPrime, maybe that's just you! you could have a horrible setup on your PC, and your bugs are unique!" NOOOOOPE. Look it up, or check the forums. Bugs were very common, and generally still are as of May 2004. The fun part is, that for many people the bugs are not even the same. It's like every user gets to pull out 5-10 bugs out of a hat that will be common to them. It's fun like that!!. Keep in mind, i'm not even mentioning the bugs that don't happen anymore. Like game save bugs, where you have to restart your campaign. Losing all progress in multiplayer unlocks and XP. Areas of the game you couldn't get past, and everyone had to wait for a bug fix, just to play through the basic main campaign. Collectibles that were bugged, and could not be accessed. You know, nothing too bad.
- Final Summary. It's kind of a okay to decent game. The developers took what Rocksteady made, in the masterpiece that is Arkham City (literally a copy/paste of all their code), then managed to not only add nothing new that was good, but ruin many things that were already amazing and downgrade them to "Meh" at best. The only good parts of the game, are the parts they left the f*** alone. So yeah, this is a pretty terrible game, and a horrible effort by this new Developer in the Arkham Franchise "Splash Damage/WB Montreal". Just terrible.
**TL;DR** Not a good game. Play either of the other Arkham games first, then if you want more, just punch yourself.

Batman Arkham Origins...what can I say? Nobody wanted this game when it was announced that original developers Rocksteady were not behind the helm, myself included, but after seeing it on sale I just had to suck up the misgivings and give it a whirl. As it turns out I was extremely pleasantly surprised. This game gives you more access to Batman's iconic arsenal and carte blanche to use it not only on the City's criminals, but also the police force. Yes, that's right, as the Dark Knight of Arkham you get to use your near super human abilities to shatter the bones and bodies of every police man you see. Furthermore, you are even given a mission to infiltrate the Arkham City Police Station, and after a few grumbles from Alfred about toning back the devastating blows when fighting the police, you are then allowed to brutally incapacitate every on duty officer inside the station. The sheer amount of officers you are allowed to perform the ingame "takedowns" and "freeflow combat combos" on absolutely blows away the miserly amount of cops you could attack in the previous games (note to Rocksteady, the mind controlled security guards in City and Asylum did not satisfy. The fans want to punch REAL cops who are fighting back on their own terms). Overall I'd say this game is one of the best Cop Smashing Games on the market and is a must have for any fans of beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of cops.

Im feeling good, even a little cocky now. I luckily found a station that offered repairs and I was able to get all my ships back into top shape though costing most of my scrap. Instead of heading for the exit i think ill take a few more chances since the danger level is still minimal and i need to gain some more scrap for upgrades. Ok, warp here and the mission is destroy all threats. This shouldn't be too much of a problem. Oh NO theres a battle carrier, torpedoes, shields failing dammit....game over.  And so goes another Distant Star Revenent Fleet run that looked promising and again ended in failure but damn lets do that again!
Distant Star Revent fleet is an addictive "one more mission" rouge type game set in space. At the start, literally,  you are immediatley thrown into battle thats set ups the familiar story and gameplay. The story begins(why was Revent Fleet added?) after an enemy ambush that leaves you as the leader of the last A'kari ship. Your mission is to traveres the galaxy, rebuild and upgrade the fleet (up to 5 ships) and destroy the enemy before they unleash their ultimate weapon that will destroy your homeworld. There are no cutscenes, pictures, voice or video. All information(other than the opening set up) is text based and unfortunante becasue while it's not an original story there are multiple occasions more art work, or sound would have provided some immersion into the world.
In order to win the game you will have to travel through 5 galaxies and complete roughly 35-50+ missions/warps depending on your courage to reach the end boss. Each galaxy contains muliptle sectors in which you warp your ship(s). This is where you can gain missions to earn scrap, upgrades and addtional ships. Choices are everywhere but the longer you stay in a galaxy the threat level from the enemy becomes higher making each warp to a sector more dangerous. Its that constant gamble that can payoff with more scrap, but also can devaste your run. Oh, and did i mention everything is procedurely generated so no run is alike. Quests, loot, ship upgrades, the galaxy is differet each time.
Gameplay is real-time/ pausable combact in the likes of the original Dragon Age and more recently Pillars of Eternity. The combat is excellent and you will constantly be pausing and startegizing your every move, every second. Battles do grow a little monotnaous after a hundred or so encounters but mixing up your fleet, equipment and passives makes each comabt session a dance of survival by number crunching. Each ship whether a tank, support, or heavy(7 different ships to choose) each has their strenghts and weakness and waiting for those countdowns to expire, pause and then position for the kill or to power up a friendlys shield or increase damage is super satisfying. All combat takes place on a randomly genertaed map with broken ships used to block oftern certain passages. Its an attractive background but it could have used some more variety, but hey, its space.
As you journey through the galaxy quests, missions and random events will be your source of income and more likely the countodwn to your impending doom. Missions in Distant Star vary from escort, destroy all enemies, protect or retake space stations, or ships to name just a few. As you warp into some sectors you will also be be given a text quests in which you will make a choice whether to steal from refugees, kill traitors, provide resources, etc but from an overall impact i do not know if playing good or evil has any consequnce. On some occasions, where i had helped refugees earlier by providing rations, later gave me a discount from a vendor but i am really not sure.
While i wish decisions did impact the world, one of the biggest problems you will face is having enough resources. Each time you warp to a sector you will consume 1 resource. As resources are limited you will occasionally/ randomly warp into a sector were you will be rewarded with a resource or 2 but my biggest issue are the vendors. As i mentioned the game is randomly generated and most vendors only sell one item. One may be a vendor for ships, another for upgrades, or another for resouces and repairs. Its really the biggest hurdle in my opinon especuilly on the harder difficulty as you have to continually warp and take on these missions and gamble  in order to build up your fleet. if you dont have resources it will cripple you in a sense that your ships(randomly) will receive critical damage. In one instance i made it to a vendor to repair my ships(no resources) but becasue of the expense i had no money left to buy resources. As i said earlier IF you have resources available and you run into trouble in a sector you can escape but with a penalty, but you have to have resources.Punishing to say the least.
Make no mistake this is not rouge 'like', or rouge 'light' this is a hard core rouge type game. One death and its the end, curtains, game over man. Its soul crushing, devasting, and sometimes just flat out ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t but damn it fun as hell. Distant Star is a great initial offering in a genre that is usually left to fanatsy and side scrollers. Its not as deep as it could go but there is stiil a lot of meat on this bone that hopefully they will be able to build on this success.

This was a pretty boring game.  The graphics, while polished for what they are, come across as very two dimensional.  Everything looks flat, like paper ships.  There is no 3D or 3D rendered or 2.5D  graphics here.  Models are flat as can be.  The backgrounds use layers to attempt to achieve depth, but this too comes across looking like nicely printed paper moving across other nicely printed paper.  The game overall was quite dark too and just not all that interesting to look at.
The pace of the game is quite slow as well.  I didn't really feel like finishing my game, but I played through to the end just to try to give it a fair review.
Sound effects are average, but the musical score will put you to sleep.  Seriously, if you have trouble getting to sleep, buy the soundtrack for this game.
Early battles for each level are way too easy.  I know the game is set up this way, but the most interesting moments in this game are when you are overpowered and really need to devise strategy and tactics to defeat the enemy.
One odd choice was the fog of war.   It just makes this already dark game look even darker, and the viewable area was too small imo.  Enemy ships appear from the fog of war just barely out of weapons range, giving the player a second or so to react.  Not good when you are already engaged with another enemy.  This negatively impacts the player's ability to mount effective strategy.
Battles can be difficult to manage.  I attribute this to the narrow zoom angle of the game.  You cannot zoom out and get a wide view of the battle.  You will find yourself often pausing the action to pan around the battle and issue orders, which further slows the pace of the game.
The ship types and weapon systems of this game are interesting.  Each ship has specific roles to play, and exploring their strengths while trying to piece together an effective battle fleet was fun.  I also enjoyed the skills system for this game, which helps make every ship in your fleet unique while tailoring them to your play style.
Though I wasn't able to defeat the boss on my one and only playthrough, it was a fun challenge.  I would like to try it again, but there is no way I'm playing through this boring game again.  I would have enjoyed other mini boss battles along the way.  Maybe a massive drone controller to defeat.  A carrier that continuously launches small craft.  A beam ship, and you can maneuver behind rocks to avoid the beams.   Anything.  Mini bosses would be more exciting and they would differentiate each level, instead of each level basically being a clone of the last.  I know, it's randomly generated, but I really felt like "didn't I just do this" at the start of every level.
Basically, as I said, this is a boring game.

Super Meat Boy will appeal to anyone who loves punishingly difficult platformers. It has incredibly tight controls, so you own every action your character takes. As a result, you'll find that every death is your fault, but you can reach levels of near perfection with practice. That, to me, is what makes a great, challenging game.
Instead of building large, sprawling levels, Super Meat Boy takes the approach that there should be many levels that are smaller, faster, more concise challenges. Many of the levels can be completed in under thirty seconds once you can actually pull them off, with only a few taking more than a minute. However, you'll also find yourself dying over and over again trying to complete each level as you grow in skill as a player, so it's not going to be often that you're actually finished with a level in such a short period of time. Additionally, there are hundreds of levels, all of which feel well-designed. There is also a level creation toolkit, and a content portal that lets you play user-made levels and worlds, many of which are quite interesting and challenging. As a result, this game offers dozens of hours of entertainment, even if you never venture into the user-made content.
Going over and above having tight mechanics and well-designed levels, Super Meat Boy is packed full of hidden content, like unlockable characters (many of which are from other indie games), retro warp zones, a dark world for every normal world, and glitch levels that can be found. These all bring personality, challenge, and intrigue to the table in a terrific way. Many of these are fairly well hidden, too, making it feel all that much more special when you come across them.
Super Meat Boy is a rewarding and incredible difficult platformer that has a fantastic soundtrack, looks great, and plays great. If you enjoy the challenge of honing your skills to perfect fast-paced and difficult levels, you'll love this.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is a game if you love words, if you love words being put together, and if you love words telling a story in your brain. Every conversation is an utter delight, with a turn of phrase or a statement that had me wheeling my chair back just to think about it, just to admire.
It's a game of choice, where your choices matter through how they effect you, those around you, and the world you're passing through. It asks questions of your actions all the time, and nothing ever is 'right' other than standing by whatever moral code you've chosen.
It's good. Very good. A true RPG, in that it's not just combat, there's choice and consequence, and conversation, and roles to play.

First and foremost, if you plan on playing this game, DO NOT compare it to Planescape: Torment, because they are not the same thing. I am a huge fan of P:T (and other CRPGs) and wound up liking this game after I stopped associating them together. Sure they call this a successor to that game, but it definitely is not the same thing.
Now that that's off my chest, let me get to reviewing this game. (I will use comparisons to older CRPGs to get my point across, but I am not judging it based off of these older games. I like this game as its own standalone series.)
First thing to know: this is definitely not a perfect game and there is a LOT of reading. If you don't like reading, this is probably not the game for you. There's a lot more reading than gameplay, in this game. I am not done playing this game. I have done 1 playthrough and still have more to do.
In a sort of "Undertale" style (I'm not a fan of Undertale, but that's the best comparison I could think of) this game allows you to almost always get through without having to battle. However, that does not make it a bad game.
You play as a character (who you can't customize, sadly, outside of being Male or Female) called "The Last Castoff". You're basically a blank slate, having lost your memories, and from there, you start the game and build up your character's personality. You can choose from 1 of 3 classes to be, before you start the game: A Glaive (warrior/fighter), A Jack (Thief), or a Nano (Witch, Wizard, Mage).
There's a lot of choices in this game, that can lead you to create all sorts of types of personalities for your character. You can be evil, good, or neutral or simply just keep changing your mind. Your actions change this thing called "tides". There are different tides that you grow attuned with, depending on how you live your life.  No choice is really right or wrong, so you can do what you want without having to be told 'BAD, YOU! Stop it!". Your companions are the only real people who will say anything, since they have their own personalities. They might conflict with you and might even love or hate you, but that's the only time anyone ever really says anything about your choices.
There aren't quite as many allies as other CRPGs and the allies you do get aren't quite as fleshed out as the ones you find in other CRPGs, as well. If you take the time to get to know them, you might find them a little interesting.
The best allies, in my opinion, are: Aligern, Erritis, Matkina, and Rhin. Alligern can be pretty bitter, but over time, he can be fun to have in your party. Erritis is basically the comic relief companion. Rhin is just adorable and I grew to see her as my adoptive daughter. Matkina is cool because she gives you insight into the other castoffs and history, etc. I found the other companions to just be bland (although it's cool that Callistege is voiced by the woman who voiced Nancy Drew in the Her Interactive Mystery Games). They just added Oom, who is cute, but I don't really know much else from that, yet.
For those, like me, who play RPGS and love romances- I'm sorry to tell you that there is no such thing as romance in this game. There is deep friendship, a sort of parent/kid relationship with Rhin, and you CAN make your companions LOVE you, but it's not quite the same as romance; more like "loyalty/familiar love".
There sadly isn't a lot of cool cutscenes or whatnot in this game. A lot of the action is either through battles or done in a sort of visual novel/choose your own adventure style.
Speaking of battle, the battles are turn based, which I know some people really hate, so take this as an FYI in case you do hate turn-based battles.
When it comes to fighting, there's a number of ways for you and your companions to fight. You can do physical damage, use a variety of weapons, or use these awesome things called "Numenera", which is part of the title of this game. Numenera are basically 1-time use things that allow you to cause lots of damage, gain buffs, make summons, etc.They can really turn the tide of a battle, but can make you sick if you hold too many of them. This is one of the coolest parts of this game, in my opinion.
Outside of battle, you gain 3 important skills (outside of being able to control the tides). These are called "Speed, Might, and Intellect. These are very important, because they're what you will use in conversations and for doing things outside of battle, like opening doors or trying to escape from danger, etc. I strongly suggest trying to level these up or you will have a hell of a time trying to play this game.
The graphics are pretty decent for a newer "CRPG-esque" game. I don't mind them at all, but some people hate them and this prevents them from playing the game.
I love the fact that I can play this using a mouse only, for the most part. Although I highly suggest you constantly keep your hand near the TAB key on your keyboard, so you can see the names of everyone, find important things, and entrances, etc. This is one of the bad parts of this game- the fact that the names of things/characters aren't just there, like in other games.
There are some bugs/bad animations in this game, such as getting stuck on invisible things or stuck in other characters, being unable to talk to characters, being unable to exit certain areas without having to try clicking on a character to talk to in order to get to the exit, or jumpy animations for characters. Sometimes the game freezes and stops working. And, sometimes the loading screens take forever.
The storyline of this game is decent, but definitely nowhere near as great as the original CRPGs or as great as other newer RPGs (Pillars of Eternity). It is cool, however, and I did get interested in it; it just took me a couple hours. The first few hours are kind of boring. Once you actually start getting into it and leave the main area, it becomes better.
If you're a fan of amazing worlds, I'm afraid that the world in this isn't quite as amazing in scale. It is definitely unique and has some cool places to look at, but the worst part of this game is that a lot of the time, you're stuck in one area for many many hours. Unlike Baldur's Gate or other older RPGS, there's not really a fast travel/world map. There are a few different areas, but they're defintely not as open as I had hoped for. However, there are a lot of interesting things to look at and some cool visuals, which makes up for the lack of vastness. I do like the setting of the game, though. It has a sort of Steampunk vibe, which I'm sure others will like.
I think that the worst part of this game is the fact that it suffers from the same issue a lot of point-n-click games suffer from: you get lost easily, because there isn't a lot of narrative that tells you exactly what to do. You do need to do a lot of reading and pay a lot of attention to literally everything you run into, because you won't truly know what you do or don't need (to know/have) until you get to that point in the story. Because of this, there are some quests and storylines that you can miss out on, which will seem pretty important in the future; so I suggest saving a lot so you can go back and do them, in case you can't go back to a certain area. SAVE SAVE SAVE LIKE CRAZY!
I think the coolest part of this game is that there are a LOT of ending possibilities and a lot of achievements in this game, on top of lots of ridiculous or funny choices, which gives this game a lot of replayability. I would suggest you at least give this game a try.

- THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PART FOR YOU TO KNOW BEFORE YOU BUY : Not a game but an interactive novel ! even tho I like to read and I understand that this is an interactive novel, the text felt overwhelming and just too much sometimes. 95 % of your "gameplay" time is just reading, the leftover 5 % is moving, exploration and combat. Expect to "talk" to some of the NPC for even more than 30 minutes until you deplete every option. And there are hundreds. Unfortunately not every NPC will tell you interesting things to read and sometimes it feels useless or even boring.
- Short and felt rushed. Completed this game in 35 hours. I expected more from the "spiritual successor of Planescape : Torment. Pillars took me 61 hours and Baldurs gate hundreds.
- I miss the AD&D mechanics and I am not really a fan of Monte Cook's Numenera world. I would prefer the classic Planescape world like in the first game. This game is absolutely not related to the first game by any means expect a few people who were working on both games. Therefore calling this a spiritual successor is out of the place.
- ♥♥♥♥♥♥ anticlimatic ending.
Conclusion :
This is still a good game with all it's flaws and I highly recommend this for all the cRPG fans. Don't expect miracles, this is not PS:T or BG but a slightly above avarage RPG with a good story and sadly not a spiritual successor to PS:T by any means. It just does not hold up to it's legacy. If you can get it on a sale, go for it. But I would not pay more than 10 $ for it. For that buck, it was a fantastic ride which I really enjoyed.

This is an fairly elaborate text-based RPG: honestly more of a choose-your-own-adventure book with pre-rendered backgrounds and, like the books, a single real through-line to the plot. The gameplay is mostly random skill-check rolls and selecting lines of dialog. Combat is primitive, with a clunky interface. You can essentially stumble your way through the story, re-trying skill-checks until you're happy. The game boils down to clicking "next" on a stupendously long and boring dialog tree. This wouldn't be terrible, but the writing is infested with Stronk characters and beta-apologist weasily wimpering. It's embarassing to read more than 10 minutes of this game. Do not play.

Wow.
So many reviews - and conflicting views on this game. I had to chip in! Here are my two cents:
Quick review: this is a very interesting and unique game. Worth your time. The kind I only saw a few times in close to 3 decades (yikes!) of gaming.
Cons:
-Yes, it's not perfect
-It does sometimes feel "unfinished"
Pros:
-Original
-Adventure RPG at it's best
-Reminds of of those 90s adventure game that just did not take you by the hand...
Rantings:
Back in the days... pc games were about experimenting and inventing new genres. When Syndicate or the original Torment or Baldur's Gate, or Xeen or even Quest for Glory came out, these were the first of their kind and pc gaming was not about emulating the previous game, they were about coming up with new game types, new gameplays, graphics, etc.
Yeah, Torment is not perfect and it's very text heavy but that's the point: this is not your typical game!
If you want to get lost in a very unique and original universe, this is an amazing game. Grab it.
It's an hommage to those early games where you had to read and picture things in your mind as well as rely on what the screen was showing you.
It's a courageous effort to go outside the box and pull you in a weird and crazy world.
It's on the edge of the new artform that pc gaming was back in the days, merging visual art, music, poetry, prose, storytelling and technology into a new artform that has since been sacrificied to the gods of profit that would rather have you play yet another game using the same old engine over and over again.
I mean, if the next elder scrolls games still has that same lock-picking system (that they have been using since Daggerfall!!!) I will stop playing right then and there. Please, evolve and innovate!
If you like checking boxes, following waypoints and getting all those achievements, you'll probably not enjoy this game.
This is meant to be an experience... this is beyond "gaming" as it's known today.
Open your mind and step in... or go play something else!
It is your right.

I enjoyed the game very much. It preserves many aspects that made its "predecessor" great. I was a bit wary, because of several negative reviews. Fortunately, there was a free weekend, and as I could not stop playing, I bought T:ToN. A good decision, as I played the game for 70 hours. I am thinking of starting a new playthrough with other characters sometime in the future.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is a cRPG with a lot of good ideas and very varying degrees of success in the implemention. When buying the game one should make sure that they know what kind of game they are buying so they won't be disappointed just because there was a misunderstanding what the product is. T: ToN is not a tactical combat simulator, action in any way, decision making simulator or character builder. It is a cRPG with an emphasis on roleplaying and exploring the wonderous world and story from the perspective of the PC.
Overall: 8-
Pros
+ Many memorable characters, locations and cultures
+ The main story and plot are interesting and well told
+ The game is filled with interesting mini-stories
+ The quests are  mainly well designed
+ The best looking arts assets look awesome and fit the setting spot on
Cons
- The combat mechanics are bad
- Most of the Crisises are both boring and tedious eventhough they are supposed to be "handcrafted"
- The resource management of Effort felt unnecessary and badly designed
- The ending felt unsatisfactory
Ps. I don't think I have ever come across to another game which has been dondemned so unfairly. People have complained about for example:
- The game doesn't have a proper day / night cycle
- The game is too different from Torment Planescape
- The game is too similar to Torment Planescape
- The game didn't / doesn't have all the content planned originally
- The game is not a PC exclusive
- InXile is evil
- The game is too short for an RPG
- etc.
And in most of these compains the writer makes it sound like that these are so big problems any single one of them makes the game bad. My world of advice is that don't look at average based ratings at all but instead read and watch individual reviews to see what exactly were the things the reviewer liked and disliked and compare those to your own preferences.

DISCLAIMER: I'm still pretty early in the game, so there's a lot of content I can't comment on, yet.
I *love* the story ideas in this game.  They're bizarre, beautifully realized in the game's world art, and offer excellent opportunities for stimulating story telling and character development.
I *hate* the mechanics of the game so far.  I still don't actually really understand what "tides" represent, other than facets of personality that contribute in some vague way to the ability point pools you use to interact with the game.  Different dialogue options you pick will increase (and presumably decrease, though I've not seen it yet) a tide of a particular color, and those colors line up with the colors of your various point pools.
I'm in the main city - Sagus City - with totally full combat pools, since there's been *zero* combat so far, and empty pools for what I can most simply call Dexterity and Speechcraft pools.  The main problem, of course, is 100% of the game so far has relied on the two latter, and none of the former.  The result of his disparity is basically a grinding halt of any quest progression, since I can't convince NPC's and characters to do/say/change anything with empty point pools for those interactions.
The solution?  Rest, obviously.  But resting, like in most games like this, relies on going to a place and paying some funds.  Easy peasy -- except the one place where I can do it charges more than I actually have, since I've apparently not accomplished whatever was expected of me in order to procure those funds.
The end result of all this is I'm stuck in what is basically the starting city with no apparent way to move the story forward and no way to replenish the only stat pools that apparently mean anything in the game to move the story forward.  I literally had to Google "how to rest in torment" and learned there are dialogue options you can take (which I wouldn't have done, b/c they didn't seem like choices my character would make) or quest lines you can complete to unlock free resting.  The latter requires those stat pools I mentioned that are empty, and so aren't attainable.
If I have to Google how to rest in your game, and the results are mostly about having to pick particular dialogue options that seemed dumb or premature for a character that's only been "awake" for less than a day to open up free resting options, so that I can replenish these arbitrary stat pools upon which the entire character interaction system is built, then you've failed as a game designer.  (DISCLAIMER 2: I am not a game designer, so that's just a pleb feel, I admit).
I'd love a movie of this universe. Or books.  Or a Netflix series.  The game world is vibrant and interesting, and the game's writing is excellent.  As a game, though, at least early on, it's just not good.  :\

There is a difference between 'a good game' and 'an entertaining game.' Batman Arkham Origins is a very entertaining game that had me gliding around Gotham for hours of fun. But Arkham Origins isn't necessarily a good game. Although it is very hard to back up the dynamic duo of greatest superhero games every made. (Asylum&City and yes pun intended) I would recommend Origins to people who have played both previous games before and just in general like the franchise. (Like myself) If you are new to playing the Batman Arkham games, just go get Batman: Arkham Asylum instead.....You'll thank me for it. However, in my opinion the voice acting was clearly the best part of the game with Troy Baker's outstanding performence of the Joker. The combat was the same as in Arkham City and the Riddler collectibles weren't nearly as taxing as the Riddler Trophies in Asylum and City. The boss fights in Origins where some of the best and worst times in the game. Since you don't really battle Killer Croc in Arkham Asylum and just merely avoid him, I was looking forward to an awesome Killer Croc battle when I heard he was in Arkham Origins. What I got was jump out of the way and throw a Batterang at him and occaisonally a few quick time events.....LAME.....One of the only boss' I even enjoyed fighting was Death Stroke. Death Stroke is the best boss battle in the game because it really shows how Batman and Death Stroke match each other in combat. Even though there where many quick time events, I was ok with that because the animation was stellar. I also liked the Dead Shot boss battle aswell. Keep in mind, none of the boss battles in the game were bad, they just weren't great. Compare it to Arkham City which has the best boss battles in the franchise. Arkham Origins was in the middle for me.....it wasn't bad...but it wasn't great either.

Distant Star: Revenant Fleet is an FTL-Like [is that a thing?], but not really. Really the only similarity is the map and agression buildup mechanic and having limited supplies. There are three main game phases, the universe map, sector map, and the RTS mission map. The universe and sector map are similar to FTL, but with an agression meter instead of the the encroacment of enemy controled space.
The actual game play is very differant. Many of the mission maps in DS:RF are procedurally generated. Unfortunatly they are also forgetable. There are a number of ship classes with a variety of tactics, weapons, and purchasable subsystems and semi-random level upgrades as the ships get exp. if you run out of supply or go down in a mission ships get "critical damage" which lowers one of the stats of your ship and can lead to destruction.
Where FTL created a winning combination with pretty fundementally simple mechanics, DS:RF's mechanics just don't hit that sweet spot just right, the innability to set waypoints and some difficulty with point and click targetting and navigation makes most complex tactics a chore and coordination difficult. The upgrade system is a little unsatisfying as well. The biggest problem with the game is that every time I hit "continue" after reading the flavor text at the end of the mission, the game hangs, stalls, and comes to the brink of crashing before finally snapping back after around 20 seconds (assuming you are patient and stop clicking, otherwise it will crash). Almost all of the menues and dialouge boxes do this and it kills the game.
That said, especially in the begining, the RTS space battles are visually pleasing with lots of detail put into ship destruction. It's extremely satisfying when my lancer beam cuts off part of a ship and it travels through the debris field of it's former allies. the AI is pretty basic and there are no ship collisions so you can neither ram nor block other ships. There are abilities ranging from buff's to heals and debuffs with ships representing healers, rogues, mages, tanks, dps, and "ranged dps."
If you can catch the game half off it's cheeper than the acrade, but It's also somewhat forgettable. Some of these issues shouldn't have made it to release, but it's clear that it was released in a playable state despite having some intractable bugs just beneath the surface despite work to fix them.
