Having just completed Planescape: Torment for the first time a few months ago (thanks for the Enhanced Edition, Beamdog!), spending roughly 100 hours with it, it is still very fresh in my mind as I venture through the world of Numenera for the first time.
So far, it compares very favorably to Planescape. It is an excellent game if you are a fan of Planescape: Torment and the style that game brought forth.
The story in this game and the encounters you find have deep philosophical underpinnings and heavy symbolism. There are a myriad of ways you can interpret the events in each situation, and like Planescape before it you could easily write a thesis on the many different angles this game continually presents you with. It will take a long time to peel away the layers of Tides of Numenera as there are so many choices you can make, which seem to have both far and short-reaching consequences. It looks like a very complex web that makes up the foundation of the game, from the skills you choose to develop, the companions you decide to bring along and the decisions you make.
You play the game as The Last Castoff, a literal shell of the Changing God. The Changing God likes to jump from body to body to evade his own death, and you were the last body shell he used. Or, so you think. Who you really are is as much a mystery as it was in Planescape. All you know for sure is that you were born into the world by falling like a star (or a *moon*, at best), crashing through a dome in the strange coastal city of Sagus Cliffs. You are being hunted by The Sorrow, a hideous beast that wants to devour your very being, your very existence. The Specter, a strange projection of a man in your mind, implored you to find and fix something called a Resonance Chamber, a device which he claims will keep you safe from being devoured by The Sorrow.
During the game you will explore the physical world, i.e. The Ninth World, which is Earth 2 billion years in the future. You will also explore the deepest fathoms of your mind (literally, you will explore The Labyrinth of your mind at some points during the game, which you can frequently return to) in an attempt to survive this "life" as you know it and fix the Resonance Chamber. Along the way you will meet characters who need your help and can travel with you, helping you understand more about who they are and who you are in the process.
In other words, it's very PS:T-like, and done to a very high level.
It is remarkable that they crammed the amount of detail they have into the game, with variations sometimes so subtle they could easily be missed if you aren't paying attention. Even seemingly "generic", unnamed townspeople may have 3 or 4 small, unique (and often funny) things to say to you. The fact that the game has over 1 million words (!), i.e. more words than The Bible, is an amazing feat considering the quality of the writing. And there is no way you will see all 1 million of those words in one playthrough as there are just so many varying factors in the game based on the player's choices.
Yes, there is a lot of text, as there was in PS:T. It is all excellently written, consistent and interesting, contrary to some negative memes about this game spread on the internet. There is very little superfluous, unnecessary or out-of-place text, and the introduction of the world's slang is no more jarring than givin' someone the laugh, cutter, in PS:T. Aye? The level of detail in the exposition is very, very similar in both games, and for my money Numenera is a tad more detailed and vivid while using similar amounts of descriptive text.
Questing, exploring, chatting, character developing, looting; it's all there. The thing that may surprise you is a lack of combat in general. Combat generally happens very infrequently (although your choices impact this), and can usually be totally avoided. A combat encounter in Tides is a much more critical and important situation than in most RPGs, i.e. a Crisis, rather than a random encounter giving you an opportunity to mindlessly kill things. Yet despite the lack of combat, the game is completely interesting and intriguing without having to really raise any weapon against foes if you choose. The option is generally left up to the player to decide how to handle each situation, with a combination of a possible skill check based on your character's skill, with a dice roll at times to determine success (which can also be augmented depending on how much Effort you spend, and even increased to a 100% success rate if you have the Effort available from your stat pools.) The game is more about exploring the world, finding unique, strange objects, having deep and interesting encounters with characters, objects and the environment and much more than just killing bad guys.
The graphics also help to tell the story and look quite beautiful in 4K. Much like PS:T you will get detailed descriptions of some objects in the environment, but the difference is that in Tides, you see *more* of the description with your own eyes via animations. If the description mentions bubbles or streaks of lightning surrounding an object, most of the time you will actually see those depicted in the physical environment as well. It is a step above the older games in that way, and is almost certainly a benefit of being made in 2017 with modern technology.
The game overall is very polished. It oozes a feeling of high quality. The soundtrack, graphics, UI et. al are all very nice, clean and feel like they are part of a slick, expensive production.
For my money this is up there with Planescape: Torment so far, a game which I really revere. It trims some of the fat of excess combat in Planescape and focuses the experience more. There are plenty of buttons to push, toys to tinker with and unique people to discover that make the game feel almost like an amusement park of unique, fun and interesting experiences. I'm not sure if it will fully reach the heights that Planescape did for me, but I wouldn't rule anything out as I play and examine the game more. It certainly is a worthy successor to Planescape, absolutely.
I really look forward to exploring more of this world and learning more about it. I hope InXile will make more games like this. If you like Planescape: Torment or complex, utterly interesting isometric RPGs, you should really check this game out and support the devs. It's really a unique RPG that is well worth your time if you are into either Planescape: Torment, isometric RPGs, interesting lore with a sci-fi tinge or just unique RPGs that will draw you in and immerse you deeply.
Thank you, InXile, for the excellent RPG!

'Torment' has always been in my focus ever since its inception. The original 'Planescape: Torment' remains to be one of my favorite RPGs. The expectations were high, of course, and when the game came out I madly read reviews from major webzines and what people had to say on various forums. Few things I read made me a little worried, such as reoccurring themes of lack of content, simplification of mechanics, lack of good combat, etc. I thought that, well, perhaps the Devs just couldn't meet their grand ambitions and have released a decent product but not quite the masterpiece everyone wanted. I decided to dive deep into this experience and see for myself..
TL:DR: At the very least this game needs a careful consideration, at the very most this is another RPG masterpiece in the best traditions of its older brother. My feelings tend to be on the far positive spectrum.
I spent with this game in total of three hours before I really started to explore the first city. . So what made me stomp around the same couple of locations all this time, seemingly not making much progress?
Every single character I've met along my way had something interesting to say, expanding the lore of the fascinating world and adding to it a bit of a personal touch in the form of a tragedy or a subtle comedy, or even an allegory, masterfully told between the lines. Such inspired  weaving of stories, visual art and auditory magic--and presenting it in an accessible format of a videogame--is a truly a feat. .
Torment will age like fine wine, like a work of art it is, and it will stay relevant like its older sibling for generations to come. Because its components don't need fastest hardware to realize their intent. I suppose the game is like a poem where images, ideas and feelings are presented as symbols for each individual. It is an impressionist painting that is not meant to be a modern photograph. Such approach requires from players more mental work to interpret the symbols, to read those words and imagine those worlds, all while being guided by images and sounds accompanying the experience. It is true that very seldom an individual would need to activate his reptilian brain while engaging with the game. This game could have been made purely in the text format and still remain relevant as a work of literature. Its visual part can be exhibited separately in a gallery-type environment. And the music can be played as a stand-alone performance. I am not saying that mindless shooters and titles such as Candy Crush are bad. There's time and place for everything, however, the balance is not quite proportionate, considering the current market, and the choices we have, unfortunately..
It is necessary to say few words about the sonic component of this creative manifestation that many reviewers have ignored to mention. To be honest, this game has one of the best soundtracks in any video game I ever played over two decades. It's definitely in the top 10. .  Even though I can't think of any catchy tunes, catchy tunes wouldn't have worked here, they just don't belong. Let's not forget that this is avant-garde, ladies and gentlemen. The quality of the sound itself adds to the submersion. And by quality I mean not just the artistic quality, but the quality of mixing, production, composition, clarity of the signal.. The whole nine yards. Listen to this game via a good stereo through a digital output or a nice pair of headphones, and you will get lost in a different world if you close your eyes (or keep your eyes on the screen).
Choosing not to say much about the graphics, doesn't mean that there's nothing memorable. Oh, the hand-drawn locations are mesmerizing and provide a relief from usual  castles or  space ships we see in games these days. Like its predecessor, this game breaks norms and chooses to challenge and inspire players at the same time.
Sure, there are some technical shortcomings but I don't even want to mention them. Because they pale so when considered as a part of the whole this game constitutes. My mildly biased opinion is that this game is a masterpiece and there's nothing really wrong with it..  Insert here a chuckle.. Yep, just dig into it and tell me what you think after the credits start to roll. And I bet it will be nothing about "small locations" or "lack of combat." Talking about combat, it's there if you want it, and it's not broken, yet it is your choice how you want to handle tricky situations. If you lied, persuaded or deceived your way  out of a heated trouble, well, it's no one's fault but yours.
A lot of games strive to play like interactive movies, and they somewhat succeed, more so with every passing year, as new technologies become available. However, this game plays like an interactive science fiction novel of a top tier quality. Meaning, this work will inevitably make you think about all sorts of topics that people normally don't bring up during office chit-chats. Really, it is food for brain. The kind of substance that we have a huge shortage of in our society. I am just glad that this game found its way into mainstream, and that there are people who create such things and people who interact with them, and through their support bring such gems to life.

Let me start by saying I wanted to return this game within the first 20 minutes of gameplay. I didn't feel any particular way, and the opening didn't grab me quite yet. But I thought it only fair to give it a real try, and played through it. I am so glad I did! This game is a lot of fun. The story and writing kept me glued for two days straight until I finished it in the end.
The game plays very much like, obviously, Pillars of Eternity, when it comes to the systems and basics. You can see a lot of parallels
But it works! It doesn't feel like a blatant rip off of a core function; it actually blended into the gameplay pretty well.
If you like having the ability to play through a game by talking your way out, you'll enjoy Torment. You CAN actively fight everyone and everything, but I never found myself wanting to. I really enjoyed being able to diffuse situations by talking my way out of it. It really plays more like a choose your own adventure game and less like a standard RPG, and for me that really happened to work. If you like combat heavy games, you probably will be pretty disappointed.
And speaking of combat: I wasn't a huge fan of the combat in Torment. To give it a fair review, I have to preface this by saying I am generally not a fan of turn based fighting, so take what I say with a grain of salt. It's way too slow paced, and you're always incredibly outnumbered -- which in the way of fighting, is not so bad. You can definitely hold your own in the game with limited fear that 1.) death is permanent, and 2.) you're gonna die in the first place in combat. I really hated being so outnumbered because it made the queue so much longer, and waiting for it to be one of my companions or my turn took a really boring and long time. Not to mention that sometimes NPCs and enemies will just sit and idle for a little while when it comes to their turn, making combat drag out even longer for no reason.
Another small issue I had with the game that could have really changed the way I played it was how they handled changing your party members. Every time you wanted to switch someone out, you had to open a dialog, they would get upset that you were booting them (which led me to not change party members for a long time,
, and then you had to call them back to you. I ended up missing out on Aligern for a lot of the story simply because I didn't think I could switch him out with Callistege without booting her from my party permanently.
All of my gripes aside, this game was a lot of fun to play. The characters were pretty well written. I was emotionally invested in my character's story, as well as my companion's stories. The gameplay was interesting and fun, especially because death wasn't an end, but a mechanic to gameplay.
I enjoy a game where my choices really matter, and this game doesn't let you down in that aspect. So If you're heavy into fighting and standard RPGs, this probably isn't for you! But if you're heavy into roleplaying games and choose your own adventures, then I think you'll love this game as much as I do.
It's a surprising game, really. I didn't expect much of it, and it managed to impress me all around. Give it a try if you're interested. And really give it a try, because I almost refunded a game that is now easily in one of my top favorite slots.

When one makes a spiritual successor, one must ask themselves 'how close to the original should we stay?'
For a game like Planescape Torment, one should try and re-capture the themes and story it build.
Does Tides of Numenera do that?
Yes. Yes it does. Perhaps not quite to the scale of Planescape, but it still holds the original ideas.
The tale of Tides of Numenera is a rather simple one. Save yourself.
A left over biproduct of another mans method of immortality, which is, building himself new ones and then transfering his mind into them, you are the Last Castoff. The latest in a long line of left over shells used by a man known only as the Changing God. When his mind flees from one body to another, the left over shell becomes its own person.
This odd method of prolonging his life has attracted the attention of a powerful and deadly creature that wants only to destory him and all his creations.
Set in the odd, but charming world of Numenera - you are cast into a far flung future of the Ninth World, one billion years into Earths future. Where science and magic are indistinguishable from each other. At first this will seem over whealming and alien, but in less than an hour you will settle in to this strange world and quickly learn to understand its quirks and oddities.
Tides of Numenera uses a great deal of text in its story telling, with very little voice acting, which can be a major draw back. So when you boot the game up, get ready for some eye strain. (I believe it has upwards of 1 million words in total)
The gameplay is a turn based tactics type deal, where each character has their own set of uniquie abilities and powers . That being said, one does not have to always rely on fighting to settle disputes. Tides of Numenera can be played without having to kill anyone, if you play your cards right.
The Graphics are very nice for a cRPG and and the animations are smooth. The world looks and feels very nice over all. If someone lacking in size. But I've always perfered substance of size.
So, how would I rate this game?
A very solid 8/10, and a definate worth successor to Planescape: Torment.
While perhaps lacking some of the darker tones of Planescape, and have a very large amount of text, Numenera sets it self apart enough to be its own game without changing so much, that it loses track of it self.

This is my first review personally, so please bear with me.
Let me state initially that as a fan of Planescape:Torment, Baldur's Gate I & II, Icewind Dale etc. I was intrigued when I first saw this game, however, I was deterred from engaging it by many of the negative reviews.
I purchased the game on sale and having just completed my first playthrough of the game, I can definitely see the validity of many of the thoughts offered and wanted to share some brief ones of my own.
- The game, in my mind, was definitely worth the price I paid for it on sale ($18), however, I would not recommend paying the full price for it ($45)
- If you are looking for a more immersive, story-rich RPG, where your choices have impact, I might recommend exploring other titles first, such as Divinity Original Sin (1 & 2), Pillars of Eternity (and its sequel slated for release in 2018), or even Tyrrany
- If you are looking for more involved skill/ability tree development and/or combat rich game, this is probably not the game for you
- If you don't mind a heavy mixture of reading and weighing the benefit of using force, cunning/guile, persuasiveness, inquisitiveness, and diplomacy in a variety of situations this game is quite fascinating
- Although the companion characters, as others have noted, might not possess the depth present in other games such as those in the Dragon Age series or Divinity: Original Sin titles, nevertheless, if you immerse yourself in both the larger narrative arc and the choices present in assisting your companions the experience can be delightfully haunting as you contemplate virtue/vice, loss/fulfillment, love/hate, and vengeance/forgiveness
- Personally, although I have already completed the first playthrough in the game, there is definitely a re-playability factor. I am intrigued to see how the game feels differently if I choose a different route for the main character (initial run I chose an intellect based character) and I would like to explore all the companions that I did not fully work with (5 more by my current estimation)
Overall, I would definitely recommend the game at its sale pricing, however, I would also highlight that it might only appeal to a niche audience. Be mindful of what the game is and what it is not when entering in and it can be quite an enjoyable experience.

Borderlands 2 holds true to its looter shooter origins, continuously and consistently rewarding players with loot piles after loot drops after loot piles – most of which scales as the players do. You’ll quickly find that most of it isn’t worth picking up due to its low value or obsolete stats though. This acquired junk instead will be used to trade-in for cash, but Borderlands 2 doesn’t do much to give players an incentive to save up. With money, players can go to stores and vending machines, only to find items not as good as what they already have after a few hours of gameplay, or they can blow it on the slot machines. The slots are the game’s way of giving players a fun chance at earning more valuable loot, the most valuable of which are the super-duper-rare orange items and Eridium, the latter of which can be used on the Black Market to buy permanent player inventory upgrades (i.e. more ammo storage or inventory space).

On the surface, Duckie Dash doesn’t bode well: bad physics, repetitive levels, and plethora of level design oversights. Still, thanks to the lack of challenge, it is a surprisingly soothing little thing.
Duckie Dash looks and feels like a cheap Unity asset store product. It is a time trial game, where the player has to navigate a little ducky through 3×10 courses, using slipstreams, geysers, and boosters, all the while avoiding some unfriendly beavers and whirlpools.
Since there are no opponents and the par times are incredibly generous, the only hazard the player faces are the physics, or more like the lack of them: there is no acceleration, collision stops you instantly, and the water is more like some transparent jelly.
Still, there is something soothing about playing a game with no chance to lose. Also, the stages are super short (30-180 seconds), so Duckie Dash can be used as something like a calming treatment, if you like these challengeless titles (and if its price drops to a reasonable level).

Well. This is it. The first game I've had to give a thumbs down. It's also the first game I asked for a refund over.
Is Dark Void Zero the worst game I've ever played? No. But it's also not very fun. Which is a shame because it has all the components for a good game: colorful graphics, action platforming, and a cool sci-fi theme. But the problem is that none of those things are done particularly well. Dark Void Zero tries to bank on its retro-for-retro's-sake aesthetic without actually delivering a solid experience like the games it hearkens back to.
The gameplay of Dark Void Zero boils down to navigating large, maze-like levels with the aid of a jetpack. You shoot enemies and dodge obstacles. There are level objectives thrown in, like hitting a switch or finding an item. And the game is short, too, only having three levels to play through.
So what's wrong with it all? To begin with, the graphics, while bright, do not look good. Take a step back and compare a game like Batman: Return of the Joker to Cybernoid. One looks much better than the other. Now take a step forward and compare a game like Axiom Verge or Odallus to Dark Void Zero. When the ability to make gorgeous pixel graphics is as accessible as it is today, there's no reason for Dark Void Zero to look this bad.
Moving on, the controls suck. 8-way navigating should not be frustrating. In Dark Void Zero it is. It doesn't help that the level design, instead of being open and wide, is tight and cramped. The freedom of zooming about, shooting bad guys is replaced with being corralled around narrow corridors and shafts. What makes that even worse is that oftentimes any powerups you might have found (which are more difficult to get than they're worth) are taken away from you to which you're then forced to use another, more inferior weapon for a portion of the map.
Why give me the freedom to explore when you take away the fruits of my labor? That would be like playing the original Zelda, and after working hard to find all of the extra Hearts and the Magic Sword and the Red Ring, walking through a door only to be reduced to four Hearts and the Wooden Sword. Why? Why give me the option of finding secrets that only aid me in finding secrets that in turn don't help me in completing the stage?

You want a good "retro" NES game? Play Shatterhand. Or Vice. Or Ninja Gaiden III. Or Batman. I could keep going, but my point stands: 8 bit graphics and sound do not excuse a bad game.
Poor game design like that is what held this game back. Poor game design, along with its poor controls and poor level design, make this game too difficult for the wrong reasons. I find this very similar to the original Dark Void: full of potential, but flying just short of quality.

I never experienced the 80s, but I was around back when NES games where still being made. I remember playing on it when I was a kid and having so much fun. If a game didn’t work just blow on it, once in the console and just try again. Graphics didn’t matter, there were only 64 colors anyway.
Originally Dark Void Zero was created as an April Fools prank, but somehow the devs thought to make it an actual game. However this game turned out to be much better than the one it was promoting.
Dark Void Zero is kind of a throwback to the 80s, same colors, same sounds, same clunky controls. It all fits perfectly. I actually own this game twice, I downloaded it first on the Nintendo DSi, where I played it much more than I did on the PC. The PC version only differs in one point, which is the death cam at the end, where you see every point where you died during your play. Now actually I like it better on the DSi than I do on the PC, but that’s not the point.
Beyond all of that, I’m not that sure that there’s more to it. It has a story, like most games, that has been done. It has three levels, most games in the 80s where relatively short due to soft-and hardware limitations. To make up for their lack of longevity, they made them hard. Playing this game on easy would be more in the line of above normal. Playing it on hard, would be hard as ♥♥♥♥. You will definitely get what you ask for.

-------------
If it is good enough to own twice, it’ll be pretty okay to own once.

Undertale is such a unique take on an 8 bit game. In a time of unreal and unity engines how can a primitive looking game even compare? It lies in the story and flow of the game. On one play through it seems linear, through another playthrough you see your choices matter much more than you ever thought.
In a word it can only be described as surprising. playing it requires you to challenge the idea of how a game should be played and every aspect of it has so much depth. The characters have personalities beyond what you originally thought, the soundtrack match your feelings and the battles (or lack of battles) stay interesting through and through.
It is not a perfect game and may not even appeal to majority of gamers. But if you enjoy a game for its story and design then you should help yourself to a play-through. This game draws on your thoughts of humanity without forcing the subject. It stays comedic and up-beat while slapping you with heart-string-pulling.
Lastly I want to say I nominate this game for soul of vitruvius award due tot he main character, which is vicariously you. You are silent and your words are your actions. You will come to find yourself meeting both great and horrible people and you have a chance to influence them. You can influence through force, sacrifice or abandonment. Depending on your choices you find your appropriate ending.

After the few years of Undertale having been shown to the public, and the fandom has became worse than cancer and died out, I believe it is time for a review.
Undertale is a simple game where your choices impact the game in ways that you won't even realise until much later in another playthough. The game is best played blind, however, if you are reading this you are most likely someone who has fully decided their stance on the game, so I won't be changing minds anytime soon.
Pros:
-The game's soundtrack is simplely outstanding
You're seeing the pricetags right, the soundtrack is as much as the actual game itself, and for 100 sound tracks, it seems to be a good deal.
-Creative
The game will make you laugh at the jokes it plays and puzzles it shows will be a little mind wraping your first run.
-The Combat
the "combat" point of the game is fun enough to not get stale throughout the play time until your 5th run or so.
Cons:
-Repeating Tracks
I swear to god four songs that are all the same fricking song, and I asked a couple of my friends and they swear they're not. Listen to "Ghost Song", "Dummy", and "Spider Dance" and you'll notice it, they are the same song.
-Preachy
Of course going down the Genocide path is bad, but my god, did the game have to make it so boring to do? Other then the two major bosses, genocide is just plain boring. I get it, I'm killing people, but really, could we have SOMETHING else to do during the in genocide route.
-Reruns
Returning to the game after doing a few runs feels wrong, you lose your sence of wonder after that first run, this is not a game to constantly replay after your first few runs.
Overall-
Undertale is a good game that I do recomment playing, however, with it's fanbase being as toxic as it is, is not something to get into... However, as a game, Undertale is loved for the right reasons, if you don't like it, you most likely either didn't play it, or the Cons of this list are the only things you think about (along with the bad fans)
Undertale is a game to be played, and a game that most people should play for a good time.

There's a lot to love in this imperfect game.  Conceptually it's fantastic.  The gameplay is unique and fun.  Like all good platformers, the gameplay mechanics evolve as you progress.  I love the artwork, and the background music is quite pleasant.  I like the small details like the lights switching on and the birds flying away and the appearance of butterflies. I really like the story concept and the parallel perspectives of father and daughter.
However, the big weakness in this game is the repetition of dialogue. There is already significant repetition since the daughter's dialogue repeats with the fathers (but I like that).  The problem is that the dialogue repeats a lot of the same information across chapters.  And then, in a short, five chapter game, the last chapter completely repeats the first chapter (although it does add some new elements).  Another slight issue is with the controls - if you hold down the jump button for Sally, you will repeatedly jump.  This is fine except that oftentimes if you aren't just tapping the jump button, you might get two jumps in a row you don't want.
Despite these two issues, I recommend the game.  I was able to do a full playthrough and collect all the collectibles in about 2 1/2 hours.  I also had 17/20 achievements by the end of that. The remaining three aren't hard to get, but they involved doing things I didn't naturally do while I was playing.
Unfortunately, I'm not sure there is much replayability here. I really like that you can unlock character skins.  Some of them are very cool - like the foxes and the Christmas ones. The platforming is solid but slow at times to allow the player time to read the dialogue. The dialogue is so repetitive in a single playthrough that I don't imagine people wanting to read it over and over across multiple playthroughs.
Regardless, this game is absolutely worth a single playthrough and at full price if you enjoy indies with a casual pace and can forgive some imperfections.
Lastly, thank you to the devs for explaining the title on the store page.  Apparently Sally's Law is supposed to be the opposite of Murphy's Law (anything that can go wrong will) because things usually go right for Sally with her father watching out for her. Sweet idea.

I think it's save to say that this is one of the beyt games I ever played. Especially in this genre. And yes I plaey PS:T. Right befor this one actually, so I had a rather good and fresh comparison. And while I love PS:T, Numenea has something... more.
It's just utterly fascinating, strange and wonderful. I loved searching for every little bit of text that showed me more of this starnge world and enjoyed all the unique items that can be found.
And while the game is very reading focused I really liked the small bits of gameplay it has. The battles were rare but fun and you could do a lot despite them being quite simple. Also the thing with the skills like speed, strength and intelligence (dunno how they are named in English xD ). It's a bit more than just depending on pure luck, since you can decide how much percent you want to have or you can spend level points in edges.
The text itself was fantastic to read, although the German translation was quite often really messy and sometimes utterly bad (Like: Google translator quality). InXile should definitely hire someone else for the job for the next game. >.>
Sure I could just have played in English, but it's just way more tiring to read so much text in a non-native language.
What I also really loved was how much your companions were included into the world. That was a thing PS:T really lacked a lot. You found your companions, talked to them until you had all dialogues comleted... and then they were just mindless NPCs for the majority of the game. Numenera included them very often into dialogues, so it felt as if they were really with you.
My first playthrough took me around 70 hours and I only had the same 3 companions with me all the time. (Since I want to start a second someday and take the others with me then).
Buy this game if you are:
- not afraid of reading tons of text
- a fan of avoiding every battle you can (or just don't)
- interested in an utterly fascinating and strange world that surprises you at every corner
Don't buy the game.... if you dissagree with anything above. xD

I wish I could give this game a score instead of a binary recomendation. But after investing many hours to play this game the ending among many other CONS made this game a BIG DISAPPOINTMENT.... therefore thumbs down :(
Such a shame this game has such potential...
PROS:
- Game design is overall extremely detailed, colors, lanscapes and level design... really, the team which did this put so much love into it... congrats on that!
- smooth running game engine with a steady 60fps cap which gives excellent gameplay without nausea
- Awesome Brawler Combat a la Batman. I'm quite sure that they've bought the code from Rocksteady studios. The type of enemies and the way boss fights feel are almost identical to the Batman Arkham games. Somehow they have improved it. Combat feels much more polished.
- Car combat! (Extremely fun at the beginning, but after....have a look at the CONS)
- Chumbucket (the mechanic) improves the game atmosphere with his hilarious comments and entertaining pseudo religious jabber
CONS:
- Towards the end the game feels rushed, many balancing issues and the story gets weaker towards the end
- HUGE balancing issues regarding magnum opus, almost all of the enemy vehicles had better handling although they were much more robust
- even with the highest armor, magnum opus is a fragile piece of machine. after 10-15 hours in the game instead of ramming cars you end up jumping out of yours and the game becomes something like a matador simulator with cars...
- wonky collision detection car gets stuck at most annoying times (happens a lot during the gastown race)
- story is VERY inconsistent, ok I didn't expect a big story from this game but the way Max behaves is just very inconsistent. But the story also does not give the impression that this inconsistencies are there due to his madness. He actually speaks and behaves quite normal. So to describe his behavior I'd call him "Schroedingers Max"...
- UTTERLY DISSAPPOINTING ENDING! To be clear I did not expect a fuzzy warm happy ending from a Mad Max game but this???
TLDR;
If you don't care about the weak story and character inconsistencies and only want to play a good brawler with some car combat you should definitely buy this game
but if you expect a bit more.... don't waste your money and time

So... Mad Max.
First of all, you get to play as a good ol' Max in his endless quest for... I am not quite sure what. But in this game, the main goal is to make a new car. So, you get to personalize your car from a parts that you'll find you your quests and journeys. The main story is good and actually quite interesting, so are the quests. Side-quests, given to you from wastelands lords and some random encounters are good too. Some even quite challenging. Can't say the same about open-world activities. Don't get me wrong, some of these are fun to do, but it gets quite repetitive after a while. And you must do quite a lot of these, if you want to unlock more parts for you car. The ones I do like, though, are the "Convoy attack". These are really fun to do. Combat could be a little strange at first, but you'll get used to it eventually. Game can be played with controller or keyboard, depends on what do you prefer, it's quite comfortable to play both ways. Ammo is scarse, but it's not that big of a problem. But in case if it is a problem for you... You can get more max ammo storage as you level up. And I haven't seen much bugs in game, as I played it. Yes... It's a bit lineal and there isn't much choise of what you can change (Except for your car, of course), but there is an open world for you to explore and secondary quests and another activities to do, if you feel like taking a break from main quest for a bit. I even encourage you to do so, if you want to unlock more upgrades for your car. So, to finish this review... It's a good single-player game with interesting main story and well-made and fun road-rage rampage. It's a solid 8 of 10 and I do recommend it.

I came to this game late in the day. I love Batman, but having been burned by game breaking glitches in both Asylum and City, I refused to pay top dollar for Origins. especially at launch. Add that to no Conroy and no Hamill, and I had real concerns about how Origins would stack up. So I waited, and eventually it went on sale.
Well, I was partly right. Troy Baker is no Hamill as the Joker. He puts in a valiant effort, amd he should be applauded, but he is in the master's shadow.
Otherwise, though, Origins is superb, perhaps even the best in the series. The combat is the most enjoyable of the games so far, and the villains - most of whom it is fair to say are in the Batman B cast  - are actually very engaging.
The writing is also top notch, the highlight for me being when Joker's rhapsodizes the bat at the same time as seducing Doctor Quinzel. It's also fun to play Batman as he finding his feet. Detective vision takes on a more literal meaning for the 'world's greatest detective', actually used to solve some mysteries, as opposed to finding out where the nearest grapple point or wall to explode is (though you still use it for that).
So, it's great. If you love the series, or enjoy seeing Batman done well, you should enjoy this.
Edit: Some people have said this game has issues with Mouse and Keyboard controls. I used a controller, and had none.

I'd precaution that I don't think this game is a bad game, I just can't recommend this version.
I bought this game in a sale a while ago and am just playing it seriously now. If you have any interest in this game, and if you own any Nintendo handheld from the DSi onward, buy that version instead. I haven't played the DSiware version, mind you, but from videos of gameplay I figured the PC version would be somehow better in it least resolution, but a better look at the graphics here only serve to the games' detriment; the native resolution on the DS makes it look as if it were a unique step beyond 8-bit, the 2 options (windowed and fullscreen)  on PC make it look like poor mockery of a NES game. One problem I have which I presume is present in both versions is that the sound design (other than the music) is inconsistent with the "retro" theme, with some sounds being appropriate and some just being poorly masked modern sound effects, which is jarring when noticed. I had to drag the windowed screen to a much smaller size to make the graphics decent looking, and also put the sound effects down to minimum and the music 3 notches above it - there was some definite oversight with whoever made the default options so bad. If you've made the same mistake of already buying this version of the game, this is at least the most optimal way to play it.
Now, my biggest gripe with this port is the blatant removal of an integral feature: the map. The DSiware version gives it to you on the bigger top screen the entire time, like the DS Castlevania games. Here, Mr. Tesla is constantly referring to having updated your map, and THERE IS NO MAP. There isn't even a button to bring it up. You could argue that the map is unnecessary given how simple the map is, and maybe this is a direct throwback to Metroid I & II, but again, it is CONSTANTLY referred to in game, and those are the only games in the series that are too obtuse to play now without the use of a guide. I could have overlooked it here if they only removed that from the dialogue. That Capcom hasn't is obscenely lazy, and as a result, there is no justification for having released this game in the state it is in.
I had no issues with the CD-Key, but it was still an unnecessary and inconvenient step in the process further defining this version as the inferior port.
Edit: Nevermind, the M key brings up the map, which is explained nowhere and I had to find out online! Still can't recommend this version.

I stumbled upon this quirky, lovely, casual platformer by chance. Considering the price and the cute visuals I decided to buy it. The gameplay itself is ultra simple platforming coupled with a twist - how you finish a level determines how it will be "replayed" with the second character. Although I did tend to mess up sometimes I did not find the game (or the achievements) difficult. Some of the jumps detract from reading the story though, as do a couple of English language mistakes. But the story is what makes the game worth it for me. Right from the beginning it grips your heart and squeezes. It touches the tipic of single parents but anyone who does not see their parents often can deeply relate. It is hard to say if I can connect with the story better because I'm older. And I do wonder what I would think of it if I was 12 again (or younger). Sadly, the writing got a bit worse by the end, repeating the same thing over ("she is courageous", "I was lucky"). Though I got the message of WHY it was worded like this it kind of feels like it could have been replaced by something else to make the ending a bit better. Do I recommend this game? Well, how could I not if it made me actually call my folks! It's cute, relaxing and makes you think about the parent-child relationships. Try it!

This is a beautiful, casual game I just purchased, about a father and daughter at odds who eventually reunite after quite a few years apart.
The art is well done, and the music is soothing. Basically you play as Sally who, after dreaming of being a writer, runs off to the city leaving her father behind. There aren't any enemies per se, but you can fall to your "death," and unopened columns and un-trampled spikes/bushes can harm Sally; causing you to start part of the level over. There are only 3 sets of keys to remember, space bar so Sally can jump, the directional keys so the father can move, and the left shift key to speed Sally up when playing as the father. As far as I can tell, there's no need for the mouse in any part of this game.
The biggest difficulty in this game comes with obtaining all the memorial pictures, as well as the last couple of levels. I've spent most of my play time attempting to finish the last couple of levels, while at the same time getting the memorial photos. For me, there is only one minor negative, and it's that you don't keep a memorial photo if you fail that specific part of the level. Which is somewhat understandable. That being said, I guess the music can become a bit irritating if you're spending a lot of time repeating the same sections over and over. One other thing, timing is quite important in some parts of this game. It almost requires you to think ahead, since the father can only "jump" by bouncing off of Sally. And to clarify, you first play the level as Sally, then after a couple of sections you play as the father with Sally taking the exact same route you took to complete the level just before.
So yes I would recommend this game, but it is rather short. So if that bothers you, wait for it to go on sale again. As I was able to pick this game up for $1.99, and I don't regret it in the least.
P.S. No need to worry about being stuck in this game, the level restarts after several seconds of no movement.
P.P.S. I nominated this game because I found it fairly addicting, and really just wanted to keep playing until I reached the end. Since I've finished it I'm going back for the rest of the memorial photos I missed.

Sally’s Law is a play on Murphy’s Law, because, with her law, nothing goes wrong, unlike Murphy’s.  However, Sally’s has a specific reason for that, and it’s a touching one.  I enjoyed my time with this family, helping Sally get to her dad one last time, at all costs.  Nothing would stand in her way.  Though short, that means it doesn’t overstay its welcome, but in this case, it’s both a blessing and a curse.  On the one hand, there’s satisfaction in the completion and you don’t get bored, on the other, you don’t have much incentive to replay it unless you fall in love with the story or are a completionist.  In the end, it’s really up to the individual player to decide to go back or not, but before that, this is still a game worthy of being in your library if you’re a puzzle game fan.  A sad, yet touching story with simple mechanics and puzzles for a good price.  You could do so much worse.

Distant Star : Revenant Fleet (from here on out I'll call it DSRF, because I like my fingers and typing that over and over will murder my keyboard) is one of the "Second Generation" of Early Access games, having now seen and made it through the initial wave of Early Access highs and lows, we're now seeing a more matured approach to the Early Access platform, with more specialised projects and more consistent and constrained planning resulting in products that actually deliver on their promises. DSRF was sold as a Rogue "lite" in space, where you'd assemble a small fleet of ships, guide them across the solar system, and then engage in a showdown in a final battle much like the genre definer FTL.
Much like FTL, you work your way across multiple sectors, each sector contains multiple jumps, however, unlike FTL, there's only four sectors that you'll be working your way across as you head towards the final battle, meaning your average playthrough is much closer to two to four hours, as opposed to the four to eight in FTL. However, unlike FTL, instead of managing -one- ship with a few upgrades, here you'll be managing a full fleet, each with their own weapon systems (in some cases, multiple weapons systems), sub systems, and passive systems.
The blend of upgrades means that fleets can in theory be quite unique (in practice, there's usually one generally optimal approach for fixing the deficiencies for each ship, straying too far is a bad idea). The ships too will upgrade with experience, granting bonuses in various ways, again, helping you compensate for their weaknesses or exaggerating their strengths. These upgrades are not exactly anything amazingly unique, but there's a good enough variety per ship to keep things interesting.
Of special mention are the weapon systems, of which there is a serious number, all with their own strengths and weaknesses, allowing for a significant degree of tactical flexibility and nuance within your fleet, this is extremely useful, and can allow for a player to adapt on the fly, particularly if things go sideways and they lose a valuable ship during the course of the voyage.
Once you jump into a sector, the game moves to a top down view of your ships, moving around a two dimensional "pane" of space, with the sun behind it, filtering light through to give a sort of 3D effect. It's rather effective, and pretty. Combat therefore works by ordering your fleet (up to five units) around the 2D map and having them reposition, attack, use specials, cover each other, heal each other, etc. Line of Sight can be used and abused to cover each other (units are solid objects, so weapons will hit the first thing they make contact with), and specials are often "skillshots", which means that moving can disrupt or even cause them to miss.
This should sound very much like a singleplayer version of most MOBA type games, and that's because in a sense, it is. It carries a lot of the fundamentals of that type of game in the genesis when you're playing the tactical map mode, but you have the benefit of a pause mode that allows you to issue orders and activate specials whilst the pause is set, then allow time to proceed on its' merry way once more, pausing when you need to issue fresh orders. Disabled units will suffer critical damage at first, represented by debuffs that carry over from sector to sector, however, with each critical suffered, the chance for them to be entirely destroyed begins to tick up, if they take too many criticals, well, you may lose a ship altogether, and in this game, that can be a punishing blow, especially late game. Units in this game are extremely valuable, and losing one can be crippling, enough to trash a game and force a restart.
The A'kari are not a pleasant or amiable lot. Their culture is very warrior caste, and it's very clear as you travel through space that you are just "a side" in the war, if anything it's quite possible that you're the bad guys. This moral ambiguity is both interesting and potentially a downside, the problem with such a situation is that for some players, it's important to have the belief that they're on the "good" side when playing these kinds of games. The A'kari often resort to less than wholesome tactics to make their way through the game (as the necessity of their mission requires), but that will come with a moral weight to it, and if you become invested or put some time into thinking about the lore or backstory of the game, well, it may leave you wondering if you're actually playing for the right side.
The graphics aren't -quite- Homeworld Remastered, but nonetheless, they're definitely good enough to pass muster, presenting clearly defined racial ships for both the A'kari and the Orthani, along with a third set of ships for the neutral Pirates. The backdrop itself is colourful and clear, with a good set of nebulae and lighting presentation being well handled and running smoothly throughout. This is a well designed and imagined game. Of specific mention is the soundtrack, which is really,
good. We're talking standout quality, easily worthy of being a standalone OST if ever they decide to release it as such.
When combat takes place, the playfield is colourful and bright, the music sweeps up to an orchestral swell, the explosions are many, debris litters the place as ships disintegrate in style. This game makes space combat look -good-, and does a good job of hiding the MOBA style combat under it's interface and behind the active-pause button, but with the limited number of sectors, and the fact that the game doesn't support the same level of replayability as FTL, this is a game to play in shorter bursts, as a side dish to things like FTL.
DSRF does a lot right, and in some areas it does break some interesting new ground, however, it doesn't -quite- do enough to break free of FTL's shadow, and it doesn't quite do enough to stand far enough away to net it my unguarded praise. Which is a shame, because there's a lot to like about this game, for people who are big on Sci-Fi and Roguelites, this may prove to be too tempting to miss, for people who are looking to get "into" such games, FTL is still the daddy.
Verdict :

This has been described as a roguelike in the vein of FTL, but with RTS elements thrown in. Objectively speaking, that's true, but it's not as 'roguelike' as people looking for that specific genre might be looking for. As a rogue fanatic myself, I'll be honest with you; It's a roguelike in the sense that it has random world generation and random encounters down pat, along with permadeath and proper consequences for actions that are more often than not your own fault. That said, there isn't as much depth to the management of your fleet as you'd expect, and so I can't really consider this a full-fledged rogue experience. It's more half-and-half than anything, and while some people have complained that it's not really sure what it wants to be, I think the devs know exactly what they're aiming for, and that it just needs some tuning to get there.
The only real connection it bears to FTL is in navigation between sectors and the fact that it's set in space. The gameplay is entirely different beyond that. So rather than compare it to another game and judge it based on how it measures up, I'm going based on its own merits, and that leaves me with a rather positive first impression. With a bit of polish to work out the kinks, I can easily see this becoming just as popular.
As it stands, the game is fun. Possibly not worth the heft 19 dollars being charged for an indie game from a company you've likely never heard of, but still a fun title that won't leave you disappointed. If the price were dropped to a more reasonable 10 dollars, or even 5, it would enter impulse-buy territory, and I promise you would not regret picking it up.
That about summarizes my review, but if you want a more detailed breakdown, I've posted a full review in the Forums

White phosphorus is a material made from a common allotrope of the chemical element phosphorus that is used in smoke, tracer, illumination and incendiary munitions. Other common names include WP, and the slang term "Willie Pete", which is dated from its use in Vietnam, and is still sometimes used in military jargon. As an incendiary weapon, white phosphorus burns fiercely and can ignite cloth, fuel, ammunition and other combustibles.
White phosphorus can cause injuries and death in three ways: by burning deep into tissue, by being inhaled as a smoke, and by being ingested. Extensive exposure by burning and ingestion may causes fatal result.
Burning:
Incandescent particles of WP cast off by a WP weapon's initial explosion can produce extensive, deep second and third degree burns. One reason why this occurs is the tendency of the element to stick to the skin. Phosphorus burns carry a greater risk of mortality than other forms of burns due to the absorption of phosphorus into the body through the burned area, resulting in liver, heart and kidney damage, and in some cases multiple organ failure. These weapons are particularly dangerous to exposed people because white phosphorus continues to burn unless deprived of oxygen or until it is completely consumed. In some cases, burns are limited to areas of exposed skin because the smaller WP particles do not burn completely through personal clothing before being consumed.
Smoke inhalation:
Burning white phosphorus produces a hot, dense, white smoke consisting mostly of phosphorus pentoxide. Exposure to heavy smoke concentrations of any kind for an extended period (particularly if near the source of emission) has the potential to cause illness or death. White phosphorus smoke irritates the eyes, mucous membranes of the nose, and respiratory tract in moderate concentrations, while higher concentrations can produce severe burns. The Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry has set an acute inhalation Minimum Risk Level (MRL) for white phosphorus smoke of 0.02 mg/m3, the same as fuel-oil fumes. By contrast, the chemical weapon mustard gas is 30 times more potent: 0.0007 mg/m3.
Fume inhalation:
Long term inhalation of derivative fumes causes a condition called phossy jaw or osteonecrosis of the jaw, which is a painful, debilitating and ultimately lethal condition that afflicted factory workers involved with the manufacture of matches that contained white phosphorus. The mechanism for necrosis is clot formation leading to bone ischaemia or infarction, leading to the putrid rotting of the bone of the lower jaw. For this reason, the Berne Convention (1906) was enacted to forbid the manufacture, sale or purchase of matches containing white phosphorus. This condition may also be caused by high doses of lead, cadmium and bisphosphonate based cancer drugs.
The assumption that white phosphorus is considered a chemical weapon, and thus constitutes a violation of the Chemical Weapons Convention, is false. During the testimony of Prof. Michael A. Newton at the United Nations Fact Finding Mission on the Gaza Conflict he said "the law is clear that there are some authorized, perfectly valid uses of white phosphorus munitions".

Side missions, camps to take over, races to race, cars to collect, scrap to collect which is basically currency in the game world which you would need to max max out, and to upgrade your vehicle which started of as a piece of junk but by the end of the game you will have a beast.
The world is beautiful, the graphics are dam pretty and ran at a solid 60 fps. The wastelands are a dangerous place random npc cars will try bash your car off the road, which at times can get a little annoying but once you upgraded the car enough you be able to rip drives out of their cars with the harpoon and drag the drivers across the wastelands to punish them for bashing into you. There are also random sandstorms, and thunderstorms, in these storms. Scraps of metal can hurt you, or lighting strikes so you best of finding shelter and wait for the storm to end, but there will be large amounts of scrap in the storms to award you for your bravery or stupidity.
Combat is a bit like the arkham games, it is simple yet brutal if you half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥play it you will probably lose a lot of health, but it becomes easer and easer once you upgrade max, you can pick up weapons from fallen enemies, or blast your shotgun right through them if you have the ammo. There is no regenerating health you will either have to find some food to eat, or drink water from your flask which will need to be refilled often. Vehicle combat is fun, you have the shotgun, the harpoon, thundersticks, and flamethrowers to use, you often be fighting multiple cars, you can pick of weaker cars by shooting the fuel tanks or ripping of their tires with the harpoon gun, others you will have to ram into them to weaken, if you take too much damage your car would explode unless you get out and let your buddy chumbucket  fix it.
This is a great open world game for mad max fans, if you want something to keep you busy here it is.

I was fully aware that Mad Max will be a game cast from Batman/Shadow of Mordor mold. I was fully aware that if I found Shadow of Mordor boring, I may find Mad Max boring. But, sweet Jeebus was I bamboozled. I am amazed that I was able to log this many hour in this game. It is simply because Mad Max is, after a while, soul-crushingly boring.
After the charm of customizing your car wears off, what you are left with is a mindless grind through pointless activities. Looting locations are not worth your time, enemy camps are almost a carbon copy of each other, races are barely entertaining, destroying sniper towers almost requires no imput, and enemy convoys are just a bigger bunch of regular enemy cars.
Story is just as bad. Maybe it is my fault, but I have absolutely no idea what is going on and what am I supposed to aim for. We meet the big baddie 2 minutes after the opening, we kill him 1 minute after that, then we find out he is not dead. He still could be for all I know, though. After almost 30 hour I have not even heard the scum taunt me over loudspeakers or otherwise manifest his presence somehow. But frankly, I do not even care at this point.
The only good thing about Mad Max is the built-in Capture Mode. This cool little gimmick allows you to take screenshots. You can use it to make quite neat screens if you are into such thing.
Apart from that the game is just boring. Plain and simple. I would even go as far to say that even if the game is on sale, you enjoy the setting, and you love collecting stuff in games, still do not bother. I bet there are better games on offer somewhere.

If you liked the other FNAF games, this one sets a new standard for the series.
Whereas the other FNAF games were more focused on staying in one place and doing the same things for five nights with growing intensity, Sister Location bucks the trend with each night introducing a new element or twist, requiring you to think on your feet and be very clever to survive. It focuses more on a "horror story" aspect rather than single room survival, requiring you to do things like sneak across dark rooms using eery music to determine how close the danger is, or hold a cupboard door shut while tiny animatronics try to wrestle control away from you, or even work on (supposedly) offline animatronics in the parts and service room to fulfill your nightly goals.
That's right, goals. No more 12am-6am, this game is all about challenges.
It's all very tense and wonderful, and I feel like it speaks wonders about Scott Cawthon's ability to change things up and push himself to a new level. I look forward to your future games Scott, whether they are FNAF or not!

While it says I don't have much time shown on steam, I played this game years ago and have thoroughly put many, many hours into this game. Back then I just took whatever I wanted into each game. Now I can look back and say holy hell, this is such a great game.
The combat is a turn-based tactics-style strategy with some rpg elements thrown in. While there is a 'cash shop' (by what I remember) as you progress you can get more 'radiance' (the secondary currency for buying more characters) by simply completing levels and by daily quests. With enough time you can get pretty far.
The web-based version didn't have voice acting, and while the steam version does, I think it was still well done though not the greatest in the world. The story was great back then and I hope it added more over the years (I'll update this post once I get a few hours in :P)
The animation is something I really liked about this game, at least during the combat. They are clear and readable skills and spells, even the passive buffs are easily read with distinct colors. Each summon has their own sets of skills, and while two or more can heal there is specialists-- the priest being the main healer, the tree-ent the best tank as far as I remember it, and the druid doing the best sustained field-control with her summons and rocks that stun things for at least a turn. I didn't get a mage type summon until later on, but the nukers were there.
All in all one of my favorite games of all time that ever came from the internet-- well done Tactics Studio. :)

Hitman Absolution to me wasn't a great game and after hearing the announcement for another Hitman game I really wasn't as excited as I was for previous Hitman games. Also after looking at the reviews of the game my first impression of Hitman was really a poor first impression, Online DRM? Episodic Releases? These aren't very good ideas?! I was wrong on the episodic release part. Episodic releases gave IO-Interactive the ability to really focus on a single area of the game at a time and really master each destination. So far every destination i've visted has been fantastic! Especially Italy and Bangkok. Originally I had no intentions of purchasing Hitman and finally I decided to give it a chance, and i'm glad I did and here's why.
The gameplay of this Hitman is by far the least clunky, and most realistic Hitman to date. The AI in the game is very smart compared to many other games in the stealth genre. The AI can become suspicious very quickly over small details like crouching or standing in a place watching an event happen too long, and the AI will follow you until you successfully lose them or until they apprehend you. Once you've been apprehended the rest of the AI will search for you and your mission is basically compromised. Another great addition to Hitman that wasn't in the past Hitman games was saving at anytime and loading back your saves from any point. Another outstanding aspect of the game is replayability. This game has so many different options and choices on how to take your target out from taking your target out from a distance, to getting close and using the fibre wire or silverballer, poisoning them, or even making their death look like an accident. This game has been a pleasant surprise and i'm very glad I invested in the Full Experience, its much more efficient to purchase the Full Experience rather than episodically, their has been many complaints about buying the game episodically.
Like previous Hitman games you play Agent 47 tasked with objectives to take out various targets in various locations all over the world, This game has missions and contracts, but also unlike any other Hitman games you have the option to explore destinations that are purchased in each episode. The story is a solid experience with lots of replayability and is faithful to the original Hitman games.
The visuals in this game are stunning, with DirectX 11 and 12 compatability! The graphics in this game can compete head to head with any other game currently out with little to no stutters or performance problems, i've had 60 fps constant with no frame drops and the game looks fantastic especially in places like Italy and Bangkok.
Hell yeah! This game has so much replay value in it that the full price of $60 is well worth the price of this game, each level has over 40 challenges that you can achieve by completing the challenges these challenges include ways to kill your target, how you enter the targets building, and how you escape, and complete the level unseen.
Definitely give this game a chance, this game is an impressive game with many hours of replay value and story.
1. Optimize. Speed up the game menu, it takes almost 30 seconds to load the Gear, Planning, and Save/Load option.
2 .Create a showcase area and shooting range/testing area, the old Hitman games had this and I really miss it.
3. More clothes, gear, weapons, upgrades, and attachments for my weapons, I feel like Hitman is lacking in terms of customization and weapon variety.
4. First Person. I know the older hitman games had the option for first person, I think at some point IO-Interactive should look into adding the ability to go into first person.
5. Sandbox. This would be seperate from the story, but look into building even larger worlds, city sized worlds with random scripted events, places like skyscrapers where you can snipe your targets, with hundreds of things to do whether it's exploring, or doing contracts. The option to get contracts while roaming the city, and areas where you can get agency drops, or purchase upgrades and stuff. I think this would be a great idea for lots of replayability. This game would never run out of things to do.
I may get a little flak for this, but I personally think the sandbox addition would make for an awesome unique addition to the Hitman series.
All of the down votes really kept me from buying the game for a long time. But once I bought it I was WOWed! This is one of the best games I have ever played.

FOR HITMAN FANS:
RECOMMENDED, but: the game has some serious issues. My PC crashed several times (one of which was quite serious and required a repair with an external OS disc). Furthermore: game freezes, poor performance compared to other 2016 games.
FOR NON-HITMAN FANS:
NOT RECOMMENDED: wait until there is a full version of the game. Until that time: play Blood Money or Contracts: similar set-up (as opposed to Absolution), but complete and less buggy. Plus, non-PC-wrecking.
AS FOR THE GAME:
I've only been able to play the first two contracts, Paris and Sapienza, and thus far I'm happy with the large maps present in the game. It takes the good from Absolution and mixes this with what made the series great. This means that unlike Blood Money and earlier games, there are certain triggered events, meaning that you have less issues with timing and don't have to wait in a box or in a corner for 10 minutes. The maps are huge and daunting, and Sapienza has a large area that is outside of the area where your targets are, but still there are interesting things to be found in these 'extra areas'. Plus, the online component opens up opportunities for using these areas fully. It will be awesome once fully released and decently optimised. Until then, for non-hitmen, skip this title. Fellow hitmen, enjoy but beware.

It's not a good game, nor a bad game. Supposedly a tribute to NES titles, but aside from odd choise of graphic filter and the soundtrack that screams "I wanna be Mega Man 2  to associate myself somehow with a popular and successful game", it really nails the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ aspect of shovelware cash ins of yore. Which is weird, because *almost* everything that Capcom did during the NES era was gold.
The game has very stiff controls. You cannot aim effectively while moving, and taking aim directly upwards frequently has you aiming diagonally first, then firing one shot, then aiming upwards. Granted, you can aim directly upwards if you let go of your D-Pada and then press Up. But it's a hassle when you're already used to a fluid quarter circle motion that doesn't hinder you in other games.
The screenshots suggest that any given level is divided into several screens (with their respective transition), when in fact the entire level is displayed upon entering it. Conceptually, it doesn't sound bad. But having the camera follow your character at all times without staying fixed means being unable to see what is directly below you. since the camera is fixed at an angle where your character is always in the lower half of the screen instead of dead center. Good luck being able to see what is directly below you whenever you collect a weapon, as the developers decided it was a good idea to display a huge text message everytime you did, obscuring everything beneath your character's feet.
It's not THAT bad, though. Once you adjust to the bad controls (and even more awkward flying/hovering mechanics), it becomes a modest challenge. But the game is both too short (being only 3 levels long, with the same boss with minor upgrades being recycled), as it is too repetitive (every level consists of having you fetch keycards that open other parts of the level, which have more keycards that open more sections, until you run out of keycards and then you're made to walk half-way across the map to fight a boss).
Fortunately, the key activation issue that plagues the majority of the current reviews seems to have been resolved. However, further research indicates that you're ony allowed to install this game up to 20 times before you lose your license to the game, after which you permanently lose the right to play the game. There is a workaround available on one of the Community guides, but I thought it would be nice to mention it now so you keep this in mind.
I would only recommend getting this game if it's 90% off, and you're terribly bored. It's really not worth your money or time otherwise.

Hey everyone!
I have been playing this game on my YouTube channel and wanted to post here for anyone that wanted to check out what Sally's law was like! I do want to preface and say that this game is honestly fantastic it is a very well done platformers with a great story so far and just enough challenge to let it be interesting but still let's you focus on the story.

Sally's Law is a sidescrolling puzzle-platformer from Korean indie developer Nanali Studios. And it's a good one.
This game tackles theme as old as time itself - struggle between different generations, relationships of parents and children, a conflict between passion of the young and caution of the elder. We are being told the story of Sally, a girl, brought up by single father, loving, but very protective of her. The plot unfolds as Sally journeys back to the home she left a long time ago pursuing her dreams. And during this trip she reminisces about her father, how she used to resent him for not being there for her in the past. But little by little Sally is starting to realize that her dad did his best to help her and support her, even when she didn't notice it. All the obstacles she overcame with such ease, all the pitfalls she avoided - he always been there, carrying her through thick and thin.
Gameplay is a simple but solid puzzle-platformer, which doesn't open new horizons or revolutionizes the industry but does enough to differentiate itself from hordes of other platformers and to keep gaming process compelling. The brilliant thing about it is that gameplay mechanics are inseparably intertwined with storytelling and the big theme of this game. Playing as Sally you are rushing towards the end of the level, towards the future, whatever it brings. Playing as her dad, you watch over your girl, clearing obstacle on her way and helping her to get to her goal. This approach enhances the storytelling aspect immensely, allowing you to experience the message on both intellectual and emotional level.
The game is rather short and I would not describe it as challenging in any way, not that it's a bad thing. Sally's Law offers solid two hours of game time full of puzzles that are just hard enough to make your cogs spin but neither of them will take you more than a minute to figure out. Same goes for platforming - it's relaxingly smooth and moderately easy. This game doesn't strive to be Braid or Meatboy, it's a game which knows what it is, knows what it set out to do and does it quite well.
Animation takes after a certain plain but compelling style and music fits the general mood of the game, organically adding to the experience. As for the techincal part - controls are very simple and rebindable, basic graphical options, such as resolution, can be tuned in the menu and english translation seems alright. I noticed a few odd phrases, but then again, I'm not a native speaker myself, so that might have been a mistake on my part. The game runs smoothly on my fairly old PC, providing a good 60FPS performance you would expect from such a title. A couple of minor fps drops or hitches occured during my playthrough, but they are barely worth mentioning and didn't impact my experience in any way.
There is a few things that in my opinion could been done better. Spawn animations and pauses at the start of each stage are unnecessary and disrupt the pace of the game. A one key bind to restart current stage would be helpful as well as ability to restart the whole level without going back to the main menu. The way the story is told requires you to shift focus from the gameplay to read text or risk missing a piece of the plot. Still, these are very minor issues that don't take away from the general experience.
Sally's Law is a beautiful and bittersweet story about love and caring and forgiveness. If you're up for two hours of enjoyable platforming, puzzlesolving and sweet heartache, this game is for you.

Pretty disappointing overall.  I was pretty excited about a game that looked like FTL with an RTS engine for the battles; and that’s exactly what this game is, unfortunately it was just executed very poorly.  I'm going to refer to FTL repeatedly in my review, and if you haven't already played that, stop reading, point your search to there and go buy it.  It's a great game and this is but a poor shadow.
The good:
The RTS engine is actually quite well done.  Graphics are smooth, tactics actually matter, and they’ve done some interesting (although in some cases not very well balanced) things with dodging, cover, and tanking.  Controls are not very responsive, but I can live with that as it makes good tactical choices even more important.
The bad:
The strategic portion of the game (i.e. the FTL clone) is absolutely terrible.  Imagine if FTL had worse balance, very little choice in the actions available, very few strategic build choices, and no achievements or unlocks.
The balance of the game is similarly pretty awful.  I’m all for a hard roguelike, but I do prefer some sort of achievement or progress system that makes dying fun.  Nothing like that here, the game is terribly random and punishingly difficult.  Actually getting anywhere feels more like luck than skill in most cases.
Overall, I’d say that this feels like a game that was developed by two teams: one reasonably competent and the other with very little game design experience.  I also suspect that the game was probably rushed out before it was finished.  I do note that the developers are still patching it, so maybe it will improve over time, but at the moment I can’t recommend anyone to put either time or money into it.
