This is for me about nine-tenths a masterpiece, with only some minor balance changes needed to be great, and any additional content would be icing on the cake.
The game plays just like how you would expect seeing comparisons to RTS and FTL. Build your fleet, try to scrape together enough resources to keep them repaired and up to date, and engage in real-time space battles.The upgrades and ship options are dynamic enough that they can drastically alter your combat strategies from hit-and-run, full-frontal engages, to micro-mechanic tech battles. This alone gives each playthrough the ability to be unique, and the procedural universe only adds to that.
The sole issue with this game at the moment comes from the difficulty balancing on a razor's edge, which is currently tipped toward you dying horribly. The battles are fierce, the economy sparse, and certain missions you simply give up on all objectives and focus solely on surviving. This to me is not a very large drawback, games that are as challenging as this currently is feel incredibly rewarding for even minor achievements: Succesfully complete all mission objectives? Survive a massive enemy force with no ships disabled? Actually made it to the final sector?! Haven't scored a win yet (EDIT: Have now), but I hardly notice because all of these steps along the way feel like wins in their own right.
A game that gets EVERYTHING right but needs minor balance tweaks? Sold. Not to mention what could be done with more content.
EDIT: Balance HO! Early game is now much more forgiving, making it far easier to develop the basics needed for a run. Defense and escort missions in particular are now realistically achievable even with 3 and 4 ship fleets. I think overall more starting money wasn't needed as long as the rewards were tweaked to reflect risk/reward, but it accomplishes the same goal.
If you were holding back on this, don't. I really couldn't ask for more at this point, the game is amazing. And more seems to be coming anyway.

Spec Ops: The Line is an amazing game that does an excellent job of mind-♥♥♥♥ing the player. This is
a happy good-guys-kill-bad-guys type of game. This is a gritty and violent dive into the awful real world where things are not so black and white. Where things are grey, and people who are put into terrible situations have to do terrible things to reach the end goal. And when they reach that goal they are forced to contemplate if the ends really did justify the means. This is the kind of game that teaches people that sometimes the 'good guys' have to do a lot of very bad things.
I was so grasped by this game that, without meaning to, I played through the entire campaign in one sitting. And by one sitting, I literally mean one long session where I did not leave the chair for the six hours it took me to finish the game. So engrossed was I by this game that I forgot about the outside world. It was truly the most immersive gaming experience I've ever had. To experience it in this way I would recommend that you go offline, disable the Steam overlay, close Skype or any other messaging programs you have, turn your cell phone off, and just play through it all. It won't happen at first, but by the middle of the game you will have forgotten that you are playing a game.
I do not wish to go into detail about the dialogue, characters, or choice-making system, for fear that it would spoil something in one way or another. Just know that Spec Ops: The Line is honestly one of the best things I have seen to ever grace the gaming market. It is the perfect blend of action packed third-person shooting, and excellently written plot development.

I loved Borderlands. It had wry humour, a great look a neat variety of guns (oh...about 3,000,000) and was a fun sandbox overall. Then like a small child whose antics are cute when are young but get annonying as they age Borderlands 2 grew up (or rather sideways).
The basics are all still there but there is much less cohesion of it's elements. Here are the things that changed for the worse in the sequel:   [spoilers]
>Lack of diferentiation on gear. This game always had an element of tedious looting. You were forever comparing the just-slightly-better gun you found to one you are using. Fortunately this was mostly optional because you could make a go of it with most guns without the fretting over stats. In B2 now there is no real diferences anymore; every gun does everything. There used to be one 'Nade that was homing, another that was sticky or breaks into smaller bombs. Now your gun shoots grenades that  launch flaming bullet storms while dealing electrocution damage and the clip explodes  when you toss it (but for some reason it looks like you tossed your whole gun), and all of the guns are like that. The old naming convention for the weapons, grenades and shields gave useful cues to help you navigate the dizzying variety. Now the guns sound like they named by adolescent gangbangers using text shorthand or just plain bad spelling.
>TMI. During combat the screen looks like riot of color and flashing lights. It resembles a carnival midway more than a battle.I'm not shooting bullets so much as hosing my enemy down with a neon rainbow-colored bands of damage-indication that are fountaining from the top of my enemies head as well as twelve other NPCs while claptrap is chattering, bad guys are reciting Shakespear (or purile taunts), critters are scurrying amid the exploding oil-drums and now my gun is talking to me. Its techicolor mind-mush on tap. I wonder if that twinge in my frontal lobe is an epileptic fit about to happen. The sequel did not evolve or refine itself. It feels more like some headbanger just turned the noise up to eleven.
There was a time when games were unable to deliver much on screen due to limitations of the available  technology. Now that there are no technical limits we will have to decide for ourselves how much is too much. Borderlands 2 failed to draw a line anywhere so we are left with a cocophony of sound and an average 0f 300 moving elements on the screen at all times. Cerebral overload is a poor path to bliss.
>'Change everything!'. Things seem to have been updated pell mell. Aspects of the game that were just fine the way they were have been altered without improving them. eg. the user interface is now on three separate pages requiring scrolling. No more comparing skills at a glance, now you must navigate within the UI adding tedium. Oh and wouldn't it be cool if the pages floated around making reading the scattered text more dificult or making us hunt around to hit a moving button while peering through three layers of animated watermarks. No it would not. Yes I am old...and blind...but I like to play games too. (snif)
>Humor? Borderlands (the Original and expansions) walked a perfect line with it's humor. I am an older player (cut my teeth on Space Invaders) and I never felt like the game was too adolescent. Like the original Warner Brothers cartoons Bordelands apealed to a wide range of ages. B2 seems like it was engineed to apeal to 14 year old boys with O.C.D. and a sugar addiction. A solid demographic to be sure but what about he rest of us?
>Annoyance. I liked ALL of the original Boss characters. Claptrap was the main source of anoyance and like a bitter spice, he made for some variety in the original. Now we are stuck with Handsome Jack. And I mean stuck since the Devs have put all their eggs in the Jack basket.  I hate Jack. He is not funny, or clever or a workable Boss. His dialog adds nothing to the game. He just makes you want to kill him...which you will never be able to do. See below.
>Why Jack is the worst boss fight ever. OK, so I have slogged though the entire game and wasted 3 billion baddies over five continents and now comes the climax. The moment I have been waiting for: I am going to kill that guy once and for all. Except...
-I'm not fighting him. Mostly it's just some giant bird but I still have to listen to his blathering.
-Didn't I already encounter multiple Jack-doubles. How do I know that this is not just another clone?
-Oh thats right Jack is the CEO of a company that owns the technology that has been respawning me for the last four years. Almost like he has been toying with me all along. (He could just revoke my respawn rights and leave me for dead at any time.
-And for that matter what is the point of 'killing' Jack anyway. Wont he just respawn like I do 30 seconds later? Could this get anymore meaningless?
>Misogeny anyone? Lilith is a super hottie. Maya is Emo/Goth gorgeous. Tannis has a sexy librarian thing going. Moxy is a blow-up doll. Any other body types on this rock? .....hmmmmm there is Ellie; Morbidly obese and with attitude. No range of 'normal' body types exist between the unattainable and the gross caricature that is Ellie. Really? This is 2015 people and this crap has no place in the modern world. Somehow the male characters in the game manage to have a wide range of body types as seen IRL. Also, Tina Ebonic-Mouth is even more anoying than Claptrap and a terrible role model.     ; ]
>Trashing the original cast. I played each of the characters in the first game and became attached to them after having had many adventures together. I have fond memories of them and I played them each differntly. When gamers play a role playing game they project into their characters and, like actors, may enjoy the imersion into another personality. It can be an intimate and personal thing.
Now I am playing 'The New Guy/Gal' as one of the new playable cast members. The old cast are still in the game fulfilling mundane gate-keeper duties for the new story...and they are a pathetic lot.
Mordecai has been reimagined as a drunken, skater-dude with a slacker attitude (with his goggles it is impossible not to think of Poochie when he talks. All he needs is a backwards baseball cap). Roland is whipped and socially awkward, too distracted by Lilith to lead the movement anymore. Lilith is a phycho with an Eridium problem. Brick is still Brick, just more brutal and less intelligent.
My heroes...how far you have fallen. I don't recognize these clowns. I was never that guy or that woman. Why have the game makers♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥all over my memories and connection to these characters? What a waste! How hard would it have been to just make up some new NPCs? This was a huge mistake. Anyone who understands Role playing would know this was a daft idea so who makes these bone-headed decisions? I can't fault the people on the ground doing the grunt work for the blunders. I have to conclude that this franchise is being badly led astray by it's manegement.

There's 2 things I'd like to get out of the way first before starting my review. I got the "Full Experience" (entire game) for free from a Steam friend - although this should have no effect on my review, it's obviously a bit harder for me to gauge whether this game is worth full price or not. Second,
The episodic model this title uses is polarizing, a lot of stupid decisions have been made and the game lacks a lot of polish like most early access games do (ironically we were repeatedly told Hitman wasn't an early access title). Now with that out of the way... how is the new Hitman game?
HITMAN is closer to the fourth Hitman game "Hitman: Blood Money" than its predecessor "Hitman: Absolution". As a big fan of the series, it was disappointing to see Hitman: Absolution divorce itself so much from the gameplay we have come to love and expect in favour of odd game mechanics. So it’s nice to see HITMAN makes a return to what made Hitman games great. Like the past games there's a story, but it exists solely to connect the levels together rather than hinder the gameplay or steal the focus. While this all sounds well and good, there's some glaring issues that people need to know about. Everyone will feel differently about these of course but here they are:
An internet connection being needed to get the most out of HITMAN. When this game first released you essentially needed an internet connection to do anything, but over time far more features have dropped this requirement and if you do lose your connection to the servers: there's options to reconnect or play offline now. This requirement still annoys me though, as Hitman was always a singleplayer game and the excuse that this was done to make HITMAN a "live" game is simply not good enough.
Features that were present in Hitman: Blood Money and in some cases, Hitman: Absolution, are currently not present in HITMAN: first person view, human shields, sniper rifle case, collecting weapons from past levels, upgrading weapons, dual wielding, civilians using dropped weapons against you, guards following blood trails and difficulty settings.
The "opportunities" system. I'm happy to report this isn't as much of a problem as it used to be but basically opportunities meant listening to NPCs nearby, picking up a document and activating an object or two, in that order usually, which would then allow you to murder your target in a really unique way. What I hated about this system was assassination targets refusing to go to a certain area just because I hadn't followed them around and listened to a certain conversation. This mainly applies to the Paris level, and clearly the developers learned from feedback, because I don’t remember having to do this in the later levels.
American voice actors being American. Personally this hasn't bothered me too much but all of the released levels feature tons of shared American actors and actresses who are very easy to recognize. I have admittedly found myself going once or twice "ah that's generic American guard actor #1". Again, it's not a huge problem but I'm a little bit baffled as to why previous Hitman games had tons of different accents and this time around the developers didn't think to put this higher on their budget list.
Optimization. While I haven't had too much trouble playing this game on mostly medium settings and I think the latest patch has made my performance and load times a bit better, the game still runs less than average for a lot of people and I've even had quite a few crashes.
Many bugs that have come and go. I believe the worst have been finally patched out for good but this game is notorious for issues that were previously fixed (like the audio missing)  being reintroduced later on. I honestly haven't had as many bugs as a few individuals have had but this game is undoubtedly buggy at times.
Looking past these issues and putting aside some of the stupid decisions that have been made by IOI/Square Enix (e.g. people that didn't buy the "Full Experience" are not able to buy the bonus missions at the moment), HITMAN is a game which will easily give you value for your money. Right now I have 124 hours on this title and I've barely played half of what's been released thus far. The game's fun, highly replayable and probably the most accessible Hitman game to-date. Here are my reasons for why I think this is the case:
Huge non-linear sandbox levels (bigger than any of Hitman: Blood Money's maps) that are chock-full of objects, NPCs, and things to interact with. They’re mostly pretty too. If that’s not enough, you'll notice easter eggs here and there as well as areas that will remind you of a classic map from one of the older Hitman games. The "Intro Pack" (episode 1) contains 2 small tutorial maps and the first large map called Paris. Episodes 2, 3 and 4 contain Sapienza, Marrakesh and Bangkok respectively. While all of the maps are excellent in my honest opinion, episode 3's Marrakesh is the weakest of the bunch.
There's around 70 challenges, 8 opportunities and 20-30 hours worth of content in each map. If you don't want to do the opportunities, there's still tons of different ways to eliminate a target. Completing the challenges earns you "mastery" which will allow you to unlock new weapons, items and even starting locations and areas for you to smuggle in items. The inclusion of a score system with no negative feedback in-game, as well as leaderboards, also gives players another reason to keep playing maps over and over.
A few good game mechanics from Hitman: Absolution are brought back (subduing, throwing equippable objects, the cover system) which help make HITMAN feel less clunky than some of the older titles.
The return of traditional Hitman gameplay and the introduction of the best disguise system in the Hitman series. How the disguise system works is only a few people in your current disguise can blow your cover. There may also be a few people not in that disguise that can also blow your cover but overall it feels like an improvement over Hitman: Blood Money's unchallenging disguise system.
The music and dialogue. The soundtrack’s no Jesper Kyd but it’s decent. As for dialogue, it’s entertaining and at times well-written. I’m running out of room to say more!
Contracts mode returns and you can use it on any of the huge maps.
The "live" nature of this game gives us new official contracts and escalation contracts about every week. On the odd occasion there's even an "Elusive Target" which gives you one shot at taking on a target. If you kill the target you cannot restart the mission and if you die, fail to meet the requirements, or even miss the real-life time limit placed on the Elusive Target? That's it - you can't attempt it again. I personally love all of this live content.
Don't like some of the HUD elements cluttering your screen or the neutered-but-returning Instinct Mode being in your game? Practically everything's toggleable in the options menu.
In the end this game’s a 7/10 for me. It’s slowly shaping up to be the Hitman sequel we always deserved but make no mistake – it’s still far from perfect in its current state. As such I recommend this game to everyone, providing they’re okay with the issues I listed above (this applies especially to those who are hardcore Hitman fans).

Pros
------

- Different paths and methods to discover and use (I reccomend turning off hints)
- Favors the more planned and methodical approach rather than the "Absolution" approach
Cons
------
- The game runs atrociously. I get about 30-60fps on a r9 390, and an i5 6500.
- Episodic releases are kind of annoying
- Can get boring after a while, definately not a game you can pour hundreds of hours into in my opinion
Overall, I would reccomend the game to other, I like it. Ultimately though it's up to you to decide whether episodic releases and sub-par performance on many machines is acceptable. Being someone who used to run on a very short budget PC, I am perfectly used to running games at around 30fps.

Do yourself a favor and buy the full experience from the get go! If you liked hitman in the past then your in for a great time here. The staggered release dates put me off at first but now I love them. It gives you time to really explore these huge and intricate levels before going off towards the next mission. The game is perfect by no means but a great game none the less.

This game is worth every cent, but be sure to buy the once-off or the upgrade pack, so that you can get all the extra content. If you buy it episodically, you're gonna get screwed.
As for performance, it's intensive but runs well on my GTX 760. I was getting just over 30fps on Ultra with DX12, but managed to get upwards of 55fps just by dropping a few settings and reverting back to DX11. Also, I experienced a lot of random crashes when using DX12, but I can't say if that was my GPU's fault or the games fault. If you're struggling with performance, try change your DirectX API in the options on the splash screen at launch.
Levels are expansive, immersive and fun. It's like Blood Money and Silent Assassin all over again. I find the game mechanics and movements to be very fluid, and it's easy to forget about Absolution when you're playing this game.
If you're unsure because of all the bad reviews, buy Episode 1 on its own, and decide about upgrading later. That's what I did, and it paid off. Episode 1 has more than enough content to be considered a very big, very substantial Demo. Get it!

What a lot of reviewers here are neglecting to tell you about the always-online component, is that if you do suffer a disconnection, this game, unlike others, allows you to try to reconnect, rather than forcing you out to a menu and losing your progress. I have a really unstable internet connection in my country, and I've only been disconnected a few times in the 100 hours I've played so far, and each time, I've been able to reconnect and carry on without losing anything.

Really great game. After the more story driven approach to Hitman we saw with Absolution, this new installment is a real return to the more open-ended and creative roots of the franchise. The game gives you a lot of freedom, leaving how you assasinate your targets completely up to you. While the progression system is quite gimmicky, it gives a nice amount of replayability, even if you've only bought one mission.
The graphics look absolutely amazing, and the game runs at a constant 60 frames with all settings maxed out on a GTX 970 even in largely crowded areas.
The controls can be a bit glitchy, leading to some frustration when instead of silently taking someone down you initiate a combat sequence attracting the attention of nearby guards.
The thing that lets this game down is it's always-online DRM and the slightly unusual episodic pay-model. But it's really a minor thing, and if you can look past that it's a real return to form for the Hitman series. Don't be discouraged by the mixed reviews like I was at the start, give the game a shot and there's a high chance you'll enjoy it.

It's a great game if you have decent internet access.

First of all i have to say RUST is my first "survival" game, so i don't have comparison to other titles (and i probably won't as i hate zombies and most other survival games are full of them). Got RUST few months ago, so i'm not very familiar with the changes since it's "release".
(I play mostly in duo/trio on european community servers with my friends.)
I really liked it from first hours, but in time i realized few things.
1. If you consider yourself mature, stay away from this title. In my 600 hours of experience i haven't got shot when spoke to geared player as naked one maybe 5 times... and most of the time when i got shot i heard insults and laugh of a 12 YO (at most) boys. I spent 5 years in LoL, and i consider community there more mature than here...
2. Community is not only toxic (look at 1. + chat mostly looks like mix of pre-school and prison), but also dumb and lazy (you will see "when was wipe?" question in chat even if it's enough to press ESC and see the exact time in description of most servers).
3.* It doesn't matters how much time you will put in building a base, you WILL get raided, and usually it will be an easy task, unless you will build a freaking castle or hide your base in some very rarely visited place on map (REALLY far away from crafting materials).
4. Low populated servers - you can build easily, but there's no fun as there's nothing to raid nor anyone to fight with.
Well populated servers - good luck in finding resources and building a 2 by 2 without getting slayed before even chopping wood for your twig construction.
5. You must have time for it. Like 5h minimum, because most likely you will start from scratch every day (before situation from next point comes).
6. Servers usually die after few days. 130/150 (for example) players right after wipe, 50-80 next day, 20 on 3rd day, and on 4th you can usually raid abondonned server if you're so bored.
7. You HAVE TO look for servers according to your group size... unless you like uneven fights like one versus a clan.
8. If you want to play on PvE server you also might get raided (even when you build a well defended base).
9. Very few crafted objects you can move - even small wodden box have to be destroyed if you want to place it elsewhere.
10. Wildlife clipping through walls and foundations... Yes, the bear or wolf can kill you in your stone base.
11. If you fall off after wipe, you mostly won't get anywhere.
12. Crouching people don't make ANY noise. Even if someone passes in front of your face you won't hear anything if he's crouching, even a crupmled grass.
13. Air drops can provide decent guns, but mostly you will find crap like clothes and land mines.
14. No safe zones/immunity for fresh spawns - you can get killed by animal or player before you get up right after game loads.
15. You need only materials for crafting in vanilla... seems too easy, even considering the drop rates of good crafting materials (modded servers with old blueprints system are way more interesting in gameplay, but unfortunately mostly dead), but at the same time...
16. this is not freaking asian MMO, yet still you need a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of time to get resources for building a base and gear up in solo/duo... unless you play on empty server, but wait, why would you need to gear up than?
17. It is possible to meet fully geared player with AK 30min after wipe... when most people will still run around with bows.
18. Some changes are totally unrealistic (example: only stone nods give stone, even if sulfur and metal ore nodes are mainly made out of stone like you see them in game and like they are in real life).
19. With full HP you can survive a headshot and run away with a spear or an arrow in your head... NAKED.

21. Look down... oh, it seems like you're arms of your character hovering above the ground. ;)
22. Price: 20E on the release, 14E from dec 2014 till feb 2016 and...
23. ...the regular price now is freaking 20E again, and...

25. With additional micro-payments for skins... Like they wouldn't get enough from selling the game itself.

This game is really good - old style tactical RPG. Provides lots of fun! It has great potential. At the moment of the review there were not much of game content yet for a MMO. I really hope that this game gets futher development!
Pros:
+ Many characters: some you can play from the beginning, some you will unlock by playing the game
+ The "VIP" in-game currency is easily earned by playing the game, so you can farm it to unlock a new character, like, each day!
+ Arena "gauntlet" system is really fun - facing waves of monsters with friends, and at higher levels a simple mistake may get the whole team killed!
+ Nice plot
+ No restrictions on player inteaction: free trade, free partying etc - play with friends or random people as much as you want!
+ Your character is as powerful as you design him - how good you are at the game depends on your build, skills and choices - and not on random.
Cons:
- Game is quite short, and mostly you end up farming gauntlet arenas, which become repetetive, as they are not randomized.
- Again, lack of content: all items look the same with some little exceptions, monsters and player characters have all the same spells and skills. Hopefully it gets repaired with futher development.
- It might be tricky to learn to play for new players: most likely you will have to start over after first attempt of playing, considering your past mistakes. Not sure if this is a con though.
- Lack of players: there are probably not more than 100 players online at peak moments. This game deserves more attention, however, it should be filled with more content to get it.
For anyone who like RPGs and tactical games - this one will surely grab your attention for at least a week. It is worth time playing and getting more support and development!

Mad Max takes a little bit to pick up and kind of trails off at the very end, but the mid-game missions and exploration elements make this a fantastic game! You really do feel like a wasteland survivor in the world of Mad Max and it seems like the whole world is out to get you, especially during intense storms, where visibility is reduced and debris flies at you at high speeds. The driving controls are fantastic and the environments, while brown and gray, have character and an unexpected life to them. This game is everything but boring, with loot and secret areas hidden in every corner. The world may look like a bleak desert at first glance, but you'll find plenty to do once the world opens up. Highly recommended.

That being said the game could have had alot more to it,  They laid the ground works for a great game if they were to go into as much depth as say a witcher game does story wise with the side quests and all that this game would have easily been one of the best games around.  However is doesnt, its main story is decent, but dont expect much in the side quests department, for the most part your left with scavenging the map and taking down difffernt objectives kinda in a just cause fashion, slowly lowering the control in the different areas of the map.  Some may just find that sort of thing boring.
Theres alot of different character customization and leveling up, alot of different cars and customizations that can be made on them. The devs did a really good job in that aspect. The fighting system is really good, very comparable to the batman games.  Vehicle combat is solid, taking down convoys was one of my favorite parts.
If you love the Mad Max Movies you will probably enjoy the heck outta this game.

"Five Nights at Freddy's: Sister Location" is the new installment to the Five Nights at Freddy's series. However, it is important to also seperate the previous 4 from Sister Location, as Sister Location is very different. It is more connected to a point and click game than hunkering down in one room and survive like the other installments. This will be as spoiler-free as possible.
Sister Location showcases new animatronics all with their own voice. The voice acting may be the best thing about this game. The voices are creepy, adding to the atmosphere, but balances it enough to where you might enjoy the voices if you weren't in this situation (just a customer during the morning). Along with this, Sister Location does well with crafting the atmosphere first (making smart choices that becomes memorable moments), instead of throwing jumpscares, and the tenseness that might come if Sister Location was real. It also has humour that, as I can tell, is supposed to wind you down and it works. While Sister Location does bring in references from previous games, those who have no previous knowledge.
However, with any newly released game, there are bugs and improvements that can be worked on. Others have reported bugs in the forums that cause a hault in progress in Night 2. Night 4...Night 4 in particular. I also wish the game didn't seem so short so far, the new mechanics show up either once or twice (and in case of especially Night 4 not explained well).
Five Nights at Freddy's: Sister Location comes off as a spin off from the originals, and with this comes new mechanics and more focus on a story. While these are refreshing, it comes short with the lack of letting the player understand the mechanics. While I do recommend Sister Location, there are bugs that does come with being newly released and you may want to wait if you want a bug free experience.

I've only played the game for about an hour but so far it is a fun game. It is a very difficult rogue like/rpg hybrid with a space setting. You explore a map jumping from sector to sector. I did encounter a few minor bugs which I was going to report but when I checked their bug thread I found the dev had already acknowledged them and said they were working on fixes.
I played two games and got killed in both. The first game I only made it to two areas. The second game I explored about 2/3 of the map before a giant battleship wiped me out.
I hope they work on the rpg and upgrade elements more. When I started the game I only had money to purchase 3 ships for my fleet (you are allowed 5). Later on I had got more money but the fleet screen wouldn't let me click the button to go to the ships screen. There was very little gear and weapons to find and although I was only a couple jumps from the final fight when I died my ships hadn't progressed very much. I'm not sure if I was doing something wrong or if those features aren't quite implemented yet. Regardless, I couldn't buy more ships or do repairs and I got very few upgrades.
The descriptions for the weapons need more info so we can compare them. For example, I had 3 missiles I could equip on my main battleship. But the descriptions didn't provide things like damage, rate of fire, shield piercing vs. hull piercing, etc.
Overall I think it looks like it's going to be a good game. The devs seem to listen to feedback and are working on the bugs and balancing. It's already a fun game with very nice graphics and a solid framerate.

This is the first review I have ever posted for a game on steam. That being said I felt moved to do so because I think I have input that may prove helpful to the players and developers alike. I spent a great deal of time watching videos and reading reviews before I made my purchase discision and I must say that in the very short time that I have played and with the promising involvement of the develpers I am confident I won't be dissapointed with spending my money on this game.
Within the first few moments of battle I started to scratch and itch that I've had for a very long time. I have been craving a fast-paced space rts of a certain type for a long time. Distant Star: Revenant Fleet has a great feel and an excellent balance of fleet combat control and ship modability plus its a roguelike to boot. I would recommend anyone who enjoys the space genre as well as the roguelike genre to consider getting this game.
As for helpful information, I want to say that after watching several videos and reading many comments I feel that perhaps many players do not have a very solid grasp on the most effective way to play. I don't mean for that to sound arrogant. What I do mean is that the developers have made it difficult for new players to jump straight in. I haven't done the research to see if the features I'm about to suggest are in development but I do feel that if they were they would have been implemented with the transition from alpha to beta. The game offers a excellently executed tactical drop in and out of combat pause system. Understanding how to use this effectively is in my opinion the key to playing the game successfully. On some of the videos I watched the commentators talked about having to constanly be on the move and not being able to activate ship abilities or a sense of not having enough control over what is actually taking place in the battle in relation to the players ships. The reality is that all the control you need is right at your fingertips. The problem is that is never told or shown to you. If a player doesn't intuitively recognise that a certain level of control is necessary and doesn't search for the controls in the menu then their first couple of experiences in battle can sour their opinion of the game. What I'm suggesting is that the developers incorporate a tutorial like experience in the first mission. Instead of dropping you into a battle and just saying survive please add tips that say press spacebar for tactical mode. Then once the player does so add some more tips explaining the benifit of tactical mode and just what the player can do. Features like hotkeys for your ships and their abilites and basic commands like defend this target are an absolute must in this genre and the game has them. It just doesnt tell the player. Because of this I feel like the game is not as unbalanced per say as players believe. I was able to take the starting ship and just a lancer with no additional upgrades to the end of the first sector and through several combat nodes with relative ease simply by utilizing the tools that are there.
--Feature Suggestions--
1. Tutorials
2. I would love to be able to que multiple movements for my ships. In other words Holding shift and creating waypoints for my ships to travel along.
3. I'm not sure if this isn't already implemented in some fashion and I just haven't discovered it yet but I would like to see information about enemy ships. Nothing game breaking of course but just simple stuff for the sake of immersion.
4. I would like to be able to zoom out just a little bit further. you can't see the max range of the lancer's laser without panning your screen. This left me unaware that it could target a location instead of a specific ship which is tactically useful information.
Sorry for the excessively long post and thank you to anyone who took the time to read it.

This is one of the most popular indie games out there for good reason. Super Meat Boy takes the platforming genre and perfects it. Meat Boy controls flawlessly, and you'll need that level of control to fling him through the insanely hard levels in this game. Aside from the first five or so levels, which serve as (a very brief and fun) tutorial, the game never holds your hand. You will die thousands of times before you beat it, and many thousands more if you want to complete everything the game has to offer. And you will love it, because death is only a minor setback that causes you to instantly respawn - no penalties except starting the level over, and when the levels are usually 15 - 25 seconds long, it's no big deal. The difficulty seems like it would make this game inaccessible, but the fact that you can start within a second of dying completely eliminates that concern and actively encourages you to finish the level, even after dying dozens of times on a single level.
Aside from the gameplay itself, Super Meat Boy also has one of my favorite soundtracks ever. Every single level or boss theme is great, and the music plays through death, too. The music ranged from fast, rock songs to a booming orchestrated choir and everything in between.
The game is also bleeding with charm. The graphics are excellent, the cutscenes are funny, and there are references thrown in everywhere. Warp zones take you to retro worlds with 4-bit or 8-bit graphics and chiptune versions of the music in the world you're playing. Everything meshes together into one solid package.
So buy this game if you like platformers at all. Or even if you don't - it may change your mind.

This game is worth every cent, but be sure to buy the once-off or the upgrade pack, so that you can get all the extra content. If you buy it episodically, you're gonna get screwed.
As for performance, it's intensive but runs well on my GTX 760. I was getting just over 30fps on Ultra with DX12, but managed to get upwards of 55fps just by dropping a few settings and reverting back to DX11. Also, I experienced a lot of random crashes when using DX12, but I can't say if that was my GPU's fault or the games fault. If you're struggling with performance, try change your DirectX API in the options on the splash screen at launch.
Levels are expansive, immersive and fun. It's like Blood Money and Silent Assassin all over again. I find the game mechanics and movements to be very fluid, and it's easy to forget about Absolution when you're playing this game.
If you're unsure because of all the bad reviews, buy Episode 1 on its own, and decide about upgrading later. That's what I did, and it paid off. Episode 1 has more than enough content to be considered a very big, very substantial Demo. Get it!
-UPDATE-
========
What a lot of reviewers here are neglecting to tell you about the always-online component, is that if you do suffer a disconnection, this game, unlike others, allows you to try to reconnect, rather than forcing you out to a menu and losing your progress. I have a really unstable internet connection in my country, and I've only been disconnected a few times in the 100 hours I've played so far, and each time, I've been able to reconnect and carry on without losing anything.

Really great game. After the more story driven approach to Hitman we saw with Absolution, this new installment is a real return to the more open-ended and creative roots of the franchise. The game gives you a lot of freedom, leaving how you assasinate your targets completely up to you. While the progression system is quite gimmicky, it gives a nice amount of replayability, even if you've only bought one mission.
The graphics look absolutely amazing, and the game runs at a constant 60 frames with all settings maxed out on a GTX 970 even in largely crowded areas.
The controls can be a bit glitchy, leading to some frustration when instead of silently taking someone down you initiate a combat sequence attracting the attention of nearby guards.
The thing that lets this game down is it's always-online DRM and the slightly unusual episodic pay-model. But it's really a minor thing, and if you can look past that it's a real return to form for the Hitman series. Don't be discouraged by the mixed reviews like I was at the start, give the game a shot and there's a high chance you'll enjoy it.

So after 15 hours of playing I believe I have a grasp of the game.
---Pay2Win---
First of all I don't like how its pay to win, but I will say I was hesitant at first to say this, because the game makes it easier than most games to earn in-game currency simply by completing quests or by killing enemies. But it still is an excrutiating grind if you were setting out to get even one paid for character, assuming you play for 1 hour a day you can expect to make 150 radians on a good day. So it would take you 5 days to get 1 paid for character. Its not as bad as many games I've played but its still rather long and the quests get alot harder so don't actually expect getting it in 5 days.
---Encourages Friendship---
The game as I've found it really encourages playing with friends, which is nice of course but I'm a lonewolf and if you are too then its gonna be a hard time leveling up. I made the mistake of using all of my 5 characters at my disposal and trying to level them up equaly, but you end up finding out pretty quickly that this simply won't work. The monsters get really strong really quick and will need to concentrate your fire into one or two characters but this leaves you unable to defend against enemies that have your weaknesses all figured out. So then you need a party that helps defend you.
---Pvp---
I haven't played much of this mode so you may have to hear someone elses voice in the matter, but what I could tell is its a small version of lol. Simply capture territories on the map to earn points for your team or for yourself depending on if you clicked 1v1, 2v2,3v3,etc. But It was oddly fun, but it may just be because my crew if characters was actually really well at handling these battles, because alot of people were just coming in with one or two super strong op characters,
I could come in with one semi-decent character or two to distract him from 3 characters ready to take down the totems, ending the game quickly before he has time to recapture.
---Storyline---
I couldn't care about anything they were saying.
---Overall & Verdict---
It was suprisingly fun, but it is a fan of microtransactions. I recommend it being played with a friend but thats usually said about every game isn't it? The artstyle is simple and clean-cut, the skills are limited if your playing with 1 or two characters it will feel, the game encourages making friends and punishes ones that don't want ones.
Final verdict:7/10 playing alone, 8/10 if your with friends.
Either way, play it, you'll love it for either a few hours,or years.

First of all I should mention that I played this game awhile back when it was on kongregate and I haven't gotten a chance to try it out with the changes since I last played (probably a couple of years ago now) and although kongregate doesn't keep track of play time, my play time on there for this game was probably over 500 hours. I'll update this at some point after I've played through it again.
This is a very good tactical rpg (same style of game as final fantasy tactics, xcom, etc.; in this one you control six characters if I remember correctly) but it also has multiplayer options (three modes last time I played, pvp, gauntlet (co-op arena style combat), and co-op campaign. It's a free to play, but legitamately free to play if you want (the premium currency can be farmed in-game at a reasonable pace with no limit).
Now with that out of the way onto the review (I'll update this at some later time, for now I'm just giving the short version).
The short version:
Pros:
-Excellent tactical gameplay
-Can be competitive (and even the 'best/highest rank/however you want to phrase that' player) as a free to play player.
-Diverse classes/characters (every class has their own set of abilities and plays differently from all of the other classes).
-Motivated and active developer. He hangs out in the game chat now and then (sometimes he's on quite a lot).
-At least reasonably good story (at least of couple of surprises and some decent replay value because you can go back through to get the dialogue options you didn't take the first time).
-Fun single player (or if you prefer co-op) campaign and multiplayer options.
-Probably several other things that aren't coming to mind at the moment.
Cons:
Noteworthy:
-In the past there hasn't been a large player basis. In part this is probably because the game was released in stages and by the time multiplayer and the full campaign were out most people had moved on. Hopefully the steam release has fixed that :)
-Tournaments weren't built into the game and instead were run by the developer which sometimes lead to confusion about the rules/guidelines for tournaments. Hopefully this has been fixed or at least there is some pvp mode with built-in prizes now.
Minor:
-I wouldn't be too surprised if pvp still needs some balancing but it will probably take awhile to figure out in what way. That said I wouldn't be too worried about it, as said the developer is quite dedicated to the game and is willing to listen to the games community and incorperate suggestions.
-The graphics weren't great but it looks like they have gotten a major update so that's probably less of a con than it was and honestly this is a game you play for the gameplay not the graphics.
-Initial loading time: When you first load the game and the first time you load it after any major update it takes a long time to load. This was an intentional choice by the game designer and the pay-off for it is that subsequent load times are fairly quick, (a lot faster than most of the other games I have played).
-Probably a few other things that aren't coming to mind, but there weren't any other noteworthy issues that I can recall.
Long Version: (Coming in a later update to this review)

An unfortunate mixture of a 'realistic' approach in design and a severe lack of control in combat. I quit just before the last level after dying multiple times for the stupidest reasons, reasons I cannot condone :/ Figured I'd write a review before uninstalling. I'll list some appreciated pros and then why I can't personally recommend it. (minor editting done)
+Interesting narrative (the♥♥♥♥♥♥that swayed me into buying it...)
+AI Alies make your game livelier and not so lonely, and can be commanded (only focus target or heal ally)
+Highly destructible environment; the game makes great use of the setting (Dubai & sand) and the frequent sandstorms make for some epic scenarios
+Great sound effects; maneuvering terrain, breaking structures and walking through sandtorms sound great (if it doesn't 'cause some eargasm - don't leave it too loud))
+/- AI is quite challenging (Suicide Mission difficulty~), you can't run at them from the front or stick your head out of cover for more than a few seconds and expect to be okay.
+/- There are a few choices in the storyline - what course of action to take - but they mostly don't seem to have any lasting effects or matter at all.
: As a cover-based third-person shooter the game has some really bad level design, and combat (more on that below). One could argue that being pretty open is rather realistic compared to very conveniently placed covers, but having a single safe cover in the area and then having multiple enemies throw grenades at you (which you can't throw back, veeery realistic~), an enemy shooting RPGs at you, and everyone else firing unlimitted bullets at you in this barren land where bullets are so scarce is NOT (mainly describing the levels around which I quit...).
: a few incredibly stupid implementation choices. One is that, as mentioned above, you CANNOT throw grenades back at enemies, a grenade means awkwardly detach from cover and run (i.e. sprint uncontrollably) and possibly die or stay and die - someone said your allies will sometimes throw a grenade at an enemy directly in front of both of you, I didn't see this.
Second is that uncontrollable sprint. When you sprint, Walker (our unfortunate hero) behaves like the Tank in Left4Dead; he becomes extremely difficult to steer or stop and you can essentially only go in a straight line until you stop moving completely.
Melee is limitted to wacking people with your gun which isn't all that stealthy but from behind it kills enemies (headshot).
: The game tells u bullets are scarce, and it's reflected in the fact that I can't go past one area/level without changing weapons; this is pretty counterintuitive considering I'm sometimes presented with the opportunity for a stealth attack for example and I don't have my 1 pistol with the silencer, so there goes that. Even stranger is how enemies have unlimitted bullets and can spray them all day long. Another thing is the HEAVY enemy, that one arsewhole that I feel almost all devs don't think rationally about when they include them in the game. It takes 2 grenades (your full load) and several shotgun hits or more than your full load of rifle bullets to take one down, and he just keeps walking up to you spraying bullets until he reaches your cover and then there's an invisible barrier preventing him from going any further - that's when you can more easily kill him.
Anyway, I'm not even glad I got it on discount. Maybe it'll be more playable in easy mode though.

As close to torment as possible!

NOTICE:  The developers called this game, "The Spritual Successor to Planescape: Torment."  What you need to know as a consumer is that the game world is different, the engine is different, and the story in no way impinges upon or builds from the Planescape: Torment.
Moving past that fact, this game gets a solid "meh" from me.
PROS:
- Stable & relatively glitch free.
- Decent artwork, and music.
- Okay-ish voice work (not completely voiced)
- Some compelling characters.
CONS:
- Very poor character customization, covered up by falling back on the old "nameless wanderer" trope.
- A ton of cookie cutter, easily forgotten characters.
- Tons of unnecessary pseudo-mysticism.  Every single bum on a street doesn't need to be a five thousand year old trancendental diety whose only purpose is to give you riddles and second guess every choice you make.
- Overall, while the story is interesting, it's neither engaging or relatable.
FINAL THOUGHTS:  I like the concept of a world on the edge of reality that's a mash-up of many times & places.  The destruction of infrastructure, the struggle to survive, and the conflict of various tribes is a good stage to set a role-playing game.  But game tech & RPG expectations have changed over the years.  This is a quaint little game, but serves to remind me of why isometic video games will never completely replace table-top RPG's.

Because of the eridium, the Hyperion corporation has arived to mine the eiridum. The leader of Hyperion, Handsome Jack has found the location of another vault, which is said to house a alien warrior powerful enough to murder the entire planet,  which he will use to civilise the Borderlands once and for all.
This is where you come in, you are a Vault Hunter, searching for the vault for your own fortune and glory. You begin the game on a Hyperion train where some Hyperion robots are trying to murder you and the train blows up. You (and your buddies in co op) is the only survivor(s) and you are found by the robot Claptrap. This is where your story begins.
Now what this game mainly is build around is its bazilions of guns. In order to get some of those guns you need to farm some of the bosses which you can easily spend a lot of time on, if you are not going for max level (50 without DLC)

Cons:

Is it fair to write a review with less than 1 hour play time?  In this case... I think so.
The game is basically FTL with a completely different combat mechanic.  On the surface that sounds great since I liked FTL.  And this game is early access so maybe my complaints will go away over time.  However, right now the combat seems to devolve into a slugfest.  There's almost no tactics involved that I can see.  Every combat turns into trying to engage as few enemies at a time as possible, focusing fire one at a time, using almost all cooldowns asap every chance, and basically standing there trading blows hoping your ships are more powerful than the enemy.  The only "tactic" I've been able to come up with is hiding my lancers behind more powerful ships to try to have attacks against them absorbed.  But that is still just a slugfest.  I want to think there's potential, but with the recent addition of a "save" system that actually punishes you for saving if you need to leave the game and come back later, I'm not holding out much hope.
No, I don't recommend this game.

"Dream Daddy" is a ** M/M dating simulator ** for folks who crush on daddy figures (pun intended).
There are options for romances OR hookups: hot dad, chubby dad, cosplayer dad, pastor dad, badboy dad, coffeehouse dad, etc.  The love interests have kids that vary in age and personality.  While the player's kid is amazing and the player's relationship with said kid is awesome (... well, I guess that would count as a fantasy element, so to speak ...), the other dads' kids  run the gamut from non-verbal newborn to shy overachiever to intentionally creepy twins.
Pros ::
... You can design the player's "dad" icon, with body type, hair/beard, and outfits.
... Pretty art and design for the npcs.
... Decent writing.  The dads all come with their own baggage, some of which remains hidden if you are not romancing that particular dad on that particular playthrough.
... Minigames for each of the romances.  Some of the minigames are: a fishing game, a mini-golf game, finding a lost dog, and a "bragging standoff" where two dads go head-to-head for bragging rights about their kids.
... Some funny bits with the different dads.
... Theme song.
Cons::
... The art for the player's icon is rough in comparison to the game's npc art.
... Short game: a first playthrough may take 4 to 5 hours to complete.  Each dad has three "dates," but I believe you can only get a third date once you've decided on which dad you will romance.
... Earnest but not very interesting player character.  I was scratching my head as to why he was so sought out by the local dads and why the other dads (who were interesting) weren't dating each other instead.
Every so often, I check Steam for more by this developer.

Distant Star is an excellent real-time, space-strategy adventure with roguelike elements.
The game features fleet-based combat with persistent ship upgrades in a dynamically generated galaxy. In Distant Star, you take control of the last remaining ships of a near-destroyed A’kari fleet, and must rebuild your forces as you battle through ancient, galactic battlefields towards a final showdown with an alien race. You can mix and match your small fleet of ships, upgrade their weapons, gain experience, new skills and traverse the galaxy, system by system, experiencing a series of mission types. Each sector in the galaxy and the missions within each system are dynamically generated so each playthrough is a different experience. Story events offer you a range of choices which may affect whether or not you are attacked (or you attack your enemy), are rewarded or the option to upgrade your ships. - Recommended!

-progress: not monitoring this game for a long time yet, but the amount of released updates is promising

stuff that needs improvement:

Very basic and simplistic "tactics" game that looks like a game from the 80s with 16-bit sprites yet saddled with a "modern" microtransaction currency, in this case a "radiance" currency that you either buy with real money or farm at an excruciating slow pace.
This wouldn't be so bad if it was only for optional stuffs like skins etc but most of the classes are paywalled behind by this radiance. 4 out of the 5 classes you get for free are melee and this game heavily favors ranged (it uses a time action system and moving to melee range means you loses attack/time while ranged characters get free attacks before the enemies get to you).
Each of the classes is priced at an absurd 750 and you only get 15 per daily. You may get some extra from challenges (5 per) but these are doable only once per map unless you repeatedly create/delete character over and over.
The dev reply to this is that you also get 1 radiance per kill (my experience is that it's more like every 2 kills) but this is a misdirection play as it is valid only when the mob is within 5 levels of your hero level (total levels of all your chars in your party). You can't choose to not levelup your hero level (even when you choose not to levelup the individual immortals) - i.e. you'll quickly outlevel everything you fight just by playing normally and end up getting no radiance, more so if you play it typically and add in extra immortals in your party.
Add in other radiance sinks like runes/enchants/gear/respec (and even deleting a char from your party costs like 15 per level! ) etc.. and you'll quickly realise it's your typical cashgrab p2w game from a former flash/java applet game.

Combat is mediocre and derivative of the Batman Arkham series except slower and less fluid. There are 6 enemy types: the unarmed guy, the guy with a shiv, the little guy that craws on all four, the guy with a stick, the guy with the stick and shield, and the guy with the sniper that puts away his gun when you get close. There are several bosses in the game. The bosses are basically just the guy with a stick but with a bigger lifebar. All of the bosses fight exactly the same and the fighting arenas are all basically the same except one or two have easily avoidable firestreams that you can let the boss run into too. All the bosses even have the same execution animation of Max bashing their head with the shotgun.
There's a bunch of different cars in the game but that doesn't really matter since they all drive pretty much the same (some are slower and heavier) and you're really only going to want to use one, the Magnum Opus. The Magnum Opus is the only car you can repair, the only car you can use the grapple hook with (to open doors or pull down towers), the only car you can use the rocket launcher with, etc.
Blowing up enemy cars is kind of fun but there's very of that in comparison to the rest of the game, which as I mentioned earlier is trudging on foot through camps and settlements picking up rubbish.
The story is a waste of time with underdeveloped characters and a rushed ending. The emotional aspect comes off as forced and ineffective
What's probably the worst part is that there's hardly any music anywhere in the game and what's there is so dull and forgettable it might as well be nonexistant. And there's no ambient sounds to make up for it besides the revving of your engine which even that you don't get when going on foot.
And once you've played through the first mission to get the first car body you've experienced just about all the game has to offer.

Short version: Excellent sandbox game that is faithful to the atmosphere of Mad Max Fury Road.  Interstate '76 + GTAV.
Playtime: ~60 hours to finish the storyline (but I had done every side mission, every scavenge location, collected all the historical relics, lowered the threat to zero in every area, and had almost every achievement and probably 95% of the legend challenges done.  I was a level ~120 Road Warrior).  I'll likely play a bit more to unlock the last few achievements.
I normally avoid movie tie-ins like the plague, but I took a chance based on great reviews and a love for this style of game.  It reminded me a lot of Interstate '76 - desert car wars, upgrading your car with better weapons and armor, scavenging for parts among the defeated enemies, and so on.
The basic premise is similar to all of the Mad Max movies.  Max loses his family or car and is forced to help out a bunch of people before he can continue on his journey alone.  After losing your Interceptor in the opening scene, you spend the game scrounging for scrap to build a new car with the help of a mechanic that rides along with you. This allows him to repair and upgrade on the fly, so dying is pretty easy to avoid.  If your car becomes too damaged, you have to exit the vehicle while the mechanic puts out the fires.  Since you usually have enemies in vehicles around you, it's a matter of dodging them, shooting out tires/gas tanks if you have some (scarce) ammo, or getting them to get out of their vehicles to fight hand to hand.
The combat system is a page right out of the recent Batman games - punches and kicks paired with parry/counters.  You chain hits together to fill your Fury meter which allows you to hit harder.  As you progress, you can unlock new finishing moves that can be ground attacks, using your shotgun or a shiv to instant-kill, or using the environment to finish them off.
In addition to being able to unlock new clothes (armor and melee power), shotgun upgrades, and your ammo belt capacity, you can also unlock upgrades to customize your appearance.  Similar upgrades and can be purchased and earned for your car - better armor, better tires, etc.
Starting out, you'll find that food and water is pretty scarce, and they're the only way to replenish health.  For that reason, the early part of the game is a bit tough when find yourself outnumbered.  However, this is an open-world wasteland, so you can leave the storyline idle while you seek out various tasks to do that will allow you to complete objectives and tasks that will earn you both scrap metal (the in-game currency for all upgrades) as well as tokens that you use with a wandering mystic.  This mystic will allow you to upgrade your health bar, your ability to scavenge, your skill with melee and weapons, and more.  As you visit strongholds and complete improvement tasks for the leaders there, the game becomes exponentially easier.  You'll be able to set up food and water sources, create crews that pick up the scrap left behind when you destroy an enemy vehicle (so you don't have to stop), a crew that scouts all the scavenging locations in the area, a crew that gathers scrap while you're offline, and an armory that fills your ammo belt.  All of this plus the scrap you earn from dismantling enemy camps and populating them with allies makes your life a lot easier..  You can add cars to your collection by stealing them from enemies or by winning races in the numerous "Death Run" races scattered throughout the map and then driving them to a stronghold.
- because the game has so many things you can do, it is very easy to out-level the story.  For example, I was about 3/4ths of the way through the storyline and had to do a race.  The race leader turns me away saying I can't race in the heap I'm driving.  I'm given an objective to come back after I upgrade to make the car faster.  The problem was that I had already unlocked and purchased every upgrade available, so I ended up having to downgrade my car in order to compete. Later when I finally got the V8 Engine in the storyline, I had enough scrap to immediately buy every upgrade for it. Huge fights near the end of the game were much easier with every melee, armor, and ground combat ability unlocked.  They should have scaled the enemies with the player level.
Customizing your car is something you'll do a lot - you can upgrade bumpers, armor, spikes (to keep people from jumping on your car), spiked wheels for grinding against other cars, suspension and lift kits, and so on.  Some have trade-offs (better armor makes you slower and have worse handling) and some tires are good on sand, others on asphalt, but the rest just get better with each upgrade.  The main reason they have all the variation is that you can select a ready-made builds called an Arch Angels.  Each requires certain types of each component, so as you progress through the game you'll be able to make more varieties of them.  There are in-game legend achievements to complete that are specific to some of the builds.
Lastly, once the game ends you are back in the wasteland and basically have free play to do things you missed.  As I said, I had already cleared the camps, the scavenge locations, etc so I've got just a few achievements to get for racing in the Death Runs.

It saddens me to give a thumb down to this game but I have to. I'm a Numenera RPG player and maybe I had too high expectations for this title, I really couldn't wait for it.
I was hoping to live again the same wonder as I experienced when I played Baldur's Gate almost 20 years ago, but sadly TToN's gameplay has NOTHING to do with that old classic.
There are many reasons why, but I'll jot down here the first two:
1. There is no free roaming at all: once the plot takes you from A to B you can't get back to A. No "world map". Very few "side quest" and the words must be spelled within quotes because at the end of the day they are still part of the main quest.
2. Waaaay to much dialogue: before you say "duh", let me argument. Out of the 28 hours it took me to complete the game, I can bet my money that I've spent 5 of them fighting, maybe another 4 solving puzzles and walking around, and the rest reading endless dialogues. I'm sorry if both fans and developers will be offended by my heavy words, but saying "two players will never have the same game experience" it's plain and simple false advertisement. Sure, there are soooo many dialogues and options that it's statistically impossible for two players to always choose the same. But once you know the plot via becoming friends with faction A and hostile towards faction B there is no way you are going to play again the game just to see what happens, waaaay to much unbalancement towards dialogue.

I've played Planescape Torment around 15 years ago and that game certainly redefined my notion of game story so I bought Torment: Tides of Numenera with very high expectations and interest. Well... I certainly did not expect this game! Simply put , I found almost no similarities between the games except the strangeness of their universe . I think it is better to keep the two games separated and evaluate each in no relation to the other.
For me,  Tides of Numenera was an amazing story in an universe where each speckle of dust seem to have layers over layers of old and forgotten history. And this comes at a price ... if you know yourself incapable of reading lines over lines over other hundreds of lines of descriptive text , beautifully written yet hellishly sophisticated and philosophical... well this game is not for you. Beyond that ,the story is great , graphics acceptable , some of the characters are memorable, the dialogues well written . The character progression while complicated in choices doesn't actually lead to much difference in the end game where you will end up with such overpowered characters that many of the skill checks are a breeze and the end fights feel like punching a bunch of untrained punks. Bottom line , this is more of an interactive book than a game and if you like a good book , you're in for a treat.
On the downside , the ending chapter was disappointing, felt lacking and rushed, by far not at the same level as the rest of the game  and the ending itself so anti-climatic that it almost begs for a redesign.
Overall , I enjoyed this game a lot and while it was not what I expected , was certainly a pleasant surprise.
It's good in its own right. Not as good as Planescape: Torment. But I do enjoy it and I'm glad to see companies trying to revive the CRGP genre.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is an awesome piece of fiction, but it's not a good game.
Some context -- Planescape: Torment is probably my favoite CRPG of all time, and I gladly backed Numenera on Kickstarter a few years ago. I'm happy to say that the writing in Numenera easily rivals that of Planescape, and I have enjoyed every line of Monte Cook's prose.
The main problem, for me, is that there is very little "game" here.  Unlike Planescape -- which, while it was not generally lauded for its combat, at least had "dungeons" in the classic roleplaying sense -- Numenera has very little in the way of combat, at least if you play an intelligent, dialogue-focused character.
While this could make for an interesting roleplaying game if it had other gameplay mechanics -- perhaps simulation or management aspects -- in Numenera, it means that the game amounts to little more than branching dialog trees with some interesting choices to make. This was relatively enjoyable for the first ten hours or so of the game, but after twenty hours I have had a grand total of two fights. I would say I wished for more, but the actual gameplay for these turn based combats is simply terrible.  Player combat abilities are boring, there is nothing of tactical interest, and in general they are a total slog.
In some ways, Numenera is the opposite of Pillars of Eternity, which I found to have at least passable encounters, but vapid writing that left me totally uninterested in continuing to play.
If you're looking for a great RPG that brings back some of the magic of 90's RPGs, I'd recommend Divinity: Original Sin and its sequel which are quite likely the best RPGs of their generation.  Sadly, Torment: Tides of Numenera is not.

This is a long review, consider yourselves warned.
I think that the mixed feelings about the game in the steam community and in general express my own feelings about it as well. While there are some aspects that are wonderful, there is also a sense that something is missing or amiss. So, rather than being a extremely coherent essay-like review, this is more of a catalogue of my views on individual aspects of the game. Also, I wil be overtly comparing this game to Planescape: Torment and not treating it separately, because I cannot go back in time and unmake myself playing PS:T and not basing my expectations of this one based on that one. Also, this review is focused much more on the game's content, philosophy etc rather than on more formal aspects such as combat or difficulty. So, being clear on that,  strap yourselves in and we may begin.
1. The Story. This is the the key point in the mixed feeling I have. As the guys in inXile claim, the game is supposed to be a spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment. PS:T had a quite a long story, in my view, compared to this one, and therefore I'm a bit disappointed. While there are many side-quests and a lot of lore an worldbuilding, the main storyline is quite short and straightforward. I would expect more twists and turns in the main plot, more obstacles to overcome, more tension-build up, and more flashbacks. To put in another way, I expected the story to be like a novel. Instead, it is a short story. I expected it to be long and (moderately) narrow, instead, it is short and quite broad. More about that later.
2. Thematically, i'd say the story utilizes very powerful tools. Questions of identity and decisions, mystery and discovery, abandonment and bonding. And herein also lies the novel vs. short story issue. The game wants to explore these themes into a great depth, which is very commendable, but it does so by being broader rather longer. By this I mean that instead of exploring a theme, say, loss, through successive encounters with more situations where this theme is prominent and looking at it from various angles successively, it sets up just one or few such situations and allows the player to choose the way (or the angle) in which they explore the theme. This, as I said, makes the game broader but not longer in the linear sense. It might, however, make the game longer in the sense that it has substantial replayability potential.
The problem is, if you don't explore a theme linearily, that is, in a successive encounters in one gameplay, the theme doesn't really stick. Once you have made your choice about the approach you take towards the given theme, your decision is done and you move to another one without being too much reminded of the former. Repetitio est mater studiorum. That's what I liked about the old Torment - the themes it explored came up frequently and always in a diferent manner. For example, the very theme of suffering (torment) was so appealing to me because as I played the game, I encountered it on so many occasions - the pain in memories, the pain of companions, the tattoo, the shadows, the scars, etc. So when a character started talking about torment, I felt like - yeah, good old torment theme again. this game IS indeed about it-. So this is what I miss severely in T:ToN. The themes dont stick. But maybe they will once I have re-played the game a couple of times.
Moreover, it seems that PS:T wanted to tell something about the themes it explored, that it had a message. Yes, the player was free to make their own choices and have their own attitudes, but there were some foundations that didn't shake, such as thirst for immortality leads to torment or that one has face one's past in order to become whole, or that one is not bound by one's past and can be freed from it etc. However, T:ToN appears to give no message about the themes it explores but rather leaves it up to the player to take whatever attitude they want. This might be in line with the aim to make the game's narrative as personalized as possible and make the choices really matter, but I feel it was taken too far, so the game can say anything you want it to - and that, I think, is not good storytelling.
The only themes that really stuck were that I'm free to decide and that my decisions have consequences. BUT those themes aren't the themes of the game or the story itself. The story isn't about dealing with consequences of one's actions. Those are the gameplay themes and features, so bacisally they are just the formal aspects of the game - alebeit good ones.
3. Setting. I have mixed feelings about this one as well. On the one hand, the Ninth World and Numenera setting is a wonderful idea. Original, creative with a lot of potential to create the most various contents without disturbing the game world's internal coherence. The sheer breadth and variety of the world is astonishing, and that I like very much. On the other hand, it is also a drawback, because the more varied and broad a world is, the more haphazard, erratic or just plain chaotic it feels. There were very few locations in the game where I had the feeling that they are internally consistent. While that is the nature of the setting, I wonder if it is good for the gameplay and storytelling. I feel that we as humans need things and places that have some internal logic and orderly structure in order to be recognized as specific rather than just random spaces in the world. So, the internal inconsistency of the locations ruined the joy from being in , say, "good ol' Government District". Instead, I was just in another messy place that happened to be called the Government District. There were, of course, exceptions, including, but not limited to, The Labyrinth, The Order of Truth or the Anchorage, but that just wasn't enough for me. Miel Avest almost did it, though.
4. The visuals. For the great part, I am well pleased. The precision and invention with which the locations are designed is amazing and I derive pure beauty just by looking at some of the Ninth World's buildings or other numenera. The game's interface is also pleasing to the eye. No greatness, but no lame design either. I also like the geometrical patterns appearing in the Ninth World, the Labyrinth, the interface... those circles, lines and polygons work really well for me. But that, I guess, is just a matter of taste. More objectively, though, I like inner consistency in them. At least here the haphazardness doesn't irritate. Colorwise, I thikn the game coveres the whole spectrum pretty well. Originally I was about to write that I miss white and black, but then I relized that the merecaster episodes supply enough of that. I also like the non-classical way the game treats the color schemes. The 5 tides are red, blue (which are "traditional") but then go indigo, gold and silver - which is quite original. I also like the dark grey-purplish / purple-greyish design of the Labyrinth and the interface. What I also like is that in the interface (as well as in the game wordl) the colors are toned and tuned. So you don't get plain red, yellow and blue on your stat pools. Rather, you have rust red, cadmium yellow and purple. Same thing with the experience bar - azure blue to purple. These aspects contribute to the game's uniqueness quite well, even though they are just cosmetic ones. The one and only thing about visuals that I don't like is the design of the tides in the main menu and at the background of the character views. They are thin, and when someone says the word tide, I imagine a large surge of water or the Golf stram or something. Having those tides like thin worms just doesn't do the job for me. Combat and effect animations are fine. Nothing groundbreaking, but working.
End of part I.
