Arkham Asylum was a revolutionary game. Arkham City was as well. By contrast, Arkham Origins is viewed as an evolutionary game, and between that and the fact that the principal actors and development studio have been replaced a lot of people figured "eh, I don't need to play this for a year." Technically speaking, Arkham Origins does feature revolutionary additions over the previous games, but it's in an area that nobody particularly asked for in the first place: online competitive multiplayer. I myself have yet to even launch it, but given that it's developed by Splash Damage I'm sure it's not slapped together. They did after all make the Return to Castle Wolfenstein multiplayer (which got carried over into Enemy Territory, and then Quake Wars, etc).
The thing about the single-player is that while it's good, you literally cannot help but compare it against Arkham City the entire time. The combat system and animations are completely carried over, with some additions. You have some new gadgets (one is allegedly "new" but in reality is functionally identical to something else from Arkham City) and face a few new common foes. Luckily, one of the gadgets is straight out of Super Inframan and makes combat even more satisfying since you trounce everyone with it, and the others give you more options during the Predator encounters. The enemy AI is altered since the rate at which you counter rather than strike has gone way, way up. Boss battles are VASTLY improved over the previous games, as each one emphasizes that you do different things. At no point do you feel "well, this is the same thing I did for the last boss."
But even with that said, at most points you DO feel "well, I've done this before." Aside from the combat, the sidequests have you doing the same gameplay mechanic as 2 years ago (and 4 years ago) albeit for a different cosmetic reason. Example: in Arkham City you have to quickly travel across the city to answer phones in time to stop a killer. Here, you have to do the same to defuse bombs. It's the same map as Arkham City, albeit with some new zones. It helps a little that you can now fast travel. But there must be fewer grapple points because getting from place to place is a little trickier than it used to be.
You'll be fighting and fighting, and with the random "crimes in progress" that spawn, you'll fight more. You're rarely going to be scanning the environment unless you're prompted to do so. Crime scene investigations are a new addition, but much like the show CSI you aren't really doing anything yourself. The computer is magically reconstructing a series of events based on your having scanned a body and a spot of blood (which they can't show as red). Then you go beat up a guy. You can't inadvertently defeat the person you meant to interrogate either, so there's no "save this guy for last" aspect to combat. But you are now given grades for each encounter, such that higher grades yield XP bonuses. Winning is largely a foregone conclusion given that you're Batman, but winning with an A or S rank is the tough part. In fact, I still haven't gotten the last one because it doesn't always play the *wham* sound effect to denote you KO'ed someone with a hit (I call this the "BATMAAAAAN!" since if I could mod this game I would replace that sound with the screaming pug). The game offers various challenges for additional bonuses and upgrades, but it's buggy about deciding whether or not some of them "count." I busted my ♥♥♥ doing the "do 4 exotic takedowns in a Predator section" and then it didn't count it. And then it turned out there were no more Predator sections in the game. AND it won't let you complete those challenges on the challenge maps, so if you don't do it during the story you're screwed...unless you replay it on the much harder New Game+ mode...
The reduced architecture grapples and increased enemy attack rates are somewhat minor, but if there's a major "step backwards" here it's one of atmosphere. This Gotham City isn't yet overrun with supervillains who've marked their territory and themed their gangs. The incentive to see the world isn't really as strong. The Riddler's challenges were designed to direct you to all the cool little references, but at this point there is no "Riddler" etc so you're basically completing the challenges for the sake of hearing the "extortion data that's going to harm innocent people" recordings. Except pretty much all of them pertain to supervillains and corrupt civil servants whom you take down anyway. It feels more like a task since there's less "reward" for doing it. Why oppose this so strongly? That's the REAL enigma.
The strong negative online backlash to Arkham City's criminal dialogue means that EVERYTHING pertaining to threats or abusive language is long gone (that already got walked back since the Arkham City DLC) so pat yourselves on the back, Team Social Justice. Between that and the fact that Batman is less infallible at this stage of his career, the writing has gotten a lot more praise compared to Arkham City. But for me, it feels less satisfying to beat people up because I overheard them saying they're cold and hungry, or that they're resorting to crime because they lost their job and now they have to not be home on Christmas Eve. This definitely plays into the "Batman as fascist authoritarian conservative" reading of the character. I kind of wonder if the writers just hate Batman as a concept, since the villains all expose the flaws in his approach and morality and Batman has no answer because he can't admit "the reason I can't kill you is because you're all too profitable as IP."
Also, the game takes place over a few hours on Christmas Eve into Christmas Day, yet the amount that happens is absurd. True, a lot happened during Arkham City, but there was planning leading up to it. How can these locations be THIS devastated and re-renovated in just a few hours? And it's not even accidental; the game points out "yeah, it's been 3 hours." On the other hand, James Gordon isn't Commissioner yet, so the cops are pretty much all dirty. In this game you get to beat up SWAT team guys, which is the part of "Year One" that is the most important.
The Assassin's Creed guy as Batman has his highs and mids since he's mostly forced to imitate Kevin Conroy, but with a name like "Roger Smith" you'd think he was BORN to impersonate Kevin Conroy's Batman! Troy Baker (who already nailed his Richard Moll Two-Face impersonation in Arkham City) is about as dead-on a mimicry of Mark Hamill's Joker as one could hope, given that Mark can no longer really do that voice anymore. Richard Epcar (voice of the Joker in the fighting games) has a few background lines that jump out to me, but I guess he also directed a lot of the secondary dialogue recordings.
I enjoyed Arkham Origins, but I'd still say to hold off on getting it. Not so much because of the issues described above so much as the fact that there's a ton of DLC and all of it's spread out across platforms and retailers due to exclusivity (Challenge maps where you're Bruce Wayne in training, etc). There's a Season Pass which includes that stuff, but it costs another $20 and for now is almost entirely cosmetic. They say there'll be at least one story DLC, but what'll it be about? Maybe something inspired by The Long Halloween? I don't know, so I don't know if that, a few challenge maps, and some cosmetic skins are really worth the money. For now I'd say to pick this up once a "complete edition" is available unless you happen to buy a new video card that bundles it.

This is a sloppy, dull, unimaginative mess. If you haven't played any entry in the series, stick with Asylum and City and then wait for Knight; if you've played the first two already, again, wait for Knight.
The voice acting isn't up to par with the previous games, thanks in no small part to the distraction of hearing replacement actors do imitations of Conroy and Hamill. I know it's not necessarily the studio's fault that the original actors weren't there, but a review's a review. The story doesn't match up with several details established in the first two games (the Joker was well-established before Harley Quinn or the Penguin arrived in Gotham, Quinn met the Joker in Arkham and not Blackgate, etc.). Gotham is visually much more boring than the art shown in the previous two games; it's very sterile and plain. Batman's dialogue is crude and angry, with very little nuance. I know it's supposed to be him in his early days, but the relentlessly dour, thuggish delivery and word choice wear thin pretty quick. Enemy taunting upon Batman's death, somewhat amusing in the previous two games, is intolerable here. It's boring in terms of writing, but worse it either takes too long to skip or can't be skipped at all. The player could swiftly jump past it in previous games if they weren't in the mood.
From a technical standpoint, this game is very poor. Combat is all over the place; Batman will frequently target the wrong enemy (or nothing at all), counters are touchier and less responsive. The game overall is absurdly buggy for a title of this level; Batman's radio dialogue will cut off abruptly for no reason, enemies will be unconscious but still standing, NPCs will get stuck on the environment, changes won't register or save, and so on. The game design is frustrating and uncreative: in Asylum and City, it was almost always clear why Batman could or couldn't interact with portions of the environment (generally in regards to his grappling). Here, there are countless ledges that can't be grappled onto, but which are indistinguishable from the ones that CAN be grappled onto. Time and time again one wonders why a particular area requires arbitrary rigmarole to interact with when identical surfaces are straightforward and intuitive.
In summary, this game has all the symptoms one would expect of handing successful material over to second-rate writers and designers. With two excellent games already available and a third on the way by original developer Rocksteady, I recommend spending money on those titles and avoiding this one.

I've played the previous FNaF's, and this is definitely different, I liked it, but from what I've heard, it's short... too short to warrant:
1. Night 4
2. Even $6.5
First, the scares... it's just not... scary. I know, I dislike people who say this too, but I'm a pretty big wuss and enjoy being scared, not so much that I've built up a dumb immunity; I enjoy immersing myself, and thus I let myself become scared easier.
That being said it's not as scary as the previous FNaF's, even accounting for the fact that sometimes you know what's coming. The way the game plays detracts from the scares, why? Look below:
Night 4, and honestly a lot of the nights period:
Night 4 ramps up to an insane difficulty. There's plenty of reviews discussing why it sucks, read them, watch a youtube video "FNaF Sister Location Night 4". MY review will focus on why this game design decision, and truly the game in general, is flawed.
In horror games you often have jumpscares, this game revolves around them. There's a semi-psych aspect in the form of narration, but mainly it's jumpscares. Here's the problem with jumpscares: They're not scary after you've been "scared" by the same one 12 times.
Crawling through a room as an evil robotic death harbinger dances around you, waiting to kill you due to your movement, scary. Getting caught in the same way 12 times... not scary.
Being placed in an animatronic suit, and forced to move your mouse over springlocks, to avoid being "jumpscared" by a little puppet, scary... but not when you do it 40+ times (this is night 4).
Why are other games with jumpscares fun? Because after you get scared you normally don't die (they're easy?) OR, you only die once, because after that you know what to watch for.
And this is why FNaF fails. It's not due to the jumpscares being random. It's due to their MECHANICS, being random. Resulting in the SAME jumpscare happening, every time, in exactly the same way.... (Night 4, once again).
Walking through Foxy's room is scary at first. But after you die 5-6 times it just becomes annoying.
FNaF 1 and 2 were great, because they involved a touch of randomness. Sometimes you had your eyes on one animatronic... only to be surprised by the one that snuck down the hall, or the vent. BUT, despite that, and even if you did die a good amount, each scare/scenario felt a little different.
The scenarios in this... are not different. When you die the first time, it'll be the same the second time.
It can be a little hard to explain, since you could attribute this to a lot of horror games, but again, the reason it fails, is become you fail so much, in the same way, that this "horror" game stops being scary, and just becomes frustrating.
Do yourself a favor, either wait until Night 4 gets "fixed" (difficulty tuned down), it goes on sale further ($2? maybe $3?), or just watch the let's plays of it.
TL;DR
The actual story and scares are great, it's more the fact that redoing the "horror" parts just make you forget how scary it was, and just make you think how many more times you have to do the same thing until you get to the next part.

This morning, while looking at the "Featured" page on Steam and scrolling through what Steam thought I would like, this game popped up. I liked the banner/whatever you want to call it. Nice sci-fi-y name. And only 6.99. So, I thought for 6.99 I might as well see what this game is - expecting another space 4x game (that isn't bad) -
Instead, I started reading reviews and kept running into "It's like FTL mixed with (2D) Homeworld". And that just isn't fair. How am I supposed to NOT spend a mere 6.99 when multiple reviews are dangling one of my favorite games, FTL, and one of my favorite RTS games, Homeword, and saying that this game is like both of those games....in one package... So I bought it.
So, first off, are the reviews that compare this game to FTL and Homeworld (a 2D version of Homeworld) accurate? Basically, yes. I definitely would compare it to FTL. Homeworld, is a bit more of a stretch since it's basically a 2D space RTS when it comes to combat, but I have no problem with the comparison to Homeworld because of the atmosphere of the game. If you like both, this is worth checking out.
It is early access, though, so it's currently rather short (replay value is there, though, due to it's roguelike nature). And although I have no experience with Blazing Griffin when it comes to early access, all signs point to them being a developer who is wanting to do early access right. They urge players to join the forums and leave feedback/get involved and they seem genuine. Plus, the price is rather low, so it's not a huge risk. If you're worried about early access titles, throw this on your wishlist/watch list and keep on eye on it. If you like FTL and RTS games and Blazing Griffin does things right, then this will be a title you will want one day.

Well I saw the trailers and screenshots and a mostly positive review so I decided to buy the game. I kinda regret my decision. I understand it is in the alpha stage which is why I'm really not too mad about paying 7 bucks, but this game is just not what was advertised by the Curators. There were several issues that I ran into:
-Heavily borrows from FTL to the point of ripping it off.
I can see where they were influenced by FTL. In fact it even has the same basic story, jump mechanic, and star map, which is not that big of a problem. I mean if it ain't broke don't  fix it right? However, unlike FTL this game just isn't very fun.
-Tagged as RTS but it has no strategy
Every encounter I came across was being ambushed by an enemy fleet and trying to defend myself after being hit with opening volleys. I soon realized that the best strategy is to just select all of you ships and just have them fly circles around the enemy to avoid their fire while dishing out your own. It works because unless you fly away and run the enemy ships that aren't drones don't move.
-Drone imbalance
The enemy drones will absolutely rip your ships apart. If you stand still for even a few seconds, the drones will likely disable or severly hurt at least one of your ships, but my drones merely flew around and most of the time did not shoot.
-Ship targeting issues
My ships often targeted drones instead of large assault ships right next to them.
-Pacing is kinda weird
The pace of the game seems off. Its too fast to really use positioning to get a tactical advantage, but the ships are just too slow to dodge and manuver sometimes.
-Minor issues
Maybe a select all button for the ships or the ability to hotkey them.
Selecting the ships abilities doesn't always work and targeting with them is also unresponsive at times.
Pathing is also poor at times resulting in ships getting caught on random objects.
Overall it is a pretty good idea, but still needs a good bit of work. I do hope they use some more original ideas instead of just ripping FTL off and improve the user interface. I look forward to when it is finished though, but I do suggest people wait a little longer before buying it.

First Impressions:
Distant Star: Revenant Fleet reminds me of FTL but with RTS elements.  To sum this up, you'll jump from point to point and encounter various events (pirates, enemy fleets, dialogue choices, etc.).  When docked at a friendly station, you can purchase new ships and/or upgrades for your existing ones.  Unlike FTL, the action sequences are less crew specific and more about controlling 1-5 ships inside an arena-esque map and activating their individual abilities timely.  Some things do rub me the wrong way: no difficulty setting, encounters/enemy waves tend to be too long, and the battles tend to be stacked against you to the point where you're dancing and running constantly.  I never felt like I was powerful enough to stand toe to toe with enemies in these events.  The right click sound (when moving) is incredibly annoying as well.  Still, $7 is a pretty good value for what the game has to offer thus far...though I'd personally play this more if the game had an easier difficulty setting or at least scaled in difficulty appropriately.  I suppose we'll see if this gets addressed throughout the course of development.

This is a great game.  I spent hours clearing this game's map with the sound turned down and a podcast on in the background.  If you like what you see in the story page, then chances are you'll enjoy the game.
As far as the story goes, you can pay attention to it or ignore it entirely.  You could probably go into this game without watching any of the movies first, though I recommend checking out fury road (which takes place after this game) so you can have some idea of the world your going into.  I've also seen the original Mad Max movie, but I wouldn't say it's vital to watch before starting the game.  The story is decent with a few cliches, but it's not the main reason you should check out this game.
There's 2 main things that you will be doing in this game, car combat and ground combat.  The car combat consists of you driving around in the magnum opus (your customizable car), and using the weaponry at your disposal (or even the car itself) to take down any enemies you come across.  The ground combat is similar to the Batman:  Arkham series, though with a shotgun, shivs, and melee weapons.  Going around clearing camps and scavenging locations is pretty enjoyable, and you feel pretty satisfied when you finally clear the game's map.
The only thing I wasn't too big of a fan of was that if you're not careful and clear too much of the map too soon, you can make some of the challenges a lot harder to complete.  If you don't plan on getting all the achievements, then this is no big deal, but if you want to try to do that, you'll need to have a game plan for when you're going to do the non-repeatable challenges so that you don't have to spend a ton of time waiting for a storm to come or to run into a certain enemy vehicle.
All in all, I highly recommend you pick this game up when it's next on sale.  Get a feel for the story, then turn down the in-game volume and put on some music or a podcast of your choice.  I'm sure you'll be able to put quite a few hours into it.

This game makes you do what is says in the title; walk a very thin, and eventually cross, a proverbial line.
I have the utmost respect for any soldier; they are beyond politics, they're doing their duty, and in situations where you never know whether the next civilian could be a potential hostile, when you live on the edge all the time, I do believe black and white turn into grey at best.
I have never served in the military, but based on what I know, what friends in the armed forces told me, and what I've seen in documentaries, this game gets very close to reality.
There is nothing glorious about combat, it's survival. Sure, there is a mission to complete, whatever that may be, but ultimately it's about making quick decisions and living to tell about them.
The game shows that it's not about being a hero, it's at best about respect; respect that, in my opinion, every soldier who has ever been through a combat situation deserves.
They will see things that no news report, no photo, no movie can show. Approximate perhaps, but no more. This game puts you one step closer by giving you the choices. And unlike other military shooters where you hardly ever see the aftermath, here you will. You make a call and the game will slap you in the face with the often harsh reality of that choice. It will show you what you did, and tell you to live with it. Welcome to the suck.
I guess the only thing we, the gamers, can take away as a good thing is, that, in this case, it IS just a game. Your decisions won't change the world, or someone's life, or end it. Based on how the game shows you what's going on, that is, however, not easy to keep in mind while playing, and maybe some part of your soul will end up paying regardless.
Beautiful surroundings are in stark contrast to the atrocities that await around the next corner. You want to know war without actually having to physically live through it?
Go ahead. Walk "The Line"...
A quick word about the gameplay: It's sharp, precise, the controls are fluid, and the game blends the play part with cut scenes seamlessly. The controls are in fact so well balanced in my opinion, that it almost feels as if you are pulling a trigger instead of pushing a mouse button.
If you want to give the game the extra bit of polish, then follow one of the guides regarding anti-aliasing which can be configured within your GPU drivers. It's worth it.

I started playing this game with fairly high expectations and I must say I was not dissapointed. Even though the game is fairly linear - with little decision making in terms of the events unfolding - it still instills a sense of freedom as to how you choose to go about it.
The game is clearly trying to grapple with the moral choices during times of war and battle, survival and necessities and in many ways it succeeds quite well.
The setting and graphics are both very nice, while the locations are well thought out and quite detailed. The story (while nothing to jump out of your clothes for) drives you forward quite well, more than anything because it succeeds in instilling the feeling that you have to move on, that there is no choice but to move on...
There isnt extraordinary variety in the weapons and most dont feel much diferent between them, but the momentum of the game doesnt really allow you to think about it much. You mostly grab whatever weapon you have some ammo for.
I played it at the hard settings, which in some situations challenged me, but was overall an enjoyable experience (I believe normal dificulty might be a bit too easy).
Finally there are a few points in the game where your (moral) decisions affect [if only partially] how the game unfolds.
All in all it is a very nice story driven third person shooter, full of intense moments of combat. Not sure if there is a lot of replayability, unless you are after all the achievements, but I can see myself going back and playing it all over again.

A really solid story based RPG. While it doesn't quite achieve the heights of Planescape: Torment, the game it aspires to be, as piece of RPG story telling it is excellent and memorable.
The ninth world of Numenera's setting is as equally weird as that of Planescape. Whereas Planescapes City of Doors was linked to other worlds via gateways, the ninth world is built upon the ruins of the preceding eight civilizations. The Numenera are the detritis of these past worlds: ancient war machines, weapons, artifacts and oddities that are barely understood by the current inhabitants of the world to the extent that they might as well be magic in most cases. This mish mash of present and ancient cultures makes the world of Numenera a weird and dangerous place to inhabit as the artifacts scatterered about are as likely to kill you as make your life easier.
The game is heavily story focused and it is often possible to avoid combat altogether via your characters skills and abilities. Which may be for the best as combat is not the games strong point. While I don't have the same level of loathing for it as some other reviewers, for me it was the weakest part of the experience. Given that results are nearly always more interesting if you can avoid combat, I didn't really have an issue with this. Another thing working in the favour of avoiding combat is that you geneerally dont get XP for it. This puts the focus on finishing quests and discovering the worlds secrets as opposed to bashing everything until its stops moving. Fortunately the writing in the game is excellent and it's closest ties to Planescape, outside the utterly bizzare setting, are the ways it tries to deal with immortality and personal responsibility.  It's good stuff and I don't want to spoil it here but trust me it's a journey well worth taking. As mention in the opening paragraph, it never reaches the heights of Planescape, but that game is seeming more and more like lightning in a bottle and I'm unsure if anything will quite reach that height.
The game is based on the Pillars of Eternity engine and for the most part it does a pretty adequate job of displaying the world around you. It's nothing fantastic but to be honest, most of the world buidling in this game takes place in the text anyway. As mentioned the combat is not the best but it is servicable and I found once I got the gyst of it I was able to win those rare instances when I had not choice but to fight.  There are still some odd bugs kicking around though. I got some strange slow downs in combat that would require a reboot to fix. Ive read of other people experiencing bugged quests, but fortunately I lucked out and did not experience it myself.
This game presents a weird and wonderful world and if you are prepared to invest in its text heavy experience, its a rewarding game. If you value story and world building over hack and slash XP grinding, you wont mind the average combat as its mostly avoidable.
Really recommended.

Very differant type of rpg. While most, if not all, rpg's require conflict & fighting for resolution for a given situation, this game does not. Which is why I liked it. With few exceptions, solutions can be found that don't require fighting. So if you are into the hack & slash approach this game may not be for you. The non violent approach will require a lot of reading and understanding of the background details, many of which will contain clues to solving the "problems" that come up. But you will get more drawn into the story that way. The only critisim I have is that the devs seemed to find it neccessary to invent new terms and words to describe things. For example, battles are known as "crises". Many words are totally made up slang terms that are nonsensical and so it took me almost a third of the way thru to fully understand what the hell they were talking about. After you learn to "translate" what is being told to you, the story becomes very immersive. If you do all the side quests it will take about 60 hrs to complete this because of all the reading. Not neccessarily a bad thing. So if you want to try something different, and ready for something less combative than usual, try this.

Put simply I think this game is unfinished.
Sister Location has some good ideas going for it, but unfortunately it completely lacks in execution. The game mechanics are terribly implemented, with little to no feedback and overall clunkiness. The lack of feedback when using the game mechanics makes the game feel like a guessing game leading to a frustrating experience for the player, who may struggle to determine what they are doing wrong/ what they are supposed to do. The creator of this game tries to deliver a scary experience for its player, but the unjustified level of difficulty (exemplified in night 4) ruins the scary atmosphere and replaces it with an overwhelmingly frustrated one.
The game also falters on a design level at times, with night 4 being a good example of this. The game practically tells you not to wriggle in night 4, but then it turns out that you need to wriggle in order to complete the night. The game basically lies to the player for no good reason and it honestly baffles me how this design choice made it into the final product.
The voice acting of the female voice that speaks to you throughout the game is also painfully cheesy and works to the detriment of the game.
Overall, Scott Cawthon needs to fix the game mechanics of this game in order for the cost of it to be warranted.

Don't get me wrong. If you're a fan of the Arkham series, you will like this game. Single player is very much like Arkham City, except the city seems a bit more expansive, and there are newer gadgets and harder enemies. The story is pretty good, too.
Developers had a great idea when it came to multiplayer. This was something that should have been done before. Only problem is that it's very, very limited. It strongly feels like they threw their ideas together one afternoon during lunch and finished it by quitting time that day.
There are two game types, one of which I've never even found anyone willing to play, so I can't review it. Both are 3v3v2 (Joker thugs vs. Bane thugs vs. Heroes). The concept was great, but the levels are small, and there are only 4 of them. This is ridiculously fun at first, but gets old quickly. In fact, today I couldn't even find any players for the "good" game mode, which was sad but expected. People got burnt out.
It would have been AMAZING if there were a Team Deathmatch, 10v10v2, in a dozen large maps. But maybe next time.
All in all, you're basically buying this game for single player, which is good, even though much of the time it just feels like a large expansion to Arkham City.

I love a good visual novel, dating sim or no, but I sometimes feel I still don't play enough of them. This one was really making noise at PAX Australia 2017 this year, and while they'd already convinced me thoroughly I wanted to invest the money into buying it, I was fortunate to be the lucky winner of a copy in a competition that was held during said convention. Onto the review details, though:
Yes, it's a bit gay, but honest to goodness, unless you feel really uncomfortable with that, this is one of the best. I'm looking back at my playtime and am surprised I already sunk 4.4 hours into the game, and you can bet I'm going to want to play through this one over and over because there's a fair bit there in a single playthrough without the game being achingly long.
The characters are beautiful, with each of them having their own flaws and positives, and the art is consistent to its own style and never feels repetitive. The dialogue is well-written and there's been plenty of times I've laughed at the awful dad jokes, and nearly cried at the heart-warning family-centric themes. Things have been painted in an overall very positive light, characters and diversity are very realistically portrayed with with no truly "bad" characters. This is sincerely one of the best dating sims out there.
There are some light mini-games you'll play, but they don't influence your play too much, so much as break up the monotony. I am unsure if you can actually "fail" them so to speak, and what the consequences of doing so are, but in my playthrough I had not managed to come close to doing so.
If you want a great story that will not fail to make you feel good, play this game. If you're not into dating sims, visual novels, the like, just play the game anyway - if you don't like this, you'll very possibly never find one you'll enjoy and you can feel confident in giving up on the genre for good.

I love this game. If you have played previous hitman games, it is very similar to blood money. You have complete control over how you approach the mission, you can choose an entry point, loadout, and ICA drops. Each level is massive and gives an infinite amount of ways to take out a target. There are challenges that you can look at if you need help deciding how to kill the targets, and if you get stuck, you can use the opportinity system to help you along the way. I do not personally prefer the opportunity system (i feel it holds your hand too much), but it is very helpful for new players or those who have gotten stuck. The graphics are beautiful, but you will need a good computer to run it on high settings. The DRM bothers a lot of people, but I do not have a problem with it as i have a reliable internet connection as does 89% of North America and 74% of Europe. The episodic model also bothers a lot of people, but I'm actually a fan of it. It makes the game more immersive and exciting by making you wait for your next mission. I find that the levels are easily large enough to last until the next one comes out. It also makes it possible for the developers to release a season 2 and 3 without creating an entire new game. In effect, it shortens the amount of time between new content. If the episodic mode really bothers you, just wait until season 1 finishes and buy the game then. The six main episodes, plus two mini-levels, plus 2 training facility missions will be more than enough content to stand as its own game.

I would make a pros and cons list but I'll just list it plainly.

You're driving through the destroyed landscape and notice a pillar of smoke behind the hill. Let's check it out! Before you reach it, you are attacked by a car patrol protruding with spikes and flamethrower nozzles. After defeating them, you notice on the minimap that there is a treasure cache nearby. Let's check it out, I need some more scrap! Before the last bend, you see a big ramp beckoning you to try out the newly upgraded boost and jump wherever it leads. After jumping you are notified that you reached a new wasteland level and that you should go and upgrade your skills at the shaman/psychotherapist.
Where was I and what did I want to do?
This is Mad Max in summary. Just as other games in the genre, you keep getting distracted by myriads of activites everywhere. This is held together by two things: Threat level, a number representing how much activities in the region you already did, and the story.
Of the similar games in the genre, Shadow of Mordor, Arkham City, Assassin's Creed and Mad Max I enjoyed Mad Max the most. It is definitely not without flaws, but as far as 3rd-person distractathons go, its gameplay holds well together. It is mostly well written, the two combat modes are fun and the distractions hold well together for the most part.

I've been pretty disappointed. This could have been great. But it's due to the writing  that I simply cannot recommend this to anyone.
It starts with the intro. The graphics look horrible. It's almost as if the design is unfinished - too much unused space, cheap looking images. Then the text:
Bombastic, grandiose, and unbearingly pretentious, without a lot of actual content. And to my amazement, it kept going exactly like that. Maybe you gotta be a fan of that prose, but I'm not. I prefer brevity and density over elaborate grandstanding that simply has no meat. Read it, and tell me honestly: Isn't 90% of this game's prose atmospherical prattling?
I did enjoy the small quests. But it all felt entirely disconnected. The numera (ancient artifacts/technology) do exactly what  they need to do. There is no system to it, no inner-world laws that give this story the feel that it's real. Instead, there's all those visions, flashbacks, ghosts, memories, all jumbled together into one big mess. It reminds me of a teenager writing his first fantasy story: The girl has a flute that can conjure an army of dragons, but she only uses it once and dismisses  the dragons omce they carried her off the mountain. Nevermind that with this flute she could have defeated the evil overlord, or conquered the whole world.
Instead, the authors seem to revel in this mess. They pile those unconnected little tales onto each other, until it's arbitrary.
Arbitrary. That should probably be the name of the game. "Torment: Tides of Arbitrary." Just googled it, 0 results. So if you see that elsewhere, they've stolen it from me.
One more thing that irked me: the battle system. I've had zero problems fighting people until I got to that one dude with the cultist  groups in the tunnels that you can bypass. Well I wanted to fight them, so I did, and they obliterated me. No chance to win. That's a glaring balancing problem, because none of the other fights were even remotely a hassle. I felt railroaded into sneaking past the cultists and simply brute forcing the boss with a persuasion check. That's when I finally stopped caring.

Review updated April 4th, 2015.
I played 1.7 hours of the game the past two days so I could update my review. My 6 and 4 year old sons were providing armchair Admiral support (both of my sons play FTL regularly so they have valuable insight).
Summary review:
I don't really have a desire to play more Distant Star Revenant Fleet (DSRF) right now. It's not because DSRF is bad. I simply want more from a game than an FTL map clone with some better graphics and  controlling a small fleet of ships. What made FTL fun, for my family, was the feeling that each ship-to-ship combat with crew playing vital role might be your last. What FTL lacked was freedom and openness. DSRF is FTL with better graphics and small fleet to fleet battles that lacks freedom and openness. That may appeal to some people and I would recommend the game to that crowd. I simply want space to feel like space: vast, open, and full of surprises. I want to spend my time with a vast, open, and full of surprises space survival game with RPG elements.
Detailed review:
Distant Star Revenant Fleet (DSRF) is a 2D space game about your small fleet of 1 to 5 ships moving through space to save your home world. The map and galaxy are straight out of FTL. When you fight it's your small fleet battling one to many waves of enemy ships in real time. The developers added an ability to pause the game so that is nice to pause, asssess situation, issue commands, then resume combat. The battles can be hectic so this is a nice feature.
Some ships don't fire unless you specifically click on that ship, click on the weapon, then click on enemy. Even if your ship has 1 weapon, that weapon doesn't autofire. I would like a toggle option to autofire on a particular ship or fire manually. The toggle autofire or manual would be nice on a weapon by weapon basis or ship repair.
The developer added the ability to save your progress. Exiting after you clear out a section after a jump incurs no penalty. When I exited after I jumed into a sector (my boys wanted food right then) before I even engaged any enemy I got this message stating I'd have some kind of penalty for leaving mid-conflict. This particular design choice creates a horrible user experience. Sometimes I like to exit a game when I must deal with real life issues and any game that penalizes me for that automatically gets a fail recommendation.
The maps appear to be randomized as well as the encounters. I do enjoy the options when jumping into sections. That being said I haven't played the game enough to experience the variety and depth of choices. The designers used the layout and theme from FTL where the "galaxy" is really about 8 sections of space with last section having some type of "boss". You jump section to section. Within each section is ~20 systems that you'll jump to. You consume some kind of fuel when jumping system to system. The systems have a difficulty rating from 1 to 10 (10 being highest).
The ship to ship combat is drag box right click or point and click, you highlight with left click, then right click to move/target. The exception are some ship guns or special modules that require additional clicking. The battles are all real time. You cannot ram into enemy ships you simply pass thru them. Your ships can earn experience and credits after each system is completed. At some systems you can upgrade ships in your fleet (the weapons or modules), add ships to your fleet, or buy fuel.
The permanent death is nice so you have to play smart. I like the persistent damage mods. The maps are a bit off when playing at 5760 x 1080 but it's playable.
I stopped playing and wanted to update this review after I experienced an annoying design choice and what I think was a bug. When entering a system I was hailed by "pirates" and "cargo" ships / victims. The choice was to leave them them alone or side with either pirate or cargo ships. Since I wasn't presented with an option to kill pirates and then loot the cargo ships (I am at war) I'll talk about the choice I did take. I sided with cargo ships to provide an escort. What happened next was an escort mission that included defeating all the pirates and escorting three vessels (A, B, and C). You escort ships one at a time. Ship A appears on map when mission starts, B shows up after A is destroyed or makes it to starbase, C shows up after B is at starbase or destroyed. The cargo ships simply fly without any care in the galaxy straight into the horde of pirate ships. If I had known this I would have sided with the pirates. If your life / cargo depends on your security escort you had better take commands from the security escort. For the cargo ship to simply fly head long into the pirates is poor design and ignores a realistic option that beings don't ask for help then simply suicide it. Give the player control of moving the cargo ship. Save the developer the labor of creating cargo ship AI in escort duty. Then if cargo ship is lost there is really only one person at fault, the player and not developer AI. I did manage to save ship B and escort that ship to the single space station. Ship A and C did not fare well. A morale aspect or fair reward system would be nice. I'm not sure what was so valuable a cargo that was worth the 30+ pirate vessels (large and small) being destroyed. You would think that at some point morale would fail and pirates would give up or the reward from the cargo ship captain would scale to the risk.  Here is were the bug kicked in...after all that fighting, the mission failed. I never found out what the reward would have been. I completed killing all the pirates and ship B escort (green check next to objective). Failed A and C ships (red in boxes). The mission message said I failed because I failed to escort ANY of the ships to station even thought I did escort B.

Very much FTL meets a 2D version of homeworld.

As of v0.0.0.3:
Distant Star: Revenant Fleet is an interesting mix of FTL-like overworld and roguelike style of random encounter with RTS combat mechanics.
The game has simple, but nice visuals, pretty good music and solid sound effects.
Well, maybe aside from that strange sounds that's made when you give a command to your ships - it can get annoying pretty quick.
Even though at the moment the game does not have too much content (you can beat it in ~20 mins if you are lucky), the core mechanics are all there and all are pretty solid.
You can clearly see what the game wants to be, it wants you to jump from sector to sector and resolve variety of random RTS encounters with the ships you have.
If that sounds simple - think again. Since your ships is a limited resource and you cannot just build more "on-the-fly", you have to be pretty careful about handling them.
On top of that - the game's quite cheap.
So, even if you don't want to buy in right now and want more content - it's definitely worth tracking.
If you are OK with current amount of content - then I'd say buy it, it's pretty enjoyable and probably will get only better.

The graphic are simple, I like these kind of 2 dimensional top down space games and I like the style.
-----The music is spacey and pleasant. It reminded of magic carpet of all games with it's (middle eastern?) string instrument sound.
-----There is some dialogue at each encounter, against the back drop that you are from a dominant space faring faction which is served by other factions and at war with another major faction the Orthani. I liked it.
-----It would be nice if units didn't talk every single time you give them a command, that is not every split second lol
I haven't played FTL, but I've watched people play it. It basically seems to work on a similar concept. That is between encounters you select your next Star System destination within a randomly generated network of Star Systems. Encounters can be hostile or neutral. You can choose to attack, intimidate or avoid conflict at most encounters.
-----You also come across shops where can attain additional ships and equipment to fit to them including weapons and active abilities.
-----There is no fleet control tutorial yet. In combat, ships in your fleet by default fire upon the closest hostile vessel. You seem to be able to prioritize specific targets if you wish. You also tell ships where to move during an encounter. Basically it plays exactly like at RTS.
-----Most ships other than the Assault class type are very fragile. Usually these weaker ships in my fleet tended to be destroyed almost immediately because I couldn't move them out of harms way quickly enough. Any of your ships that aren't moving or are doing so in a straight line are basically sitting ducks and will destroyed very quickly.
-----So ultimately my strategy ended up boiling down to flying only assault class ships and kiting the enemies I encountered. This was a very effective strategy. But it wasn't a satisfying experience. Your ships will not move by themselves, without your intervention they will just sit there. You have to constantly micromanage their movements, which potentially is demanding with a progressively larger fleet at your control. Encounters typically consisted of flying circles around a wave of enemy ships until they were destroyed and repeat several times until the encounter is over, there wasn't really any challenge. I wasn't really fond of constantly directing ships, which you must do because of the games pace.
-----You can basically finish the game in just a few minutes. You can just travel directly to the 'exit' system while avoiding every hostile encounter along the way. And Bob's your auntie, you win!
-----In the games current state, if want an extended space adventure you need to avoid traveling directly to your final destination. That is visit all the star systems which aren't on the way there.
-----I had a few technical problems with the game. I couldn't scroll the view to the right with the mouse cursor because the cursor would travel outside of the game on my first screen and into my second screen, I had to awkwardly reach around my microphone with my left hand to scroll with the arrow keys. Shops didn't appear to function properly and I had to fiddle around a lot with the menu to purchase items successfully. You are supposed to be able to pause the action by pressing space however this was completely non-functional for me. Lastly
-----So I think the game-play needs to be fleshed out to make it more satisfying interesting and challenging, I think most people might agree with that. But personally I would prefer if units autonomy wasn't restricted to firing at the closest hostile ship. Or alternatively if more advanced commands were implemented to reduce the need for micromanagement being so constant. Lastly with pretty much any single-player game I would like there to be some way of enjoying the game online with friend or other people aka multi-player.
I think this a good foundation for a great game. Hopefully the developers will keep working hard to produce a complete and polished title.

First, I do recommand this game - It's an excellent game, but do not buy it over the original game. If it wasn't for its predecessor, BL2 would have a "thumb up" from me.
The story is more solid in BL2. The NPCs are full of interesting personalities (even the generic ennemies have interesting bits, like the Shakespeare-reciting psychos), and some of them even move. The cutscenes are more elaborate, and the visuals are (of course) lushier. There is also more of something like an actual story, with lots of humor. And yet somehow the playing pleasure is diminished. Why?
It's a combination of many factors. One of them is the substitution of Weapon Proficiencies for Badass points, wich are unfair for the new player and dull to boot. Another one is the over-cafeinated UI (why do companies insist in giving us badder UI than they did in their previous games is beyond my comprehension). The "Fight for your Life" which is nearly impossible in single-player, but the one that takes the cake for me are the poor loot and guns.
Guns are un-sufferingly bad for a game that's all about them. Apart for snipers, which are generally okay, they are un-workeable gizmos that shoots way too much ammo for what they do. They do everything except shoot straight (yeah, I'm looking at you, Hyperion). I had debates with friends about it, and my winning argument was the "golden keys" gimmick; In the first game, you didn't need internet-fetched code to get a decent weapon - regular loot sufficed.
The guns also get quickly out of style. And the fact that your character no longer has weapon preferences, combined with the general rarity of ammo on the field, makes it that you are forced to carry one (or two) of every type, all the time. This, in turn, makes weapon swapping from "inventory" to "equipped" common as you depletes all ammo for a type of gun you had equipped. But with the wonky, multipanel UI, swapping guns like that is a risky operation in multiplayer.
Dropped loot is so insignificant It's becoming a chore picking them. The only valid items are the ones you get as rewards for quests, anyway. Elemental tech weapons and scoped assault rifles are rarities. Character customization "evolved" from colour-chosing in the first game to rigid, spit-the-money-out all made-up outfits and heads, but as you never see your own character anyway, it's mostly for showing off to your partners.
And since we're at it, another irritant is the constant buying pressure: Some of the extra playable characters and outfits you've got to pay for, and they're far from being cheap; But even if you don't buy the extra characters, you will consistantly find loot for them, which IMO is a moneymaking scam. Such coercing manners makes the caricatural corporate greed in the game an irony.
Now, as I write, it's still a good game, it really is... But playing it just urged me to go back to the first BL. I heard the DLCs were quite good, thought.

I love this game. If you have played previous hitman games, it is very similar to blood money. You have complete control over how you approach the mission, you can choose an entry point, loadout, and ICA drops. Each level is massive and gives an infinite amount of ways to take out a target. There are challenges that you can look at if you need help deciding how to kill the targets, and if you get stuck, you can use the opportinity system to help you along the way. I do not personally prefer the opportunity system (i feel it holds your hand too much), but it is very helpful for new players or those who have gotten stuck. The graphics are beautiful, but you will need a good computer to run it on high settings. The DRM bothers a lot of people, but I do not have a problem with it as i have a reliable internet connection as does 89% of North America and 74% of Europe. The episodic model also bothers a lot of people, but I'm actually a fan of it. It makes the game more immersive and exciting by making you wait for your next mission. I find that the levels are easily large enough to last until the next one comes out. It also makes it possible for the developers to release a season 2 and 3 without creating an entire new game. In effect, it shortens the amount of time between new content. If the episodic mode really bothers you, just wait until season 1 finishes and buy the game then. The six main episodes, plus two mini-levels, plus 2 training facility missions will be more than enough content to stand as its own game.

text:
An unforgiving and difficult game, Super Meat Boy is a very polished platformer with a steep difficulty curve. The amazing soundtrack keeps you hyped through every death, and the moment where you finally master the level patterns (or simply luck your way through it) feels amazing.
The controls are incredibly responsive and tight, and though the game recommends playing with a gamepad, I had no difficulty whatsoever playing with a keyboard. The art style is also very unique; it doesn't quite stray into the territory of pixel graphics that many indie games use, but it is cartoony and colourful without sacrificing small details in levels. If you enjoy games that throttle you over and over until levels become imprinted in your muscle memory, you'll love find Super Meat Boy highly entertaining.
TL;DR: Play this game if you enjoy difficult platformers and/or aren't prone to ragequitting.

One of the best platform games I have ever played, though admittedly I haven't played many. It has a very attractive art style and an amusing story. The game controls perfectly, i.e the controls are simple and very responsive but the game itself is very challenging. Every time you die attempting to clear the level, your actions are recorded and in the end when you do manage to clear a level, all your attempts are shown simultaneously as multiple meat boys jumping to their collective doom as a lone one emerges victorious. I felt this was a great payoff, since all my failed attempts weren't just forgotten away. Also, the BG score is very good as it keeps you going even after dozens of failures in each level. And all this is just the core game. There are massive secrets waiting to be unlocked including new characters with their own move set, not to mention a level editor and workshop support.
All in all, this is a must buy.

Hella fun game, not too taxing on a 2GB card at max settings.  (I'm running an nVidia 670 card which supposedly is below minimum and had zero issues with everything turned on) And you'll want max settings since the wasteland details and explosions are fantastic.  Half driving game, half melee like Arkham Asylum style, it's hours of apocalyptic mayhem.
My only beef was the final story chase car fight that is near impossible since you can barely navigate a maze without crashing and dying.  It litereally took hours to complete that one segment of the game with much frustration.  It wasn't about skill or some boss fight but just a badly designed race imo that knocks your car around like a pinball machine.  The physics and mechanics of the game were really well done on 99% of the game  so it was annoying to hit this speedbump in the game that makes you want to rage quit. So be warned and prepare to spend some time researching tactics on youtube and you'll see the volume of poeple♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at this part too.
That said, really I didn't find this repetitive at all being a massive open world that takes a LONG time to drive around end to end.  The driving physics are excellent and your car drives differently on different terrain be it sand, dirt road, asphalt or rocks.  Upgrades are very noticeable, and even weight of the car affects it's handling.  Enemy AI is well done, and you won't be able to outrun other vehicles until you get a V8 engine, but some cases the AI will run away if you damage them enough or hide in a minefield.  Hand to hand combat is very enjoyable, and maxs fighting skills level up really fast to give it a lot of variety early on. Clearing scavenger sites is probably the only repetitive element as the developers were sneaksy hobbitses about hiding scrap you need to find at each site.
Having played this on both Mac and PC, the graphics on the Mac are not quite as good and a bit laggier than PC, but that's to be expected.  I kept medium settings on the Mac and it ran well.  The nice thing is all achievements are saved cross platform so in my case running Boot Camp, anything you manage to complete on one is saved to the other platform.
All and all great game, definitely a keeper and worth replaying.

This is one of the best games ever made and the only reason it is not regarded as such is that it is not very accessible. I can imagine many critics have started Terraria, played for some hours trying to figure it out, and put it away. Very often, critics have drawn misguided conclusions that Terraria resembles Minecraft (or is a Minecraft clone), but in fact nothing could be further from the truth. Terraria is a procedurally generated sandbox survival metroidvania. Learning curve is steep, the game is hard and often requires you to consult to wikis and guides (even more so than the Souls series) but once you gain control of the game mechanics, you will find a very deep, hard core gem. Don’t let its eye-candy graphics fool you…
You are dropped into a world surrounded by many dangers. Initially, you are expected to make your first shelter, first weapon and just survive. This is the very core of the whole game. In order to beat stronger creatures, you need better weapons for which you need better crafting material. To get better crafting material, you need to mine deep into the earth, which leads you to find secret chests, face gazillion creatures including “bosses”. Boss fights not only require skill, but also need you to have the weapons, armors, potions, items necessary to beat them. Last, but not the least, there are plenty of events such as Halloween, Christmas, Pirate Invasion etc. with their own unique bosses and loots.
While you are working on mining for better tools, armors, weapons to be able to beat stronger enemies, you also need to keep expanding your “shelter”. A chair, ceiling and door is not sufficient any longer. You need to keep building new rooms to have room for new crafting centers and chests (for inventory). Every new room invites a new NPC to your shelter who can be crucial in your quest to beat the world of terraria, whether they sell unique items or provide healing.
Being a true sandbox game, you can also ignore progression and spend hundreds of hours just building. Your limit to what you can build and how you can customize it is your imagination. People at Terraria subreddit still manage to amaze me with their creativity and sometimes totally mind-blowing architecture.
Whether you choose to play it as a metroidvania or as a sandbox 2d Minecraft, you will love Terraria. In my opinion, it is one of the best games ever made.
Buy it full price. Developers are still updating content and supporting the game after all these years (without any paid DLCs whatsoever), they really deserve some support.

It may not be the game everyone was expecting, but it is still a thoroughly enjoyable experience. I like the fact that there are several ways to resolve each quest and you don’t have to resort to combat to get things done. The flip side to that is if you like games where you are constantly grinding for loot and killing everything that moves, this may not be your cup o’tea.
It is certainly not cutting edge in terms of graphics, but the game has a nice look to it and the splashes of purple and gold in Sagus Cliffs kind of remind me of the Clerk’s Ward in the original Torment, which is cool.
The thing I disliked the most was that each area is isolated, so once you leave there is no going back. I tend prefer games that are more open and allow free exploration.
Also, the game is a bit on the short side, I did virtually all the side quests available to me and I finished it in about 25 hours. That being said, the game does appear to have a fair bit of replayability, as choices you make will prevent you from playing every questline in a single playthrough. Also it looks like the dev has added additional content through a patch so it definitely looks like to would be worth a 2nd playthrough.
This is an amazing world with so many weird, fun, and believable little quests to complete.

Batman: Arkham Origins is the unofficial third game in the series, I say unofficial because it wasn't developed by Rocksteady, who made both Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. Most people view Origins in a bad light due to this fact, and there are certain points that feel strange when transitioning from City or Asylum to Origins, for one the sound seems a little off, adjusting to the new voice actor for Batman is a little strange, but you get used to him eventually, the graphics seems somewhat off, not standing up like Cities impressive visuals, however the enviroment designs are beautiful such as Gotham in snow and the hotel and other such locations. Fighting feels off as well, the usually fluid combat feels somewhat strange when the visuals tend to pop weirdly with a filter or two, however it still is the old City style combat so it fits okay within the series.
However one of my biggest problems is the lack of variety in characters to play as. Asylum had a single character to play as (Or two depending if you had Joker), which was fine, it was a great game, then City upped the Ante by having Batman, Nightwing, Robin AND Catwoman, each with their own unique fighting styles, Deathstroke, whilst an appreciated addition to a cast list borrows a lot of his moves from Arkham City Robin, which makes him feel less unique in this work, and the third character is simply a variant of Bruce Wayne, from the Initiation DLC. Going from City to origins, you will feel it lacks a lot of the polish and shine that City had, but for being developed by another developer, they did an alright job with what they could, I liked my experiences with the game and would recommend it for someone who has played the other 2 games first. Also, as a side note, the Multiplayer did feel tacked on, and the fun of it lasted a short while. Overall I'd give Batman: Arkham Origins 7/10, It lacks enough spirit and polish to push it beyond City and Asylum, Since it was built upon the foundation laid out by Asylum and City, it doesn't do enough to warrant a higher score, it feels too much the same, however the enviroments are beautifully done and Gotham is really fun to explore around, with this unique look in the usually gothic and gloomy city, it's nice to see a more festive take on the city. Still, as a stand-alone experience, it's stands alright on it's own, I wasn't bored by this, and so I'd recommend it to someone who likes Batman or the DC universe.

The Five Nights at Freddy's franchise is a beloved franchise (in certain circles). And it is no secret that for the most part, the last four games (not counting FNAFW) have stayed fairly similar in presentation.
In Sister Location, Scott mixed it up a bit and instead introduced the new game in segments that task you as the player to complete specific events, sometimes in a allotted amount of time. Each new night presents new tasks for the player to overcome.
There's no denying that what Scott has done here new (for his games) and a refreshing change of pace as far as the FNAF franchise is concerned. The game looks better and it's a nice change of pace being able to go between rooms in the new game.
With that being said, each night really only feels like a string of mini games sewn together. And unfortunately these events can become repetitive and quickly frustrating depending on how many times you have to do them. It'd be different if each completed task had a check point, so if you failed, you'd just start off from where you failed, but they don't. When you come to a part in the game you are having problems with, instead of being able to try again, you instead are (usually) pushed back behind several other events.
(Spoilers) A good example is on the third night. You'll need to cross through Funtime Foxy's domain and then perform maintenance on Funtime Freddy. If you fail either of those events, you'll have to complete both over again.
Similarly, while the game may give you vague directions on what it expects you to do, often times, it's still very unclear on what you actually need to do, resulting in you performing the same "puzzles" over and over again until you get it right. Othertimes it is simply downright hard and frustrating to complete a task simply on how it is designed.
I don't have a problem with mini games and puzzles, far from it. But when players are complaining on Reddit, when players have to do the same task over and over and over again, it seems like there may need to be some tweeking involved to balance out the difficulty a little.
This was clearly one of Scott's best works. And I applaud him on his effort, he did well. But for players who are not nearly as engaged to the franchise, this can be a frustrating experience that will ultimately cause them to quit playing. I really wish STEAM had a middle of the road decision for rating games besides recommending the game or not, because it isn't a bad game by any means.
For die hard fans of the franchise, who love Scott and his games, then it's simple, I recommend for you to play the game, it's not even a question. For people who  have been casually following the game and may want to check it out, not so much, those players would be better left to watching a playthrough on YouTube where they don't have to deal with the frustration.
As for me? I got involved in the franchise because of the story and less because of the scares, because ultimately as you are exposed to the jumpscares they will gradually lose their impact on how they effect you, to the point you are completely unmoved. For me, personally, I wouldn't recommend this game to my friends or family.

Decent co-op TBS with a good ammount of single player content. Perfectly playable without spending money but like all FTP it's a question of how long you can resist the temptation to splurge.
There are a couple of opening tips that the game doesn't make clear and you will want to take note of:
Each time YOU level up you can only level a single skill/attribute/feature of a single character. This means you will be most useful if you only ever have one character. Your first character's name will also be YOUR name as far as your community presence goes. The first thing you should do when you start this game is hit the "?" and read the help notes. Or you will want to start over from scratch very quickly. Many players prefer to play with a single character as this provides the fastest way to create a powerful presence for gauntlet games. I have revised my opinion on this because making a party for your first account is more fun, familiarises you with hero types, and you lose nothing by it because you can still create "solo" accounts later and use your party account for farming. "radience" the in game currency is effected across all accounts linked to your steam acct and items can be passed down through other players. Given that it's "free" it's certainly well worth a look. But be prepared for some grind.

An unforgiving and difficult game, Super Meat Boy is a very polished platformer with a steep difficulty curve. The amazing soundtrack keeps you hyped through every death, and the moment where you finally master the level patterns (or simply luck your way through it) feels amazing.
The controls are incredibly responsive and tight, and though the game recommends playing with a gamepad, I had no difficulty whatsoever playing with a keyboard. The art style is also very unique; it doesn't quite stray into the territory of pixel graphics that many indie games use, but it is cartoony and colourful without sacrificing small details in levels. If you enjoy games that throttle you over and over until levels become imprinted in your muscle memory, you'll love find Super Meat Boy highly entertaining.
TL;DR: Play this game if you enjoy difficult platformers and/or aren't prone to ragequitting.

One of the best platform games I have ever played, though admittedly I haven't played many. It has a very attractive art style and an amusing story. The game controls perfectly, i.e the controls are simple and very responsive but the game itself is very challenging. Every time you die attempting to clear the level, your actions are recorded and in the end when you do manage to clear a level, all your attempts are shown simultaneously as multiple meat boys jumping to their collective doom as a lone one emerges victorious. I felt this was a great payoff, since all my failed attempts weren't just forgotten away. Also, the BG score is very good as it keeps you going even after dozens of failures in each level. And all this is just the core game. There are massive secrets waiting to be unlocked including new characters with their own move set, not to mention a level editor and workshop support.
All in all, this is a must buy.

After playing 200+ hours of playing Prison Architect I can say with certainty that this game is one of my favourites of all time.
When I first bought the game in Alpha 20 (give or take) on a Steam sale I soon realized I purchased much more than my money's worth. This game provides a rich, cartoony experience of a nineties management sim while also fusing the serious undertone accompaning the modern prison system and its legal factors.
As a previously Early-Access game the development cycle was absolutely amazing (Which unfortunately can't be said for most in-dev games on Steam these days). Introversion Software did a really good job keeping their game interesting with fun and meaningful monthly updates which changed how I played frequently. It contained the same buzz, which in one way or another reminded me of the excellent progression of the developing stage in the golden days of Minecraft.
I highly recommend this game. As it molds from its Alpha versions and launches into its full release stages, I still feel that Prison Architect can only get better form here.

Immortal Empire is a game I have found myself enjoying, it is not often that we get strategy turn based RPG's that are free to paly, and even rarer that we get one that is not complete garbage.  In Immortal Empire you play as an immortal or party of immortals and fight your way through the campaign alone or with co-op. So far the story seems to be primarily about riding the world of this corruption that its found itself in, as of me writing this review I have not progressed very far in the story.  The immortals themselves are your playable heroes who respawn after death, there is a pretty decent variety of immortals to chose from, the majority falling under standard RPG class system, dps assassins, melee tanks, healers, supports and even a few immortals who have hybrid skill sets.
The combat is turnbased and functions around a unique resource called time, not only does movement and attack run off of this resource, so do most ability cool downs, so when running a large party its always good to have an idea what order you should use your skills in. When it comes to game modes, aside from the campaign, there is gauntlet mode, from what I can tell you try to survive with a group of co-op players against waves of enemies for increasingly valuable rewards. I have not played much gauntlet as of this review.  Immortal Empire also has PvP or some sort, but I have not seen or tried PvP at this time.
Overall I feel like Immortal Empire balances RPG gameplay and strategy in a way that makes it a fun co-op game, and would recommend it to people looking for a combination of co-op, strategy and RPG in some way, shape or form.

I'm not sure what it is. Have I become to critical of games these days? Or maybe my expectations for this specific game were just too high? Or maybe the game really is just mediocre. Since this game first appeared on kickstarter, which feels like ages ago, I was beyond excited about it. After all these years, a successor to the original Planescape Torment, which is a game that to this day still holds up as a true classic (and so much fun), except this new one would have updated graphics, a new story that I haven't already beat more times than I'd care to admit and surely a new creative interface. And I waited patiently for it until it finally came out. Finally that day came. But It's just... disappointing and painfully boring.
The story isn't particularly interesting when starting out (not really bad, just nothing special), the characters are uninteresting, the gameplay isn't all that exciting or fun, the interface and combat is just bad, the music is unmemorable at best, and to top it off even the movement feels a bit clunky. There are still a few touches they tried to add in that are similar to the old Planescape. For example, you can still interact with many of the objects in each screen and gain experience or items depending on your choices, but I honestly don't think they did a very good job with it; most of these interactions are just not very interesting. Just strange random things for the sake of being strange and random. I started getting bored with it, and this is something I'd normally love. So I just couldn't get into this one... I don't know if the game picks up after a few more hours in (from other reviews it sounds like it doesn't though), but honestly, with all of the amazing new games that come out on steam every week, I doubt I'll ever find the time to get back to this one.

Excellent game, I would highly recommend it to anyone who has enjoyed the previous Hitman games. This game is the true successor to Blood Money, returning back to the big open levels that we loved from the previous games. Each level in this game is massive and there is so much more to do in each levels compared to Blood Money. The escalation missions and elusive targets will keep you coming back for more! This is one of the rare examples of a game that is perfect for the episodic release method.  While the over-arcing story (though this is something that has always been weak in the Hitman series) does suffer due to episodic release, the stories contained within each level more than makes up for it. Another thing that is great is that by replaying levels and completing them in different ways, you unlock new weapons, gadgets, and entry points into levels. I would highly recommend you purchase the full experience rather than the other offers since you will not have to pay extra for the bonus episodes.

If you like open world games, you'll like Mad Max.
If you liked the fist fighting style of the Batman Arkham franchise, you'll like Mad Max (not such an elaborate fighting system tho, but it keeps you entertained)
If you liked Farcry, you'll like Mad Max.
The game has a lot of the above mentioned mechanics, which include: open world, fighting, racing (there are some racing circuits in which you can get more cars as rewards), destroying stuff to gain area control, side quests, crashing cars, treasure hunt, tactical enemies, yanking enemies out of their cars... Even massive electric sansdtorms that reward the player with some extra loot!
So far I've played 38 hours and I have a bit over half the world under control, I can customize Max to a certain degree, but the car has a much higher level of options available.
I did get this game in a sale offer, but I've had so much fun playing (it's actually a bit addictive for me) I would have bought it anyway. Heh! Even cruising around just because is fun!
The main story? Haven't finished it yet... but it's Mad Max!
Give it a try, you won't regret it!

When I finished playing Arkham City, all I wanted was more Arkham City. Arkham Origins delivered on this while adding some new enemy types and some special boss battles and a whole new story on a different map. Having been skeptical about how the franchise would do under a different studio, I was definitely put off by the mixed reviews the game has received. The good news is that the story mode holds up very well next to its predecessor, although I liked the predator maps in Arkham City a lot better. It is disappointing that some bugs were left in the game even over a year after its release. There is one trophy I simply can't get because of a game-breaking bug. There is a room in the back of the night club that causes the screen to turn black. Your game then saves, and there is no way to leave the black room. That is unfortunate, but it doesn't make it impossible to complete the storyline or enjoy the game, and there is an unofficial workaround that allowed me to exit the room.
One place where I was very disappointed was the challenge maps. I really enjoyed the challenge maps in Arkham City and played them again and again, but I just don't feel compelled to do that there. Arkham City had more characters and better maps. In Origins we have only Batman and Deathstroke. You can play as Bruce Wayne if you buy the DLC, but it's hardly worth it.
All in all, Origins is a  decent entry into the series in spite of a few flaws. Arkham City was an absolute masterpiece, and this one doesn't quite reach the same level, though it's pretty darn close. If you liked Arkham City, you will like this game.
