Dark Void Zero brings back the classic "NES difficulty", where games were short but hard as balls to beat.
Besides the difficulty, it also captures the rest of the 8-bit feeling perfectly. Play this for a couple of hours straight and you'll probably think that you were playing some obscure NES game on an emulator this whole time.
The levels follow the old "get keycards, open new part of level, repeat until end of level is reached" formula. This is then layered on with hard enemies and deliciously kind-of-frustrating controls (it's more frustrating when you're using the jetpack power-up, when you're on foot, the controls are actually extremely simple and straight-forward).
As if this wasn't enough to make it a controller smashing game, there aren't any continues. You die 3 times (or more, since there are 1UPs through the levels) and you gotta start the level all over again and get the keycards again.
Buy it, play it, do whatever you want with it.
EDIT: !!READ THIS PART, PLEASE!! --- I forgot to mention something that some people love to complain about because... I dunno, they just do (I understand the frustration this brings, but calm yourselves. If this is a dealbreaker for many of you, then what in the actual ♥♥♥♥ is wrong with you?). There is an extra layer of DRM on this game, aside from Steam. The overall hated SecuROM.
This piece of DRM imposes a set number of times your game can be activated.
There's a limit of 20 activations now since Capcom raised the number, instead of the 5 activations it had before.
>>NOW THIS IS THE IMPORTANT PART!<<: There's a way you can avoid using the activations. Before you uninstall the game for whatever reason, do this: right-click the game on your Steam library, go to "Properties" and then "Set launch options", write "/revoke" (without the quotation marks, of course) and RUN THE GAME (you must do this before uninstalling it!!)... and now you're safe to uninstall it without losing one of the activations!
Have fun without having to worry about the DRM!
Oh, and one more thing: whatever is said about SecuROM using the CPU like crazy is NOT true.

Inmates is a solid and well constructed adventure. It held my interest and provided several hours of respite from real life. While it is not ground-breaking, it is definitely worth playing for those who favor exploration and story.  Read my full review at
.  Grade = B

Inmates is a game that preys on the creepy factor of prisons, and their hostile, unpredictable incarcerated. Players become Jonathan, a man who has woken up in a seemingly abandoned prison with absolutely no recollection of how he got there. He soon discovers that his cell door isn't locked, and he leaves in hope of finding help and answers, but he also uncovers that he's not truly alone. Evil is lurking around the prison, and he must find a way to escape. The full plot isn't revealed until the very end, but gamers with even a little bit of horror background can probably hazard a guess as to what happened. The conclusion is very predictable.
It should be stated right off the hop that the second video on the store page is extremely misleading. Events happen in that trailer that never actually occur in the game itself, and it makes the title look far more exciting than it actually is. There isn't even a run button included, so expect to wander around the prison at a medium stride the entire time; a painpoint that becomes increasingly frustrating during all of the inevitiable backtracking that is needed. The estimated game length of 3-4 hours is also very wrong, as even exploring the environments completely will create for a maximum play time of about 2 hours.
Even though the idea behind Inmates is promising, the overall execution comes across as cliché and uninspired. It's a glorified key-finding simulator with some very basic puzzles thrown in. The majority of the game is spent exploring prison cells, some contain matches while others contain notes, some offer up both or neither, while three of them lock you in until you can solve the easy enigma inside. There are only a few scares that happen, and all of them are cheap and ineffective; half-naked guys whose heads shake around alot.
Additionally, this title does include game breaking bugs. About halfway in I decided to take a break and I closed up shop, when I went back a few hours later the game had jumped me forward in the story, and I missed one of the puzzles. While that isn't horrible, it also glitched out the door that I needed to open in order to progress any further at all. Taking a look at the forums, I see that numerous other people have also experienced this problem, but I also see that the developer has been helpful in the matter and has promised an update to fix this issue.
Don't be too fooled by the graphics in the screenshots and trailers on the store page, they're not as spectacular as they may seem. Most of the textures turn into mud up-close, including the ground, and overall the game is far too dark. Even using the matches that are laying around is counterproductive since they create a harsh glare that hinders visibility rather than helping at all. Their lifespan is also ridiculously short, but luckily there's a plethora of them laying around.
Inmates could be a much better game if some more love and polish went in to it. Still, the fact of the matter is that the horror world is oversaturated with key finding and basic puzzle solving to the point that games are almost guaranteed to fail if they include these elements; especially in tandem. If the story was salvagable, the shallow gameplay would be acceptable, but it's more of the same tried-and-true "amnesiac with a predictable plot twist" scenario. For what it's worth, the optimization is excellent, although the menu could use a bit of sprucing up as well. Once the bugs get ironed out, give it a shot for $5 or less, but the current asking price of $11.49 CAD is too steep.

From the very first moments of Inmates, you are thrown into a topsy-turvy world in which all prisoners are issued with esoteric reading matter (running the gamut from quantum physics to demonology), children are imprisoned next-door to grown psychopaths (at least they're given toys), and matches - while in plentiful supply - only last about ten to fifteen seconds from the time you light them to the time they snuff themselves out.
Yessir, you're in for a wild and woolly - if somewhat short yet slow-moving - ride.
The voice acting is mediocre at best; the graphics a long, long way from anything to write home about; the technical performance a bit wonky considering how underwhelming the graphics are; and the character models ugly in the extreme (and not always in a DELIBERATE way). By comparison, the atmosphere is quite strong; the jump scares sufficiently effective and not overly crude; the mapping quite nice without being exceptionally imaginative; and the puzzles mildly distracting without ever being frustratingly difficult. The story is...actually, it's pretty good, and definitely one of the game's strongest suits. (Though you'll be mighty sick of the name "Roy" by the time it's over with, guaranteed!)
Look, I'm definitely recommending it, but I'm hardly GUSHING over it. It's a solid indie horror game/moody walking simulator (with one chase scene), and it's probably overpriced at ten dollars but worth picking up in a sale. If, you know, it's your kind of game to begin with. I've played much better, I've played much, MUCH worse, and there's not a great deal more I can say beyond that.
Oh, except that anyone with a particular grudge towards heaving breathing sound effects should avoid this game like the plague (it didn't bother me much personally, but it really does sound like your character is borderline asphyxiating for the entirety of the game's duration. Hey...it's "horror").
Verdict: 7.5/10.

Played the game on GOG, but the free weekend gives me a chance to review it here.
Pros:
- The original Kickstarter brought up a lot of interesting ideas about combat and NPC design and showed an admirable ambition to create a more intellectually stimulating, meaningful type of game. Almost all of these ambitions were abandoned during the game's production, but those backer updates are still interesting to read through.
Cons:
- reams upon reams of unbearably purple prose, using 50 words where 10 would work just as well. It seems like the writers simply could not write down a noun without putting at least one adjective in front of it.
- combat encounters where you fight up to a dozen enemies at once, each moving with super slow animations (a speed slider should be a base requirement for any turn based game)
- most of the gameplay consists of chance-based skill checks, even more so than in Wasteland 2. Contrary to the developers' claims, failing one of these checks is generally not "rewarding" or "interesting" in its own right, so I ended up reloading a lot. Many of the skill checks cannot even be properly failed: if you get a bad roll on one of those checks, you just pay a penalty point and try again. This will repeat again and again until you succeed. That's just about the opposite of "interesting failure" - it's tedious as hell.
- the displayed percentage chances for these skill checks are often contradictory and don't follow the game's own rules (see this thread:
). If we want to be charitable, we might say that the game is applying hidden modifiers to make these checks harder or easier according to the developers' secret wishes; if we don't want to be charitable, we might say that the skill check calculation is broken.
- the replacement of many potential fail states with "retry options" also means that the game has considerably less replay value than advertised. Most of the checks in the main quest can always be passed if you just keep retrying them, and I generally found it easy to arrive at my preferred outcome for a quest. Most of the reactivity in the game is either minimal (a slightly tougher skill check that can be infinitely repeated anyway) or purely cosmetic (an ending slide that changes depending on your dominant tide, an extra piece of lore unlocked by your focus on Intellect skills). Resting can force a few failure states for time sensitive side quests, but I never had to rest once during the entire game.The different endings just boil down to one choice at the end of the game.
- mismanaged development (by inXile's own admission) resulted in massive cuts that are very noticeable in the game; you can't join a faction anymore, but the factions still talk about taking new recruits, you can't go to the Oasis anymore, but the plot points that were supposed to happen there are still being foreshadowed with no payoff. Certain NPCs are completely pointless, but were meant to be important quest givers or faction leaders before their quest/faction was cut, etc. etc.
- the main plot also feels thin; large pieces of it were cut or simplified when the Oasis was cut, and the impact of the Tides and the Factions was diminished greatly from the original concept. What remains is pretty dull and by-the-numbers; maybe I set my expectations too high, but I was hoping for something that was at least in the rough vicinity of the Nier games, or the original Torment, in terms of complexity and emotional resonance. In an alternate reality, this plot could have been the basis of Pillars of Eternity 2, or Neverwinter Nights 3. From the Kickstarter, I had envisioned something unique and artistic; as it stands, I'm not even sure if this story was really worth telling.
- the same cuts also forced some shortcuts in visual design: the character models are ugly as sin (both in strictly aesthetic terms and in terms of polygons/texture quality), and the animations are best described as "minimal". Environmental art is wildly inconsistent - some stuff looks good (particularly at the start of the game, which was reworked and polished several times during Early Access), while other assets seem to be transplanted from a late 90s 3D game). The 3D assets generally look worse than the 2D assets. People were speculating that the stuff we saw in Early Access had to be placeholder art; no, it wasn't.
- Intellect builds rule all; since the game is so focused on skill checks, and nearly 80% of all available skills are based off Intellect, there's no advantage to playing a Might or Speed character. The remaining 20% of skills can easily be covered by your companions. Most damningly, those skill checks that can only be taken by your main character are 95% Intellect based, focusing on memory, perception, lore, etc.
- borked difficulty: no matter what build you choose for your main character, by the halfway point your party will be able to pass every skill check with at least 90% probability. This kind of design totally trivializes the second half of the game; you can sleepwalk through every check right through the endgame.
- The only remaining challenge lies in the game's sparse combat encounters, most of which can be bypassed with an easy skill check. One of the few combat encounters that cannot be bypassed in this way can be completed without any ill effects by simply pressing "End Turn" over and over again. Your greatest enemy in combat is the interface; you can't hotkey abilities, there's no combat log, and the line-of-sight calculations are... very strange. You can't even set up a formation or move a ranged party member away from the enemy group before you start a battle; your party always starts in a clump right next to the enemies. And there is no setting to make the combat harder or easier; the game has no difficulty options whatsoever.
- still lots of bugs and unpolished features, but no signs of further patches. The Lazaret quest still bugs out when you try to do it peacefully, certain background sounds become louder or quieter as you play until you restart the game, alt-tabbing will randomly cause a blast of audio to burst through your speakers, companion banter will spoil future plot developments (this could have been fixed by changing a single line in a conversation file, but was never addressed), certain choices will be misinterpreted or confused with another choice, etc. etc.
In brief: the game bears the scars of a badly mismanaged development. It still needs a couple of major patches, at least one more balance pass, and ideally an Enhanced Edition. Unfortunately it was also a commercial flop, and the last patch came out 5 months ago. As it stands, I would wait for a bundle sale, which shouldn't be too far off.

TL;DR While not necessarily a bad game by itself, Tides of Numenera utterly fails when measured against its predecessor or comparable isometric RPGs and also has to stand up to its unfulfilled promises.
As a big fan of old school RPGs and having played Baldurs Gate, Icewind Dales, Neverwinter Nights and Planescape Torment, I was incredibly excited about this game. The setting (Numenera by Monte Cook) is fresh and the question about 'What one life matters' is intriguing and promises for a great self reflecting story. While some of this actually makes it into the game, it also proofs to be its biggest challenge.
Setting out as the Castoff shell of an ancient being, the changing god, you crash land on a corner of the Ninth World. While most areas are overall ok (not good or bad...just ok) to explore and are definitely designed with a love for detail, some still feel disconnected and (for those who actually know the source material) not hardly as interesting as they could be. The same must regrettably said about the companions which, while by no means being completely horrible, never really reach the heights or being as memorable as most from the previously mentioned games. This is a shame since the source material actually does have so much more to offer (there isn't a single non human character in the group - in a world with AIs, Trans dimensional/Alien beings and Mutants).
Combat is just plain awful, while not unplayable, it is utterly dull and utterly dissappoints when compared with references such as Pillars of Eternity, Tyranny or Divinity Original Sin (I am not even going to compare it to Original Sin 2). And while one might argue that combat is not supposed to be a main feature of the game, it can easily be countered that someone who roleplays as a more evil or emotionally reactive type of character, certainly does have a LOT of opportunities to pick fights. This creates a problem since Tides of Numenera must allow itself to be measured against similarly kickstarted games which, in case of Divinity Original Sin, managed to put together a significantly better system with a much smaller budget. This goes on top of the fact that inXile, used Pillars of Eternity technology, as the game proudly reminds the players, which means a good part of the engine work had been done for them, where other studios developed things from scratch.
The overarching story disappoints, despite the great outset and overall good writing. Some of the 'surprising' story turns concerning the Changing god or his motivations can be figured out within the first 1-2 hours. Even worse, the initially menacing antagonist ultimately ends up as a wasted potential and remains hardly memorable. Location wise there is a big disconnect between the first and second part of the game and again, given the source material, a lot of wasted potential.
Lastly, the game and its developers must stand up to the broken promises of the kickstarter campaign. While it can be said that it doesn't matter for people who buy the game now, the truth is still that this game is well below the bar that it set itself out to reach. Things such as Numenera crafting (which despite developer arguments would have fit perfectly into this setting - the source material even has rules for it), an additional Major City: Oasis of M'ra Jolios, a
companions and factions have been cut and are not included in the game. Other bits such as the Crystal Dimension, an
(A single slide with a small paragraph) or the vast
appear to have been significantly reduced or reshuffled/recycled in other game bits instead of being fully fleshed out.
At the end of the day (since people often argue in response to the above that 'resources are limited and people gotta make a call') I'd recommend (for real time enthusiasts) Pillars of Eternity and Tyranny or (for turn based strategists) Divinity Original Sin or Divinity Original Sin 2 over this game (I can't help but rub in that DoS 2 is significantly more expansive with full voiceover and had HALF of ToN kickstarter funding).

Old-school CRPG. Good, but has flaws, mostly storytelling-wise. Pick up on sale if interested. Pick up now if craving good-old CRPG fun. No PS:T, but more or less on par with Icewind Dale.
So, let me get something out of the way first. Is it as good as Planescape: Torment? No. No it isn't. I will explain why I find that is after review proper.
Despite Tides of Numenera being touted as a "spiritual successor" to PS:T, and don't get me wrong, it absolutely is, I find it shouldn't be judged while looking back through nostalgia-tinted glasses. So, does it stand on it's own? Well, yes, yes it does. But it's not "the masterpiece", not by a long shot.
Pros:
+ Music is nice
+ Art direction is pretty
+ Companions are interesting
+ Dialogues are well-written
+ Quests don't feel like chores (mostly)
+ Combat mechanics are enjoyable and fit for purpose
+ Actual game mechanics are sensible
Cons:
- Voice-acting is next to nonexistent, and there's a lot of text. I don't mind that much, but I know people do.
- Progression system is needlessly convoluted and at the same time rather shallow. That's one really strange combo.
- Pacing is inconsistent
- Theme is inconsistent
- Overarching story is mediocre
- Endings are underwhelming
First thing you notice is music is rather nice, especially the main theme. Not something I would listen by itself, but complements the rest of the game rather well, so no complaints there at all.
Second thing you notice is graphics is rather colorful. Art direction is rather interesting as well. Granted, it's trying to emulate ye olden CRPG style with it, but it works rather well, I think.
Third thing you notice is voice-acting.... is almost nonexistent. Well, that's a minus, obviously, but I don't mind reading. And literally the next thing bears mentioning is there's a LOT of reading involved.
Dialogues are rather well-written. Companions are... interesting, each has their own quirks, which may or may not play into the grander scheme of things.
There's a distinct lack of straight up fetch and/or "kill 20 rats" quests. Most if not all quests feel at least somewhat meaningful -- obviously some are more so that others.
Combat system is deep enough to keep my attention, but this is not a combat-heavy game, not by a long shot.
Actual mechanics of interacting with environment given a chance of failure are rather sensible.
Progression system I found needlessly convoluted though.
It would seem there's a lot to like here. But it's not all good. I found the story, both writing and execution, rather mediocre.
First of all, pacing is inconsistent. Basically, first two acts work well enough, then second act cuts somewhat abruptly, third act is rushed, and fourth act is basically railroaded. And I will resist the urge to compare this to PS:T, see below.
Secondly, the game is thematically inconsistent. This very page says the theme is "what does one life matter?". This comes up exactly twice throughout the whole game, once in the middle and once at the end. Nowhere else I could see this at play. And again, see below.
Last, but not least, story itself is somewhat... jumpy and underwhelming? There are random plot threads sticking out from time to time, evidently leading nowhere, Character motivations are all over the place. It's just... weird. Some plot threads are planted there at the very beginning, and you can see the "big reveal" almost from the very start, so when it's actually revealed it's presented as this big revelation, and my only reaction was "meh, called it". Other "twists" seemingly come out of nowhere at the last second.
And don't get me started on endings. Basically they amount to being an egotistical jerk, being an indecisive jerk, or being a suicidal jerk. And your actions during the game don't affect what endings are available in a given playthrough, basically the ending is decided via one dialogue at the very end. Underwhelming to say the least. Well, of course there's a bit of an epilogue for side quests, and those don't get decided in one dialogue, but main quest does.
So overall, it's an interesting setting, rather solid game mechanically, and you can tell that inXile tried their best. But it is brought down by inconsistent pacing and overarching story.
I don't regret buying it and sinking about 34 hours into it, but it's definitely not everyone's cup of tea. So do I recommend it? To old-school CRPG fans, yes in general, and definitely on sale. To everyone else... well, it's a tough sell, but I'm leaning to yes. It's not a bad game. Not amazing either, but it's good enough to play through once (or twice if you need something to occupy yourself with)
First thing I'd like to point out is ToN tries to emulate PS:T even when it shouldn't, and sometimes it emulates only form without substance.
For example, I've complained about pacing in ToN. PS:T had the exact same problem: first half of the game is somewhat open, that than shifts gears abruptly to more and more rushed and railroaded experience. Did ToN need to emulate this particular aspect? I don't think so. But it did, and we have what we have now.
When I'm talking about how ToN is thematically inconsistent, PS:T also had a "theme" stated in form of a question. And that question also was asked of the protagonist exactly twice, in the middle and at the end of the game -- almost exactly like in ToN.
But! In PS:T this theme plays in rather early, if implicitly, in form of an implicit answer to the question posed, and that answer is consistent with the setting, and everything comes together beautifully at the end, provided you play your cards right. Gameplay options at the very end are limited by what you did or did not do during the time leading up to that moment.
Compare and contrast with ToN: First, stuff happens. Near the middle we suddenly remember, "oh, right, better ask the question now!". Then more stuff happens. And by the end, you're not even asked the same question again, your previous answer is just reaffirmed. Nowhere else this comes into play.
There was a profound meaning in asking the question twice in PS:T -- your character experienced a lot after being asked the first time, and should have a better grasp on his reality. It should be the same in ToN, in theory. But in practice, execution is abysmal. As I said, form without substance.
There are a lot more superficial similarities, where ToN relies more on evoking feelings of familiarity and nostalgia from PS:T players by emulating form with little regard if it makes sense in context.
It might feel like I'm being too harsh on ToN. I'm trying not to be. But it's rather disheartening to see it failing by trying to emulate PS:T too closely. It might've been a much better game if it didn't have to grow in the shadow of PS:T, frankly.
What I'm trying to say is, ToN lands squarely in the uncanny valley of being too similar to PS:T without actually being PS:T. That's it's primary failing in my opinion. Distancing itself from PS:T somewhat might've helped it flesh out it's own identity.

Let me clarify two things before moving forward with this review:
1) I have not encountered one single bug / glitch throughout the game during my playthrough. Perhaps one thing could be mentioned: Batman occasionally does some strange movements once in the air whilst gliding. But when you stop it and do the gliding again it is fine. So, I have to assume that by the time I played this game WB had patched it properly eliminating all (or most) of the annoying issues.
2) I have not tried multiplayer out, at all. I just didn't care. This franchise is all about the single player experience for me and after completing the story I moved on to other games simply skipping the multiplayer component. So, whether good or bad, I do not know and my review is based on the single player experience.
Additional criticism towards Arkham Origins (beside the handful of glitches) was its incremental nature. So, while Arkham City offered a couple of new things Origins does not do so. Media cited it should have been a more transformative sequel. But why? It prepares Arkham Knight for that - Rocksteady will do that (we already know vehicles have more involvement in the new Batman game), in the meantime, Splash Damage simply picked a working formula and created a game with that.
With that in mind Arkham Origins has one new thing: its story. This is now a prequel so Batman is just after his disappearance (the journey during which he honed his skills) and just started apprehending the bad guys of Gotham. Police, at this point, do not trust him (meanly because they fear him and another reason for that is them being corrupt). Of course, we have Gordon as the outstanding, good, by-the-book guy who can accept Batman (albeit he is making this decision reluctantly). So, it's interesting to be there from the "beginning" and see - for instance - how difficult it is for Batman to cope with Joker (he's quite worked up after their first encounter). I liked the story and I liked the new villains - Black Mask, for instance, or the assassins he hired to kill Batman.
So, in essence, the game offers the same thing, but instead of Arkham we are in Gotham City. This is quite huge (perhaps even bigger than Arkham); there's the usual riddle trophies we can collect and many side missions. Also, there are a lot of cutscenes and one thing I found very interesting: Both Batman's and Joker's voice actor changed, but they do a very good job indeed! You can barely hear the difference (yes, even Mark Hamill's replacement is that good).
I found the game a bit more difficult. You need to act much faster and there's a new enemy type who can counter Barman moves so you need to counter the counter (it makes sense, right?). Some predator challenges can be annoying as if you mess with the bad guys one by one there's always one who grabs a hostage and if he sees you he simply eliminates the victim resulting in a game over. So, even these encounters require a bit more focus.
I do not know about the DLCs (I understand there's one with titled Cold, Cold Heart and it is with Freeze) but the core story is really good and the game offers a long-lasting experience just like its predecessors. Perhaps Origins sticks out a bit; this will be even more alarming probably once Arkham Knight is released; in the meantime, let's just enjoy this installment which I believe is an important part of the franchise and true fans of the series should not skip this one.
UPDATE:
Cold, Cold Heart DLC - The downloadable content pits Batman against Mr Freeze. We have an extra 4-5 hour long single player content that is to be launched separately from the main menu. After completing the introduction section we find ourselves in Gotham once more with "all gadgets available". I guess all gadgets means all you have obtained in the main game. There is no levelling up and only a relatively small section of the city is available as a playable are.
Still, the DLC content offers a new enemy, a new boss battle and exciting cutscenes. I like how Batman faces a frozen Gotham - the snow / ice effect on his cape is brilliant. And of course completing the story still allows us to go back and pick-up the remaining collectibles. This is a good DLC - while for 10 bucks it may be a bit expensive if discounted true Batman fans must get it!

I have only managed to get to Night 4 as of now, but I can say this: Those getting into this game expecting the resource/camera management gameplay that made FNaF popular will be dissapointed. I have heard that there is something like that as an end game bonus, but I don't want to risk spoiling myself to find out.
That said, what you get in this game is pretty good, if not a tad unfair at times. The first three nights do a good job of indicating what you need to do, and the stuff you do on those nights are a good mixture of fun, challenging, and tense. Night 4, however, doesn't do a good job of telling you what you need to do (aside from the primary objective; anything about how to reach that objective is not indicated to you, and it took me a good 3-4 deaths to figure out the pattern).
Sister Location also does a good job of being more story driven than any previous entry. The voice acting is excellent, the writing is a good balance of humor and horror, and the visuals are as horrific as you would expect from a FNaF game.
Overall, the game so far is worth the price tag. Again, those looking for a true FNaF experience, similar to one or two, will have to look elsewhere. But if you're a horror fan looking for a good, cheap game to get for Halloween season, I highly recommend this one, regardless of your familiarity to the FNaF series.

Inmates is described as a Psychological Horror title with Adventure themes and a thought-provoking storyline. Unfortunately, this title starts out promising but quickly declines over the first hour of gameplay (roughly 2-3 hours total to finish it). The environment is creepy, and immersive, but jarring, unspooky jump scares become an interruption instead of a fear motivation. At first, the plot seems to be interwoven with all kinds of Occult and Religious themes, but eventually these elements just seem out of place and seemingly irrelevant to the storyline. I also was unable to run the game any higher than the lowest setting, and it made the shadowy landscape frustrating rather than unnerving. The matches as a source of light were a nice touch but I eventually had so many of them that there was no hesitation use them quickly.
I don’t want to give away too much of the plot, but the dialog present here about Mental Health topics was a disappointing but all-too-common twist on legitimate experiences. It’s essentially a first-person walking simulator in a dank, decrepit building, but Inmates just doesn’t reach its full potential. The voice acting isn’t super strong or bad, but the cut scenes leave a lot to be desired. Still, it’s an ambitious beginning for a single-developer team, and some enhanced optimization, volume/lighting controls, and some more explanation about the story fodder found in the prison would go a long way towards turning my Not Recommended over to Recommended. The price tag is currently too high for the content and the satisfaction level upon completion for me to recommend it.

This is a first-person walking sim where you have to find your way around a seemingly abandoned prison complex searching for clues to trigger cutscenes and reveal the next portion of the game. If you’re familiar with this genre it will hold no surprises for you, it’s pretty standard stuff.
The main feature of the game is that much of the environment is hidden in darkness, but there are boxes of matches festooned all over the place that you can pick up, store in your match inventory and use to illuminate the blackness for ten seconds at a time. I guess this is a variation on the torch you often find in games like this to supposedly create a spooky atmosphere.
There’s a storyline revealed by scraps of paper you find around the place with cryptic handwritten notes on them. I’ll avoid any spoilers but the self-character talks to himself and wonders whether this is a dream or reality. I have to say I did enjoy the ending of the game when the story finale was revealed, it was above average in my experience.
Erm, that pretty much describes the entire game really. It’s short, I would guess it could be speedrun in an hour or two.
I’ve seen what Unreal Engine 4 is capable of, and I’m afraid this is not it. The graphics here are low definition, unimaginative and repetitive. The items you can interact with – apart from the main cutscene-triggering items – are:
a) Endless plain books – mostly bibles, occasional scientific or satanism – which you can’t even open, you just look at the title and put them down again.
b) Scraps of paper with handwritten notes.
c) A small number of assorted random objects that serve no purpose whatsoever.
One example of c) that sticks in my mind was a cube shaped ornament on a side table in a prison cell. I picked it up and wondered what to do with it – was it part of a puzzle? Would I need to keep it with me for later? No, it just existed there for no apparent reason. It might as well have been a frog, a stick of dynamite or a custard trifle. Utterly pointless. It didn’t even look nice. In retrospect I’ve come to the conclusion that the developer must enjoy browsing asset store catalogs and when he sees something that takes his fancy he chucks it into his game somewhere, like a home-made soup containing whatever is in the cupboard, whether it’s appropriate or not. Anyway, this list is not just examples of what’s available, it covers everything in the game. There’s nothing to see here… in many cases quite literally, until you light a match. And then there’s still nothing.
There’s no music, just the usual ‘spooky’ noises droning away in the background, the heavy-breathing of the character, and the odd random jump scare, because why not.
There are three puzzles that I can remember. There may have been a few others so dull that I can’t even remember them, but certainly no more than half a dozen or so. They are all extremely obvious. I did enjoy the one that had to be accomplished in an anti-gravity room, floating around like a spaceman. That’s probably the only memory I’ll take away from this.
Steam
12 achievements – I got 10 of them by completing the game, and I suspect at least one of the others should have popped but didn’t. Too early to say whether or not there will be Trading cards. No Steam Cloud mentioned, and no Linux.

I haven't played Planescape, so the the game was totally new to me. I was looking for a tactical RPG with turn-based combat, something similar to Banner Saga or Blackguards. That's precisely what this game isn't. That, however, definitely doesn't mean this game is bad. I'll go through few main points:
Setting
Game world is incredibly original and unlike pretty much anything I've ever seen before in a computer game. That's both good (fun, original) and bad - unless you invest a lot of time to learn about the world, it will seem very alien and incomprehensible.
Combat
Unlike its competitors which are built around combat, in Tides the battles aren't really fun. Weapons are uninteresting, there aren't many tactical options or combos and the game kinda promotes brute force. Fortunately, it is possible to avoid almost all combat situations, just as I've done.
Quests
Game has many side quests that are definitely worth playing, as they are among the most memorable I've seen. Just like the game world, though, you need to be prepared to invest a lot of time to really enjoy them. Looking back at the game, I'd say the Ghostly Woman quest was the best one.
Graphics
Tides just are not about graphics. This fact has one big advantage in that you can run the game even with a low-end graphics card (I don't even have a dedicated graphics card). On the other hand particularly the character graphics are really bad. On most NPCs you can't even tell if it is a man or woman, which is worse than even Icewind Dale all those years ago. It's a shame, because the game has countless very well written characters and horrible graphics just put them down. Fortunately, the areas are beautiful and you will sometimes find yourself walking around the map, trying to remove fog-of-war from every corner so that you can enjoy every little hand-drawn detail.
Character creation & leveling
First thing that struck me was rather simple character creation. I couldn't even alter my character's appearance. While this matters little to me, I guess many players will take that as a big minus. I also missed the good RPG feeling as in "I want to achieve that particular ability, so that my character can be far more powerful or will be able to use a particular combo etc." Here character leveling is not something you look forward to.
Overall
This game was something totally different from what I expected, but I still enjoyed it a lot. That's why I'm recommending it, but I definitely suggest you read many more reviews first, so that you can get a good idea what to expect.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is the thematic successor to Planescape: Torment, one of the most critically acclaimed role-playing games of all time. Immerse yourself in a single-player, isometric, story-driven RPG set in Monte Cook’s Numenera universe. What does one life matter? Find your answer.
Tides of Numenera is an old school RPG in the likes of Baldur's Gate or, wait for it, Planescape Torment. For the fans of the genre it has some nice things to offer, but it also can be a little rough around the edges. And that's easy to see. Literally. The graphics are serviceable, and that's all. ToN uses the same engine technology that powers Pillars of Eternity, but PoE looks much better.
Then the game mechanics. Numenera does some things differently and/or calls some things differently and that can be confusing if you're not paying attention. And it might not be easy to pay attention as there is a lot of reading. And I do mean a lot. The story is interesting enough to keep you playing, but the obscureness of some sidequests can be annoying. It's so oldschool that you really need to be very thorough and click on everything or consult a walkthrough to do some quests.
Now, it's not all bad. There are a few things that this new Torment does very well, like the fact that you can avoid most fights by talking your way out. The fights, when you can't or don't avoid them, are turn based. Each turn you can one move action and one attack action, you can also use one of many skills/spells (here called cyphers) which cost you one attack or move action. Whether in or out of combat your companions are very well written, they are quite witty and it's a pleasure listening and talking to them. The story can suck you in (even if the endings are kinda lacking). All in all Torment Tides of Numenera is mechanically ok-ish story wise interesting addition to roleplaying genre. It's not a great game, but I had decent amounts of fun in my almost 30hrs with the game.
I liked:

Get this if:
* you'd like to play a solid(ish) oldskool isometric rpg
* you like reading
Don't get this if:
* you'd like pretty graphics or visual character customization
* you don't like to read

I love Monte Cook's work, I love Planescape, and I loved Planescape: Torment. So why did this one not hook me? I didn't want to give this a thumbs down, because it isn't a bad game, but I cannot recommend it to people who would agree with my first sentence and want to buy this title based on that alone.
First off, the world. Numenera is a weird place. Planescape is also weird, but at least in that game, the denizens of the City of Doors belong there. They are just as weird as their setting, and just as dangerous. Most importantly, this includes your companions. In Numenera, however, *no one* belongs. You're an alien, a trespasser on your own homeworld. Your companions are (at least superficially) just as out of place, and that hindered my ability to ever feel anchored to the world. I never felt like I was supposed to be there.
Second, the combat. While it's true that you can play a significant amount of this game without ever making an attack (and I really dig that), the few times I was forced to draw weapons was when the game literally fell apart. I mean serious save game-breaking bugs. Failures to initiate combat, failures to end combat, failures to advance turns, failures to recognize range or movement restrictions, etc etc etc. I had to start playing as a more diplomatic character simply because getting into battle was an almost surefire way for my game to come to a grinding halt.
Third, flow and direction. There is a LOT of narrative going on here and much of it feels... unnecessary. Words are really the only way Tides of Numenera can convey what's happening (there are no cutscenes or robust character animations), and those words break down and turn into nonsense pretty frequently. Particularly when an alien device behaves in a way that defies logic and physics, defies how we understand the universe to be. Plus I straight up got lost multiple times trying to figure out just how to advance the main story. What was relevant? What was not? I had no idea.
The game's definitely interesting with a lot of cool ideas, but missed the mark pretty severly when claiming to be the thematic successor to Planescape: Torment. Don't buy it for that reason alone.

THIS IS A REVIEW IN PROGRESS.
Planescape: Torment is one of my favorite PC games, ever, And this game takes that setting and really runs with it. You play as a fallen hero with no memory, kind of predictable, but you get over it, fast. It takes place in a world so far into the future of Earth that uncountable societies have risen and fallen, history is lost, and you can't tell what is magic and what is technology. Like most isometric RPGs, there is a lot of reading to get the story, but that is just part of the experience. All of the recruitable characters have their own goals which you can help with or completely ignore. And each party member brings something new to the combat.
Speaking of combat, you don't need to fight. You can talk your way out of most battles. Which is a good twist on the formula.

Fantastic RPG. The writing was excellent and Monte Cook's science-fantasy Numenera setting made for an interesting diversion from the standard tropes.
While I love the old Infinity-engine style RPGs, with their fiddly ports of tabletop rules, the simplified skill and combat system in Torment made for a nice change as well. It was crunchy enough to have interesting character development choices, but I felt like I could make quick choices about the playstyle I found interesting without having guess or do a lot of mental arithmetic (I found this annoying in Pillars of Eternity -- less so in the old D&D ports, since that's long been comitted to memory).
Most of the conflicts in the game could be resolved without combat -- while you can often jump in with guns (or whatever) blazing, it is often more interesting to explore some of the clever conversation options (or good skill use). This also reveals more layers of backstory for situations and characters (and there is an absurd amount of content to discover).
I'm about 80% through the main storyline at this point and will likely try an alternate playthrough next.

Mad Max is the first video game introduced into the franchise and serves as a prequel to the Mad Max: Fury Road film that released in theatres back in 2015.  This game was made to introduce the iconic anti-hero to a new generation of moviegoers after his long cinema hiatus.
Moreover, it is a game that proves not all video game tie-ins should be avoided.  It is a solid game packed with high-octane fun that serves the franchise well and will hold your interest until the ending credits roll.
The combat, which is a large portion of the game, is fast paced and gets the adrenaline pumping.  As Max delivers jaw busting blows to his enemies you can’t help but feel his every hit. The hand-to-hand combat mechanics are reminiscent of the Batman Arkham series. That is, it’s a mixture of free-flow combat and quick-time events.

However, what sets Mad Max’s combat apart from other titles is the sheer brutality in which Max dispatches is foes.  Every punch, stab and counter fuels his rage meter, and once it is full, enemies beware.  His attacks become more brutal and other combat options open up making you feel like an unstoppable force.  Watching Max destroy his enemies in such a brutal fashion felt very rewarding to me and I had to stop and remember to breathe after every encounter.
Upgrades can be purchased in the game using scrap that can be obtained by completing missions and scavenging at designated points dotted throughout the game world.  Equipping said upgrades to Max and his steel steed make him all that more deadly to hostile waste landers and warlords.

As great as game this is, it does have some things in it that make it far less than perfect.  One of my major gripes is its receptiveness, most enemy strongholds are captured in the same way and upgrading your ally strongholds all feels like it was done before.  It is an unfortunate aspect make the gameplay feel stagnant after a few hours of playing through it and it mostly serves as a means to artificially extend the games length.
Another issue I ran into was the day/night cycle in the game. The cycle felt a little too long and time could not be manipulated by the player.  This may not seem like a big issue until some missions require it to be a certain time of day to start.
My final issue is the game’s ending.  It did leave me with a sense of having wanted more from the conclusion and did not seem very rewarding considering the amount of hours I put into it.
In the end, I did enjoy this game a lot and it was a steal as I had bought it during a sale.  It is a one-time roller-coaster ride that delivers with solid gameplay and impressive voice work.  I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the Road Warrior franchise, or someone who is new to the franchise and wants to be introduced into the world of Max.

Let me clarify two things before moving forward with this review:
1) I have not encountered one single bug / glitch throughout the game during my playthrough. Perhaps one thing could be mentioned: Batman occasionally does some strange movements once in the air whilst gliding. But when you stop it and do the gliding again it is fine. So, I have to assume that by the time I played this game WB had patched it properly eliminating all (or most) of the annoying issues.
2) I have not tried multiplayer out, at all. I just didn't care. This franchise is all about the single player experience for me and after completing the story I moved on to other games simply skipping the multiplayer component. So, whether good or bad, I do not know and my review is based on the single player experience.
Additional criticism towards Arkham Origins (beside the handful of glitches) was its incremental nature. So, while Arkham City offered a couple of new things Origins does not do so. Media cited it should have been a more transformative sequel. But why? It prepares Arkham Knight for that - Rocksteady will do that (we already know vehicles have more involvement in the new Batman game), in the meantime, Splash Damage simply picked a working formula and created a game with that.
With that in mind Arkham Origins has one new thing: its story. This is now a prequel so Batman is just after his disappearance (the journey during which he honed his skills) and just started apprehending the bad guys of Gotham. Police, at this point, do not trust him (meanly because they fear him and another reason for that is them being corrupt). Of course, we have Gordon as the outstanding, good, by-the-book guy who can accept Batman (albeit he is making this decision reluctantly). So, it's interesting to be there from the "beginning" and see - for instance - how difficult it is for Batman to cope with Joker (he's quite worked up after their first encounter). I liked the story and I liked the new villains - Black Mask, for instance, or the assassins he hired to kill Batman.
So, in essence, the game offers the same thing, but instead of Arkham we are in Gotham City. This is quite huge (perhaps even bigger than Arkham); there's the usual riddle trophies we can collect and many side missions. Also, there are a lot of cutscenes and one thing I found very interesting: Both Batman's and Joker's voice actor changed, but they do a very good job indeed! You can barely hear the difference (yes, even Mark Hamill's replacement is that good).
I found the game a bit more difficult. You need to act much faster and there's a new enemy type who can counter Barman moves so you need to counter the counter (it makes sense, right?). Some predator challenges can be annoying as if you mess with the bad guys one by one there's always one who grabs a hostage and if he sees you he simply eliminates the victim resulting in a game over. So, even these encounters require a bit more focus.
I do not know about the DLCs (I understand there's one with titled Cold, Cold Heart and it is with Freeze) but the core story is really good and the game offers a long-lasting experience just like its predecessors. Perhaps Origins sticks out a bit; this will be even more alarming probably once Arkham Knight is released; in the meantime, let's just enjoy this installment which I believe is an important part of the franchise and true fans of the series should not skip this one.
UPDATE:
Cold, Cold Heart DLC - The downloadable content pits Batman against Mr Freeze. We have an extra 4-5 hour long single player content that is to be launched separately from the main menu. After completing the introduction section we find ourselves in Gotham once more with "all gadgets available". I guess all gadgets means all you have obtained in the main game. There is no levelling up and only a relatively small section of the city is available as a playable are.
Still, the DLC content offers a new enemy, a new boss battle and exciting cutscenes. I like how Batman faces a frozen Gotham - the snow / ice effect on his cape is brilliant. And of course completing the story still allows us to go back and pick-up the remaining collectibles. This is a good DLC - while for 10 bucks it may be a bit expensive if discounted true Batman fans must get it!

I recommend getting this game, but only for a cheap price. I loved Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, and I was excited to get Origins. I bought it off of Amazon during their black friday sale for $20, a month after the game's release. There are 6 major assasins wanting to kill batman for 50 million dollars. The gameplay from Arkham city, is largely similar; you glide around the city stopping crimes in progress, beating up criminals, and sneaking by guys with guns. One welcome addition to this game is fast travel. However, you must unlock fast travel points before you can fast travel to a location. The boss fights, are POORLY designed.
*Spoilers*
-Electrocutioner, literally goes down after one punch. I thought, "hmm, maybe you fight him again later, since he's talking about fighting Batman and wanting to take him down so much." Nope, he ends up getting shot in the chest and you take his gear off his dead body.
-Fighting Deathstroke, was extremely anti-climactic and just flat-out poorly designed. The trailer shows and epic hand-to-hand fight between Deathstroke and Batman; the actual fight is as followed: Hit Deathstroke 3-5 times, evade explosive barrels, repeat. After about 1/2 of his health is gone, he'll begin using his staff more and this is where the game decides to get really cheap. You have to time your strikes very carefully and evade constantly. If you mess up your timing, you have no choice but to take a flurry of unblockable/unevadable hits. Your only option is to evade and use the batclaw slam to get through this annoying boss fight.
-Firefly. You chase him around on the bridge and on several occasions, you have to run/jump through fire. There is no way to beat him unscathed, so if you took a lot of damage right before a checkpoint and die, you are pretty much screwed.
*End Spoilers*
Overall, what could have been an amazing game, turned out to be a mediocre disappoint. 5/10. If you have an Xbox 360 or PS3, rent the game for a weekend or two, or buy it when the price drops down to about $5.

"
And so ends
The Line. But what did it all mean? Well, I don’t ﬁnd that a particularly interesting question. Many people think
The Line is about how horrible war is, or how horrible military shooters are. I don’t think that is so. For me, The Line isn’t about statements or answers, but about questions.
Its theme is not one of criticising the military shooter, but simply critiquing it, asking questions about its nature. What is actually going on in these games that some of us play with reckless abandon, and which some of us dismiss outright? What do these games contribute to a broader culture of disassociated violence and dehumanised others? What does it mean that as these games increasingly depict war with more realism, reality itself increasingly begins to look like a videogame?Tese are not the questions that The Line answers; they are the questions that The Line left me with. Trough my complicity in Walker’s descent into madness, I learned things about myself. Once I stood before Andrew Ryan in Bioshock and realised I had never before made a choice in a videogame, and absolved myself of all my sins. Now, I stood before my own reﬂection and realised that just because I had no choice, that didn’t mean I had no responsibility over my actions. My sins are my own. Maybe it seems like a copout to conclude 50,000 words with “it’s complicated,” but war, violence, videogames, humanity, everything truly is complex. And that is the beauty of The Line: it is complicated. Too many games—not to mention other media forms, critics, journalists, politicians, everybody and everything—want to ﬁnd the nice and easy dichotomies. The good and the evil. The human and the other. The start and the end. The right and the wrong. The Line stubbornly refuses such dichotomies. There is good and evil in everyone. Every start is an ending, and every ending is a start. Every human is monstrous. Every right is a wrong.
The Line refuses to give us a simple answer. Instead, it embraces contradictions to expose just how fraudulent simple answers are.
"

Torment: Tides of Numenera feels like it really wants to prove something, but fails to deliver in almost every way.
Story
The title, though refering to a great classic, the original Planescape: Torment, has nothing to do with that unique game. The only torment here is that of the player having to sit through all the pointless, uninspired, extremely bloated dialogue, terrible, boring and basically broken combat, all set in a world where everything is 'super unique', but does not make any sense. The great potential of the setting has been ruined by a medicore story with no real premise. The side quests feel like they were all done by different people and usually have no meaningfull connection to the main storyline. The writing in general feels like reading a cheap fantasy magazine where you can find stories written by junior high students. The game has tons of text, but it just doesn't make much sense and is simply amature, leaving the impression that the developers wanted a lot of words, because Planescape had a lot of words, but forgot about making it meaningful storywise. In my opinion the game fails at being a good RPG for those reasons alone, but there is more...
Graphics
The graphics look like they were developed in 2005 at best. The art style fails to convey the feeling of the world. And finally, the animations simply look funny. Loading times are very long, even on SSD drives, which is hilarious considering how the game looks and runs.
Music and sound
Just like almost everything about the game, the music feels uninspired and bland, but fortunately, it's bearable. On the other hand, the ambient sound and sound effects will make you see red just after a few hours into the game. At a point I had to tun off the sound completely because it was so unbearably loud and annoying.
Inference
The game is bad in every aspect. There are many mechanics that feel unfinished or pointless. The graphics are bad. The sound is terrible and the story is a disgrace to the original Planescape. In one word - this game truly is TORMENT.

I had to cut this review down in order to fit Steam guidelines. You can find the full text here: pastebin dot com /d7WpDW4H
Bottom line: Torment: Tides of Numenera (TToN) is a flawed game, just like Planescape: Torment (PT), but it is a mostly rewarding story. If you are a fan of atmospheric RPGs, cRPGs, or the Numenera setting, I don't think you will be disappointed in the overall experience. I enjoyed TToN, but I cannot say that it delivered everything I hoped for, and the resolution to the game felt lacking. TToN requires a lot of reading. If you don't like reading, TToN is not the game for you.
Why are Steam reviews so mixed? TToN was Kickstarted. It had a lot of content changed, remixed, or outright removed from the initial Kickstarter pitch. That made a lot of people angry, hence the negative reviews. I was one of the Kickstarter backers, but I played the game for the first time almost a year after it was officially released. The original release contained a lot of bugs and issues which are common of cRPGs. Several bug fixes and a content patch later, TToN is a far more polished, balanced game. It's far from perfect though.
STORY AND SETTING
The setting in TToN is put to excellent use. The world of Numenera is imaginative, weird, sometimes bizarre, and filled with things to see, do, and learn. The Bloom gets a special mention here because it's a really cool place/being, something that fits both PT and TToN: The Bloom is a giant, living creature that some call home. It is both a place, an intelligence, and a gateway to many other worlds. It's the Sigil of TToN, a peculiar quagmire of concepts and worlds, and it just works. Suffice to say, the setting and world building is strong in TToN.
The writing in TToN is also good, but I seldom found it great. The Twisted Metal Merecaster is an exception, and it is by far my favorite bit of writing in the game. I can't say the same about the companions. TToN companions are decent, overall, but lacking in some aspects. PT had you start out with two great companions: Morte and Dak'kon. You wanted to keep those two in your party to discover their individual stories because of how closely these stories associated with the Nameless One. You could always ditch them if you didn't care. Callistege and Aligern appear at the beginning of TToN, and neither character is bad or poorly characterized. They just happen to be there by complete happenstance and are not connected to the Last Castoff in any meaningful way; moreover, you can't bring them both along. You have to choose, and neither really brings anything special to the overarching narrative. The two characters that I consider mandatory for a playthrough are both optional: Matkina and Rhin. Former more than the latter, but I really like Rhin. Not to mention that all of the companions in TToN are human, aside from Oom. This is odd, given the setting and some of the NPCs you encounter: mutants, sentient monsters, nanoclouds, visitants, etc.
Personal torment was at the center of PT. It was about the Nameless One's journey to root out his hidden adversary and regain his mortality. TToN is not about personal torment. It is about a broader, more conceptual theme of what qualifies as individual existence, family, and even love. I don't think this is as emotionally gripping as it could be, not as relatable. The player is given a lot of choice in how to respond to the events taking place in TToN, but I am not sure if the player is placed at the heart of the conflict, where they form an emotional connection with, a stake in, the final outcome. I also found the ending to be lacking, partly because it was full of exposition, partly because I was not satisfied with how it was handled and the choices given. I was particularly disappointed with the final encounter with the Sorrow.
MECHANICS
TToN uses an odd system for skill checks: Checks are percentage-based, but you can invest effort from stat pools in order to increase your chance of success. You can also use your companions for most checks. The narrative doesn't differentiate when you do that, so it ends up sort of strange when you're trying to climb a wall and have someone else do the skill check--to have you scamper up the wall. Quite odd. This is not my preference as far as skill checking goes, but I suppose TToN does an alright job with what it had to work with, though in the latter game this is trivial because you learn to max the important stats. Intelligence is the most important stat this time around, like Wisdom in PT, and mind reading is highly encouraged. Unfortunetly, there are only three Foci, which grant additional character abilities and customization, considering far more were promised initially.
Tides handle character alignment, and I feel they are well implemented. Considering that most cRPGs place a character in the good and evil alignment spectrum, the Tides present something different. The vast majority of the dialog choices in TToN increase your Tides, which in turn influences the legacy you leave behind. Tides don't work in combat, but can influence social situations and interplay with the game's story.
Speaking of combat, it's love it or hate it. PT had really bad combat, almost an afterthought, and TToN actively tries to remedy that by making combat almost entirely optional and introducing it only when it's relevant. There's no monster thumping in TToN. Combat doesn't really involve just killing everyone else, though that's usually an option, as there are alternatives on how to handle a tense situation. I found the combat, when it did happen, to be relatively fun. I do wish there were more options for some well-developed dungeon-crawling, with traps, fearsome enemies, and you get the idea. As it is, you spend the game honing your group's combat skills, but you have to actively encourage violence to participate in it.
One really cool thing that I absolutely adore about TToN is that death doesn't usually mean a game over. When the Last Castoff dies, which you have to do in order to finish some quests, he or she is transported to the Castoff Labyrinth (the Calm), a sort of psychic construct dimension. The problem is that the Calm itself is underused. During the Kickstarter campaign, the Calm was pitched as a major area of the game with its own set of rules and NPCs to interact with. A place that would grow during the course of the game and allow new insights on the Ninth World. While the Calm still serves this function to an extent, and is more important than it first appears, it is not fleshed out enough.
MISC COMMENTS
Something that stands out to me is the lack of narration and voiced dialog in TToN. Early on, after the Kickstarter pitch, important NPCs were to have recorded, voiced dialog lines. This makes sense to me, and there are several plot-important characters in the game worthy of voiced dialog. The final game only voices the companions. Not even the main antagonist, the very thing the Last Castoff is desperately trying to escape, is voiced. Comparing that to Tony Jay's excellent performance as the Transcendent One in PT, and you can probably reason out why I am disappointed.
CONCLUSION
TToN is a larger experience than PT, one with more reactivity, choice, and technical savvy. And it's also a game with some bits of really great writing. But TToN does not surpass the original thematically, which is a shame, and suffers from a few fundamental storytelling faults that keep it from reaching its full potential. I will recommend it, but maybe wait on the vain hope that it gets a director's cut edition, like Wasteland 2, for a fuller, richer experience.

If you know what to expect, this is an absolutely amazing, uniquely original, and thoroughly rewarding game. If you’re expecting nail-biting combat, labyrinthian skill trees, oodles of loot, and a robust class system…this is not the game for you. However, if you’re after detailed and rich storytelling, complex characters, and an immersive and unexpected world that demands your focus and attention, then look no further.
In some ways, I was fortunate in coming to this game late, as it gave me a chance to read lots of reviews and reactions. I can definitely understand how it may have been mis-marketed early on, setting up some false expectations, but I think enough time has passed that the game can be understood and judged for what is now, rather than for what people were expecting it to be.
Furthermore, I was actually drawn to this game specifically due to some of the things that others have complained about. Chiefly: the insane amount of text (serious, this makes War and Peace look like a pamphlet), and the lack of combat. In short, this game offers an alternate take on what an RPG can be, and that’s exactly what I was looking for.
Still, there are pros and cons. Other reviews here have done a better job of this, but here are some that stand out for me.
I really like how combat is handled. An encounter is called a “crisis”, and there are multiple ways to resolve it that don’t require fighting. Essentially, based on how you want to play the game and types of characters you build, you can choose to either take a social approach (lie, bribe, intimidate, etc), a mechanical approach (lore, repair, manipulating things), or the old standby of fighting. This gave me more choices as to how I wanted to play a scenario, based on how I was feeling at that time, and it also gives the game more replayability. My first play through (based on someone else’s advice) focused on the social skills (I basically lied my way through most encounters, which was great), but now I’m curious to go through again with a different focus. And, as I said, it’s nice to take a break from hack-n-slash once in a while. The flipside is that each crisis, no matter what approach you take, is unfairly stacked against you. Things usually go terribly wrong (you’re always outnumbered, never have enough supplies, and AI is irritating). You will die a lot, but that’s actually the point. Much like Planescape, death is merely a gateway to another realm, with it’s own set of quests and characters and things to do, and then you can easily re-enter the world of the living and try again (note that there are a few deaths which are permanent, so saving frequently is still a good idea).
The other criticism of combat is true: there isn’t much of it. For a game of this length, there are probably no more than a dozen crisis encounters. Maybe that’s an exaggeration, but combat was very, very, very few and far between. However, each crisis is a major event, so they make up for frequency with complexity. Some of the encounters can require a long-haul commitment and take quite a while to get through, so that also makes up for the lack of numbers.
Now, if the lack of combat is a turn off for you, then it’s best to give the game a pass. However, in my opinion, it more than makes up for the reduced role that fighting takes, by expanding on some of the other things that role playing can offer. Things like story, character building, choices, exploration, interactions, are all extremely rich, detailed and rewarding.
And I suppose that’s where the other justified criticism comes in. All of the aforementioned role playing elements are almost entirely text based. Yes this is a modern game with visuals, sounds, and UI…but the heart is un-abashedly old-school text. Seriously, reams and reams of it. However, the writing is, with few exceptions, fantastic. And sometimes, the images conjured in my imagination are more powerful than anything a visual could render. The scenes, descriptions, ideas, dialog and details are simply mesmerizing. This is a thoroughly constructed and very deep world. It is worth every syllable.
You do run into some hammy lines now and then, but considering the sheer volume of text, a few throw-away phrases hardly dent the epicness of the whole. I can’t stress enough just how rich and imaginative this game is. There are enough ideas in here for a hundred games, if not more. Some are fanciful, others disturbing, and yet others quite profound.  Ultimately whatever you do think of the game, there are many ideas and images in here that will stay with you for a very long time. Maybe haunt is the better word. This is also true to the mood of the game, as it is just as cruel as it is verbose. This is a painful, spiteful, gruesome, and utterly disgusting world that you are inhabiting. Nothing turns out well, for anyone, ever. But it’s also insatiably riveting.
The only other complain that I might add, which isn’t a bad thing depending on your viewpoint, is that items and trade are rather disappointing. There is finite number of items in the this game, and finite number of merchants who have a finite amount of money. Maybe I’m just spoiled by games where looting is a reward, and trading is a skill. Not so here. If you get carried away and use up all the healing potions, life will suck for you, as there are no more. And the merchants are dirt poor, so you’re never going to get rich, which is fine as there’s nothing of interest to buy anyway. The most coveted objects in the entire game world are the Numenera themselves. These are basically single purpose objects that can do amazing, deadly, or powerful things in combat and beyond. And the whole Numenera system is really cool and well executed in the game…BUT there are just so darn few of them in the world that I wound up hoarding them, rather than using them, because I wasn’t sure I’d ever find more. As for the weapons, there’s almost zero point in trying to upgrade. The difference it makes in a crisis is minimal, and there just aren’t many options to choose from. Not to say there aren’t surprises, the Merecasters are fun, for example. When activated they essentially launch you immediately into a mini side quest, a sort of choose-your-own-adventure. Depending on how you do, you might gain a bonus or something from them, plus they’re a nice departure from the main narrative.
Despite any minor flaws, I definitely recommend this game to anyone looking to try something that’s beyond the rote RPG. It’s very rare for me to want another playthrough of a game. But I do have to honestly say that I will revisit Torment in the future, and I wish there were more like it. Imagination will always be more powerful than spectacle.

TL;DR :
O jogo é uma mistura de conceitos de x-com com DOTA. Assim é um jogo de batalha por turno com criaturas chamadas de imortais, que possuem 6 habilidades e 2 ultimates que podem ser utilizados consumindo uma unidade de tempo.
Cada turno você possui X unidades de tempo para usar com cada unidade, assim você precisa derrotar outros inimigos para cumprir algum objetivo.
Análise:
Pontos Positivos:
* Todos diálogos do jogo apresentam as vozes dos personagens.
* Mistura de conceitos, o que torna este jogo bem único.
* Me pareceu relativamente rica a possibilidade da customização do seu immortal.
* Possibilidade de multi-player, o que torna o jogo bem mais competitivo.
* Diversos elementos de RPG e DOTA.
Pontos Negativos:
* A parte visual do jogo é bem simples.
* Número baixo de immortals, além de poucos que são de graça.
* Os items apresentarem sprites muito semelhantes.

The origins of this game, whether they are true or not, certainly ring true after having played the game. The reason being, this game handles as if it was designed in the early days of platforming, when game creators hadn't quite gotten the hang of how things should handle.
The movement of your character isn't abysmal, but using the jetpack is far from the joy it is in the previous (or...  later?) Dark Void game.  You can hold the jump button down to rocket, which is OK for going up, but the delay makes coming down tricky to control, or you double tap, which is probably the preferred method but has some weird quirks, like a slight bob that makes aiming while hovering trickier than it should be.  The controls overall feel oddly unresponsive. This combines with moving, which re-adjusts your aim, making you have to do a lot of fiddly jiggering to really point the way you want.  All the while, getting blasted by aliens.  This could have been fine if it were a dual stick shooter instead, but the way it is makes dodging and firing a real chore if you want to be safe.
And you do want to be safe.  Because if you take a lot of damage, you WILL have a "low health" alert.  That goes on and on.  And is annoying.  This just adds to the likelyhood that this game really was created in the 80s.
The entire first level consists of collect keycard, open next door, collect another keycard, which is OK, but again, makes it feel dated.  I got to the first boss, and promptly lost all my lives.  And yes, since this is claiming to be an arcade game, having lives makes sense, but it feels just like worthless punishment here.
For a bonus, while it's not the WORST music, it sounds like Mega Man cast-offs to me, uninspiring stuff that didn't make the cut for their better tracks.
I guess for me, they either really found this game and decided to do absolutely no modernization, or they concocted a story meant to play on nostalgia and went out of their way to make it play poorly.  I really hope it's the first, which is forgivable.  The thing about nostalgia is that, people would have had to play the game before now to have nostalgia for it.  Either way, poor mechanics without the memories to back them up are a disappointment, and make this game overall not worth it to me.

Unlike some games where you can choose to be stealthy or go full commando, if you get caught pulling out a gun by several guards you'll get mowed down in a second.
However this game definitely has graphical issues. DX12 is really buggy. It crashes quite often and even 100% of the time when stepping into the military area in Marrakesh (Episode 3). The only solution seems to be switching to DX11 and while I haven't experienced any issues with it, many people seem to have buggy lighting in DX11. At this point I'm wondering if IO will ever fix it because people have been reporting these bugs for months now.
Despite the issues, the game is still incredibly fun. I'm really looking forward to the other episodes and, hopefully, a 2017 season for this game. Hitman is a strong contender for my game of the year.

Edmund McMillen is a freaking genius, Part 1.
Stunningly brilliant retro-styled painfully hard platformer, SMB is one of those gems to come from the wonderfully wacky mind of Edmund McMillen (and co-conspirator of Team Meat, Tommy Refenes). Based on the original flash prototype that you can find on Newgrounds/Kongregate and in
, the improvements made to the game and the game engine are what truly elevates this game from un-Super to Super.
The level design is rather well made, and you have to be microscopic-precise to clear a lot of levels. Really easy to follow and rather straightforward. Figuring out how to complete the level is chicken feed - actually completing it is, more often than not, a different story.
You need a decent gaming rig, though - some of the later stages with tons and tons of saws really lags my computer hard, I did find it hard to complete those. Not to mention I get a few annoying crashes in the middle of my playing, but that's probably because a) crap computer and b) I keep alt-tabbing out to check other stuff.
There
a way to hack the command line option to lower the detail so it does not lag so much, though...
This game has also made me consider buying a gaming controller. The warnings given at the start of the game ring true - even with a keyboard, I periodically stress out my left hand playing this.
Finally, wanting to complete all the levels with A+ and all bandages before proceeding to the next stage has brought out the inner OCD freak in me. I love the sense of satisfaction derived from the success of completing the level with a pixel-perfect run, after dozens upon dozens of abject failures.
Steam Sale or trade for a bundle key. Worth full price, though. Support indie developers today!
