"
And so ends
The Line. But what did it all mean? Well, I don’t ﬁnd that a particularly interesting question. Many people think
The Line is about how horrible war is, or how horrible military shooters are. I don’t think that is so. For me, The Line isn’t about statements or answers, but about questions.
Its theme is not one of criticising the military shooter, but simply critiquing it, asking questions about its nature. What is actually going on in these games that some of us play with reckless abandon, and which some of us dismiss outright? What do these games contribute to a broader culture of disassociated violence and dehumanised others? What does it mean that as these games increasingly depict war with more realism, reality itself increasingly begins to look like a videogame?Tese are not the questions that The Line answers; they are the questions that The Line left me with. Trough my complicity in Walker’s descent into madness, I learned things about myself. Once I stood before Andrew Ryan in Bioshock and realised I had never before made a choice in a videogame, and absolved myself of all my sins. Now, I stood before my own reﬂection and realised that just because I had no choice, that didn’t mean I had no responsibility over my actions. My sins are my own. Maybe it seems like a copout to conclude 50,000 words with “it’s complicated,” but war, violence, videogames, humanity, everything truly is complex. And that is the beauty of The Line: it is complicated. Too many games—not to mention other media forms, critics, journalists, politicians, everybody and everything—want to ﬁnd the nice and easy dichotomies. The good and the evil. The human and the other. The start and the end. The right and the wrong. The Line stubbornly refuses such dichotomies. There is good and evil in everyone. Every start is an ending, and every ending is a start. Every human is monstrous. Every right is a wrong.
The Line refuses to give us a simple answer. Instead, it embraces contradictions to expose just how fraudulent simple answers are.
"
- Brendan Keogh: Killing is Harmless

This is a very generic (though competent) 3rd person cover shooter (with very, very basic squad mechanics) with a striking story. Especially the ending will probably keep you thinking for a while (and/or make you watch Youtube videos about the (multiple!) endings). The graphics and sound are also quite awesome and support the setting in the middle of the desert. Also all the hidden "intelligence" pickups in this game are actually worth it, as they are all voice acted, interesting and fit into the story.
My main problem with this game is that in between the iconic story moments of the game, the generic shooter part can become quite boring. Shoot at enemies, stay in cover until health regenerates, repeat until everyone his dead, proceed to next cover or segment of the game, repeat. There are some badass moments but also a lot of dull moments. At some point in the middle of the game I just wanted to finish the game to finally delete it. But the ending is really worth it! If they had put this story on a good shooter, that would have been one of the best shooters out there. And the fact that ammo is actually scarce, you have to switch weapons regularly and that all weapons are useful in one situation or the other distinguishes this game at least a bit gameplay-wise from other cover shooters.
If you crank up the difficulty the game will be quite challenging as you are not able to take many hits (enemies will still die after 1 (most enemies) or 2 headshots). And there is also a coop mode which makes every game better. ;)
But who the **** came up with these heavies? That was the worst design decision of the game. These are some heavy armored enemies, that take WAY too many hits to kill. Like I said before, all the the other enemies in this game die after at least 2 headshots but this guy takes several grenades and/or 10-40 (depending on your weapon) headhots while shooting at you with an LMG or shotgun. I know that he has a very tough armor and therefore moves very slowly but this enemy just don't fit into the game and is just annoying as an enemy. Also his visor cracks after the first headshots but you still need many more headshots RIGHT INTO HIS FACE before killing him...
Anyway, after finishing the game I would definitely recommend this game if you can get it cheap (it's only ~6 hours of gameplay on the highest difficulty (so with quite a few deaths)). The story is worth it but nevertheless, the game is quite short and I see no replay value as the story (any maybe the coop mode, which I did not play) is the only thing that keeps you playing.

Full disclosure, I bought this game because I'm gay and it's gay, and sometimes that's enough to get me to buy something.
What do I think of it though? It's cute, and the first playthrough is fun, but it's definitely not a masterpiece. I like the character creator, but I don't like that your dadsona is almost always gonna look silly. It was fun making my idea of a male version of myself named Oscar Byron (after my faves Oscar Wilde and Lord Byron) but on subsequent playthroughs when I was playing around with it more, my new dads just looked cartoon-y, which feels off considering that the other characters look really nice.
The story's cute, and on my first playthrough, I went on all the dad's first two dates (you have to commit on the third) and I felt like I got a good length out of it. The rest of my playthroughs though, were REALLY short. I made new dads for each of them, and each run through my date's storyline took maybe half an hour? I also ended up fast-forwarding through a lot of the scenes since I didn't feel like watching the same story bits five times in a row, especially since the story outside of the dates can get pretty old.
The minigames are probably the biggest negative aspect of the game. Can you win in the psuedo-pokemon daughter battle against Brian? Probably not, but the game makes you think you can win. Brian's golf minigame is also garbage, and honestly I don't think I can ever do his full track because it's all minigames and they all suck. Some of the other minigames in the other dating tracks present themselves as things that can be won or lost, but they really aren't, they're just interactive bits where you don't seem to be able to mess up (ex. wood carving with robert, playing the piano with matt). This game was an extremely good move by Scott Cawthon. Not did he just manage to completely change the formula on FNaF successfully, but he pushed through our expectations like a friggin train conductor on cocaine.
Firstly, the game no longer has the "Sit & Survive" technique where you try to keep animatronics away from you by staying in one spot, thereby creating an atmosphere or terror everywhere.
Secondly, you now have to be more strategic to plan your escape, such as timing when to look at Funtime Freddy while rebooting errors.
Thirdly, and the largest change, you no longer have to survive until 6:00 AM. This requires you to do what you are told to do, and if you fail at any given task, you die. Once all chores are done, you proceed to the exit.
These are just a few reasons why Scott Cawthon did a good job and finally creating something different. Any fans of the series will enjoy this, and new fans may finally find out what they've been missing. Thank you Scott for everything, continue what you're doing with FNaF and any other projects you may be working on, we will all support you no matter what happens.
...Also you can watch TV and eat popcorn. Can't get any better than that, can ya?

So, seeing a number of negative reviews, I felt the need to post my opinions.
Like a lot of people, I jumped on-board with financially supporting this game from the very second I learned about it. Also, like a lot of people, I *loved* Planescape: Torment and consider it to be the finest example of an RPG that I have seen to date. I still sing its praises for the depth of its story, characters, environment, gameplay (yes, even combat), and really anything about it, I love it that much.
With that said, I don't think Torment: Tides of Numenara failed to deliver. Is it everthing that the developers said it would be? Probably not, because it turns out pitching an idea off the cuff is really hard and can involve a lot of things that later turn out to be unrealistic. But is it a spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment? I certainly think so.
Overall, Tides of Numenara is an interesting game, it has a lot of story to it and a world that I think is equally interesting to that found in Planescape: Torment. I will admit that the latter had better characters (to be honest, it's hard to compete), but I think that for what it is, Torment: Tides of Numenara still delivers solid characters with some having very interesting stories and interactions.
Combat is something I can't weigh in on too much. I didn't like Planescape: Torment for its combat, that was just a way to interrupt the story, and so I picked the story mode for Torment: Tides of Numenara. If you're looking for a game that involves varied combat and challenge and what not, beats me, I wouldn't know. But for what I wanted, the game definitely delivered.
In short, if you've never played Planescape: Torment, I don't think you'll be disappointed so long as you realize you're playing a game that is really only good if you take the time to relax, read (a lot of reading is involved) and get into the environment. If you have played Planescape: Torment, I still think you'll like it, because it has a lot of depth to the parts that, to me, are important.
I can't claim that people with negative opinions are wrong, or that they don't have valid opinions you should consider, but if you're looking at this game in the light of The Game that was important to you, or looking at this based on the combat mechanics, I think you're looking at it in the wrong way.

I nominated Undertale for the "The World Is Grim Enough..." award, because I think it is - to this day - one of the most compelling uses of non-violence in gaming. You can clear the whole game without harming a fly, even though you have the option to do so. There is conflict in the game, but its specific choice to build non-violent solutions in a genre that's usually all about murder-hobos killing giant rats to take their gold is refreshing and unique.
You can hardly have a story without conflict - if you want literally zero conflict, maybe try Kerbal Space Program, or anything that has the word "Idle" in it. For my nomination, it's gotta be the game that gives you the option of violence and makes you want to choose peace. And yes, I know this nom doesn't really fall within the description of the category, but depending on how you play it, it CAN involve less violence than Mario Party - and that's saying something.

There is a good reason why this game has  97% positive reviews out of over 150,000.  I bought Terraria in 2013, just over four years ago now, and it has continued to evolve bit by bit during this time.  Since I started playing, no fewer than five bosses have been added, and at least three more events as well (and heck, I still haven't managed to get an alien invasion to occur in my most advanced world...).  From my first forray around the surface of my lovely world of Neverland, to the horror that was the Wall of Flesh, through my struggles against Plantera and my first Solar Eclipse I have prevailed in the face of hardship.  Though the Dungeon was dark and mysterious, crawling with all sorts of arcane horrors (and one really nasty Paladin), I stuck with it to unlock the special biome chests (but...not all of them, yet).  I mastered the minishark to defeat the Golem, and I took my flail to the King Slime.  Time after time I found myself with victory, though often as not preceeded by multiple defeats.  Until finally....*finally*...I approached the newest, latest, greatest challenge:  the Moon Lord.
I swear it took me ten hours alone to defeat this guy.
Such a sense of accomplishment when I finally defeated the Moon Lord, only to realize...I need to do it again if I want to craft some of the more awesome end game items.  Still...the Portal Gun was worth it.
Clocking in at over 350 hours in Terraria, I have judged this game to be well worth the low cost.  Additionally, all this time spent has been, for the majority, played in singleplayer-- I estimate only twenty hours has been spent playing with friends.  To this day I still look for friends who want to start a new adventure with me, and every time I open the game up I look forward to the excitement that awaits!

Edmund McMillen is a freaking genius, Part 1.
Stunningly brilliant retro-styled painfully hard platformer, SMB is one of those gems to come from the wonderfully wacky mind of Edmund McMillen (and co-conspirator of Team Meat, Tommy Refenes). Based on the original flash prototype that you can find on Newgrounds/Kongregate and in
, the improvements made to the game and the game engine are what truly elevates this game from un-Super to Super.
The level design is rather well made, and you have to be microscopic-precise to clear a lot of levels. Really easy to follow and rather straightforward. Figuring out how to complete the level is chicken feed - actually completing it is, more often than not, a different story.
You need a decent gaming rig, though - some of the later stages with tons and tons of saws really lags my computer hard, I did find it hard to complete those. Not to mention I get a few annoying crashes in the middle of my playing, but that's probably because a) crap computer and b) I keep alt-tabbing out to check other stuff.
There
a way to hack the command line option to lower the detail so it does not lag so much, though...
This game has also made me consider buying a gaming controller. The warnings given at the start of the game ring true - even with a keyboard, I periodically stress out my left hand playing this.
Finally, wanting to complete all the levels with A+ and all bandages before proceeding to the next stage has brought out the inner OCD freak in me. I love the sense of satisfaction derived from the success of completing the level with a pixel-perfect run, after dozens upon dozens of abject failures.
Steam Sale or trade for a bundle key. Worth full price, though. Support indie developers today!

I loved Borderlands. It had wry humour, a great look a neat variety of guns (oh...about 3,000,000) and was a fun sandbox overall. Then like a small child whose antics are cute when are young but get annonying as they age Borderlands 2 grew up (or rather sideways).
The basics are all still there but there is much less cohesion of it's elements. Here are the things that changed for the worse in the sequel:   [spoilers]
>Lack of diferentiation on gear. This game always had an element of tedious looting. You were forever comparing the just-slightly-better gun you found to one you are using. Fortunately this was mostly optional because you could make a go of it with most guns without the fretting over stats. In B2 now there is no real diferences anymore; every gun does everything. There used to be one 'Nade that was homing, another that was sticky or breaks into smaller bombs. Now your gun shoots grenades that  launch flaming bullet storms while dealing electrocution damage and the clip explodes  when you toss it (but for some reason it looks like you tossed your whole gun), and all of the guns are like that. The old naming convention for the weapons, grenades and shields gave useful cues to help you navigate the dizzying variety. Now the guns sound like they named by adolescent gangbangers using text shorthand or just plain bad spelling.
>TMI. During combat the screen looks like riot of color and flashing lights. It resembles a carnival midway more than a battle.I'm not shooting bullets so much as hosing my enemy down with a neon rainbow-colored bands of damage-indication that are fountaining from the top of my enemies head as well as twelve other NPCs while claptrap is chattering, bad guys are reciting Shakespear (or purile taunts), critters are scurrying amid the exploding oil-drums and now my gun is talking to me. Its techicolor mind-mush on tap. I wonder if that twinge in my frontal lobe is an epileptic fit about to happen. The sequel did not evolve or refine itself. It feels more like some headbanger just turned the noise up to eleven.
There was a time when games were unable to deliver much on screen due to limitations of the available  technology. Now that there are no technical limits we will have to decide for ourselves how much is too much. Borderlands 2 failed to draw a line anywhere so we are left with a cocophony of sound and an average 0f 300 moving elements on the screen at all times. Cerebral overload is a poor path to bliss.
>'Change everything!'. Things seem to have been updated pell mell. Aspects of the game that were just fine the way they were have been altered without improving them. eg. the user interface is now on three separate pages requiring scrolling. No more comparing skills at a glance, now you must navigate within the UI adding tedium. Oh and wouldn't it be cool if the pages floated around making reading the scattered text more dificult or making us hunt around to hit a moving button while peering through three layers of animated watermarks. No it would not. Yes I am old...and blind...but I like to play games too. (snif)
>Humor? Borderlands (the Original and expansions) walked a perfect line with it's humor. I am an older player (cut my teeth on Space Invaders) and I never felt like the game was too adolescent. This game ran my life for a good while. I personally think it's a fantastic game but it's definitely not for everyone. First things first since this is the PC version you would want to know if there are any performance issues and as far as I know there is none. The options menu is one the best i've ever seen with a proper FOV slider, multiple graphics options, etc. The story revolves around you being a vault hunter who hunts vaults which can contain anything from immense power, very powerful weapons, wealth, etc. The main antagonist Handsome Jack is a very charismatic character who's the owner of the megacorporation known as Hyperion that basically owns Pandora (the location in which this game takes place.) Handsome Jack attemps to kill you from the very start of the game by blowing up the train in which you come to pandora in. He's very cocky and confident that he will kill you and the Crimson Raiders (an Anti-Hyperion rebellion) before you even get near him. There are plot twists and multiple characters re-appearing from the original Borderlands like Mad Moxxi, Marcus, Roland, Lilith, Mordecai, and Brick to name a few as well as completely new characters such as Tiny Tina, Handsome Jack, Zero, Maya, and Salvador. The gameplay is your typical FPS but it has an awesome stat and skill tree RPG system (imagine an RPGFPS) and lots of loot. the weapons range anywhere from pistols to rocket-launchers and 5 rarity types White, Green, Blue, Purple, and Orange. White is very common loot while Orange is Legendary loot (also the rarest and most powerful most of the time). The game also has incredible voice acting and dark humor (which I am biased to) with some examples being "BURN ALL THE BABIES!!!!" and "You're worse than the midgets." to name a few. Graphics are nothing special it's your standard cell shaded art style that many other games have used in the past. They are not bad but it's no Crysis 3 what it does have is some of the best PhysX I have ever seen. One thing that might but you off from this game though is that HEAVILY promotes you play the campagn at least 3 TIMES in order to get your character to max level, and not only that but since the game has 6 playable classes (4 default and 2 DLC) you are almost guaranteed to have at least 2 classes that you really like so that means if you want to get at leat 2 classes to max level you are going to have to beat the game a total of 6 TIMES. Another thing that I also love about the game is that the DLC is not BS. each DLC gives you a huge new area to explore with loads of bosses, quest, bad♥♥♥♥♥ranks, new characters to meet, and even more loot and loot rarity. Overall if you enjoy grinding out levels, farming for weapons, extreme replay value, good story and characters then  I would recommend that you pick up the game of the year edition of Borderlands 2 since it will be alot cheaper than just buyng the base game and all the DLC with it.

A rather difficult game to rate.
I've played 3 of inXile games (wasteland 2, pillars of eternity, and this), and they all have a somewhat limited audience, due to their somewhat dated structure and heavy amount of reading.
And I will say that I think tides is my least favorite game I've played from them.
The good:  The setting is like nothing I've seen before, and is easily its strongest component.  Far, FAR, future, where anything is possible.  Very original set pieces, characters, puzzles, etc.  It took a couple hours for me to get really invested in the story, but it's a pretty great one, all in all.
The bad:  Combat is pretty dull.  Found that auto-attacking pretty much did the trick the entire game through.
Some of the exposition can get a bit longwinded, even more so than pillars at times.
In general, this is almost an interactive book.  The combat challenge is almost non-existent.  And that's ok!  It's an interesting and original story.  The lack of challenge is striking from that of pillars, which I had to turn down to baby mode.
However, I think my biggest problem is that it's ~$45, and I was stunned that I finished it in about 15 hours.  And that's after chasing down every side quest I could find.  Plus, I only found 4 party members, which seemed low.  It felt like I was just getting into the story and then END.
Anyways, I feel that its gameplay to dollar value is quite low, especially compared to other inXile games.  If you're a fan of the setting, and of reading, it's a decent buy.  If you like InXile games, it's much the same, just surprisingly short.  In either case, I'd recommend waiting for sale (I did).
But if you're new to inXile or 90s isometric RPGs, I'd easily recommend wasteland 2 over this.

I backed this game on Kickstarter as soon as it was announced- the original Torment is my all time favorite game/novel. I followed the development and was pretty excited, despite the long wait. Unfortunately the game did not live up to it's predecessor in any dimension; writing, art, itemization, even combat- and thats saying something, consider how lackluster combat was in the original Torment.
The writing and artistic direction was adequate. I never felt all that drawn in, but it was serviceable. Some of the gameplay elements were baffling. I understand that a game based around skill checks is difficult to make, and every one that exists has its share of (fair) criticism (Torment, Age of Decadence, etc.). As many users have noted, the skill checks are quickly trivialized by the aggregate skills of your party, and the combat system was really uninspired.
What really prompted my negative review was the lack of support from the developers. The game arrived very late and incomplete, with many promised features missing. I waited a few months after launch to wait for some patching and smooth things over, but still encountered major bugs that stopped my progress. As of today, these issues are still not fixed. This is pretty disappointing, especially compared to something like Pillars of Eternity; I didnt like that game at all at first, but the devs were constantly patching and tuning it, and eventually became a much more enjoyable experience. Alas, T:ToN clearly doesn't have this kind of support and I doubt it will ever get much better.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is a story driven, party based RPG from the developers of Wasteland 2, using the Pillars of Eternity engine. You are a Castoff – a new consciousness born into an adult body, which was previously inhabited by the Changing God, a being who can move from one body to another at will. You have fragments of the Changing God’s memories, and you are being pursued by the Sorrow, a demonic creature who wants to devour you and the other Castoffs.
While the main story is good, the game has a slow pace. There isn’t a lot of combat, and you’ll spend most of your time talking to NPCs. There’s almost no voice acting, so be prepared to do a lot of reading. I don’t really know how to describe the theme of the world. Its not your typical Tolkien style Elves/Dwarves/Orcs/Goblins fantasy, nor is it a traditional Star Trek/Mass Effect style sci-fi. Its an unusual setting, which can be a good thing, however I don’t think the developers did a good job of explaining things to begin with. I spent the first few hours fairly confused, as NPCs kept referring to people, places, creatures, and events that I had no knowledge of. I suppose you could argue that, having just been born, my character is supposed to feel that way. I did enjoy the game more after I left the starting city.
Combat, on the rare occasions that it happens, is very enjoyable. Its a turn based system where each character attacks once per turn, in an order determined by speed/initiative. The Castoff and each of your companions have stats for Might, Agility and Intelligence, and T:ToN uses these in a unique way. For example, let’s say you’re using a heavy melee weapon which uses Might, and you’ve got 10 points of Might. When you attack, you have to choose how many points to spend, where 2 points could give you an 80% chance to hit and do 8 damage, and 3 points could be 100% hit chance for 12 damage. But then after the attack, your Might will reduce by the amount of points spent, so now you have 8 or 7 points remaining. This results in an interesting gambling mechanic, where if you try to save points for the rest of the fight, you risk missing the attack. As you level up you can acquire “edge”, which is basically free points (a 4 point attack with 1 edge will only reduce your stat by 3 points). You can restore stats by using items or resting.
Might/Agility/Intelligence are also used outside of combat, for other quest challenges. For example you could need to lift a heavy object that is blocking your path using might, or maybe you need to use intelligence to understand how to activate an unusual artefact. Most non-combat challenges will allow you to select which companion attempts the challenge, so you can pick whoever is most likely to succeed, and this encourages you to have a balanced party. Many quests can be solved in multiple ways, and you can sometimes avoid combat by talking your way out of it or intimidating the enemy.
Companions are interesting. My favourites were Callistege, a female mage who can speak to reflections of herself in other dimensions, and Erritus, a boastful adventurer who often flirted with my other companion Matkina (who would usually respond by threatening to kill Erritus). However, companions don’t gain experience when not in your party, which means you’ll be weaker if you constantly switch companions. Its better to stick with the same 3 for the whole game, forcing you to ignore the others.
I didn’t suffer from any bugs or crashes, and this isn’t the kind of game where you need to worry about framerate. It took me 30 hours to finish the game and roughly 75% of the side quests, so value for money is good.
Overall, Torment: Tides of Numenera is a good game, but not a great game. For every interesting idea, there was something else that I didn’t enjoy as much. However, I would still recommend this game to fans of the RPG genre, assuming you’ve played all the other important games and you’re looking for something new. Although this is described as a spiritual successor to Planescape Torment, the story doesn’t continue, so you don’t need to play that game to enjoy this one.

Simply put, if you were playing CRPGs in the 90s, this game feels like a natural extension of the era. Much like those games of the 90s, you'll spend a lot of time reading. If you're not ready to read, then this game isn't for you.
Otherwise, Torment:ToN successfully delivered on it's promise to be the spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment. I may even be hated for saying I preferred Torment: Tides over Planescape: Torment.
Give it a go. I hope to see more from inXile in this setting.

No, it's not up to the legend of Planescape: Torment, but yes, it can be enjoyable; it's odd, sometimes too much, but interesting enough to keep going forward. Where PS:T aided by the planescape setting relied on a greatly coherent structure, both thematical and design wise, this feels sometimes messy, sparse and "undefined", the numenera setting itself seems to be a great cauldron of...things, among different time-spans or different "humanities", giving writers the chance to write some exotic weird stuff, but also the possibilty to not care about any kind of coherence and thematic unity. This game feels like an expansion to Arkham City in every aspect. As soon as you start the game, you already have most of the gadgets and abilities from Arkham City. The mechanics are the same, there are no new enemy variants introduced, only a few new abilities and modifiers. Although this might look like a bad thing, it is actually not, since everything still works very well even though there is no innovation. The aspect where this game shines is story. The story is just great, better than all previous Batman games, although shorter.
One big step back is the new challenge mode. Previously, we had combat and predator challenges. Now we have combat and campaign challenges, the last is a series of 3 levels mixing predator and combat, where you have to complete all 3 in order. The drawback is that you cannot choose which predator map you want to play, and you have to replay combat challenges you have previously completed, for a new score. This really feels like milking the game mode in order to make the game last more hours, but is very off-putting.
Another annoying aspect is that certain upgrades are unlocked only after you completed certain in-game achievements. Some of them are very difficult and you will find yourself spending hours repeating yourself just trying to unlock an upgrade.
The riddler trophies in this game are the easiest of all games so far, most of them you have to go to the location and it pick it up, no puzzle solving required. I liked when there were lots of puzzles.
Played a little bit of multiplayer, it is quite fun, but the biggest drawbacks are that matches are too short (less than 5 minutes, it ends when it is getting fun) and takes a long time to set up the next match.

Batman: Arkham Origins manages to be the worst Arkham game that, disappointingly, barely does enough to justify its asking price of £30, especially if you have played Arkham City.
Lets start with the good things.
- The story in Origins is very good, possibly the best out of the current trilogy. While there are pacing problems, the overall plot is deep, thought out and even manages to surprise in a few areas.
- Sound design and the soundtrack are superb; feeling like they had a real production value and weren't just simply overlooked. (unlike some other things)
- The voice acting is incredible, for the most part, with Troy Baker as The Joker stealing the show. (though Roger Craig Smith as Batman does a pretty good job at emulating Kevin Conroy from previous games) I must admit it's jarring to hear Batman's voice at first, (being so used to Conroy's work) but it doesn't take long to get acclimatised, with halfway through the game, barely noticing the difference.
- The game manages a decent length of around 10-12 hours for the main story.
Now on to the negatives.
- The game world, while being of a decent size, is too cumbersome to travel round. Most of your time in the open world will be spent travelling from A to B by grappling rooftops. The fast travel does alleviate this, but you have to unlock the various points by overtaking radio towers as side missions, making the whole thing feeling a bit like too much work.
- Most of the side missions are now completely seperated from the main plot, they are now mostly unintresting and uninspiring filler.
- The combat is only slightly improved from City, and with the inclusion of the new shock gloves, makes it far too easy to beat enemies.
- Most of the little refrences and in-jokes to other DC comics which made the previous games that little bit more awesome are gone, it feels like most of the devs aren't as passionate as Rocksteady and it would have be nice for a couple of easter eggs here and there.
- The first part of the plot (about the assassins) doesn't quite gel with the rest of the story and feels like an excuse to shoe horn some D-list DC villans.
- The Penguin's 'assistants' are some of the worst characters I have ever seen in a Batman game. Plus the thick (what I assume is meant to be cockney) accent of one of them is so horrible, it's on par with Bolo Santosi in Just Cause 2.
- While I haven't played much of the multiplayer and while it was fun, it lacks depth to keep my interest, making it only passable at best.
- The biggest flaw of Arkham Origins, however, is its MOUNTAIN OF BUGS. While most of the game breaking bugs have been reportedly fixed, there are still a plethora of visual bugs, such as the skybox having circular clouds covering it, textures spazzing out and not unlocking certain areas of the game. Fortunately, in my personal experience, all it needs it a checkpoint restart. Others haven't been so lucky. As WB Montreal aren't fixing the game anymore a minority will most likely never finish the game, buy at your own risk.
This game is nowhere near worth its full asking price, and some of it is really good and well done, which only makes it more painful to say that if you have never played the Arkham games NEVER EVER PLAY THIS. If you have played the previous two then wait for a sale, only then it will be worth at least a vague look.
4/10

Arkham Origins is the third Batman game from Warner Brothers but not, the company likes to point out, either a direct sequel to Arkham City nor even necessarily something that is connected to the previous two games, by external developer Rocksteady, in any particular fashion. This entry, by WB Games Montreal, is sort of like a Year Two Batman story, which immediately raises any number of questions. First, because it's clear that Jim Gordon and Batman have very little history together at this point, it's not a tale that directly follows Frank Miller's Year One. Second it's not really an origin story of anything: Batman has already been operating for some time and Arkham Asylum, as a facility that is distinct and separate from Blackgate Prison, on the other hand, does not exist at all. This is, however, very much a WB Batman game, as the new developer takes Rocksteady's work and makes no substantial alterations beyond telling a different story. For good or ill, this is indeed your father's Batman game.
The game begins on Christmas Eve with Batman going after Black Mask, who has apparently put a bounty of $50 million on his head, and this has attracted some of the most dangerous assassins in the world to Gotham. Because this is early in Batman's career he does some dumb things like forgetting his razor and neglecting to secure a subdued "super"villain (the ridiculously-named and ill-fated Electrocutioner); additionally, half of Gotham isn't convinced that he's real and most of the police force is out to try to arrest him or put him six feet under (compare this to the deferential treatment he receives in the opening cutscene of Arkham Asylum). Also, there are quite a few other things going on during this particular December 24: a certain Mr. E Nigma hijacks Batman's navigation towers and leaves blackmail files around the city; Anarky has planted bombs on major landmarks; and the Mad Hatter does his best Jonathan Crane impression. The entirety of the main story's action takes place during this single evening so it's a very busy night for the Bat.
The main elements of the previous games return here: the free-flow combat, unlocking a succession of Bat-gadgets, side missions and collectibles. The only new facets to the game are the Team Fortress-like multiplayer, the fast-travel system needed to traverse the much-larger bit of real estate that is Gotham City, and the training simulator (although this is basically a reworking of the combat and stealth room challenges from the previous games, which are also present).
Multiplayer is disappointing, in some measure because it's never been a strong suit of mine in any game, but also because it's the first time I've ever felt like a 95-lb. weakling when playing as Batman in a game. Players are randomly assigned to teams of criminals with two random players being selected to play as Batman and Robin. The regular criminal types are loaded to the gills with gear that ensures that simply lying in wait as if you were playing a predator challenge as Batman is not a viable option, as you will quickly be spotted and shot. There is also the possibility of the gang leaders, Bane and Joker, turning up during a match. Matches are won by holding control points in the case of criminals or filling an intimidation meter (by taking out criminals) when playing as the Dynamic Duo. It's all bog-standard stuff, in other words, and not something I was too interested in spending much time on.
Disappointingly, this and the challenge maps are the only places where one can utilize the various DLC costumes available. I'm not sure why this is. The official explanation had something to do with cutscenes being pre-rendered in such as way that the use of alternate Batman skins is not an option, but this is evidently a limitation of the engine being utilized by WB Montreal because Rocksteady released a code that allowed anyone to use unlocked DLC skins at any time during Arkham City's story.
The story mode action, then, is very familiar to players of previous Arkham games. Is this an inherently bad thing? Not really. If you liked the Rocksteady games, you'll probably like this one, because it is largely more of the same.
Several odd design decisions occurred with the production of this game, which will affect your experience but not in a terribly detrimental way. For whatever reasons the corporate gods determined, Warner had Montreal working on this while Rocksteady was quietly and concurrently (it would seem) creating Arkham Knight in secret. Where the latter sees the return of fan-favorite Kevin Conroy as the voice of Batman, WB opted to go with a different voice cast for the roles of Batman, The Joker, and Harley Quinn in Arkham Origins. This is somewhat distracting at first, but the Origins cast do well enough in their respective roles. Troy Baker, in particular, is quite good as The Joker, which is a bit of a relief because Mark Hamill is probably done with the part for good. The number of Riddler collectibles was halved from Arkham City's absurd 400 to a more manageable 200. While some reviewers have said the freeflow combat doesn't feel as "tight" in this entry, I can't really say that I've noticed a difference; on the other hand, I'll be the first to concede that I'm not exactly a freeflow-combat master.
There are a lot of goofy aspects to the unfolding narrative here. While Arkham City presented us with the bizarre notion that an entire area encompassing dozens of city blocks would be cordoned off as a kind of "death zone" substitute for an actual penitentiary, I've come to realize that this could either be viewed as something presented in a realistic fashion (in which case it is kinda batshit crazy) or as a Swiftian satire on the phenomena of white flight, the "war on drugs" and an increasing reliance on the expansion of prisons in a society where the percentage of the population that is incarcerated seems to be growing exponentially. In either case, it would make sense that there would be no ordinary citizens on the streets of such an Escape from New York-style dystopian penal zone. Here the only explanation provided for this incongruous phenomenon is that police have warned people to stay off the streets. At various points in the game, we're introduced to Batman and Alfred's insanely-fantastic analytical equipment, which can produce antivenoms to unknown neurotoxins in a matter of minutes and provide DNA matches from bodily fluids at a crime scene with equal celerity. The crowning absurdity has to be the game's naive proposal that any kind of high-voltage equipment can be used as an effective defibrillator; in fairness, this is the sort of thing that one tends to see on television on an almost weekly basis, but this doesn't make it any less nonsensical.
The main story will take you around 30-35 hours to knock out and you can count on an extra 10-15 hours getting the collectibles and beating challenge maps. Annoyingly, the "Initiation" DLC is itself just a series of challenge maps rather than being a full-fledged story prologue. "Cold Cold Heart," however, does consist of a new story, a somewhat-rehashed origin tale of classic Bat-villain, Mr. Freeze. Outside of the wintry tale, there are a few new things to do, such as finding new Anarky tags and unfreezing cops and security guards. For a completionist, the Mr. Freeze DLC will take about another 7 hours, and it's well worth a few bucks, but I wouldn't buy it at the current full asking price of $10.

If Arkham Asylum offered the thrill of becoming Batman, and Arkham City offered the thrill of exploring Gotham in free flight, and Arkham Knight will (supposedly) offer the thrill of piloting the Batmobile, then Arkham Origins seems to be offering the thrill of experiencing the genesis of Batman's most important relationships: Alfred, Gordon, and an array of his iconic nemises.
However, Arkham Origins does not, as you might think, tell the story of how Bruce Wayne became the Batman. In fact, the circumstances of Wayne's childhood tragedy, training, and return to Gotham as reborn vigilante is already in the past, before the game begins, and he is already equipped with batarangs, grapnel, and Batwing jet. Instead, the 'Origins' referenced are the seeds planted in the story that will eventually mature into the Arkham City future. Along the way, Batman grows from a shadowy rumor to a renowned crime-fighter, having already taken bites out of local threats like Penguin and Black Mask, but also starting to attract enough attention to himself to begin to tip the established balance of power that will change Gotham forever.
Unfortunately, where the previous Arkham Games have built and expanded on the fantasy of 'becoming' the Batman and living his adventure, with his gadgets, intelligence, and fortitude, Origins deviates very little from the City forumla of roaming the night, dealing justice to criminals, solving crime, and saving the city from an overarching threat. There's nothing new here, which is probably good news if you enjoyed City, but will disappoint if you're looking for the Arkham franchise to raise the ante. In a very real sense, Origins is a sort of deluxe-sized expansion pack for Arkham City that transposes that sequel's gameplay back in time.
The good is that the polish and production values are as high as ever. The animation, cinematics, voice acting, and so on are extremely immersive, and Gotham looks great as a proud, post-industrial metropolis beginning to decay from the inside out. All of Batman's gadgets return, and there are now even more districts to explore, with never a shortage of thugs to beat into unconsciousness. There is a full compliment of challenge maps to medal in, side quests to complete, and obscure objects to find and collect, as in City. The main addition to the Arkham series overall is the "Crime Scene" sequences where Batman explores and reconstructs various crimes in order to solve a problem. While these are very, very simple puzzles, the actions and narrations do give the player a solid sense of being the "World's Greatest Detective", which is often neglected in Batman movies and games.
The bad is that it will feel very much like playing Arkham City all over again, in a more mundane environment, and with a story campaign that feels noticably shorter when you consider it apart from all the diversions that you might explore along the way. Batman gains new abilities by completing various challenges according to the Dark Knight system, but what might have been enjoyable can easily become a frustrating grind when the challenge requirements do not properly align with the actual given opportunities within the game, forcing you to replay the game over if you want to maximize your potential. Lastly, this is clearly the least stable, most buggy iteration of the Arkham franchise. While most of the issues have been resolved by now, the game does not seem to have been coded cleanly or elegantly. Expect to experience crashes along the way.
Concerning the DLC: The Initiation Pack only features Challenge Map content, which is a good value if you like that gamplay (I do). You can play pre-Batman Bruce Wayne in a weaker, stripped-down form on all the standard maps, along with a difficult, 5-map campaign simulating his training as part of the League of Shadows. Conversely, the "Cold Cold Heart" DLC is a standalone, story-only campaign, with no challenge maps, that doesn't interact with the main Origins storyline at all. If you just like the Batman story and experience without the tedium of Challenge medals, then this is perfect content for you, featuring a complete set of side quests, equipment upgrades, open-world exploring, and plotline with new enemies and characters, and a challenging new boss fight integrating stealth, combat, and gadgets together. As for the Batman costume skin packs, I didn't find them ultimately worth the value. The various suits and costumes generally did not fit well into the strong, well-established artistic design the game already possesses, and were at best comical and at worst distracting.
In summary, Arkham Origins is retelling stories you have probably already heard before. If once was enough, you should probably take a pass, but if you can't just get enough, Origins is happy to offer more.

This is a pretty fun game if you're looking for something to really challange yourself with. Playing as the Germans, you'll walk into the battle and roll over the early Soviet units, and then all of a sudden everything turns sour and the Soviets start pushing back. I play it because it's fun, but I don't see it as a historical game, which is a bad thing since this is literally called "Drive on Moscow" and based on a historical battle. Soviet cossack horsemen will beat your Panzers 8 out of 10 times, which probably isn't realistic. In my opinion, there's way too much RNG in the game, which makes sense if you're trying to make a balanced wargame, but this isn't supposed to be balanced. The Germans are supposed to steamroll the Russians and then only get beat once winter comes around. This RNG also means that halfway through the game, your units will be fighting constant battles over and over with the same group of Soviet units with no outcome, because there's always woods or buildings or something that absorb hits and at the end of the day, no one dies and no one moves. I play the game in school so I don't die of boredom.
In a nutshell, you will move your units twice, and then never move them again because they'll get themselves into an eternal stalemate.
Good thing it's only ten dollars.

A small and slick game that will give you a few hours of entertainment. Easy to learn, hard to master. The game plays out on an operational level in very chess like map divided into provinces. The A.I plays pretty well and the game implements a few special rules for the russians as well as the germans to simulate real world events. The game utilises a very unique system of phases during a turn in which you only can activate and move units in particular province before the phase returns to the opposing player. That means you can not coordinate things in advance but have to take into account every countermove from the opponent. Interesting system which forces you to prioritize which units to move and attack with.
Unfortunately the same map is used in all scenarios and the campaign and will soon become repetitious unless you can find a human hotseat opponent.
For sale I highly recommend this game.

With such a large game world comes the problem of filling it with interesting content to experience. Unfortunately Mad Max is filled with the same content in each divided region. There is some very beautiful world, and level design, however the repetitive gameplay leaves you mindlessly slogging through the game as you hold buttons to perform mundane actions. On a side note, I groaned at times when a puzzle was presented to Max of which he would verbally acknowledge; However the solution was conveniently placed two steps away, every-single-time.
The fighting mechanics are ripped from the Batman series and simplified. The combat is most simple in the beginning of the game, but gives you the ability to upgrade it through Max's character menu. Even with all combat skills acquired, and weapon and ammo fully upgraded, the combat is still rather dry, yet addicting.
The physics engine is a little wonky at times, and the car mechanics don't feel as if they were fully designed as well as they aught to have. So, although you'll be able to have fun zooming around the wasteland, at times you'll find yourself flying through the air in amusing pirouettes. You'll most likly do the latter during the car combat which is actually quite entertaining. The only thing I was wishing the game had more of were the caravan routes where your task was to take out the lead car while the support cars buzz like a swarm of angry bees.
A large part of upgrading your vehicle relies on Max eliminating certain threats within each region of the map. As mentioned above, dealing with convoys is a part of this. Max is also tasked with destroying landmarks and sniper posts as well as diffusing mine fields with his bomb sniffing dog. With the decrease of regional threats comes the decrease of enemies within that region. Makes sense, but this results in a somewhat empty world. Again, makes sense, the world is a sparse desert, but the entertainment value drops a bit.
The story was nothing to get all geeked up about: it is pretty shallow and predictable with forced character interactions. I will say that the last act had a Mad Max 1 moment that got me pumped with motivation until the game took a nose dive into the depressingly short final battle.
I do plan on keeping the game installed for now as I would like to read the in game character bios, vehicle designs,  and location information. As many things as I didn't care for in the game, it is aparent that a good deal of interesting design went into it and builds off the world of Mad Max.
Bottom line:
-------------
The world:          Beautiful
The fighting:      "I'm Batman(tm)"
The driving:        Passable
The car combat: Entertaining
The leveling:       Hopelessly repetitive
The questing:     Go to 'X' location; Hold 'A' to gather; Return
The story:           MEDIOCRE! THE GATES OF VALHALLA DO NOT OPEN FOR THEE!
If this game didn't carry the MAD MAX name, I never would have purchased it. If you'd like to try it, wait for a sale (as I did).

Mixed feelings. I have played this game alot on PC and iPad. It is interesting but flawed in my mind. I like the system but the whole game will depend on special rules, like prepared offensives, command confusion and then weather which can raise and lower the defensive value of terrain for just one side. Some is realistic but it drives the game a little too much in my opinion. You must master movement planning and the special rules or you will always lose. At first it is easier to play the Soviets as they have no real movement problems and fewer units to move. The Germans rarely can get their army moving, especially if you spread out. I have had half my army stationary for most the game at times. In fact, if you are Soviet you can use it to your advantage.
Against good or expert players it will be hard to beat the German player. You learn how to make about five or six key attacks, exploit through and get units adjacent to Moscow or even in it before the mud hits. There is not much the Soviet can do but react and hope for bad combat results. Defense is absolutely supreme and you cannot displace anything other than small units without special rules or some very good luck meaning if the panzers get close to Moscow you will have a bad time trying to dislodge them even if you severely outnumber them.
Having said that, it can be fun to play. If you are the Soviet and can survive the first five turns in good order and punish the lead mobile units you have a chance. It is a long long wait to your offensive and the German army is much stronger given you may lose 60-80% of your army at the start.
I give it a middle of the road rating, say 3 of 5. I think with revisions it could be great like it's brother, Battle of the Bulge which I prefer. Given the low price I would say it is worth buying and then playing in multiplayer after you do some learning with the AI. This new version has better AI than the old which will help. Then go play the great players for some eye openers and a steep learning curve.

Dream Daddy: A Dad Dating Simulator is, as the name implies, a dating sim. Not just any dating sim-oh no! It is a simulator where you are a single dad who can date other dads! There are seven datable dads, each with their own character type and personality. It is a basic dating simulator where you are mostly reading with some choices of dialougue and actions that will determine which dad you will end up with.
Throughout your quest for a boyfriend, you also have choices to make with your daughter that will determine what kind of relationship you will have with her as she moves off to college. So while you are managing your love life you are also cementing (or not, depending on your choices) your relationship with your child. There are also mini games on some of the dates you go on with the dads.
Overall, I really enjoyed the game, finishing it (except the currently unachievable) in about 29 hours. It wasn't a complicated dating sim/visual novel, but for me it was still very enjoyable to read and to experience anyways. I felt that the characters, dialogue, and descriptions were really well-written and although the structure of the game was quite simplistic (date a dad three times to get the ending) and the rest of the story in between the dates doesn't really change, I still liked playing!
The music was good for background noise and didn't detract from the experience. There were some bugs here and there, but none that were game breaking. The devs fixed quite a few of these, but there are still a couple things that I still didn't like even after the fixes. There is an achievement that cannot be unlocked at this point without manual overriding, so I am hoping that is something they fix in the future (or just get rid of the achievement). Another thing was the FRICKIN MINI GOLF ACHIEVEMENT! UUGGGHH - everything else in the game is either wonderful or passable, but SCREW THAT ACHIEVEMENT!
Despite that, I liked the game and I recommend it! If you are a person looking for a more complex dating sim/visual novel I would look elsewhere. Because of the currently broken achievment and the simple structure of the game I would suggest getting it on sale if you aren't sure whether you should get it or not. I personally enjoyed it because it was finally some good lgbt+ representation, and the characters have an interesting depth to them that makes them likeable.

Honestly one of the best FPSes I've ever played if not THE best FPS I've ever played.
Pros? Hundreds, if not at least a thousand+ hours of replayability. Six classes with, as the game advertises, millions of guns will guarantee that gameplay feels fresh the whole way through. The humor doesn't always quite hit the mark but Handsome Jack is one of the funniest and most well written characters I've seen in a video game in a long time. Hundreds of character skins, heads, and vehicle cosmetics are fun to collect and use in a multiplayer enviroment. Finally, because of the batshit crazy nature of some of the guns, there is ample opportunity for screwing around, but if it's your thing the game includes a surprisingly deep build system and tough as nails bosses for the "hardcore gamers™"
The cons? This game's really ♥♥♥♥ing expensive unless you pick it up during a sale, around $40 USD for the main game with each main DLC Expansion being $10. Picking up all the headhunter DLCs will drop you around $25 as well. Luckily, the game goes on sale fairly often so price shouldn't really be a problem unless you need this game NOW. Also, the really late-game (I'm talking levels 55 - 72) is unbalanced as♥♥♥♥♥♥and are almost unplayable without a second person or a lot of time spent grinding for weapons. And oftentimes, you'll find yourself struggling to get even a single kill before death due to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ luck finding weapons.
Overall though, it's a great game. I've spent several hundred hours in BL2 at the time of writing and I can easily find myself spending several hundred more before I shelf this game for a while. Would definitely recommend.

All in all, this is a fine game which did manage to remind me of its illustrious predecessor. Many things to like: funny dialogs, fine irony, easter eggs, detailed world, original items and puzzles, memorable NPCs, cool forms of damage and a solid set of skills and abilities, Monty Pythonesque scenes (e.g., taking colorfully described surgical enhancements), some fascinating interior sites (e.g., the Necropolis). The plot is sophisticated and abounds in interesting philosophical and psychological topics and memes.
On the downside, the game is definitely too short and lacks nice expansive locales characterizing The Planescape: Torment. Battles are too easy (would be a good thing to have a difficulty slider or something such) and too few. Many useful items come too late in the game, and others are simply too cheap (or there is too much money in the game, prices should be higher). And there could be more recruitable companions -- I hope some could be still added via updates, like Oom was.
And I do sincerely hope for a sequel!

Torment: Tides of Numenera is a hard game to rate. I know it is supposed to be a spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment, but the it feels like the game is trying to hard to emulate something else instead of standing on its own legs.
I didn't like the RPG character system, it is mostly based on how many points you have in Might, Speed or Intellect (Hint: Intellect is clearly the most important and used). These stat pools are drained as you use them in combat, dialog or just to touch stuff, but can be refilled by items or just sleeping.
Combat is boring (the little there is), and you can avoid most of them by dialog, sneaking or devices nearby.
The world is a mismatch of things (laser guns and old swords anyone?) and nothing really seems to fit together properly.
I'll just put it simply. If you have played Planescape: Torment, you can skip this one. If you have not played Planescape: Torment, you can pick up Torment: Tides of Numenera whenever it is on sale and give it a try.
I'd give this game 6/10, Above average.

Never seen a game at this price range delivering so much depth through a simple structure of mechanics. At my first look I thought that the gameplay was a bit odd and simplistic, but oh man, I was so wrong! After playing an hour of the campaign I realized that every single move is VERY important and every single mistake that might seem insignificant is in fact, a game changer.
The AI destroyed me and forced me to find weak points and rely on every single mechanic of the terrain system. After beating this type of AI, the victory feels very good and significant especially if the AI will beat the c**p out of you the first three matches(my case).
My single problem with the game is that the Operation Typhoon feels very unbalanced and unfair for the Germans. It is nearly impossible to win against Soviets.
Pros:
- The gameplay feels very refreshing to me (not a war gamer veteran), but I love it because you have a limited number of units and Replacements/Reinforcements and every move can have multiple consequences.
- I really like the Replacements/Reinforcements mechanic and how you can change the whole rhythm of the game.
- The AI is very good and will take advantage as soon as the player commits a mistake.
- It really looks and feels like a war boardgame and I like the way tiles are positioned throughout the map.
- Love the hotseat mode that adds to the boardgame factor.
- Have not played the multiplayer yet, but I was not expecting one at this price (This is the first time I play a Shenandoah/Slitherine game).
- The game scenarios do not feel repetitive.
- THE PRICE!!
- The learning pattern because you will get better and better at this game (and it's kind of addicting)
- The Briefing menu will give the player any information needed.
- The rules are well written and the terrain system is awesome. The players will have to learn the advantages and disadvantages of every terrain type.
- The historical accuracy of the game.
Cons:
- The Operation Typhoon scenario feels unbalanced being almost impossible to win as Axis.
- Could be hard for newcomers (I am not bothered by this, because the AI will force you to think and find new strategies, helping you to become much better at the game).
I recommend the game to any war strategy enthusiast, because it is an excellent price/quality product that delivers a unique gameplay feeling.

You will probably like Drive on Moscow if you like turn based board games (RISK, Chess) or strategy games which rely more on planning ahead than microing unit healthbars. The game does a good job of presenting historical context, and the scenarios have specific win conditions for both factions (Soviets or Axis) so that playthroughs feel different. Moreover, to help the replayability, the AI is quite competent and will give you a run for your money. You won't beat it in your first 2 or 3 games and that's okay, because the mecahnics are easy to get into, but you need to factor the future of your mission: where you want to strike, which points you want to hold or leave, where are the reinforcements coming etc.
An aspect which I don't agree with is a bit of randomness, which happens to determine winners in combat (it happens seldom enough, though, to lose a fight just out of pure bad luck).
The multiplayer is also fairly accessible, and works in a similar way to chess by mail: once a game is started, each player receives a notification when the other has finished his or her turn, and so on, so moves can be squeezed in a match even in a tight schedule.
All in all, Drive on Moscow is a challenging but easy to understand strategy war game, and if you like this sort of stuff the you could try it.

With such a large game world comes the problem of filling it with interesting content to experience. Unfortunately Mad Max is filled with the same content in each divided region. There is some very beautiful world, and level design, however the repetitive gameplay leaves you mindlessly slogging through the game as you hold buttons to perform mundane actions. On a side note, I groaned at times when a puzzle was presented to Max of which he would verbally acknowledge; However the solution was conveniently placed two steps away, every-single-time.
The fighting mechanics are ripped from the Batman series and simplified. The combat is most simple in the beginning of the game, but gives you the ability to upgrade it through Max's character menu. Even with all combat skills acquired, and weapon and ammo fully upgraded, the combat is still rather dry, yet addicting.
The physics engine is a little wonky at times, and the car mechanics don't feel as if they were fully designed as well as they aught to have. So, although you'll be able to have fun zooming around the wasteland, at times you'll find yourself flying through the air in amusing pirouettes. You'll most likly do the latter during the car combat which is actually quite entertaining. The only thing I was wishing the game had more of were the caravan routes where your task was to take out the lead car while the support cars buzz like a swarm of angry bees.
A large part of upgrading your vehicle relies on Max eliminating certain threats within each region of the map. As mentioned above, dealing with convoys is a part of this. Max is also tasked with destroying landmarks and sniper posts as well as diffusing mine fields with his bomb sniffing dog. With the decrease of regional threats comes the decrease of enemies within that region. Makes sense, but this results in a somewhat empty world. Again, makes sense, the world is a sparse desert, but the entertainment value drops a bit.
The story was nothing to get all geeked up about: it is pretty shallow and predictable with forced character interactions. I will say that the last act had a Mad Max 1 moment that got me pumped with motivation until the game took a nose dive into the depressingly short final battle.
I do plan on keeping the game installed for now as I would like to read the in game character bios, vehicle designs,  and location information. As many things as I didn't care for in the game, it is aparent that a good deal of interesting design went into it and builds off the world of Mad Max.
Bottom line:
-------------
The world:          Beautiful
The fighting:      "I'm Batman(tm)"
The driving:        Passable
The car combat: Entertaining
The leveling:       Hopelessly repetitive
The questing:     Go to 'X' location; Hold 'A' to gather; Return
The story:           MEDIOCRE! THE GATES OF VALHALLA DO NOT OPEN FOR THEE!
If this game didn't carry the MAD MAX name, I never would have purchased it. If you'd like to try it, wait for a sale (as I did).

Outside of the story and endgame the game plays like a typical Ubisoft open world (Just Cause 3, Assassins' Creed, etc.). If this is a deterant for you, remember that the majority of this content does not have to be cleared if you strictly follow the story.
Overall:
Graphics: 5/5
Optimization: 5/5
Story: 4/5 (Starts a bit slow)
Entertainment Value: 4/5
Overall: 4.5/5
Out of several open worlds I have played recently, this is the only one I have been able to finish. Perhaps it is because I am a fan of the Mad Max series, but for the frequent running $5 price tag, this game is worth a shot.

Undertale - A Choose Your Own Journey game.
A game that is worth more than it's price.
An average run being 6 hours across multiple different endings creates lots of replayability.
The story itself immerges into a story that isn't so much like others. It has a unique consequential side.
Therefore what you do has actual consequences on the story. I love impacting the game in multiple different ways
There is a unique character set, nothing you could imagine. Creativity through the roof.
This game has so much heartbreak and twist and turns and an overall amazing story that could be continued in a second game if Toby so chose to.

In one sentence:
Undertale is a special game that you'll remember for a long time, but it's not perfect.
Story?
It's a excellent story with memorable characters, even characters that don't really affect the story you'll remember.
Gameplay?
There's really two parts to this. I feel like this is where Undertale fails the most.
1: Combat is 8-bit fashioned with high stakes, high reward kinda thing. At times it's honestly annoying.
2: You move through the world mostly on foot. I feel like this slow movement takes away from the feeling of freedom to explore the world.
How much content am I buying?
Allot, if you invest the time.

Q: What exactly is the "live component" of HITMAN?
A: It covers many things. Get ready for a long read.
Elusive Targets
The Contracts that are available for a limited-time are what we call Elusive Targets. An Elusive Target is the closest thing to the Hitman fantasy that we've ever created. These targets will be custom-created characters that are added to existing locations and are only there for a limited time in real-time. You'll only have one chance to take them down. If they escape, they are gone for good. If you kill them, that's the way that you killed them. There are no do-overs and no second chances. When an Elusive Target leaves the game world (one way or another) they never return.
Each Elusive Target will have a custom briefing video, a backstory and a unique reason for being in that location. When you're actually playing in the location, the Elusive Target will not appear on the map and will not appear in Instinct. In order to find them, you'll need to use clues from the briefing video and a photograph that you will be able to review. You'll need to explore, find your target, learn their patterns and come up with a plan to eliminate them - all whilst playing. The pressure will be on when you've got the target in your sights. If you miss the shot and chaos breaks loose, you will need to have a plan B, because the save-game is disabled during an Elusive Target. If you kill the wrong person or die when trying to exfiltrate, that's it. Game over, the target escapes.
As the season unfolds, you’ll earn in-game rewards for completing multiple Elusive Target contracts. The rewards are signature suits from previous Hitman games and versions of those suits with gloves. There’s also a version of the signature suit from the new HITMAN with gloves.
We know that Elusive Targets are not going to be easy, they were designed that way.

Escalation Mode
Escalation Mode is something else completely new for HITMAN and was created as a way to regularly provide a fresh challenge to players. You'll need to master the location as well as the gameplay mechanics to complete a hit that will escalate in difficulty by adding new elements. As an example, the first stage could be to eliminate your target with a sabre. Then, the second stage could be to eliminate your target with a sabre whilst dressed as a waiter and removing any security camera recordings within two minutes. We are able to change where the security cameras are and also add additional ‘security’ measures to the locations, such as laser trip-wire explosives that you’ll need to avoid.
Escalation Mode has a strong focus on having fun with the game mechanics and mixing them up – pretty much anything goes in this mode. It’s more about being playful than realistic. For each Escalation Contract, there are five stages and you're free to replay them as you wish to climb the leaderboards. As with Elusive Targets, the save-game functions are disabled.
All Escalation contracts and Elusive Targets are created by IOI and will be released between the location releases as part of the live content.

Contracts Mode
On top of those new features, we also have Contracts Mode. You'll know this from Absolution. Play-to-create, mark your own targets, choose how to kill them and compete against your friends. IOI will also pick the best of the bunch and put them in the Featured Contracts list so you've got something fresh to play whenever you load up the game.

Live Challenges
Additionally, we have the ambition of adding community-inspired challenges into the game. As you'll have seen from the recent Beta period, the game is full of challenges you can complete to prove your mastery of a location. We are looking into creating new challenges that we can periodically add to the game. These challenges will be an homage to some of the more elaborate, amusing, difficult or creative feats that we see our players complete. As an example, one of the first ‘live challenges’ we are looking at creating is called “Hammer Time” and was inspired by a ‘2AngryGamers’ livestream of our PS4 Beta, where they used only a hammer to knock out almost every guard in the ‘Final Test’.
At this stage, Community-inspired challenges (or whatever we actually decide to name them) are just one of the ideas we are working on to keep the game fresh and live as we go through the season. These are not a guaranteed feature but something we’re testing and trying out.

All of those things are part of the live component of HITMAN. We'll be watching and listening to what you do in our game world and want to shape that world to what you've already done in it.

Numenera invites you to explore a weird and unknown world, playing as a character who doesn't know much and can't understand fully what's happening to him/her. Although the combat system is a little complicated at first (you get used to it), most of the game is not really about fighting but more about exploration, dialogue and decision-making. Every one of the decisions you make will have an influence on the world, the people you meet and yourself. Some of them minor and some very significant.
It's really interesting that in many situations, you don't fully understand what's happening, what you're supposed to do or just what is the right thing to do. Remember PS: Torment, waking up in the morgue, greeted by a talking, floating skull, go meet that guy you never heard about before... well, that's the feeling.
The places you explore couldn't be more alien, yet with a little bit of familiarity. I like the fact that the technology you encounter is so new, so advanced and sophisticated, it almost looks like magic (Clarke's third law right there).

Tides of Numenera is a mixed bag when it comes to recommending it to someone. While the first few hours were quite incredible, and caused me to become excited, these feelings ultimately did not last. The main reason is the combat--it felt like a flaccid♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ There was no real talent system, and the abilities themselves felt underwhelming.
Furthermore, many of the companions you'll be playing with are absolutely useless until the end game. Why, developers, oh why, did you make it this way? You had a beautiful world, and interesting story breaks ("meres") that are slightly similar to Divinity: Original Sin 2 cannibalism trait, except in Divinity you actually have the chance of acquiring new abilities through the memories of others. Still, the meres offered quite a uniqe way of weaving in the story and lore.
Now, one aspect of the game that had me quite enthralled were the various choices you are allowed to make. Some will make no difference, while others might save your life (or make future fights more interesting.)
The story was quite enjoyable, although by the middle of the game you could see where it was going, and know what will be expected of you. Still, some things pleasantly surprised me during the final act.
I think that it's a tad overpriced for the content and all of its flaws, so I'd recommend you buy it at a sale ($30 or less).

This is one of the best, most original games I've played in recent memory. To start, my very small list of gripes:
The ending: I felt the ending was a little lackluster. I loved the revelation of a large chunk of the plot however, I felt the end decisions were too open-ended. I would much prefer to be forced into only a couple of decisions via my choice-making throughtout the game.
Length: I felt the game was too short. I accomplished the vast majority of tasks in my first play through and spent about 30 hours total. This game is so great I just want more of it.
Equipment: I love inventory management and felt that there weren't enough weapon and armor choices.
What I did love
The World: The Ninth World is super cool. I love the mix of ancient, decaying tech with limited magic, some divine interference, and a splash of high-fantasy. If a sequel is made I hope it utilizes this same world with its rich history.
Combat: I love that, especially in the beginning, the use of ability points is soooo agonizing. It makes every decision feel very important and also challenges the player to think outside the box and try to use the environment around them.
The Story: Very fun and interesting story. I felt each chapter did a good job of fleshing out my character and what he/she was. I daresay by the end I actually cared about my character, which rarely happens.
Environmental Interactions: It felt like nearly every other thing could be interacted with, and, most importantly, if a skill check failed it wasn't a big deal because sometimes something even better happened as a result.
In summation, if you enjoy story driven games with inventive combat and good environmental interaction this game is for you.

Tides of Numenera's strength is also its shortcoming.
On the upside you got 20 different ways to solve a quest. On the downside you got 20 total quests in the game. The game is short and I feel that many will just run through it without realising what they missed in the game.
As wide as a puddle. As deep as an ocean.

I've played a number of RPGs and I highly recommend this one. Compared with other text-based games, it has rich descriptions that make the world vibrant, accentuating the unusual setting. The world feels real and your choices have consequences. Taken in isolation, some aspects of the game are under-developed and the combat's a little clunky. In spite of this, I found the game thought-provoking and felt it had a bigger emotional impact than anything I've played in a long time. If you play RPGs for the story and the world, this is one for you.
Lots of early reviews were rather negative, and I appreciate some of their concerns, but many of their criticisms come from unrealistic hype or a rigid idea of what the game should have been. I believe if you approach it with an open mind and engage with the world, the whole experience rises above most CRPGs and approaches the sublime.
