Well, I'm giving the game a thumbs up.  But whereas I've seen many reviews of this game that give it a thumbs down, yet then list its virtues, I likewise will be taking this opportunity to list its many sins.  It does, of course, have the wonderful writing of its spiritual predecessor, so if what you're looking for is a story that will draw you in and blow you away, then what are you waiting for?  Buy the damn thing already!  But as for everything else...
SINS:
1.  Ambiguous dialog options.  Nothing ruins immersion more than looking between several dialog options and thinking... "What?"
2.  OP cyphers with no cause for use.  The game kept giving me awesome cyphers, but even the final fight I was in didn't seem to need them.  In FACT... I managed to get an extremely powerful combat cypher... AFTER the last combat had occured.
3.  Unclear direction.  Occasionally the game left me with nothing much to do except wander around and talk to people at random, hoping to stumble on storyline.  The bloom could be particularly bad for this.
4.  Small party size.  I get that this was for balance, but I started to feel like I couldn't experience everyone's story properly.
5.  Optional main quest portion.  Part of the main quest was in the form of an optional side quest.  I get that this was to underemphasize the side quest, so that its importance would come as a big plot twist, which I'm fine with, but getting out of Sagus without completing that quest would have been trivial, and then where would I be?
6.  Unchallenging combat.  Covered slightly in number 2, but the crisis events were usually trivially easy, and few and far between.  And this annoyed the heck outta me.  I get that I'm here for the story, but this game's spiritual predecessor at least broke up the story with a few sections where you fought rats and demons and undead and crazed philosophers.  This one... had very little, and what was there was generally beaten without so much as a reload.
Well, that's all I can think of.  But like I said, a beautiful game with a great story, so despite my griping, get it anyways, it's a great spiritual successor to the original.

By now you're probably aware of the game's gimmick. It's an emotionally punishing morality based knock off of Dark Heart (Apocalypse Now) masquerading as a generic FPS. The game aims to put you into a series of morally conflicting positions. Situations you would likely have faced in many other FPS's but it tries to humanise your opponents and confront you with the ramifications of your actions. Cute. If you want to get a better idea of what the themes are and how they're implemented Extra Credits has two good videos about it on YT (one with, one without spoilers), if you can put up with the pretentious high-morality fapping to the game.
So let's look at this one three levels: the morality mechanic, the themes of morality and PTSD from a narrative perspective, and the actual quality of the game play otherwise
The themes of morality manifest themselves as game mechanics when you periodically come across “moral” situations and have to make a decision about how to proceed. Here's how they've utterly ♥♥♥♥ed it up:
* At times, and one scene in particular everyone keeps raving about, you're presented the illusion of choice but no actual choice. You do the one thing the game lets you do, and are treated to what I assume was meant to be an emotional cut-scene to punish you for it. I cannot feel bad for doing the thing the game required. This isn't console players blubbering into their controllers, this is the PC master race. We've been dropping chemical weapons on civilians since Postal. You gotta bring something better than that.
* The majority of the time the game misleads you about your options. There are hidden “high morality” alternatives in a lot of cases. Sure it's nice for the game to put explicit and hidden alternatives in, but the thing is you can just play the game the way the game tells you to and it still works fine. There's no reason to look for alternatives. In fact I'd've been more morally invested had I seen the high-morality option and still felt I needed to take the low morality choice.
* And finally, and probably most egregiously: the moral choices you make seem so to have
. Why would I make the moral choice here? I'm trying to get from this level to the next one and I will shoot a civilian in the head if that's what the game says I need to do to progress the story. I absolutely loathe ending changes based on a morality meter (à la Bioshock, Dishonored) but if you implement a morality mechanic it needs to at least change the game-play somehow. The entire game seems to assume that everyone who plays a game like BF or CoD must spend their entire time vacillating over how they could solve each problem in a moral way. I, like I think most normal PC gamers, just did what the game said I should do. I'm not interested in the lives of NPC's who don't even get a name tag. I don't care. It's a game, it's a challenge to get from A to B. You need either REALLY good storytelling or something particularly special to make me feel things, or harder still, to make my feelings factor into my game play style.
The terrible implementation into the game-play not withstanding, the artistic value here is pretty high. The story is kind of interesting, despite its obvious plot-holes, the way they represent constant descent, the psychosis colour schemes, loading screen accusations, the 4th wall breaking. They're not all immediately obvious, but they're there and they're pretty well thought out and it'll give you plenty to mull over and wonder about on a second play-through. I mean yes it's so so agonisingly obvious that this is a port from a console game, and it has what are pretty standard mechanics for a console game I guess so fine, but I'm sitting on PC, wondering why I spend half my time hiding behind a bench or wall or ornamental plant pot, taking turns to fire at enemies who are also hiding behind whatever debris magically happened to be there. The most tactical thing in the game is blowing up explosive barrels or taking advantage of the ridiculously contrived breaking-glass-to-unleash-an-avalanche-of-sand mechanic the whole handful of times the game remembered it wanted that to be a thing. A fortunately all the miniguns scattered around shopping centres can be turned around and used to mow down waves of suicidal enemies.
But the worst, the absolute worst, and this I cannot forgive a game, are your NPC's. In theory you have a sniper and a heavy and you can light up a target for them to take out. Yeah good luck with that. They're useless as all hell, they get in your way a LOT, by the time they eliminate a target for you, you could just have done it yourself since you need to have the reticle on the target anyway to tag them. But to top it off, if they get shot, you need to run in and revive them. And they have no idea of how to not get shot. ♥♥♥♥ stealth, these guys assume that not only are you going to speed-run-n-gun this game, but that you will somehow provide much better cover for them than mere concrete or sandbags ever could, so eschew both in favour of just sitting out in plain sight. Possibly the worst example of NPC's ruining any hope you have of making good tactical choices is one scene where you see a yacht in the desert. Plenty of openings, no aerial cover, and a reasonable amount of open ground between you and it. Open ground which has an inbound truck load of enemies. I wanted to stay put in my indestructible aircraft hull, with a box of nades, a box or ammo, high ground advantage, and crucially, one small controllable entrance. But my highly trained delta force sidekicks thought our only hope for survival would be to run like idiots for the yacht and then stay put half way when I didn't run with them. Needless to say they got mowed down and I lost the game for not reviving them fast enough. Good idea; implement it better. Time to review Undertale!
My review will be as follows-
-Gameplay
-Story
-Characters
-Soundtrack
-Graphics
-Summary
-Gameplay
There really is not alot of real gameplay as you are just walking and checking options
with the few random fights. The encounter rate gets lower the farther You get in the game
which for me is ok. The combat is a standerd turn based RPG system, HOWEVER there is a bullet hell like
way of dodgeing enemy attacks which really got me in the combat. You can also check enemy stats to see if they are hard or not. Which leads me to my major complaint the game is WAY to easy, even on the "Bad route" (Trying to avoid spoilers) even the final boss was easy, but there were some bosses that were at a good difficulty. There are not many stats
in the game like speed, magic ect but that doesnt mean the gameplay is boring. With each level up you gain 2 attack and 4 more HP every 5 levels is 1 Defense. While it says you have 0 Defense or Attack you really have 10 so dont worry. Overall Decent Gameplay
-Gameplay: 7.7/10
-Story
There are 3 routes to take in Undertale each with a wonderful lead up to their final boss (With great music) and the final bosses all have unique attack patterns that set them apart. The story is good there are good times and some sad times in the story from makeing jokes to having a boss almost destroy everything. its a good balance and I think that had thought put into it. However the whole "Spare everyone" did not really sit well with me. I did not feel bad when i killed the final boss of the "Neutral" route because to me they deserve it. If you disagree then thats ok.
-Story: 8/10
-Characters
There are a good amount of characters from skeletons to fish to goat-people weilding fire magic. Some were in one way or another relateable while some were annoying. But they each have their own personality to set one apart from the other. Many people praise for the great humor while i never really laughed although one part did make me have a good laugh. Another thing about the characters is that a few of them might change troughout the story. You may hate a character then at the end care about them. (or you kill them like i did and never see their changes :P) A good example would be (Minor Spoiler) a guard who chases you relentlessly trying to kill you, if you spare the guard. The guard will tell you about their life and what you would need to do to make it out of the Underground.
-Characters: 8/10
-Soundtrack
Holy crap the soundtrack is the best soundtrack i ever heard in gaming. The music is wonderful and sometimes sets the mood to a calm guitar to a crazy "what the hell is happening" music. Its amazing and I never found the 8-Bit music to be a pain.
-Soundtrack: 10/10
-Graphics
I really dont judge a game on its graphics but I do think graphics are important, Undertale has uh well not great graphics. Some people might say it look like a kid drew it :P. To me it was passable. But if you really care about graphics you might be disapointed
-Graphics: 5/10
-Summary
Overall Undertale is one of those games where its either great, meh or bad. If you like a good story and a retro style RPG I recomend it. If your looking for a emotional deep story with a crap ton of gameplay with great graphics then you might want to look for something else. If you disagree with my review, thats ok just dont be like "f*** you". Also dont go near the fanbase lol. Well the cringy side anyways.
-Undertale: 8/10

TL;DR Version:  Well, I enjoyed it more than Fallout 4.
It's Batman Arkham meets Carmageddon and GTA w/ the Mad Max license.  If that doesn't entice you, I don't know what will.
Don't rush through the story missions and do try to unlock fast travel spots ASAP.
Always carry a spare gas can.
------------------
Maybe it was just me, but the game did not feel as repetitive as some others have complained about.  Yes, the landscape looks similar all over, but it's to be expected when you're in the middle of the desert.    Yes, tasks do repeat, but how many games these days don't follow some kind of grind cycle?  I never really felt bored through it, though.  Part of this may be a result of me spending a lot of time clearing scrap sites and knocking out territories as much as I could and really only advanced the story when I needed to do so.  The base story itself doesn't really have a sense of urgency (at least to me) until I start the quests specific to getting the Big Chief (a V8 engine), so in a way I felt more encouraged to take my time.  It probably would have felt like more of a grind if I just blitzed through the story missions ASAP and didn't do the side quest options.  So if there is one recommendation for playing a new game, it's take your time and explore.
I would also recommend unlocking fast-travel spots as soon as you can.  The Hot Air Baloons (which allow you to scout the area) as as fast-travel spots, but so do the Death Run spots.  Just drive right into the Death Run spot (not just passed it when gives you the bio for the place) and you have and automatic fast travel zone.  It does makes traversing the desert a lot quicker.  One thing I will note is by using fast-travel, you always spawn with your Magnum Opus.  So if you actually do play around with the specialty cars (not counting your Archangel mods for the Opus), it will reset and you will need to go back to a stronghold to re-obtain your car.
The combat is mostly akin to the Arkham games, but now you have a shotgun, shivs, and can actually use the melee weapons.  Controls feel very responsive.  I don't feel “quite” as responsive as Batman in Arkham City, but I am playing as burnout ex-cop/soldier with bad knees and a death wish, so it isn't jarring for me.  It might just be me.  Even with that, the vast majority of times I died it was due to stupidity and not bad or unresponsive controls.  The camera can, at times, go a bit stupid.  That said, it's not enough to detract me from the experience.
I have now beaten the game, but not 100%.  The ending was bittersweet, which is fitting for the Mad Max universe.  At some point I may go back and just scrounge around for scrap and history relics and collect the one car I am missing, but for the most part I am done and ready to tackle another game.  I will say I actually want to go back spelunking in the game at a later point, which I can't say about some other games I have beaten.
My largest gripe about the game is actually nothing to do with the overall scenery, story, mechanics, or anything else of that nature.  It's actually the pointless product placement rammed in it via the (admittedly minor) DLC which comes with purchase.  Two of the hood ornaments and one of the cars unlocked in the game are just ads for Rockstar Energy Drinks.  Kind of wrecks the immersion just a bit.  The hood ornaments are at least useful in early game (before you unlock the others), but the unlocked car is a pig's♥♥♥♥♥♥
All that aside, I still enjoyed my time in the game.  As of this writing, the game is currently retailing for $19.99 and I would consider it money well spent.  Lord knows I've bought other more expensive games which were greater letdowns.

I've never played a HITMAN game before but a friend gave me a code for it and it's already one of my most favorite games to come out in 2016. The graphics are stunning and how you finish these missions is 100% up to you. There's no wrong way to complete a mission.

First let me say that I played the original Hitman: Codename 47 for probably 2-300 hours when it first came out? I was rocking it hard on my Pentium 3, as it was the first game of it's kind that I had ever seen; and it blew me away.
So now we're y'know, 15 years on and there have been many imitators and some stealth action games that are definitely better, and some stumbling blocks in the Hitman series as well. Some are great, some are bad, everyone has their favorites and  everyone (seemingly besides me) hates Absolution....
Well this years version of Hitman is pretty great. You have 47, looking slightly made over but voiced by the right man for the job, and since you spend most of the time looking at the back of his head anyway it's all good. You've got Diana, and the agency and a new batch of interesting things happening, all of which is still quite vague and hazy given the nature of the episodic release they've decided to go with this time round, so I'll focus on the good and the bad instead of the DRM business everyone else seems to complain about.
Good:
Throwing stuff!
Stealth is still fun, disguising is still fun and done well.
Diversity of levels, creativity of the hits.
Graphics (if you can handle it, early release FPS stutters were horrible).
It's the Hitman we've all come to know and love, just upgraded a little and seemingly taking itself somewhat less serious than before, while still being incredibly good.
Bad:
AI sometimes is moronic, othertimes they're mutants with insane powers of omnipotence and perfect accuracy.
There's the always online thing, but seriously in modern times if your computer isn't constantly connected to the internet then what the heck are you doing?
FPS Stuttering and not so hot rendering when the levels first load which usually clears up within a minute or so.
Some people seem to genuinely not like this rendition?
I'm not really sure what all the complaining is about? At least this isn't a deep sad emotional thing like Absolution which is I think why everyone kind of hated it despite it's excellent gameplay. This game also has excellent gameplay, and intentionally bakes in clues as to assassination options, as well as a lot of other fun oddball stuff and "mastery" of levels and achievements all which give you the sense that they were truly going for replayability with each and every level of this game. It's almost not so much a story based "GAME" as it is the devs practically breaking the fourth wall and saying "Here's a bunch of hitman missions loosely tied together with a story. Go crazy!!"

I was kinda worried when I realized it was a sci-fi game, but they've really captured the essence of Planescape: Torment, despite the setting being so... new. Frankly, apart from a few things that are rather too outlandish, I'm very impressed with the setting. It's not easy to create a compelling setting without relying on previously-known elements, but they've pulled it off.
I wouldn't necessarily recommend playing this game and Planescape: Torment back-to-back. I think much of the beauty of Numenera happens when something is vaguely reminiscent of something you saw long ago... especially since that fits the theme of the game so well. But I can recommend you buy both games, play Planescape: Torment now, and then play Numenera some time later. ;)

This is an excellent game, but it won't appeal to everyone. Don't expect an another Baldur's Gate. There is not much combat here and about ~90% of the game consists of reading. I found the story interesting and engaging. There are many similarities with the storyline of Planescape: Torment, which is an obvious nod to its fans. However, it should be noted that TToN is neither a sequel nor a prequel to the PS:T and should not be treated as such. The world and the characters are different and while some concepts are similar, TToN is a separate game.
It should be noted that this is not an open world and the locations themselves are not that big. There are two "hubs" and various smaller locations. When you leave the first hub at a certain point in the game, you won't be able to return (the player is notified about this). Same in case of the second hub. All in all, exploration is not a heavy focus of TToN. This game is a bit similar to Shadowrun Returns: Dragonfall and Shadowrun Returns: Hong Kong in that regard.
TToN begs for more content, because it's obvious that during the development many cuts had to be made. I would love to see an expansion, a DLC or a Director's Cut edition, although I'm afraid that we won't get any. Anyway, even without an expansion/DLC/DC, I will replay TToN in a few months and I'm sure that I will enjoy it.
During the course of my playthrough I had one CTD and the game froze two or three times. During some of the longer dialogues, the dialogue window can become laggy, which is annoying although not game-breaking. Fortunately, I was able to finish all quests without problems.
IMO many reviews on Steam are unfair. This game definitely deserves a recommendation even if it's not perfect. I guess that the standard price (~45 €) may be a bit too steep, especially considering the fact that TToN was KS-funded. ~30 € would probably be more appropriate. If you cannot afford TToN ATM, be sure to put it on your wishlist to watch for sales.

If you're the kind of gamer that finds themselves impatiently flipping through dialogue to get to combat, then this one isn't for you. This game is heavily weighted on its story and the results of your character's decisions. You can sort of brute force your way through the world if you know the twists and turns, but trying to do so on your first playthrough will leave you lost and frustrated.
Combat is easy, sparse, and a little too simplified.
Graphics (for an indie isometric RPG) vary between poor and above average, depending on the scene you're in. Character models exhibit an unusual blandness.
Character development could use some fleshing out. However, the options available still allow for decent customization and replayability.
The real reason to play is for the setting and story. Though a little rough around the edges, it's well-written, fantastical, and engrossing. This is a game that really begs for additional content / sequels. It's worth supporting if you like story-rich, choose-your-adventure style games, and weird fantasy/sci-fi/cyber-steam-whateverpunk worlds.

At the time of writing, I'm a bit over 14 hours into the game, which has, in my opinion, given me enough experience with it to rate it fairly (at least up to this point - I'm almost out of Sagus Cliffs, I believe).
Without prattling about, so far Torment: ToN is superb, an amazing and worthy successor to PS:T (I've played Planescape only last year, and for the first time, so there was no nostalgia clouding my judgement of it).
It starts off slow, and its very intro is not the most spectacular event. The falling sequence and initial introductions won't immediately grip you like PS:T's mortuary tutorial. After a bit of chit-chat with your starting two companions, you'll be set free to roam a small-ish area called Reef of Fallen Worlds. It's an interesting, flashy and mysterious location, although without much interactivity.
The real fun begins some thirty minutes into the game (if you're a curious person like myself and touch and activate everything in sight), when you'll be presented with the city of Sagus Cliffs. There's a lot to do in Sagus, you can join two different factions, explore the uses of many flashy and colorful numenera, small and large, and find some very unique and interesting characters. You've got your criminal alleyways (more of a large cave in this case), government district, slums (on the very edge of the cliff Sagus was built on), air-docks and other memorable locales, such as a tavern made especially for Sagus Cliffs' psychics to rest in.
As for the combat, there are no random encounters and each combat situation (or 'Crisis', in Torment's terms) can be averted or forcibly stopped through persuasion, deception, intimidation, creative use of environment etc. If, by mistake or on purpose, combat does ensue, you'll be thrown in a turn-based brawl and you better start thinking tactically. Battles work something like X-Com, without the cover and a bit more simplified. You have to wage your chances of each action's success and failure, and you can expend extra Effort from one of your three pools - Might, Speed and Intellect, to improve those chances and increase potential damage. Those pools are character-specific and refill through item use or fully while sleeping. They are also expended when you try an especially difficult task, like persuading someone to do your bidding, climbing a particularly steep cliff (and coming down from it), lifting debris etc.
The core of PS:T was its personal stories, interesting and quirky characters and unique companions. T:ToN has, so far, proven worthy in all of those respects. There's something intriguing about each companion, but they keep to themselves; if you want to know them better, take them with you and talk, share your opinions and watch them react to your decisions. Your companions will, after a time, reveal theirs. Without spoiling anything, just to grab your attention, your companions range from a combat-inefficient girl with a god in her pocket to an overly-energetic 'heroic adventurer' with a strange golden glow which he doesn't seem to notice and odd, impersonal thoughts (if you've got the Scan Thoughts ability) which give the impression there's something very off about him.
I could write about Tides of Numenera for days, but I don't want to spoil this experience for anyone. I've got over 14 hours out of this and my gut tells me there's much more of the game I haven't seen. If you liked PS:T, you'll love this, and if you haven't, try both of them out. Both games share ideas, structure and design philosophy, but their tone, characters and storyline are distinctly different.

I don't know what to say about this game, so here is a recipe for pancakes,
Ingredients:
4tbsp plain flour (about 100g)
1 large free range egg
½ pint semi-skimmed milk + water (about 300ml - ¾ milk ¼ water)
Pinch of salt
Butter for frying
How to make pancakes:
Sieve the flour and salt into a large bowl and make a well in the mixture.
Break in the egg and stir to make a breadcrumby mix.
In a jug add 1/3 of a pint of milk and top up with water to make 1/2 a pint (200ml milk, 100ml water) - this makes a lovely light batter.
Add the milk and the water mix bit by bit, beating constantly to avoid lumps.
Tip:*If you have a food processor just throw all the ingredients in and zap until smooth!
Pop a large frying pan over a medium heat.
Add a large knob of butter (roughly 50g) and melt.
Pour the excess butter into a small bowl and reserve it for later.
Using a ladle pour a spoonful of the pancake batter into the hot pan and swirl to get a full covering - cook for about 1 min each side (it's ready when it's easy to flip over).
Serve immediately with sugar and lemon or other exciting toppings. We love cheese and Marmite for an extra British twist! Delicious!!

Becoming jealous of Dan's bromance with his best friend
Dino, the evil princess turns to dinonapping in a desperate bid to get Dan outside and away from his man cave. After a lifetime of rescuing princesses, collecting coins, avoiding spikes and watching out for pitfalls, it's time to do the complete opposite.
Playing  through 20+ levels over 4 distinct worlds, you will slowly retrain your brain in the ways of the platformer. Starting with ignoring all road signs since they usually point straight toward death. Each level has hidden collectables which after further progress gives you the ability to unlock
sidequests. Timed leaderboards were also available for speedrunners. Would suggesting using a gamepad but controls were manageable with a kb+mouse.
Outside of the constant tongue in cheek humour the visuals are where the game really stands out. Rendered beautifully in 2.5D and standing somewhere between old classics like Super Mario World and the modern era of platformers. Couple that with a wonderful soundtrack by
of DKC, SMW, Megaman (and more!) fame, which only added to the nostalgia.
While 20 levels may not seem like a lot of content, Default Dan will make you rage and keep coming back just to perfect runs. For it's decent price point and the bizarrely backwards trip down memory lane it gets my recommendation. Cheers. :)

First let me say that I played the original Hitman: Codename 47 for probably 2-300 hours when it first came out? I was rocking it hard on my Pentium 3, as it was the first game of it's kind that I had ever seen; and it blew me away.
So now we're y'know, 15 years on and there have been many imitators and some stealth action games that are definitely better, and some stumbling blocks in the Hitman series as well. Some are great, some are bad, everyone has their favorites and  everyone (seemingly besides me) hates Absolution....
Well this years version of Hitman is pretty great. You have 47, looking slightly made over but voiced by the right man for the job, and since you spend most of the time looking at the back of his head anyway it's all good. You've got Diana, and the agency and a new batch of interesting things happening, all of which is still quite vague and hazy given the nature of the episodic release they've decided to go with this time round, so I'll focus on the good and the bad instead of the DRM business everyone else seems to complain about.
Good:
Throwing stuff!
Stealth is still fun, disguising is still fun and done well.
Diversity of levels, creativity of the hits.
Graphics (if you can handle it, early release FPS stutters were horrible).
It's the Hitman we've all come to know and love, just upgraded a little and seemingly taking itself somewhat less serious than before, while still being incredibly good.
Bad:
AI sometimes is moronic, othertimes they're mutants with insane powers of omnipotence and perfect accuracy.
There's the always online thing, but seriously in modern times if your computer isn't constantly connected to the internet then what the heck are you doing?
FPS Stuttering and not so hot rendering when the levels first load which usually clears up within a minute or so.
Some people seem to genuinely not like this rendition?
I'm not really sure what all the complaining is about? At least this isn't a deep sad emotional thing like Absolution which is I think why everyone kind of hated it despite it's excellent gameplay. This game also has excellent gameplay, and intentionally bakes in clues as to assassination options, as well as a lot of other fun oddball stuff and "mastery" of levels and achievements all which give you the sense that they were truly going for replayability with each and every level of this game. It's almost not so much a story based "GAME" as it is the devs practically breaking the fourth wall and saying "Here's a bunch of hitman missions loosely tied together with a story. Go crazy!!"
All in all? Quite enjoyable for me. Easy to play through with the controller OR the M+KB which is how I control primarily as of writing, so I can actually aim the weapons.

By now you're probably aware of the game's gimmick. It's an emotionally punishing morality based knock off of Dark Heart (Apocalypse Now) masquerading as a generic FPS. The game aims to put you into a series of morally conflicting positions. Situations you would likely have faced in many other FPS's but it tries to humanise your opponents and confront you with the ramifications of your actions. Cute. If you want to get a better idea of what the themes are and how they're implemented Extra Credits has two good videos about it on YT (one with, one without spoilers), if you can put up with the pretentious high-morality fapping to the game.
So let's look at this one three levels: the morality mechanic, the themes of morality and PTSD from a narrative perspective, and the actual quality of the game play otherwise
The themes of morality manifest themselves as game mechanics when you periodically come across “moral” situations and have to make a decision about how to proceed. Here's how they've utterly ♥♥♥♥ed it up:
* At times, and one scene in particular everyone keeps raving about, you're presented the illusion of choice but no actual choice. You do the one thing the game lets you do, and are treated to what I assume was meant to be an emotional cut-scene to punish you for it. I cannot feel bad for doing the thing the game required. This isn't console players blubbering into their controllers, this is the PC master race. We've been dropping chemical weapons on civilians since Postal. You gotta bring something better than that.
* The majority of the time the game misleads you about your options. There are hidden “high morality” alternatives in a lot of cases. Sure it's nice for the game to put explicit and hidden alternatives in, but the thing is you can just play the game the way the game tells you to and it still works fine. There's no reason to look for alternatives. In fact I'd've been more morally invested had I seen the high-morality option and still felt I needed to take the low morality choice.
* And finally, and probably most egregiously: the moral choices you make seem so to have
. Why would I make the moral choice here? I'm trying to get from this level to the next one and I will shoot a civilian in the head if that's what the game says I need to do to progress the story. I absolutely loathe ending changes based on a morality meter (à la Bioshock, Dishonored) but if you implement a morality mechanic it needs to at least change the game-play somehow. The entire game seems to assume that everyone who plays a game like BF or CoD must spend their entire time vacillating over how they could solve each problem in a moral way. I, like I think most normal PC gamers, just did what the game said I should do. I'm not interested in the lives of NPC's who don't even get a name tag. I don't care. It's a game, it's a challenge to get from A to B. You need either REALLY good storytelling or something particularly special to make me feel things, or harder still, to make my feelings factor into my game play style.
The terrible implementation into the game-play not withstanding, the artistic value here is pretty high. The story is kind of interesting, despite its obvious plot-holes, the way they represent constant descent, the psychosis colour schemes, loading screen accusations, the 4th wall breaking. They're not all immediately obvious, but they're there and they're pretty well thought out and it'll give you plenty to mull over and wonder about on a second play-through. While we're at it, the general visuals are pretty sweet actually, so good job there.
I won't say that graphics
matter, or that narrative
matter, but I will say and I will defend this to the hilt, they matter
than mechanics. A game with a pretty poor delivery can still be good if its mechanics are solid. But the opposite is rarely true. Spec Ops: The Line does
have good mechanics. I mean yes it's so so agonisingly obvious that this is a port from a console game, and it has what are pretty standard mechanics for a console game I guess so fine, but I'm sitting on PC, wondering why I spend half my time hiding behind a bench or wall or ornamental plant pot, taking turns to fire at enemies who are also hiding behind whatever debris magically happened to be there. The most tactical thing in the game is blowing up explosive barrels or taking advantage of the ridiculously contrived breaking-glass-to-unleash-an-avalanche-of-sand mechanic the whole handful of times the game remembered it wanted that to be a thing. A fortunately all the miniguns scattered around shopping centres can be turned around and used to mow down waves of suicidal enemies.
But the worst, the absolute worst, and this I cannot forgive a game, are your NPC's. In theory you have a sniper and a heavy and you can light up a target for them to take out. Yeah good luck with that. They're useless as all hell, they get in your way a LOT, by the time they eliminate a target for you, you could just have done it yourself since you need to have the reticle on the target anyway to tag them. But to top it off, if they get shot, you need to run in and revive them. And they have no idea of how to not get shot. ♥♥♥♥ stealth, these guys assume that not only are you going to speed-run-n-gun this game, but that you will somehow provide much better cover for them than mere concrete or sandbags ever could, so eschew both in favour of just sitting out in plain sight. Possibly the worst example of NPC's ruining any hope you have of making good tactical choices is one scene where you see a yacht in the desert. Plenty of openings, no aerial cover, and a reasonable amount of open ground between you and it. Open ground which has an inbound truck load of enemies. I wanted to stay put in my indestructible aircraft hull, with a box of nades, a box or ammo, high ground advantage, and crucially, one small controllable entrance. But my highly trained delta force sidekicks thought our only hope for survival would be to run like idiots for the yacht and then stay put half way when I didn't run with them. Needless to say they got mowed down and I lost the game for not reviving them fast enough. If the game had let me I'd've shot them in the first 5 minutes and gone on alone but alas the point of the game seems less about killing the enemies and staying alive than it does basically babysitting two idiots with the survival instincts of a screamapillar through a war zone dodging bullets to shoot them full of adrenalin.
Over all the idea of the game was fine – put players in a situation where they question their actions despite playing a game, or even question their actions in all games. The problem is it didn't work, must like the “Would you kindly” scene in Bioshock, it didn't work. Because I did what I did because that's how you make game progress. The designers may have tried to go meta and accept that players rage-quitting would just be one of their “endings”, or try to argue that the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanics are there to fill you with a sense of unease to foreshadow the descent into madness theme, but really, it didn't work. Good idea; implement it better. The visuals were stunning and some of the little bits and pieces of depression were nice (like the slowly decaying soldier in the menu screen) but the core mechanics were♥♥♥♥♥♥ the game-play was highly linear, it was all cover based shooting, the shooting itself was clunky and frustrating, the NPC's are worse than the enemy, and even the storyline needed tidying up. If you're making an FPS, make an FPS; once you've managed to do that well, then we can talk about themes and story. But at the end of the day morality does NOT belong in games. Old-style isometric RPG, very similar to Planescape: Torment and Baldur's Gate 2. It differs from these older games in having even more lore, lower tempo, and much less combat -- I'm about 20 hours in, and I think I've fought two battles, total. You can nearly always talk your way out, and get as much or more XP.  Choices have consequences, and you can basically think of this game as the biggest and best Choose Your Own Adventure book  you've ever read. And I mean read, there's a LOT of text to read here.
The game is set a billion years in the future. Civilizations have risen, reached for the stars, and collapsed over and over and over again. In the game, technology level is approximately medieval, but ultra-high-tech relics from earlier civilizations litter the world, and can be used for good or evil. The game is billed as the "spiritual successor" to the fantastic RPG Planescape: Torment. It isn't quite THAT good, but it's good, and it does remind me very much of Planescape: Torment.
Anyway, highly recommended to the person who RPGs but find the constant battles in Baldur's Gate 2 annoying, or who would like a game reminiscent of  Planescape: Torment, or who just wants a novel and intelligent RPG and don't mind reading a lot.

Ultimately, my verdict on this game is that I can definitely recommend it, while still having many points of criticism.
The visual style is starkly different from the original Torment. Whereas the former has a horror vibe, Numenera is vibrant and colourful. The element that carries over from the first game is the idea of the setting as a melting pot for lots of different weird concepts. Secondly, some story elements such as the protagonist being unable to die properly are carried over.
T:ToN really has more in common with the Planescape setting in general than with the prequel's interpretation of it. This can be good or bad, but if the dark horror vibe contributed to your appraisal of the first game, then this is clearly bad.
The quality of the writing is good, for comparison with more recent games clearly better than Pillars of Eternity. The writing style is also uncannily similar to the original in some places. What we lack is really slightly more interesting companions.
Game mechanics-wise T:ToN is in many regards opposite to the first game. The combat system is excellent but underused. Combat situations ("crises" in the lingo of the game) are all too rare but often offer interesting tactical choices. Hard optional crises are sadly all but non-existent, leaving the existing ones like a quickly fading sweet savoury drop on the tongue, a taste of what could have been. Where the first game required you to min-max attributes to not miss out on story, T:ToN instead offers you many different solutions to reach to reach the same end. This does not pan out well and leaves you with a feeling of handling any problem with ease with the many consumables spread out through the game.
In the end, the shortcomings of the game are mostly irritating because you feel it could have been so much better, but it is worth playing and buying for the writing alone.

TORMENT: TIDES OF NUMENERA (alpha/early access), v0.1.2
PUBLISHER/DEVELOPER: InXile Entertainment
GENRE – RPG (Infinity Engine-type)
THE BASICS:
You are a blank slate – The latest of many vessels that a chaotic deity has chosen to empower. Some of your brethren have long since passed on from this world; others are very much alive. You had a former life – several, in fact – and bits and pieces of them come back to you as the game progresses and events happen around you. Whoever you were before you were “lucky” enough to be chosen, they're gone now.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
You start out within your own freshly-minted mindscape. You perform a few simple tasks, and how you choose to resolve them determines how many points you have to spend in each of three stat “pools” (might, sped, intelligence) once you begin the game proper. You also get to decide which of several past lives will influence your skill loadout – but, just before things get serious, the game gives you the opportunity to choose a new loadout, improve one or two of your stat pools, and figure out just what you want to be: A Glaive, well-versed in the use of arms and armor? A Jack, nimble and silver-tongued? Or a Nano, who proves that sufficiently advanced tech really is indistinguishable from magic?
Once you've decided who and what you are, you face your first great struggle: A combat tutorial that has you defend your mind against the first incursion of The Sorrow, a mind♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥entity that really has it in for your sire's vessels. As in, with murderous intent.
Once you've dealt with that, you are able to emerge into the real world, where you find that your body heals miraculously quickly (well, in the story; not during normal gameplay), and that death is really more of a temporary inconvenience than anything else. Sometimes, death will bring you back to your mindscape, which has since been altered in some way. Other times, you'll end up in a gradually-expanding, grey void. You could also wind up in the company of some friendly cannibal cultists who really just wanna have a nibble of your juicy flesh...in exchange for proper compensation, of course.
CONTROLS:
Fully mouse-driven with optional keyboard commands and shortcuts. Click to move (no hold-to-move, though), move mouse to the edge to scroll, etc. During both dialogues and in combat (“crises,” as this game calls them), you choose to “invest” points from your pools to improve your odds of success. Your base chances are based on your skills, and having points in Edge can reduce the costs, even down to zero. The pools replenish only when you take a rest, and upon the occasional critical success (in which case, you only get back what you spent on that action), so you have to choose carefully. Currently, doing anything useful as a Nano (mage) requires a massive Intelligence pool, unless you've also put several skill points into weaponry in order to give yourself a realistic chance to actually hit something.
Interacting with the plethora of devices, statuary, pools of detritus, et al, throughout the areas will grant you new toys to play with (Cyphers), and occasionally, even a shiny new weapon or suit of armor. Just be careful – Each character can only hold so many Cyphers before beginning to take stat penalties (aka “Fetters”) simply due to overload.
GRAPHICS:
Looks like a world with elements of both fantasy and advanced tech (mostly the former), set up to mesh together. While the setting has a definite Steampunk vibe to it, you won't see any people running around in brown & brass overalls with goggles on their heads, wielding wrenches as they chase down their lazy assistants. What you will find are merchants and hidebound officials; public executions and slavers (who, of course, are just making sure that those poor folks have a place to live and food to eat...or so they say); sentient machines and rock-encrusted giant bugs who eat electricity; airship captains, war veterans, and that one guy whose body is covered in toes.
SOUND:
Good music. Ambient sounds in the city suit the area. Combat audio works, as well.
OVERALL:
A great start to a Kickstarted game by folks who have shown obvious love for the Infinity Engine (Baldur's Gate/Icewind Dale/Planescape: Torment) type of CRPGs. The team behind this also did the original PS: Torment, to which this is a successor, of sorts. It was made in the modern engine that Pillars of Eternity uses. . Nearly 100 thousand people backed this game on KS.
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:
Pros:
Interesting, minimalist stat “pools” system rather than the usual suspects; this is based on a wholly separate PnP RPG system than D&D, and it shows – in a good way
Mild overtones of Steampunk without hitting the user over the head with the stereotypical Steampunk “look”
Nice music; the voice acting is well-done
Lots and lots and lots of dialogue. According to the loading screens, the game had over a million lines set up for it as of this past Spring, with more to come
Cons:
Still suffers from the “Linear warriors, quadratic wizards” issue that all RPGs ultimately face. Physical combatants improve at a steady, predictable pace, while Nanos start out with maybe 2-3 spells per rest, tops, and even that assumes that they don't use their Intelligence pool on smooth talking an NPC or delving into their knowledge of ancient history, for example. “Magic” ability use (and some others, as well) during combat requires you to burn off points from the relevant ability pool, and is not reduced by Edge

You just can't describe the feelings you get from this game. It's mellow, but also filled with monster slaying and crazy weapons that make Mega Man's arsenal look like a toybox. The process of finding materials is enjoyable, with nearly every trip underground revealing more ores, treasure chests (which can contain some of those weapons, and cool gear too!) and more enemies to test yourself against. The game can suck you in for hours at a time, which you spend working toward goal after goal. Cool! You finally made that Blade of Grass you wanted. Now you can try to free that mysterious old man guarding the dungeon from his curse. After that... This NPC needs a house. Let's see what you can come up with, huh? The game is just filled to bursting with cool stuff. Almost every item feels unique, with unique effects, attack radiuses, designs, attack speeds, damage, uses, and ways of obtaining them. Interface is great, too. You can sort your inventory in the middle of a fight seamlessly, thanks to the fact that you can still attack while your inventory's up. The only complaint I have is that the first few nights seem to drag on, since you probably aren't confident fighting off zombies and demon eyes with a copper shortsword. But it'll open up soon after that. Also, the game costs ten bucks. That's really freaking awesome.

One night in the World of Jihan Fahira, Valencia woke up with a set of tools in her inventory. The land was green, filled with trees and wild plants. The rabbits and squirrels running around, the bird chirps, it was quite peaceful even though she wokes up with no memories on her mind. But there are also some weird creatures running amuck, like this blue blobs jumping around.
Not knowing what to do and where she came from, she did what her instinct told her to do, survive.
After walking for a while, she saw a person strolls peacefully. So she greets him and maybe he knows this world more. After approaching him, he introduce himself as ' Jeff the Guide'."This is your new Home" Jeff said. New Home? So she will be staying here forever?
"If you want to survive, you will need to create weapons and shelter. Start by chopping down trees and gathering wood." Jeff speaks with a calming tone.
So she chopped some trees, lots of trees. With some woods in her pockets she try to build her own shelter. She doesnt remember how, its like these architectural and craftsman skills has been implanted to her brain and muscle memory. Putting together some wood and placing it carefully to make a livable shelter of her own. When she asked Jeff where do he lives, Jeff just smiles. "Wherever i can find a place to sit." well that was weird.
Come to think of it, Jeff told her to make weapons. What for? The Blobs? The World was already peaceful as it is. The Night comes, Valencia doesnt feel that tired as she has an infinite amount of stamina. So she thought to wander the beautiful night alone maybe chop some more wood or find some ore to mine. After a couple of miles, she saw something flew in the sky. Is that a ball? And the ball keeps coming closer to her. It was a giant eyeball, with veins stretch out of its core, looking at her as if its going to kill her. She was so scared that she ran as fast as she could to her shelter. But the eyeball keep chasing and tackled her into the ground. She then uses her pickaxe to puncture the eyeball, putting it on the ground. The blood squirts and some chunk of it explodes on the ground. She thought it was over but then she heard an agressive moaning from nearby. It gets closer and closer. She cant believe her eyes. an army of corpses roams around the land. "Stay Back!" she screams. She tried to fight them with her pickaxe but the numbers of the corpses got the best of her. Her arm was ripped off and her head got bit. The corpses starts munching her entrails and she screams in pain knowing this is the end of her. All fading to black.
After a while Valencia woke up at the first place she woke up. " I thought i was dead" she mumbles. She ran as fast as she could to her shelter and reminded on what Jeff said to craft some weapons. So she crafted some bow and arrows, jumped to the rooftop of her shelter. These creature of the nights are surrounding her shelter but she doesnt falter. "COME AT ME YOU WORTHLESS TRASH" She starts shooting at their heads, killing the corpses. Using her pickaxe she slashed every flying eyeballs coming at her. After all the blood spilled she starts to scream internally and that screams turned into laughter. She starts to enjoy the bloodrage and head on straight to face the army of the dead, only ends up to be killed again.
She woke up again at the same place, this time its already in the morning. All the creatures has vanished and nowhere to be seen. "I Can't die" She thought. Realizing that shes an immortal in these plains made her think if she could make it alone. So she stands up and determined to prepare more for the upcoming nights. Survival is not an option, its a must.
Then suddenly a person appears at the same place she spawns.
"Where am i? " He asked. At this point Valencia knew that this person is the same as she is. She grins and pull out her hands.
"This is your new home. If you want to survive, you will need to create weapons and shelter. Start by chopping down trees and gathering wood."

When I first started hearing about Dream Daddy, I thought it was going to be a creepy, kinky kind of thing, because dating sims are usually...well, rather gross [to me].
But I decided to give it a go anyway, and I'm so glad I did. It's actually really funny and makes so. many. references. It even referenced Die Antwoord, which made my little heart happy. On top of being funny, it's actually really wholesome and heartwarming at times.
The characters are all very well written and designed, and I love how they're all flawed; I also love how you can either help them overcome their flaws, or you can let them keep on dawdlin' by with heavy drinking problems or just severe insecurity, whatever ails them.
Create-a-Dad was done beautifully, because you can make your Dadsona look so ridiculous that if you start taking the game too seriously for a moment, once you see him again, you're brought back down to earth. (You can also make a fairly attractive Dadsona, but he won't be nearly as hot as the datable dads. ;D)
Lastly, major props for inclusion. There's a super diverse set of characters, and even one that is canonically transgender!
Overall, I give it a 10/10. It was lots of fun and had some great stories!

Mad Max opens with as direct a setup as you could hope for: bad guys stole Max's car, he meets a fanatical mechanic building a bigger badder car, and they agree to work together to build the biggest baddest car and kick the bad guys butts. There's the hook of the game, and its biggest strength: putting together your very own rad wasteland death machine is super compelling. You're never far from the next substantial upgrade to your Magnum Opus, as it's called, which pulls you along through a typical array of Open World Action Game Activities.
With the exception of a handful of story missions and odd jobs for some of the less evil warlords, those activities are mostly what you'll be doing for your 20-plus hours in Mad Max's gorgeously rendered wasteland. And really, you'll mostly be clearing camps. There are nominally a few varieties of camp, but they mostly boil down to tearing down the camp's outer defenses from your car, then running in and punching a lot of dudes. Melee combat in Mad Max is a simplified version of the standard design from games like the Batman Arkham series or Shadow of Mordor. The simplification is justified by Max's character: he doesn't go in for a bunch of fancy flipping around when he can just punch a dude real hard. Some fine animation work reinforces this, making fights look weighty and brutal. Even so, such a simple combat system in such a long game gets repetitive by the end.
Up to this point, Mad Max would get a marginal recommendation: it goes cheap on sales, get it then if you're into the genre and setting. What tips the scale is the hard dive it takes near the end, so I need to talk vaguely of spoiler things. The rest of this paragraph has vague spoilers about the last part of the game.
I have to give Mad Max a thumbs down, which I hate doing because there's so much good in it. The wasteland is one of the most beautiful in video games, and it's so cool making your Magnum Opus incrementally more awesome. But hoo boy, that ending drags everything down. I'll update my marginal recommendation: if you're into the genre and setting, get it cheap, then stop playing immediately after that one big fight in Gastown, you'll know it when you get there. Pretend that's the ending and you'll have a far better time.

All the mechanics work great, but this is a prime example of a game that is too big, something the developer Avalanche Studios, creators of the Just Cause franchise, seem to do a lot in their games. While Just Cause has many different methods of travel, Mad Max has only one, drive. The driving is good, it has weight behind it and the car combat hasn't been done anywhere else, but the enviroments are typical Mad Max large open deserts. Thats not to say they're bad enviroments, a lot of effort went into the world design, the entire map is vertical despite being one big desert. You start in the ocean bed and make your way up sand dunes until eventually you're driving past church steeples submerged in the sand. But at the end of the day, they're still open deserts, with the only things populating them being ubisoft icons; 100s of scavenging locations (to upgrade max and his car), dozens of camps and a massive amount of destructable collectables. The game could've benefitted from a smaller game world.
The gameplay loop of exploring/fighting, getting scrap and improving max and his car (which has nice aesthetic and stat increases) is really great at short bursts. I haven't even left the 2 large ocean areas yet, since I just pop on for an hour and play until it peaks my interest. Story is alright, obviously not the focus, but I would've liked to see a bit more effort after Fury Road's decent attempt. Again, it's one of those 'Ubisoft' styled games where there're only 10-20 actual story levels in the game intermingled with outposts and repetitive side content. On foot combat is great, although it is essentially Batman Arkham's combat. Get the game if you're going to play it in bursts, otherwise it'll drive you mad.
I'd probably give it a 6/10. Above average and worth a glance but the fact that I can't get myself to properly sit down with it and play for an extended amount of time on account of it being too repetitive means it's not an all-around 'good' game. If you want something similar but executed better, try Shadow of Mordor, the Batman Arkham games and Just Cause. As I said earlier however, the car combat while underutilised is definitely unique.

Best story in a video game I've seen, hands down. It even surpasses Planescape: Torment in some regards. The ending is superb, and the amount of details the writers put in the universe, the characters and the story is staggering.
The gameplay is also surprisingly strong. Where Planescape: Torment was built around conversations and most other elements weren't very well thought out, Tides of Numenera also introduces a complex system of interaction with characters and objects through using various skills, such as Smashing, Persuasion or Lore knowledge, and the amount of possible interactions is enormous. The interaction may fail, which sometimes leads to unpredictable (not necessarily negative) outcomes. These interactions are also the cornerstone of the combat system, where, aside from the usual attacks and spells, you can interact with objects nearby to damage or disable your enemies or to shield or heal your group, or sometimes you can talk to some of the enemy characters and convince them to lay down their weapons.
The soundtrack is amazing; I haven't checked, but I strongly suspect that the composer is the same as in Planescape: Torment, or, at the very least, he/she was strongly inspired by it. The visuals are dated and don't always match the narration, but the artists did an a good job with the engine and managed to create very atmospheric locations.
---
My only points of criticism are the companions and the sound effects. The companions are by no means boring or poorly written, but somehow they aren't very memorable. Where Planescape: Torment had a flying skull, a naughty tiefling, a levitating burning man or a succubus keeping a brothel specialized on intellectual activities, Tides of Numenera has a bunch of humans (except for Oom; Oom is on par with his/its Planescape counterparts) with somewhat generic sub-stories. Sound effects are good on their own, but their volume isn't balanced properly, and every so often some annoying sound will dominate the background, making it difficult to read the dialogue lines without being distracted, or to feel immersed in the area.
---
Overall, this is a perfect spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment, with a lot of elements refined/improved. Precisely what I wanted from this game while waiting for it all these years, and frankly, much more than I hoped for from a Kickstarter project.

I funded this game on Kickstarter. I regret that.
There are two games that I naturally compare this one to. First is, of course, "Planescape: Torment", whose shoes TToN tried to fill. Well, it failed to even to find those shoes and to approach them. The old classic is a deeply philsophical tale of a person in search of himself. It is huge (in word-count, close to a large novel), the world is coherent despite being rather bizzare, companions' tales are (mostly) related to the main story and are big and deep by themselves. TToN is none of that. The story is about a man on the run from an unknown but deadly threat, which he fails to understand up until the end (and, arguably, even then). It is much smaller, the world is bizzarre, but incoherent, piecemeal. Companions are shallow, don't make you feel emotionally connected to them (well, except for Rhin-the-lost-child, but even her writing is shallow).
The other game is "Pillars of Eternity". I funded both games on Kickstarter at the same time. And, boy, yes, Pillars is flawed too, but it delivers so much more thatn TToN. I finished both games and Steam tells me I spent twice as much time with Pillars. Good. Other comparisons, in no particular order:
* Visual presentation. Pillars looks so much better. TToN visuals are blurred if zoomed in, or glossy 3D-renders if you zoom out. Almost if someone tried to faithfully reproduce the flaws of Planscape graphics from 90s.
* Character classes. TToN has three: fighter, thief and mage. Period. Mage is too powerful, thief is underwhelming, fighter is OK - like D&D of old. Pillars have many classes, most of them interesting, some of them *very* novel. Consequentually, combat in Pillars is much more interesting. Yes, most fights in TToN are avoidable, but the few that are not are *dead* boring.
* Companions. Pillars companions are well-written. One of them in particular, the priest that lost his faith, was the most memorable RPG companion ever for me. TToN companions are shallow and boring, for the most part.
* Story. The main story sucks in both games. The main villain(s) of TToN are just boring, the one in Pillars isn't just that, he's also way too cliche. But I had fun travelling the world of Pillars, seeing places, doing side quests, and the final decision of the storyline made a lot of sense. On the contrary, the trip around the Ninth World of TToN is a slog. The final decision made no sense, because I failed to feel emotional connection to any of the parties involved. Including "myself", the main character.
The final verdict: don't. Don't buy this. Don't play this. Save your time and money and spend them on some other RPGs.

A masterfully crafted game. I honestly can't believe how much of a homerun this game is for Scott. It's so good and fun, I especially like the way it takes 7 years to do every activity. I have never seen a feat captured by another game except this one. Every time I boot up this masterpiece I'm already trembling in my britches, every pixel so perfect, every sound effect so chilling; it's hard to not be terrified. And who could forget when the main menu music kicks in, the ambient sounds blend perfectly with the beautiful soundtrack. Which, by the way, is nothing short of a masterpiece. Now, Scott is known throughout the world for his nail-biting and thrilling gameplay. From the really fun crawling sequence that takes only 5 minutes each time you go through to the breaker sequence that barely makes sense; there's a little something for everyone.   Scott really doesn't disappoint when it comes to the gameplay of this game. And who could forget, the most important part of a FNAF game, the animatronics. Freddy's back and he's better than ever with a whole new gang of beautifully crafted animatronics. I know what you're thinking and yes they are as terrifying as they are beautfiul and graceful. The game is just a mix of every previous FNAF game but on 'roids; interesting characters, addicting gameplay, beautiful soundtrack, gorgeous visuals, and who could forget the wonderful backstory. And of course the mini games are back and better than ever, but I don't want to spoil too much of those, I want you to experience those for yourselves. So, grab some popcorn and set five nights aside to play this horror classic.
Graphics: 9.5/10
Soundtrack: 10/10
Gameplay: 11/10
Audio: 9/10
Story: 10/10
Characters & Animatronics: 9/10
Closing Statements: This game is truly what horror games should strive to be like, Scott did it again. He's truly back at it again with the white vans.
Final Rating: 21/10

This was sold as an episodic game with an incredibly slow delivery schedule. Players were given the choice of either purchasing all the content up-front, even if they wouldn't receive most of it for over a year, or else buying it episodically. However, after getting most users to pay $35 for three episodes in separate installments, they suddenly announced that some content would be available free only to those who paid in full up-front. Those who paid in installments would have to wait a long time to get it and pay even more for this "free" content, even though they were already paying far more for the game than those who paid in full up-front. Given the publisher's lousy recent history with this franchise and the slow delivery schedule, most users had the sense to buy each episode separately, and now they're being punished for it.
♥♥♥♥ you, square enix. ♥♥♥♥ you.
On the other hand, the game at its core is quite good. It's certainly the best Hitman game in a while. The magical way that events trigger at the most convenient moment for you is at times a little silly, but it's all part of the fun of trying to pull off a bunch of achievements in a single run. The quality of the levels varies; Paris was a little weak and probably not the best way to start the series. Later levels have been better, although Thailand just feels like a reskinned Paris in too many ways.
Overall, I can't recommend this right now. Wait until the whole game is released and buy it as a discounted package.

Also, they have done a good job of keeping fresh content coming in between episodes with contracts, escalations, and especially the Elusive Targets.

For me, it's a very small knock against a very good game.

HITMAN is excellent, hands down. Just go buy the full experience right now and get playing.
If you want more of an explanation, then allow me to discuss essentially the three main aspects of it, the core game and level design, the "extra" modes, and the episodic experience as a whole.
The core game is simply pure Hitman Blood Money bliss, and I don't say that lightly. Each level we have gotten so far is massive, with multiple environments, crowds, hallways, multiple routes, many different killing methods, and stealth good enough that you can do them all silently with only the suit. There is nothing possibly bad you could say about the level design except that there are far fewer levels than Blood Money so far. But, every level is extremely good, where BM had a few stinkers spread about padding out the length. Here, each level has such a huge number of routes, kill methods, and opportunities, that it dwarfs even the best BM levels in variety on offer. The only serious trick added that BM did not have is that certain guards can see through certain disguises. Usually, these are important guards or important characters; i.e. the target will see through you in the uniform of his personal guard, or the guards running the checkpoint will see through you in the uniform of a guard, but not if you are dressed as a waiter. But then the chef might pick you out...
Beyond that, all I have to say is this is the heir to Blood Money, which was one of the finest games ever made. If you have had the pleasure of playing BM, that is all the endorsement you need.
But beyond even the variety of the main levels, Eidos has provided quite a bit of extra content. Contracts, the mode from Absolution where you create a custom challenge to kill an NPC in a level a certain way and can upload it for others to play, is back, though a few of the options are stripped from Absolution. Eidos also provides Escalations, which are much the same thing, but Eidos has scripting users do not, and with it they have made some clever challenges (Kill three people with a battle axe, but they are at opposite ends of the party, and there is only one axe, and if anyone at the party sees you with the axe... you will be in trouble. Stuff like that.). Elusive Targets are a similar deal, only there the levels are changed a bit. A new NPC and some guards are added, some new parameters are put in, and you only have one attempt (Technically, that attempt is only spent if you die. You can retry as much as you like provided you did not die.) and a limited amount of real world time to try the mission.
What makes these all alike is that they take place in the same massive, sandboxy levels as the story missions, but these are generally much tighter puzzles, you have less control, no scripted events to help... It boils the game down to the core mechanics. Distractions, disguises, poisons, stealth, peeling away guards to shadowy corners to knock them out and hide them to get at the target alone, exploiting the AI as best you can with precise distractions... These are not usually as fun. Tougher play of these tends to involve some trial and error as you are really battling the quirks of the stealth AI and systems rather than the elaborate scripting of the main story targets. These are not bad... it is just a different focus.
As far as the episodic experience goes, I think HITMAN is about the only episodic game I have seen that really justifies its price. With every content drop, Eidos improves the game with patches, updates, quality of life improvements. Each level in the game is meant to be replayed and savored, even more than Blood Money's levels. The immense variety of the story missions and the amount of bonus challenges in Escalations, the Elusive targets, and user-made Contracts... Eidos is providing a lot of support and the game really does work well with the wait between levels. If you are not marathonning the game, you have time between episodes to really play the level and associated challenges as much as they deserve.
So I do not think you should wait for the full release to get HITMAN. The content we have now is of exceptional quality, and by the time you finish that, more levels will be available. The game is worth your time and money, easily.

There isn't much to say about this game so I was going to write up a short list of pros and cons to sum it all up, but after a few moments of consideration I realized that there were no "pros" to share.
The game is cheap, especially so on sale. I picked Scribble Space up for half a dollar hoping it would be a short, casual sidescrolling shooter I could play through without much effort. Now that I've played it a short while, I know that if this game were freely available online, I would not have played it for more than a few seconds. Since I paid for it I felt inclined to at least get my money's worth, but this is one of the few times I have legitimately regretted a purchase on Steam. Again, it wasn't much money in the first place, but this game is much more frustrating than it is fun.
Though the concept is simple, the gameplay issues are too frequent and obvious to overlook. The player hitbox isn't made clear, which makes creatively designing your own ship more dangerous to the gameplay than it is fun. Taking damage removes all your power ups, and this really wouldn't be a problem if the hitbox made more sense. Even then, though, it is almost impossible to avoid taking damage in this game, rendering you without the power ups (which are rare as it is) for the majority of the time playing. Boss fights are a nightmare to deal with, and it isn't always obvious what you are supposed to be attacking or how to even avoid taking damage. Most of the time you have to hope to just get lucky and get enough shots in to defeat the boss before you die.
The game has cards and achievements, so if you want it for either of those then go ahead. Be warned, though, that one achievement requires a lot of luck and mastery of the game, so you may spend quite a bit of time playing it if you want to 100% it.

Mad Max opens with as direct a setup as you could hope for: bad guys stole Max's car, he meets a fanatical mechanic building a bigger badder car, and they agree to work together to build the biggest baddest car and kick the bad guys butts. There's the hook of the game, and its biggest strength: putting together your very own rad wasteland death machine is super compelling. You're never far from the next substantial upgrade to your Magnum Opus, as it's called, which pulls you along through a typical array of Open World Action Game Activities.
With the exception of a handful of story missions and odd jobs for some of the less evil warlords, those activities are mostly what you'll be doing for your 20-plus hours in Mad Max's gorgeously rendered wasteland. And really, you'll mostly be clearing camps. There are nominally a few varieties of camp, but they mostly boil down to tearing down the camp's outer defenses from your car, then running in and punching a lot of dudes. Melee combat in Mad Max is a simplified version of the standard design from games like the Batman Arkham series or Shadow of Mordor. The simplification is justified by Max's character: he doesn't go in for a bunch of fancy flipping around when he can just punch a dude real hard. Some fine animation work reinforces this, making fights look weighty and brutal. Even so, such a simple combat system in such a long game gets repetitive by the end.
Up to this point, Mad Max would get a marginal recommendation: it goes cheap on sales, get it then if you're into the genre and setting. What tips the scale is the hard dive it takes near the end, so I need to talk vaguely of spoiler things. The rest of this paragraph has vague spoilers about the last part of the game.
I have to give Mad Max a thumbs down, which I hate doing because there's so much good in it. The wasteland is one of the most beautiful in video games, and it's so cool making your Magnum Opus incrementally more awesome. But hoo boy, that ending drags everything down. I'll update my marginal recommendation: if you're into the genre and setting, get it cheap, then stop playing immediately after that one big fight in Gastown, you'll know it when you get there. Pretend that's the ending and you'll have a far better time.

All the mechanics work great, but this is a prime example of a game that is too big, something the developer Avalanche Studios, creators of the Just Cause franchise, seem to do a lot in their games. While Just Cause has many different methods of travel, Mad Max has only one, drive. The driving is good, it has weight behind it and the car combat hasn't been done anywhere else, but the enviroments are typical Mad Max large open deserts. Thats not to say they're bad enviroments, a lot of effort went into the world design, the entire map is vertical despite being one big desert. You start in the ocean bed and make your way up sand dunes until eventually you're driving past church steeples submerged in the sand. But at the end of the day, they're still open deserts, with the only things populating them being ubisoft icons; 100s of scavenging locations (to upgrade max and his car), dozens of camps and a massive amount of destructable collectables. The game could've benefitted from a smaller game world.
The gameplay loop of exploring/fighting, getting scrap and improving max and his car (which has nice aesthetic and stat increases) is really great at short bursts. I haven't even left the 2 large ocean areas yet, since I just pop on for an hour and play until it peaks my interest. Story is alright, obviously not the focus, but I would've liked to see a bit more effort after Fury Road's decent attempt. Again, it's one of those 'Ubisoft' styled games where there're only 10-20 actual story levels in the game intermingled with outposts and repetitive side content. On foot combat is great, although it is essentially Batman Arkham's combat. Get the game if you're going to play it in bursts, otherwise it'll drive you mad.
I'd probably give it a 6/10. Above average and worth a glance but the fact that I can't get myself to properly sit down with it and play for an extended amount of time on account of it being too repetitive means it's not an all-around 'good' game. If you want something similar but executed better, try Shadow of Mordor, the Batman Arkham games and Just Cause. As I said earlier however, the car combat while underutilised is definitely unique.

I first became interested in this game after hearing that my favorite author, Patrick Rothfuss, actually helped write out a character. And let me tell you, it shows. I don't at all mind some game in my book, and the game system is excellent and well implemented. The is passable, the characters are unique in a way that transcends stat blocks, and the setting is fresh and interesting. The game provides one of the best sets of non-combat solutions to problems I've seen. Those are the good parts.
By far the biggest fault is how painfully obvious it is that the writers think they are so very, very clever when they are, in fact, not. Prepare for a lot of mainstream dystopian philosophy, tired tropes with a very thin coat of new paint, and rails so strong you'll wonder why this wasn't just a movie. Despite deep dialogue trees with plenty of skill checks hidden in them, decisions that matter inevitably come down to "Pick A or B" with a stellar "Pick one of three" for the ending. The game mixes ♥♥♥♥♥♥ damsel/purity tropes, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mary sue urwoman tropes, and a not-so-subtle matriarchy, all while railing about how gender doesn’t matter. Don't worry though, the villain’s still a straight (probably white) dude. Classic. The game's "morality" system is obtuse at best, and is further subject to the writers’ opinions of the philosophical underpinnings of decisions. Oh, and just in case you care about the actual gameplay: it's also buggy, from broken animations, to characters getting stuck on terrain, to asking a question locking you out of a series of quest options without warning, to a save system that apparently failed to learn from the past decade of gaming.
Somewhere out there there's probably a writer yelling "That's the point, you idiot!" (Or more likely, "Like your opinion matters, idiot." while looking for grammar mistakes.) This game’s head is so far up its own♥♥♥♥♥it's a wonder they managed to ship it. They took a beautiful setting and great rules system and proceeded to systematically ruin the experience with babby's first grim fantasy novel writing, writing which would have been perfectly acceptable except the game spends a great deal of time talking down to the player. I finished this game mostly out of disbelief that a game selling itself on writing could possibly be this trite.
