This is a game for people who want to read a lot, and find wonder in books like A Wrinkle in Time, Mister Bass, or Golden Compass.   There are so many great ideas here, just spread out for you then thrown away, entire series just flashed on your retinas then discarded.
If you're here for a balanced RPG or combat, just forget it.   This is not your thing - this is an RPG that attempts to recreate a creative human GM spilling his guts with creativity, and your wonder and a frission down your spine at what this means for your lovingly created and curated character.  By the end of the game you'll be OP, but who cares?  It's the journey that matters.  You have the all the options here, there has never been more choice in an RPG.
The question is whether wading through piles of color text is a pleasure or a burden for you.  For me it's a pleasure, so I'm enjoying the hell out of it after a slow start.  But if you don't like, seriously LIKE reading, you'll miss the point and give it a 7/10 like most reviewers who've been trained for Shooty McFace.

Good game, lots of negativity from folks who kickstarted it thinking it would be something different.
Combat is weird but if you play the game focusing on diplomacy and smarts you can avoid almost all encounters in the game. I think I had to fight maybe a total of five times in the 40+ hours it took me to finish the game.
The story is interesting and fun to follow. Plenty of side quests and LOTS of flavor text everywhere.
Items and their descriptions are almost an art form all on their own. Even things that are seemingly "vendor trash" have rich, interesting descriptions and sometimes can be used in weird ways. I don't think i have had this much fun reading item descriptions since Baldurs Gate 1.
Biggest flaws in the game are the linear progress in each "act" and the very abrupt ending of the game.
There are no marked "acts" or chapters in the game but there are about four distinct location hubs, with the fourth one being the end game one that is pretty much linear. The districts are interesting and pretty large but still seem pretty locked tight compared to even Baldurs Gate series.
The final of the game comes out of nowhere, you are literary doing some questing and following the story and BAM final mission comes up. Depending on your choices in game and how well you did in certain "mares" the options at the end of the game will change but ultimately it doesn't feel as fun as the ending of even Planescape. And of course your in game choices will be described along with their consequences at the end in a series of static text blocks... Well, at least its better then the initial Mass Effect 3 ending.
Overall its a good game, well worth the price tag, takes over 40 hours which include probably about 10 hours of reading if not more. Perhaps the biggest flaw of this game is the inevitable comparison to Planescape: Torment.  This is obviously an intentional comparison on the part of the designers, and you can see some elements that are the same in both games: an amnesiac main character that can't stay dead, an unfamiliar alien world, belief shaping reality, a mysterious force hunting the main character, etc.  The truth is that if this game hadn't invited the comparison to Planescape: Torment, it would still likely be judged the same way.
This game stands on its own, with some flaws detracting from the otherwise good quality.  I had originally started playing this game on a PS4 console, and quickly abandoned that experience as it was clear that the experience was intended for PC even if console releases were simultaneous.  I found the story to be compelling, the dialogue to be fresh and interesting, and the sheer artwork to be awe-inspiring.  The more I play, the more I get drawn into the rich world which they have created from the ground up.
The few flaws that exist with this game mostly have to do with mechanics relating to combat and the points system.  Rather than opting for a system inherent in the Baldur's Gate series and Planescape: Torment in which the characters will continue to attack, cast spells, etc. until you choose a different action for them, this game is entirely turn based.  This means that you have to choose each and every action for your characters each and every time, from movement to special abilities to attacking the same monsters.  Although this system is inherent in games such as XCOM, Wasteland 2, and others, it somehow feels out of place in this type of game, especially since its predecessor Planescape: Torment did not feature a turn-only system.  And although the points system each character features allows you to increase your chance to hit with a weapon or to use a special ability in combat, these points are used so frequently that you will find yourself working hard to replenish them simply to get an edge from battle to battle.  Add to the fact that these same points are used outside of combat in scripted encounters to activate certain abilities, and you understand some of the frustration inherent with such a system.  And if you choose to rest to replenish these points rather than use inventory items to replenish them, the game actually advances certain quests and story elements independently.  This makes resting a tricky proposition if you're trying to solve certain quests that may advance without you.
But even with these flaws, that's not enough to make me dislike this game.  It's too interesting, too beautiful, too engrossing to put it away and dismiss it.  It's not Planescape: Torment, and it will never be.  But on its own, it is a solid game worth the time of anyone who plays and enjoys  similar games, especially games that give you such a rich world with surprises around every corner.

Rust has a unique game design concept where a lot of the texture and guns and items are designed to look sort of unorthdox. Essentially rust is a sandbox shooter survival game that allows players to create and form social dynamics in a world without rules. This game can be absolutely infuriating and also can cause extreme frustration due to hardships endured by toxic individuals. On the other side this game can be rewarding and fun as the excitement of raiding and building and accumulating resources motivates and empowers players to forge futher into the gameplay to find more regions to explore.
Some downsides of the game as many people have stated are the resistance to not leave the server after being raided which can be quite demoralizing. Solo progression is limited as one person can only invest so much time into base defense and foraging. Clans can be overwhelming at times and more times than not adolescents and pre-pubescent children are acting out of control. So with that said the overall community can be harsh. Combat can also be very onsided as more times than not you will probably be out gearerd and out classed.
Some upsides of the game are, besides a large segment of the community you can find some decent individuals to meet and explore the game with. Once you understand how to setup a base and effectively resource the game is not very difficult. The challenge of overcoming hardship and establishing yourself can be rewarding. The developers seem to work diligently on constantly modifiying the game and updating its playability. Rust is always a new adventure and each wipe brings new obstacles player dynaimcs which keeps the game interesting and playable. Overall the game is very different from anything that I have played before and could really turn into something extraordinary if the community and developers continue working together.

8/10. A nice and funny tycoon game. To my wife I said "it's like Theme Hospital but if too many patients gather in one place they start fighting".
The Good:
- funny graphics, and nice sound (especially the background sound in different rooms and the hilarious prison fight/riot ambients)
- it's interesting to plan rooms and build from individual tiles, not just as rectangles
- the game tries to give both views on whether the prison system should be more about punishing/deterring or about treating/educating
- the game is frequently updated, and new features keep getting added, so it's worth to replay it after a few months
- every prisoner has his own biography and personal data. One biography even said "I am a real person!"
- the game runs pretty fast. As a programmer, I wonder how all those hundreds of characters on the screen do their pathfinding calculations so efficiently.
- the tutorial missions are very well designed and make you feel comfortable by giving you a few already running prisons and letting you add minor stuff
The So-so:
- the game shows a US or Western European prison, which feels more like a student dormitory or a 0-star hotel where the only bad thing is dangerous neighbors. The prison itself gives you food, a separate room with a TV, even free education and medical treatment - things 3/4 of working people in the word might not have. So I guess for players outside the golden billion the game creates a strange feeling of absurdity - but at the same time it is an educational experience, like "gee, those rich guys are nuts!". Even work is done voluntarily and for payment! And a prisoner who kills a guard doesn't get an electric chair, just solitary for 8 hours?! The main source of revenue is Prison Grant (taxpayers' money), and the prisoners themselves produce very little. I guess I could go to the US and kill somebody just to save on rent :) I guess they'd let me place a PC in my cell? I heard in German prisons they even get a free session with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ once in a while :)
- the story is pretty mediocre, but honestly I don't think one could come up with anything better because we've seen tons of crime movies and most crime-related real-life stories are pretty banal.
- it's a sandbox game like Mincraft, and you can share your prison with others. I checked a few dozens, but it's either just some random prison you can get when you play without any special purpose - or a prison which tries to look like something well known (e.g. Star Trek spaceship). Apart from aesthetics, this doesn't change the game much, suggesting that, as good as it is, it's a pretty much fixed experience which you will get on most replays.
- the Escape mode is completely broken but it's nevertherless fun for an hour.
The Bad:
- given the complex systems this game has, much is left unexplained. E.g. what defines how many prisoners can work in a Laundry? Or what at all defines the efficiency of a Laundry? How many wash machines I need, how big the room should be - all that I had to find out in online wikis. Nothing is explained about CCTVs, remote doors and phones (does one have to connect them or not? Why do some CCTV links become red?)
- it seems that the Programs scheduling is bugged somehow. Often I'd have lots of "Queued" prisoners for a program but none would participate - pretty annoying when you can't start any Workshop production without training first. I guess this might be due to overlapping classes, or if you add/remove objects into rooms there will be more/less places, or some prisoners may be a few days into a program already and their progress is taken into account somehow etc. This system is overcomplicated - even if it worked bug-free, most players would be overtaxed by it. And I'd wish to have the option to send any prisoner to obligatory training and obligatory jobs, even if that makes him angry.
- I was surprised when the game ended after just the 5th episode. I did have a prison for 300 prisoners already with all rooms built, but I expected at least one more mission where CCTVs and other maximum-security elements were explained.
- Dormitories don't work well. Is there a minimal 4-tile requiement for a prisoner to live in a dorm? The game should say that or there should be no minimal reqs.

+++++ to developers this is how a early access game should get treated.

So me and my friends played this one time when it was on a free Steam weekend.  Needless to say, it was a keeper for the three of us.  We're all fans of weird humor, and violence.  So when we got to try this amazing game, we all decided, "Let's buy the game and beat it together!"
Best and worst decision.
This game is addicting.  The violence is just top notch.  The humor is spot on.  The characters are so well written.  This is one of those games that will go from "super robot violence fun time" to tearing your heart out.  Who knew a game about senseless violence would make you feel such strong emotions?
The weapon designs are beautiful.  Each one - be them white, orange, or pink - are so beautifully designed.  Purple and magenta Maliwans have
to be the best, though.  It is so satisfying to pick up a Torgue shotgun and just watch an enemy's head blow up in a bloody mess.  These guns are just that nice.  They feel real, and it's so nice to get a beautiful gun in your hands as you go to usurp an "evil" corporation.
The download content is definitely worth it.  The extra levels help a lot, Gaige is a wonderful DLC character (along with Krieg), and my god do I love Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragonkeep.  Best.  DLC.  Ever.  Torgue's Campaign of Carnage is pretty okay.  The humor helps out with a fairly decent campaign, turning it into a pretty fun one.  Can't say much on Sir Hammerlock's just yet, but Captain Scarlet's is pretty fun so far.  So 10/10 on the DLC.
If you're a stickler about graphics, don't be.  The graphics are nice, the style is wonderful, and still holds up well.
I can't say much about the multiplayer servers since I never went on them, but the multiplayer mode with friends is amazing.  The developer's original intention shines through without the game seeming nothing like it's inspiration: it feels like a Fallout multiplayer....but isn't.  It's what my friends and I (mostly) want in a Fallout multiplayer.
This game is one of the greatest games I've ever played.  And it's made my friends fear getting into a car in which I'm behind the wheel.  So good things all around.
11/10 would totally recommend.

SMB is a cartoon style platformer, similar to other recent indie games in paying tribute to the 8-bit titles of yesterday.You gotta help Meat Boy, who’s trying to reach his one and only love while surviving the dangerous environment filled with weird creatures and wicked traps. Despite the „Super” title, Meat Boy’s only abilities are jumping and sticking to walls with his bloodied body. Just make one mistake and you have to start over (it occurs quite often).
This game has a huge amount of levels: each of the chapters contains 20 „light” levels and a boss fight. By beating a time limit, you get to play the „dark” version of each level (even more difficult). You can also stumble upon warp zone portals, by entering them you get to a retro 8-bit world where you can unlock new characters. The majority of these guys come from other indie games (Bit.Trip, Minecraft, VVVVVV etc.) wielding different powers which can be used to collect all the band aids spread over levels. By grabbing all of them you might purchase even more heroes to control. This way the number of levels is already over 300 but we shouldn’t forget about Super Meat World with hundreds of community made levels and scenarios and a random map generator!
All in all, Super Meat boy packs a considerable amount of fun even with its extreme difficulty. While most of its levels can be completed in 15 seconds (preceded by hours of practice in some cases though), you’ll need lots of free time to get a 100% out of it.
SCORE: 8/10

The description is totally accurate.
The difficulty goes from hard to ridiculous, but that's what makes it so satisfying to finally beat a level or achieve the A+ score on it. The levels take less than a minute to beat (when you finally do it) but even in the first world it'll take many minutes of failed attempts to get your actions just right. When you do, you get a replay showing all ways you didn't make it in parallel, making victory even more satisfying.
The game strongly (and humorously) suggests that it's best played with a controller, and it's probably right. Playing on a keyboard is doable, but I feel like it'd be easier to get the moves just right with a controller. On a keyboard you'll have to get used to pressing Shift to run and Space to jump, while using Left + Right arrow keys. Those are the only inputs you'll need while jumping around a level, so you'll get used to it. I finished the first world on a keyboard, and I'm not planning to buy a gamepad yet.
The soundtrack is great, very fitting. The audio keeps running when you respawn, and the game doesn't penalise you at all for dying on a level. It's totally expected, and after half a second you respawn back at the beginning ready to try again. Ready to jump at just the right moment this time.
Replayability is fostered through hard-to-get bandages on some levels, and "A+" time targets. In most cases it's not too hard to reach the "A+" goal time after you've passed a level, but the bandages can be a bit trickier. After you collect the bandage, you still have to get to the end of the level (without dying) for it to be saved.
Graphics are fitting for what is essentially a pixel-art game.
The storyline is thin, but it doesn't need any more. A few cut scenes to tell you what's going on, but it's really all about the platforming - getting from A to B.
Verdict: Hard, satisfying, hilarious. Four stars.

Overwhelmingly positive.
This was an impulse buy.  It was cheap, and I was intrigued:  overwhelmingly positive reviews?  For a truck-driving simulator.  I mean, I like driving games all right, but really?  Overwhelmingly positive?
In recent months, I've bought a lot of games:
Mad Max, X-Com 2, Assassin's Creed Syndicate, Assassin's Creed Rogue, and Tom Clancy's The Division.
These are all great games ... and yet the game I keep coming back to almost every day is Euro Truck Simulator 2.
This is a brilliant game.  Here's why:
1.  It's beautiful.  Sure, it's not the most beautiful game out there, nor even the most beautiful game I own, but the scenery is beautiful nonetheless.
2.  It's SOOOO relaxing.  As the end of a hard day, it's nice to load up a 1 hour stand-up comedy special in YouTube and then hit the road.  Just drive and listen to comedy.
3.  It IS challenging.  I get scored on getting my cargo to its destination in a timely manner, and UNDAMAGED.  Navigating tight corners, trying not to get speeding tickets when the speed suddenly changes, trying not to run into cars that suddenly slam on the breaks on the freeway, trying not to have an accident when I have to suddenly change lanes because my lane is "turn only" and I don't want to get off course.  Not to mention trying to map out and mark my turns, and plan where and when to stop for gas and sleep.
This is a game that understands that "challenging" and "frustrating" don't have to be synonymous.  This is a game that challenges my driving accuracy, while also making me think.
4.  There's motivation.  Sure, just going for a drive is nice, but this game adds another layer:  building an empire.  I save up money, get some loans, buy a garage, buy some trucks, and select drivers.  I quickly learn that loans aren't a bad idea:  I can repay them quicker if I have more people driving for me.  I'm now at the point where I no longer need loans because my drivers earn enough money that, in the time it takes me to run a reasonably long route, I can buy another garage and three more trucks.
The only downside I've run across so far:
1.  Roads sometimes don't make sense.  Signs sometimes say both lanes go to "X"ville, but only the left lane goes:  the right lane MUST turn.  In America and Japan, for the most part, if I'm on a two-lane freeway, it STAYS a two-lane freeway.  If the speed is 100kph, it STAYS 100kph until you exit.  Sometimes I see a sign indicating a speed change ... but my gps speed limit doesn't change.  Sometimes I don't see a speed limit sign, but still get a ticket.
However, I don't really mind because, even though it doesn't make sense, it keeps me on my toes.
2.  Drivers are STUPID.  I've had people come to a COMPLETE stop on the freeway.
If I'm turning across traffic, or even changing lanes, oncoming traffic rarely slows down.  They'll plow right into me at full speed, damaging my truck and/or cargo, and I get a ticket.
However, I don't really mind.  Drivers in my hometown do some pretty boneheaded things too, and if anything, the drivers in ETS 2 are LESS boneheaded than the people in my hometown (after all, ETS drivers don't suddenly change their mind at a red light and cross against the light).
Overall:  my feelings about this game are "overwhelmingly positive".
I had worried I would get bored playing this game, but after over 90 hours of play, I'm nowhere near bored.  I still love this game.  It's not for everybody.  No game is.  But there IS a good reason why the reviews for this game are so high:  it's an outstanding game.

And it didn't go very well for the game I'm afraid.
Because it's so similar, it also needed to be either *that* much better, or different in a few obvious ways. It was neither.
P:T Felt real. Felt personal. You were trying to figure out yourself and in the process You learned about soooo much.
The companions felt real and personal. They each had strong, believable reasons to follow You around. Even non-companions had "soul" there.
Here, I liked Erritis and loved Rhin, but the rest of the NPCs was mediocre. Unrelatable.
The biggest issue I have here though is that the game was externally focused. You had to go and save the world. Yes, Sorrow was chasing Your kind, but You had to save the world from castoffs or sorrow or both.
When You compare it to the internally focused P:T where all You were asked was to understand and act accordingly, You feel like it was more Baldurs Gate than P:T. It should be clear which game I deem superior in narrative.

Not for everyone, but one of the best games in history for those who like this style of gameplay.
This game is basically all the plot-solving and discovery of Baldur's Gate 2, polished and on steroids. The setting is the best I have ever experienced in an RPG: It allows the writers to make all NPCs super interesting and varied, it has a constant sense of mystery and it means that even the flavor material has that exciting sense of discovery, rather than just reading about political factions and historical events.
The reason this game is not for everyone is that this quest solving and discovery is *all* you do. Baldur's Gate also had a great strategic combat system. This game actually has some interesting combat mechanics, that still make it exciting to build and equip your characters but:
- There isn't a whole lot of combat. This is partly because the game makes it so much more fun to explore the non-combat solutions to problems.
- The combat mechanics are a bit slow, cumbersome and with various UI issues (e.g. can't see if your AoE effects cover enough of a target to affect them). This sadly also means that you can't use stealth a whole lot, because you can only activate it when you're in combat, and combat is slow as hell. The lack of control over your characters' turn order, also makes it unpractical to use many of the synergies that the combat system technically has the potential for.
If in BG2, you liked running around in Amn, hand-crafted quests and NPCs around every corner, this game does that better than you have ever experienced. World, plot and writing are all amazing.
The only question you need to ask yourself, is if you will still enjoy that kind of game, when combat is 10% of your experience, rather than 75%.

Arkham Origins can be a good game. It can be at times. The casefiles are well done and the challenges are actually difficult to complete and require you to think encounters out in order to complete them. The new voice actors do a good job. The story is interesting. The boss fights, unlike the previous games, are fun and are all unique. But that's where it ends, because the bugs absolutely break any enjoyment you manage to suck out of this game.
First we had the glitch involving a Riddler Tower that made completion of a main side-quest impossible. Thankfully it's patched, but it sent up red flags about the QA. 6 months after release we still have bugs involving the glide mechanics, crashing/stability issues, and my personal favourite which involved every gadget I used to be a Concussion Detonator when aimed and fired completely negating a New Game Plus run.
Is WB going to fix these issues and many others that people are experiencing? No. In fact they've come out and said that they won't be patching the game any further despite all the known issues, in favour of working on the DLC. So basically we have a good game plagued by terrible technical issues by a QA team staffed by monkies with a developer/publisher at the helm saying, "We got your money already, go **** yourself. But only after you buy more of our product."
And I haven't even got to the multiplayer, which interests me on a personal level about as much as playing a game of Roshambo. Make no mistake, if the multiplayer was not in this game and instead that money and time was spent on the singleplayer I have no doubts that this would have been a better game for it. Instead it's a fragmented mess that pulls left and right and splits apart at the seams.

I'll say this right off the bat. This game is great if you're looking for something really laid back. It has a cute, light-hearted story; nothing too deep, and the gameplay itself is quite simple. It also has a bit of a Star Trek feel to it. You can definitely tell the creator is a fan.
Basically, you're the captain of a spaceship. You travel from planet to planet  chasing down your threat-to-the-unverse first officer while collecting some alien friends along the way. You can either try to save the universe and win over your second officer, or like me, stab everyone in the back and make it with your first officer~
The game is pretty non-violent. Even your strongest weapon is actually just a relocator device. You "fight" enemies by walking into them. If that enemy poofs, you've won. If your weapon isn't strong enough, you'll get bumped back and take on a little damage.
Honestly, you can probably just edge around most enemies. They won't chase you, but I'd advise having a strong enough weapon just to avoid the nuissance of it. (There's no need to bother with shields.)
The game offers some fun, self-aware humour. It's filled with amusing, silly dialogue and options.
One thing that particularly stood out to me was the unique option to choose your own gender and pronouns. There isn't the typical drop down list, so whatever it is you'd like your character to be referred as, you can literally type in anything.
---
IN A NUTSHELL VERSION
- gameplay simple, story light-hearted and not too deep, great if you're looking for something laid back
- non-violent, focuses more on character interactions than combat
- choose your own gender and pronouns
- has some fun, self-aware humour
* In good concience, I do feel I need to give fair warning... This game is very social justicey. This is just one extra thing to take into consideration when buying the game, because it's not subtle. If you're all for that, cool! Get the game. If not, the game still has it's charm, but it's just the one extra thing to keep in mind.
Either way, I think the game was fairly priced. Really. It costs nothing. I enjoyed it's humour throughout and I genuinely hope more people will try it out~ Good job to the creator.

Positives:
• Interesting character interactions.
• I've only played it once, so I can't confirm this, but there are numerous decision points that feel significant.
• Detailed and varied environments.
• A built in system to help the player identify important locations if they get stuck. This is a real frustration saver!
• Some self-aware humor.
Facts:
• The game follows a very directed path. The story itself doesn't feel linear, but the gameplay does.
• The setting is a space ship and several (very visually different) planets.
Negatives
• Too much inventory management. There are two important equipment categories—keys and tools—that you have to frequently navigate through several menus in order to change which ones you have equipped. You must do this with regularity.
• It can often be difficult to determine what terrain elements are passable and which aren't.
Overall, I enjoyed the game and feel that it is at a very fair price point.

First things first--this is basically a visual novel.   That's fine, I like visual novels, but it might disappoint others.  There is, nominally, combat, but when you run (usually by accident) into an enemy, you either defeat it and get one Spacebuck or you don't and take damage.  Enemies almost never block your path, and the main reason to use currency is to buy weapons, and weapons...allow you to beat stronger enemies.  Hmmm.
Aaaaanyway, this game is for people like me who just wanted a story about cute alien girls running around and trying to save the universe.  For that, it delivered.  While the main cast is a teeny bit simplistic, they, and the story, are endearing and occasionaly surprising.
Bad♥♥♥♥♥♥  This game had a staff of three people, and it shows.  Both the editing and programming have notable oversights (look!  there's a typo in that screenshot up there).  Neither the occasional mispellings or the walking through walls is ever bad enough to affect my enjoyment.  Even when some odd decisions or errors would slow you down, the programmers have put in optional Helpful Dolls to guide you to all solutions and difficult-to-find exits (they're downright neccesary on the fourth planet; the sprites that are meant to guide you never spawn).
Edit:  I'd also like to point out the puzzle-solving mechanic.  Obstacles present themselves as either locked doors or blockages that are easily surmounted with the correct tools: a shovel to dig up things, gardening gloves for thick weeds, etc.  You utilize the keys and tools by equipping them to your main-character Captain...and ONLY your captain.  Despite the fact you can equip tools and keys to all of your party members and you can even remove the Captain from the front line or even your visible party, only the items your Captain has currently equipped will influence what doors or obstacles you can deal with.  To get past a blocked tunnel that occasionally pops up, one has to go to the menu, go to the equip screen, equip the shovel to Captain Whomever, dig away the loose soil, go back to the menu, enter the equip screen AGAIN, and equip a pickaxe to finally open the way forward.  It was not a dealbreaker for me, but it easily could be for someone else.
Edit 2: Electric Boogaloo :  As of Jan 2017, the above comment about the mechanics has been fully fixed. Gameplay: This game is deceptively simple. You'll think you have the hang of it until it you realize you've made one mistake, try to fix it, and watch everything fall apart. A game that's easy to be good at, but hard to master, and perhaps the most fun if you're not good at all.
Graphics/Visual Experience: While Prison Architect looks like an indie game, playing the game will reveal that this really works out as a strength. The game can get quite chaotic, and if the graphics were any different than they are the game would slow to a crawl not long after starting a new prison.
Sound: There's not a lot of different sounds in Prison Architect, another way in which the simplicity is nice. If you like listening to music while you play without feeling like you're missing out on anything, this is your game.
Replayability: The game isn't terribly restrictive. Prisoners are (I think) both randomly generated and drawn from a pool of names of people who contributed money towards the game's development. The number of random elements per game means that each playthrough is quite unique, even if you did your best to make them the same.
How it Runs: No computer should have a hard time running this unless you decide to do what I did, in which I gave all my prisoners a lighter and they decided to set the whole prison on fire. That got a little challenging for my computer to handle.

For 10$ more (or 20$ if you are upgrading from one of the other versions) you can have your name in the game, as if that couldn't be done by modifying an .INI file somewhere.
As I said, prison architect is a great game, but horribly overpriced. Get it from one of the bundle sites or at a steep discount because if you are paying 30$ for this, you are getting ripped off.

This game, while hard for most people, is a great challenge and well thought out. Unlike some games (looking at you, I Wanna Be the Guy), this game is a Fair platformer, meaning that traps are obvious and won't come out of nowhere to kill you unfairly. It is well balanced and controls like... Well, Meat. It has some of the finest controls in a game I have played to date, but beware wireless keyboard users or laggy pc-ers, this game might be too much for you. All in all, I'd give this game a 5/5, for two reasons. Firstly, it lacks obvious negative attributes, and secondy, any death or frustration in this game isn't the game's fault. The fluid controls and straight-forward gameplay let you know that every death isn't your fault, but the game's. A classic that more people should enjoy (or if you're short tempered, despise). I'd say the replayability is good for people that like a challenge or like completionism.
Collectables like bandages and A+ times are a goal that can seem unreasonable at first, but progressively getting better and being able to do what you weren't before is extremely rewarding and satisfying. As previously mentioned, the collectables not only add heavy replayability but also unlock whole new characters. Most characters have unique abilities that change how they are used as well as different speeds and jump heights. For example, Flywrench can triple-jump but is more floaty and slow and slides up walls instead of kicking off of them.
This game shouldn't be compared to the flash game prequel! A lot of people try it and then pass on this game, and it makes me sad for them. I personally don't much like the flash game either, but that's because it lacks a lot of positive traits this one has (a big one being the flash game has very sticky and slow controls).
All in all, I would definitely recommend this game. It is a must-have purchase for anyone who enjoys platforming or a challenge. 5/5!

If you somehow still haven't played this game, get it. Easily stands out from the rest of the swaths of "omg teh harderest gaem ever!!" out there. Good design, addictive, and most importantly, fun and rewarding. This is no I Wanna Be the Guy. The game is hard, yes, but it remembers what fun is.
The only minor thing holding this game back is the bugs that can occur due to the game's odd way of handling lag. Player control is given absolute priority, and well it should be, since this game is difficult, but Meat Boy moves at a constant speed no matter what, meaning that he will sometimes fly right through walls if your FPS isn't up to the job. Lag will make the game almost, if not literally unplayable. Performance is something to consider for this game, even though it's not exactly graphically intense.

I bought this game as a late birthday present for my younger brother (who is transgender and gay), but also for my interest in one of the bachelors (I personally am nonbinary and pansexual). We went into it pretty excited for what awaited us.
We both liked most of the characters and while we lamented how short the routes are, it was generally fun. We've since dropped the game and try to forget it exists and have not bothered to 100% complete it after hearing about the "secret ending" on Twitter.
While we both enjoyed what we played of this game, the appearance of the infamous "secret ending" (I won't reveal it here for spoiler reasons, but you might have heard about this) ultimately ruined the entire thing for us. The fact that other routes contain details that imply this secret ending is the canon ending just further upsets me and others who were expecting a pure game.
I
Dream Daddy was marketed as a sweet and simple game for homosexual men/the LGBT+ community, so by including a secret, implied canon ending that completely destroys your impression of the game once you know it is... heartbreaking.
The response by the developers to the backlash regarding this ending makes me even angrier. If this game was meant to be a social commentary on dating sims, I think it should at least be warned or tagged as such. I know people who were triggered by the content from the secret ending as it is something that gay men have literally experienced.
I don't know if the content was included as some kind of zany "shock factor" that people for some reason think is a
addition to the visual novel/dating sim genres (
), but it was in very poor taste here. Post-secret ending, it feels like the game means to say that gay men are a joke and don't deserve genuine happiness. That's literally how it sounds to me and my friends and my 16-yo trans brother.
I would not have such a huge issue with the content if it were in a more appropriate game; the problem is not necessarily the content itself, but the setting it was presented in. This game was not marketed at all to include any kind of psychological horror and the inclusion of it (regardless of whether it's accessible or not; the information is out there and it's true so that is now irrelevant) is, again, in very poor taste and judgement.
I do have a few friends who genuinely enjoy the game, however, and I'm glad if others are able to have fun with it, but after all that happened with it and how upset my brother is over it, I'm extremely saddened and I can no longer say that I like it. Also, if you try a game and decide you want to refund it, make sure you don't leave the game running in the background.

There's a few things people look for that are into visual novels:
- A deep storyline with fascinating characters and an immersive universe, and all that stuff entails.
- Oh yeah, that stuff up above, there.
The sad thing is, while the art was super gorgeous, and an interesting and original universe was created, the storytelling and lack of any sort of genuine seriousness made it fall short. They fooled you into thinking it would be really in-depth with the little "Make Your Dad" thing. But it was comical and no matter how hard you try, your dad will look silly and ugly in comparison to the other dads, which ruins the dynamic completely. (Who wants to imagine hunky-azz Craig getting frisky with a dude who looks like the creepy uncle from a 90s cartoon? Not me, and golly did I try to make him not look uggo.)
I appreciate comedy in all its forms, I just don't think it had a place in visual novels, to be honest. I enjoyed the hilarious puns and little jabs in the beginning, but it ended up tiring and over-played by the end of even 1 story. (I couldn't get through another.)
Pros:
- Funny
- Wholesome
- Endearing
Cons:
- Short
- Boring
- Lack of options in both story and character.
- Lack of art/scene splashes.
- Voice acting was uneeded, too frequent, and cringy, since they say maybe 1 word, the rest is grunts and other weird noises.
- Lack of any genuine feelings aside from those shared with your daughter. For example, Craig's storyline. He was one of your oldest friends, and at the end of  the storyline, you still kiss and then f*cking say, "BRO..." Like really?
All in all, this was a mockery of visual novels, which it very well may have meant to be, in which case it fulfilled its purpose, I just wish they had said that from the get go instead of taking 15 bucks from me and taking JUST long enough for me not to be able to get a refund for it.

This game was great. Though it might not live up to my rose-coloured glasses view of the original Torment. It provides a lot of interesting quests to complete, to grow stronger and eventually face the final encounter using the skills built up over the game.

Like Planescape, Tides is a cerebral text-heavy game where you can talk yourself out of most combat situations or avoid them all together. If you build a strong combative character, you can find yourself fighting quite a bit. But no matter how aggressive you play, the fighting will be dwarfed by the amount of reading you'll be doing. While the combat is solid and has a nice feel to it, this is hardly the best game for strategic turn-based combat. What you should be coming to this game for is the engrossing world and story, it's unique cast of characters, and the special mood this game offers.
Both games feature a protagonist unsure of their identity who is faced with philosophical and existential situations in highly imaginative bizarre/alien worlds. Both deal with similar themes but remain different enough to branch into separate areas. "What can change the nature of a man?" is at the heart of Planescape, and "What does one life matter?" is at the heart of Tides.
If you have played Planescape, I feel it's important to go into this one with limited expectations to be pleasantly surprised at all the similar feelings and nods to planescape rather than looking for what does or doesn't measure up. I think the mixed reviews are partly do to that, and also from people buying the game expecting something like Pillars of Eternity, where combat plays a much larger role and is significantly less text-heavy.
Despite PS and Tides being in different universes, you'll recognize some names and items and even some of the areas+characters will remind you of those in planescape - again being different but resminicent. Tides takes place in the numenera table top world which itself is largely influenced by the planescape D&D campaign setting.
There are some mechanics I really enjoyed in this game - such as failing skill checks can often lead to interesting variations in the quests, and may open up new doors that you otherwise wouldn't get to. In a few negative reviews I saw people saying that they wish they could do this or that not knowing that they totally could if they had made different choices previously. inXile's previous game Wasteland 2 offered an incredible amount of ways to navigate situations and complete quests, and Tides continues the possiblities by adding depth to skill check success/failure
Overall, this game offered a great 40 hour ride with future replayability. I'll continue thinking about it. Highly recommended!

The original Torment is still one of my favorite games and this very much delivers as a spiritual successor or reboot.  The story and characters are all well drawn and engaging. The game is not perfect-some of the quests were buggy and it could stand to be more challenging.  Some areas contained encounters that felt unfinished or underdeveloped, but this was fairly minor.  I enjoyed the combat system, though it could have used more depth.  Overall, though, this was an excellent game that kept me hooked until the end.  Hope we'll see more in this setting.

Mad Max ist ein großartiges Spiel, und neben der Fallout reihe eines meiner liebsten postapokalyptischen spiele.
Diesmal hat man keine Power Rüstung, oder ein Casino oder einen Alien Blaster. Nein

Dies ist ein Muss, denn in Mad Max ist euer Auto euer zuhause, eure Lebensversicherung, ohne geht nicht.

So kann man direkt im Spiel seine ohnehin schon tollen Screenshots mit diversen Fitern, Brushes, Lichtverhältnissen, Distanzen uvm anpassen. So macht das Monotone rum fahren weiteren Spaß auf der suche nach neuen Bildern.

In the short time I have owned this game I have learned three things.
1. Chumbucket is the best traveling compainion I have seen.
2. Raming things with your car after some bumper (ramming prow) upgrades is absolutely fun to do.
3. I very rarely use fast travel for some unknown reason.
You will see that people mention a lot of grinding, well they are not lying.
Best thing to do is enjoy the absolute slaughter fest that you cause in melee combat and act like a serial killer shark when you drive. Trust me, it will make the grinding much more enjoyable.
You will spend quite a bit of the game going from warcamp to convoy, destorying everything that you don't like the look of. You decide wether or not that pitiful warboy in his little buggy gets to live or not, but most of the time it will be not.
***WARNING SOME SPOILERS PAST THIS POINT***
Now your two biggest limiting factors is going to be threat level and scrap. As such i suggest that at your first oppertunity you get a cleanup crew at each stronghold as that will allow you to do hit and runs on random scouts without stopping for the scrap they drop. This will also be useful when you take down convoys as they have quite a few vehicles in them (Which respawn if you don't kill the fuel truck).
As for region threat level, try and enjoy the fun that is killing all the warboys in each camp. I suggest using whatever equipment you have to weaken the defenses at each one before going in (AKA kill that damn war crier before hand). If you find a warcamp a bit too hard go out, do random crap for griffa tokens, get better equipment from leveling, see Griffa for upgrades, and go murder some armies inside that camp.
Last of all, THE CAR! That is your everything in the game, it will end up with harpoons, a sniper riffle, EXPLOSIVE harpoons, as well as better rams, armor, engines, wheels, anti-boarding spikes, wheel spikes, nitros, and some other interesting things to make it your own. Seriously, the armor and ram will affect the weight of the car meaning you will need a better engine and suspenstion for it to work, and you can work all that to your benifit. A long time back when this game came out someone I knew let me mess around and I constructed a car with no armor, best engine and suspenstion, and a MASSIVE RAM! Needless to say it could ram the scrap off a war-rig if they existed in-game.
So before you get this game remember that you will be grinding and improving your stuff before you can progress. This game is LONG and you will have a lot of time in this game before you finish it. Even then you can spend more time getting the last few parts for your car and getting 100%. As such game at the risk of your already limited social life and say goodbye to your cousins and other family members that do not live within a mile of you if you do get this game.
If you're a fan of the Mad Max film series you'll be glad to know that this is one of the best uses of a license for a game ever. Highly recommend you get it next time it's on sale.

Sure, it's episodic and you are (potentially) paying full price for a game that you will receive over time with no guarantee of on going quality.
I have to say though, the individual locations are massive, and there is a ton to do in each of them. If you're the kind of player who tends to run through a level and be done with it, then sure, this probably isn't for you. For me however, I've had a blast going into each location multiple times finding new items, new intel, hearing new conversions, not to mention finding new ways to eliminate my targets without ever being seen. It's definitely Hitman.
I also have to commend the number of gameplay/UI options they've included for tweaking the experience. There isn't anything quite like being dropped into a mission with no waypoints or hints, and having to scope out your targets manually.
If you're unsure, drop the $15 on the first mission (which actually includes 2 somewhat beefy training missions, in addition to Paris), play it a few times, then see how you feel. If you're like me, you'll promptly drop the $50 for the upgrade. In the end, you'll only be paying $5 more than what you would on a typical full release.

My personal favorite Batman game to date. It's darker, grittier, and more sinister than both Arkham Asylum, and Arkham Origins. It may not be Kevin Conroy as the Caped Crusader, but Roger Craig Smith does a decent job at a younger, inexperienced Batman. Troy Baker also takes over the mantle as The Joker, the unstable, unshakeable, villain we know and love; and he pulls it off well! While combat hasn't changed drastically from the previous games, Arkham Origins still delivers that Batman feeling we know and love. I don't recommend the multiplayer, however.

Do not misunderstand me: compared to most games today, Arkham Origins is a GREAT game, so by all means, buy it! The one true Achilles' heel about it, is that it is a sequal to two idiotically AMAZING and revolutionary games. That is what truly killed it for me, because there are so many things that is half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥compared to Arkahm Asylum and City. The one thing that was the most annoying, was the revamped character models and (partly) background story. Yes, I'm looking at you Bane and Riddler!
So by all means, buy it and enjoy it, because it is actually pretty good. Just be mindful of a few things if you've played the other two Arkham games.

"Oooh!" -I thought. "Another Arkham game! How exciting!"
Alas, I was fooled. It's not a new Arkham Game, it's the same Arkham game: Arkham City.
They just renamed some skills (ice gun is now the glue grenade), re-skinned parts of the map, juggled some locations around, made the characters look and sound younger (with mixed success) and wrote up a story that would have made sense if this game was released BEFORE the other two.
So yes, it's a prequel that explains the origins of the Joker in the Arkahm universe. I'm not regarding that as a spoiler since the game drops that ball pretty quickly and then forgets to properly pick it up again. The game starts off as a setup to get Batman to fights 8 big-name(?) assassins, but then the JOKER is name-dropped. "Who is this Jokey -guy? He seems very unpredictable and DANGEROUS!" -wonders Batman aloud, while the player is gritting his/her teeth in impotent frustration.
Then the assassins get picked off with ridiculous ease (Example: you punch one of them. You punch the assassin once. That's it. He drops on the first punch and that's it. The game lets you think he's coming back but he isn't and that is LAME.)
Lastly: the game seems to get bored of itself towards the end. When you get the shock -gloves the combat becomes straightforward button-mashing with little else. Most special enemies are not seen until the last moments of the game, and I managed to beat several boss-fights simply by mashing attack, since blocking does not seem to always work for some enemies.
No recommendation, since the original two games do all the same things but better.
Oh, wait! There's COLLECTIBLES! Just like in the last two games! So you can pump up the 100% completion time all the way to 30+ or maybe even 40+ hours! (If you are a psychotic achievement-♥♥♥♥♥ completionist, in which case this is your dream game!)

I definitely have mixed feelings about this game. I've played it for 2 years off and on and it definitely has it's pros and cons. It's customization system gives a very wide variety of ways to make unique characters, the base weapons (ones that don't require premium/money) are fairly easy to pick up and overall this game seems very good aesthetically.
HOWEVER, the relevance and playability of this game being completely multiplayer have dwindled more and more with every update. The way that Gamer First and the community has pushed the idea of paying being more rewarding than grinding has destroyed the opportunity for new players to get anywhere in the game. Premium and weapons are expensive, $40 dollars being the minimum price to buy and keep a gun from Armas. Weapons like the rocket launchers and reskinned assault rifles with insane fire rate while cool conceptually make it impossible for lower ranked players with less experience to have a chance of winning.
Because grinding for some of the base (and mediocre) versions of some of the "best" gear takes tens to hundreds of hours to raise money for without premium or winning constantly, anyone who hadn't gotten into the game a year or so earlier can't compete the the very few who still play.
Now this isn't entirely the fault of the community although they share a lot of the blame too. Gamer First seems to only care that they keep making money and it takes them years to make any big change to this game. Anti cheat was added less than a year ago and it's been out since 2011. It still doesn't keep hackers and triggerbots out. To Gamer First they're running out of people to syphon money out of with the community down to 100-200 people being online at once max, so they've decided to announce that they'll 'revamp' the matchmaking system that currently forces casuals against the people that pour money into the game and play daily.
They probably won't really fix anything relevant to what the casual community wants though. The graphics have not really changed beyond that of a would-be GTA IV (if that), items that are attractive in design to most people are a huge gap in price from earlier items (example: slow moving and amusing cop car to extremely fast sports car that's been custom designed from licenseplate to tailpipe).
As for the community's fault in all of this, people pay for this game to keep up, to make the grind less strenuous. But their view can be even more narrow than those of the casuals. Because they put money into it, the logic is that they deserve to be where they are in the game. It doesn't matter what group/stereotype is in it either. They meet casuals with hostility and often push new players away from the game. Hostility does not bring about banter or intellectual conversation. And understanding that this is a video game makes it just as bad to take it seriously.
TL:DR : This game is a lost cause, regardless of what the updates might say. It was beautfiul in it's initial design, it's cosmetics are great and back when it was starting out the community was friendly and viable. Now because of money and hostility from those who spend it, only people who have poured out their wallets play this game (100-200 people online max).

Mad Max ist ein großartiges Spiel, und neben der Fallout reihe eines meiner liebsten postapokalyptischen spiele.
Diesmal hat man keine Power Rüstung, oder ein Casino oder einen Alien Blaster. Nein
Dieses mal hat man ein Auto mit V6 und V8 Motoren Nitro und coole Waffen.
Eine Wunderschöne Wüstenlandschaft und einer Tollen Nebengeschichte in Form von Postkarten die die Menschen vor der Apokalypse und während dessen verfasst haben. Diverse Postkarten sind sehr emotional so das man mehr in die Spielwelt eintaucht.
Wenn ihr viele Quests wollt, dann seid ihr bei Mad Max falsch, neben der eigentlichen ebenfalls schönen aber kurzen Storyline liegt die stärke darin, alle Orte zu besuchen, um Metal, Benzin, Wasser, Karrosierien, und besagte Postkarten zu finden.
Dies ist ein Muss, denn in Mad Max ist euer Auto euer zuhause, eure Lebensversicherung, ohne geht nicht.
Ihr werdet oft das Gefühl haben nur das gleiche zu tun da es relativ monoton werden kann, aber der reiz alles zu sehen und zu schauen was die Landschaft noch so bietet zahlt sich aus. So kann man zb den versteckten Ort vom Menübild finden.
Aber das eigentliche Highlight ist die Ingame Screenshot Funktion.
So kann man direkt im Spiel seine ohnehin schon tollen Screenshots mit diversen Fitern, Brushes, Lichtverhältnissen, Distanzen uvm anpassen. So macht das Monotone rum fahren weiteren Spaß auf der suche nach neuen Bildern.

In the short time I have owned this game I have learned three things.
1. Chumbucket is the best traveling compainion I have seen.
2. Raming things with your car after some bumper (ramming prow) upgrades is absolutely fun to do.
3. I very rarely use fast travel for some unknown reason.
You will see that people mention a lot of grinding, well they are not lying.
Best thing to do is enjoy the absolute slaughter fest that you cause in melee combat and act like a serial killer shark when you drive. Trust me, it will make the grinding much more enjoyable.
You will spend quite a bit of the game going from warcamp to convoy, destorying everything that you don't like the look of. You decide wether or not that pitiful warboy in his little buggy gets to live or not, but most of the time it will be not.
***WARNING SOME SPOILERS PAST THIS POINT***
Now your two biggest limiting factors is going to be threat level and scrap. As such i suggest that at your first oppertunity you get a cleanup crew at each stronghold as that will allow you to do hit and runs on random scouts without stopping for the scrap they drop. This will also be useful when you take down convoys as they have quite a few vehicles in them (Which respawn if you don't kill the fuel truck).
As for region threat level, try and enjoy the fun that is killing all the warboys in each camp. I suggest using whatever equipment you have to weaken the defenses at each one before going in (AKA kill that damn war crier before hand). If you find a warcamp a bit too hard go out, do random crap for griffa tokens, get better equipment from leveling, see Griffa for upgrades, and go murder some armies inside that camp.
Last of all, THE CAR! That is your everything in the game, it will end up with harpoons, a sniper riffle, EXPLOSIVE harpoons, as well as better rams, armor, engines, wheels, anti-boarding spikes, wheel spikes, nitros, and some other interesting things to make it your own. Seriously, the armor and ram will affect the weight of the car meaning you will need a better engine and suspenstion for it to work, and you can work all that to your benifit. A long time back when this game came out someone I knew let me mess around and I constructed a car with no armor, best engine and suspenstion, and a MASSIVE RAM! Needless to say it could ram the scrap off a war-rig if they existed in-game.
So before you get this game remember that you will be grinding and improving your stuff before you can progress. This game is LONG and you will have a lot of time in this game before you finish it. Even then you can spend more time getting the last few parts for your car and getting 100%. As such game at the risk of your already limited social life and say goodbye to your cousins and other family members that do not live within a mile of you if you do get this game.
If you're a fan of the Mad Max film series you'll be glad to know that this is one of the best uses of a license for a game ever. Highly recommend you get it next time it's on sale.

Please note: My thumbs down would flip into a thumbs up as a recommendation to fans of wordy visual novels, but only on deep discount (75% off).
Torment: Tides of Numenera has some great writing and fascinating 'what if?' characters, all of whom you'd never want to read as a main character because their fantastical situation is all-consuming (in some cases, literally). While there are witty barbs and amusing banter exchanged between your accumulated and chosen party members, it only works because of the humanity in their words, not the weirdness of the setting. I'm sure there were tons of situational remarks that could crop up, depending on who was in your party and which conversational fork you go down, choosing your own adventure in this trippy science fanstasy setting.
And really, that's what Torment comes down to: a lore dense world of imaginative characters hanging out. You click on them and engage in a dialog tree thats reads like mini-choose-your-own adventures, just like in Ultima IV... from 1985. Don't get me wrong, many of the choices are interesting, varied and thoughtful. It is a highly evolved conversastional structure, but it is entirely inside the box Lord British's built. For as weird as Torment tries to be, it adheres to very old conventions, often to the detriment of play.
Navigating around the dated 1990's interface to read a scattered stack of (mostly) good choose-your-own adventures, some that do cross-over with other characters, often standing within easy earshot, isn't something I want to do on my computer for more than $40. Especially given the looped animations, repetitive sound effects and the sameness of the conversational structures.
While I was okay with the game interface as total Baldur's Gate/Pillars of Eternity/Planescape: Torment, combat came up so rarely that the whole game felt like a Pillars of Eternity mod. Like a walking simulator, we're stuck clunkily marching the whole party around to interrogate anyone standing about or pacing, waiting to show me their choose-your-own adventure. To be fair to the game, I conceived of a gentle and wise character during creation. I avoided the first fight, as well as the very few obvious opportunities I was presented with for a scrap. Still, even had I been bloodthirsty, I imagine that 95% of the game was reading. Why make us wander around like we're in a pausible tactical RPG?
Combat did not reappear for a VERY long time (about hour 10 of my play through), and when it did it felt super bad, first time awkward. I had no idea what any of my characters could do. Not having any practice with the system, beyond the tutorial that I'd played hours/days earlier, I stumbled through it, accepting that (as part of the premise of the game) my character was probably going to die at some point in the story. Resurrection, reincarnation and reinvention are all themes of the Torment: Tide of Numenera. Right then was as good a time as any to see if my choices had amounted to anything in my sweet afterlife home base.
To mark big decisions, game provides glowing colors as indicators of the merits of your choices (wise, aggressive, proud, compassionate, etc). Some options are only available if you're sufficiently advanced in a particular color. But in ten hours I didn't feel like any of that made any difference to my story. That though my dialog within that particular choose-your-own adventure might be changed, the larger story appeared unaffected. Perhaps all those choices were affecting things, dramatically, but given the strangeness of the setting (I mean, there are some seriously odd characters loitering about), I couldn't really tell if anything I'd done had any effect. However, given the breathless introduction of weird character after weird character, mostly behaving in pedestrian, static ways, waiting to sell you a healing potion or offer a quest... well, I found that I  didn't really care all that much about any one of the characters, least of all my own.
But Death was so dull that there wasn't even anything to read, adding not a single between-lives choose-your-own adventure.
So I resurrected in a temple of cannibals, looked at the half-dozen choose-your-own adventures that I'd need to slog through to try and figure out where I was, what was going on, what they wanted me to do, and then click on everything in the scene, in case there's a bit of writing that's actually important to driving the plot; instead, I just quit the game.
Torment did stay with me a few days. For more than a week, I considered picking it back up, but it felt like just that: a weight that I carried for reasons past understanding.
While much of the written dialog is quite good (but long and front-loaded with lore and nomenclature), parts are performed as voice-over. I didn't think any of it was particularly good. A few actors were terrible. Weird is the long abscence (most of what I played, in fact) of ANY voice-over at all, then came lengthy periods of unlikable characters talking. I turned that off fairly fast, because for the few characters that I liked, I'd already come up with my own voice for them that I enjoyed far more than hearing the uneven performances. It felt like a half-baked Kickstarter stretch goal to voice all the main characters and the game was worse for it.
Were this game conceived of and marketed as a linked series of easy-to-navigate mini-games and scenes that let you play out stories in their imaginative universe, through a tablet and for less than ten dollars, I'd think Torment: Tides of Numenera was pretty great.
Instead, the thing is old, dressed-up Ultima dialog trees, sending you on a colorful Avatar quest that you have to navigate in an inappropriate Baldur's Gate interface. The story has all the indications of depth and lore and mystery, but there's no effective device, scuba or otherwise, to dive in and feel like you're actually creating your own tale. Maybe I'd only scratched the surface, and a fantastic story with reveals and twists and turns awaited me after talking to all the cannibals, but I lost interest because all their neat ideas and fine writing didn't make me feel much of anything.
Oh, and they want more than $40 for a giant choose-your-own adventure. So I say: no.

The good is that this game does have a really good story with plenty of choices in how to respond to NPC's, everything is very well written. The big downside for me is the combat just isn't fun. I've played a lot of Planescape, and other CRPGs, where they have automatic combat, which isn't fun at all, but the turn based crisis system in this game just isn't enjoyable at all. I have no problem with turn based combat, I really love the combat in Fallout 1&2. This game, it doesn't work that well, like the fights take too long. The worst is an area where there's about 20 drones and a few major ones, so if you and your party have good stealth, you can slowly creep through and deactivate the terminals and get a better reward. If you fight, expect to be there forever, especially with drones that waste turns spinning around for no reason. Only one class specializes is combat and has weapon training, in a game with minimal combat, so what's the point? I've tried very passive characters with nano and jack, but there are still parts where you're forced into combat and it sucks, so a bad build will wreck you. There is a lot to like, but a lot to be annoyed by. Like, Planescape, you always come back from defeat in combat, only here there's some story areas where if you die, that's game over, which can get super irritating. I wish they were serious about being able to avoid combat, because some enemies don't have reason. Also, one other thing I have mixed feelings about is the morality, for better or worse, there is no punishment. Like you can do the good thing, some people will be nicer to you, but that's it. Or you can kill something in cold blood or other acts of cruelty, and get very impresive rewards, some people will hate you after that, but it's just to make you feel bad, while you get wealthy. It's better than punishing you for role playing, but it also feels very soft on being a jerk. As far as time spent playing, I played almost 17 hours, then my computer died, so I bought the PS4 version, and spent way more time playing that, got pretty far into the game, but started to lose interest. It's like I'd want to cheat because of the bad combat, but trainers kinda suck, either flagged by antivirus or they want you to pay for cheats. There's let's plays, but it's a text heavy game, so the player must be a great talker, good luck at that. I'd like to know how it ends, but I don't care to play more.

The best review I could possibly give is that this is a worthy successor to its namesake, and I think that it is. It doesn't surpass the original Torment, but it certainly comes the closest to it of any game in recent memory. The writing is just stellar, which is somethign I almostnever get to say about video games. Truly thought-provoking stories are rare in video games these days, at least in ones that have any reasonable amount of actual gameplay (i.e., not walking simulators), and those that do achieve it usually either dig shallow or hit a single isolated point or feeling. Tides dives deep in almost every area, nearly every conversation delving into a different, difficult moral/philosophical dilemma. It's difficult to play this game without seriously reflecting on what you are doing and why, and who that makes you.
Beyond the deeper issues, Tides is one of the most creative universes I've ever seen, really bringing Monte Cook's remarkable source material to life. Every little thing is a wonder, every description is amazement. In one early area, there is a fountain made entirely from synthetic fish that constantly leap and spiral as though they were water. If you're fast, you can catch one and examine it. This has no story consequence whatsoever-- it's a random detail, but things like this are everywhere, and they give so much life to this post-post-futuristic world. It feels like everything is accounted for.
On the negative side, two critiques: first, the characters, while well-crafted, just didn't capture me as much as I'd hoped. I still think fondly of Morte, Falls-From-Grace, and the Nameless One from the original Torment. While the Last Castoff's story will still be with me in 20 more, I doubt that I will remember his companions, let alone have their names at my fingertips. Second critique: I enjoyed the effort system, but frankly it felt a little too easy, particularly after the early levels. I suggest ramping up the difficulty any way you can, because at a certain point, I never worried about conserving my effort (recharging was always near) and I nearly never failed a challenge.
Overall, I highly recommend this for any fan of RPG games, and particularly for anyone interested in storytelling, philosophy, or world-building.

Sooo.......... Ages ago I backed this game on Kickstarter. However, once InExile started making development decisions that seemed to reverse promises made in the Kickstarter I became skeptical. Only having backed for a $20 digital game didn't make it worth refunding. But I felt as though there were intrinsic aspects of Infinity Engine-style games, and Torment in Particular, that the developers either didn't understand, or wanted to shortcut, and that these decisions were exemplified by their conception of "Crisis Encounters" and turn-based mechanics.
Well, after finally playing the game, I feel that me concerns were eminently justified.
The idea that you should be able to interact with characters and the environment to resolve encounters makes toooooooooons of sense, and it's good to see. But mixing it with turn-based mechanics is a terrible, awful, no-good, and vile fundamental flaw. The Torment devs think nothing of tossing a dozen random mobs into encounters that revolve around your characters essentially flipping a couple switches or have a few conversations without dying. You then find yourself taking thirty quadrillion zillion years per encounter to talk to a couple NPC people because you have to wait for all the mobs to cycle through their turns. Even worse, sometimes the AI bugs out during encounters and you have to restart the whole damned thing. (Not to mention some of their graphics and effects choices are weirdly non-performant relative to quality while at times being rather overdone and innelegant.)
If they'd stuck to typical Infinity Engine-style "Real Time With Pause" during these things it'd have been fine. But they didn't, and it's miserable. Even weirder, there's no coherent reason for adopting the encounter system: the game isn't remotely a tactical turn based game like XCOM or something. And bringing that style of gameplay into a game based less on combat and tactics and more on dialog and interactions makes no cohesive sense. What does the player gain out of enemies taking a dozen sequential turns when all that's going to happen is that you're going to flip a couple text-encounter switches and resolve them with some "effort?"
Now if you ignore the terrible terrible terrible encounters the game is actuall more than half-decent or even good. At least two of the companions are interesting (if a tad underdeveloped, which is weird and crazy considering the amount of text in the game). (Others are kind of boring.) The world is interesting. The plot is interesting, though at times hard to grasp if you aren't making sure to investigate every damn thing. This is a game that could have been great, but somebody tried to frankenstein the idea of "turn based-encounters" into what's fundamentally a mostly dialog-based game and it ruined it. Narratively, I think it really deserved to have the Last Castoff forge some more meaningful bonds with non-party based (particularly castoff) NPCs, and the lack of said meaningful bonds between the castoff and all but a couple in-party characters really makes some of the decisions fall flat, feel a bit empty. (I think the Merecaster thing was supposed to be a way to sidestep this issue, but I don't really feel like it worked.)
If somebody could figure out a way to mod the encounters into behaving like combat in Pillars of Eternity or Baldur's gate the game would probably be many times better. Help me tan the dead horse's hide: "It's just not fun to have to spend 1+ hours to have two conversations because of pointless turn-based mechanics." I question devs who couldn't grasp this... They are certainly not ones I'd ever trust with what was essentially a preorder again.
I feel bad writing this review because most games these days aren't remotely as interesting. Yet I'm not sure it's right to praise something so flawed just because the attempt was made and it is rather interesting...
I definitely would love to see another RPG set in the Ninth World, at least.

I went into this thinking I wasn't going to like it, if I'm honest. I was expecting it'd either be Tumblr bait, a low effort meme game, or a little of both. And yeah, there are some minor elements of those things, but it's surprisingly well written and quite sweet. It's not
tier, and doesn't try to be, but I felt way more involved with the characters than I expected to, and they're not just big obvious stereotypes. It was a refreshing change to play a VN that had a predominantly upbeat tone and a story/setting grounded in the real world, and while it's not 100% played for laughs there are moments of genuine humour as well as some emotional scenes. Overall I liked it way, way more than I was expecting to.
The main downside to the game is that it's pretty short. My first playthrough clocked at under 2 hours -- though I'm quite a fast reader -- and while I've occasionally played shorter VN's, it's definitely on the low end of the scale. As far as I can gather there's also not a huge amount of branching routes; I believe the surrounding story stays the same with the only changes being which of the six dads you decide to date. (I think the store page description is wrong when it says there are 7 options.) Again, this isn't a deal breaker, as there are plenty of kinetic visual novels (i.e. ones with no choices at all) that manage to be really enjoyable, but if you're replaying to see what the routes are like with other characters you're going to be doing a lot of fast forwarding. Personally, I can't see myself replaying it to see every route as there were some characters I just wasn't very interested in, but that's down to personal taste.
I also experienced a few technical issues with the game. The most obtrusive was that certain sounds were much louder than others, in contexts where the sound has no reason to be that loud. This made playing on headphones somewhat uncomfortable as I never knew when I was going to get ear blasted by a high volume clip. The second hitch is that you click to advance the text, but the choices are in the exact same place as the regular text, so it's super easy to accidentally reach a point where you have a choice and click on one of the options before you can see them properly. I had to reload on a number of occasions due to this problem, and I feel like it would have helped to have the choices in a different part of the screen. A more rare issue (only happened twice) was where the game was stuck on a loading screen for an unreasonably long time.
Apparently some of the achievements are bugged. I do not care about achievements, though, so it's not something that matters to me personally, but YMMV.
Overall it's by no means one of the best VN's out there, but it's certainly not bad. We're talking 7/10 material here; it has a good deal of charm and wit, but it's probably not going to stay with you for a long time.

Definitely a lot of good things to be said about Amygdala, and definitely a lot of bad. A lot. To begin, after wiping out the entire campaign in a very short amount of time, not a single achievement unlocked, which while not important, isn't cool at all.
Clearly artistically inspired by Binding of Isaac, with contextual black and white doodle intro to boot, Amygdala throws you into a visually interesting platformer with a lot of surrealist monstrosities roaming the landscape and a dorky looking wizard to hunt and kill. Taking out the wizard is your main objective to regain your body, but you can take your time exploring the randomly generated levels and collecting gems to make your third eye bigger. That third eye serves as a sort of dual health meter/jetpack gauge, as it shrinks both when you take damager and when you literally♥♥♥♥♥♥bricks to gain some extra height. It's weirdly fun, and using your buttstuff to save yourself from falling into the abyss is definitely a good feeling. While initially disarming, the lack of a UI is a welcome change, and I appreciate the attempt, even though in some ways this game among others would've benefitted from some sort of number count or something. When you succeed you're presented with a lot of stats, and it was only after a few matches did I connect the third eye was more than just a bulletshooter. Also, for those who do take the dive into this game, where the eye is looking is where the boss is more or less located. Quite well done in both theory and execution, so serious props.
Where the game faulters is sadly in the gameplay itself. Even after seeing the majority of the game and the monsters it offered, most served little other purpose than to just be bulletsponges. Platforming is wonky but functional, and I could more or less guide my disembodied grandfather head fairly well to dodge stuff and make certain jumps, but the amount of deaddropping I experienced and weird jump lag or random loss of inertia often made me have to♥♥♥♥♥♥bricks to save myself. I do not regret typing that. The bullets that I shoot I could never tell were getting stronger or weaker either, which wasn't the best, and most fights involve jumping and spamming the bracket buttons (of all things) to win, so prepare for a lot of repetition.
Is it bad? No. It's better than the majority of games on Steam now. Amygdala is a key example as to why a maybe button is keen at the moment, because that would be my choice. This game needs a lot of work, but it's also not that bad in the first place. I can't recommend it in good faith, but I do respect what they've done here. Hopefully whatever MachineSpirit makes next will take whatever they've learned here and really apply it to whatever they do next. Worth a buy maybe if it's super on sale, but otherwise pass this one.
