Whilst buggy, this game is seriously underated.
Most of the hate comes from the large amount of game breaking bugs, which were not removed quickly enough, though at this stage I managed to complete the game only having to restart twice, both of which were not during the story, and I only need to "restart from last checkpoint", and not the entire game. [SPOILER ALERT]
Apart from that, the 'lack of innovation' in this game is the another reason that this game is hated. Whilst in comparison to the other two Arkham Games, that is true, this game has one huge area of innovation: The Multiplayer. Unfourtunately, this was not the audience wanted, so it was largely disregarded. But in fact, the multiplayer is quite fun, and at the time of writing has an active multiplayer community. This is really what I would have wanted from an Arkham multiplayer mode. Stealth against real people. Whilst I will admit playing Batman or Robin is alot more fun than the thugs, there is an equaliser. The fact that at one point in the game, one player will be able to play as the Joker or Bane. This actually can be really challenging for Batman or Robin, especially if the player of the Joker or Bane is good at the game. Of course there is one bug that *still* hasn't been fixed is multiplayer data being wiped. Though by launching the game from singleplayer mode this will prevent this bug, no matter what (from my experience). Some may also have to launch singleplayer again one they are finished, but I haven't experienced this. Now my favourite bit from this game is the Story. Now, obviously some will be dissapointed (see the spoiler) by the plot, but I still think that the story was gold. It was really the first Arkham Game to try to show the flaws in Batman's actions, as he seriously hurts people to stop them hurting others. Some of the corrupt police or common thugs are in desperate positions, and don't have much hope elsewhere, yet Batman will still knock them out cold. Still angered by his parent's death, Batman is demanding, somewhat ungrateful and unable to listen an opinion other than his own, I cringed with every conversation Batman and Alfred had, until the *incident*. Not a single thank you, shouting because Alfred opposed his views, Alfred's relationship with Batman is one of the most heart-breaking of all. The ending was uplifting, and somewhat smart. One pointer is how ubsurd it is how much happens in one night. I'd rate it 7/10, based on the fact Arkham Assylum is a 10/10 for me.

Tides of Numenera is a CRPG in the vein of the great RPGs of the late 90s and early 2000s. As such, it targets a very specific kind of customer: those who have played those games in the past or at least always wanted to try them. Hence, in this review I will not go into the specifics of the gameplay or genre. Instead, I would like to offer my take on whether or not Tides of Numenera successfully achieved its goal to be a spiritual successor of possibly the greates of all CRPGs: Planescape Torment.
There are three main reasons why people think it didn't and why it's getting such controversial reviews here on Steam (in stark contrast to the overwhelmingly positive critical reception in the gaming press):
1.) The story and the setting are completely different even though they share some fundamentals. It feels like the developers tried to recreate the "feel" of Planescape Torment. Some people think they tried to hard and that it comes across as somewhat by-the-numbers. (I disagree.)
2.) The battle and character development systems and mechanics are completely different and actually rather innovative and unconventional.
3.) Kickstarter stretch goal controversy: not all features that were planned initially as part of the crowdfunding campaign made it into the game.
Now, do these things detract from the enjoyment of playing Tides of Numenera? I would strongly disagree. This is a great game focussing completely on its story, world building and player-NPC interaction. Absolutely ridiculous amounts of mostly well-written texts (conversations, descriptions, lore) take your mind on a journey where you travel to strange places to meet hundreds of interesting characters. In this sense, while by nature it feels somewhat derivative of games like Planescape Torment, it is still almost unmatched in todays gaming market.
The game systems are rather innovative and hence take some getting used to. This is true for the conversation and skill-check system, and even more so for the battle or "crisis" system that the developers came up with. The latter might not be the most elegant or engaging system you have ever used, but it gets the job done once you understand its idiosyncrasies. Certainly not up to par with the proper turn-based or real-time-with-pause-combat systems and traditional loot- and stat-based character levelling systems of the genre's very best, it is still servicable and fun if you invest the time to get behind how it works. What's more: You can play most of the game without every killing a single enemy, but you can also get some pretty nice gear and invest in the proper skills and make your characters into killing machins - or strike a balance somewhere in between. It's all up to you and how you want to confront the crises.
Lastly, the controversy about the missing Kickstarter goals might affect some backers' enjoyment of the game. This differs on a person-to-person basis. I backed the game originally and couldn't care less about the specifics of what made it into the game and what didn't. Others are not so lenient. Rest assured, for people who did not follow the development process of Tides of Numenera, the game as it stands now is a fully realized, fleshed-out experience true to the original vision. It might lack some of the peripheral bells and whistles, but that should not detract you from trying it.
Tides of Numenera certainly is not a perfect game and can't quite match what Planescape Torment achieved at the turn of the century. But judging from how many of these types of CRPGs of such a quality we have gotten in the last 15 years, this is not really something to critizise Tides of Numenera for. Rather, the developers should be applauded for how close they came to making a game that matches such a masterpiece in spirit, scope and execution.

I bought and played this game after it was patched to 1.1.

This is a game about atmosphere mostly, and lots of lots of words, oh god the words.
The combat system is rather simplistic, but functional and the enemy set-ups never gets very interesting, The crisis system itself I enjoyed since even if you found yourself in a sequence you'd rather want to avoid you can usually solve it by some other means and avoid fighting the enemy all together with some clever thinking which I enjoyed a lot .
The art in the game itself is fantastic. While it might not be graphically impressive, it sure do have some of the most interesting areas and design I've seen in a role-playing game in a long time and the colors are vibrant.
The story and the premise of the game  is interesting, and might leave yourself questioning your own morality sometimes, though the story gets a bit rushed towards the end which is a bit of a shame. As for the main cast, they are all interesting though I find them to be a bit underdeveloped, as for the side characters, there are lot of odd personalities around which are fun to interact with.
As for the gameplay - it's mostly reading honestly. If you don't like reading, you won't like this game - period. Some sequences feels like they were meant to be played trough but are instead experienced trough only text and pictures which is a shame and leaves you with the feeling that there were supposed to be more to it. The RPG system feels like a real P&P RPG and leaves you with lot of dialouge choices and a very fair point based RNG system to improve your choices.
Overall I can wholehartly recommend this for anyone who don't mind lot of reading. If you don't enjoy reading, well as I said earlier this game might not be for you, but you'll miss out on on of the best written stories in modern RPG history.

I honestly wasn't sure if I'd enjoy this game when I first considered buying it, but now I'm really glad that I did.  I had a surprising amount of fun playing Mad Max.  The environment is beautiful and for the most part the driving is good.  I thoroughly enjoyed upgrading Max's car, the Magnum Opus, and realizing that the best options weren't always the most powerful or top-tier.  Certain combinations are better for speed versus durability.  Yes, the game gets grindy since you're doing the same things over and over, but each camp is a unique layout, each territory is its own character.
The only parts of this game that had me raging were the two mandatory races for the story; Gastown especially.  The driving mechanics are rather touchy for such areas and often send your car spinning out of control.  I actually had to switch to a controller for the Gastown race just so I could have that fine steering control that WASD just doesn't provide.
One of the wasteland encounters also glitched for me which kept me from 100% completion; there are some bugs still in the game and I doubt that the developers are still maintaining this title.  But it was a minor issue for me and certainly not enough to keep me from playing.
I wish there were more open-world games that also gave me the ability to upgrade a personal vehicle in such detail.

Firstly I would call myself a veteran Call of Duty player, having been playing Call of Duty since 2011 starting with Black Ops 1. I have played Call of Duty on Xbox 360, One and PC and have improved my Call of Duty skills drastically over the years that I have been playing. I find myself enjoying Call of Duty more on the PC since I am better on PC than 360 (I have a 1.21 K/D on BO2 Multiplayer PC and 1.00 on 360). Overwhelmingly positive.
This was an impulse buy.  It was cheap, and I was intrigued:  overwhelmingly positive reviews?  For a truck-driving simulator.  I mean, I like driving games all right, but really?  Overwhelmingly positive?
In recent months, I've bought a lot of games:
Mad Max, X-Com 2, Assassin's Creed Syndicate, Assassin's Creed Rogue, and Tom Clancy's The Division.
These are all great games ... and yet the game I keep coming back to almost every day is Euro Truck Simulator 2.
This is a brilliant game.  Here's why:
1.  It's beautiful.  Sure, it's not the most beautiful game out there, nor even the most beautiful game I own, but the scenery is beautiful nonetheless.
2.  It's SOOOO relaxing.  As the end of a hard day, it's nice to load up a 1 hour stand-up comedy special in YouTube and then hit the road.  Just drive and listen to comedy.
3.  It IS challenging.  I get scored on getting my cargo to its destination in a timely manner, and UNDAMAGED.  Navigating tight corners, trying not to get speeding tickets when the speed suddenly changes, trying not to run into cars that suddenly slam on the breaks on the freeway, trying not to have an accident when I have to suddenly change lanes because my lane is "turn only" and I don't want to get off course.  Not to mention trying to map out and mark my turns, and plan where and when to stop for gas and sleep.
This is a game that understands that "challenging" and "frustrating" don't have to be synonymous.  This is a game that challenges my driving accuracy, while also making me think.
4.  There's motivation.  Sure, just going for a drive is nice, but this game adds another layer:  building an empire.  I save up money, get some loans, buy a garage, buy some trucks, and select drivers.  I quickly learn that loans aren't a bad idea:  I can repay them quicker if I have more people driving for me.  I'm now at the point where I no longer need loans because my drivers earn enough money that, in the time it takes me to run a reasonably long route, I can buy another garage and three more trucks.
The only downside I've run across so far:
1.  Roads sometimes don't make sense.  Signs sometimes say both lanes go to "X"ville, but only the left lane goes:  the right lane MUST turn.  In America and Japan, for the most part, if I'm on a two-lane freeway, it STAYS a two-lane freeway.  If the speed is 100kph, it STAYS 100kph until you exit.  Sometimes I see a sign indicating a speed change ... but my gps speed limit doesn't change.  Sometimes I don't see a speed limit sign, but still get a ticket.
However, I don't really mind because, even though it doesn't make sense, it keeps me on my toes.
2.  Drivers are STUPID.  I've had people come to a COMPLETE stop on the freeway.
If I'm turning across traffic, or even changing lanes, oncoming traffic rarely slows down.  They'll plow right into me at full speed, damaging my truck and/or cargo, and I get a ticket.
However, I don't really mind.  Drivers in my hometown do some pretty boneheaded things too, and if anything, the drivers in ETS 2 are LESS boneheaded than the people in my hometown (after all, ETS drivers don't suddenly change their mind at a red light and cross against the light).
Overall:  my feelings about this game are "overwhelmingly positive".
I had worried I would get bored playing this game, but after over 90 hours of play, I'm nowhere near bored.  I still love this game.  It's not for everybody.  No game is.  But there IS a good reason why the reviews for this game are so high:  it's an outstanding game.

I got this game to laugh at the sillyness of dads dating other dads. The game seems that way on the outside, but it gets deeper than that. I personally have always found dating sims and other visual novels to be kinda creepy/cringy. Dating virtual people (especially anime girls) has always looked so weird to me (I still think it's weird). Something about this game is different though. Relationships feel like relationships, everything isn't about how hot someone else is, the characters are great
, and not everything is about dating. It actually feels like a story rather than a place to trick fake anime people into sleeping with you. Aside from it being well-written to the point where I was laughing at the jokes the game presented instead of the game's concept, this game has great queer representation. If you haven't already caught on, this game features men dating men, and I think the diversity deserves praise. You can also play as a trans character. It doesn't really affect much, but it seems to have made many in the trans community happy, and I think it deserves to be a virtue of this game. Now one of the best things about this game, besides the humor, is there are more characters to interact with outside of the dads you can date. The most important relationship is with your child, and this game seems to talk a lot about the ups and downs of fatherhood. It's great to see a dating sim actually nail it. I've personally always hated the genre, but I highly recommend this game to anyone who wants good comedy, story, and representation.

Disclaimer: I was given a key to this game from the developer.
If this game were in early access (and it should be) I would give it a passing grade. To consider this a final product is a bit short-sighted, and it's not nearly worth $10. Don't get me wrong, I've had a bit of fun with this game. I was actually going to recommend this game until something happened.
I beat the first level. I finally got past the clunky, loose controls and beat the first level. I managed to find the wizard (the boss who I had never found before) and kill him. Then a portal appeared and I got excited to see what came next.
The title screen. The title screen is what came next. Am I missing something? Was that IT? Imagine playing Risk of Rain but having no items and nothing past the first level. Just the first level over and over again. According to another reviewer you can unlock hats, so that's... something. Other issues I had. (In addition to things I listed above)
In the end, this feels like the type of thing I would create if I had the time to learn how to develop a game. I would be proud of it, but I wouldn't think it's worth $10. I probably wouldn't even release it. I would take what I learned and start working on the next project. This feels like a tech demo for a bigger (and very fun) game.

Amygdala offers Risk of Rain-style roguelite platforming with runthroughs that are different every time, along with baddies that get slowly tougher the more boss wizards you kill.
First looks can be deceiving here - it's easily written off at a glance as a poor man's roguelike. But the original Binding of Isaac had a similar barrier to entry, a game whose graphics didn't appeal to everyone and had player movement that didn't feel right until a few plays in. So don't run away yet.
Gameplay highlights video:
At the heart of the game is a neat mechanism that means you CAN go and kill the boss wizard on each level straight away, but you'll probably die. Instead, you hunt for gems that both increase your energy level and increase the size of the third eye on your face. This eye, once large enough, is a handy compass that tells you where the boss is.
The other unusual mechanism is that you can poop out bricks. YOU CAN POOP OUT BRICKS. This acts as defence from some enemy attacks, plus sends you flying up in the air to reach difficult places. Doing this saps your energy, so you can't go mad.
Amygdana suffers a bit from a main character that lacks presence in the world - he slides around without much animation and has floaty jumps. But his reaction to being hurt is genuinely funny, his cute look of terror making up for anything else.
The graphics in general are a touch inconsistent. Most things look great - goofily charming enemies, vertigo-inducing backdrops, large tentacle-waving bosses etc. But a few feel slapdash; one of the basic wizard boss forms has a fairly ugly green shield and tiny missiles that look like placeholders.
Amygdala is an enjoyable and charming platformer with flaws, but has plenty of replay appeal (although it could do with a few more rare and random items). It's not a twitch shooter, so don't expect your heart to pound at every turn. So bring your explorer's hat, get past the occasionally shonky bits and you'll be pleasantly surprised.
Also there are hats. Hats there are. Everybody likes hats.

As I speed around the long, sweeping, dusty bend, I see a two cars coming in from the right.
"A War Party!" Yells my sidekick, Chumbucket.
They immediately make a beeline for my car, attempting to slam into it.
I harpoon one of the vehicles front tyres and swerve to left and hit the Nitrous. The tyre snaps right off, leaving the warboy stranded. I chuckle. So easy since upgrading my harpoon.
WHAM! The other warboy slams into me so hard i go swerving off into the dunes at high speed.
Not to be outdone I hit the Nitrous again and swerve to the right, back onto the road, neck and neck with the remaining warboy. Utilising my grinders on my tyres I slam hard into the side of the bad guy, sending him skidding off the road into the dunes. With little damage.
"Even the littlest ones are amoured up!" Chumbucket yells.
Fine then!. As he rejoins the road I harpoon his passenger side door and rip it off at high speed.
My sidekick reloads whilst we trade blows, side slamming into each other at high speed, whittling away the armour of the other.
"Ready to fire!" Yells Chumbucket!
The harpoon flies into the now unprotected cabin of the car, piercing the driver and retracting him from the vehicle, which swerves off right, into the dunes.
Just before I can chuckle a victory chuckle to myself, I spot another war party, but this party is parked on the side of the road, waiting.
I line up one of the cars and hit the Nitrous. Just before impact I do a commando roll out of the car and the second i'm on my feet I throw a heavy punch. CRACK! It connects with the jaw of a now-dazed warboy, who I then spin around and drag a steel blade across his throat. His warbuddy comes running at me and throws a punch...which I counter and release a flurry of quick punches before knocking him down to the ground, face first. Bad position to be in, as I quickly kneel,  cradle his head in my arms, and twist.

Mad Max is an action-packed and very fun game to play.
On my list of my all time favourites : Along with GTA V and Red Dead Redemption.
Best names for bad guys : Rim Jobbie for example.
The fighting system is brutal and often after a long fight of many enemies, i'll find myself staring at the screen in awe of what I just witnessed.  Not many games have a fighting system this good.
The driving is a little sluggish but thats just how things are in the wasteland. You'll find yourself slipping and sliding all over the place. For me, this just adds to the feeling that you are in a wasteland on mostly unsealed roads.
This game receives my "Environment Award" alongside games such as Red Dead Redemption. It just feels like I'm in a brutal wasteland, scavenging for what little I can find.
Which brings us to another topic. Repetitiveness. This game has loads of it. This is the game's biggest flaw. Not that I cared. The fighting is fun enough to keep me interested. The scrap grinding is very repetitive, but I no longer pick up every little piece.  Because the more strongholds you beat, the more free scrap you'll periodically get. Also, here's a hint, don't seek shelter during a storm. I made a 1000 scrap every storm :)
I've read a few other reviews which mention the scrap-grinding feature, but for me it wasn't an issue. I didn't just focus on the main story much or even worrying about where I was on the map. For the first 30 hours of gameplay I just killed whatever got in my way. And a LOT got in my way...in between me taking screenshots that is. The game looks amazing.

Great fighting system, similar to Batman.

Good storyline
Character audio / conversation is great.
One of the best games I've played.
Cons

Repetitiveness.
Short Main Story (Although, I dragged it out to 60 hours by doing side missions and generally killing things)
Scrap Grinding (Can be minimised by not rushing the main story)

This is a super early review (note my time played) but I had to get this kinda nitpicky point out there. If, like me, you are playing for the "Numenera" part and not the "Torment" part, you will be shocked.
This game gives you three foci.
No, not three foci at once, or three foci you can rotate between at will, or something like that. That would actually be kinda cool. No. There are three foci available for you to choose, period. THREE.
For those of you who haven't played the tabletop and who have only experienced Numenera via this game, let me clarify: the main sourcebook for Numenera gives you 29 options for your character's focus. Then they published a "Character Options" supplement that added 25 more, for a total of 54, which you may recognize as EIGHTEEN TIMES what you get here.
And they're not even cool ones, like Talks To Machines, Rides The Lightning, or Fuses Flesh and Steel. No, you get Masters Defense, Brandishes a Silver Tongue, and Breathes Shadow. Fighty, talky, sneaky. Presumably budget or time constraints stopped them from doing much with foci but SHEESH.
Other than that, pretty good game so far, awesome writing, nice to look at (even if everything kinda looks like a cutscene from The Longest Journey), combat's a little lackluster so maybe find ways to avoid it. I'm still recommending the game. Just be warned if you're coming from the tabletop and expecting to Master Insects or Exist Partially Out Of Phase.

As these kinds of RPGs go, I quite enjoyed Torment: Tides of Numenera. The most important thing was that combat wasn't especially common, and could usually be avoided or ameliorated through some cleverness or another. I really appreciated that - fighting through tons of trash mobs is not what I play RPGs for. The RPG mechanics themselves, with three stat pools that you spend from to perform actions, was really interesting, worked intuitively, and never really got in the way.
The setting is also spectacular - this is really interesting science-fantasy, and while there are some body-horror elements I'm not a huge fan of, I found the texture and the mood of the world to be really interesting. The writing is occasionally overly verbose, but for the most part it works nicely to establish the atmosphere, and the party members are interesting to have around and occasionally have neat story arcs.
I did have a bit of a hard time with the game's treatment of failure, though that's partly my fault. The game has contingencies built in to help you move forward from just about any failure, even failed stat rolls in conversations, but it's very hard to shake the feeling that you need to do everything you possibly can to succeed. I'm not sure how this could have been designed for, though - it's really about the prior baggage most players will be bringing to the experience.
The art style also didn't really do much for me - it felt a bit drab and a bit muddy, which is a shame given how the setting is so fantastic. There could have been a lot more to play with.
But overall, a cool world and fun RPG mechanics are what I play these games for, and this game delivers on that front. Give it a go!

mission structure, and keeps the game fresh with weekly targets, bonus missions, and
the exciting addition of "Elusive Targets", which are timed contracts with a one-try-only
sort of approach, the perfect challenge for a seasoned Hitman player.
There are only three episodes out at the time of this review, with a planned release
of seven in total, but there's enough varied content and complexity to the maps that
it'll keep you revisiting them for weeks.
This is a great entry for both new and old fans, whether you want to go in without any
guidance, or if you want a little push in the right direction.

You can -again- choose your equipment before the mission, don't have checkpoints, approach the target in way many different ways just like the games before Absolution and not follow the arrows pointing you to your target which was something we hated about Absolution, right?
Neutral:

Cons:
- The DRM ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t: For this one, I didn't have any problems myself since I'm playing on a desktop but in order to play it, you need to have a stable internet connection. As much as it shouldn't be bothering me, I think this might sometimes make it impossible to play for the people who game on a laptop since they don't always have internet connection when they are outside. Being able to play outside is one of the few reasons why some people choose to buy gaming laptops and considering you won't always have internet connection, thank the developers because you won't be able to play this
- Performance issues: Besides the often texture bugs, this game doesn't look THAT good even on the ultra settings. That's not a problem for me since I don't play games for their graphics but what annoys me the most is the mediocre frame rate with those graphics. I am pretty sure that it's about the game since I play/ed games that look much better than this such as Arkham Knight, MGSV and have an overall better frame rate.
